**Besides these 41 shakhas, the remaining 45 are no longer found today** — they may survive only as sub-branches subsumed within the shakhas already named. The names of these sub-branches, and the regions where they were current, are explained at length in the following section.

#### Sāmaveda Saṃhitā {.lv2}

**The Samaveda Samhita is not, strictly speaking, a wholly independent text.** It is the Samhita containing the mantras useful specifically to the Udgātṛ — the ritvij responsible for the Samaveda's own chanting (sāmagāna). **Although this Veda is traditionally said to have a thousand shakhas, at present only three Samhitas are chiefly available: Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya, and Jaiminīya. Among these, the Kauthuma Samhita is the principal one.**

**The names of the principal Samhitas are given below:**

1. Kauthumāḥ — 10. Kālabavinaḥ
2. Jaiminīyāḥ — 11. Śāṭyāyaninaḥ
3. Rāṇāyanīyāḥ — 12. Raurukiṇaḥ
4. Sātyamugrāḥ — 13. Kāpeyāḥ
5. Naigeyāḥ *(?)* — 14. Māṣaśarāvyaḥ
6. Śārdūlāḥ — 15. Karadviṣaḥ
7. Vārṣagaṇyāḥ — 16. Śāṇḍilyāḥ
8. Gautamāḥ — 17. Tāṇḍyāḥ
9. Bhallavinaḥ

<div class="pgmark">original p. 22</div>

**This Veda [Samaveda] is divided into two parts: Ārcika and Uttarārcika.** The earlier part, the Ārcika, contains 585 mantras, and the Uttarārcika 964, 1,549 in all. Of these 1,549 mantras, apart from 75, all the rest are also found within the Rigveda Samhita itself. These mantras are generally composed in meters suited for chanting — chiefly Gāyatrī and the Pragātha-type meters. Among the Rigveda's own mantras, [the Samaveda's borrowings] are generally found in Maṇḍalas 8 and 9; the remaining 75 mantras belong to other Samhitas.

**The Samaveda has seven svaras (musical accents).** The accents used for reciting the Samaveda differ from those used for the other three Vedas. In the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda, there are three accent-types: Udātta, Anudātta, and Svarita. In Sāmagāna, however, corresponding to the musical notes Pañcama, Madhyama, Gāndhāra, Ṛṣabha, Ṣaḍja, Dhaivata, and Niṣāda, there are seven distinct accent-registers, named Kruṣṭa, Prathama, Dvitīya, Tṛtīya, Caturtha, Pañcama and Ṣaṣṭha. **There are many different styles of chanting (gāna), each bearing its own distinct name. It is said that this Sāmagāna is itself the very root of the science of music.**

#### Atharvaveda Saṃhitā {.lv2}

**The Atharvaveda goes by many names — Atharvāṅgirasa, Bhṛgvaṅgirasa, Brahmaveda, Atharvaveda.** This Veda has 9 shakhas. Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya states:

> नवधाथर्वणो वेदः ।
> *navadhātharvaṇo vedaḥ |*
> "The Ātharvaṇa Veda is ninefold."

**And the Caraṇa-vyūha, in its Ātharvaṇa-pariśiṣṭa, states:**

> तत्र ब्रह्मवेदस्य नव भेदा भवन्ति । तद्यथा ।
> *tatra brahmavedasya nava bhedā bhavanti | tad yathā |*
> "There, the Brahmaveda has nine divisions, as follows —"

1. Paippalādāḥ — 6. Jaladāḥ
2. Staudāḥ *(?)* — 7. Brahmavadāḥ
3. Maudāḥ — 8. Devadarśāḥ
4. Śaunakīyāḥ — 9. Cāraṇavaidyāḥ
5. Jājalāḥ

**The Atharvaveda Saṃhitā has 20 sections (kāṇḍas).** Across these 20 sections there are, in total, 731 suktas and roughly 12,000 mantras. **Many of its portions — the 20th section entirely — consist of mantras drawn directly from the Rigveda, with only minor variations here and there.** The first section has small suktas of four verses each; the second, suktas of five verses; the third, suktas of six verses; the fourth, suktas of seven verses. The fifth section has suktas ranging from eight to eighteen verses. The sixth section has 142 suktas, generally small suktas of three verses each. The seventh section has 118 suktas, some containing only one or two mantras. The eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, seventeenth and eighteenth sections have large suktas of more than 21

<div class="pgmark">original p. 23</div>

**verses each.** In the fifteenth and sixteenth sections, much of the content is in prose form. The nineteenth and twentieth sections generally consist of Rigveda mantras.

**This Veda's mantras closely resemble Rigveda mantras in language, style, and meter, and its subject matter is similar as well — though no strict rule governing meter is evident here.**

### Brāhmaṇas {.lv1}

**"Brahmanas" are specialized treatises that explain, at length, how the Samhita's mantras — which take the form of hymns of praise — are to be used in yajnas and similar rites: at what time which acts should be performed, and so on.** Taken as a whole, the Brahmanas serve as a kind of commentary (vyākhyāna) upon the Samhita. Each Veda has its own distinct Brahmanas.

**The Brahmanas connected with the Rigveda are the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and the Kauśītakī Brāhmaṇa.** Of these, the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is the principal and more ancient one. It comprises 40 Adhyāyas in total. It is said that one Mahīdāsa arranged this Brāhmaṇa. **The Kauśītakī Brāhmaṇa is also called the Sāṅkhyāyana Brāhmaṇa.** It comprises 30 Adhyāyas: the first six describe the procedure for the Darśapūrṇamāsa and similar rites, and Adhyāyas 7 through 30 describe the procedure for the Soma-yāga. The subject matter of this Brahmana broadly follows that of the Aitareya Brahmana.

**The Brahmana-portion, throughout, explains the procedure of the yajna in full.** Detailed discussion of the individual acts comprising the rite, the derivation of ritual terms, and similar matters are especially prominent here. Where the mantra-portion is bound to meter, the Brahmana-portion is generally in prose. **The Brahmanas may be regarded as representing the earliest stage of Sanskrit prose.**

**Of the two Brahmanas connected with the Rigveda, the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa belongs to the Śākala shakha, and the Kauśītakī Brāhmaṇa to the Bāṣkala shakha.** The reason for the name "Aitareya Brāhmaṇa" is this: Mahīdāsa, son of a woman named Itarā, once, at a yajna performed by his father, was not permitted to sit upon his father's lap alongside his other brothers. Grieved by this, he performed austerities directed to the Earth-goddess (Bhūdevī), and as the fruit of that penance obtained this Brāhmaṇa and its accompanying Āraṇyaka. **For this reason, these texts came to bear the names "Aitareya Brāhmaṇa" and "Aitareya Āraṇyaka" [after his mother Itarā].**

**This Brāhmaṇa is divided into 8 Pañcikās, each containing 5 Adhyāyas** *(cf. the 40-Adhyaya total already given above)*. The first fourteen Adhyāyas concern the Agniṣṭoma-yāga; Adhyāyas 15, 17 cover the Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, and Atirātra sacrifices, and so on. Other Adhyāyas describe the duties of the Hotṛ, the Yajamāna, the Grāvastut, the Subrahmaṇya, and six further officiants. **The final ten Adhyāyas describe the yajnas a Kṣatriya may perform, and explain the mutual relationship between Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 24</div>

**Yajurveda Brahmanas** — for the Shukla Yajurveda, there is the **Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa**. Just as this Veda's Samhita has the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina shakhas, so too does this Brāhmaṇa. It comprises 14 Kāṇḍas and 100 Adhyāyas — and, having 100 Adhyāyas, bears the name "Śatapatha" ("Hundred-Path") Brāhmaṇa. **Its final portion is known as the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad.**

**For the Krishna Yajurveda, there is the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.** This Brāhmaṇa explains many matters not covered in the Samhita, and so may be regarded as a later portion of the Samhita itself. It comprises three Kāṇḍas and twenty-eight Adhyāyas.

**Besides these, this Veda has several further Brahmanas, now extinct and found nowhere. Only their names survive:** Caraka-brāhmaṇa, Kāṭhaka-brāhmaṇa, Śvetāśvatara-brāhmaṇa, Maitrāyaṇī-brāhmaṇa, Jābāla-brāhmaṇa, Khāṇḍikīya-brāhmaṇa, Aukheya-brāhmaṇa, Hāridravika-brāhmaṇa, Āhvaraka-brāhmaṇa, Kaṅkati-brāhmaṇa, Gālava-brāhmaṇa.

**Samaveda Brahmanas** — this Veda has three principal Brahmanas: **Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa, Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa**, and **Jaiminīya-brāhmaṇa** (also called Talavakāra-brāhmaṇa). Besides these, it has further Brahmanas: Mantra-brāhmaṇa, Daivata-brāhmaṇa, Sāmavidhāna-brāhmaṇa, Saṃhitopaniṣad-brāhmaṇa, Vaṃśa-brāhmaṇa, Jaiminīyārṣeya-brāhmaṇa, and Gopatha-brāhmaṇa. **A further, now-extinct set — Bhallavi, Śāṭyāyana, Kālabavi, Raurukī, Tumburu, Āruṇeya, Paiṅgi, Saulabha, Śailālī, Parāśara, Māṣaśarāvi, Kāpeya, and Anvākhyāna Brāhmaṇas — are known only by name, from mentions in the Sutra-literature, showing they were once current.** The Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa has 25 sections and so also bears the name "Pañcaviṃśa-brāhmaṇa"; the Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa is a later portion of this same text. **The Jaiminīya-brāhmaṇa is considered more ancient than the Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa.** Among these, there is yet another Samaveda Brahmana called "Śāṭyāyana" — the last two mentioned have not survived in complete form.

**Atharvaveda Brahmanas** — this Veda has only a single Brahmana, the **Gopatha-brāhmaṇa**.

### Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads {.lv1}

**The Āraṇyakas closely resemble the Brahmanas in most respects.**

> अरण्याध्ययनादेतदारण्यकमितीर्यते । अरण्ये तदधीयीतैवं वाक्यं प्रचक्षते ॥
> *araṇyādhyayanād etad āraṇyakam itīryate | araṇye tad adhīyīta evaṃ vākyaṃ pracakṣate ||*
> "It is called 'Āraṇyaka' from its being studied in the forest; texts declaring 'one should study this in the forest' pronounce it so."

**This verse is stated in connection with the subject matter of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.** Because these portions exist [in a form requiring careful guidance], and because they must be studied specifically in the forest, and since they contain much deeply secret Vedāntic material,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 25</div>

and because it was considered improper for these to be known to those not properly authorized, they were taught to disciples in the forest — for this reason, these texts came to be called "Aranyakas" (forest texts). Not all the subjects touched on within the Aranyakas have been explained in dedicated reference works, and even the scope of what they cover is a matter of some disagreement among scholars.

The Aranyakas discuss ritual action (karma) at a subtler, more philosophical level, leaning toward knowledge of Brahman, and are similar in character to the Upanishads. They suit the needs of a particular stage of life. Householders following the path of ritual action (karma-marga) — the Brahmanas — describe such rites in full external detail; the Aranyakas, by contrast, do not dwell on the external procedure but instead explain the deeper, hidden significance of these same acts. For this reason, the Aranyakas are associated with the path of renunciation (sannyasa), while those seeking the path of pure knowledge (jnana-marga) turn to the Upanishads. What belongs to the karma-marga is set out in the Brahmanas — though some hold, alternatively, that the three portions (Brahmana, Aranyaka, Upanishad) correspond respectively to the three paths of ritual action, meditative worship (upasana), and knowledge (jnana).

The most widely known and discussed portions of the Veda are the Upanishads, properly called "Vedanta" — the culminating portions of the Veda. Depending on the tradition, a given Upanishad may belong to a Brahmana, to an Aranyaka, or stand as an independent text. All together the Upanishads are said to be 108, though now as many as about 200 are available; and only 10 or 11 are generally regarded as the principal ones deserving special attention.

The word "Upanishad" literally suggests "sitting near" (upa + ni + sad) — a disciple sitting close to the teacher — referring to knowledge conveyed in this intimate, one-to-one manner. As this concerns the guru-disciple relationship rather than our present subject, it need not be discussed further here.

> इदं वाव तच्छ्रेष्ठाय पुत्राय पिता ब्रह्म प्रब्रूयात्प्रणाय्याय वा चान्तेवासिने ।
>
> *idaṃ vāva tac chreṣṭhāya putrāya pitā brahma prabrūyāt praṇāyyāya vā cāntevāsine* (Chāndogya Up. 3-11-5)
>
> "This indeed should a father teach to his most worthy son, or to a devoted resident-disciple."

The point: sacred knowledge should be imparted to a humble, deserving son or disciple. One who studies the Upanishads must be of refined character, well-disciplined, and genuinely eager to learn; the teacher, when a disciple comes to him, should examine him thoroughly before teaching. The dialogue between Nachiketas and Yama in the Katha Upanishad, and between Pratardana and Indra in the Kaushitaki Brahmana Upanishad, both illustrate the qualities expected of a true disciple.

Each branch of the Veda has an Upanishad. Among those now extant, the Aitareya and Kaushitaki Upanishads belong to the Rigveda; the Chandogya to the Samaveda; the Taittiriya, Katha and Shvetashvatara Upanishads to the Krishna Yajurveda; and to the Shukla Yajurveda, the

<div class="pgmark">original p. 26</div>

Brihadaranyaka and Isha Upanishads; and to the Atharvaveda's Mundaka, Mandukya, and Prashna Upanishads. Thus the Brihadaranyaka, Aitareya, Chandogya, Taittiriya, Isha, Kena, Katha, Prashna, Mundaka, and Mandukya — these ten Upanishads — are the celebrated ones. They are not easy to understand: "What is this world? Who am I? What is the nature of the self? Where does ultimate truth reside?" — such questions are addressed across their various sections. Schools of thought such as Sankhya, Yoga, Vaisheshika, and Nyaya have all, in their own ways, drawn on and interpreted the Upanishads to support their own doctrines — worth noting, since each school's interpretation often stands opposed to another's, with authors frequently writing against rival schools. What truth is to be learned from the Upanishads is itself a matter of dispute.

#### The Aranyakas and Upanishads presently available, by Veda {.lv2}

**Rigveda:** the Aitareya Aranyaka and the Shankhayana Aranyaka; the Aitareya Upanishad; the Kaushitaki Aranyaka and the Kaushitaki Upanishad (also called the Kaushitaki-Brahmana-Upanishad).

**Shukla Yajurveda:** in the Shatapatha Brahmana (both the Kanva and Madhyandina recensions), the final portion of the last kanda serves as the Aranyaka; its concluding section is well known as the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. The last chapter of this Veda's Samhita is known as the Ishavasya Upanishad.

**Krishna Yajurveda:** the Taittiriya Aranyaka and the Maitrayaniya Aranyaka, containing the Taittiriya Upanishad, the Mahanarayana Upanishad, the Katha Upanishad, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad.

**Samaveda:** the closing portion of the Tandya-Mahabrahmana serves as this Veda's Aranyaka, containing the Chandogya Upanishad; also the Talavakara Aranyaka (or Jaiminiya Upanishad-Brahmana, also called the Jaiminiya-Aranyaka), containing the Kena Upanishad (also called the Talavakara Upanishad).

**Atharvaveda:** the Mundaka Upanishad, the Mandukya Upanishad, and the Prashna Upanishad.

These are the principal Aranyakas and Upanishads. Given their difficulty of language and philosophical depth, they are generally regarded as belonging to the very latest portion of the Vedas. Many ancient scholars and teachers have written numerous commentaries on them from many different viewpoints, and they have since been translated into languages around the world.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 27</div>

Beyond these [ten], many further Upanishads exist — tradition holds there are 108 in all, though manuscript copies of some 200 are actually available today. Many of these cannot be confidently assigned to a particular Vedic branch, and modern Western scholars differ on how to classify them; even so, since some display real literary depth, their importance cannot be dismissed outright. These can be broadly grouped into six categories:

1. Upanishads generally expounding Vedantic philosophy.
2. Upanishads explaining the practice of Yoga.
3. Upanishads expounding devotion to Vishnu.
4. Upanishads expounding devotion to Shiva.
5. Upanishads expounding Shakti (the Goddess).
6. Upanishads expounding renunciation (vairagya), the sannyasa order, and other deities such as Ganapati.

Listing every individual title is not essential here, so they are omitted.

## Chapter Three — The Vedangas

"Vedanga" does not simply mean correctly interpreting portions of the Veda — these are dedicated, specialized texts explaining subjects necessary for correctly understanding and reciting the Vedas. They are six: **Shiksha, Vyakarana (Grammar), Chandas (Metrics), Nirukta, Jyotisha (Astronomy), and Kalpa.** Let us examine each in turn.

### 1. Shiksha {.lv1}

Shiksha is the discipline teaching the correct pronunciation, accent, and clarity of Vedic mantras. Sayanacharya defines it:

> शिक्ष्यंते वेदनायोपदिश्यंते स्वरवर्णादयो यत्रासौ शिक्षा ।
>
> *śikṣyaṃte vedanāyopadiśyaṃte svaravarṇādayo yatrāsau śikṣā*
>
> "That [text] in which the accents, sounds, and related features of Vedic mantras are taught — that is Shiksha."

At the start of the first chapter of the Taittiriya Upanishad (of the Krishna Yajurveda), there is a section beginning "śikṣāṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ" ("We shall now explain Shiksha"), concerning the [correct pronunciation of] Vedic mantras

<div class="pgmark">original p. 28</div>

and the associated rules that assist correct recitation are set out in Pratishakhya texts specific to each shakha (recension) — one Pratishakhya per shakha of a Veda. The Rigveda has two principal shakhas: Shakala and Bashkala, with no essential difference between them beyond arrangement and ritual custom. Among the authors of Shiksha-texts, the principal ones are Bharadvaja, Vyasa, Yajnavalkya, Narada, Panini, Vasishtha, Shaunaka, Shambhu, and Vararuchi; each shakha's Shiksha corresponds to its own Sutra-text, called a Pratishakhya.

For the Rigveda's Shakala recension, the Pratishakhya author is Shaunaka (who also authored the Atharvaveda's Chaturadhyayika Pratishakhya); for the Yajurveda, Katyayana. The Shakala Pratishakhya has 3 adhyayas, each made up of six patalas: 18 patalas in all. The first patala is the Paribhasha-patala, describing letters, accent, consonants and the like. The second is the Samhita-patala, on the combination of letters and, within it, the combination of 2-3 vowels. The third is the Svara-patala, which teaches the manner of pronunciation. Patalas 4, 5 and 6 explain the sandhi and changes of consonants; patalas 7 to 9 deal with the svarita accent; and the remaining patalas with the origin and power of letters, meter and similar topics.

For Shukla Yajurveda, the Vajasaneyi Pratishakhya (8 chapters) was composed by the sage Katyayana, citing earlier Pratishakhya authors of the Shaunaka and Kashyapa lineages. For Krishna Yajurveda, the Taittiriya Pratishakhya names about 20 such authors. For the Samaveda, there are the Sama-Pratishakhya, the Pushpa-sutra, and the Panchavidha-sutra. For the Atharvaveda, the Atharva-Pratishakhya.

### 2. Vyakarana (Grammar) {.lv1}

The grammar tradition specifically tied to the Veda survives today only in scattered fragments. Among the earliest grammarians, Shakatayana, Gargya, Shakalya, and Yaska are the principal figures; Panini came after them. According to Shakatayana, all words ultimately derive from verbal roots (dhatus) denoting action. Panini composed his own grammar largely building on the views of these earlier authorities, addressing, among the Vedic material then in current use, the part

<div class="pgmark">original p. 29</div>

tied to Vedic word-forms and their derivation. Since Paninian grammar became especially renowned, and no other principal grammar text exists apart from it, this is the one in current use today.

This work has eight chapters, hence its name "Ashtadhyayi." Exceptions to grammatical rule relevant specifically to the Veda are relatively scarce within it. Paninian grammar is celebrated for teaching correct classical Sanskrit usage, but for that very reason it cannot always be fully relied upon to reflect actual Vedic forms. In composing grammatical works generally, later authors have taken care not to disregard any part of received usage — this has become well-established practice.

Beyond Panini, the Unadi-sutras and Phit-sutras remain in use. The Unadi-sutras explain suffixes attached to particular roots — words formed this way are called "Unadi words," and are considered part of the broader Vedic grammatical tradition. The Phit-sutras, meanwhile, concern specifically the accentuation of Vedic mantra-words. Both, like the Pratishakhyas, are counted among the Vedangas.

### 3. Chandas-shastra (Metrics) {.lv1}

Chandas-shastra explains the metrical patterns of Vedic mantras. Pingala's treatise on this subject is the one in current use, though — unlike Paninian grammar — it is not the earliest such text. Discussions of meter already appear in the Brahmanas and Aranyakas, forming the real foundation on which Pingala's later, more systematic treatise builds. The key defining features of the meters found in the Rigveda are given in a separate chapter later in this book.

### 4. Nirukta {.lv1}

The Nirukta-shastra was composed by the sage Yaska, in two parts: the Nighantu and the Nirukta proper. The Nighantu gathers together Vedic words that share a common or synonymous meaning; the Nirukta then explains the form and derivation of these words, tracing their meaning in context and setting it out in connected, coherent form. This work is specifically and solely tied to the Veda.

The Nighantu (also called "Samamnaya") has three sections. The first section has three chapters; each of the remaining two sections has one chapter. The first section, the "Naighantuka-kanda," lists the names of objects and words of several meanings in its first chapter; living beings and their limbs in its second; and the qualities of the things and living beings of the first two chapters in its third.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 30</div>

The next section is the "Naigama-kanda": words that, though found only in the Veda, share their form with ordinary words but carry a different meaning there — these are gathered here. The final section is the "Daivata-kanda," listing the names of the various deities.

The Nirukta proper is the major work explaining the Nighantu's contents, and the modern Sanskrit style begins from it — it is the earliest surviving text specifically devoted to explaining Vedic meaning. Yaska explains meaning independently, by his own method, though never in a way that would contradict the Veda's own intent; he states himself that his interpretations generally rest on the authority of the Brahmanas and the Aranyaka tradition.

The Nirukta has 12 chapters, plus two further supplementary chapters. The first three chapters explain the Naighantuka-kanda; chapters 4–6 explain the Naigama-kanda; from chapter 7 onward, the Daivata-kanda is explained. For Vedic study, the first chapter and half of the second chapter are especially interesting and useful.

At the very outset, Yaska defines nouns, verbs, prepositions, and particles. Some hold that words are naturally nouns and the like; others hold that every word derives from a verbal root; Yaska belongs to this second group, deriving nominal forms from roots by showing a fitting semantic connection between them, wherever the explanation comes easily and naturally, and deciding between competing senses on the strength of the best-supported reading. Yaska also acknowledges that one and the same object may carry several names, or several objects may share one name (i.e., synonymy and homonymy both occur), and that not every word's origin can be traced to a clear founding principle — some function as mere conventional labels, a point grammar itself does not claim to fully resolve, and Yaska addresses this candidly in his own introduction.

Yaska then states the Nirukta's purpose: to help ascertain the Veda's meaning. This raises an objection: if the mantras have no meaning, explaining their meaning is a senseless thing. Yaska answers that the objects are there before us; a blind man not seeing them is no reason to say the objects do not exist, and such talk is the talk of the ignorant. Ascertaining the Veda's true meaning is genuinely difficult, and only through sustained effort can one hope to grasp it

<div class="pgmark">original p. 31</div>

properly. One who knows the Veda's meaning is blessed — with this, Yaska closes his first chapter. From the second chapter onward, wherever a word in the mantras admits multiple possible senses, he lays out the principles for settling on the correct one: chiefly, rules concerning pronunciation and rules concerning word-form. Where a word is regular in grammar and its meaning bears a direct relation to its root, the derivation should be made directly; where the meaning cannot be found so easily, the derivation should be made on the basis of a similar meaning or similar letters. Everyone who wishes to read and understand the Veda must read the Nirukta; no one can forget the service done by Yaska. That the Nirukta's whole purpose is to aid correct understanding of the Veda is thus firmly established.

Many works must have existed as the basis of the Nirukta, but none of them is available now. Though to moderns Yaska's explanations often seem unjustified, without his Nirukta the meaning of many mantras of the Veda would not be known at all. Two points stand out in this matter of the Nirukta. First, Yaska is generally held to belong to a fairly ancient period: Panini's own grammar contains a sutra referencing the name "Yaska" (in the sense of his clan/gotra — Panini-sutra roughly 2-4-63), without further explanation, showing grammatical scholarship was already well established by then; yet Yaska, in the Nirukta, first explains the noun and the like and then goes on, so the grammatical matters must have been new at the time the Nirukta was composed. Second, some scholars question whether the compiler of the Nighantu and the author of the Nirukta are the same "Yaska," since the Nirukta occasionally appears to alter the Nighantu's exact word-order when explaining it — for instance, where the Veda has "akūpārasya," the Nighantu-compiler changed it to "dāvane akūpārasya," while the Nirukta-writer follows the order of the mantra. At the end of the work a sentence is found, a salutation to Yaska; this must be meant for the Nighantu-compiler himself. Therefore the two must be different people.

### 5. Jyotisha-shastra (Astronomy) {.lv1}

Jyotisha does not much go into explaining the science of astronomy. These sutras are of no use to those who wish to learn the motions of the planets and from them to fix the good and bad results in a person's life; their aim is to state the planetary motions only so far as is needed to fix the time for performing yajnas and the like and the muhurta at which to begin them. References to such matters appear scattered through the Brahmanas and Aranyakas, including the idea that time can be reckoned by the moon's motion through the lunar constellations. A compact treatise, the Jyotisha-Vedanga, exists for this purpose: 36 verses for the Rigveda tradition and 43 for the Yajurveda tradition, treating the sun, moon, constellations, and the twelvefold zodiacal division in careful detail — a discipline that helps determine the correct, auspicious timing for yajnas and similar rites.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 32</div>

### 6. Kalpa-sutras {.lv1}

These are texts composed to set out the practical rules and procedures governing mantras, yajnas, and related rites. Authorship of these texts varies by shakha — for instance, Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra is named for its author. They fall into four principal types: **Shrautasutra, Grihyasutra, Dharmasutra,** and **Shulbasutra**.

The **Shrautasutra** sets out, step by step, the procedure for yajnas and similar rites, together with the mantras required at each stage. The **Grihyasutra** explains the rules for life-cycle rites (samskaras) — birth-rites and the like — that Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas are to perform according to their station. The **Dharmasutra** sets out the general rules of right conduct expected of people. The **Shulbasutra** explains the construction of ritual structures — the fire-pit, the altar, and the sacrificial implements — including their precise measurements.

Each Veda (and each of its shakhas) traditionally had all four kinds of Sutra composed for it, though today only a fraction survive. These Sutra-texts are of great help in understanding Vedic meaning. Officiating priests, needing to know the correct procedure for the rites they performed, are why these Kalpa-sutras came to be composed in the first place. Sayanacharya puts it this way:

> बोधितानां कर्मणां सुखावबोधाय भगवान् बोधायनः कल्पसूत्रमकल्पयत् ।
>
> *bodhitānāṃ karmaṇāṃ sukhāvabodhāya bhagavān bodhāyanaḥ kalpasūtram akalpayat*
>
> "For the easy comprehension of the rites already taught, the venerable Baudhayana composed the Kalpa-sutra."

The Brahmanas do describe yajnas and similar rites, but this material is interwoven with spiritual, historical, and etymological matter, making it hard to extract on its own — which is exactly why the Kalpa-sutras became indispensable for performing these rites correctly and in proper order.

Many Kalpa-sutras exist, one per shakha. For the Rigveda: the Ashvalayana and Shankhayana Sutras. The Ashvalayana Shrauta-sutra has two parts and twelve chapters in all, each chapter further divided into sections called Kandikas, describing the Darsha-Purnamasa (new-moon/full-moon) rites and others. For Krishna Yajurveda: the Baudhayana and Apastamba Sutras. For Shukla Yajurveda: the Katyayana Sutra. For the Samaveda: the Latyayana and Drahyayana Sutras.

It was through these Kalpa-sutras that a new era began among those who study the Veda. From the time they were composed and came into use, the importance of the Veda itself kept diminishing, until finally

<div class="pgmark">original p. 33</div>

the Kalpa-sutra itself became the chief basis. The Vedas were neglected. It also became the custom to say that a part of the Veda belongs to such-and-such a charana or shakha. Even now, when reciting the gotra and pravara after the sandhya-vandana and the like, people follow these sutras and name schools such as the Ashvalayana, Baudhayana and Apastamba.

#### Shrautasutras {.lv2}

These sutras primarily explain the procedure for performing yajnas. The person on whose behalf the yajna is performed is called the *yajamana*; priests called *purohitas* are engaged to help him carry out the mantras and ritual components correctly. As already noted, a yajna has four principal officiants — Hotr, Adhvaryu, Udgatr, and Brahma — with further officiating priests, up to 16 in all, depending on the kind of yajna. Three sacred fires are principal in a yajna: Dakshina-agni, Garhapatya, and Ahavaniya.

The first and most fundamental act in any yajna is establishing the sacred fire, either through the Agnyadheya rite or by transferring it from an already-consecrated fire. Fire is produced specifically by friction using two designated pieces of wood (Arani) — only fire kindled this way may be used in a yajna; fire started by matches or other modern means is not proper. Maintaining this sacred fire involves numerous ancillary rites and mantras, and every element of a yajna proceeds strictly according to the Sutra-texts' prescribed rules.

Among yajnas, the Agnihotra, Darsha-Purnamasa, Soma, Chaturmasya, and Agnishtoma rites are the principal ones. "Darsha-Purnamasa" refers to the rites performed on the new-moon and full-moon days. The year's three seasonal divisions each begin with a rite called "Chaturmasya" (the four-monthly rite), itself with several sub-varieties. Soma-sacrifices likewise come in many distinct kinds, governed by particular rules concerning the relationship between the yajamana and the officiating priests from the initiation (Diksha) rite onward; a Soma-yaga may run for up to 12 days or, in its most elaborate form (the "Sattra"), for as long as a year.

Central to the Soma-yaga is the construction of the fire-altar (vedi) itself — the Agnishtoma rite requires it as an essential preliminary. The required number and type of bricks, their composition, and the exact sequence for laying them are described in painstaking detail, down to precisely when and with which mantras each brick is consecrated. In this Agnicayana as many as 10800 bricks are used, and 16 officiating priests carry it all out by rule, working to strict procedure — none of it left to improvisation. It is precisely this demand for exactness that makes these Sutra-texts so indispensable.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 34</div>

**For the Rigveda:** two Shrautasutras exist — the Ashvalayana and the Sankhyayana. The Sankhyayana Shrautasutra is especially current in Gujarat and northern regions, while the Ashvalayana is current especially in the regions south of the Godavari river. There is no especially significant difference in subject matter between the two, though the Sankhyayana treats rites such as the Ashvamedha and Rajasuya in greater detail. The Sankhyayana Sutra generally follows the Kaushitaki Brahmana; it has 18 parts, and its last two parts appear to be later additions, following material from the Kaushitaki Aranyaka specifically.

The Ashvalayana Shrautasutra has 12 parts and generally follows the Aitareya Brahmana. Some say the sage Ashvalayana was a disciple of Shaunaka and also the author of the fourth chapter of the Aitareya Aranyaka.

**For Shukla Yajurveda:** the Katyayana Shrautasutra, in 25 chapters; the three chapters 22 to 24 relate to Samaveda matters, and the rest largely follows the Shatapatha Brahmana.

**For Krishna Yajurveda:** six Shrautasutras exist, of which only a few have been printed. The Baudhayana and Bharadvaja Shrautasutras are quite ancient. The Apastamba Shrautasutra (30 chapters) has the Hiranyakeshiya as its supplementary text; both follow the Taittiriya tradition. The Manava Shrautasutra, connected to the Maitrayani Samhita, is very ancient. The Vaikhanasa Shrautasutra remains unprinted, surviving only in scattered manuscripts.

**For the Samaveda:** the Arsheya-kalpa (or Masaka-sutra), the Latyayana, Drahyayana, and Jaiminiya Shrautasutras, and the Samavidhana-Brahmana. Of these, the Masaka-, Latyayana, and Drahyayana Sutras are the principal ones in current circulation. The Masaka-sutra, the oldest of the three (also called "Arsheya-kalpa"), details the Soma-yaga rites described in the Panchavimsha Brahmana. The Latyayana Shrautasutra is the principal text for the Kauthuma shakha, following the Panchavimsha Brahmana; the Drahyayana is connected with the Ranayaniya shakha — the two do not differ significantly.

**For the Atharvaveda:** only the Vaitana Shrautasutra exists, closely following the Shukla Yajurveda's Katyayana Sutra and this Veda's own Gopatha Brahmana. This sutra does not appear to be especially ancient.

#### Grihyasutras {.lv2}

These same authors composed further Sutra-texts as well — the Grihyasutras and the Samayacharika-sutras. Where the Shrautasutras belong to the Shruti tradition, these are *Smartasutras* (belonging to Smriti). The Grihyasutras set out the rules a householder should follow in family and domestic life, along with the customary practices expected of each person in society — hence also called Dharmasutras. Later works such as the Manusmriti and Yajnavalkya-smriti drew on these.

The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra has four chapters, each divided into further sections (Kandikas). Among its subjects: the Pakayajna, Balikarana, and the daily duties of a twice-born person — Chaula (tonsure), Upanayana (sacred-thread initiation), and other rites of passage, sixteen in number altogether. These rites are far simpler than the Shrauta rites, needing little preparation or material — the aim of performing these rites appearing to be that the purpose of every act a person does should not be worldly gain alone, but that there should be fruit in the world beyond, with the touch of sin and merit.

**For the Rigveda:** two Grihyasutras — Ashvalayana and Sankhyayana. The Sankhyayana Grihyasutra (6 parts) generally follows the Kaushitaki Brahmana; related to it is the Shambhavya Grihyasutra, covering some distinct matters, though unprinted and surviving only in manuscript. The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra is closely tied to the Aitareya Brahmana and is described as the latter portion of the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra, in 4 adhyayas, with 24, 10, 12 and 2 sections called "Kandikas" respectively.

**For Shukla Yajurveda:** the Paraskara (also called Kathiya or Vajasaneya) Grihyasutra, largely following the Katyayana Shrautasutra's subject matter; its influence is visible in the Yajnavalkya Dharmasutra as well.

**For Krishna Yajurveda:** seven Grihyasutras, of which only 3–4 are printed. The Apastamba and Baudhayana Grihyasutras are especially popular in South India; the Hiranyakeshiya Kalpasutra closely follows Apastamba. The Bharadvaja Grihyasutra is not widely used. The Manava Grihyasutra mainly expounds subjects from its corresponding Shrautasutra and uniquely describes the Vinayaka-puja procedure, absent from other sutras. The later Kathaka-Grihyasutra follows the Manava Grihyasutra, quoting many of its passages directly.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 36</div>

The Vaikhanasa Grihyasutra, though not especially ancient, sets out many new subjects.

**For the Samaveda:** the principal Grihyasutra is the Gobhila Grihyasutra, very ancient, and sets out its subjects well and completely. It follows mantras drawn from the Samaveda Samhita used specifically in domestic rites, in their traditional compiled order — a companion "Mantra-brahmana" gathers, selected from the Rigveda and other Vedas and put together in one place in an order, the mantras needed for domestic rites that are not found in the Samaveda, and is cited repeatedly within the Gobhila-sutra. Also notable is the Khadira Grihyasutra of the Drahyayana shakha, also used by the Ranayaniya and other shakhas, with no significant difference in content from the Gobhila-sutra.

**For the Atharvaveda:** the Kaushika Grihyasutra, which uniquely details the Atharvaveda's kamya-karmas (rites performed for specific desired outcomes) — a level of detail no other sutra provides, making this text especially valuable for understanding the social life of the Vedic era.

##### The Sixteen Samskaras {.lv3}

From birth to death, a twice-born person undergoes numerous prescribed rites — around 40 in all — of which the principal ones are known as the Shodasha-samskaras, that is, the 16 samskaras. The chief among them: Jatakarma, Namakarana, Chudakarma, Upanayana, Vivaha, Garbhadhana, Simanta, the Pancha-yajnas, and the Antyeshti (funeral rites).

**Jatakarma:** the rite to be performed soon after the birth of the child, that is, as soon as the birth-impurity (jatashauca) is over.

**Namakarana:** the naming ceremony, in which parents give the child both a chosen name and one based on the birth star (nakshatra), usually performed on the eleventh day after birth. Naming convention prescribes that a Brahmin's name end in "-sharma," a Kshatriya's in "-varma," and a Vaishya's in "-gupta."

**Chudakarma:** the first tonsure, ordinarily performed within the child's third year, the hair being cut by rule and a tuft (shikha) left according to custom.

**Upanayana:** among the most important rites for a twice-born person — it is from this rite that one gains the authority (adhikara) to study the Vedas. The boy is dressed appropriately, invested with the sacred thread (yajnopavita), and taught the sacred Gayatri (Savitri) mantra by his guru. This rite is also called a "second birth" — hence Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, once they undergo it, are called "dvija" (twice-born).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 37</div>

This rite is prescribed for a Brahmin boy in his eighth year, a Kshatriya boy in his eleventh, and a Vaishya boy in his twelfth. Afterward, the boy, or brahmachari, serves his guru, subsisting by begging alms and devoting himself continuously to Vedic study — performing the morning and evening twilight (sandhya) rites daily, living on alms alone, sleeping on the ground, not sleeping by day, and acting according to the guru's instruction at all times. This entire way of life is called the Brahmacharya-ashrama, the first of the four ashramas; one may not pass to the later ashramas without keeping its rules. Having studied the Veda in it for twelve years, finishing other studies, and, upon completing the Samavartana rite (marking the end of studentship) and proving themselves worthy, becoming eligible for marriage (vivaha).

The marriage rite includes several significant elements: Panigrahana (taking the bride's hand), circumambulation of the fire, Saptapadi (seven steps taken together), and the viewing of the pole star and the star Arundhati, among others — the Rigveda's Surya-sukta (Mandala 10, Sukta 84) supplies the mantras specifically used in marriage. Panigrahana signifies that the couple are no longer to be separated. Having the bride step on a stone (Ashmarohana) signifies she should remain as steadfast as that stone. The Saptapadi — seven steps taken together — signifies that from that point on, the couple will share equally in life's joys and sorrows. Parinaya is the couple's walking round the fire together three times. Aupasana is to be performed by the couple morning and evening for life, the fire established at the marriage being kept at all times for the Aupasana; hence the fire is also called Grihapati. The viewing of the pole star and of Arundhati signifies that the couple should live together lovingly and inseparably, or that, as Arundhati, wife of the sage Vasishtha, was devoted to her husband, the bride should be a devoted wife, serve her husband, bear ten sons and live happily. Since these marriage customs have changed little since Vedic times, much the same practices continue even today. Through marriage, a man enters the householder stage (Grihastashrama) — regarded as foremost among the four life-stages, since it alone makes possible the fulfillment of all four aims of human life (purushartha).

Beyond these life-cycle rites, a householder has ongoing daily duties, among which the **Panchamahayajnas** (five great sacrifices) are most important. The Taittiriya Aranyaka (Krishna Yajurveda), Prapathaka 2, Anuvaka 10, states:

> पञ्च वा एते महायज्ञाः सततं प्रतायन्ते सततं संतिष्ठन्ते देवयज्ञः पितृयज्ञो भूतयज्ञो मनुष्ययज्ञो ब्रह्मयज्ञ इति ।
>
> *pañca vā ete mahāyajñāḥ satataṃ pratāyante satataṃ saṃtiṣṭhante deva-yajñaḥ pitṛ-yajño bhūta-yajño manuṣya-yajño brahma-yajña iti*
>
> "These five great sacrifices are continuously extended and continuously maintained: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to [all] beings, the sacrifice to humankind, and the sacrifice of sacred study."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 38</div>

That is: Devayajna, Pitriyajna, Bhutayajna, Manushyayajna, and Brahmayajna together make up the Panchamahayajna. These must be performed daily, begun and completed within the same day. The Taittiriya Aranyaka details each:

> यदग्नौ जुहोत्यपि समिधं तद्देवयज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यत्पितृभ्यः स्वधा करोत्यप्यपस्तत्पितृयज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यद्भूतेभ्यो बलिं हरति तद्भूतयज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यद्ब्राह्मणेभ्योऽन्नं ददाति तन्मनुष्ययज्ञः संतिष्ठते, यत्स्वाध्यायमधीयीतैकामप्यृचं यजुः साम वा तद्ब्रह्मयज्ञः संतिष्ठते ॥
>
> "Offering even a samidh into the fire constitutes the sacrifice to the gods. Offering 'svadha' with even water to the ancestors constitutes the sacrifice to the ancestors. Giving 'bali' (a food-offering) to [all] beings constitutes the sacrifice to beings. Giving food to fellow humans constitutes the sacrifice to humankind. Reciting even a single verse of the Rig, Yajus, or Sama constitutes the sacrifice of sacred study."

**Devayajna:** offering the Purodasha and other oblations into the fire with a simple homa, worshipping the intended deity — complete in a single such offering, requiring no elaborate effort.

**Pitriyajna:** since an ordinary householder cannot make elaborate offerings, he simply honors the ancestors with a water-offering accompanied by the "svadha" formula — this alone, via the Tarpana rite, completes the Pitriyajna.

**Bhutayajna:** as part of the Vaishvadeva rite and similar daily observances, offering food ("bali") to crows and other creatures.

**Manushyayajna:** giving food and other necessities, honestly earned, to Brahmins, guests, and people generally.

**Brahmayajna:** studying one's own Vedic shakha — or, having done so, studying one of the other Vedas as well. Its manner of performance is described in detail in the following eleventh Anuvaka; for fear of length it is not described here, and will be described later as occasion arises.

Those devoted to their duties perform these five great sacrifices daily even now.

Turning to practical customs: **Garbhadhana** is the rite performed to properly solemnize conception after a wife reaches fertility (also called "Nishekaprashasti"). Simanta is the rite to be performed for the wife in the sixth or eighth month of her first pregnancy.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 39</div>

Besides the Panchamahayajnas described above, the householder must perform yajnas such as the Darsha-Purnamasa on the parva-days, the new-moon and full-moon days. Optional (kamya) rites and other yajnas such as the Soma may be undertaken when opportunity offers; there is no rule that they must be done.

**Antyeshti:** after death, the rites performed on behalf of the departed — cremation (Dahana), gathering of the remains (Sanchayana), the daily rite (Nityakarma), and further rites (Ekoddishta, Sapindikarana, Parvana-shraddha, Masika-shraddha, the annual Pitrimedha, and others) performed during the twelve days from the day of death and recurring yearly thereafter. These funeral (Shraddha) rites are distinct from the daily Pitriyajna discussed earlier, and are treated in great detail both in the Grihyasutras and in dedicated works such as the great work of Hemadri, the Shraddhakalpa — not elaborated further here.

The subjects of the Grihyasutras have now been surveyed. While the overall pattern of these rites is broadly shared across all Vedas and shakhas, considerable variation exists in specific procedure and mantra.

#### Dharmasutras {.lv2}

The reason for this name should already be clear; these texts are also called Samayacharika-sutras, since they teach proper conduct for the four social classes (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and the four life-stages (Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sannyasa) according to established custom — offering real insight into how thoroughly ancient society regulated conduct.

Tradition holds each Veda or shakha once had its own Dharmasutra, though only three survive today, all from the Taittiriya branch of Krishna Yajurveda. The **Apastamba Dharmasutra** is the most important, covering varna-ashrama customs, marriage, inheritance, and punishment for wrongdoing in detail; it predates even the Paninian era and remains current in South India. The **Hiranyakeshiya Dharmasutra**, though later, closely follows Apastamba with only minor wording differences, and is followed along the western (Konkan) coast. Third is the **Baudhayana Dharmasutra**, considered quite ancient — good evidence suggests Apastamba drew on Baudhayana rather than the reverse — and equally thorough

<div class="pgmark">original p. 40</div>

in its treatment of subject matter; it too remains current in South India. Sayanacharya himself, the celebrated Veda-commentator, belonged to the Baudhayana tradition. The sutra's later portion is thought to be a later addition rather than part of the original text.

Among these Dharmasutras is also the **Gautama-Dharmashastra**, traditionally linked to the Samaveda's Ranayaniya shakha — its twenty-sixth chapter follows the Samavidhana-Brahmana word for word, supporting this connection, though its antiquity makes it hard to date with real confidence; its date is said to be not later than 500 BCE.

The **Vasishtha-Dharmashastra**, in 30 chapters, survives in error-ridden manuscripts with no reliable commentary; its later chapters seem to have a different origin than the earlier ones, and its middle portion includes verse material. It appears ancient and, as in the Apastamba-sutra, describes six kinds of marriage, not eight as at present; Kumarila Bhatta says in his work that the Rigveda schools studied it well and followed it, and he quotes many parts of it as authority. Since northern Indian scholars relied on it for Vedic custom, it likely gained wider currency in the north; and since it quotes the Gautama-sutra while the Manava-Dharmashastra quotes it in turn, it is dated between the two — a few centuries BCE — though evidently followed by northern Rigvedins even earlier.

Beyond these, several other Dharmasutras are known only by citation in other texts. The **Manava-sutra** is notable among these, mixing prose and verse; some of its sentences are quoted elsewhere. A prose-verse Dharmashastra by the brothers Shankha and Likhita survives similarly only in scattered citations, evidently once a substantial work, since it treated many subjects — later authors such as Parashara

<div class="pgmark">original p. 41</div>

cited many of its statements as authoritative. This text belongs to the Vajasaneya Samhita of Shukla Yajurveda, as Kumarila Bhatta (c. 700 CE) says; this is confirmed by many sentences in it.

**The Vaikhanasa Dharmasutra** is not very ancient. Its four-part Prashna section discusses matters connected to Narayana/Vishnu, alongside Varnashrama-dharma and the duties of the Vanaprastha stage, as in a Grihyasutra; it belongs to the Taittiriya tradition.

#### Shulbasutras {.lv2}

These describe the construction of yajna-altars and are thus tied to the Shrautasutras. Only three survive: the **Apastamba, Baudhayana,** and **Katyayana Shulbasutras** — all connected to the Yajurveda; no equivalent texts are known for the other Vedas. The Apastamba Shulbasutra has three commentaries (Kapardi-bhashya, the oldest, in 6 patalas/26 khandas; Sundararaja's; and Karavindiya's) and has been printed as No. 79 in the series of the Mysore Oriental Library. The Baudhayana and Katyayana Shulbasutras have been translated into English with diagrams and printed at Kashi (Benares), with commentaries by Dvarakanathayajvan (on Baudhayana) and by Someshvara's extensive *Somasudramanchandrika* (on Katyayana). These texts describe, in painstaking detail, the construction of the fire-pit and ritual implements, their use, and the precise dimensions required for the brick-built altar in the Agni-chayana rite — an established and carefully followed ancient custom. The Shulbasutras are considered the foundational source of the discipline of geometry/architecture (shilpa-shastra).

### Parishishtas (Supplements) {.lv1}

A few further Veda-related texts from this same era belong here: the Parishishta-sutras, the Anukramanikas, and the Charanavyuhas.

The Parishishta-sutras are generally not as compact as the earlier Sutra-texts; they are written in the Anushtubh meter, on Vedic subjects, though in a comparatively later style of composition. They fill in matters left incomplete in the Vedanga-related Kalpa-sutras — 

<div class="pgmark">original p. 42</div>

which, being composed concisely, left many such points untreated or barely touched on. Later generations, wanting fuller, more convenient guidance for performing yajna-related rites, compiled these more detailed supplementary works — hence "Parishishta": that which comprehensively completes what was left unaddressed.

Among the Parishishtas, the **Ashvalayana-Grihya-Parishishta** (4 chapters, all Rigveda-related) is important. The **Gobhila-Sangraha-Parishishta** is its Samaveda counterpart, covering domestic and especially kamya-karma rites. Related to it is the **Karma-pradipa** (also called Samagrihya, Chandogagrihya-Parishishta, or Gobhila-smriti), attributed either to Katyayana or to a Gobhila-follower, covering subjects that overlap with the main Grihyasutras plus additional material.

Katyayana, connected to Shukla Yajurveda, composed several further Parishishtas — three worth noting: the Nigama-parishishta, explaining words; the Pravaradhyaya, giving the gotra-pravaras and genealogies of the rishis, useful for determining gotra in marriage matters; and the Charanavyuha, listing the names of the shakhas.

### Anukramanikas (Indices) {.lv1}

An "Anukramanika" is a systematic index of the mantras, words, and other elements occurring in a text, in their original sequence. The Rigveda's Anukramanikas list its suktas, rishis, meters, deities, and other details in the order they occur in the Samhita. About 7 such indices exist for the Rigveda, all attributed to Shaunaka; similar information also appears within the Rigveda's own Pratishakhya texts. The best known is Katyayana's **Sarvanukramanika**, covering every sukta's order along with rishi, deity, and meter, tied to the exposition of Vedartha; its commentary, the Vedarthadipika, written by Shadgurushishya, says that before the Sarvanukramani there was a separate anukramanika for the mantras, the rishis and the deities, now lost, said to be Shaunaka's; Katyayana must have composed his work taking these in.

There is also, for the Rigveda, the **Arsha-Anukramani** (about 300 shlokas), listing which rishi composed which mantra. Similarly, the **Chandonukramani**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 43</div>

(about 300 shlokas) gives the names of the meters of the Rigveda, how many mantras of each meter there are in each Mandala, and how many in the whole Samhita; of the Chandonukramanis only 5 texts are now available. The Anuvakanukramani has only about 40 shlokas. It gives the opening words of the Rigveda's 85 Anuvakas and the number of suktas in those Anuvakas, and states the Rigveda's total as 1,017 suktas, or 1,025 suktas according to the Bashkala shakha, 10580 mantras (the mantra count given here is not correct), 153826 words and 432000 syllables, along with some other details.

The **Padanukramani** catalogs the Veda's individual words; the **Suktanukramani** would detail the suktas themselves, though this text does not appear to survive. The **Devatanukramani** lists the deity names, but only partially survives. Sage Shaunaka is also credited with the **Brihaddevata** and the **Rigvidhana**. The Brihaddevata (1200 shlokas across 8 chapters) explains at length which deities belong to which sukta each chapter explaining one Ashtaka of the Rigveda; the Rigvidhana explains the practical ritual application of the Rigveda's mantras. Both are extremely ancient — and the Rigveda Samhita was arranged as it now stands in their time and has remained unchanged since then, without the slightest alteration.

For Shukla Yajurveda's Madhyandina branch, Katyayana composed an Anukramanika broadly following the Rigveda's Sarvanukramani in covering rishi, deity, and meter (with some differences), and separately describing the Samhita's meters, based on the Rigveda's own model.

For Krishna Yajurveda, two Anukramanikas exist. The Atreyanukramani has two parts (part one in prose, part two in verse); it gives the names found in the Samhita, without much further detail. The **Charayaniyanukramani** belongs to the Kathaka shakha and gives the names of rishis and the sequence of mantras; with regard to the Rigveda mantras it differs in many places from the Rigveda's Sarvanukramani and indicates many new names; it is said to have been composed by the sage Atri and taught to a disciple named Laugakshi.

For the Samaveda, the **Arsha** and **Daivata** Anukramanikas list rishis and deities respectively, following the Samaveda's

<div class="pgmark">original p. 44</div>

Naigeya-shakha tradition. Across these various indices, the names of Yaska, Shaunaka, Ashvalayana, and other sages, along with citations from their works, appear at many points.

Connected to the Atharvaveda's Parishishtas is one called the **Charanavyuha**. More than 70 Parishishtas exist for the Atharvaveda in total, this being one of them; it states that the Atharvaveda contains 2,000 suktas and 12380 mantras.

**Prayoga and Paddhati texts:** beyond understanding ritual procedure in the abstract, separate practical manuals were composed to make actual performance convenient for ritual specialists — of great help to those handling Shrauta and Grihya rites. A **Prayoga** text lays out, step by step, exactly which act comes first and which follows, together with the specific mantra each officiant uses at each stage — invaluable to the ritvijas actually conducting the rite. A **Paddhati** gathers together, in one place, everything the Sutras say on a given ritual topic. Besides these there are also works called Karikas, written following the Sutras and the Paddhatis, which describe the rites in verse. Of these Karikas, the one written by Kumarila Bhatta (c. 700 CE) is the first.

## Chapter Four — The Shakhas (Branches) of the Veda

The previous chapter raised the question of how the Veda came to be divided into so many shakhas, and why. The Veda was originally a single, unified body of text. Consider first whether it would even be feasible for one person to study it in that undivided form: by ordinary human capacity, attempting to study it exactly as it originally existed would make serious Vedic study nearly impossible — and recognizing this is itself the reason behind its division:

> पूर्वं भगवता कृष्णद्वैपायनेन जगदुपकारार्थमेकीभूयस्थिता वेदा व्यस्ताः ।
>
> *pūrvaṃ bhagavatā kṛṣṇa-dvaipāyanena jagadupakārārthamekībhūyasthitā vedā vyastāḥ*
>
> "Formerly, by the venerable Krishna-Dvaipayana [Vyasa], for the benefit of the world, the Vedas, which stood as one, were divided."

> सकलवेदपरिपालनं तैश्चैव पुरुषेणेति शाखाभेदप्रवृत्तिः ।
>
> *sakala-veda-paripālanaṃ taiś caiva puruṣeṇeti śākhā-bheda-pravṛttiḥ*
>
> "So that the entire Veda could be preserved by these very people [his disciples] — this is how the practice of dividing it into separate branches (shakhas) came about."

That is: Vyasa, having mastered the whole Veda himself, divided it and taught its parts separately to different disciples, who carried their respective portions forward within their own family traditions — whatever one makes of this account, dividing the Veda clearly became a practical necessity. This explains why the Veda was first split into its four parts. But this alone doesn't fully capture what "shakha" means: a shakha is not a distinct portion of content so much as a distinct line of oral transmission — since different gurus took on the task of teaching disciples, each taught according to his own particular tradition, and although it was one and the same Veda, small variations crept in simply because the teaching lineages differed. That is: even within a single shakha, mantras handed down in different manuscript lines occasionally differ slightly from one another

<div class="pgmark">original p. 45</div>

and even the sequence of pronunciation could vary from teacher to teacher — though no substantial difference of principle exists between shakhas. This is why some are said to follow the "Shakala reading" and others the "Bashkala reading" when studying the Rigveda — both traditions remain current today.

All four Vedas originally had numerous shakhas; only a handful survive in practice now, and some are known only by name. The Rigveda has 21 shakhas, of which the Ashvalayana, Sankhyayana and some others are well known. The Yajurveda first splits into Shukla and Krishna; Shukla Yajurveda has 15 shakhas, of which only two, Kanva and Madhyandina, are prominent, and Krishna Yajurveda 86, of which a few, such as Apastamba, are in use. Of the Samaveda's 1000 shakhas very few are found today, and of these only Kauthuma is in currency. The Atharvaveda has nine shakhas, of which Shaunaka is well known. These are all Samhita-portions.

Brahmana-portions are believed to have once existed for many of these shakhas too, though only a few survive: for the Rigveda, the Aitareya and Kaushitaki; for the Yajurveda, the Shatapatha and Taittiriya; for the Samaveda, the Tandya, Shadvimsha and others; and for the Atharvaveda, the Gopatha Brahmana.

Shakhas do not differ significantly in antiquity, but do show some variation in matters of pronunciation and recitation sequence — for instance, the Shakala-shakha recites the suktas seen by Gotama, Kutsa, Kashyapa and Kakshivat in a different order: after the hymn seen by Gotama they recite those seen by Kutsa and Kashyapa and then the hymn seen by Kakshivat, whereas the Bashkalas recite Gotama, Kakshivat and then Kutsa, and the Ashvalayana followers are thought not to include certain Khila-suktas that the Bashkala tradition does. Such differences are essentially a matter of textual lineage rather than substance.

The text here gives the "Sankhyayana Samhita Krama" (सांख्यायनसंहिताक्रमः) — a short reference table showing where key suktas begin and end within the Sankhyayana sequence, by opening/closing words and Mandala-Sukta-Mantra reference:

| Opening words | Reference | Closing words | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| अग्निमीळे *(agnimīḷe)* | Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-1-1 | वा पुरस्तात् *(vā purastāt)* | Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-48-15 |
| अभि प्रवः *(abhi pravaḥ)* | " 8-49-1 | न आयुः *(na āyuḥ)* | " 8-59-7 |
| अग्न आयाह्य *(agna āyāhya)* | " 8-60-1 | सु सहासति *(su sahāsati)* | " 10-191-4 |
| संज्ञानमुशना *(saṃjñānam uśanā)* | (Pariśiṣṭa 36) | सु सहासति *(su sahāsati)* | — |

This is the Sankhyayana Samhita-krama. In this Samhita the Valakhilya suktas are included. The Parishishta-sukta of 15 mantras which in the Shakala Samhita begins "saṃjñānam uśanā" is, in this Sankhyayana Samhita, included in the Samhita as its final portion; it is not regarded as a Parishishta, but is counted as a final sukta of 4 Vargas.
