Looking at all these variants, the author settles on three reconstructed name-pairs as most likely correct, based on the Brahmanda Purana's readings specifically:

> पैंगश्चाद्दालकिस्तथा । पैंग्य औद्दालकिस्तथा । पैंग्यः शैलालकस्तथा ॥
>
> *paiṅgaścāddālakistathā | paiṅgya auddālakistathā | paiṅgyaḥ śailālakastathā ||*

(read as **Painga** and **Auddalaki**; **Paingya** and **Auddalaki**; **Paingya** and **Shailalaka**).

#### 1. The Paingya Shakha {.lv2}

A genuine Rigveda-related shakha, as already established from evidence discussed earlier. Its Brahmana and the existence of an associated Kalpa-sutra

<div class="pgmark">original p. 87</div>

were stated at the very beginning of this section. Whether this shakha has its own Samhita remains entirely unknown to this day. The Charaka Samhita's opening names a sage "Paingi," whose son was likely "Paingya" — a person by this name is separately listed among those present at Yudhishthira's assembly hall (Sabha-parva, 4-23). Paingya's own son, **Madhuka**, is cited in the Brihaddevata (1-24) and referenced in passing across the Shatapatha, Aitareya, and Kaushitaki Brahmanas, as well as frequently in the Sankhyayana Shrautasutra — including his view on the Agnyadhana (fire-establishment) rite, which later commentators note as differing only slightly from the Kaushitaki view; on the question of Soma's associated deity, Paingya's view, according to the Kaushitaki Brahmana's statement, turns out to be the same as that of the Bahvricha. The Madhyandina Shatapatha Brahmana (14-9-3-16) further records that Madhuka-Paingya received special teaching from Yajnavalkya connected with the Vajasaneya sacrifice. Evidence for a Paingya-Grihyasutra or Dharmasutra appears in the Smritichandrika (Ashaucha-kanda, p. 14), the Maskari commentary on the Gautama-Dharmasutra (14-6-17), and Haradatta's Anakula commentary on the Apastamba Grihyasutra (8-21-9) — this branch's texts appear to have been more prevalent specifically in South India.

#### 2. The Auddalaki Shakha {.lv2}

Uddalaka, of the Gautama lineage (son of Aruna, hence also called "Aruni"), was the father of the famous Shvetaketu. Uddalaka Aruni — a resident of Panchala, contemporary with King Janamejaya, and a disciple of Dhaumya-Ayoda — has his story begin in the Adiparva (3-19). Owing to his Gautama lineage, this branch is known in the world as the "Gautama-shakha," though the Vyakarana-Mahabhashya and other texts call it "Aruneya" (a separate discussion of the Aruneya-Brahmana follows elsewhere in this chapter). A teacher named Gautama appears frequently in the Ashvalayana Shrautasutra and must have been a Rigveda teacher.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 88</div>

(A separate Samaveda "Gautama-shakha" also exists and should not be confused with this Rigveda branch — details given elsewhere.)

#### 3. The Shailalaka Shakha {.lv2}

Possibly an alternate reading for "Auddalaki" in the Brahmanda Purana variants — which of the two readings is original cannot be determined with certainty. This shakha's Brahmana is cited in the Ashtadhyayi (4-3-110), and Sudarshanacharya's *Shruta-prakashika* commentary on the Shri-Bhashya quotes a lengthy passage from it (p. 681, with further references at pp. 909, 910, 1368).

#### 4. The Shatabalaksha Shakha {.lv2}

This name appears with several variants across the Brahmanda, Vayu, Vishnu, and Bhagavata Puranas (Shvetabalaksha, Shvetavalaka, Balaka, Babalaka, Vyalika), with "Shatabalaksha" the most commonly used form today. The Nirukta (11-6) names a Shatabalaksha Maudgalya, son of Mudgala (the same Mudgala-shakha discussed earlier) — and per this same Nirukta passage, Shatabalaksha himself became an author of Nirukta material. If this Shatabalaksha was indeed a disciple of Shakapurni, the likelihood strengthens that he is one and the same as this Nirukta-author.

##### Shakapurni's Fourth Disciple {.lv3}

Beyond the three disciples who became shakha-founders, Shakapurni had a fourth disciple named (with variant readings) Gaja, Naigama, Niruktakrit, Nirukta, or Viraja — the authentic form cannot be determined with confidence. One associated Kalpa-sutra text is called "Hrasvika." The Shabara-bhashya on the Mimamsa-sutra (1-3-11) lists examples of Kalpa-sutra texts: "Mashaka, Hastika, Kaundinyaka," and similarly named works — raising the natural question, if "Gaja" is indeed the correct disciple-name, of what connection might exist between him and this "Hastika-Kalpa" text.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 89</div>

### The Final Puranic Divisions of Shakha-Founders {.lv1}

#### Bashkali Bharadvaja {.lv2}

Distinct from the earlier-discussed Bashkala lineage. The Skanda Purana's Nagara-khanda (41-6) mentions a "Danavendra Bashkali" — not a rishi and shakha-founder. Shankaracharya's Vedanta-sutra commentary (3-2-17) separately mentions "Badhva questioned by Bashkali" — plausibly referring to the actual shakha-founder. The Brahmanda Purana (earlier section, ch. 35) gives his lineage:

> बाष्कलिस्तु भरद्वाजस्तिस्रः प्रोवाच संहिताः । त्रयस्तस्य भवन्तीष्ट्या महात्मानो गुणान्विताः ॥ ५ ॥ धीमांश्च त्वापनीपश्च पन्नगारिश्च बुद्धिमान् । तृतीयश्चार्जवस्ते च तपसा संशितव्रताः ॥ ६ ॥ वीतरागा महातेजाः संहिताज्ञानपारगाः । इत्येते बह्वृचः प्रोक्ताः संहिता यैः प्रवर्तिताः ॥ ७ ॥
>
> "Bashkali Bharadvaja taught three Samhitas; he had three great-souled, virtuous disciples: the wise Apanipa and the learned Pannagari, and a third, Arjava, of keen vows through austerity — passionless, of great splendour, masters of the knowledge of the Samhitas; these are called Bahvrichas, by whom the Samhitas were propagated."

That is: Bashkali Bharadvaja had three disciples.

**Disciple 1 — "Apanipa":** variant readings include Apanapa, Nandayaniya, Kaalaayani, and Baalaayani; the last two seem closer to the original, but nothing can be said with certainty.

**Disciple 2 — "Pannagari":** variants include Pannagaani, Gaargya, and Bhajya across different Puranic manuscripts — of which the first name seems the more fitting. A possible connection to "Bhujyu Lahyaayani" (named in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, 3-3-1) is considered, though this identification has its own complications given the Brihadaranyaka-Kaushitaki tradition's own account,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 90</div>

leaving the third disciple's identity (whether a mere messenger or a genuine shakha-founder) unresolved from the Bhagavata account. Per the Ashtadhyayi (2-4-61), Pannagari was of the eastern (Prachya) country. The Brahmanda Purana instead names this third disciple "Arjava," with further variants:

> आर्व्व । कथाजन । तथाजन । कासार ।
>
> *ārvva | kathājana | tathājana | kāsāra |*

— again, no confident determination among these is possible.

**Tally:** across these Puranic accounts, the Puranas name 15 Samhita-founding teachers of the Rigveda's shakhas in all — five of the Shakala group, four of the Bashkala group, three of Shakapurni's disciples, and three of Bashkali Bharadvaja's disciples. Bhartrihari, in the commentary on his Vakyapadiya (1-6), writes:

> एकविंशतिधा बाह्वृच्यम् । पञ्चदशधा इत्येके ।
>
> *ekaviṃśatidhā bāhvṛcyam | pañcadaśadhā ity eke |*
>
> "The Bahvricha [tradition] is twenty-one-fold; some say fifteen-fold."

— reflecting a genuine, acknowledged difference of scholarly opinion inherited from his own teachers, rather than a settled figure.

##### Other Rigveda Shakhas Not Clearly Connected to Those Already Described {.lv3}

##### 1. The Aitareya Shakha {.lv3}

The existence of the well-known Aitareya Brahmana itself confirms a corresponding "Aitareya" shakha. The Ashvalayana Shrautasutra (1-3) and the Nidana-sutra (5-2) both use the terms "Aitareyin" and "Aitareyakam" for it; the commentator Gargya Narayana likewise treats "Aitareyin" as a specific shakha-type, as does Varadatta's son in his Sankhyayana-Shrauta commentary ("Aitareyiṇām," 1-4-15). Medhatithi's commentary on the Manu-sutra (2-6) states directly:

> "The twenty-one Bahvricha [shakhas], distinguished into the Ashvalayana, Aitareya, and other such divisions."

That is: among the Rigveda's 21 shakhas, Ashvalayana, Aitareya, and others are counted — confirming Aitareya's place as one of the recognized 21.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 91</div>

**The Aitareya-Grihya:** though this shakha's Brahmana and Aranyaka are well known, its Grihyasutra is only inferred. Haradatta's commentary on the Ashvalayana Grihyasutra (1-6-20) notes: "And the Aitareyins' statement — [the mantra beginning] 'bhava,' etc., is common everywhere" — suggesting a shared marriage-rite recitation, plausibly drawn from an actual (if now-obscure) Aitareya Grihyasutra.

**The Aitareya Shakhas and the Nine-Shraddha Question:** Devanabhatta's *Smriti-chandrika* and a related citation (attributed to Shivaswami) preserve variant readings of a verse on how many types of Nava-shraddha (ancestral rites) different shakhas recognize:

> नवश्राद्धानि पञ्चाहुराश्वलायनशाखिनः । आपस्तम्बाश्च दित्याहुः पञ्चभिः षड्भिरैतरेयिणः ॥
>
> "Ashvalayana-shakha followers say the nine shraddhas number five; the Apastamba followers say six; the Aitareyins reckon them, with some flexibility, as five or six."

Since this distinctly Aitareya view doesn't appear in known Ashvalayana texts, the author raises — without resolving — the question of what independent Aitareya text this view might originally have come from.

#### 2. The Vashishtha Shakha {.lv2}

Bühler edited and published the Vasishtha-Dharmasutra as Rigveda-related, though which specific shakha it belongs to remains unclear. Kumarilabhatta's Tantravartika (1-3-11) writes as follows:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 92</div>

> गैरेव च परिगृह्येते । वासिष्ठं बह्वृचैरेव । शङ्खलिखितोक्तं च वाजसनेयिभिः । आपस्तम्बबोधायनीये तैत्तिरीयैरेव प्रतिपन्ने इत्येवम् ॥
>
> "...are each adopted through their own Grihya[-text]. The Vashishtha [text] is used only by the Bahvrichas; the Shankhalikhita-prescribed [text] by the Vajasaneyins; the Apastamba and Baudhayana [texts] only by the Taittiriyas..."

That is: just as Pratishakhyas differ by shakha, so do Grihyasutras — Samaveda followers use the Gautama and Gobhila sutras; Bahvricha-shakha followers (i.e., Rigvedins) use the Vashishtha-sutra; Vajasaneyins use the Shankhalikhita material; and Taittiriya-shakha followers use the Apastamba and Baudhayana sutras. If Kumarila is right that the Bahvricha shakha is genuinely distinct, this confirms the Vashishtha tradition's specific association with it — though the Vasishtha Shrauta- and Grihyasutras themselves still merit closer investigation.

That is, the Vasishtha shakha has 152514 words; in that Samhita the 23rd varga of the third adhyaya of the third Ashtaka, beginning "Indrotibhih," is absent, and that varga's word-count is 71 — confirming that the **Vasishtha shakha was indeed treated as a genuinely distinct branch.**

#### 3. The Sulabha Shakha {.lv2}

Attested in the Vyakarana-Mahabhashya (4-2-66 and 4-3-105); that Brahmana belonged to the Rigveda, as the Rishi-tarpana section of Ashvalayana shows, where the names Sulabha-Maitreyi (or Sulabha and Maitreyi) are written. Whether the lady Sulabha had any connection with this Brahmana, or whether some special teaching of Sulabha in a Brahmana text led to that part being called the Saulabha-Brahmana, is open to inquiry.

#### 4. The Shaunaka Shakha {.lv2}

The sage Shaunaka was a resident of Naimisharanya; great sacrifices were performed in his hermitage, and for this reason he was called Bahvricha-simha (lion among the Bahvrichas). One of his disciples was Ashvalayana. According to the Mahabharata story, Ugrashravas told this after Janamejaya had performed the snake-sacrifice (Sarpa-satra).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 93</div>

In the Prapancha-hridaya a Rigveda shakha called Shaunaka is written of. In the second and fourth chapters of the Ananda-samhita of the Vaikhanasa tradition a Shaunakiya sutra of the Rigveda, different from Ashvalayana's, is also quoted. Nothing more than this can be said about this shakha.

### Summary — All the Rigveda Shakhas Discussed in This Chapter {.lv1}

1. Mudgala Shakha
2. Galava Shakha
3. Shaleeya Shakha
4. Vatsya Shakha
5. Shaishiri Shakha
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*— these five are the Shakala shakhas*

6. Baudhya Shakha
7. Agnimatara Shakha
8. Parashara Shakha
9. Jatukarnya Shakha

10. Ashvalayana Shakha

11. Sankhyayana Shakha
12. Kaushitaki Shakha
13. Mahakaushitaki Shakha
14. Shambavya Shakha

15. Mandukeya Shakha
16. Bahvricha Shakha
17. Shaingya Shakha
18. Uddalaka = Gautama = Aruna Shakha
19. Shatabalaksha Shakha
20. Gaja = Hastika Shakha
21–23. The three Bashkali-Bharadvaja shakhas (Apanisha, Pannagari, Arjava)
24. Aitareya Shakha
25. Vashishtha Shakha
26. Sulabha Shakha
27. Shaunaka Shakha

<div class="pgmark">original p. 94</div>

The Vyakarana-Mahabhashya states the Rigveda has 21 shakhas, yet the list just compiled runs to 27 names. The author reconciles this by suggesting that some of the additionally-identified names should properly be understood as sub-divisions nested within the main twenty-one, rather than fully independent branches — though confirming exactly which ones is not straightforward given the limited evidence currently available: the six extra shakhas must be included within some of the others, and the first nine names and names 11–13 are settled. The Anubhashya's citation from the Skanda Purana, and a separate account in the Anandasamhita, both give the figure 24 Rigveda shakhas — suggesting either that a few names in the present list are duplicates/overlaps counted separately, or that all these sources made their count on a broadly similar (if not perfectly reconcilable) basis. Neither possibility, the author notes, would be especially surprising.

**Footnote:** The Brahmanda Purana's earlier section (chapters 33-35) treats the division of the Veda, the names of Vedic shakhas, and the shakha-founders connected to the Shukla Yajurveda and Vajasaneya-Samhita at much greater length than could be included here — what appears in this chapter is only a focused extract, gathered and gone into in detail specifically where it bears on Rigveda shakha-founders. **This Brahmanda Purana has itself been published, with Kannada explanations, as part of the "Sri Jayachamarajendra Grantharatnamala" series** (see the list of Books published by Palace Authorities, Mysore). Chapters 33-35 referenced throughout this chapter are in the second part of this work (the Purana).

**— Chapter Five (The Branches of the Rigveda) concludes here. —**

## Chapter Six — The Branches (Śākhās) of the Yajurveda

<div class="pgmark">original p. 95</div>

**ಆರನೆಯ ಪ್ರಕರಣ — The Sixth Chapter**

##### The Śukla and Kṛṣṇa Yajurvedas {.lv3}

Although the sage Bhagavān Vyāsa taught the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda alone to his disciple Vaiśampāyana, in the ancient tradition the Śukla Yajurveda held great esteem. In the earlier part of the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa (1-29) it is said:

> इषे त्वोर्जे त्वा वायवः स्थ देवो वः सविता प्रार्पयतु ।
> श्रेष्ठतमाय कर्मण इत्येवमादिं कृत्वा यजुर्वेदमधीयते ॥
>
> *iṣe tvorje tvā vāyavaḥ stha devo vaḥ savitā prārpayatu |*
> *śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇa ity evam ādiṃ kṛtvā yajurvedam adhīyate ||*
>
> "'You (are) for sap, you for vigour; you are the winds; may the god Savitṛ impel you to the most excellent act' — beginning in this way, the Yajurveda is studied."

That is: one must study the Yajurveda beginning with the mantra stated above; and that mantra is the first mantra of the Śukla Yajurveda.

In the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, after the words *vāyavaḥ stha* there stands the reading *upāyavaḥ stha*; that reading is therefore absent here. From this it is clear that for those who study this Brāhmaṇa the first mantra of the Śukla Yajurveda was the one accepted here; they used to regard this alone as the Yajurveda. In the 26th chapter of the Vāyu Purāṇa the same is stated:

> ततः पुनर्द्विमात्रं तु चिन्तयामास चाक्षरम् ।
> प्रादुर्भूतं च रक्तं तच्छेदने गृह्य सा यजुः ॥१९॥
> इषे त्वोर्जे त्वा वायवः स्थ देवो वः सविता पुनः ।
> ऋग्वेद एकमात्रस्तु द्विमात्रस्तु यजुः स्मृतः ॥२०॥
>
> *tataḥ punar dvimātraṃ tu cintayām āsa cākṣaram |*
> *prādurbhūtaṃ ca raktaṃ tac-chedane gṛhya sā yajuḥ ||19||*
> *iṣe tvorje tvā vāyavaḥ stha devo vaḥ savitā punaḥ |*
> *ṛgveda eka-mātras tu dvi-mātras tu yajuḥ smṛtaḥ ||20||*
>
> "Then again he thought of a syllable of two *mātrās* … [the sense is not certain] … 'iṣe tvorje tvā vāyavaḥ stha devo vaḥ savitā punaḥ' — the Ṛgveda is of one *mātrā*; the Yajus is remembered as of two *mātrās*."

The Kannada comment: "The first mantra of the Śukla Yajurveda is declared to be the first mantra of the Yajurveda."

#### The antiquity of the Śukla Yajurveda {.lv1}

The name "Śukla Yajurveda" is very ancient. In the closing statement of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the Mādhyandina branch:

> आदित्यानीमानि शुक्लानि यजूंषि वाजसनेयेन याज्ञवल्क्येनाख्यायन्ते ।
>
> *ādityānīmāni śuklāni yajūṃṣi vājasaneyena yājñavalkyenākhyāyante |*
>
> "These white Yajus-mantras, belonging to the Sun, are proclaimed by Yājñavalkya of the Vājasaneya [line]."

Thus this Śukla Yajurveda, which originated from the Sun, is called by the name of Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya. Why did the Śukla Yajurveda come to have the name *Vājasaneya-saṃhitā*? What is the connection between the Śukla Yajurveda and Yājñavalkya? Such matters are described at length in chapters 34–35 of the Pūrvabhāga of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. This subject has already been explained in subtle detail earlier.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 96</div>

#### How ancient is the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda? {.lv1}

In the bhāṣya on the first kaṇḍikā of the *Pratijñā-sūtra*, and again at the end of the bhāṣya on the second kaṇḍikā of the *Caraṇa-vyūha*, Ananta (in the former) and Mahidāsa (in the latter) use the word *kṛṣṇa* together with Yajurveda. Sāyaṇācārya, in two places in the bhūmikā of his bhāṣya on the Kāṇva-saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda, uses the term *kṛṣṇa-yajus*; and in the Muktikopaniṣad (1-2-3) too the term "Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda" occurs. Besides these, a further authority is given by Ananta in the bhāṣya on the *Pratijñā-sūtra*; it cannot be said from which work it comes. That authority follows:

> शुक्लं कृष्णमिति द्वेधा यजुश्च समुदाहृतम् ।
> शुक्लं वाजसनं ज्ञेयं कृष्णं तु तैत्तिरीयकम् ॥
>
> *śuklaṃ kṛṣṇam iti dvedhā yajuś ca samudāhṛtam |*
> *śuklaṃ vājasanaṃ jñeyaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ tu taittirīyakam ||*
>
> "The Yajus is declared to be of two kinds, white and black. The white is to be known as the Vājasana [Vājasaneya]; the black is the Taittirīyaka."

> तत्र हेतुः —
> बुद्धिमालिन्यहेतुत्वात्तद्यजुः कृष्णमीर्यते ।
> व्यवस्थितप्रकरणं तद्यजुः शुक्लमीर्यते ॥
> इत्यादि स्मृतेश्च ।
>
> *tatra hetuḥ —*
> *buddhi-mālinya-hetutvāt tad yajuḥ kṛṣṇam īryate |*
> *vyavasthita-prakaraṇaṃ tad yajuḥ śuklam īryate ||*
> *ity-ādi smṛteś ca |*
>
> "The reason there: because it causes dullness (blackening) of the intellect, that Yajus is called black; that Yajus whose sections are in an ordered arrangement is called white. — And so on, from the Smṛti also."

There is a book named *Mantra-bhrānti-hara* ("Remover of confusion in mantras"), also called *Sūtra-mantra-prakāśikā*; its name too is cited as an example in the *Caraṇa-vyūha*. In it:

> यजुर्वेदः कल्पतरुः शुक्लकृष्ण इति द्विधा ।
> सत्त्वप्रधानाच्छुक्लाख्यो यातयामविवर्जितात् ॥६१॥
> कृष्णस्य यजुषः शाखाः षडशीतिरुदाहृताः ॥६४॥
>
> *yajurvedaḥ kalpataruḥ śukla-kṛṣṇa iti dvidhā |*
> *sattva-pradhānāc chuklākhyo yātayāma-vivarjitāt ||61||*
> *kṛṣṇasya yajuṣaḥ śākhāḥ ṣaḍaśītir udāhṛtāḥ ||64||*
>
> "The Yajurveda is a wish-fulfilling tree, of two kinds, white and black. It is called white because *sattva* predominates and because it is free from *yātayāma* [staleness]. The branches of the black Yajus are declared to be eighty-six."

That is: the Yajurveda has two kinds, Kṛṣṇa and Śukla; and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda is said to have 86 branches. This book is somewhat ancient; but nothing more could be learned about it.

#### The branches of the Yajus (*Yājuṣa-śākhās*) {.lv1}

The sage Patañjali, in the Paspaśāhnika of his grammatical Mahābhāṣya, writes:

> एकशतमध्वर्युशाखाः ।
>
> *ekaśatam adhvaryu-śākhāḥ |*
>
> "The Adhvaryu [Yajurveda] has one hundred and one branches."

The Kannada explains: "Patañjali writes that the Yajurveda has one hundred and one branches."

In the second Veda-chapter (*veda-prakaraṇa*) of the *Prapañca-hṛdaya* it is written thus:

> यजुर्वेद एकोत्तरशतधा ।………। यजुर्वेदस्य —
> माध्यन्दिन-कण्व-तित्तिरि-हिरण्यकेश-आपस्तम्ब-सत्याषाढ-बौधायन-याज्ञवल्क्य-भद्रंजय-बृहदुक्थ-पाराशर-नामदेव-जातुकर्ण-तुरुष्क-सोमशुष्म-तृणबिन्दु-वाजिंजय-
> श्रवस-वर्षवरूथ-सनद्वाज-वाजिरत्न-हर्यश्व-ऋणंजय-तृणंजय-कृतंजय-धनंजय-सत्यंजय-सहंजय-मिश्रंजय-श्रैरुण-त्रिवृष-त्रिधामश्विंज-फलिंगु-उखा-आत्रेयशाखाः ॥
>
> *yajurveda eko-ttara-śatadhā | ………… | yajurvedasya —*
> *mādhyandina-kaṇva-tittiri-hiraṇyakeśa-āpastamba-satyāṣāḍha-baudhāyana-yājñavalkya-bhadraṃjaya-bṛhaduktha-pārāśara-nāmadeva-jātukarṇa-turuṣka-somaśuṣma-tṛṇabindu-vājiṃjaya-*
> *śravasa-varṣavarūtha-sanadvāja-vājiratna-haryaśva-ṛṇaṃjaya-tṛṇaṃjaya-kṛtaṃjaya-dhanaṃjaya-satyaṃjaya-sahaṃjaya-miśraṃjaya-śrairuṇa-trivṛṣa-tridhāmaśviṃja-phaliṃgu-ukhā-ātreya-śākhāḥ ||*
>
> "The Yajurveda is divided one hundred and one ways … Of the Yajurveda [the branches are]: Mādhyandina, Kāṇva, Tittiri, Hiraṇyakeśa, Āpastamba, Satyāṣāḍha, Baudhāyana, Yājñavalkya, Bhadraṃjaya, Bṛhaduktha, Pārāśara, Nāmadeva, Jātukarṇa, Turuṣka, Somaśuṣma, Tṛṇabindu, Vājiṃjaya, Śravasa, Varṣavarūtha, Sanadvāja, Vājiratna, Haryaśva, Ṛṇaṃjaya, Tṛṇaṃjaya, Kṛtaṃjaya, Dhanaṃjaya, Satyaṃjaya, Sahaṃjaya, Miśraṃjaya, Śrairuṇa, Trivṛṣa, Tridhāmaśviṃja, Phaliṃgu, Ukhā and the Ātreya branches."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 97</div>

That is: these branches of the Yajurveda were either obtained by, or known to, the writer of the *Prapañca-hṛdaya*. Among these, many names are not stated to be the names of the sages who created branches.

In the Buddhist work named the *Divyāvadāna*:

> एकविंशति अध्वर्यवः ……… अध्वर्यूणां मते ब्राह्मणाः सर्वे ते ऽध्वर्यवो भूत्वा एकविंशतिधा भिन्नाः । तद्यथा — कठाः । काण्वाः । वाजसनेयिनः । जातुकर्णाः । प्रौष्ठपदा ऋषयः । तत्र दश कठा दश काण्वा एकादश वाजसनेयिनः त्रयोदश जातुकर्णाः षोडश प्रौष्ठपदाः पञ्चचत्वारिंशदृषयः ॥
>
> *ekaviṃśati adhvaryavaḥ ………… adhvaryūṇāṃ mate brāhmaṇāḥ sarve te 'dhvaryavo bhūtvā ekaviṃśatidhā bhinnāḥ | tadyathā — kaṭhāḥ | kāṇvāḥ | vājasaneyinaḥ | jātukarṇāḥ | prauṣṭhapadā ṛṣayaḥ | tatra daśa kaṭhā daśa kāṇvā ekādaśa vājasaneyinaḥ trayodaśa jātukarṇāḥ ṣoḍaśa prauṣṭhapadāḥ pañcacatvāriṃśad ṛṣayaḥ ||*
>
> "Twenty-one Adhvaryus … in the opinion of the Adhvaryus, all those Brāhmaṇas, having become Adhvaryus, were divided into twenty-one ways; namely: the Kaṭhas, the Kāṇvas, the Vājasaneyins, the Jātukarṇas, the Prauṣṭhapada sages. Of these, ten are Kaṭhas, ten Kāṇvas, eleven Vājasaneyins, thirteen Jātukarṇas, sixteen Prauṣṭhapadas, [and] forty-five sages."

The Kannada author says: "We have written this passage after some investigation [i.e., with some correction]; but where it reads *ekaviṃśati* (twenty-one) it may be *ekaśatam* (one hundred). According to the count of the *Divyāvadāna* there are 10 Kaṭha, 10 Kāṇva, 11 Vājasaneya, 13 Jātukarṇa and 16 Prauṣṭhapada [branches]; thus 60 branches in all. To these the sages (45) are added; if this is the meaning of the passage quoted earlier, then according to this Buddhist work the Yajurveda has in all 105 branches [the printed figure is read from small print; the sum 60 + 45 = 105 agrees]. This division of the Yājuṣa branches is very strange; nor is there anything elsewhere to which it can be compared."

#### Two lists relating to the Yājuṣa branches {.lv2}

We have two lists describing the Yājuṣa branches. The first list was found in the house of Śrī Yajñeśvara Dājī Maitrāyaṇīya, a Pañcavaṭī-resident living within the Nāsik sacred region (*Nāsika-kṣetra*); it is a copy of the list he gave. The second list is a copy that Paṇḍita Śrīdhara Śāstrī, son of Śrī Aṇṇā Śāstrī, who lived in the same Nāsik-kṣetra, made himself and gave, in accordance with the list he had. According to the first list the details of the Yājuṣa branches are as follows.

In stating the names of these branches, where "Jābāla branch" is meant it is written *Jābālāḥ*; likewise the Baudheya branch, the Kāṇva branch, and so on, should be understood at the outset [as such]. Among these, most of the names are not those of authors of branches, but are the names of various Brāhmaṇa clans (*kulas*) —

<div class="pgmark">original p. 102</div>

in the Pariśiṣṭa of the Atharvaṇa *Caraṇa-vyūha* it is written thus:

> तत्र यजुर्वेदस्य चतुर्विंशतिभेदा भवन्ति । तद्यथा —
> काण्वाः । माध्यन्दिनाः । जाबालाः । शापेयाः । श्वेताः । श्वेततराः । ताम्रायणीयाः । पौर्णवत्साः । आवटिकाः । परमावटिकाः । हौष्याः । धौष्याः [औख्याः] । खाडिकाः [खाण्डिकाः] । आह्वरकाः । चरकाः । मैत्राः । मैत्रायणीयाः । हारिकर्णाः । शालायनीयाः । मर्जकठाः । प्राच्यकठाः । कपिष्ठलकठाः । उपलाः । तैत्तिरीयाश्चेति ॥३॥
>
> *tatra yajurvedasya caturviṃśati-bhedā bhavanti | tadyathā —*
> *kāṇvāḥ | mādhyandināḥ | jābālāḥ | śāpeyāḥ | śvetāḥ | śvetatarāḥ | tāmrāyaṇīyāḥ | paurṇavatsāḥ | āvaṭikāḥ | paramāvaṭikāḥ | hauṣyāḥ | dhauṣyāḥ [aukhyāḥ] | khāḍikāḥ [khāṇḍikāḥ] | āhvarakāḥ | carakāḥ | maitrāḥ | maitrāyaṇīyāḥ | hārikarṇāḥ | śālāyanīyāḥ | marjakaṭhāḥ | prācyakaṭhāḥ | kapiṣṭhalakaṭhāḥ | upalāḥ | taittirīyāś ceti ||3||*
>
> "Of these, the Yajurveda has twenty-four divisions; namely: Kāṇvas, Mādhyandinas, Jābālas, Śāpeyas, Śvetas, Śvetataras, Tāmrāyaṇīyas, Paurṇavatsas, Āvaṭikas, Paramāvaṭikas, Hauṣyas, Dhauṣyas [Aukhyas], Khāḍikas [Khāṇḍikas], Āhvarakas, Carakas, Maitras, Maitrāyaṇīyas, Hārikarṇas, Śālāyanīyas, Marjakaṭhas, Prācyakaṭhas, Kapiṣṭhalakaṭhas, Upalas and Taittirīyas."

(The words in square brackets are the Kannada editor's corrections as printed; there are two.)

Of these, the first ten belong to the Śukla Yajurveda; the following fourteen belong to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. There are many errors in the printed text of the Atharvaṇa Pariśiṣṭa; as shown in brackets, only two readings have been corrected.

Now let us examine closely Yājñavalkya, the exponent of the Śukla Yajurveda, and the subject matter of the Śukla Yajurveda.

#### On Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya {.lv2}

##### Birth-place {.lv3}

In the time of the Mahābhārata there was, to the west of Bhārata, a large province named Saurāṣṭra. One part of it was called Ānarta. Camatkārapura was another chief town of the Ānarta country; it was famous under the name Nagara. It is the original home of the Nāgara Brāhmaṇas. According to the Nāgarakhaṇḍa of the Skāndapurāṇa (175-55), Yājñavalkya's hermitage was somewhere near Camatkārapura. In the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the work *Yogi-yājñavalkya* (1-1) and in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* (1-2), at these places Yājñavalkya is said to have been a resident of Mithilā, that is, of the city of Mithilā. Because of his friendship with King Janaka, it is also possible that Mithilā was one dwelling-place of Yājñavalkya.

##### Many names of the clan, gotra and father {.lv3}

According to the Vāyu Purāṇa (61-21), the Pūrvabhāga of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (35-24) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3-5-3), the name of Yājñavalkya's father was Brahmarāta. According to the Vāyu Purāṇa (60-41) his name is Brahmavāha. According to the Śrīmad Bhāgavata (12-6-64) his name was Devarāta. The name of Śunaḥśepa also was Devarāta. This Śunaḥśepa was regarded as a son of the sage Viśvāmitra. According to the Vāyu Purāṇa (91-93) the real name of this Viśvāmitra was Viśvaratha. Members of Viśvāmitra's clan are called Kauśika. According to the Vāyu Purāṇa (91-98) and the Madhyabhāga of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (66-70), Yājñavalkya too belonged to Viśvāmitra's clan. In the Anuśāsana-parvan of the Mahābhārata also (7-51) in this very manner

<div class="pgmark">original p. 103</div>

has been said. And by indicating Yājñavalkya with the epithet "famous" (*vikhyāta*), [the Mahābhārata] makes his renown extend to the ends of the quarters. For that reason it is also possible that Yājñavalkya was the very son of Devarāta. Devarāta may have had another son named Brahmarāta, and it would also be right to say that Yājñavalkya was this Brahmarāta's son. Or Devarāta himself may have been called Brahmarāta, and for that reason his name may have been given as Brahmarāta. Later, at the end of the account of Yājñavalkya's lineage, a proof from the Śānti-parvan of the Mahābhārata (315-4) will be given; by it the name of Yājñavalkya's father is established with certainty as Devarāta.

Viśvarūpa, the commentator (*ācārya*) on the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, is known to have lived about the eighth century. In his commentary named *Bālakrīḍā* he writes thus:

> यज्ञवल्को ब्रह्मा इति पौराणिकाः । तदपत्यं याज्ञवल्क्यः । (१-१)
>
> *yajñavalko brahmā iti paurāṇikāḥ | tad-apatyaṃ yājñavalkyaḥ | (1-1)*
>
> "According to the Paurāṇikas, there is a Brahmā named Yajñavalka; his offspring is Yājñavalkya."

That is: according to the Paurāṇikas there was a Brahmā (Prajāpati) named Yajñavalka, and Yājñavalkya was his son — so it is written in the Vāyu Purāṇa (60-42):

> ब्रह्मणोऽङ्गात्समुत्पन्नः ।
>
> *brahmaṇo 'ṅgāt samutpannaḥ |*
>
> "Born from a limb of Brahmā."

That is: Yājñavalkya arose from a part of Brahmā.

In this very chapter of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

> अथान्यस्तत्र वै विद्वान् ब्रह्मणस्तु सुतः कविः । (३४-४४)
>
> *athānyas tatra vai vidvān brahmaṇas tu sutaḥ kaviḥ | (34-44)*
>
> "And another there, a learned man, a poet, the son of Brahmā."

That is: Yājñavalkya is said to have been a son of Brahmā.

#### Other relationships {.lv2}

To Janamejaya at Takṣaśilā, the revered sage Vyāsa related the whole story of the Mahābhārata; Vyāsa had a dear disciple named Vaiśampāyana. This Vaiśampāyana, the famous Carakācārya, was also Yājñavalkya's maternal uncle (mother's brother). In the 323rd chapter of the Śānti-parvan of the Mahābhārata it is written thus:

> कृत्वा चाध्ययनं तेषां शिष्याणां शतमुत्तमम् ।
> विप्रियार्थं सशिष्यस्य मातुलस्य महात्मनः ॥१७॥
>
> *kṛtvā cādhyayanaṃ teṣāṃ śiṣyāṇāṃ śatam uttamam |*
> *vipriyārthaṃ saśiṣyasya mātulasya mahātmanaḥ ||17||*
>
> "Having caused a hundred excellent disciples to study it, in order to displease my great-souled maternal uncle together with his disciples."

That is: "I composed the work called the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa in full and had my hundred disciples study it. This matter was displeasing to my maternal uncle, the sage Vaiśampāyana"; that is, he could not tolerate it.

Their maternal uncle Vaiśampāyana followed the text of the Caraka branch of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda; therefore the currency of the Śukla Yajurveda was not agreeable to him.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 104</div>

Concerning Yājñavalkya's son and grandsons, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skānda Purāṇa, chapter 130, says:

> एवं सिद्धिं समापन्नो याज्ञवल्क्यो द्विजोत्तमः ।
> कृत्स्नोपनिषदं चारु वेदार्थैः सकलैर्युतं ॥७०॥
> जनकाय नरेन्द्राय व्याख्याय च ततः परम् ।
> कात्यायनं सुतं प्राप्य वेदसूत्रस्य कारकम् ॥७१॥
>
> *evaṃ siddhiṃ samāpanno yājñavalkyo dvijottamaḥ |*
> *kṛtsnopaniṣadaṃ cāru vedārthaiḥ sakalair yutaṃ ||70||*
> *janakāya narendrāya vyākhyāya ca tataḥ param |*
> *kātyāyanaṃ sutaṃ prāpya veda-sūtrasya kārakam ||71||*
>
> "Thus having attained perfection, Yājñavalkya, best of the twice-born, and having expounded to King Janaka the entire Upaniṣad, beautiful, joined with all the meanings of the Veda, and thereafter having obtained as son Kātyāyana, the maker of the Veda-sūtra …" (the sense of the first line is as read from the print; the grammar is not entirely clear.)

And in the next chapter, 131:

> कात्यायनाभिधं च यज्ञविद्याविचक्षणम् ॥४८॥
> पुत्रो वररुचिर्यस्य बभूव गुणसागरः ॥४९॥
>
> *kātyāyanābhidhaṃ ca yajña-vidyā-vicakṣaṇam ||48||*
> *putro vararucir yasya babhūva guṇa-sāgaraḥ ||49||*
>
> "… named Kātyāyana, skilled in the science of sacrifice; whose son was Vararuci, an ocean of virtues."

That is: Yājñavalkya's son was Kātyāyana, and Kātyāyana's son was Vararuci.

It was said before that Yājñavalkya was a Kauśika. His son Kātyāyana too must have been a Kauśika. In the Pariśiṣṭa of the *Pratijñā-sūtra* composed by Kātyāyana:

> सोऽहं कौशिकपक्षः शिष्यः । (खण्ड ११)
>
> *so 'haṃ kauśika-pakṣaḥ śiṣyaḥ | (khaṇḍa 11)*
>
> "I am of the Kauśika side, the pupil."

That is: "I, Kātyāyana, belong to the Kauśika side."

The sage Kātyāyana who composed the *Yajña-sūtra* [the Śrauta-sūtra] is Yājñavalkya's son. This matter will be discussed later.

#### Could there have been two persons named Yājñavalkya? {.lv2}

In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (4-4) it is written:

> ततश्च विश्वसहो जज्ञे ॥१०६॥ तस्माद्धिरण्यनाभः । यो महायोगीश्वराज्जैमिनेः शिष्याद्याज्ञवल्क्याद्योगमवाप ॥१०७॥
>
> *tataś ca viśvasaho jajñe ||106|| tasmād dhiraṇyanābhaḥ | yo mahāyogīśvarāj jaimineḥ śiṣyād yājñavalkyād yogam avāpa ||107||*
>
> "And from him Viśvasaha was born; from him Hiraṇyanābha, who obtained yoga from Yājñavalkya, the great lord of yogins, the disciple of Jaimini."

That is: in the Ikṣvāku family, a long time after Śrī Rāma, there was a king named Viśvaratha [the Sanskrit above reads *Viśvasaha*]. From him Hiraṇyanābha was born; he learned yoga from Yājñavalkya, the disciple of Jaimini and great lord of yogins.

The Śrīmad Bhāgavata (9-12-3, 4) also mentions the same matter.

According to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, after this Hiraṇyanābha, the twelfth in this dynasty was a Kosala king named Bṛhadbala, who was killed in the Bhārata war by Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son.

Since the Viṣṇu Purāṇa says here *prādhānyena mayeritāḥ* ("stated by me according to importance"), mentioning only the principal kings, this point should be kept in mind.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 105</div>

Mahārāja Hasti, resident of Hastināpura, had a second son, Dvijamīḍha; after him the eighth king was Kṛta. About him the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (4-19) says:

> कृतः पुत्रोऽभूत् ॥५०॥ यं हिरण्यनाभो योगमध्यापयामास ॥५१॥ यश्चतुर्विंशतिः प्राच्यसामगानां संहिताश्चकार ॥५२॥
>
> *kṛtaḥ putro 'bhūt ||50|| yaṃ hiraṇyanābho yogam adhyāpayām āsa ||51|| yaś caturviṃśatiḥ prācya-sāmagānāṃ saṃhitāś cakāra ||52||*
>
> "A son, Kṛta, was born. Hiraṇyanābha taught him yoga. He made twenty-four saṃhitās of the Prācya Sāma-singers."

That is: Kṛta learned yoga from Hiraṇyanābha. This Hiraṇyanābha was the exponent (*pravacanakāra*) of the text of the 24 saṃhitās of the Prācya-sāmans.

The Vāyu Purāṇa (99-190) joins the name of the sage Kauthuma with this same Hiraṇyanābha.

Again, in the Madhyabhāga of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, chapter 64, it is written thus:

> व्युषिताश्वसुतश्चापि राजा विश्वसहः किल ॥२०६॥
> हिरण्यनाभः कौसल्यो वरिष्ठस्तत्सुतोऽभवत् ।
> पौष्पञ्जेश्च स वै शिष्यः स्मृतः प्राच्येषु सामसु ॥२०७॥
> शतानि संहितानां तु पञ्च योऽधीतवांस्ततः ।
> तस्मादधिगतो योगो याज्ञवल्क्येन धीमता ॥२०८॥
>
> *vyuṣitāśva-sutaś cāpi rājā viśvasahaḥ kila ||206||*
> *hiraṇyanābhaḥ kausalyo variṣṭhas tat-suto 'bhavat |*
> *pauṣpaṃjeś ca sa vai śiṣyaḥ smṛtaḥ prācyeṣu sāmasu ||207||*
> *śatāni saṃhitānāṃ tu pañca yo 'dhītavāṃs tataḥ |*
> *tasmād adhigato yogo yājñavalkyena dhīmatā ||208||*
>
> "The son of Vyuṣitāśva too was King Viśvasaha, it is said. His son was the excellent Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya, who is remembered as the disciple of Pauṣpañji in the Prācya Sāmans — he who studied five hundred saṃhitās. From him yoga was obtained by the wise Yājñavalkya." (The verse numbers are 206–208.)

That is: Yājñavalkya learned the science of yoga from Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya, the disciple of Pauṣpañji.

This view conflicts with the view of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa. It is understood that in these places the Purāṇic text is much corrupted. Let it be so.

Elsewhere, in the Vāyu and other Purāṇas also, in the passage that speaks of the Sāma branch, the relation of the exponents (*pravacanakāras*) of the Sāma branches is written as follows:

- **Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana**
  - **Jaimini**
    - **Sumantu**
      - **Sutvā**
        - **Sukarmā**
          - **Hiraṇyanābha Kauśalya** (a king, *narādhipa*), a Prācya Sāmaga
          - **Pauṣpañji**
            - **Laugākṣi**
            - **Kuthuma**, etc.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 106</div>

According to this lineage, Hiraṇyanābha belongs to the time of the Mahābhārata. According to the first genealogy, he is twelve generations earlier than Bṛhadbala, who belonged to the time of the Mahābhārata. What is found to be true is difficult to determine. If one trusts the first view, it is possible that there were two Yājñavalkyas: one the Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, and the other a much earlier Yājñavalkya, disciple of Jaimini and teacher of Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya. But the Purāṇic text itself is more likely corrupt, and Hiraṇyanābha and Kausalya may have been two persons; in the same way there may have been only one Yājñavalkya. Or the reigns of the twelve Kosala kings before Bṛhadbala may have been very short. Or there may have been several persons named Jaimini; among them the first Jaimini's teacher may have been not Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa but someone earlier, bearing another Vyāsa's name. According to the Skānda Purāṇa, Nāgara-khaṇḍa (5-6), a certain Yājñavalkya used to perform the Udgātṛ's work in the sacrifice of Triśaṅku, king of the Solar dynasty.

#### The Teacher of Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya {.lv2}

It is known that Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya had two teachers. One of them was the famous Carakācārya Vaiśampāyana; the Purāṇas say that he quarrelled with this teacher. The name of his second teacher is known from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (14-9-3-15 to 20) to be Uddālaka Āruṇi. In the 12th chapter of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skānda Purāṇa there is an account concerning Yājñavalkya; according to it, Yājñavalkya's teacher was Śākalya, a tiger among Brāhmaṇas, born in the Bhārgava lineage. That Śākalya lived in Vardhamānapura and was the *purohita* of King Supriya of the Solar dynasty.

#### Yājñavalkya — a long-lived Brāhmaṇa {.lv2}

When, in the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, the famous Rākṣasa Maya, who had survived for another reason, built a beautiful assembly-hall for Mahārāja Yudhiṣṭhira, many sages and groups of kings came to the city of Indraprastha at the time of the festival of its entry. Among them was Yājñavalkya. The Sabhā-parvan of the Mahābhārata, chapter 4, writes thus:

> तित्तिरिर्याज्ञवल्क्यश्च ससुतो रोमहर्षणः ॥१८॥
>
> *tittirir yājñavalkyaś ca sasuto romaharṣaṇaḥ ||18||*
>
> "Tittiri, Yājñavalkya, and Romaharṣaṇa with his son …"

Later, at the time of Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice, when the sage Vyāsa had the officiating priests summoned, the names of the disciples are given in the 36th chapter of the Sabhā-parvan of the Mahābhārata thus:

> ततो द्वैपायनो राजन्नृत्विजः समुपानयत् ॥३३॥
> स्वयं ब्रह्मत्वमकरोत्तस्य सत्यवतीसुतः ।
> धनंजयानामृषभः सुसामा सामगोऽभवत् ॥३४॥
> याज्ञवल्क्यो बभूवाथ ब्रह्मिष्ठोऽध्वर्युसत्तमः ।
> पैलो होता वसोः पुत्रो धौम्येन सहितोऽभवत् ॥३५॥
>
> *tato dvaipāyano rājann ṛtvijaḥ samupānayat ||33||*
> *svayaṃ brahmatvam akarot tasya satyavatī-sutaḥ |*
> *dhanaṃjayānām ṛṣabhaḥ susāmā sāma-go 'bhavat ||34||*
> *yājñavalkyo babhūvātha brahmiṣṭho 'dhvaryu-sattamaḥ |*
> *pailo hotā vasoḥ putro dhaumyena sahito 'bhavat ||35||*
>
> "Then, O king, Dvaipāyana brought the priests. Satyavatī's son himself took the Brahmā-office there. Susāman, the best of the Dhanañjayas, became the Sāma-singer. Then Yājñavalkya, most devoted to Brahman, the best of Adhvaryus, [officiated]; Paila, son of Vasu, became the Hotṛ, together with Dhaumya." (Line 2 is printed *brahmatvam akarotsya*; the form *akarot tasya* is read.)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 107</div>

That is: at that Rājasūya sacrifice the sage Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, was himself the Brahmā-priest. Of the disciples who came with him, Susāman served as Udgātṛ, Yājñavalkya as Adhvaryu, and Paila as Hotṛ at the sacrifice.

At the end of this Rājasūya, at the time of the concluding avabhṛtha bath, the Sabhā-parvan (chapter 72) describes the honouring of the officiating priests, Yājñavalkya and others:

> याज्ञवल्क्यं च कपिलं कपालं (कालापं?) कौशिकं तथा ।
> सर्वांश्च ऋत्विक्प्रवरान् पूजयामास सत्कृतान् ॥६॥
>
> *yājñavalkyaṃ ca kapilaṃ kapālaṃ (kālāpaṃ?) kauśikaṃ tathā |*
> *sarvāṃś ca ṛtvik-pravarān pūjayām āsa satkṛtān ||6||*
>
> "Yājñavalkya, and Kapila, Kapāla (or Kālāpa?), and Kauśika likewise — he honoured all the chief priests, having shown them hospitality." (The query after *kapālaṃ* is in the print.)

In the Aśvamedha sacrifice later performed by Yudhiṣṭhira too it is described that Yājñavalkya came there:

> अयं पैलोऽथ कौन्तेय याज्ञवल्क्यस्तथैव च ॥३॥
>
> *ayaṃ pailo 'tha kaunteya yājñavalkyas tathaiva ca ||3||*
>
> "Here is Paila, O son of Kuntī, and Yājñavalkya likewise."

Later, when Yudhiṣṭhira and his brothers set out for their ascent to heaven, at the time of consecrating King Parīkṣit as king, many sages came there, and it is said that Dharmarāja had them all fed. The sage Yājñavalkya was one of them:

> द्वैपायनं नारदं च मार्कण्डेयं तपोधनम् ।
> भारद्वाजं याज्ञवल्क्यं हरिमुद्दिश्य यत्नवान् ॥१२॥
>
> *dvaipāyanaṃ nāradaṃ ca mārkaṇḍeyaṃ tapo-dhanam |*
> *bhāradvājaṃ yājñavalkyaṃ harim uddiśya yatnavān ||12||*
>
> "Dvaipāyana, Nārada, and Mārkaṇḍeya, rich in austerity, Bhāradvāja and Yājñavalkya — with effort, in the name of Hari."

After Dharmarāja, Parīkṣit ruled for 60 years, and Janamejaya and his son Śatānīka for 80 years. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa (4-21) says that this Śatānīka learned the Veda from Yājñavalkya:

> जनमेजयस्यापि शतानीको भविष्यति ॥३॥ योऽसौ याज्ञवल्क्याद्वेदमधीत्य कृपादस्त्राण्यवाप्य विषमविषयविरक्तचित्तवृत्तिश्च शौनकोपदेशादात्मज्ञानप्रवीणः परं निर्वाणमवाप्स्यति ॥४॥
>
> *janamejayasyāpi śatānīko bhaviṣyati ||3|| yo 'sau yājñavalkyād vedam adhītya kṛpād astrāṇy avāpya viṣama-viṣaya-virakta-citta-vṛttiś ca śaunakopadeśād ātma-jñāna-pravīṇaḥ paraṃ nirvāṇam avāpsyati ||4||*
>
> "Of Janamejaya, Śatānīka will be [the son]; he, having studied the Veda under Yājñavalkya and obtained weapons from Kṛpa, with a mind turned away from the harsh objects of the senses, and skilled in knowledge of the Self through Śaunaka's instruction, will attain supreme liberation."

The Mahābhārata states in one place that Yudhiṣṭhira's lifespan was 108 years. Before going to the forest Yudhiṣṭhira ruled for 23 years; at the time of the Rājasūya sacrifice Yājñavalkya is known to have been 40 years old. From there on, according to the evidence available to us, his years work out as follows:

| Period | Years |
|---|---|
| At the time of the Rājasūya sacrifice (Yājñavalkya's age) | 40 |
| After the Rājasūya, for those setting out for the forest | 10 |
| Forest-life and the year of concealment | 13 |
| Yudhiṣṭhira's reign | 36 |
| Parīkṣit's reign | 60 |
| The time of Janamejaya and Śatānīka | 80 |
| **Total** | **239** |

Yājñavalkya may have lived even longer than this.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 108</div>

#### A brief life-history of Yājñavalkya {.lv2}

Many matters concerning Yājñavalkya's life have been stated earlier. Here we mean to state one or two further matters. Yājñavalkya was a Brāhmaṇa of great splendour. For some reason he quarrelled with the sage Vaiśampāyana, who was both his teacher and his maternal uncle (see chapters 33–35 of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa); he vomited out the Yajurveda that he had received from him and gave it back; and Vaiśampāyana's disciples, taking the form of Tittiri birds, took up the Veda thus vomited. For that reason there is an ancient account that that Veda (the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda) came to be named the Taittirīya-saṃhitā. Afterwards Yājñavalkya practised austerity towards the Sun and, by the Sun's favour, obtained the Śukla Yajurveda. Because the Sun taught Yājñavalkya the Veda directly in the form of a *vājin* — that is, a horse — that Veda came to be named the Vājasaneya-saṃhitā. This Śukla Yajurveda Yājñavalkya taught to fifteen of his disciples, beginning with Jābāla. Those fifteen disciples became the originators of the branches of the Śukla Yajurveda; this will be explained later.

Yājñavalkya had two wives, named Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. Maitreyī was a *brahmavādinī* who knew well the truths of Vedānta. Kātyāyanī too was accomplished in all learning. Yājñavalkya had great friendship with Janaka, king of Videha, and often discussed Vedāntic questions with that king. He therefore probably lived many times in Mithilā, Janaka's capital. It is believed that he composed many works of Dharma-śāstra and Smṛtis. He is a supreme lord of yogins; there is the saying *yogīśvaraṃ yājñavalkyam* ("Yājñavalkya, the lord of yogins"). In the end he is known to have taken up the saṃnyāsa stage of life.

#### Works famous under Yājñavalkya's name {.lv2}

It can be said without doubt that Yājñavalkya is the exponent (*pravacanakāra*) of the Vājasaneya Brāhmaṇa and other such works. Besides these there are:

1. the *Yājñavalkya-śikṣā*;
2. the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*;
3. the *Yogi-yājñavalkya*.

These three works were composed by Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya himself; or one of his disciples or disciples' disciples may have composed them. About the eighth century the ācārya Viśvarūpa wrote a commentary on the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*. In his view Yājñavalkya himself wrote this Smṛti; and it is understood that this Smṛti is earlier than the Kauṭilya Arthaśāstra, and that the same person who composed this Smṛti composed the Yoga-śāstra. In the Yatidharma section of the Prāyaścitta chapter of the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 109</div>

> ज्ञेयमारण्यकमहं यदादित्यादवाप्तवान् ।
> योगशास्त्रं च मत्प्रोक्तं ज्ञेयं योगमभीप्सता ॥१००॥
>
> *jñeyam āraṇyakam ahaṃ yad ādityād avāptavān |*
> *yogaśāstraṃ ca mat-proktaṃ jñeyaṃ yogam abhīpsatā ||100||*
>
> "The Āraṇyaka that I obtained from the Sun is to be known; and the Yoga-śāstra declared by me is to be known by one who desires yoga."

That is: those who wish to know the subject of yoga may read and understand the Yoga-śāstra composed by me. In the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* he is described as *yogīśvara* (1-1) and, in other places (1-2 and 3-324), as *yogīndra*. The work *Yogi-yājñavalkya* has two parts. One part is in print; the second part does not appear to have been printed. Devaṇabhaṭṭa [Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa] cites many passages of the *Yogi-yājñavalkya* as authority in his own works, such as the *Smṛti-candrikā*. The *Yājñavalkya-śikṣā* too has two parts. This work has been printed in this way.

#### Yājñavalkya and King Janaka {.lv2}

In the 315th chapter of the Śānti-parvan of the Mahābhārata (chapter 315, and the chapters after it): when Bhīṣma, lying on his bed of arrows, begins to relate to Yudhiṣṭhira the dialogue of King Janaka and Yājñavalkya:

> याज्ञवल्क्यमृषी दैवरातिर्महायशाः ।
> पप्रच्छ जनको राजा प्रश्नं प्रश्नविदां वरः ॥४॥
>
> *yājñavalkyam ṛṣī [sic] daivarātir mahāyaśāḥ |*
> *papraccha janako rājā praśnaṃ praśna-vidāṃ varaḥ ||4||*
>
> "King Janaka, the very famous, best of those who know how to question, asked a question of the sage Yājñavalkya, Daivarāti."

Here, instead of *daivarāti* one ought to have *daivarātiṃ*, it seems; for this epithet applies to Yājñavalkya himself. Since he was Devarāta's son, there is a possibility that Yājñavalkya is called *Daivarāti*. As said before, in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa the name of Yājñavalkya's father is Devarāta. So there may be a slip in this verse.

After this, Bhīṣma, informing us of the dialogue of Janaka and Yājñavalkya, narrates incidentally in chapter 323 the story of Yājñavalkya: the manner in which he received the Veda from the Sun, and the manner in which the fifteen branches of the Śukla Yajurveda were propagated by his disciples. Yājñavalkya says to King Janaka: "O great king, I myself held the purohita's office at your father's sacrifice and brought it to completion with all its limbs. At that time Sumantu, Paila and Jaimini were my helpers in the sacrificial work" — and so on; and his dialogue with the Gandharva king Viśvāvasu on Vedāntic questions is also related. Hearing these teachings, King Janaka was pleased, gave the sage Yājñavalkya and other Brāhmaṇas much wealth — gold, jewels and many other objects — and cows, put the burden of the Videha kingdom on his son, and himself became eager to accept saṃnyāsa.

#### The fifteen Vājasaneya branches {.lv1}

That Yājñavalkya's fifteen disciples were the originators of fifteen branches of the Śukla Yajurveda has been shown earlier. These originators of branches were all called Vājasaneyas. In this matter the names of Yājñavalkya's disciples are described in chapter 61 of the Vāyu Purāṇa as follows:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 110</div>

> याज्ञवल्क्यस्य शिष्यास्ते कण्ववैधेयशालिनः ॥२४॥
> मध्यन्दिनश्च शापेयो विदिग्धश्चाप्य उद्दलः ।
> ताम्रायणश्च वात्स्यश्च तथा गालवशैशिरी ॥२५॥
> आटवी च तथा पर्णी वीरणी सपरायणः ।
> इत्येते वाजिनः प्रोक्ता दश पञ्च च संस्मृताः ॥२६॥
>
> *yājñavalkyasya śiṣyās te kaṇva-vaidheya-śālinaḥ ||24||*
> *madhyandinaś ca śāpeyo vidigdhaś cāpya uddalaḥ |*
> *tāmrāyaṇaś ca vātsyaś ca tathā gālava-śaiśirī ||25||*
> *āṭavī ca tathā parṇī vīraṇī saparāyaṇaḥ |*
> *ity ete vājinaḥ proktā daśa pañca ca saṃsmṛtāḥ ||26||*
>
> "These were Yājñavalkya's disciples: Kaṇva and Vaidheya, Śālin; Madhyandina, Śāpeya, Vidigdha and Uddala; Tāmrāyaṇa and Vātsya, likewise Gālava and Śaiśirī; Āṭavī, Parṇī, Vīraṇī, Saparāyaṇa. These are declared to be the Vājins, remembered as fifteen."

In the same matter, in chapter 35 of the Pūrvabhāga of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:

> याज्ञवल्क्यस्य शिष्यास्ते कण्वो बौधेय एव च ।
> माध्यन्दिनस्तु सापत्यो वैधेयश्चाद्ध बौद्धकौ ॥२८॥
> तापनीयाश्च वत्साश्च तथा जाबालकेवलौ ।
> आवटी च तथा पुण्ड्रो वैणोयः सपराशरः ॥२९॥
> इत्येते वाजिनः प्रोक्ता दश पञ्च च सत्तमाः ।
>
> *yājñavalkyasya śiṣyās te kaṇvo baudheya eva ca |*
> *mādhyandinas tu sāpatyo vaidheyaś cāddha bauddhakau ||28||*
> *tāpanīyāś ca vatsāś ca tathā jābāla-kevalau |*
> *āvaṭī ca tathā puṇḍro vaiṇoyaḥ saparāśaraḥ ||29||*
> *ity ete vājinaḥ proktā daśa pañca ca sattamāḥ |*
>
> "These were Yājñavalkya's disciples: Kaṇva and Baudheya; Mādhyandina, Sāpatya, Vaidheya, and Addha and Bauddhaka; the Tāpanīyas and Vatsas, likewise Jābāla and Kevala; Āvaṭī, Puṇḍra, Vaiṇoya, with Parāśara. These are declared to be the Vājins, fifteen, the best."

In one variant of the *Caraṇa-vyūha* as well it reads thus:

> वाजसनेया नाम पञ्चदशभेदा भवन्ति —
> जाबालाः बौधायनाः काण्वाः माध्यन्दिनाः शाफेयाः तापनीयाः कपोलाः पौण्डरवत्साः आवटिकाः परमावटिकाः पाराशराः वैणीयाः वैधेयाः अद्धाः बौधेयाश्चेति ।
>
> *vājasaneyā nāma pañcadaśa-bhedā bhavanti —*
> *jābālāḥ baudhāyanāḥ kāṇvāḥ mādhyandināḥ śāpheyāḥ tāpanīyāḥ kapolāḥ pauṇḍaravatsāḥ āvaṭikāḥ paramāvaṭikāḥ pārāśarāḥ vaiṇīyāḥ vaidheyāḥ addhāḥ baudheyāś ceti |*
>
> "The Vājasaneyas have fifteen divisions: Jābālas, Baudhāyanas, Kāṇvas, Mādhyandinas, Śāpeyas, Tāpanīyas, Kapolas, Pauṇḍravatsas, Āvaṭikas, Paramāvaṭikas, Pārāśaras, Vaiṇīyas, Vaidheyas, Addhas and Baudheyas."

In another variant of the same *Caraṇa-vyūha*:

> काण्वाः माध्यन्दिनाः शाबीयाः तापायनीयाः कापालाः पौण्डरवत्साः आवटिकाः परमावटिकाः पाराशर्याः बौधेया नैनेयाः गालवाः ओधेयाः बैजवाः कात्यायनीयाश्चेति ।
>
> *kāṇvāḥ mādhyandināḥ śābīyāḥ tāpāyanīyāḥ kāpālāḥ pauṇḍaravatsāḥ āvaṭikāḥ paramāvaṭikāḥ pārāśaryāḥ baudheyā naineyāḥ gālavāḥ odheyāḥ baijavāḥ kātyāyanīyāś ceti |*
>
> "Kāṇvas, Mādhyandinas, Śābīyas, Tāpāyanīyas, Kāpālas, Pauṇḍravatsas, Āvaṭikas, Paramāvaṭikas, Pārāśaryas, Baudheyas, Naineyas, Gālavas, Odheyas, Baijavas and Kātyāyanīyas."

Sāyaṇācārya too, in the bhūmikā of his bhāṣya on the Kāṇva-saṃhitā printed by Chowkhamba, cites this same reading. But the manuscript text found in the libraries of Lahore and Madras reads as follows:

> जाबालाः गौधेयाः काण्वाः माध्यन्दिनाः श्यामाः श्यामायनीयाः गालवाः पिङ्गलाः वत्साः आवटिकाः परमावटिकाः पाराशर्याः वैणेयाः वैधेयाः गालवाः ।
>
> *jābālāḥ gaudheyāḥ kāṇvāḥ mādhyandināḥ śyāmāḥ śyāmāyanīyāḥ gālavāḥ piṅgalāḥ vatsāḥ āvaṭikāḥ paramāvaṭikāḥ pārāśaryāḥ vaiṇeyāḥ vaidheyāḥ gālavāḥ |*
>
> "Jābālas, Gaudheyas, Kāṇvas, Mādhyandinas, Śyāmas, Śyāmāyanīyas, Gālavas, Piṅgalas, Vatsas, Āvaṭikas, Paramāvaṭikas, Pārāśaryas, Vaiṇeyas, Vaidheyas, Gālavas." (*Gālavāḥ* occurs twice in the print.)

The reading of the book called *Pratijñā-pariśiṣṭa* also deserves consideration:

> जाबालाः बौधेयाः काण्वाः माध्यन्दिनाः शापेयाः तापायनीयाः कापोलाः पौण्ड्रवत्साः आवटिकाः परमावटिकाः पराशराः वैनतेयाः बौधेयाः कौन्तेयाः बैजवापाश्चेति ।
>
> *jābālāḥ baudheyāḥ kāṇvāḥ mādhyandināḥ śāpeyāḥ tāpāyanīyāḥ kāpolāḥ pauṇḍravatsāḥ āvaṭikāḥ paramāvaṭikāḥ parāśarāḥ vainateyāḥ baudheyāḥ kaunteyāḥ baijavāpāś ceti |*
>
> "Jābālas, Baudheyas, Kāṇvas, Mādhyandinas, Śāpeyas, Tāpāyanīyas, Kāpolas, Pauṇḍravatsas, Āvaṭikas, Paramāvaṭikas, Parāśaras, Vainateyas, Baudheyas, Kaunteyas and Baijavāpas."

Mahīdhara writes in the opening of his Yajurveda-bhāṣya thus:

> जाबालबौधेयकाण्वमाध्यन्दिनादिभ्यः पञ्चदशशिष्येभ्यः ।
>
> *jābāla-baudheya-kāṇva-mādhyandinādibhyaḥ pañcadaśa-śiṣyebhyaḥ |*
>
> "To the fifteen disciples, Jābāla, Baudheya, Kāṇva, Mādhyandina and the rest …" (the quotation continues on the next page.)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 111</div>

In all, 25 names of branch-originators of the Śukla Yajurveda are found in these places. Of these, the 10 names in excess [of fifteen] may be corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of some of these 25 names; that is, they may have arisen through the carelessness or error of copyists. The reading of the *Pratijñā-pariśiṣṭa* may in general be correct; but in the place of the number 14, *Kaunteyāḥ*, one should read *Odheyāḥ* or *Kātyāyanīyāḥ*. Now, so far as is known, the matters concerning the fifteen branches of the Śukla Yajurveda will be examined here.

#### 1. Jābālāḥ {.lv2}

Our conjecture is that Mahāśāla Satyakāma Jābāla, the well-known ācārya of the *Jābāla-upaniṣad*, was the exponent of this branch. He was a disciple of Yājñavalkya and a contemporary of King Janaka. According to the Sabhā-parvan of the Mahābhārata (7-55) a certain Jābāli belonged to the family of Viśvāmitra —

<div class="pgmark">original p. 112</div>

— and was probably also the founder of a gotra. According to the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skānda Purāṇa (112-24) those of the Jābāla gotra lived in the town named Nagara. In the Matsya Purāṇa also (198-4) Jābālas are called Kauśikas. The text of this matter is not present in the Vāyu and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas. References concerning Jābāla are found in the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (3-7-2).

At the present time, apart from the *Jābāla-upaniṣad*, no other work of this branch is known to us, and none is found in any library.

One reference concerning the Jābāla-śruti is found in the work *Bālakrīḍā*, in the 2nd part, at pp. 94, 95. Although the *Bṛhaj-jābāla-upaniṣad* is a recent work, there are many proofs of the antiquity of the *Jābāla-upaniṣad*.

Śaṅkarācārya has quoted this Upaniṣad in his Vedānta-sūtra-bhāṣya (3-4-20); there is also a statement concerning Jābāla in Śaṅkara's Brahma-sūtra-bhāṣya (3-3-37). A statement of the Jābāla-śruti is quoted on page 112 of the work *Madana-pārijāta*. In the Maskarī-bhāṣya on the Gautama-dharma-sūtra, at pp. 28, 61, 66, 85, 86 and 247, there are statements concerning the Jābāla-śruti. In that same work, at pp. 267 and 389, the Jābāla-gṛhya-sūtra, belonging to this branch, is mentioned. In the pariśiṣṭas composed by the sage Kātyāyana the Hautra-sūtra of this branch has become famous. A bhāṣya on it by Tarka-upādhyāya is also available. In the 2nd adhyāya, 8th khaṇḍa of that bhāṣya:

> नववतीश्चि कीर्षेत्-इति जाबालाः ।
>
> *navavatīś ci kīrṣet iti jābālāḥ |*
>
> "… so the Jābālas [say]."

That is: here the Jābālas hold that other ṛks should be gathered. Of those fourteen ṛks only the first is given, as an example. Tarka-upādhyāya gives in his bhāṣya the text of those ṛks in full. Some of them are found in the Ṛgveda and some in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa. Since only the *pratīka* (the opening words) of the mantras is given in the Hautra-sūtra, it is understood that those mantras may be in the Jābāla-saṃhitā. The following evidence concerning the Jābāla-śruti is quoted by the sthapati Gārgya in his *Pāraskara-gṛhya-paddhati*:

> दक्षिणपूर्वद्वारे द्व्यरत्निके जाबालश्रुतेरेतदुपलब्धम् ।
>
> *dakṣiṇa-pūrva-dvāre dvyaratnike jābāla-śruter etad upalabdham |*
>
> "At the south-eastern door, of two cubits — this is obtained from the Jābāla-śruti."

#### 2. Baudheyāḥ {.lv2}

In describing the branches of the Bāṣkala of the Ṛgveda, a few matters were said earlier concerning Baudhya, son of Bodhana of the Āṅgirasa gotra. That Baudhya, connected with the Ṛgveda, was the originator of that branch. The son of another Bodhana, of a different gotra, is called Baudhi. The word *Baudheya* arises from *Buddha* or *Bodha*. But it cannot be said definitely with which gotra the originator of this branch was connected.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 113</div>

At King Janamejaya's snake-sacrifice there was an officiating priest named Bodhipiṅgala. Since he did the Adhvaryu's work, he must have belonged to the Yajurveda. In chapter 48 of the Ādi-parvan it is written thus:

> ब्रह्माभवच्छार्ङ्गरवोऽध्वर्युर्बोधिपिङ्गलः ॥६॥
>
> *brahmābhavac chārṅgaravo 'dhvaryur bodhipiṅgalaḥ ||6||*
>
> "Śārṅgarava was the Brahmā-priest; Bodhipiṅgala the Adhvaryu."

That is: at this sacrifice one named Śārṅgarava was the Brahmā-priest and one named Bodhipiṅgala was also the Adhvaryu. It is not clear that these Bodhipiṅgalas had any connection with the Baudheyas.

In some manuscript copies of the *Caraṇa-vyūha* work, where *Baudheya* stands, the reading *Baudhāyana* is also found; and although the connection of the Baudhāyana-śrauta-sūtra is in general with the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of both the Mādhyandina and Kāṇva branches, it is closer to the Kāṇva Śatapatha. This matter is discussed at pp. 94–101 of the introduction to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the Kāṇva branch published by Dr. Caland. From this it appears that *Baudheya* and *Baudhāyana* may have been brothers; or that one person had two different names. But since there is not much evidence in this matter, nothing can be said with certainty.

#### 3. Kāṇvāḥ {.lv2}

Of the Kāṇva branch only the Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇas are found. The scholar named Weber was the first to publish this Saṃhitā in print, in Sanskrit, in 1852. After that, in 1915, at the Ānandāśrama, an edition revised (*parishkṛta*) by Brāhmaṇas of the Kāṇva branch was printed. This edition, having been well critically edited, deserves acceptance. Besides, in Germany the Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇas of this branch have been printed in carefully edited form. An edition of the Kāṇva-saṃhitā was also printed in Grantha script at Kumbhakoṇam.

The Kāṇva-saṃhitā has 40 adhyāyas, 328 anuvākas and 2086 mantras. Their details are given below.

##### The founders of the Kāṇva branch {.lv3}

The disciples of Kaṇva are called Kāṇvas. This Kāṇva branch was at first current among Kaṇva's disciples, that is, among the Kāṇvas. The sage Kaṇva has a gotra; and yet it is known that there were many sages of the name Kaṇva. Among sages of this name the principal ones are: Kaṇva Nārṣada (Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa 2-126), Kaṇva Śrāyasa (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5-4-7-5, Kāṇva Saṃhitā 21-8, Maitrāyaṇīya Saṃhitā 3-3-9), Kaṇva Sauśravasa (Kāṇva Saṃhitā 13-12), Kaṇva Ghaura (Ṛgveda-saṃhitā 1-36 to 43) and others. It is known that the Kaṇva who lived in the time of Mahārāja Duṣyanta belonged to the Kaśyapa gotra. In his hermitage Śakuntalā lived. The sage Kaṇva described in Kālidāsa's play *Śākuntalā* is this same person. He had performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice for King Bharata. In the Ādi-parvan (69-48) it is said *yājayām āsa taṃ kaṇvaḥ* ("Kaṇva made him sacrifice").

In the first chapter of the Śānti-parvan of the Mahābhārata there is a description that the sages Dvaipāyana, Nārada, Devala, Devasthāna and Kaṇva, with their disciples, after the Bhārata war, went to console Yudhiṣṭhira. Again, in the 344th chapter of the Śānti-parvan it is stated that there was a king named Upacarivasu, a disciple of Bṛhaspati, called after the son of Aṅgiras, Citraśikhaṇḍī; that he performed a great Aśvamedha sacrifice; and that among the 16 officiating priests of that sacrifice there was a sage named Kaṇva. The real names of these many Kaṇvas are not known to us. In the Mausala-parvan too (2-4) the name of a Kaṇva is indicated; it is said that this Kaṇva, who was with Viśvāmitra and Nārada, cursed that the Yādava clan would perish.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 115</div>

It is more probable that Kaṇva and his disciples mentioned at the beginning of the Śānti-parvan were connected with this Kāṇva branch. The Kaṇvas belonged to the Āṅgirasa gotra. In chapter 32 of the Harivaṃśa it is written thus:

> एते ह्यङ्गिरसः पक्षं संश्रिताः कण्वमौद्गलाः ॥६८॥
>
> *ete hy aṅgirasaḥ pakṣaṃ saṃśritāḥ kaṇva-maudgalāḥ ||68||*
>
> "These, indeed, are attached to the Āṅgirasa side — Kaṇva and the Maudgalas." (The last word is printed *naudgalāḥ*; the sense suggests *maudgalāḥ*.)

Likewise in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (1-112) and the Vāyu Purāṇa (59-100), in these places too, the Kaṇvas are said to belong to the Āṅgirasa gotra.

##### Kaṇva's hermitage {.lv3}

According to the Ādi-parvan of the Mahābhārata (64-18) Kaṇva's hermitage was on the bank of the river Mālinī. This place lies in the Madhyadeśa of ancient times. In the Kāṇva-saṃhitā there is a reading:

> एष वः कुरवो राजैष पञ्चाला राजा ।
>
> *eṣa vaḥ kuravo rājaiṣa pañcālā rājā |*
>
> "This is your king, O Kurus; this is your king, O Pañcālas."

In the Mādhyandina-saṃhitā, in this same place, it is *eṣa vo 'mī rājā* ("this is your king, O these [people]"). In the Taittirīya and other saṃhitās, in the portion where this reading occurs, the names of other places are given. From this it is known that Kaṇva's hermitage was in the neighbourhood of the Kurus and Pāñcālas.

One *āgama* of Kaṇva is quoted in the Devapāla-bhāṣya (5-8) on the Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra. Some verses concerning Kaṇva are quoted in the Śrāddha section of the *Smṛti-candrikā* (pp. 67–68). Many authorities concerning Kaṇva and the Kāṇva-dharma-sūtra are found abundantly in the Maskarī-bhāṣya on the Gautama-dharma-sūtra. In the Āpastamba-dharma-sūtra two ācāryas named Kaṇva are mentioned.

##### The Kāṇva kings of India {.lv3}

To the west of the Śuṅga kingdom established by Puṣyamitra there was a kingdom named Magadha; that, for another reason, came into the hands of the Kāṇvas. These Kāṇva kings were Brāhmaṇas. In the Purāṇas they are called *Kāṇvāyanas*. The family of these Kāṇva kings too must have been Brāhmaṇas.

##### The connection of the Kāṇva branch with the Pāñcarātra-āgama {.lv3}

It is known that those of the Kāṇva branch had some special connection with the Pāñcarātra-āgama. In the first chapter (*paṭala*) of the Saṃhitā named *Jaya* of this āgama it says:

> काण्वीं शाखामधीयानावौपगायनकौशिकौ ।
> प्रपत्तिशास्त्रनिष्णातौ स्वनिष्ठानिष्ठितावुभौ ॥१०९॥
> तद्गोत्रसम्भवा एव कल्पान्तं पूजयन्तु माम् ।
> जयाख्येनाथ पाद्मेन तन्त्रेण सहितेन वै ॥१११॥
> अत्राधिकार उभयोस्तयोरेव कुलीनयोः ।
> शाण्डिल्यश्च भरद्वाजो मुनिर्मौञ्जायनस्तथा ॥११५॥
> इमाश्च पञ्चगोत्रस्थाः मुख्याः काण्वीमुपाश्रिताः ।
> श्रीपाञ्चरात्रतन्त्रीये सर्वेऽस्मिन् मम कर्मणि ॥११६॥
>
> *kāṇvīṃ śākhām adhīyānāv aupagāyana-kauśikau |*
> *prapatti-śāstra-niṣṇātau sva-niṣṭhā-niṣṭhitāv ubhau ||109||*
> *tad-gotra-sambhavā eva kalpāntaṃ pūjayantu mām |*
> *jayākhyenātha pādmena tantreṇa sahitena vai ||111||*
> *atrādhikāra ubhayos tayor eva kulīnayoḥ |*
> *śāṇḍilyaś ca bharadvājo munir mauñjāyanas tathā ||115||*
> *imāś ca pañca-gotra-sthāḥ mukhyāḥ kāṇvīm upāśritāḥ |*
> *śrī-pāñcarātra-tantrīye sarve 'smin mama karmaṇi ||116||*
>
> "The two, Aupagāyana and Kauśika, studying the Kāṇva branch, versed in the science of surrender (*prapatti*), each established in his own duty — let those born in their lineage worship me until the end of the aeon, together with the Pādma tantra called *Jaya*. In this matter the authority belongs to those two, the well-born; Śāṇḍilya, Bhāradvāja and the sage Mauñjāyana likewise: these five gotras, who are chiefly dependent on the Kāṇva [branch], [stand] in the Śrī-Pāñcarātra system, in all this my rite." (The verse numbers are given as printed: 109, 111, 115, 116.)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 116</div>

That is: those who follow the Pāñcarātra-āgama, and among them in particular those of the five gotras Aupagāyana, Kauśika, Śāṇḍilya, Bhāradvāja and Mauñjāyana, used to follow the Kāṇva branch in their rites. Many of their ācāryas also belonged to the Kāṇva branch.

#### 4. Mādhyandināḥ {.lv2}

Of the fifteen branches of the Śukla Yajurveda, this Mādhyandina branch alone is the most widely current of all the remaining branches. In Kashmir, Punjab, Rajputana, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madras, Bengal, Bihar and the United Provinces — generally in all places — the currency of this branch is the greater. In manuscript copies of the Saṃhitā it is generally called simply the Yajurveda or the Vājasaneya-saṃhitā.

It cannot yet be said who the sage Mādhyandina was or from which country. Those who study this branch say that this Saṃhitā contains in all 1975 mantras; this count is according to the division of mantras called *kaṇḍikā*. Besides, if the different mantras within the kaṇḍikās are counted separately, the number of mantras becomes larger. The number of these mantras is found at the end of the *Vāsiṣṭha-śikṣā*; it is quoted and written here:

> ऐकीकृत्य ऋचः सर्वा मुनिषड्वेदभूमिताः ।
> अब्धिरामाथ वा ज्ञेया वसिष्ठेन च धीमता ॥१॥
> एवं सर्वाणि यजूंषि रामाश्विवसुयुग्मकाः ।
> अथ वा पञ्चभिर्न्यूनाः संहितायां विभागतः ॥२॥
>
> *aikīkṛtya ṛcaḥ sarvā muni-ṣaḍ-veda-bhūmitāḥ |*
> *abdhi-rāmātha vā jñeyā vasiṣṭhena ca dhīmatā ||1||*
> *evaṃ sarvāṇi yajūṃṣi rāmāśvi-vasu-yugmakāḥ |*
> *atha vā pañcabhir nyūnāḥ saṃhitāyāṃ vibhāgataḥ ||2||*
>
> "All the ṛks taken together are measured by *muni, ṣaṭ, veda, bhū* [7, 6, 4, 1 — read in reverse order, 1467]; or, as known to the wise Vasiṣṭha, by *abdhi, rāma* [4, 3 — the source does not explain this alternative]. So also all the yajus-mantras are *rāma, aśvi, vasu, yugmaka* [3, 2, 8, 2 — read in reverse, 2823]; or less by five, according to the division within the Saṃhitā."

In this Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā there are in all 1467 ṛks. The remainder are yajus-mantras; their number is not clear in the print. According to this the total number of mantras becomes 2823 or 2818.

That is the count of ṛks and yajus-mantras. Now the number of anuvākas is stated according to the *Anuvāka-sūtra* adhyāya. The verses at the end of the *Anuvāka-sūtra* adhyāya are written below:

> दशाध्यायेषु समाख्यातानुवाकाः सर्वसंख्यया ।
> शतं दशानुवाकाश्च नवान्ये च मनीषिभिः ॥१॥
> सप्तषष्टिश्चितौ ज्ञेयाः सौत्रामण्यां द्वाविंशतिस्तथा ।
> अश्वे एकोनपञ्चाशत्पञ्चत्रिंशत्खिले स्मृताः ॥२॥
> शुक्रियेषु तु विज्ञेया एकादश मनीषिभिः ।
> ऐकीकृत्य समाख्यातं त्रिशतं त्र्यधिकं मतम् ॥३॥
>
> *daśādhyāyeṣu samākhyātānuvākāḥ sarva-saṃkhyayā |*
> *śataṃ daśānuvākāś ca navānye ca manīṣibhiḥ ||1||*
> *saptaṣaṣṭiś citau jñeyāḥ sautrāmaṇyāṃ dvāviṃśatis tathā |*
> *aśve ekona-pañcāśat pañcatriṃśat khile smṛtāḥ ||2||*
> *śukriyeṣu tu vijñeyā ekādaśa manīṣibhiḥ |*
> *aikīkṛtya samākhyātaṃ triśataṃ tryadhikaṃ mataṃ ||3||*
>
> "In the first ten adhyāyas the anuvākas are declared, by total number, one hundred and nineteen (*śataṃ daśa nava*), by the wise. In the *citi* [the Agnicayana section] sixty-seven are to be known; in the Sautrāmaṇī twenty-two; in the Aśvamedha forty-nine; in the *khila* thirty-five are remembered. In the Śukriya [portion] eleven are to be known by the wise. Taken together, three hundred and three (*triśataṃ tryadhikam*) is the accepted [number]."

That is: in the first 10 adhyāyas there are 119 anuvākas. In adhyāyas 11–18, which describe the Agnicayana, there are 67 anuvākas. In adhyāyas 19–21, which deal with the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, 22 anuvākas. In adhyāyas 22–35, relating to the Aśvamedha sacrifice, 49 anuvākas. In adhyāyas 26–35, which are called *khila* or *pariśiṣṭa* adhyāyas, 35 anuvākas. In the last 5 adhyāyas, called *Śukriya* (36–40), 11 anuvākas. Adding all together: 119 + 67 + 22 + 49 + 35 + 11 = 303 anuvākas.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 117</div>
