That is: the Aitareya Brahmana and Aranyaka show extensive similarity in both language and word-usage, confirming the two texts' close mutual connection.

##### 2. The Sankhyayana (or Kaushitaki) Aranyaka {.lv3}

The Sankhyayana Aranyaka has 15 chapters in total, divided into sections (khandas) as follows:

| Adhyaya | Khanda | Adhyaya | Khanda | Adhyaya | Khanda |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 6 | 20 | 11 | 8 |
| 2 | 18 | 7 | 23 | 12 | 8 |
| 3 | 7 | 8 | 11 | 13 | 1 |
| 4 | 15 | 9 | 8 | 14 | 2 |
| 5 | 8 | 10 | 8 | 15 | 1 |

This Aranyaka resembles the Aitareya Aranyaka in every respect — its description of the Mahavrata and related rites matches closely. Chapters 1–2 cover the material of the Aitareya Aranyaka's 1st and 5th Aranyakas, and chapters 7–8 that of its 3rd Aranyaka. Chapters 3–4 are the well-known **Kaushitaki Upanishad** — since some manuscript copies lack these Upanishad chapters entirely, there is reasonable suspicion that this portion may have been appended to the Aranyaka at some later date.

At the end of this Aranyaka appears a closing statement:

> गुणाख्याच्छांखायनादस्माभिरधीतं ॥ १५ ॥
>
> *guṇākhyāc chāṃkhāyanād asmābhir adhītaṃ ||*
>
> "This has been learned by us from Gunakhya-Sankhyayana."

The word "asmābhiḥ" ("by us") here may refer to the many disciples of Gunakhya-Sankhyayana; alternatively, Sankhyayana himself may have compiled 14 chapters, and his disciples the last chapter.

## Chapter Ten — The Rishis of the Rigveda

<div class="pgmark">original p. 176</div>

Before reciting a sukta's mantra, one must first state that sukta's rishi, meter (chandas), and deity — a tradition inherited from ancient times. It is said that reciting a mantra without knowing these three yields no benefit and constitutes a wrongdoing. Sayanacharya states, in the introduction to his commentary:

> अविदित्वा ऋषिं छन्दो दैवतं योगमेव च । योऽध्यापयेज्जपेद्वापि पापीयाज्जायते तु सः ॥
>
> *aviditvā ṛṣiṃ chando daivataṃ yogam eva ca | yo'dhyāpayej japed vāpi pāpīyāj jāyate tu saḥ ||*
>
> "Without knowing the rishi, the meter, the deity, and the [ritual] application, whoever teaches or recites [a mantra] becomes, indeed, a greater sinner."

What exactly are this "rishi," "deity," and "meter"? Katyayana, in the Sarvanukramani, defines them:

> यस्य वाक्यं स ऋषिः । या तेनोक्ता सा देवता । यदक्षरपरिमाणं तच्छन्दः । अक्षैस्स ऋषयो देवताश्छन्दोभिरसाधारणम् ॥
>
> *yasya vākyaṃ sa ṛṣiḥ | yā tenoktā sā devatā | yad-akṣara-parimāṇaṃ tac-chandaḥ | akṣais sa ṛṣayo devatāś chandobhir asādhāraṇam ||*
>
> "He whose utterance it is — he is the rishi. She who is addressed by it — she is the deity. Whatever the syllable-count is — that is its meter. [The correspondence of] rishis, deities, and meters, [determined] through syllables, is specific to each [mantra]."

That is: the mantra's composer is its rishi; the deity the mantra addresses is its deity; and the systematic arrangement of syllables is called meter. Rishis, seeking prosperity, pleased the deities through these metrically-structured utterances.

Saying the rishis "composed" the mantras is not, strictly, Vedic doctrine — rather, they are the mantras' "seers" (drashtaras): the mantras became manifest to them. As Sayana's commentary puts it:

> अतीन्द्रियस्य वेदस्य परमेश्वरानुग्रहेण प्रथमतो दर्शनात् ऋषित्वम् ।
>
> *atīndriyasya vedasya parameśvarānugraheṇa prathamato darśanāt ṛṣitvam |*
>
> "Rishihood consists in the first perception, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, of the Veda, which transcends the senses."

Mantras are not perceivable through the ordinary senses; whoever it was to whom these mantras first became manifest, by divine grace, is a rishi — so Sayana's commentary explains.

### The Rishis {.lv1}

"Rishi" means "one who knows" — derived from the root *ṛṣ* in the sense of knowledge ("*ṛṣa-jñāne*"). By that logic, any knowledgeable person could be called "rishi." But the word "rishi" [in the specific Vedic sense]

<div class="pgmark">original p. 177</div>

does not carry this generic sense of "anyone who knows anything." Only those who directly perceived the mantras themselves are counted as their rishis — this is the general view; "perceiving" here means the mantras became revealed to them. Anandatirtha's own Rig-bhashya states:

> यः पश्यति स्वयं वाक्यं स ऋषिस्तस्य कीर्तितः । (ऋग्भाष्य)
> यथा यः स्वयमध्ययनेन विनैव यद्वाक्यं पश्यति स तस्य वाक्यस्य ऋषिः प्रकीर्तितः । (ऋग्भाष्यटीका)
>
> *yaḥ paśyati svayaṃ vākyaṃ sa ṛṣis tasya kīrtitaḥ | (Ṛgbhāṣya)*
> *yathā yaḥ svayam adhyayanena vinaiva yad vākyaṃ paśyati sa tasya vākyasya ṛṣiḥ prakīrtitaḥ | (Ṛgbhāṣyaṭīkā)*
>
> "He who himself perceives an utterance — he is declared its rishi." (Rig-bhashya)
> "That is: whoever perceives a given utterance by himself, without prior study, is proclaimed the rishi of that utterance." (Rig-bhashya-tika)

Whoever, without prior study, perceives the mantras through divine grace alone is that mantra's rishi. Before reciting any Vedic mantra, we must state its rishi, deity, and meter — those named as rishis in the Anukramani and similar texts are likely those who first attained the mantras; examining the Puranic statements about the rishis makes this clear. That is: those named in the Anukramanika, or spoken of in yajnas as the mantras' "seers," were most likely the very first seers of those mantras.

> अर्वाक्तु द्वादशावृत्तेरधीत्याप्यृषिरेव सः । (आनन्दऋग्भाष्य)
> एवं यो द्वादशावृत्तेरर्वागधीत्यापि प्रतिपद्यते सोऽप्यृषिरेव ॥ (ऋग्भाष्यटीका)
>
> *arvāk tu dvādaśāvṛtter adhītyāpy ṛṣir eva saḥ | (Ānanda-ṛgbhāṣya)*
> *evaṃ yo dvādaśāvṛtter arvāg adhītyāpi pratipadyate so'py ṛṣir eva || (Ṛgbhāṣya-ṭīkā)*
>
> "Even having studied it fewer than twelve repetitions, he is a ṛṣi." "Thus he who, having studied it fewer than twelve times, still grasps it — he too is a ṛṣi."

Those who have studied the mantras and made them their own may also be counted as rishis; but they must have studied and mastered the mantra fewer than twelve times. Thus rishi-hood may apply not only to the first seers but to others too.

The matter of the rishis is described in some detail in the Vāyu, Brahmāṇḍa and Matsya Purāṇas. The verse numbers given here follow the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, but the readings of all three Purāṇas have been compared and as correct a reading as possible is given.

> ऋषीणां तप्यतामुग्रं तपः परमदुष्करम् ॥ ६७ ॥
> मन्त्राः प्रादुर्बभूवुर्हि पूर्वमन्वन्तरेष्विह ।
> असंतोषाद्भयाद्दुःखात्सुखाच्छोकाच्च पंचधा ॥ ६८ ॥
> ऋषीणां तपः कार्त्स्न्येन दर्शनेन यदृच्छया ।
>
> *ṛṣīṇāṃ tapyatām ugraṃ tapaḥ paramaduṣkaram || 67 ||*
> *mantrāḥ prādurbabhūvur hi pūrvamanvantareṣv iha |*
> *asaṃtoṣād bhayād duḥkhāt sukhāc chokāc ca paṃcadhā || 68 ||*
> *ṛṣīṇāṃ tapaḥ kārtsnyena darśanena yadṛcchayā |*
>
> "To the rishis practising fierce austerity, most difficult, the mantras became manifest here in the former Manvantaras — in five ways: from discontent, from fear, from sorrow, from joy and from grief …"

That is: in this and the earlier Manvantaras the rishis practised hard austerity — some with the aim of obtaining mantras, others for reasons such as discontent, fear, sorrow, joy and grief. As the fruit of their austerity the mantras became manifest to them. So, as said before, all who saw the mantras are rishis. The same view is in the Nirukta and the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 178</div>

The rishis of the first Mandala begin with Madhuchchandas and others; those who saw a hundred mantras are called "Shatarchina." The rishis of Mandalas 2–7 — Gritsamada, Vishvamitra, Vamadeva-Gautama, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha, Pavamanya, and others — are termed "Madhyama," while the 10th Mandala's rishis are called "Kshudrasukta" and "Mahasukta." The Ashvalayana Grihyasutra confirms this:

> अथ ऋषयः शतर्चिनो माध्यमा गृत्समदो विश्वामित्रो वामदेवोऽत्रिर्भरद्वाजो वसिष्ठः प्रगाथाः पावमान्यः क्षुद्रसूक्ता महासूक्ता इति ॥
>
> *atha ṛṣayaḥ śatarcino mādhyamā gṛtsamado viśvāmitro vāmadevo'trir bharadvājo vasiṣṭhaḥ pragāthāḥ pāvamānyaḥ kṣudrasūktā mahāsūktā iti ||*
>
> "Now, the rishis: Shatarchina, Madhyama, Gritsamada, Vishvamitra, Vamadeva, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha, the Pragathas, the Pavamanyas, the Kshudrasuktas, and the Mahasuktas — thus."

##### These Are the Rishi-Classifications {.lv3}

Among the rishis, there are said to be several classes — Maharshi, Rishi, Rishika, Rishiputra, and Shrutarshi. Harishchandra's commentary on the Charaka-sutra (sutra 1-7) states four kinds:

> मुनीनां चतुर्विधो भेदः । ऋषयः, ऋषिकाः, ऋषिपुत्राः महर्षयश्च ।
>
> *munīnāṃ caturvidho bhedaḥ | ṛṣayaḥ, ṛṣikāḥ, ṛṣiputrāḥ maharṣayaś ca |*
>
> "The division among sages (munis) is fourfold: Rishis, Rishikas, Rishiputras, and Maharshis."

According to Harishchandra, excluding Shrutarshi, there are only these four divisions.

> अतीतानागतानां च पंचधा ह्यार्षकं स्मृतम् । अतस्त्वृषीणां वक्ष्यामि तत्र ह्यार्षसमुद्भवम् ॥ ७० ॥ इत्येता ऋषिजातीस्ता नामभिः पंच वै शृणु ॥ १५ ॥
>
> *atītānāgatānāṃ ca paṃcadhā hy ārṣakaṃ smṛtam | atas tv ṛṣīṇāṃ vakṣyāmi tatra hy ārṣasamudbhavam || 70 || ityetā ṛṣijātīs tā nāmabhiḥ paṃca vai śṛṇu || 15 ||*
>
> "… thus the Ārṣa is remembered as fivefold. Therefore I shall tell of the rishis, of the origin of the Ārṣa there. Hear these five classes of rishis by their names."

##### 1. Maharshi = Ishvara (the Divine Ones) {.lv3}

> भृगुर्मरीचिरत्रिश्च ह्यंगिराः पुलहः कृतुः । मनुर्दक्षो वसिष्ठश्च पुलस्त्यश्चेति ते दश ॥ ९६ ॥ ब्रह्मणो मानसा ह्येते उद्यूताः स्वयमीश्वराः । परत्वेनर्षयो यस्मात् स्मृतास्तस्मान्महर्षयः ॥ ९७ ॥
>
> *bhṛgur marīcir atriś ca hy aṅgirāḥ pulahaḥ kratuḥ | manur dakṣo vasiṣṭhaś ca pulastyaś ceti te daśa || brahmaṇo mānasā hyete udyūtāḥ svayam īśvarāḥ | paratvena ṛṣayo yasmāt smṛtās tasmān maharṣayaḥ ||*
>
> "Bhrigu, Marichi, and Atri, and likewise Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Manu, Daksha, Vasishtha, and Pulastya — these are the ten. These are indeed mind-born of Brahma, ... lords themselves; since by supremacy they are remembered as rishis, therefore they are Maharshis."

Among the rishis, the first rank belongs to the Maharshis. Bhrigu, Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Manu, Daksha, Vasishtha, and Pulastya — these ten are the mind-born sons of Brahma, called "Ishvara" (divine lords). Being the foremost among all rishis, they are given the designation "Maharshi."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 179</div>

##### 2. Rishi {.lv3}

> ईश्वराणां सुता ह्येते ऋषयस्तान्निबोधत । काव्यो बृहस्पतिश्चैव कश्यपश्च्यवनस्तथा ॥ ९८ ॥ उतथ्यो वामदेवश्च अगस्त्यश्चौशिजस्तथा । कर्दमो विश्रवाश्च शक्तिर्वाखिल्यास्तथार्वतः ॥ ९९ ॥ इत्येते ऋषयः प्रोक्तास्तपसा चर्षितां गताः ।
>
> *īśvarāṇāṃ sutā hy ete ṛṣayas tān nibodhata | kāvyo bṛhaspatiś caiva kaśyapaś cyavanas tathā ॥ utathyo vāmadevaś ca agastyaś cauśijas tathā | kardamo viśravāś ca śaktir vākhilyās tathārvataḥ ॥ ityete ṛṣayaḥ proktās tapasā carṣitāṃ gatāḥ |*
>
> "Know these to be the sons of the Ishvaras [Maharshis] — the rishis: Kavya (Ushanas), and likewise Brihaspati, Kashyapa, and Chyavana; Utathya, Vamadeva, and Agastya... Kardama, Vishravas, Shakti, the Valakhilyas and Arvata — these are declared rishis, who attained excellence through toil/austerity."

That is: Ushana-Kavya, Brihaspati, Kashyapa, Chyavana, Utathya, Vamadeva, Agastya, Ushik, Kardama, Vishravas, Shakti, Valakhilya, and Arvata form the second class of rishis — sons of the Maharshis (Bhrigu and others), who attained the rank of "rishi" through austerity (tapas).

##### 3. Rishiputra — Rishika {.lv3}

> ऋषिपुत्रानृषीकांस्तु गर्भोत्पन्नान्निबोधत ॥ १०० ॥ वत्सरो नग्नहूश्चैव भरद्वाजस्तथैव च । ऋषिदीर्घतमाश्चैव बृहदुक्थः शरद्वतः ॥ १०१ ॥ वाजश्रवा सुवित्तश्च वश्याश्वश्च पराशरः । दधीचः शंशपाश्चैव राजा वैश्रवणस्तथा ॥ १०२ ॥ इत्येते ऋषिकाः प्रोक्तास्ते सत्यादृषितां गताः ।
>
> *ṛṣiputrān ṛṣīkāṃs tu garbhotpannān nibodhata ॥ vatsaro nagnahūś caiva bharadvājas tathaiva ca | ṛṣi-dīrghatamāś caiva bṛhaduktaḥ śaradvataḥ ॥ vājaśravā suvittaś ca vaśyāśvaś ca parāśaraḥ | dadhīcaḥ śaṃśapāś caiva rājā vaiśravaṇas tathā ॥ ityete ṛṣikāḥ proktās te satyād ṛṣitāṃ gatāḥ |*
>
> "Know that the Rishiputras, or Rishikas, are born of [ordinary] lineage. Vatsara, and likewise Nagnaha, and Bharadvaja; Rishi-Dirghatama, and likewise Brihaduktha, Sharadvata; Vajashrava, Suvitta, Vashyashva, and Parashara; Dadhicha, and likewise Shamshapa, King Vaishravana — these are declared the Rishikas, who, true to their own nature, attained rishihood."

That is: Vatsara, Nagnaha, Bharadvaja, Dirghatama, Brihaduktha, Sharadvata, Vajashrava, Suvitta, Vashyashva, Parashara, Dadhicha, Shamshapa, and Vaishravana are called "Rishika" — the legitimate (aurasa) sons of the [second-class] rishis.

A disputed point: where rishis are elsewhere classed into "five kinds," Rishiputra and Rishika are treated as distinct categories, whereas here they are counted as one and the same — such differences of opinion recur across the Puranas, and a description of the remaining two categories has not yet been located.

#### The Rishis of the Bhrigu Lineage — 1 {.lv2}

The Puranas state there are 19 rishis of the Bhrigu lineage, named as follows:

> एते मंत्रकृतः सर्वे कृत्स्नशस्तान्निबोधत । भृगुः काव्यः प्रचेताश्च दधीचो ह्याप्नवानपि ॥ १०४ ॥ और्वोऽथ जमदग्निश्च विदः सारस्वतस्तथा । आर्ष्टिषेणश्च वनश्च नीतहव्यः सुमेधसः ॥ १०५ ॥ वैन्यः पृथुर्दिवोदासो नाध्र्यश्वो गृत्सशौनकौ । एकोनविंशतिर्हैते भृगवो मन्त्रवादिनः ॥ १०६ ॥
>
> *ete maṃtrakṛtaḥ sarve kṛtsna-śastān nibodhata | bhṛguḥ kāvyaḥ pracetāś ca dadhīco hy āpnavān api ॥ aurvo 'tha jamadagniś ca vidaḥ sārasvatas tathā | ārṣṭiṣeṇaś ca vanaś ca nītahavyaḥ sumedhasaḥ ॥ vainyaḥ pṛthur divodāso nādhryaśvo gṛtsaśaunakau | ekonaviṃśatir haite bhṛgavo mantravādinaḥ ||*
>
> (A list of the Bhrigu-lineage rishi-composers: Bhrigu, Kavya, Pracheta, Dadhicha, [and others including] Jamadagni, Chyavana, Vitahavya, Sumedhas, Pṛthu Vainya, Divodasa, Vadhryashva, and Gritsa-Shaunaka — nineteen in total, all reciters of mantras.)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 180</div>

The mantra-seeing rishis of the Bhrigu lineage, numbered in the verse above:

| # | Name | # | Name | # | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bhrigu | 7 | Jamadagni | 13 | Sumedhas |
| 2 | Kavya (Ushanas=Shukra) | 8 | Vida | 14 | Vainya Prithu |
| 3 | Pracheta | 9 | Sarasvata | 15 | Divodasa |
| 4 | Dadhyaj (Atharvana) | 10 | Arshtishena | 16 | Vadhryashva |
| 5 | Apnavan | 11 | Chyavana | 17 | Gritsa(mada) |
| 6 | Aurva (Richika) | 12 | Vitahavya | 18 | Shaunaka |

The verse states "ekonaviṃśati" (nineteen), but this list gives only eighteen names — perhaps because "Vainya" and "Prithu" were meant to be counted separately, though Vedic texts treat "Vena's son Prithu" as a single figure, "Vainya Prithu." Some one name has evidently dropped out of this particular list.

The genealogical tree of these rishis varies across different Puranas. The Mahabharata's Adiparva (60–40) gives it thus:

**Bhrigu**
- **Kavi** (Shukra, teacher of the Daityas)
- **Chyavana**
  - **Aurva**
    - **Richika**
      - **Jamadagni**

The Mahabharata treats this lineage only this briefly before moving to other rishi-lineages. Other Puranas add that Chyavana had two sons by his wife Sukanya — Apnavan and Dadhyarcha; Apnavan's son Aurva lived in the Madhyadesha and held a rivalry with Kartavirya-Arjuna over territorial matters. Vitahavya was originally a Kshatriya who became a Brahmin through the teaching of a Bhrigu-lineage rishi; Gritsamada and Shaunaka were both born within his lineage.

##### The Close Connection Between the Bhrigu Lineage and the Atharvaveda {.lv3}

Among the Atharvaveda's many names is "Bhrigvangiro-veda" (the Veda of Bhrigu and Angiras) — reflecting the view that rishis of the Bhrigu and Angiras lineages are seers of most of that Veda's mantras. Among the Bhrigu-lineage rishis listed above, Bhrigu, Dadhyaj, and Shaunaka are clearly Atharvaveda-connected rishis; indeed, this same Shaunaka is the founder of the Atharvaveda's own Shaunaka shakha,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 181</div>

which should indeed be called Shaunaka's [tradition]. Many suktas of the Atharvaveda have Bhrigu, Gritsamada, and Shukra as their rishis; several are seen specifically by the rishi Shukra, and several more by Bhrigvangiras-lineage rishis — confirming why the Atharvaveda is called "Bhrigvangiro-veda."

##### The Angirasa-Lineage Rishis — 33 {.lv3}

1 Aṅgirāḥ · 2 Trita · 3 Bharadvāja Bāṣkali · 4 Ṛtavāk · 5 Garga · 6 Śini · 7 Saṃkṛti · 8 Guruvīta · 9 Māndhātā · 10 Ambarīṣa · 11 Yuvanāśva · 12 Purukutsa · 13 Trasadasyu · 14 Sadasyumān · 15 Āhārya · 16 Ajamīḍha · 17 Ṛṣabha · 18 Kapi · 19 Pṛṣadaśva · 20 Virūpa · 21 Kaṇva · 22 Mudgala · 23 Utathya · 24 Śaradvān · 25 Vājaśravā · 26 Ayāsya · 27 Suvitti · 28 Vāmadeva · 29 Asija · 30 Bṛhaduktha · 31 Dīrghatamā · 32 Kakṣīvān

These thirty-two, with one further, lost name, make the thirty-three rishis of the Angirasa lineage. Many names among these have become corrupted in transmission, and correcting them is not something the author attempts here. Angiras, the lineage's original progenitor, must belong to a very ancient period. This lineage includes Kshatriyas such as Ambarisha and Yuvanashva — "Nabhaga Ambarisha" is referenced at many points in the Mahabharata. This Angiras, independently and together with Bhrigu, is the rishi of many mantras of the Atharvaveda.

##### The Kashyapas — 6 {.lv3}

कश्यप, वत्सार, नैध्रुव, रैभ्य, असित, देवल — *(Kashyapa, Vatsara, Naidhruva, Raibhya, Asita, Devala)*. Six rishis of the Kashyapa lineage. Asita and Devala appear to have personal connections recorded in the Mahabharata.

##### The Atreyas — 6 {.lv3}

अत्रि, अर्चनाना, श्यावाश्व, गविष्ठिर, आविहोत्र, पूर्वातिथि — *(Atri, Archanana, Shyavashva, Gavishthira, Avihotra, Purvatithi)*. Some textual variants may exist here — the rishi Gavishthira may also carry the name "Andhigu"; Rigveda Mandala 1, Sukta 101's rishi is given as Andhigu, son of Gavishthira.

#### The Vasishthas — 8 [7 named] {.lv2}

वसिष्ठ, शक्ति, पराशर, इन्द्रप्रमति, भरद्वसु, मैत्रावरुणि, कुण्डिन — *(Vasishtha, Shakti, Parashara, Indrapramati, Bharadvasu, Maitravaruni, Kundina)*. Among the Vasishthas is the rishi Parashara — father of Krishna-Dvaipayana, i.e., Veda-Vyasa himself, who holds (per the Brahma-sutra and the Mahabharata) that all the Vedas are eternal,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 182</div>

as he writes. Many modern scholars have found themselves unable to reconcile the Vedas with this view of Krishna-Dvaipayana.

#### The Kaushikas (Vishvamitra) — 13 {.lv2}

विश्वामित्र, देवरात, उद्दल (बल), मधुच्छन्द, अघमर्षण, अष्टक, लोहित, कत, कील, देवश्रवा, रेणु, पूरण, धनंजय — *(Vishvamitra, Devarata, Uddala/Bala, Madhuchchanda, Aghamarshana, Ashtaka, Lohita, Kata, Kila, Devashrava, Renu, Purana, Dhananjaya)*.

These thirteen all belong to the Vishvamitra lineage; the Matsya Purana adds two more, Shishira and Shalankayana. Many rishis appear to have carried the name "Vishvamitra," and which one founded this lineage is undetermined. One Vishvamitra, however, is especially famous: originally named Vishvaratha, son of King Gadhi, he renounced his kingdom and wealth to perform austerities and become a Brahmarshi — during which he aided King Trishanku, took the name "Vishvamitra" upon attaining Brahmarshi status, tested King Harishchandra, and famously saved Shunashepa (whom Harishchandra was leading to be sacrificed as a human offering) by teaching him a life-saving mantra, afterward adopting him as his own son. The story of Shunashepa is well known from the Aitareya Brahmana and similar texts.

#### The Agastyas — 3 {.lv2}

अगस्त्य, दृढद्युम्न (दृढायु), इन्द्रबाहु (विध्माह) — *(Agastya, Dridhadyumna/Dridhayu, Indrabahu/Vidhmaha)*.

##### The Kshatriya Rishis — 2 {.lv3}

वैनस्वतमनु, पुरूरवा (इलराजा) — *(Vainasvata-Manu, Pururava/Ilaraja)*.

##### The Vaishya Rishis — 3 {.lv3}

भलन्दन, वत्स, संशील — *(Bhalandana, Vatsa, Sanshila)*. These three are held in especially high regard among the Vaishyas.

**In total, then, there are 92 principal rishis:**

| Lineage | Count |
|---|---|
| Bhrigu | 19 |
| Angirasa | 33 |
| Kashyapa | 6 |
| Atreya | 6 |
| Vasishtha | 7 |
| Kaushika | 13 |
| Agastya | 3 |
| Kshatriya | 2 |
| Vaishya | 3 |
| **Total** | **92** |

*(19 + 33 + 6 + 6 + 7 + 13 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 92.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 183</div>

According to the Brahmanda Purana the number of rishis in these lineages comes to 90; according to the Matsya Purana, 92. Most probably the reading of the Brahmanda Purana is corrupt.

### These Rishis Are Not Always the First Seers {.lv1}

It was noted at this chapter's outset that the rishis named for a given mantra are not necessarily its very first seers. Supporting evidence:

**1.** A shared account appears across the Taittiriya Samhita (3-1-9-30), Maitrayani Samhita (1-5-8), and Aitareya Brahmana (5-14): Manu had many sons and distributed his wealth among them, but his youngest son, **Nabhanedishtha**, was away studying at his guru's household. On completing his studies and returning to claim his share, he found the wealth already divided. Manu therefore directed him to a group of Angirasa rishis performing a yajna to attain heaven, whose ritual procedure contained errors — instructing him to correct their rites, for which they would reward him with their own share of wealth as dakshina. The suktas Manu taught him are the well-known Rigveda 10-61 and 10-62. Bhatta Bhaskara's Krishna-Yajus commentary references this same Brahmana episode; mantra 10-61-18 itself names "Nabha Nedishtha." The point: though these mantras predate Nabhanedishtha, because he derived special benefit from them, tradition came to regard him as their rishi.

**2.** The Aitareya Brahmana (6-18) and Gopatha Brahmana (6-1) suggest that Mandala 4, Sukta 19's opening mantras were first seen by Vishvamitra, and only later imparted to the wider public by Vamadeva in a subsequent generation — yet the Anukramanika names Vamadeva alone as this sukta's rishi.

**3.** The sukta beginning "kasya nūnam..." (Rigveda 1-24) is assigned by the Sarvanukramani to "Ajigarti," that is, Devarata, son of Ajigarta — the same Ajigarti, taught by Vishvamitra, who praised Prajapati with this very sukta, per the Aitareya Brahmana (33-3, 4). Yet Vararuchi's *Nirukta-samuchchaya* says the seer of this mantra is Ajigarta himself.

**4.** The Taittiriya Samhita (5-2-3) and Kathaka Samhita (20-10) state that Rigveda Mandala 3, Sukta 22 was seen by Vishvamitra personally — yet the Sarvanukramani names its rishi as either Gathi or Gadhi.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 184</div>

For this reason, these rishis are not always the first seers of the mantras attributed to them; it may freely be said that the mantras were in use even before these rishis studied them. Rather than seers of the mantras, these rishis may be said to have made the meanings of the mantras manifest, or to have first employed the mantras in sacrifices and the like.

The Veda's date cannot be fixed from these rishi genealogies alone. Bhrigu, Angiras and the others are known as seers of the mantras; they lived thousands of years before the Mahabharata era, which is fixed at about 3139 BC. Since these seers are older still, the statement that the Vedas were composed in 2000–1500 BC is a mere delusion. The philologists' statement, following Philology, that the Vedas were composed in 2000–1500 BC is likewise improper. Considered historically, philology is not very useful for fixing chronology, and it is clear that these named rishis are not the very first, and that earlier rishis likely composed the mantras before them; Vedic mantras should accordingly be understood as existing since beginningless time, used across whatever periods they were actually current.

### Rishis Who Were Seers of the Mantras' *Meaning* {.lv1}

From what is known so far, mantras have appeared again and again: the same mantra was seen by different rishis at different times. Not only this: one mantra came to be understood differently by different rishis across different eras — even within the same received Brahmana material, a single mantra could be applied differently by different rishis depending on context, because its meaning was understood differently by different interpreters. That "seeing" a mantra (drashtritva) and interpreting its meaning are two distinct things is shown by the following:

**1.** The Nirukta (2-8) records that Shakapuni held all deities should be known; the deity of a certain sukta became established through Shakapuni's own interpretation specifically, though who first discovered that deity is unknown. Finally the deity taught him a rik (Rigveda 1-164-29) and made known that she was the deity of that rik. This mantra was well known before Shakapuni and he himself had studied it, yet he received it again from the deity, that is, he received instruction in the meaning of the mantra.

**2.** The Nirukta (13-12) states:

> न ह्येषु प्रत्यक्षमस्त्यन्येषां तपसस्त्वेषाम् ॥
>
> *na hy eṣu pratyakṣam asty anyeṣāṃ tapasas tveṣām ||*
>
> "For among these, direct perception does not belong to others [who lack it] — rather, it comes through their own austerity (tapas)."

That is: mantras do not become directly perceivable to the ignorant or to those who have not practiced austerity — this must be the intended sense of this statement.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 185</div>

There are as many mantras as are plentiful. But depending on the specific mantra, the power arising from it and who receives that power becomes clear only from context — the same mantra proving useful differently for different purposes. Since the quoted phrase is explained with the locative case (those with vision in the mantras, that is, knowers of the meaning of the mantra), the rishis were not only seers of mantras but also seers of their meaning.

**3.** The Nirukta (10-10) states:

> ऋषेर्दृष्ट्यर्थस्य प्रतिभावात्ख्यानसंयुक्ता ।
>
> *ṛṣer dṛṣṭyarthasya pratibhāvāt khyāna-saṃyuktā |*
>
> "[Narration] joined with the insight arising from the rishi's perceived meaning."

Here, the word "dṛṣṭyārthasya" establishes that the rishis directly perceived the mantra's meaning as well [as its form].

**4.** Vatsyayana's commentary on the Nyaya-sutra (4-1-62) states:

> य एव मुक्तब्राह्मणस्य द्रष्टारः प्रवक्तारश्च ते खल्वितिहासपुराणस्य धर्मशास्त्रस्य चेति ।
>
> *ya eva mukta-brāhmaṇasya draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca te khalv itihāsa-purāṇasya dharmaśāstrasya ceti |*
>
> "Those who are indeed the seers and expounders of the [corresponding] Brahmana are also, indeed, [the seers and expounders] of Itihasa, Purana, and Dharmashastra."

And another sutra (2-2-67):

> य एवास्या वेदार्थानां द्रष्टारः प्रवक्तारश्च त एवायुर्वेदप्रभृतीनामिति ।
>
> *ya evāsyā vedārthānāṃ draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca ta evāyurveda-prabhṛtīnām iti |*
>
> "Those who are the seers and expounders of the Veda's meanings are the very same as those of Ayurveda and similar [auxiliary] sciences."

These statements establish that rishis are both seers of the mantras and, in Brahmana form, seers of the mantras' meanings — "seers of the Brahmana" meaning those who understood the mantras' various meanings and applications.

**5.** The Shukla Yajurveda (ch. 7, mantra 46) reads:

> ब्राह्मणमुद्वीच्यं शिक्ष्यमुच्चं स्विष्टमुच्च्मषिणा शीयम् ।
>
> *brāhmaṇam udvīcyaṃ śikṣyam uccaṃ sviṣṭam ucca-ṛṣiṇā śīyam |*
>
> *(a technical liturgical phrase whose precise construction is difficult to render exactly)*

Commenting on this, Uvata glosses "rishi" as "*ṛṣir mantrāṇāṃ vyākhyātā*" — "one who explains the mantras is a rishi."

**6.** The word "rishi" also occurs in the Baudhayana Dharmasutra (2-6-36); the commentator Govindasvami explains it as one who understands the meaning and intent of the mantras.

**7.** Medhatithi's commentary on the Manu-smriti (ch. 1, verse 1), glossing "maharṣayaḥ," states:

> ऋषिर्वेदः । तदध्ययन-विज्ञान-तदर्थानुष्ठानातिशययोगात् पुरुषेष्वप्यृषिशब्दः ।
>
> *ṛṣir vedaḥ | tad-adhyayana-vijñāna-tad-arthānuṣṭhānātiśaya-yogāt puruṣeṣv apy ṛṣi-śabdaḥ |*
>
> "The Veda itself is 'rishi.' Because of an exceptional connection through its study, understanding, and practice of its meaning, the word 'rishi' extends to human beings as well."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 186</div>

"Rishi" means Veda; one who studies it, understands its meaning, and practices its accompanying duties is fittingly called "rishi" too — hence both mantra-seers and mantra-meaning-seers share this title.

### Many Rishis' Names Were Taken From the Veda Itself {.lv1}

Vishvamitra's original name was Vishvaratha; after his austerities and attainment of Brahmarshi status, he is well known to have adopted the name "Vishvamitra". Similarly, other rishis seem to have taken their names the same way — the rishi "Shiva-sankalpa" took his name from the Yajurveda's famous "Shiva-sankalpa" mantras (34-1 onward). The Aitareya Aranyaka says that Vishvamitra, Gritsamada and others are words denoting the vital breaths; the Shatapatha Brahmana connects the meaning of "Vasishtha" and similar words to the senses (indriya). The rishi of the Rigveda's Shraddha-sukta (10-151) is named "Shraddha Kamayani"; this is certainly not her name — she must have had another name.

In several such cases, it becomes clear that rishis set aside their own personal names and instead adopted, as their names, words actually found within the Veda's own text. The Bhrigu-proclaimed Manu-smriti states the same:

> सर्वेषां तु स नामानि कर्माणि च पृथक् पृथक् । वेदशब्देभ्य एवादौ पृथक् संस्थाश्च निर्ममे ॥
>
> *sarveṣāṃ tu sa nāmāni karmāṇi ca pṛthak pṛthak | veda-śabdebhya evādau pṛthak saṃsthāś ca nirmame ||*
>
> "For all [beings], He fashioned, at the very beginning, their separate names, separate deeds, and separate conditions — from the words of the Veda itself."

### The Rishis and Arya-Dharma {.lv1}

The rishis are the original founders of Arya-dharma (Hindu dharma), having lived their lives for its sake — they are the founders of our culture. Whatever is renowned as the essence of our country's culture traces to them. When doubt arises today about matters of dharma and adharma amid social turmoil, peace can be found by studying these rishis' lives and following their path — each rishi grasped the essence of dharma and adharma and stands as an exemplar of righteous conduct, fair dealing, and truthfulness.

For this reason alone, rishis have held especially venerable status since ancient times — even great kings worshipped and honored them highly; a king who saw his daughter accepted [in marriage] by a rishi considered it a blessing for his lineage's continuation (Janashruti gave his daughter in marriage to Raikva) — many such examples appear in the Mahabharata and elsewhere, and instances of offering rishis the seat of highest honor (agra-puja) recur across thousands of contexts. When Lord Krishna went as an emissary to the Kaurava assembly in the Mahabharata's Udyoga-parva to negotiate peace, beholding that wondrous assembly hall and gazing into its heights, he spoke thus of the rishis gathered there—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 187</div>

> पार्थिवीं समितिं दृष्ट्व्य ऋषयोऽभ्यागता नृप ॥ ५४ ॥ निमन्त्र्यन्तां मास्नैष्टे सत्कारेण च भूयसा । नैषां सनुपसिष्येषु शक्यं केनचिदासितुम् ॥ ५५ ॥ (Udyoga-parva, ch. 94)
>
> *pārthivīṃ samitiṃ dṛṣṭvya ṛṣayo'bhyāgatā nṛpa ॥ nimantryantāṃ māsnaiṣṭe satkāreṇa ca bhūyasā | naiṣāṃ sanupasiṣyeṣu śakyaṃ kenacid āsitum ॥*
>
> "O king, having beheld this earthly assembly, the rishis have arrived as guests. Let them be invited and welcomed with the greatest hospitality — none may remain seated without first attending to them."

*(The print continues with further verses of the same passage, numbered ‖58‖ and ‖59‖, not transcribed in this file.)* They received honored hospitality; only once they were seated did Krishna and the others take their own seats. Rishis are those who have renounced everything — to look at them they seem utterly poor. Where are such persons, and where are kings among kings? Yet, as protectors and propagators of dharma and treasuries of knowledge, they have received honor everywhere without exception. The rishis were, in effect, the very life-breath of Aryan culture and Aryan dharma.

#### The Vedas Are Also Called by the Name "Rishi" {.lv2}

The statement "ṛṣir vedaḥ" ("rishi is Veda") rests on several authorities:

**1.** Dandanatha's vritti, a commentary on Bhojaraja's Unadi-sutras (2-1-159), explains the word rishi as meaning "Veda."

**2.** Haradatta's *Padamanjari* (on Panini 1-1-18) states:

> ऋषिर्वेदः । तदुक्तं ऋषिका—इत्यादौ दर्शनात् ।
>
> *ṛṣir vedaḥ | tad uktaṃ ṛṣikā—ityādau darśanāt |*
>
> "'Rishi' is Veda — this is [established] because [the derivative] 'ṛṣikā' and similar forms are seen [used in this sense]."

In the Brahmanas the phrase "*taducta-ṛṣikā*" is used in many places meaning "as stated in the Veda" — confirming that "rishi" itself can mean "Veda."

**3.** The Vaijayanti-kosha lexicon similarly glosses "rishi" as usable in the sense of Veda ("ṛṣi-sṛṣṭa vede").

**4.** Medhatithi's Manu-bhashya likewise treats "ṛṣir vedaḥ" as an established equivalence.

**5.** The Shashvata-kosha (verse 719) states "ṛṣir vede" in a verse to the same effect — this text is thought to date to the 7th century CE, indicating this usage of "rishi" for "Veda" was current up to that period.

### The Rishis and Buddhist Texts {.lv1}

> यथोक्तं भगवता—इत्येषे आनन्द पौराणा महर्षयो वेदानां कर्तारो मन्त्राणां प्रवर्तयितारः ।
>
> *yathoktaṃ bhagavatā—ityeṣe ānanda paurāṇā maharṣayo vedānāṃ kartāro mantrāṇāṃ pravartayitāraḥ |*
>
> "As stated by the Blessed One [Buddha]: 'These, O Ananda, are the ancient great sages, the authors of the Vedas, the promulgators of the mantras.'"

<div class="pgmark">original p. 188</div>

The Blessed Buddha told Ananda that the ancient sages composed the Vedas and propagated them — so even by the Buddha's own account, rishis are credited as composers and propagators of the mantras. This shows that even the Buddha accepted that the rishis composed and propagated the mantras; one may say he had at least some regard for the Veda. But for later Buddhists this is an unacceptable matter.

The Majjhima Nikaya (2-5-5 and 2-5-9) records the Buddha addressing one called Taudeyya's son while staying at Jetavana, Shravasti:

"These present-day Brahmins' ancestors were rishis. They composed the Veda and propagated it; even now, [Brahmins] teach it following that same tradition. Brahmins count among their own ancient rishis: Ashtaka, Vamaka, Vamadeva, Vishvamitra, Jamadagni, Angira, Bharadvaja, Vasishtha, Kashyapa, Bhrigu, and others."

That the rishis were speakers of the Veda is accepted by the Buddhists too. But that there were no rishis in the Buddha's own time is clear from his words "the ancestors of the Brahmins were rishis". Rishis existed across every age — in fields like austerity and knowledge one may certainly find figures worthy of the name — but truly great rishis of this magnitude are rare in later times, and in the present era, none exist in the strict sense of "seer of mantras."

Counting forward from the Mahabharata era's ruling dynasty — Parikshit, Janamejaya, Shatanika, Ashvamedhadatta and others — their reigns spanned about 225 years. Toward the end, Ashvamedhadatta's son Asimakrishna performed a long sacrificial session (dirgha-sattra). The Vayu Purana records:

> असीमकृष्णे विक्रान्ते राजन्येऽनुपमत्विषि । प्रशासतीमां धर्मेण भूमिं भूमिपसत्तमे ॥ १२ ॥ ऋषयः संशितात्मानः सत्यव्रतपरायणाः । ऋजवो नष्टरजसः शान्ता दान्ता जितेन्द्रियाः ॥ १३ ॥ धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे दीर्घसत्रं तु ईजिरे । नद्यास्तीरे दृषद्वत्याः पुण्यायाः शुचिरोधसः ॥ १४ ॥
>
> *asīmakṛṣṇe vikrānte rājanye'nupamatviṣi | praśāsatīmāṃ dharmeṇa bhūmiṃ bhūmipasattame || 12 || ṛṣayaḥ saṃśitātmānaḥ satyavrataparāyaṇāḥ | ṛjavo naṣṭarajasaḥ śāntā dāntā jitendriyāḥ || 13 || dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre dīrghasatraṃ tu ījire | nadyās tīre dṛṣadvatyāḥ puṇyāyāḥ śucirodhasaḥ || 14 ||*
>
> "While the valiant Asīmakṛṣṇa, a prince of matchless splendour, best of kings, was ruling this earth righteously, the ṛṣis — of disciplined minds, devoted to truth and their vows, upright, free of passion, calm, restrained, masters of their senses — performed a long sacrificial session (dīrgha-satra) in Kurukṣetra, the field of dharma, on the bank of the holy Dṛṣadvatī river with its pure banks."

Rishis existed in this king's era. The Kali Yuga is reckoned to begin from the time King Dharmaraja (Yudhishthira) departed the earth; by this reckoning, rishis can be said to have existed for roughly 400 years after that point.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 189</div>

The Rigveda has 1,028 suktas comprising 10,552 mantras (as already noted, p. 16). These have many rishis: generally all mantras within a sukta share one rishi, though occasionally a single sukta's mantras carry different rishis (a rare occurrence); the same holds for deities and meters — usually uniform within a sukta, though sometimes mixed.

Given this structure, the Rigveda's mantras can be classified three ways. First, gathering in sequence all suktas seen by a single rishi produces a group compiled either by that rishi himself, a well-known descendant, or his disciples, arranged in fixed order — such a group is called a "Mandala." The Rigveda has ten Mandalas, mostly organized by lineage: Mandala 1 mixes various lineages (hence its rishis are called "Shatarshina," since many contributed around 100 mantras each); Mandala 2 belongs to Gritsamada's lineage, 3 to Vishvamitra's, 4 to Vamadeva's, 5 to Atri's, 6 to Bharadvaja's, 7 to Vasishtha's, and 8 to Kanva-lineage rishis. Mandala 9 has many rishis but is instead named for its shared deity (Soma) rather than lineage, all its suktas being addressed to Soma. The current Rigveda Samhita is arranged following this rishi/lineage/Mandala sequence.

A second classification method groups suktas by their principal deity — "devata-suktas." All Agni-focused suktas form one such group, Indra-focused suktas another, and so on. Mandala 9 follows this same deity-based logic internally: every sukta in it has Pavamana Soma as its sole deity, with the order of meters and rishis the same as in the other Mandalas. Apart from this ninth Mandala, grouping the suktas of the other deities into groups and studying them so is not the custom — though modern scholars, for convenience of study, have printed deity-organized collections (even as separate volumes).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 190</div>

There is no special benefit in arranging by the third (meter-based) method here; the traditional rishi-sequence is given priority. The names of the rishis in the Rigveda, with the Maṇḍala, Sūkta, ṛks and other details of what they saw, are given in the table below in alphabetical order. It is proper to explain how to read it; as examples, 3-4 names are explained here:

**अंहोमुक् वामदेव्यः १०-१२६ [८]** *(Aṃhomuk Vāmadevyaḥ 10-126 [8])*

Here "Aṃhomuk Vāmadevya" is the rishi's name. The number 10 shows the Maṇḍala and 126 the sūkta number, and the number [8] in brackets shows the total number of ṛks seen by that rishi. That is: Aṃhomuk Vāmadevya is the rishi of the 126th sūkta of the 10th Maṇḍala, and this sūkta has 8 ṛks in all.

**अकृष्ट (ष्टाः) माषाः, or माषाः अकृष्टाः** *(Akṛṣṭa (-ṣṭāḥ) Māṣāḥ, or Māṣāḥ Akṛṣṭāḥ)*

The rishi's name may be pronounced either way, Akṛṣṭāḥ Māṣāḥ or Māṣāḥ Akṛṣṭāḥ. Where the table has Akṛṣṭāḥ Māṣāḥ without details, look under Māṣāḥ Akṛṣṭāḥ. There the details of the mantras seen by this rishi are: 9-86, 1-10, 31-40, [20] — that is, in the 86th sūkta of the 9th Maṇḍala (this sūkta has 48 ṛks) the ṛks from 1 to 10 and from 31 to 40, 20 ṛks in all, were seen by this rishi Māṣāḥ Akṛṣṭāḥ.

**अर्चनाना आत्रेयः ५-६३ ; ६४ ; ८-४२ [२०]** *(Arcanānā Ātreyaḥ 5-63; 64; 8-42 [20])*

Here Arcanānā Ātreya is the rishi's name: the 63rd sūkta of the 5th Maṇḍala (7 ṛks), the 64th sūkta (7 ṛks) and the 42nd sūkta of the 8th Maṇḍala (6 ṛks) — 20 ṛks in all are seen by this rishi.

**असितः काश्यपः ९-५-२४ [१६४]** *(Asitaḥ Kāśyapaḥ 9-5-24 [164])* — (काश्यपः देवलः ?) *(Kāśyapaḥ Devalaḥ ?)*

Here Asita Kāśyapa or Kāśyapa Devala is the rishi's name: of the sūktas from 5 to 24 in the 9th Maṇḍala, that is 164 ṛks in all, this rishi is the seer. In this way the particulars of any rishi wanted can be looked up. From this table it can easily be known whether a rishi of a given name is in the Rigveda or not, and where and how many ṛks composed by that rishi there are.—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 191</div>

**Editorial notice.** The source prints this alphabetical index of the Ṛgveda’s ṛṣis with, for every entry, the hymn references (maṇḍala–sūkta–ṛc, in Kannada numerals) and, in square brackets, the total number of verses seen by that ṛṣi. In this edition the names, descriptions and bracketed verse-counts are given in full; the hymn references are not reproduced, because at the scan quality available they could not be read with the certainty that a reference table requires. The cross-reference lines, printed in mirrored pairs (“A B … B A”), are compressed: each ṛṣi is listed once, with the ṛṣis paired with him or her.

</div>
