## Chapter Eleven — The Deities of the Rigveda

<div class="pgmark">original p. 205</div>

Among the mantras, whatever subject a given mantra primarily describes is spoken of as that mantra's deity — as already noted in the previous chapter via the citation "yā tenoktā sā devatā" ("she who is addressed by it is the deity"). If a mantra's essential subject is Agni, its deity is Agni; deities may likewise be Indra, the Ashvin-deities, the Maruts, Savitr, Surya, Rudra, Vishnu, Vayu, and others.

A sukta of one or several mantras may share a single deity throughout; or different mantras within one sukta may carry different deities; or even a single mantra's first and second halves may address different deities, or describe multiple deities together. Generally, though, one sukta (or one mantra) having a single deity is the norm.

Agni, Indra, Varuna, the Ashvins, the Maruts, Vayu, Aditya, Ushas, Ratri, Mitra, Vishnu, Rudra, Soma, the Waters, and others are the principal deities — Agni and Indra having by far the most suktas, with other deities considerably fewer. Within each Mandala's sukta-sequence, Agni-deity suktas generally come first, followed by Indra-deity suktas, then other deities in turn — a pattern generally followed across all Mandalas. Mandala 9 alone is an exception: every sukta there shares Pavamana Soma as its sole deity, with no other deities appearing; only the rishis and meters vary within it.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 206</div>

Among the principal deities named above, depending on context, rivers, pressing-stones, knowledge, the arrow, the quiver, the sacrificial altar, the mortar and pestle, and similar objects also appear as deities in certain places. In the Danastuti hymns praising a king or patron's generosity, dialogues between two speakers are likewise treated as deities in several suktas. Mandala 10 in particular contains many such minor deities.

Rishis are observed to have composed hymns of praise following certain fixed groupings: the Ashvin-deities are always praised jointly; likewise Mitra-Varuna, Soma-Rudra, Indra-Varuna, Indra-Vayu, Indra-Vishnu, and Indra-Soma are frequently praised together, while other deities are praised individually.

In Rigvedic times, people did not worship these deities in their own homes as is done now; they invited and worshipped them in yajnas and the like. Not everyone performed every ritual act described in the Rigveda — only the wealthy did. Undertaking a ritual required resources, a proper household, necessary supplies, and several assisting priests; since the poor could not perform these rites, in course of time they took up the sorcery and the like of the Atharvaveda, and in place of priests their priests were sorcerers and such, content with little.

The Rigveda is filled, cover to cover, with hopeful aspiration — famously oriented toward experiencing whatever happiness life offers. The primary intent behind praying to the deities is this: the deities are asked to give not freedom from worldly existence nor the joys of heaven and the hereafter, but longevity, wealth, valor and progeny — worldly joys. Victory over enemies, health, plenty of food and drink appear to be life's primary aims here:

> "Agni, give strength and prosperity to our leaders, the wealthy." — useful to many. (VII-5-9)

> "O Indra, satisfy us with precious things. Give our leader the sustenance he needs, abundant valor and offspring; act mercifully; by that strength may we live long." (VII-24-6)

> "May we live a hundred years." (VII-66-16)

The rishis appear motivated by experiencing life's fullness rather than any attitude of renunciation (vairagya) toward it — only here and there a single mantra in the whole Rigveda is found expressing that this body is perishable and all life dream-like.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 207</div>

> ददात नो अमृतस्य प्रजायै (VII-57-6)
>
> *dadāta no amṛtasya prajāyai*
>
> "Grant us, for our progeny, [a share] of amrita (immortality)."

The precise meaning of "amrita" here is unclear, and scholars differ: the Western scholar Roth held it means "the deathless"; Grassmann took it as "long life"; Sayanacharya himself glosses it as "water." In VII-76-4–5, the rishis describe their ancestors behaving as equals alongside the deities; in VII-59, one mantra explicitly requests immortality. Only in a few such instances are matters of the hereafter (amushmika) raised at all — nowhere does a path of renunciation (viraktimarga) appear to be taught. On the whole, the Rigveda seems to hold that safeguarding worldly happiness is itself life's proper aim.

Even though Rigveda mantras are said to serve ritual purposes, they are not, like Yajurveda mantras, entirely subordinated to ritual action — they show real simplicity and sincerity, with hymns arising from the depths of the heart and not appearing contrived.

As already noted, deities were understood to accept devotees' prayers and come to their aid — raising the question of whether these deities have a form like ours, and if so, what kind. Generally, every Rigvedic deity represents some aspect of nature that has taken on form and become an individual deity. Dawn (Ushas) was itself a source of wonder to the Vedic rishis, worthy of worship — natural phenomena of this kind came to be conceived as deities.

Even long after deity-worship began, these natural phenomena continued to inspire wonder, awe, and reverence in the rishis — who were not mere ritual technicians; worshipping embodied deities never made them forget the underlying natural phenomena. Forgetting simply wasn't in their nature.

Although embodied deities such as Indra, Varuna and Agni are found in the Vedas, the other deities are not fully embodied deities. Reading about these deities, one can readily recognize their natural origin: which aspect of nature took this particular form. This may be called **"arrested personification"** — attributing form and personality only partially to what is inherently formless. To appreciate that this personification remains incomplete, comparison with other traditions helps: the Greeks similarly conceived natural forces as deities, but over time these became entirely human in behavior. Their chief deity, Zeus — the original cause of everything, support of the whole world — is nonetheless also described (under the name "Jove") as fickle by nature, possessing the very flaws an ordinary person might have — complete humanization, in other words. The Vedic deities, by contrast, remain half in human-like form while the other half stays rooted in their original, foundational natural essence.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 208</div>

The qualities described for these deities generally recur across the Vedic pantheon as a whole. This personification is applied also to wholly lifeless things such as the door, the sacrificial post and the chariot, but not in a special degree; these occur only in some contexts.

One further point deserves attention: **Henotheism**. When a particular deity is being praised, that deity alone is proclaimed supreme for the occasion — whichever deity is invoked in context receives this "foremost" treatment, shifting from deity to deity without disrespecting any other:

> "The God in question, alone, is present to the mind of the singer; with him, for the time being, is associated everything that can be said of a divine being; he is the highest, the only God, before whom all others disappear, there being in this, however, no offence or depreciation of any other God." (Kaegi, p. 33)

This kind of description appears only occasionally; since every deity receives every kind of attributed quality, determining relative rank becomes difficult — though some individual, distinguishing characteristics can still be identified for each.

Deities can be grouped three ways, per Yaska: according to Nirukta-shastra, scholars declare deities to belong to earth (Agni), the mid-region/atmosphere (Vayu or Indra), and the celestial region (Surya) — other deity-names within the Veda are simply variant designations for these same three deities' functions, or else there may be as many deities as there are names, since each name has its own mantra. Yaska proceeds from here to discuss these deities' embodied forms.

##### "अथ आकारचिन्तनं देवानाम्" — "Now, the Contemplation of the Deities' Forms" {.lv3}

*(atha ākāra-cintanaṃ devānām)*

Three views exist on this: (1) deities have human-like form; (2) they have no form; (3) they take shape in some particular manner not equivalent to conventional embodiment. This last, ambiguous possibility is closest to the "arrested personification" concept discussed earlier.

Before examining each deity's individual characteristics, one point should be fixed first: considerable variation exists between the Rigveda's deities and those of the much later Puranic texts — variation that developed gradually. The regard accorded certain deities in ancient Indian thought differs markedly from what later tradition gives their counterparts: some deities holding especially important places in the Vedas have no place at all in the Puranas, or, if they have one, it is of a very low rank.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 209</div>

In this way, deities holding a lesser place in the Vedas gained far greater prominence in the Puranas. Among the Rigveda's principal deities — Indra, Agni, and others — their standing in the Puranas diminished considerably, with Brahma, Vishnu, and Maheshvara (Shiva) becoming foremost instead. Vishnu, who stood far behind in the Rigveda, has great honor in the Puranas. Newer deities like Lakshmi, Parvati, and Kubera came to prominence in the Puranas; meanwhile, famous Vedic names — Aryama, Bhaga, Parjanya, Ukshas, and others — appear nowhere at all in the Puranas, while Savitr, Pushan, Mitra, Surya, and similar deities came to be merged and identified as one.

Among the Rigveda's deity-groups, the two most important from the outset are Agni and Indra. Agni is the first and Indra the second; Indra has more riks, and in the number of riks Agni takes the second place. The name "Agni" itself recurs, with small variations, across related languages: Latin *ignis*, Lithuanian *ugnis*, Slavic (Old Church Slavonic) *ognis* — all meaning fire. This Agni, in the Veda, is described as a shared phenomenon spanning deity, human, and nature — among the five elements (earth, water, light/energy, air, and space), he is described in manifold forms as a kind of energy (tejas).

This Agni takes three forms: on earth, as fire; in the mid-region, as lightning; and in the celestial sphere, as the sun. Earthly fire is produced by friction, using two small sticks (called "tāyī" — VII-1-1, VII-3-9) rubbed together. Between the clouds, Indra produces Agni [as lightning], or brings it about through water. Although there is no difference between this fire and the fire kindled daily in every house, the Veda does not take up that ordinary fire at all; only the fires connected with yajnas and the fire of the five elements are discussed.

> यो अपाचीने तमसि मदन्तीः प्राचीश्चकार नृतमः शचीभिः ॥ (VII-6-4)
> *yo apācīne tamasi madantīḥ prācīś cakāra nṛtamaḥ śacībhiḥ ||*
>
> "He who, most manly, by his powers turned eastward those [dawns] that were rejoicing in the westward darkness."

As soon as day breaks, one should perform the fire-rite to Agni and begin the day's duties — the day itself begins with fire. He is the eldest among all priests. The instant ghee is offered into the fire, Agni rises up in flame; his "teeth" (the arrangement of flames) are bright and pure, his head a form of radiant energy. He is the master (yajamana) of all — the master of the household. Shuchidan, Tapurmurdha, Vishvati, Grihapati — he alone is the family's own priest (kula-purohita), performing every priestly function himself; he is not merely a priest, but a sage (jnani) too. *(the word "Kavi": VII-15-2)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 210</div>

Agni acts as a mediating messenger (duta) between gods and humans, performing this duty in yajnas — one prays to Agni to summon the other deities (*viśvasya dūtam amṛtam*, VII-16-1).

Besides helping in yajnas, Agni drives away thieves and robbers and brings about good booty (VII-6-3). Tradition holds that Angiras and other rishis first brought Agni down from heaven to earth, and that the deity Matarishvan first brought Agni to humankind — a story reflecting how lightning striking trees gave rise to fire, natural phenomena woven into human life and told in narrative/historical form.

In this way, Agni performs his role in three forms — lightning, sacrificial fire, and celestial fire — retaining individuality in each without ever becoming fully personified as human; his natural, inherent character is never forgotten entirely.

There is a legend connected with Agni. Building on this, the Mahabharata's Vana-parva (ch. 224) and Shalya-parva (ch. 48) tell a striking story: it was Agni's task to take the oblations offered to the gods and hand them over; he found this somewhat tiresome, so he slipped away and hid in the sea. The gods could not manage without Agni. Yama discovered where Agni was hiding, and Varuna, the leader of the gods, persuaded Agni to do his work again (X. 51 and 52). The Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya Samhita (2-6-3) recounts this with slight variation.

Following Agni, the next chief deity is **Indra** — with even more hymns dedicated to him than Agni; no other deity approaches these two in this respect. Unlike Agni, Indra cannot be said to be any particular element of nature. In the Zend Avesta, Indra's name appears as "Andra," though there his status is much diminished, reduced to a demon (pishacha); yet his chief epithet, "Vritra-slayer," survives there too, as "Verethraghna."

In the Veda, Indra lacks no admirable quality. Summarized briefly: Indra was born from heaven, or from earth (VII-20-5); as soon as born, he drank Soma (VII-98-3); he is the most ancient of deities, yet ever-youthful; strong, active, a hero, wise, of limitless power, radiant, wearing a fine helmet; golden-armed (*hiraṇyabāhuḥ*, VII-34-4); his horses are yoked

<div class="pgmark">original p. 211</div>

to his golden-horsed chariot; his weapon is the thunderbolt (vajra); none equals him in Soma-drinking, through which he becomes intoxicated and destroys the rakshasas (VII-22-1,2 & VII-29-1) — on one occasion drinking Soma poured from thirty vessels (VII-77-4), among other feats.

With Vishnu's aid, Indra defeated the demons Vritra, Ahi, Shushna, Namuchi, and Shambara — who had obstructed the waters — releasing what they had blocked (VII-99-4–5) and destroying the Asuras along with their cities. Indra is a great hero and warrior; his arrows slay enemies, bringing good fortune to those who depend on him. He watches over humankind as a father would, forgiving human transgressions with a generous heart, punishing adharma within his purview, and destroying the Dasyus, demons, and sinners.

Three qualities stand out among Indra's attributes. **First:** he presides over strength and power, holding authority over the external world; in religious or moral terms he has no very exalted place — though he has a grand form:

> "Indra embodies so completely the human qualities of brag and bluster, gluttony, drunkenness and lust, as to make him the peg upon which to hang scepticism." (Bloomfield, *Vedic Religion*)

These traits — ordinary human pride, gluttony, drunken indulgence, blindness, and susceptibility to desire — are indeed found in his portrayal, which could give rise to skepticism regarding deities generally.

**Second:** Indra is the ideal of martial valor, regarded as a leader in battle; those going to war pray to him and rely on his help in destroying enemies — his help is sought not only against enemies but also when they quarrel among themselves.

**Third: the slaying of Vritrasura.** A few examples on this point:

> इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्र वोचं यानि चकार प्रथमानि वज्री । अहन्नहिमन्वपस्ततर्द प्र वक्षणा अभिनत्पर्वतानाम् ॥ (1-32-1)
>
> *indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocaṃ yāni cakāra prathamāni vajrī | ahann ahim anv apas tatarda pra vakṣaṇā abhinat parvatānām ||*
>
> "Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra, which the thunderbolt-wielder performed first: he slew the serpent (Ahi), released the flowing waters, and split open the flanks of the mountains."

Indra's heroic feats are numerous — the sukta opens by promising to relate the principal ones. A demon named Ahi had obstructed the rivers flowing from the mountains and the waters descending from the atmosphere; Indra killed him with his thunderbolt and released the waters to flow again — the same episode is retold with variation across other mantras.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 212</div>

> अयोद्धेव दुर्मद आ हि जुह्वे महावीरं तुविबाधमृजीषम् । नातारीदस्य समृतिं वधानां सं रुजानाः पिपिष इन्द्रशत्रुः ॥
> अपादहस्तो अपृतन्यदिन्द्रमास्य वज्रमधि सानौ जघान । वृष्णो वध्रिः प्रतिमानं बुभूषन् पुरुत्रा वृत्रो अशयद्व्यस्तः ॥ (I-32-6 & 7)
>
> *ayoddheva durmada ā hi juhve mahāvīraṃ tuvibādham ṛjīṣam | nātārīd asya samṛtiṃ vadhānāṃ saṃ rujānāḥ pipiṣa indraśatruḥ ||*
> *apād ahasto apṛtanyad indram āsya vajram adhi sānau jaghāna | vṛṣṇo vadhriḥ pratimānaṃ bubhūṣan purutrā vṛtro aśayad vyastaḥ ||*
>
> "Like one unfit for battle, the arrogant one challenged the great hero, the mighty overpowerer, the drinker of the ṛjīṣa; he did not withstand the onset of his blows — he whose foe was Indra was crushed and shattered. Footless and handless he fought against Indra; [Indra] struck his thunderbolt upon his back; the gelding, seeking to be the match of the bull, Vṛtra lay scattered in many places."

The demon, proud that none could confront him, was a great hero yet consumed by arrogance, and challenged Indra to battle; unable to withstand Indra's blows, he began afflicting the weak and helpless. Indra's blows destroyed Vritra's limbs one by one, yet he kept fighting even so, until finally struck down and felled in many places.

Who is this Vritrasura? What water did he obstruct, and what water did Indra release? Such questions arise naturally, and scholars have offered many differing answers — even the Nirukta itself gives more than one interpretation.

**First: the "Storm Theory"** (what Westerners call the *Chandamaruta-vada*). Here, Vritra is a malevolent deity withholding water within the clouds; Indra, lord of the clouds or rain-deity, pierces the clouds through the storm's power, releasing rain. Accepting this requires reading "parvata" (mountain) as meaning "cloud" — attested elsewhere in the text:

> य एम्॒बय॑न्ति॒ पर्व॑तान् ति॒रः स॑मु॒द्रम॑र्ण॒वम् (I-19-7)
>
> *ya embayanti parvatān tiraḥ samudram arṇavam*
>
> "[The waters] which flow past the mountains, through the vast, surging ocean..."

Here "parvata" is glossed precisely as "cloud" — the interpretation followed by many Western scholars. But the Vritra-episode involves further elements the theory must also explain: after slaying the demon, Indra releases the waters, creates the sun, *and* frees the cows — three elements a full interpretation must account for together, which the Storm Theory alone does not fully cover.

**Second: the "Dawn Theory."** Here, Indra himself is the Sun, destroying darkness and spreading light across the world — "go" (cow) also meaning "ray [of light]." This theory is reasonably consistent, though it leaves unclear whether the darkness destroyed is night's darkness or darkness caused by clouds.

Both theories leave room for objections. If Indra is the rain-deity, what role remains for the deity Parjanya? — this question naturally arises.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 213</div>

A third theory also exists — that of the Western scholar Hillebrandt. Here, Vritra is a demon who freezes and obstructs the waters during winter; Indra, acting like the sun, melts them and sets them flowing again. But this view does not suit a hot country like ours.

> यः शम्बरं पर्वतेषु क्षियन्तं चत्वारिंश्यां शरद्यन्वविन्दत् । ओजायमानं यो अहिं जघान दानुं शयानं स जनास इन्द्रः ॥
>
> *yaḥ śambaraṃ parvateṣu kṣiyantaṃ catvāriṃśyāṃ śarady anvavindat | ojāyamānaṃ yo ahiṃ jaghāna dānuṃ śayānaṃ sa janāsa indraḥ ||*
>
> "He who found Shambara, dwelling in the mountains, in the fortieth autumn; who slew the mighty serpent Ahi, lying prostrate along with Danu — he, O people, is Indra."

This suggests Indra found and killed a demon hidden in the mountains in "the fortieth year" — a specific timeframe raising the question: fortieth year from when? A Puranic story explains: Indra, having completed the required 100 Ashvamedha sacrifices, attained the office of Indra; around this time, the mountains still had wings, flying about at will, landing, and causing damage, until Indra cut off their wings with his thunderbolt — an event occurring shortly after he assumed his position, to which this "fortieth year" refers.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his *Arctic Home*, offers a different reading: this Indra-demon war reflects a struggle between darkness and light. In polar regions, darkness (and twilight) persists far longer than elsewhere. The "water" in this mantra, per Tilak, isn't rainfall or river-water but the vast water believed to envelop the entire world — the Puranas describe the earth as surrounded by a sphere of water, itself surrounded by air, itself surrounded by space; light and darkness arise from the sun's movement through this system, and, per Tilak, the sun and moon's movements are linked to the movement of this cosmic water-mass. The demon's obstruction of this water-mass's movement caused damage to the world beyond imagining — so Indra's slaying of the demon and restoring the water's motion was an act of tremendous benefit to the world, which is precisely why this feat is regarded as the foremost among all his heroic deeds.

##### Soma {.lv3}

Apart from Agni and Indra, Soma is the Rigveda's most celebrated deity — the entire ninth Mandala is devoted to his praise, and references to Soma recur even while praising other deities elsewhere. When inviting Indra and Agni to a rite, the poet specifically prays they come for Soma-drinking. Tradition variously describes the Soma-vine as originally existing in heaven before coming to earth; on earth, its

<div class="pgmark">original p. 214</div>

abode was atop mountain peaks. The Soma-creeper was pressed by stones (gravana) to extract its juice, described as sweet, honey-like in taste — its drinking bringing mental joy, bodily strength, and vigor, extensively praised by the poets. This Soma-juice itself is described as being like ambrosia (amrita).

In the Avesta, the deity "Hoama" corresponds to Soma. The Rigveda describes Soma as growing on mountains, brought by the Shyena bird — called king of the herbs/forest-plants, its juice extracted with stones, warding off disease, granting immortality, and being a drink most dear to the deities; these matters are described alike in the Rigveda and the Avesta. Because the Soma sacrifices are so many and so important, its prominence can be imagined.

In a few suktas of Mandala 10, and in the Krishna Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, Soma is explained as the Moon (Chandra), lord of the herbs; in later Itihasa and Purana works, Soma is well known as Ishvara together with Uma (Parvati).

Given how much remains to be said about Soma, only a brief account is given here — a fuller discussion follows in the introduction to Mandala 9.

Having considered Agni, Indra, and Soma together, let us turn to **Varuna**.

##### Varuna {.lv3}

Varuna and Indra differ greatly, each holding an almost opposite disposition: where Indra presides over strength and worldly prosperity, Varuna is lord of righteous life (dharmic existence).

> वृत्राण्यन्यः समिथेषु जिघ्नते व्रतान्यन्यो अभि रक्षते सदा । (VII-83-9)
> *vṛtrāṇy anyaḥ samitheṣu jighnate vratāny anyo abhi rakṣate sadā |*
>
> "The one slays the foes (vṛtras) in battles; the other ever guards the ordinances (vratas)."

This mantra, addressing both deities, shows their distinction: "Indra performs the task of slaying, while Varuna performs the task of protection." Ethical integrity and truthfulness are Varuna's chief qualities; omniscience and imperviousness to deception are his as well. Because of these qualities, it is Varuna's duty to examine all sin committed in the world and punish sinners — he alone chastises those who transgress the path of dharma, the corrupt, and the wicked. (VII-65-3)

> सत्यानृते अवपश्यन् जनानाम् (VII-49-3)
>
> *satyānṛte avapaśyan janānām*
>
> "Watching over the truth and falsehood of people."

He observes people's honesty and dishonesty; his laws cannot be transgressed with impunity. Wrongdoers approach him with great humility, seeking forgiveness or compassion,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 215</div>

offering prayers. Varuna's relationship with his devotee is compared to that of father and son — people who have sinned through ignorance beg his forgiveness as a child calls out to its father.

Many further characteristics are attributed to Varuna: he is perceptible only in the devotee's mind (VII-88-2); he possesses great power and mental steadfastness; his vision reaches far; his eye is the sun; nothing in the world escapes him; he holds Asura-like (mighty/lordly) power and māyā — a distinctive power especially associated with Kshatriyas (VII-28-4); his knowledge and awareness are without limit.

##### Rita (ऋत) {.lv3}

The word describing the ethical, righteous order Varuna presides over is **"Ṛta."** This word carries three distinct senses in the Rigveda.

**First**, it means the law of nature (prakriti-niyama) — natural phenomena proceeding in fixed, unbroken order: sunrise and sunset, day and night, occurring in unvarying sequence because of Rta. Even the deities are said to be "born of Rta" — the word carries considerable weight in compounds like *ṛta-jāta, ṛta-jña, ṛta-yoni, ṛta-vayana*, and others. Every daily phenomenon in the world follows this law of Rta.

**Second**, by the same natural principle, deity-worship, yajnas, and similar rites also follow this rule — the governing order of a properly performed yajna is likewise called "Rta." Because a yajna's many ritual acts must proceed in fixed sequence, and offerings (havis) must be properly presented to the deities, a yajna too is described as proceeding "by Rta."

**Finally**, by extension, the ordered regulation of each person's own daily life is also called "Rta" — the very scripture of a truthful person's existence, which everyone must follow. Whether or not one observes this is precisely where Varuna's role comes in: "Rta" means dharma, truth, and the like; its opposite means adharma, falsehood, and the like.

Varuna created heaven and earth and is the cause of their stability; he alone causes the sun to shine and the rivers to flow, and holds authority over the ocean, the wind, and similar domains (VII-86-1, VII-87-5, VII-87-6).

Some Rigveda mantras connect Varuna with the deity Mitra — and since Mitra is associated with the sun, the question arises of what Varuna's own connection is (VII-87-1). Sayanacharya's commentary on this mantra states:

> अस्तं गर्भ सूर्य इव वरुण इत्यच्ये । स हि स्वगमनेन रात्रीर्जनयति ।
>
> *astaṃ garbha sūrya iva varuṇa ity ucyate | sa hi svagamanena rātrīr janayati |*
>
> "'[He goes] home, like the sun — thus Varuna is spoken of.' For he, by his own setting, brings the nights into being."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 216</div>

The setting sun is itself called "Varuna" — withdrawing and thereby creating the night. For this reason, Prof. Oldenberg holds that Mitra is identified with the sun and Varuna with the moon.

Ultimately, Varuna and Mitra together receive a joint designation — "Sindhupati" (lord of rivers/waters) — a name for this jointly-presiding water-deity found in the Puranas and in Sayanacharya's own work.

In the Zoroastrian tradition (Ahura Mazda, or Ormazd), "Ahura" describes a deity whose qualities and functions match the Rigveda's Varuna closely — the Veda itself calls Varuna "Asura" (most powerful), making comparison between the two instructive.

The Greek deity Ouranos also resembles Varuna — regarded as the sky covering the earth. If "Varuna" is derived from the root *vṛ* ("to cover"), this fits — hence Varuna is also called by the name "Akasha" (sky/space).

Combining these two aspects, Puranic tradition came to describe Varuna as ruling the infinite, while certain earthly suktas are held to treat him as presiding specifically over the mass of waters.

##### The Ashvin Deities {.lv3}

Mandala 7's suktas 67–74 are devoted entirely to the Ashvin deities, with many further suktas praising them scattered across other Mandalas. Famous as physicians (vaidyas), children of Vivasvat and Saranyu, they are especially fond of Soma-drinking. They are said to arrive in a golden chariot yoked with birds, aid the suffering, and cure disease — ever ready to help directly in difficult situations. Because they move so much among human beings, the other deities hesitate somewhat to include them among themselves. In the Nirukta, when asked who the Ashvins are, Yaska answers: "Some say heaven and earth; some say day and night; and some say the sun and moon" — leaving the matter genuinely open.

Many stories are told of these deities: they restored youth and long life to the rishi Chyavana, granting him worldly happiness (I-116-10); they rescued Bhujyu, son of Tugra, helplessly drowning in the ocean's depths after he prayed to them, finding him abandoned in a hopeless situation and safely bringing him to shore (I-116-5); they revived the rishi Rebha, who had been bound hand and foot and thrown into the water, and whom people supposed dead after ten days, and drew him out. (I-116-24; I-112-5)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 217</div>

The rishi Atri Saptavadhi, thrown into a fire-pit by a demon, was rescued by the Ashvins, who protect such devotees (I-116-8; VI-50-10). Rijrashva killed a hundred sheep and gave them to a wolf as food; his father, angered, cursed him to blindness; the wolf then prayed to the Ashvins to give Rijrashva sight, and they granted him eyes (I-116-16; I-117-17). Vishpala, whose leg was severed in battle, received an iron leg from them (I-116-15); when the cow of Sayu would not calve or give milk, they made her give milk (I-116-22). Many further such stories exist.

##### Surya (The Sun) {.lv3}

The sun, dim in winter, becomes bright again in spring; rising from the depths of the vast ocean each morning, he illuminates every direction as he ascends. The youthful, beautiful-eyed imagery in the Ashvin stories above is, in some views, appropriately connected to solar characteristics.

These deities hold a very important place in the Veda, though in the Puranas their place is quite ordinary: they are merely the physicians of the gods, of very radiant form.

Savitr, Surya, Mitra, Pushan, and Vishnu can, in a sense, be treated as a single deity under different names — though because the sun performs varied functions, each function came to be regarded as its own distinct deity.

The root of "Savitr" means: to give energy (chaitanya) and to fill with brilliance. After sunrise the sun's brilliance grows steadily; in this state the sun is called "Savitr." Per Sayanacharya, the sun is called "Savitr" before sunrise and "Surya" from rising until setting; Yaska holds that "Savitr" enters once the darkness has gone and light has spread across the whole sky.

Many suktas are devoted to Savitr, who — seated in a golden chariot — destroys darkness and grants people the things they desire, and who stirs and inspires the human mind. Among all Vedic mantras addressed to Savitr, the most important and significant is the **Gayatri** — renowned as the "mother of the Vedas."

This Gayatri is the tenth mantra of the 62nd sukta in Mandala 3, and recurs in the Samaveda (1462), the Shukla Yajurveda's Vajasaneyi Samhita (3-35; 22-9; 30-2; 36-3), the Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya Samhita (1-5-7-4 and 4-1-11-1), and the Taittiriya Aranyaka (1-11-3). In the Rigveda this mantra is nowhere found to be called "Gayatri"; in the Yajurveda, praise of the Gayatri is abundant.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 218</div>

Surya is so called when wholly luminous; he is the son of Dyauh (Heaven) and Aditi; Ushas is his wife. Seven horses draw his chariot; he gives life to the world of the moving and the unmoving, and is witness to the acts of all beings. In later Puranic texts, this deity retains only a small, ordinary place, considered subordinate to the world's greater regulating powers. The ṛks addressed to Surya in the Rigveda are only 60½.

##### Mitra {.lv3}

One entire sukta is devoted to Mitra (III-59); elsewhere he is praised jointly with Varuna, without particular individual emphasis on his own glory.

##### Pushan {.lv3}

This deity knows all paths and guards travelers from dangers — thieves, wild animals, and the like. He is guardian of cattle, bringing them safely home (VI-53-56), and watches over all beings. He rides a chariot yoked with goats, a staff in his hand, and is skilled in bringing back lost things.

##### Vishnu {.lv3}

Relatively few mantras are dedicated to Vishnu alone — he is generally praised jointly with Indra or Agni ("Indra-Vishnu," "Agni-Vishnu"). In later Puranic tradition, Vishnu attains the highest position, some texts even granting him supreme overlordship — but in the Vedas, he holds only an ordinary place.

Vishnu is described as measuring the world in three steps — understood as measuring the earth, the atmosphere, and the sun's orb in the sky with these three forms; some read the three steps as sunrise, midday, and sunset. Later Puranic tradition elaborated this into the full story of the three worlds (heaven, earth, netherworld) oppressed by an Asura king, whereupon Vishnu, in the guise of Vamana (the dwarf), requested three paces of land from the demon-king Bali, then assumed his true form to measure the three worlds, thereby reclaiming the kingdom through this charitable pretext and subduing the Asura. Vishnu is also celebrated for aiding Indra in the Vritrasura-slaying episode; he is also the creator of Surya, Agni, Ushas, and others.

Vishnu carries a further name, "Shipivishta," bearing two possible senses — "one whose radiance is concealed," or "possessing intense brightness." On this (VII-100-6), Tilak's *Arctic Home* states:

> "The poet, therefore, asks Vishnu not to be ashamed of this epithet, because says he, the form indicated by the bad name is only temporarily assumed as a dark armour for the purpose of fighting the Asuras, and as it was no longer needed, Vishnu is invoked to reveal his true form to the worshipper."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 219</div>

This unfavorable form was assumed only temporarily, for defeating demons; once that task was accomplished, the form became unnecessary, hence worshippers pray for Vishnu to reveal his true form.

Sayanacharya generally explains Vishnu's name via "pervasion" (vyapti) — the root *viś* meaning "to enter/pervade." Prof. Bloomfield offers a new derivation, vi + snu. In support, the Samaveda (2-1024) states: *"yasyoru viṣṇur vicakrame pṛthivyām adhi śānave"* — "Vishnu, who strode across the earth."

Vishnu is credited with creating heaven and earth, and his qualities across past, present, and future are impossible to fully determine — his capability knows no limit; he pervades everything.

##### Ushas (Dawn) {.lv3}

No other deity receives mantras as sweetly and beautifully composed as those for Ushas — roughly 20 suktas across the Rigveda are dedicated to her, with Mandala 7's suktas 75–81 devoted to her entirely. "This radiant deity, granting a full life through her own light, spreads across all directions" (III-61-4).

Ushas is daughter of Dyauh (Sky) and sister of Ratri (Night); Surya is her beloved. She is mistress of the world, bringing things into being and taking form again and again, moving swiftly to dispel darkness and awaken everyone to their tasks. She wakens sleepers and, having banished darkness, brings joy to all. Born anew each time, she is called ever-youthful (yuvati), yet is also eternal — all living beings' lives depend on her. Vedic-era poets described dawn this way and being a ritualist he could not fail to describe Ushas' part in the yajnas; she is the starting-time of the yajnas and their forerunner, and in many places she is prayed to grant wealth, progeny, and the like.

Per Tilak's reading, the Ushas so described is not the daily dawn but the dawn of the polar regions, where sunrise is preceded by dawn-light persisting for many days running. Elsewhere, the following verse conveys this same idea:

> तानीदहानि बहुलान्यासन् या प्राचीनमुदिता सूर्यस्य । यतः परि जार इवाचरन्त्युषो ददृश्रे न पुनर्यतीव ॥ (VII-76-3)
>
> *tānīd ahāni bahulāny āsan yā prācīnam uditā sūryasya | yataḥ pari jāra ivācarantyuṣo dadṛśre na punaryatīva ||*
>
> "Those were indeed many days that passed before the sun's rising, during which Dawn was seen moving about like a lover [going to her beloved], as though she would never return again."

In this "sunrise-becoming" period, many days passed, during which Ushas moved like an infatuated young woman heading to meet her beloved — implying both a many-day gap between the horizon's reddening and actual sunrise, and that all those days were counted as belonging to a single extended "Dawn." For the words "ahāni bahulāni" ("many days") here, Sayanacharya and other scholars offer differing interpretations.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 220</div>

The philosophical tradition found in the Rigveda connects to India's much broader philosophical heritage. Our country is renowned as a land of philosophy — from ancient times, people here have fearlessly questioned life's uncertainties and pursued answers relentlessly. From royal sages like Janaka and Ajatashatru, to Yajnavalkya, Nachiketa, and other Brahmin thinkers, to Shankaracharya, Kumarila Bhatta, and various social reformers, our country has deeply engaged with the world's philosophical foundations — so it is only natural that the seeds of this enduring philosophical tendency should already appear in the Rigveda itself.

The subject of philosophy is nowhere stated with full clarity in the hymns, nor addressed directly by ordinary devotional suktas — yet, in a manner anticipating the Upanishads, philosophical inquiry does begin to surface within the Samhita, if less prominently than later. Generally, in the Rigveda, natural forces have each become distinct deities — but a single, deep divine power manifesting in many forms is also glimpsed:

> एकं॒ सद्विप्रा॑ बहु॒धा व॑दन्त्य॒ग्निं य॒मं मा॑त॒रिश्वा॑नमाहुः ॥ (I-164-46)
>
> *ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ ||*
>
> "That which is One, the wise call by many names: they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan."

That is: the wise refer to one single reality by various names — Agni, Yama, Matarishvan — implying that all deities are different forms of a single underlying deity. This sukta (1-164) more broadly touches on the five elements, historical matters, and psychological subjects too — heaven and earth, days, months and years, human birth and life-rites, the origin of life, and the workings of the world are all treated within it.

While performing yajnas and similar rites, rishis began attending closely to their practical benefits and planning accordingly — but ritual technique alone didn't satisfy their minds; curiosity about the true origin of things led them into genuine inquiry and debate. In this process, simple faith in deities embodied in human-like form began to waver, giving way to the understanding that nature and its many aspects are manifestations of one divine power taking different forms.

Questions like "Who am I? Where did I come from? How did this varied universe come into being?" seem to have persistently occupied the rishis' minds. Though the things prayed for in the Veda are largely worldly — wealth, cattle, land, progeny, and similar earthly goods — questions of life, death, and what follows death clearly occupied their thoughts as well. Because the rishis held a strong desire to continue living, they came to believe that life in the world of the deities, after death, would be eternal — giving this the name "amritatva" (deathlessness).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 221</div>

Many speculative accounts exist regarding this world's origin and beginning. In (X-121), Hiranyagarbha is named as the cause of creation; in the Purusha-sukta (X-90), the cosmic Virat-Purusha is described as the world's root cause; in the 82nd sukta (X-82), everything is said to arise from water alone.

In Mandala 10's famous **Nasadiya-sukta** (X-129; "nāsad āsīt..."), the pre-creation state of the universe is described as an indescribable, wondrous condition — its treatment of creation aligns remarkably with modern scientific causal reasoning, and contains philosophical perspectives fresh even by later standards.

Whatever the case, the hopeful spirit (asha) so characteristic of the Veda is uniquely its own, renowned among ancient scriptures generally.

**Note:** The subject of the deities has been treated only very briefly in this chapter. Going forward, wherever a specific deity's suktas come up for explanation, that deity's subject matter will be discussed as extensively and thoroughly as possible.

## Chapter Twelve — Meters (Chandas)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 221</div>

Across every language, the most celebrated, elevated texts are composed in meter (chandobaddha). In Sanskrit, the Puranas, Dharmashastras, and Kavyas are all metrical works; the Vedas follow this same pattern, falling under metrical composition. Several reasons likely explain why verse became the norm from the very beginning. First: feelings naturally take the form of rhythm or meter (chandas) more readily than plain prose — meter meaning the patterned arrangement of high and low, long and short sounds. All mantras were composed to please the deities, and verse sung to a tune delights the mind more than dry prose. Above all, in a time without writing materials, the vast mass of the Veda could be preserved over long ages only in verse. Since metrical texts are far easier to memorize and retain than prose — a matter of common experience — the Vedas came to be composed in verse.

The Shiksha texts, discussing the defining characteristics of meter, state—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 222</div>

##### "छन्दः पादौ तु वेदस्य" ("Chandas is the Veda's feet") {.lv3}

Just as legs are necessary for a person to stand, meter (chandas) is equally necessary for the Vedas to endure, unaltered, across time.

The word "Chandas" derives from the root *chad* ("to please, delight" — *chadi āhlādane*). As already noted, the Veda's chief purpose is to please the deities and bring joy to those attending yajnas — over time, "Chandas" itself came to mean "Veda."

Because Vedic Sanskrit's grammar and meters are, from a modern standpoint, less strictly regularized than classical Sanskrit, the term "Bhāndasa" (i.e., "Chandas-style," archaic Vedic usage) came to cover all Vedic linguistic forms generally — and in more recent usage, "Bhandasa" has come to mean, simply, "irregular."

Chandas is one of the six Vedangas. Among works on the subject, Pingala's treatise is the oldest, covering not only Vedic meters but classical Sanskrit meters as well.

Vedic meters show no particularly rigid internal pattern — no fixed rule governs the placement of short or long vowels, or heavy/light syllables (guru-laghu). Only the **total syllable-count** distinguishes one meter from another.

The Rigveda's many suktas each contain several mantras; each mantra has two or more feet (pada) — generally three or four — and each pada has eight or more syllables. Below is given the Rigveda's principal meters, their sub-varieties, and details of pada-count, syllable-count, defining rule (sutra), an example mantra, and its location:

##### "अथ छन्दसामुदाहरणानि" — "Now, Examples of the Meters" {.lv3}

The source opens this section with a versified mnemonic listing meter-openings in compressed form:

> अयं देवाया, ऽऽभिष्टे अद्या, ऽग्ने तमद्य, ता मे अश्व्यानां, त्वावतः, पुरूतमं, स सुन्वे यो, ईशाना, आपः पृणीत, प्रेष्ठं दश ॥ ४ ॥ (१)
> *ayaṃ devāyā, ''bhiṣṭe adyā, 'gne tam adya, tā me aśvyānāṃ, tvāvataḥ, purūtamaṃ, sa sunve yo, īśānā, āpaḥ pṛṇīta, preṣṭhaṃ daśa || 4 || (1)*
>
> *(a mnemonic verse stringing together the opening words of the ten example-mantras in the table below)*

**Table of meters (columns: Meter-type | Syllable-count | Per-foot syllable pattern & rule | Example mantra's opening words | Mantra location [Mandala-Sukta-Mantra])**

| Meter-type | Syllables | Pattern | Sutra (rule) | Example (opening) | Location |

As already noted, apart from total syllable-count, no other rule governs these meters — but even this rule doesn't hold perfectly everywhere. Where a pada should carry a certain syllable-count, occasional variance appears — 11 syllables in a pada that should have 12, and 10 where there should be 11. In the verse given earlier as an example of the Pankti meter, the fourth pada in fact has only seven syllables rather than the expected eight:

> रथं हिरण्ययं दर्भ *(3rd pada)*
> मंहिष्ठः सूरिरभूत् *(4th pada)*
> वर्षिष्ठ मुक्रथश्रवः *(5th pada)*

Whether this variance arose from carelessness on the part of the Vedic poets themselves, or from some discrepancy that crept into the text as it has come down to us, cannot be said with certainty.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 230</div>

Two opinions exist on this subject. Some hold that the Vedas, being non-human in origin (apaurusheya), faultless, and sacred, make it inappropriate to imagine any discrepancy in the received text — such readers take it upon themselves to somehow reconcile any apparent metrical irregularity wherever it appears. Others hold that acknowledging discrepancies in the received text is acceptable. Neither view should be adopted unconditionally in full; a middle path between the two is more appropriate. The view of the learned is to follow a change of reading where one change applies to many mantras, and a change of metre where the metre is accepted as slightly altered and this applies to many mantras.

Scholars have agreed on the following legitimate methods for reconciling apparent metrical deficiencies:

**(1)** When two vowels that would ordinarily combine by sandhi occur — the preceding vowel eliding into the following — they should instead be read separately, avoiding the combination. This generally applies when *i, ī, u, ū* combine with *a* or *ā*, producing elision; in such cases, the elided vowel should be restored and read separately.

> प्रेद्धो अग्ने दीदिहि पुरो नो (7-1-3)
>
> *preddho agne dīdihi puro no*

This is in the Trishtubh meter, which should carry 11 syllables per pada — but as printed, only ten appear. Therefore "preddho" should be read (restored) as "pra iddho":

> प्रेद्धो अग्ने दीदिहि पुरो नोऽजस्रया सूर्म्या यविष्ठ ।
> *preddho agne dīdihi puro no'jasrayā sūrmyā yaviṣṭha |*

Here, instead of "sūrmyā," it may be read (restored) as "su ūrmi ā."

**(2)** Where an "-aḥ" ending or an elided "-e" ending has been lost, it should be restored and read as its own separate syllable.

> अग्नयोऽग्निभ्यो *(restored: अग्नयो अग्निभ्यो)* (7-1-4)
> वनस्पतेऽव *(restored: वनस्पते अव)* (7-2-10)

**(3)** In several words, the letters "y" and "r" (where historically derived from vowels via sandhi) should be restored to their original vowel form as separate syllables.

> प्रजावतीषु दुर्यासु दुर्य (7-1-11)
>
> *restored:* प्रजावतीषु दुरि आय दुर्य

**(4)** In some words, a long vowel, or the letters "e" and "o," should be read as two separate short vowel-sounds.

> ययोरसुर्य १ मक्षितं ज्येष्ठं (7-65-1)
>
> *restored:* ययोरसुर्य १ मक्षितं ज्ययिष्ठं

> वृष्टिं परिज्मा वातो ददातु । (7-40-6)
>
> *restored, as printed:* वृष्टिं परिज्मा वातो ददातु (7-40-6) — *vṛṣṭiṃ parijmā vāto dadātu* (the print shows no visible change in this line)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 231</div>

**(5)** Some words are commonly written incorrectly — for example, "pāvaka" is to be read "pavāka," and "suvānaḥ" as "svānaḥ." Many such words exist.

Not everyone accepts that these meters' defining characteristic lies in total syllable-count alone; scholars in our own country have not focused closely on this question, and opinions here vary. Western scholars, however, have pursued the matter further — examining whether any deeper rhythmic system underlies the syllable-arrangement of these mantras. It would be wrong to think the poets composed with mechanical, rule-bound precision; yet careful examination shows no single fixed method either — one context favors one meter, another avoids it, for reasons that vary. It appears that meaning alone was not given priority in these mantras; they must also be pleasing to the ear. From this balance of meaning and rhythmic structure together, it can be said with confidence that this poetry was composed with real craft.

**Prof. Arnold** wrote a book titled *Vedic Metre*, in which he identifies **four stages** in the development of Vedic meter:

**(1)** Spontaneous composition, done in a spirit of competition with one another. Mantras from this period show considerable variation in their parts, both external and internal. Mandalas 6 and 7 belong to this period.

**(2)** Free composition gradually becomes systematized and takes on fixed structure — the Gayatri and Trishtubh meters predominate here. Mandalas 3, 4, and 9 belong to this group.

**(3)** Trishtubh and Jagati meters increasingly predominate. A large portion of Mandala 1 and a small portion of Mandala 10 belong to this — the "middle period."

**(4)** Beyond this, the meters already mentioned continued in free use — most of Mandala 10 belongs to this final period.

Vedic poets were master craftsmen in the art of poetry — later poets do not compare to them in syllabic arrangement and rhythm. It is Prof. Arnold's view that modern scholars can see a development in the use of meter as well.

## Chapter Thirteen — Commentators on the Rigveda

<div class="pgmark">original p. 232</div>

Many commentators have written Rigveda commentaries (bhashya) since ancient times. Modern scholars too have tried to explain the Vedic meaning in the vernacular languages as it seemed to them. Without taking up the habit of reviewing such vernacular translations by moderns, the commentaries and explanations written in Sanskrit by the ancient scholars, with brief accounts of their lives, will be set out here as the occasion arises.

The earliest attempt at explaining the Vedas is found in the Brahmanas themselves. In time the Brahmanas also came to be counted as Vedas, and since they contain many matters besides the meaning of the Veda, it does not seem very fitting to place the Brahmanas in the class of Veda-commentaries.

Setting the Brahmanas aside, the first to attempt the meaning of the Veda were the Nirukta-writer Yaska. Since Yaska too cites many commentators earlier than himself, there may have been many commentators more ancient than he, but their works have not come down to us and are not likely to be found; so Yaska may be reckoned the first commentator. Since his Nirukta covers only some of the ṛks of the Rigveda, does not in many places explain the ṛks fully and in order, and also gives his own opinions, it cannot easily be called a Veda-commentary. Moreover, the Nirukta is counted as one of the Vedangas; so, without taking up Yaska here, this chapter gives brief life-histories of 16 commentators, beginning with Skandasvami.

Among these commentators, those who completed a full commentary specifically on the Rigveda are rare. **Sayanacharya alone** wrote commentaries on all four Vedas, somewhat more extensively than anyone else; no one has written more fully. For this reason, Sayana's commentary deserves particular emphasis.

##### 1. Skandasvami {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 630 CE)*

As far as currently known, the earliest Rigveda commentator is **Skandasvami**. Well-known later commentators drew on statements from his commentary. At the end of the first Adhyaya of the first Ashtaka a verse about him occurs; the same verse recurs at the end of the fourth Ashtaka.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 233</div>

> वल्लभी विनिवास्ये तावृग्गर्थागमसंश्रुतिं । भर्तृध्रुवसुतश्चैव स्कंदस्वामी यथाश्रुति ॥
>
> *vallabhī vinivāsye tāvṛg-garthāgama-saṃśrutiṃ | bhartṛdhruva-sutaś caiva skandasvāmī yathāśruti ||*
>
> "Residing at Vallabhi, having thoroughly learned the meaning and tradition of the Rik — the son of Bhartridhruva, Skandasvami, as tradition relates."

Skandasvami was from the Vallabhi region; his father was Bhartridhruva. His period is dated to around 630 CE, on the strength of some supporting evidence, allowing the confident statement that he composed his Rigveda commentary around that date.

Harisvami, who composed a commentary on the Shatapatha Brahmana, records in his own text:

> नागस्वामी तत्र ... श्रीगुहस्वामिनन्दनः । तत्र याजी प्रमाणज्ञ आढ्यो अल्काकृतः समेधितः ॥ तन्नन्दनो हरिस्वामी प्रस्फुरद्वेदवेदिनिर्जः । त्रियावाख्यानाध्श्रीयोऽद्गीतंत्क्रो गुरोर्मुखात् ॥ युक सम्राट् कृतवान् सप्तसोमुसंस्का स्तथक्कृतिं । व्याख्यां कृत्वाध्यापयन् श्री स्कंदस्वाम्यस्ति सेवे गुरुः ॥
>
> *(A genealogical verse, difficult to render with full grammatical precision at this resolution, tracing a teacher-lineage: Nagasvami, son of Shri Guhasvami; his own accomplished son Harisvami, renowned in Vedic knowledge, who received exposition directly from his teacher's own mouth and composed further ritual texts; concluding: "Having composed and taught a commentary, I serve Shri Skandasvami as my teacher.")*

That is: Harisvami was the grandson of Guhasvami, son of Nagasvami, and a disciple of Skandasvami, the Rigveda commentator. Elsewhere in the same text, Harisvami states his own date:

> युदाब्दानां कलेर्जग्न्य सप्तत्रिंशच्छतानि वै । चत्वारिंशच्च मासाश्चाष्ट स्यात् तदा भाष्यमिदं कृतम् ॥
>
> *yudābdānāṃ kaler jagnya saptatriṃśac-chatāni vai | catvāriṃśac ca māsāś cāṣṭa syāt tadā bhāṣyam idaṃ kṛtam ||*
>
> "When 3,700 years of the Kali era had elapsed, along with 40 [more] years — then this commentary was composed."

That is: Harisvami composed his Shatapatha Brahmana commentary in the 3,740th year of the Kali era. By one reckoning, the Kali era began in 3102 BCE, placing this commentary's composition around 638 CE. Since Skandasvami's own commentary predates this, his period can be dated to approximately **630 CE**.

Skandasvami did not write a commentary on the entire Rigveda. Among surviving manuscripts, a complete commentary exists only for the first Ashtaka; only partial commentary survives for the second through fifth Ashtakas. One manuscript notes Skandasvami's commentary concluding at the end of the fourth Ashtaka's 32nd Adhyaya; another notes the commentary running up to 6-75-6. These manuscripts are held in the Trivandrum, Adyar, and Madras Government libraries, and this commentary has recently been printed in Travancore.

Skandasvami holds that the Vedas are primarily meant for use in yajnas; at the start of every sukta, he provides a verse or gloss identifying that sukta's rishi and deities. In his view, knowledge of meter (chandas) is unnecessary for understanding the Veda's meaning.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 234</div>

> न छन्दः । अनुपयुज्यमानवचनत्वादिति ।
> *na chandaḥ | anupayujyamāna-vacanatvād iti |*
>

Skandasvami cites many authorities from the Nighantu, Nirukta, and Brihaddevata, using phrases like "smaranam," "smṛti," "smaranti," "kecit" ("some say"). In the fourth Ashtaka, commenting on mantra 7-35-4's words "viṣṭhitaṃ jagat," he writes:

> केचित्तु—विश्वशब्दः स्थावरवचनः जगदित्येतेन समुच्चीयते स्थावरं जङ्गमं च बुध्यतामिति—एवं व्याचक्षते
> *kecit tu — viśva-śabdaḥ sthāvara-vacanaḥ jagad ity etena samuccīyate sthāvaraṃ jaṅgamaṃ ca budhyatām iti — evaṃ vyācakṣate*
>
> "But some explain thus: the word *viśva* denotes the stationary; it is combined with *jagat*, so that both the stationary and the moving are to be understood."

This makes clear that Vedic commentators existed even before Skandasvami himself.

##### 2. Narayana {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 630 CE)*

Venkata Madhava writes in his own commentary:

> स्कंदस्वामी नारायण उद्गीथ इति श्री क्रमात् । चक्रुः सप्तैकवग्वाख्यं पदवाक्यार्थगोचरं ॥
>
> *(Stating that Skandasvami, Narayana, and Udgitha composed a commentary together, in due succession, covering the meaning of words and sentences.)*

That is: Skandasvami, Narayana, and Udgitha together composed one Rigveda commentary. Narayana's own portion has not yet been located; a manuscript in the possession of Pandit Sambashiva Shastri contains only small portions of the fifth and seventh Ashtakas.

It is conjectured that the Samaveda commentator **Madhava Pandita** was Narayana's son. Madhava Pandita gives a brief self-introduction:

> स्कंदस्वामिसच्चनारायणपण्डितस्य सुतश्चेति संभाव्य माधवपण्डितस्य कृतौ सामवेदव्याख्यायां...
>
> *(Identifying himself as son of the Pandit Narayana, associate of Skandasvami, in his own Samaveda commentary.)*

And:

> पंचाग्निना माधवेन श्रीनारायणसूनुना सनितुः परां भक्तिमालंब्य तत्प्रसादात् भाष्यं कृतम् ।
>
> *(By Madhava, maintainer of the five sacred fires, son of Shri Narayana, having relied on supreme devotion to Savitr [the Sun], through whose grace this commentary was composed.)*

Madhava Pandita opens his own commentary with this invocation:

> ॐ श्रीगणपतये नमः । ॐ नमः सानुवेदाय । रक्षे जुषे जन्यसत्यव्रत्ये स्थितौ प्रजानां प्रलये तमःस्पृशे । अजाय सर्गस्थितिनाशहेतवे त्रियामयाय त्रिगुणात्मने नमः ॥
>
> *(An invocation to the unborn, threefold, three-gunas-embodying deity, cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution.)*

This same auspicious verse also appears in Banabhatta's *Kadambari*. Since it's implausible that the Samaveda-commentator Madhava Pandita borrowed this verse from Bana, Madhava Pandita must predate Bana, who lived in the first half of the 7th century CE. It follows that Narayana — Skandasvami's associate and Madhava's father — lived around 630 CE, placing Skandasvami himself in this same period, as already established.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 235</div>

##### 3. Udgitha {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 630 CE)*

Skandasvami's second associate. Both Sayanacharya and Atmananda cite Udgitha's statements in their own commentaries. A manuscript of this commentary, covering Rigveda 10-5-7 through 10-83-5, is held by Bhagavaddatta of Lahore, author of *Vaidika Vangmaya kā Itihāsa* (History of Vedic Literature). Udgitha identifies himself at the end of each chapter with this formula:

> वनवासी विनिर्गताचार्यस्य उद्गीथस्य कृतौ ऋग्वेदभाष्ये चतुष्पंचाशोऽध्यायः समाप्तः ।
>
> *vanavāsī vinirgatācāryasya udgīthasya kṛtau ṛgvedabhāṣye catuṣpañcāśo'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ |*
>
> "In the work of the teacher Udgitha, who came from Vanavasi [or Vallabhi], in this Rigveda commentary, the fifty-fourth chapter is concluded."

"Vanavasi" here may originally have read "Vallabhi-vinivasi" — if "vinirgata" means "having come from elsewhere and settled," this would identify Udgitha as a resident of the Vallabhi region [the same region as Skandasvami]. Like Skandasvami, Udgitha holds that the Veda serves yajna purposes, though he does not record each sukta's rishi and deity — likely expecting readers to consult the Arshanukramani directly for that.

##### 4. Hastamalaka {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 700 CE)*

Hastamalaka was one of Shankaracharya's four famous disciples. The Veda-commentary attributed to this name is understood to have actually been written by a later person sharing the name — no copy of it has been found, nor has substantial supporting evidence.

##### 5. Venkata Madhava {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 1100–1200 CE)*

Sayanacharya's own commentary on 10-86-1 states that Madhavabhatta holds the mantra beginning "vi hi sotoḥ" to be Indrani's own statement — a view found in Venkata Madhava's commentary. This confirms Venkata Madhava predates Sayanacharya.

The Nighantu-commentator Devarajayajva (1313 CE) also predates Sayanacharya. In the introduction to his own Nighantu-commentary, he writes:

> श्रीवेंकटाचार्यतनयस्य माधवस्य भाष्यकृतौ नानानुक्रमण्याः...सरालोचनात्...स्कंदस्वामि–भवस्वामि–गुहदेव–श्रीनिवास–माधवदेव–उवट–भट्टभास्करमिश्र–भरतस्वाम्यादि विरचितानि वेदभाष्या...निरीक्ष्य क्रियते ॥
>
> *(Devarajayajva states that his own work draws on the various Anukramanis and on the Veda-commentaries composed by Skandasvami, Bhavasvami, Guhadeva, Shrinivasa, Madhavadeva, Uvata, Bhatta Bhaskaramishra, Bharatasvami, and others, in the commentarial tradition of Madhava, son of Shri Venkatacharya.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 236</div>

Devarajayajva writes that his commentary is made after examining the Namanukramani in the commentary of Madhava, son of Venkatacharya, and the commentaries of other acharyas — confirming Venkata Madhava predates Devarajayajva.

Keshavasvami's *Nānārthārṇavasaṃkṣepa* (before 1300 CE) gives the meaning "horse" (ashva) for the word "go," citing Venkata Madhava as authority:

> दृयोःस्त्व्ये तथा ह्याड स्कंदस्वाम्यश्च भूरिशः । माधवाचार्यसूरिश्च कोऽद्येत्कृच्च भाषके ॥
>
> *(A verse invoking Skandasvami and Madhava Acharya as authorities among commentators; precise construction difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

Venkata Madhava himself, at the end of the 8th Ashtaka's 3rd chapter, indicates his own era:

> विकोनषष्ट मध्यायं व्याकरोदितिमाधवः । जगतावेकवीरस्य विषये निवसत्सुखम् ॥
>
> *vikonaṣaṣṭa madhyāyaṃ vyākarod itimādhavaḥ | jagatāv ekavīrasya viṣaye nivasat sukham ||*
>
> "Madhava composed this — the fifty-ninth chapter — dwelling happily in the domain of [King] Ekavira in the world."

That is: he resided in the kingdom of a king named Ekavira. Among Chola-dynasty kings, five bore the name "Vira"; their reigns were as follows:

| King | Reign (CE) |
|---|---|
| Virarajendra | 1062–1070 |
| Vira Chola I | 1078–1088 |
| Vira Chola II | 1135–1149 |
| Vira Chola III | 1183–1206 |
| Virarajendra (later) | 1207–1255 |

The most recent of these, Virarajendra, ruled up to 1255 CE — placing Venkata Madhava's own period at approximately **1200 CE**.

In his Rigveda commentary, Venkata Madhava includes a few autobiographical verses identifying himself as son of Venkatacharya, a resident of a village called Gorma in the Chola country, contemporary with King Ekavira.

Devaraja, in his own Nighantu-commentary (at 1-14-18), cites Venkata Madhava's commentary, concluding:

> इत्युक्तं (वेंकट)माधवस्य प्रथमभाष्यम् (1-14-18)
>
> "Thus stated in (Venkata) Madhava's first commentary."

Devaraja cites Venkata Madhava's commentary at many further points in his own text — but many of these cited statements are not found in the Venkata Madhava commentary currently available. It's possible Venkata Madhava composed **two separate commentaries**.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 237</div>

##### Manuscript Copies of Venkata Madhava's First Commentary {.lv3}

1. Travancore Government Library — the first Adhyaya of the first Ashtaka.
2. In the possession of Pandit Sambashiva Shastri.
3. Madras Government Oriental Manuscripts Library (Devanagari script) — lacks the fourth Ashtaka; corrupted in places.
4. Travancore Government Library (second copy) — only the last four Ashtakas.
5. Mysore Government Library — from the middle of the first Ashtaka's third chapter to the end of the first Ashtaka.
6. Travancore Government Library (third copy) — only the first and second Ashtakas.
7. Punjab University Library, Lahore — mostly complete.
8. Dayananda College Library, Lahore — mostly complete.
9. Dr. Malayalamkar's private collection — his two copies contain the commentary of the first and eighth Ashtakas.

Apart from the Lahore manuscripts, all the rest are probably incomplete. Drawing on these along with other supporting texts, Dr. Svarupa published this Venkata Madhava commentary in four parts; a copy of this edition is held at the Mysore Government Oriental Library.

##### The Special Features of Venkata Madhava's First Commentary {.lv3}

**(1)** This commentary generally follows the yajna-oriented tradition. Like Skandasvami's and others', it is not lengthy — quite concise, in fact. The mantra's own text is woven directly into the commentary's wording; word-derivation (padasiddhi) is not extensively explained wherever it occurs. On his own brevity, Venkata Madhava writes:

> वर्जयन् शब्दविस्तरम् । शब्दैकगतिसंय्यैरिति
>
> "Avoiding elaboration of words... by a single, direct course of expression."

That is: he states there is no wordy elaboration in this commentary, though he claims to have attempted explaining every meaning, even if only briefly.

**(2)** Venkata Madhava made an unusually thorough study of the Brahmana texts, evident throughout his commentary. In his view, the Veda's meaning cannot easily be understood without knowing the Brahmana texts.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 238</div>

Venkata Madhava's own verse on his methodology:

> अस्माभिस्त्विह मन्त्राणामर्थः प्रत्येकमुच्यते । येऽज्ञाता ये च संदिग्धास्तेषां वृद्धेषु निर्णयः ॥ संहितायास्तुरीयांशं विजानन्त्यधुनातनाः । निरुक्तव्याकरणयोरासीद्येषां परिश्रमः ॥ अथ ये ब्राह्मणार्थानां विवेक्तारः कृतश्रमाः । शब्दरीतिं विजानन्ति ते सर्वं कथयन्त्यपि ॥ ताण्डके शाट्यायनके श्रमः शतपथेऽपि च । कौषीतके काठके च स्याद्यस्येह स पण्डितः ॥ ऐतरेयकमस्माकं पैप्पलादमथर्वणम् । तृतीयं तित्तिरिप्रोक्तं जानन् वृद्ध इहोच्यते ॥ न भाल्लविकमस्माभिस्तथा मैत्रायणीयकम् । ब्राह्मणं चरकाणां च श्रुतं मन्त्रोपबृंहणम् ॥
> *asmābhis tv iha mantrāṇām arthaḥ pratyekam ucyate | ye'jñātā ye ca saṃdigdhās teṣāṃ vṛddheṣu nirṇayaḥ || saṃhitāyās turīyāṃśaṃ vijānanty adhunātanāḥ | niruktavyākaraṇayor āsīd yeṣāṃ pariśramaḥ || atha ye brāhmaṇārthānāṃ vivektāraḥ kṛtaśramāḥ | śabdarītiṃ vijānanti te sarvaṃ kathayanty api || tāṇḍake śāṭyāyanake śramaḥ śatapathe'pi ca | kauṣītake kāṭhake ca syād yasyeha sa paṇḍitaḥ || aitareyakam asmākaṃ paippalādam atharvaṇam | tṛtīyaṃ tittiriproktaṃ jānan vṛddha ihocyate || na bhāllavikam asmābhis tathā maitrāyaṇīyakam | brāhmaṇaṃ carakāṇāṃ ca śrutaṃ mantropabṛṃhaṇam ||*
>
> *(Explaining that mantra-meanings should be settled, where unknown or doubtful, by consulting the elders; that present-day scholars versed only in Nirukta and grammar know but a quarter of the Saṃhitā; and that true scholarship requires knowledge of the Brahmana texts across many shakhas — the Tandya, Shatyayana, Shatapatha, Kaushitaka, Kathaka, Aitareya, Paippalāda (Atharvaṇa) and Taittirīya Brāhmaṇas — while the Bhāllavi, Maitrāyaṇīya and Caraka Brāhmaṇas were not heard by him.)*

That is: in this commentary, each mantra's meaning is explained individually; where a meaning is unknown or doubtful, it is determined by those versed in the Brahmana texts. Among modern scholars, those skilled only in Nirukta and grammar can grasp merely a quarter of the Rik Samhita's meaning — full understanding requires mastery of the Brahmana portions and the ritual procedures (karmangas) they describe. Those versed in the Tandya, Shatyayana, Shatapatha, Kaushitaka, and Kathaka Brahmanas are called scholars (panditas); one who knows our Aitareya Brahmana, the Paippalada of the Atharvana, and the Taittiriya Brahmana is called an "elder" (vriddha). Venkata Madhava states he has not heard the Brahmana portions explaining the mantras of the Bhallavi, Maitrayaniya, and Charaka traditions.

This shows that Venkata Madhava studied the Aitareya, Kaushitaka, Shatapatha, Taittiriya, Katha, Tandya, Shatyayana, and Paippalada Brahmanas — but the Bhallavi, Maitrayaniya, and Charaka Brahmanas did not come to him. Beyond all these, the **Shatyayana Brahmana** is cited most extensively in this first commentary — worth noting that its readings closely resemble those of the Jaiminiya Brahmana.

**(3)** Venkata Madhava's commentary also extensively cites the Katyayana Sarvanukramani, the Nidana-sutra, the Nighantu, the Nirukta, Shaunaka, and the Brihaddevata as supporting examples. At many points he references "Nirukta" or "Yaska" generically without naming a specific passage — and generally cites the shorter/abridged recension of the Nirukta.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 239</div>

Venkata Madhava also cites the Brihaddevata extensively, generally aligning with McDonell's manuscript "A" — and at some points, his readings appear superior to McDonell's own manuscript.

**(4)** Venkata Madhava's views on the Ashtaka, Adhyaya, Varga, Mandala, Sukta and the mantras are worth seeing; they are therefore set down below:—

The divisions into Ashtaka, Adhyaya and Varga were made by the earlier rishis in order to know the positions in the Samhitas. "Thus we accept; this is certain." Words such as "varga" may be seen in the Brahmana.

Some count the number of ṛks as 10,402; the dvipadas are included in this. If the dvipadas are counted separately, the number becomes 10480. The reading "10580 ṛks and an ekapada" (found in the Anuvakanukramani, the Charanavyuha and the like) is not right. Not knowing which shakha's count the Anuvakanukramani, the Charanavyuha and the like give, Venkata Madhava rejected that count.

**(6)** Venkata Madhava holds that the Nighantu, the basis of Yaska's Nirukta, was itself composed by Yaska.

##### 6. Lakshmana {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 1092 CE)*

*Bhāvaprakāśana* is a work on poetics (Alankara), authored by Sharadatanaya (1174–1249 CE). His great-grandfather, named **Lakshmana**, composed a Rigveda commentary — not available to us directly, but Sharadatanaya's own text confirms his father composed a Veda-commentary:

> आर्यावर्ताख्यदेशे स्थितो जनपदो महान् । मेरूत्तर इति ख्यातस्स्य दक्षिणभागतः ॥ ५ ॥ ग्रामो मातरपूज्याख्यो द्विजसाहस्रसंमितः । तत्र लक्ष्मणनावासीद्द्विजः काश्यपवंशजः ॥ ६ ॥
>
> *āryāvartākhya-deśe sthito janapado mahān | merūttara iti khyātas sya dakṣiṇabhāgataḥ || grāmo mātarapūjyākhyo dvijasāhasrasaṃmitaḥ | tatra lakṣmaṇanāvāsīd dvijaḥ kāśyapavaṃśajaḥ ||*
>
> "In the land called Aryavarta lay a great region known as Meruttara, to the south of which was a village called Matarapujya, home to a thousand Brahmins. There resided Lakshmana, a Brahmin of the Kashyapa lineage."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 240</div>

> त्रिंशता क्रतुभिर्विष्णुं कोशयावास वेदवित् । वेदानां भाष्यमकरोन्न्याव्या यो वेदभूषणम् ॥ ७ ॥
>
> *triṃśatā kratubhir viṣṇuṃ kośayāvāsa vedavit | vedānāṃ bhāṣyam akaron nyāvyā yo vedabhūṣaṇam ||*
>
> "Through thirty sacrifices, this Veda-knower propitiated Vishnu; he, an ornament of the Veda, composed a commentary on the Vedas with proper method."

That is: in the village of Matarapujya, south of Meruttara, the eminent Brahmin Lakshmana, of the Kashyapa lineage, performed thirty yajnas, pleased Vishnu, and composed a Veda-commentary titled **"Vedabhushana"** ("Ornament of the Veda"). Since Sharadatanaya lived around 1174 CE, his great-grandfather Lakshmana may be conjectured to have lived about 75 years before him.

##### 7. Dhanushkayajva {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 13th century CE)*

> त्रिवेदीभाष्यकारेण धानुष्कयज्वा तु चरणशब्दस्स्वदर्शनाभिधायीति देवता विशेषस्स्वदर्शनमिति स्पष्टं व्याख्यातम् । यद्वा—महस्सत् अरवत् खवं धन्ययज्ज्ञा व्याख्यातम् । त्रयीनिष्ट विद्गेन धानुष्कयज्ज्ञा त्रिष्टि वेदभाष्येषु सप्रमाणमुपसस्त् ।
>
> *(A technical passage identifying Dhanushkayajva as commentator on all three Vedas; precise construction difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

From these statements in the Veda-acharya's *Sudarshana-mimamsa*, it is understood that a scholar named Dhanushkayajva composed commentaries on all three Vedas and belonged to the Vaishnava tradition — though these commentaries have not been located anywhere to date.

##### 8. Anandatirtha {.lv3}

*(Period: 1197–1237 CE)*

Renowned as the Acharya who established the Dvaita philosophical doctrine, known by many names — Anandatirtha-Bhagavatpadacharya, Purnaprajna, Madhva. He states his own date in his own work, the *Mahabharata-Tatparya-Nirnaya*:

> चतुस्सहस्रे त्रिशकोत्करे गते संवत्सराणां तु कलौ स्फुटिन्याम् । जातः पुनर्विप्रतनुः स भीमो दैत्यैर्निगूढं परितत्त्वमाह ॥
>
> *catussahasre triśakotkare gate saṃvatsarāṇāṃ tu kalau sphuṭinyām | jātaḥ punar vipratanuḥ sa bhīmo daityair nigūḍhaṃ paritattvam āha ||*
>
> "When four thousand and three hundred more years of the Kali era had passed, in this manifest age, he — Bhima [reborn] — took form again as a Brahmin, and declared the truth that had been concealed by demons."

That is: Madhvacharya was born after 4,300 years of the Kali era had elapsed — corresponding to **1197 CE**. Tradition holds he lived for 80 years within the Madhva tradition.

**His commentary:** composed in verse (shloka) form, covering only the Rigveda's first 40 suktas — that is, the first two chapters and a small portion of the third. Shri Raghavendra Yati, a disciple in his lineage, states in his own *Mantrartha-manjari*—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 241</div>

> ऋक्शाखागतैकोत्तरसहस्रसूक्तमध्ये कानिचिच्चत्वारिंशत् सूक्तानि भगवत्पादैः...व्याख्यातानि
>
> "Among the thousand-and-one suktas of the Rigveda shakha, some forty suktas were explained by the Bhagavatpada [Anandatirtha]."

That is, of the 101 suktas of the Rigveda, the Bhagavatpada commented on only 40.

Every manuscript of the Madhva commentary reads "ṛgbhāṣyaṃ sampūrṇam" ("the Rig-commentary is complete") right after the 40th sukta — confirming he composed commentary for exactly 40 suktas. A devoted worshipper of Vishnu, Madhva maintains throughout his works that Vishnu alone is supreme; his commentary opens accordingly:

> स पूर्णत्वप्रमाण्नं पौरुषे सूक्त ईरितः । स एवाखिलवेदार्थः सर्वशास्त्रार्थ एव च ॥
>
> *sa pūrṇatva-pramāṇnaṃ pauruṣe sūkta īritaḥ | sa evākhila-vedārthaḥ sarva-śāstrārtha eva ca ||*
>
> "He, established by proof of his own completeness, is declared in the Purusha-sukta. He alone is the meaning of the entire Veda, and indeed the meaning of all scripture."

That is: Narayana is complete/perfect, named "Purusha" in the Purusha-sukta; that same Vishnu is expounded by every Veda, and all scriptures take him alone as their true subject.

Jayatirtha, who wrote commentarial glosses on several of Anandatirtha's texts, affirms this same view in his own *Sambandha-dipika*:

> अतस्तेषां भगवत्पक्षप्रकारप्रदर्शनार्थं कासांचिदृचां भाष्यं करिष्यन्...प्रयोजनं च दर्शयति ।
>
> "Therefore, in order to demonstrate the manner of the divine [Vishnu-centered] interpretation, [Madhva], about to comment on certain verses, ... also shows his purpose."

For this very reason, Madhva interprets the word "Agni" itself as meaning "Lord" [Vishnu]:

> आह तं स्तौत्यशेषस्य पूर्वमेव हि तं प्रभुम् । ऋगर्थश्च त्रिविधो भवति । विशस्तावत्तृषिद्धाग्न्यादिरूपः । अहस्तदन्तर्गतेश्वरलक्षणः । अन्योऽध्यात्मरूपः । तत्रितयसंगृहेदं भाष्यम् ।
>
> "He speaks of that Lord, praising him first of all. And the meaning of a Rik-verse is threefold: first, as already established in the form of Agni and other deities; second, characterized by the Ishvara [Lord] dwelling within that same form; and third, in adhyatmic [inner/spiritual] form. This commentary encompasses all three together."

That is: this teacher interprets the Veda in three ways — first, addressing deities beginning with Agni; second, describing the nature of the Supreme Self residing within Agni and the others; and third, in a purely spiritual (adhyatmic) sense. But primarily, per Anandatirtha, the Veda's ultimate subject is Vishnu.

**Some special features of his commentary:**

> अग्रेणेत्वं यदग्निष्ट्वमित्यग्रे नाम शक्ष्णेशः । एवमेवाह भगवान् निरुक्तं बादरायणः ॥
>
> *(Explaining the word "Agni" as "the foremost, most excellent one"; this reading, he notes, is stated by Bhagavan Badarayana [Vyasa] himself in the Nirukta.)*

**(1)** In his commentary on the very first mantra, since the very first word is "Agni," he interprets it as "the most excellent, the foremost" — a reading he attributes to Badarayana [Vyasa] himself.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 242</div>

> ऋक्संहितायां स्वाध्याये निरुक्ते व्यासनिर्मिते ।
>
> "In the Rik Samhita, in [its] recitation-study, and in the Nirukta, composed by Vyasa..."

Since Madhva repeatedly writes "this is Vyasa's own view" at various points, he must have had access to some Vyasa-authored text as a source.

**(2)** His works cite many "shrutis" as authorities — Paingi-shruti, Barka-shruti, Tura-shruti, Ananda-shruti, Sauparni-shruti, and others — though what exactly these texts are is not clearly known today.

**(3)** On the division of the Vedas, he records Vyasa's own view, following Puranic authority:

> अनन्ताः श्च वेदानां शाखाः कर्मानुसारतः । संक्षेपं कृतवान् व्यास शिष्यश्च तदनुज्ञया ॥ अष्टकाध्यायवर्गादिभेदं च कृतवान् प्रभुः । स्वाध्यायविश्रमार्थाय तस्मात्कृत्वा विपर्ययः ॥
>
> "The Vedas' shakhas are limitless, following [various] ritual practices; Vyasa made an abridgment, as did his disciples with his permission. The Lord [Vyasa] also created the division into Ashtaka, Adhyaya, and Varga, for the sake of providing rest-points during study."

That is: both the Veda's shakha-divisions and its Ashtaka-based divisions were made by the Divine [through Vyasa] — the abridgment following usefulness in yajnas, the Ashtaka-divisions for convenience of study. This same view appears in Venkata Madhava's commentary too:

> अष्टकाध्यायविच्छेदः पुराणैर्ऋषिभिः कृतः । उद्ग्राहार्थं श्रद्धेशानामिति मन्यामहे वयम् ॥ वर्गाणामपि विच्छेद आर्ष एवेति निश्चयः । अध्ययनाय शिष्याणां विभागो वर्गशः कृतः ॥
>
> "The division into Ashtaka and Adhyaya was made by the ancient rishis — we hold this was for aiding the faithful's retention. The Varga-division too is certainly of rishi-origin, made for students' convenience in study."

This also helps confirm Venkata Madhava's chronology relative to Anandatirtha.

Anandatirtha wrote 37 works in total, including the *Mahabharata-Tatparya-Nirnaya*, *Bhagavata-Tatparya-Nirnaya*, *Gita-Tatparya-Nirnaya*, *Gita-Bhashya*, *Rig-Bhashya*, and various Upanishad-Bhashyas. Scholars of the Madhva tradition collectively call these works **"Sarvamula"** — the foundational basis of Madhva doctrine. Later disciples and their own disciples wrote commentarial glosses (tika) and notes (tippani) on these foundational texts.

#### Jayatirtha's Gloss on the Madhva-Bhashya {.lv2}

**Jayatirtha** wrote glosses on Madhvacharya's Rig-Bhashya, Gita-Bhashya, and other works — earning him the renowned title "Tikacharya" (Master of Commentarial Glosses). He lived roughly 20–25 years after Madhvacharya, and may have begun writing his works from the year 1302 CE.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 243</div>

On Rigveda 1-3-10's word "Vajinivati," Jayatirtha notes Madhva used it as an indication without a case-ending. On this, Narasimha's own Vivriti (explanatory sub-commentary on Jayatirtha) states:

> विशेषान्नमन्नवत् क्रिया वा वाजिनीति माधवव्याख्या प्रत्युक्ता ।
>
> "Whether 'special food,' 'food-like,' or an action called 'Vajini' — Madhava's interpretation here has been countered."

This shows that, per Narasimha, Jayatirtha is critiquing Madhava's own interpretation. On this same word, Venkata Madhava's and Sayana's readings run:

> वाजिनीवति अन्नवत्त्रयाती ।

In Venkata Madhava's first commentary, this word is glossed simply as "annavatī" (possessing food) — what his interpretation says in a possible second commentary cannot be determined. If Jayatirtha's critique targets both Sayana and Madhava here, his own date would need to be placed somewhat later than otherwise assumed. Regardless, Jayatirtha's explanatory work stands as solid evidence of his own scholarly caliber.

#### Narasimha's Explanatory Commentary on Jayatirtha's Gloss {.lv2}

Narasimha's Vivriti closes noting that he composed it in Shaka year 1583.
