He is evidently a fine scholar of Vedic literature, referencing the Kashika, Nirukta, Ekaksharanamamala, Dhatuvritti, Jaiminiya Mimamsa, Nighantu, Anukramani, Anukramanikabhashya, Unadi, Unadi-vritti (Panchapadi), Amarakosha, Dhananjaya, Vishva, Vararuchi, Brahmana, Kaiyata, Abhidhana, Bhagavad Gita, Chandogya-bhashya, Nyayasudha, Ujjvaladatta (Dashapadi-vritti), and the Mahabhashya — citing the Nighantu and Unadi texts especially extensively. At one point in his text:

> कर्णाटकभाषया वाड्वीति तथा महाराष्ट्रभाषया वासलेति उच्यते ।
>
> "In the Karnataka language it is called 'vāḍvī'; likewise, in the Maharashtra language, it is called 'vāsale.'"

This suggests Narasimha resided in the border region between Karnataka and Maharashtra.

### Raghavendra Yati's Mantrartha-Manjari {.lv1}

**Raghavendra Yati** is another celebrated author of the Madhva tradition, well known for his Upanishad commentaries. He also composed an independent commentary on Anandatirtha's Rig-Bhashya. In his second auspicious verse:

> संग्रहिष्यामि ऋग्भाष्यश्लोकार्थान्सुगमां स्फुटम् ।
>
> "I shall compile the meanings of the Rig-Bhashya's verses, clearly and accessibly."

In his own commentary, he cites the Shabara-bhashya, Chandrika, Aitareya-bhashya, Sutrakara-kantharava, the Gita, Kanva-shruti, and similar works — the *Mantrartha-manjari* itself standing as good testimony to Raghavendra Yati's scholarly caliber and erudition.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 244</div>

### Narayana's Explanatory Commentary on the Jayatirtha Gloss {.lv1}

Like Narasimha, another scholar named Narayana also wrote an explanatory commentary on Jayatirtha's gloss, titled *Bhāvaratna-prakāśikā*; a copy is held at the Baroda Library. He is recorded as a disciple of Raghavendra.

##### 9. Atmananda {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 1200–1300 CE)*

For an introduction to Atmananda, commentator on the "Asya Vamasya" sukta (RV 1-164-1) embedded within the Rigveda, Max Müller offers a brief note (name only) on page 123 of his *History of Ancient Sanskrit Literature*. Müller's own view is that since Atmananda cites Skanda, Bhaskara, and others but never cites Sayana, Atmananda likely lived somewhat before Sayana.

### Texts and Authors Cited by Atmananda {.lv1}

An extraordinary bibliography for a single sukta's commentary: Skandabhashya, Udgitha, Bhaskara, Shaunaka, Vedamitra, the Brihaddevata-author, the Anukramanika-author, Vishnudharmottara, Nirukta, Pushkaroktakalpa, the Bhagavad Gita, the Mahabharata, Puranas, Smritis, Padakara, Keshavacharya (a Vedanta author), Shankaracharya, Vedanti, the Upanishads, the Vishnu Purana, the Nighantu, a Sampradayajna authority, Yoga-Yajnavalkya, Vriddha-Shaunaka, a Yoga text, Shakapuni, the Pancharatra, Prashamsa, Vriddha-Manu, the author Lakshmidharacharya (Atmananda's own elder brother), Shankha, the author of the Chandrika (an Annika text), Vijnaneshvara, Atmajnana, the Yama-smriti, the Harivamsha, Sarvajna, Gadadhara, a Bhattacharya (possibly Kumarila), the Nrisimha-mantra-kalpa, the Maha-Bhagavata, Shvetashvatara, Shivadharmottara, the Yajnavalkya-smriti, the Brahmopanishat-parishishta, the Vasishtha-Ramayana, the Skanda Purana's Kalika-khanda, the Taittiriya texts, the Brahma-Gita, an unnamed commentator, Paingi-rahasya, the Ekaksharanighantu, the Bharadvaja-sutra, Bhoja, a Vartika-author, Dravidasvami (a disciple of Shankaracharya), the Vivarana, Vachaspati, the Mahayogashastra, the Bahvricha-Aranyaka, the Vasishtha-Vedanta-karika, the Ratnashastra, the Bhoja-nighantu, and the Naradiya Purana — all cited within this single commentary.

##### Atmananda's Era {.lv3}

Among these names, **Bhoja, Vijnaneshvara,** and the **Chandrika-author** are especially worth examining. The Chandrika-author is Devanabhatta himself, who also composed the Annikakhanda. Per Pandit Pandurang Vaman Kane, Vijnaneshvara's era runs from 1070 to 1100 CE; the *Smriti-chandrika*'s era begins in the early 13th century.

Who exactly Atmananda's elder brother Lakshmidharacharya was cannot be determined with certainty — he is not the same Lakshmidharacharya who composed the *Kalpataru* (in 1142 CE),

<div class="pgmark">original p. 245</div>

whose father is named Bhattahridaya, whereas Atmananda's own father is stated as Vishnuprakashaka — confirming these are two distinct individuals. From the above record it is certain that Atmananda was earlier than the year 1217. Among Vedic commentators, Atmananda cites Skanda, Udgitha, Bhaskara, and others, but never cites Sayana's examples — suggesting Atmananda lived somewhat before Sayana, and since no stronger evidence has been found so far, it must be said that his period cannot be later than the **13th century**.

#### Manuscript Copies of Atmananda's Commentary {.lv2}

Only three copies have been located: one at Baroda, one at Punjab University (Lahore), and one at the India Office, London. The Baroda copy carries no date. One Lahore copy closes with:

> शके १७२४ दुन्दुभिनाम संवत्सरे मासे श्रावण शुद्ध ८ भृगुवासरे ।
>
> "In Shaka year 1724, the year named Dundubhi, month of Shravana, 8th day of the bright fortnight, on Friday."

That is, this manuscript was copied in Vikrama Shaka 1724. The India Office manuscript likewise carries no date, but per Eggeling (who catalogued the India Office texts), it was likely copied around 1650 CE.

##### Style {.lv3}

Atmananda opens his commentary:

> अधियज्ञ विषयं स्कन्दादिभाष्यम् । निरुक्तमधिदैवतविषयम् । इदं तु भाष्यमध्यात्मविषयमिति । न च भिन्नविषयाणां विरोधः । अस्य भाष्यस्य मूलं विष्णुधर्मोत्तरम् ।
>
> "Skanda's and similar commentaries treat the adhiyajna (ritual) subject; the Nirukta treats the adhidaivata (deity) subject; this present commentary treats the adhyatma (inner-self/spiritual) subject. There is no contradiction among these differing subjects. The root source of this commentary is the Vishnudharmottara."

That is: Skanda's commentary and similar works address the ritual dimension, the Nirukta the deity-dimension, and Atmananda's own commentary the spiritual dimension — with the Vishnudharmottara as its foundational source.

Atmananda was an **Advaitin**, following Shankara's philosophy, and the spirit of Advaita surfaces throughout his commentary. His treatment of one famous Rigveda mantra illustrates this well:

> इन्द्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुरथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान् । एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्यग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ॥ (RV 1-164-47)
>
> *indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim āhur atho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān | ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ ||*
>
> "They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; and also that divine, well-winged Garutman. That which is One, the wise call by many names — they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 246</div>

That all the Vedas' meaning rests in the Supreme Self alone is what this mantra's commentary conveys; when glossing individual words like "Agni," Atmananda selects only those senses through which knowledge of the Supreme Self arises.

Beyond this, whichever Kalpa-text Atmananda cites at the close of each mantra-commentary likewise clearly states this same spiritual meaning — a text some centuries older than Atmananda himself, identifiable as the "Pushkaroktakalpa." Though not found within the printed Vishnudharmottara, it may well be a portion of that same work. Its relevant statement:

> इन्द्रादिशब्दो गुणयोगतो वा वृत्त्युक्तिगो वापि परेशमाहुः । विप्रास्स्यदेकं बहुधा वदन्ति प्राज्ञास्त्व नानापि सदेकमाहुः ॥
>
> "The words beginning with 'Indra,' whether through connection with qualities or through their etymological function, refer to the Supreme Lord. The learned speak of this One in many ways; the truly wise, though speaking of many, declare it to be one single reality."

This confirms Atmananda's commentary is not without foundation — this same spiritual reading of the Veda was clearly current well before his time.

#### Authorities Drawn from Shakapurni {.lv2}

Atmananda's citations from Shakapurni are worth examining. On RV 1-164-14:

> चक्रं जगच्चक्रं भ्रमतीति वा चरतीति वा करोतीति वा चक्रं इति शाकपूणिः ॥
>
> "'Chakra' [wheel] — the world's wheel — [meaning] 'that which revolves,' 'that which moves,' or 'that which acts' — is 'chakra' — thus Shakapurni."

And on mantra 40:

> उदकं—इति सुखनामेति शाकपूणिः ।
>
> "'Udaka' [water] means 'happiness/well-being' — thus Shakapurni."

The first is drawn from Shakapurni's Nirukti, the second from a Nighantu — confirming Atmananda had read Shakapurni's Nirukta directly. His scholarship shines through his commentary throughout.

##### 10. Sayana {.lv3}

*(Period: 1315–1387 CE)*

Among Vedic commentators, **Sayanacharya** holds an especially venerable position. His vast study, exceptional familiarity with the Vedas, and scholarship across many disciplines are all evident from his Vedic literary output — his Veda-commentary stands as the clearest testament to his extraordinary caliber.

His commentaries on the Vedas' Samhitas and Brahmanas are not only exceptionally excellent and clear but also correctly reveal the subtle truths hidden within the vast body of Vedic material

<div class="pgmark">original p. 247</div>

in a fully accessible way — an immense service. Even accounting for all the earlier commentators, their works aren't fully available to us today, with only some names known; where Vedic commentaries do survive, they typically cover only a small, abridged portion. Among all who received honor for composing Veda-commentaries, Sayana's own achievement stands foremost. His own celebrated fellow-commentators were his brothers — ministers to the Vijayanagara kings, who protected the Vedic commentarial tradition and composed many excellent texts, achieving leading positions in scholarship. Owing to circumstance, this great man's biography has not come down to us in full detail — even so, we present here, with what help is available, a summary of the main points of his life.

Sayana was born into a well-known Brahmin family in South India, of the Bharadvaja gotra. His father was named Mayana, his mother Shrimati. His family followed the Bodhayana branch of the Krishna Yajurveda — hence Sayana first wrote a commentary on the Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya Samhita before turning to the Rigveda. He had an elder brother, **Madhavacharya**, and a younger brother, **Bhoganatha**.

Madhavacharya served as minister to the Vijayanagara kings, and was a great authority in Dharmashastra, Purva-Mimamsa philosophy, and many other disciplines. **Harihara and Bukka**, founders of the Vijayanagara kingdom, relied on these ministers in matters of state. The renowned city of Vijayanagara, the most beautiful in all Asia, rich in wealth and charming with sculpture and the other arts, is held by the chief historians to have been founded by them.

Madhavacharya is credited with many works, though not all attributions are fully certain; several, however, are well-established:

**(1) Parashara-smriti-vyakhya** — known as *Parashara-Madhava*, a very large text.
**(2) Kalanirnaya** (or *Kalamadhava*).
**(3) Jaimini-nyayamala** — an authoritative commentary on the sage Jaimini's Purva-Mimamsa philosophy.
**(4) Jivanmukti-viveka** — a Vedanta text discussing liberation-while-living.
**(5) Panchadashi** — a famous Advaita-Vedanta text.
**(6) Vaiyasika-nyayamala** — a commentary explaining the Vedanta-sutras.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 248</div>

The last two of these works were composed, when Madhavacharya gave up the ministry and took sannyasa under the name Vidyaranya, with the help of his teacher Bharati-tirtha.

Whether this Madhavacharya and Vidyaranya are one and the same person, or two different persons, is a very important question; the problem is still unsolved. Some scholars are very doubtful that these are two names of one person. Though some of their arguments look strong, even works contemporary with Madhavacharya, not only later ones, bear witness that Vidyaranya and Madhavacharya, the minister of the early kings of Vijayanagara, are identical. But in the Indian Historical Quarterly (Vol. VI, pp. 701–717) it is determined, on the evidence of inscriptions, that this Madhavacharya or Vidyaranya and the Madhava who was minister of Bukka I (known in history as Madhava-mantri or Amatya Madhava) are different persons. They too appear to have been eminent scholars like Vidyaranya.

Inscriptions describe him as "Upaniṣan-mārga-pravartanācārya" (the teacher who established the path of the Upanishads) and as a great hero who drove the Muslims settled in the Konkan out from there and administered the Goa and Banavasi regions.

Per Kane's *History of Dharmasastra* (p. 374), Vidyaranya was an extraordinary scholar and statesman who served as a pillar of support during Vijayanagara's founding days, before embracing sannyasa in old age, renouncing all worldly ties, and spending his remaining years in meditation — a guide across many spheres of life whose biography still inspires many today.

The third brother, **Bhoganatha**, though less famous than the other two, was every bit their worthy sibling. He served as a close companion-minister (*narma-sachiva*) to Sangama II, son of Kampana — confirmed by that king's Bitragunta inscription:

> इति भोगनाथसुधिया संगमभूपालनर्मसचिवेन । श्रीकण्ठपुरसमृद्ध्यै शासनपत्रेषु विलिखिताः श्लोकाः ॥ ३५ ॥ (*Epigraphia Indica*, Vol. III, p. 23)
>
> "These verses were composed by the learned Bhoganatha, companion-minister to King Sangama, and inscribed upon the charters for the prosperity of Shrikanthapura."

While Sayana and Madhava excelled in the Veda, Vedanta, Mimamsa, and Dharmashastra, **Bhoganatha was a poet of the first rank** — attested by the many works Sayanacharya cites from him in his own *Alankara-sudhanidhi*, and by the verse-form Bitragunta inscription itself. Sayana cites from six of Bhoganatha's works in total.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 249</div>

##### Bhoganatha's Six Works {.lv3}

1. **Ramollasa** — a poetic work in praise of the Ramayana.
2. **Tripuravijaya** — describing Shiva's destruction of Tripura.
3. **Udaharanamala** — a collection of example verses for Sanskrit poetics (alankara) texts, all praised even by Sayanacharya himself.
4. **Mahaganapatistava** — a hymn to Ganapati.
5. **Shringaramanjari** — on the erotic/romantic sentiment (shringara).
6. **Gaurinathashtaka** — an eight-verse hymn to Gaurinatha (Shiva).

Sayanacharya held these works in special regard, once writing that examples of poetic ornamentation should be drawn directly from them:

> तेषामुदाहरणानि भोगनाथकाव्येषु दृश्यानि ।
>
> "Their examples are to be found in Bhoganatha's own poetic works."

As evidence of his exceptional poetic skill, here are verses he composed praising his patron, Lord Sangama:

> यस्य दृष्ट्य विमुद्ध युद्ध यांरसा वार्थ् नामभिमतानुबन्धिनि । हन्त नूनमनुयान्ति सस्यं कर्णिळ्ळ तरुकामधेनः ॥ ८ ॥ युद्य शिप्रसरणेन भू यसाप्प दने युष्टिपरं जगत्रयी । अश्व शे विफलतां न चन्द्रमाः केवलं कुमुदिनीविकासनात् ॥
>
> *(Verses in praise of King Sangama; the dense poetic compounds are difficult to render with full grammatical precision at this resolution, but their overall register is clearly one of elaborate courtly praise.)*

Based on texts and inscriptions, it becomes clear that Sayanacharya was connected to **four successive Vijayanagara kings** — Kampana, Sangama II, Bukka I, and Harihara II — the brothers holding the position of minister and serving the empire throughout all four reigns.

Kampana was the second son of Sangama I — younger brother of Harihara, the empire's founder — and ruled the kingdom's eastern provinces, likely corresponding to today's Nellore and Kadapa districts. For Kampana's son Sangama II, the brothers governed efficiently during his childhood and ensured his excellent education; once he came of age, they handed him the kingdom and moved to serve at the court of his uncle **Bukka I** (1350–1379), continuing as ministers into the reign of his son **Harihara II** (1379–1399), assisting each king in turn.

That a scholar who composed commentaries on all four Vedas possessed extraordinary learning is only natural — but that this same man was also an exceptional warrior, wielding a sword in battle with real valor, is genuinely astonishing to consider. These were not merely deeply immersed Mimamsakas skilled at explaining difficult Vedic mantras — they were capable administrators of a great kingdom, and mighty warriors who themselves entered the battlefield. Immense scholarship combined with worldly shrewdness and sound judgment.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 250</div>

Mental strength, physical strength, scholarship, and heroism all combined in them. Alongside his lord Sangama, Sayana personally led an army to defeat Kampana, the Chola king, and the chieftain of Garudanagara (*Indian Antiquary*, 1916, p. 23). The *Alankara-sudhanidhi* describes his valor:

> जगद्गीर्यस्य जागर्ति कृपाणः सायणप्रभोः । किमित्येते वृथाटोपा गर्जन्ति परिसंस्थिनः ॥
>
> "The sword of Lord Sayana, of world-renowned fame, stays ever vigilant — why then do these surrounding forces roar with such empty bluster?"

He showed extraordinary administrative skill as well. When Kampana died, his son Sangama was still an infant, so the full weight of governance fell on Sayana — reflected in this verse describing the prosperity that followed under his stewardship:

> सत्यं मुखं भवति शासति सायणार्ये संस्प्राप्तभोगसुखिने सकलाश्च लोकाः ।
>
> "It is truly said: when the noble Sayana governs, all peoples come to enjoy prosperity and happiness."

His domestic life was equally blessed — he had three sons: **Kampana** (a lover and practitioner of music), **Mayana** (a skilled poet in both Sanskrit verse and prose — R. Narasimhacharya, *Ind. Ant.* 1916, p. 20, identifies him with the "Madhava" who compiled the *Sarvadarshana-sangraha*, which if true implies deep knowledge of every theistic and atheistic school of Vedanta), and **Singana** (expert in the Veda, especially its Krama and Jata recitation methods, embodying all the qualities of a true Brahmin that Sayanacharya himself describes at the close of his Shatapatha Brahmana commentary).

### According to Some Scholars (Dr. Aufrecht's *Catalogus Catalogorum*, p. 711) {.lv1}

Sayana passed away in **1387 CE**, during Harihara II's reign — placing him at the height of his career in the second half of the 14th century.

##### Sayanacharya's Works {.lv3}

Among his works, the commentaries on the Vedic Samhitas and Brahmanas are by far the most important — sufficient testimony alone to his scholarly depth. But Sayana wrote more than these commentaries; many further texts are attributed to him, or appear scattered across reference catalogues. Many of these attributions cannot be accepted as genuine — on grounds of style and treatment of subject matter, it's clear that ordinary scholars composed some of these and their works simply became attached to Sayana's famous name by reputation. The texts listed below, however, can confidently be called genuinely his on every count, and their own internal colophons support this same conclusion.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 251</div>

From the time he was engaged in politics he must have had the intention of composing works on Dharmashastra, grammar, poetics and the like; therefore, living under the patronage of the Vijayanagara kings, he composed many useful and interesting works on the different sciences. Below, so far as it can be determined, is the list of these texts in their likely order of composition.

**1. Subhashitasudhanidhi** — a compilation of wise verses (subhashitas) drawn from many texts; apparently his first work, composed while serving as minister to King Kampana, per the closing colophon:

> इति पूर्वपक्ष्विन समुद्याश्वीश्वरारिराय विशाल श्री कंपश्राज महाप्रधान—भेरद्वाजंवशमुक्तक—मायणकरत्नाकर सुधाकर—माधवाळ्वतरुसहोदर—श्री सायणाचार्य विरचिते सुभाषितसुधानिधौ—
>
> *(A dense colophon-style compound describing Sayanacharya as chief minister to the illustrious King Kampana, an ornament of the Bharadvaja lineage, and brother of the eminent Madhava; precise word-by-word parsing is difficult at this resolution given the density of the compound.)*

**2. Prayashchittasudhanidhi** (also called *Karmavipaka*) — a text on atonement rites (prayashchitta), a major branch of Dharmashastra.

**3. Dhatuvritti** — known as the *Madhaviya Dhatuvritti*, an authoritative treatment of every Sanskrit verb root (dhatu) found in Panini's Dhatupatha; named in tribute to his elder brother Madhavacharya, to whom Sayana expresses deep devotion in the text.

**4. Alankarasudhanidhi** — a Sanskrit poetics text distinguished by an unusual feature: rather than drawing its illustrative verses (udaharana-shlokas) from generic subject matter — typically devotional or panegyric — as is customary, Sayana draws his examples from events in his own and his brothers' lives, making this text a valuable biographical source in its own right.

The next three texts — Prayashchittasudhanidhi, Dhatuvritti, and Alankarasudhanidhi — are confirmed, by their own closing verses, to have been composed during the reign of **Sangama II**:

**At the opening of the Prayashchittasudhanidhi:**

> तस्य (सङ्गमस्य) मन्त्रिशिरोरत्नमस्ति मायणसायणः ।
>
> "His (Sangama's) crown-jewel among ministers is Sayana, son of Mayana."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 252</div>

> श्रेण मायणपुत्रेण सायणेन मुनीषिणा । ग्रन्थः कर्मविपाकाख्यः क्रियते करुणावता ॥
>
> "By the eminent, wise Sayana, son of Mayana, compassionate as he is, this text called Karma-vipaka is composed."

**In the Dhatuvritti:**

> अस्ति श्रीसंगमक्ष्मापः स्पृद्धीतलपुरन्दरः । तस्य मन्त्रिशिरोरत्नमस्ति मायणसायणः ॥
>
> "There is King Sangama, Indra himself upon earth. His crown-jewel among ministers is Sayana, son of Mayana."

**At the end of the Alankarasudhanidhi:**

> इति...श्रीमत्संगमराजसकलराज्यधुरन्धरस्य सकलविद्यानिदानभूतस्य भोगनाथाग्रजस्य श्रीमत्सायणाचार्यस्य कृतावलंकारसुधानिधौ ॥
>
> "Thus [ends] the Alankarasudhanidhi composed by the illustrious Sayanacharya — elder brother of Bhoganatha, foundation of all learning, and bearer of the entire administrative burden of King Sangama's realm."

**5. Purushartha-sudhanidhi** — a text of Puranic verses on the four aims of human life (purushartha), composed at the command of his new patron King Bukka, after Sayana handed the kingdom over to Sangama and moved to Bukka's court — likely the first work he composed there, before beginning the Veda-commentaries.

**6. The Veda-Bhashyas** — discussed further below.

**7. Ayurveda-sudhanidhi** — an Ayurvedic text, also referenced in the Alankarasudhanidhi:

> आयुर्वेदसुधानिधिव्यसनिभिः श्रीसायणार्योदितं भैषज्यम् ।
>
> "The medicinal remedy stated by Shri Sayanacharya, devoted to the Ayurveda-sudhanidhi."

**8. Yajnatantrasudhanidhi** — a text on yajnas and related rites. These last two texts were composed during the reign of Harihara II, Bukka's son, a king with great personal faith in Vedic ritual practice who gave it considerable encouragement, as their opening verses attest.

##### The Veda-Commentaries {.lv3}

These commentaries showcase Sayanacharya's unparalleled scholarship — his genius shines through here more than in any of his other works, earning them a permanent place in Sanskrit literature and standing as the foremost of everything he wrote. The opening verses of the Taittiriya Samhita commentary reveal something remarkable: **King Bukka first asked his own guru, Madhavacharya, to compose the Veda-commentaries**. But Madhavacharya, weighed down by his responsibilities, did not personally undertake the task — instead directing his own younger brother Sayanacharya to compose them, while himself remaining a guide and source of encouragement throughout rather than stepping away entirely. In gratitude for his elder brother's guidance, Sayana named the commentaries **"Madhaviya"** (of/belonging to Madhava).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 253</div>

Sayanacharya wrote commentaries for these Samhitas:

1. Krishna Yajurveda's Taittiriya-shakha Samhita
2. Rigveda Samhita
3. Samaveda Samhita
4. Shukla Yajurveda's Kanva Samhita
5. Atharvaveda Samhita

He also commented on the Brahmana and Aranyaka texts belonging to these Samhitas — though only the Shatapatha Brahmana commentary seems to have been composed last of all, after all the other commentaries; as the opening of that work says, it was composed in the time of Harihara II.

**A. Krishna Yajurveda**
1. Taittiriya Brahmana
2. Taittiriya Aranyaka and Upanishads

**B. Rigveda**
1. Aitareya Brahmana
2. Aitareya Aranyaka

**C. Samaveda**
1. Tandya (Panchavimsha) Brahmana
2. Shadvimsha Brahmana
3. Samavidhana Brahmana
4. Arsheya Brahmana
5. Devatadhyaya Brahmana
6. Upanishad Brahmana
7. Samhitopanishad Brahmana
8. Vamsha Brahmana

**D. Shukla Yajurveda**
1. Shatapatha Brahmana

Per this list, Sayanacharya composed his Krishna Yajurveda commentary first, before turning to the other Vedas. Yet the Rigveda is established, on many grounds, as foremost among the four Vedas — the foundation of our culture and the most ancient of the four. If one asks why Sayana did not begin with the Rigveda commentary instead, he answers this himself at the opening of his Rigveda-Bhashya-Bhumika (introduction): the Vedas' primary use is in yajnas, and whatever yajna is performed, its central officiant is the **Adhvaryu priest** — who, taking up a given form of the sacrifice, enacts/describes it (this is the sense of "*yajñasya mātrāṃ vimimīte*," "he measures out the yajna's form"). What he must follow is the Yajus [Yajurveda].

<div class="pgmark">original p. 254</div>

Hence the Veda he must know first is the Yajurveda — so Sayana composed that commentary first, taking up the Rigveda only afterward. His own family tradition was Yajurvedic besides, making this a natural order for him as well.

### The Introductions (Bhumikas) to the Veda-Commentaries {.lv1}

Sayanacharya wrote a separate introduction for each Veda-commentary — themselves significant works, discussing many important topics connected to the Veda.

The **Taittiriya-bhashya's introduction** covers the Veda's defining characteristics, its authority, and briefly its status as a valid means of knowledge; the two parts of the Veda (one connected with the four kinds of rites, the other dealing with Brahman and knowledge of Brahman); and the divisions of yajnas — the Darsha and Paurnamasa sacrifices being essential parts of all sacrifices and therefore called the prakriti (model), all other sacrifices being vikriti (modifications).

The **Rigveda-bhashya's introduction** is the most useful of all — discussing many important questions of Vedic knowledge, restating the opponent's view and establishing the settled conclusion, to the great benefit of all who study the Veda and Vedangas; making full use of the adhikaranas of Jaimini's Mimamsa-sutras and giving his own opinion on those sutras, he sets forth the matters in a reasoned manner. It covers the Veda's defining characteristics, its self-authenticating nature (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) independent of human authorship, the Vedanga tradition, and the divisions of Veda and Brahmana — explaining the Veda's purpose and showing how each Vedanga discipline illuminates its meaning.

The **Samaveda-bhashya's introduction** discusses Veda-characteristics along with Sama-chanting (samagana) and its manner of performance in detail, again drawing on Purva-Mimamsa material to settle 62 questions concerning Sama-singing.

The **Kanva-Samhita (Shukla Yajurveda) bhashya's introduction** briefly discusses that Veda's own portions, explains the intended meaning of the injunction "svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ" ("one's own Vedic recitation should be studied"), and gathers together the main subjects of the Shukla Yajurveda's 40 Adhyayas.

The **Atharvaveda-bhashya's introduction** covers, on Puranic authority, the Atharvaveda's exceptional usefulness and necessity for the king's priest (rajapurohita) and the Brahma priest; studying the Veda grants knowledge of mantra-meaning, and the introduction also covers the Veda's own authority (pramanya) and the determination of word-meanings.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 255</div>

Across all these introductions, the topics fall into two broad groups: elements common to all the Vedas, and elements specific to a single Veda.

**Common elements** include: mantra and Brahmana together defining the Veda (whatever is not mantra is Brahmana); the Veda's non-human origin (apaurusheyatva) and eternality (nitya-vada), with refutation of opposing views; that the Veda carries genuine meaning rather than being mere sound to recite; the distinctions among Rik, Yajus, and Sama; and the Veda's own two-fold division — one Kanda describing ritual action (karma), the other describing the path to Brahma-knowledge and its attainment — meaning that dharma and Brahman together constitute the Veda's subject matter, and knowledge of these its ultimate purpose.

**Veda-specific elements** include, for instance: the Darsha and Paurnamasa sacrifices, praise of one who has studied the Veda, an introduction to the Vedangas, and (for the Shukla Yajurveda) a brief survey of its 40 chapters.

### The Commentator Sayanacharya {.lv1}

The Vedas are extremely ancient texts, and their language differs greatly from the language now in use. Garbled statements, ambiguous usages, and words without fixed convention are woven throughout the Veda from the start — so anyone wishing to understand it correctly must, above all, be thoroughly grounded in the traditional Vedic scholarly disciplines, embodied in the **six Vedangas**: Shiksha, Vyakarana, Chandas, Nirukta, Jyotisha, and Kalpa.

- **Shiksha** — explains the correct method of Vedic recitation and pronunciation.
- **Vyakarana** (grammar) — based on word-formation, aids in understanding even subtle usages.
- **Chandas** (meter) — identifies the meters of the mantras.
- **Nirukta** — clearly explains distinctly Vedic-specific usages.
- **Jyotisha** (astronomy/astrology) — helps determine the correct timing for yajnas.
- **Kalpa** — explains the procedure for performing yajnas and related rites.

Beyond these six, the **Purana, Itihasa, Dharmashastra,** and the **Anukramani texts** are called Upangas (subsidiary limbs) of the Veda, and are likewise essential. For determining the precise meaning of mantras, the **Mimamsa-shastra** is absolutely indispensable — thorough study of all these is required before undertaking Vedic commentary. Mimamsa itself divides into Purva- and Uttara-Mimamsa, both ultimately serving the same goal: properly explaining the Veda's meaning.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 256</div>

> "पूर्वोत्तरमीमांसयोर्वेदार्थोपयोगे गौतिस्स्व एव"
>
> *(A heading affirming that both Purva- and Uttara-Mimamsa serve the purpose of determining the Veda's meaning.)*

As evidence of Mimamsa's usefulness, the introductions establish the Veda's defining characteristics, its non-human origin, its self-authenticating validity, and the principle that injunctive statements carry genuine meaning (not mere recitation) — all through the Mimamsa-sutras directly.

Sayanacharya himself mastered all these disciplines thoroughly before undertaking his commentary, and with the express intention that anyone seeking to understand the Veda should first grasp these same foundations, he discusses each of them extensively in his introductions.

### Sayanacharya and Modern Scholars {.lv1}

Sayanacharya's commentaries prove immensely useful not only to those studying the Veda traditionally, but to modern scholars as well. Those comparing Philology and Mythology to uncover Vedic meaning also find valuable material in his commentary. Sayanacharya determined word-meanings following Nirukta and grammatical principles wherever possible, and relied on his own independent judgment wherever those disciplines fell short — material of genuine interest to anyone pursuing deeper philosophical truth. Even in matters of accent and pronunciation, he made full use of grammatical science, and his treatment of the deities likewise contains much of value.

Moreover, it can fairly be said that **no other commentary comprehensively explains the Vedic mantras** the way Sayana's does. Others may have composed Vedic commentaries before him — some still survive — but no one else appears to have undertaken commentary on all four Vedas together with their associated Brahmanas and Aranyakas.

For modern scholars researching the special elements hidden within the vast body of Vedic material, understanding the traditionally received meaning remains essential — the very foundation-stone for their work. No other text presents this traditional interpretation as clearly and completely as Sayana's commentary. However far modern scholarship advances, it must remain grateful to Sayana — no building stands without a foundation, and Sayana's commentaries occupy exactly that place. It is impossible to imagine what state Vedic scholarship would be in today without them. The Western scholar Prof. Wilson, who translated the Veda into English, expressed this same view, writing as follows—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 257</div>

> "He (Sayana) undoubtedly had a knowledge of his text far beyond the pretensions of any European Scholar, and must have been in possession, either through his own learning, or that of his assistants, of all the interpretations which had been perpetuated by traditional teaching from the early times."

The further points relating to Sayanacharya's biography will be discussed in the following sections.

##### 11. Ravana {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 1600 CE)*

Known to have written commentaries for both the Rigveda and Yajurveda (edited in part by Fitzedward Hall); only a small portion of the Rigveda commentary has been published. From his surviving work only these points are known: he was a Vedantin following the school of Shankara; the style of the commentary is simple and clear; Atmananda's commentary resembles it somewhat, and he must be later than Atmananda.

**Dating:** Suryapandita, author of the *Paramarthaprabha* commentary on the Gita (Suryapandita is the author of the Lilavati commentary), quotes the Ravana Rigveda commentary; Suryapandita himself writes at the end of that work that his Lilavati commentary was composed in 1538 CE — so this Rigveda commentary may be conjectured to have been composed about 400 years ago.

Some scholars hold that "Ravana" is simply another name for Sayanacharya himself, not a distinct person — this is incorrect, as becomes clear from a direct comparison of the two texts' own stated aims:

> सायणभाष्यकार्य राध्यै विशाखाप्रायेण बाह्य संग्रानुविषयो दर्शितः । रावणभाष्ये तु अध्यात्म्यीत्याभ्यंतरसंग्रानुविषयो दर्शितः उपटीपाख्ये तोभयनुस...
>
> *(Distinguishing Sayana's commentary, which shows the exoteric/ritual meaning, from Ravana's commentary, which shows the inner/spiritual (adhyatmic) meaning, with a related sub-commentary combining both; precise construction difficult at this resolution.)*

**His other texts:**

**Yajurveda-bhashya** — not available.
**Rigveda-padapatha** — not found complete; only its seventh Ashtaka survives, held at the Dayananda Mahavidyalaya library, Lahore. This text differs in small ways from Shakalya's own Padapatha.

##### 12. Mudgala {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: 1413–1419 CE)*

Nothing is reliably known of his background — no solid evidence exists, and he never mentions his own circumstances anywhere in his text. Copies of his commentary exist: one at the India Office,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 258</div>

one at the Mysore Oriental Library and another at Lahore. None is complete: the Mysore copy has the first Ashtaka and the Lahore copy Ashtakas 4–5. The copy in London reads "saṃvat 147…"; the last figure has been erased. On this basis it may be conjectured that this copy was written in about the first quarter of the 15th century.

Mudgala leaves out the grammatical part entirely; as he himself says in his opening verses, he looked at all the earlier commentaries and gathered only the essential part:

> आरोच्च पूर्वभाष्यं च बध्चिचस्य समन्ततः । गहनं मन्यमानेन सुबोधेन समुद्धृतम् ॥ नवशीतं युग्णाश्चीरात् शिककायाश्चांजनम् । तथा समुद्धृतं सारं प्राशिनां बोधसिद्धये ॥ मौद्गल्यगोत्रेण च मुद्गलेन प्राक्तनभूतेन सुसंस्कृतेन । युथार्थभूतेन सुसाधकेन समुद्धृतं सारमिदं वरिष्ठम् ॥
>
> *(Mudgala, of the Maudgalya gotra, describes having examined the earlier [Sayana] commentary in full, found it profound and dense, and extracted its essence in accessible form for students' understanding — precise word-by-word construction is difficult at this resolution, but the overall claim is clear.)*

An example of his commentary style, on one ṛk (RV 5-9-1):

> हे अग्ने ! त्वां देवं दीप्यमानं हविष्पंको होमद्रव्यसमेत मर्तासो मर्त्य ईळते । अहं च जातनेदसं जातं वेदो धनं यस्मासौ जातवेदा तमेविधं त्वां त्वां मन्ये सौमि । स त्वं हेड्य हप्यवाकसाधनानि हवींषि आनुषक् निरन्तरतयानुसक्रं यथा तथा वक्षि वहसि ॥
>
> *(A worked example of Mudgala's commentary style on RV 5-9-1, glossing "jātavedasam" as "one whose wealth is knowledge" and explaining the offering-bearing role of Agni; precise phrase-by-phrase construction is difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

His commentary can fairly be called a summary of Sayana's, closely following it — though a discernible method governs his condensation, as this example on a single mantra shows.

##### 13. Chaturvedasvami {.lv3}

*(Approximate period: end of the 15th century CE)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 259</div>

> जज्ञान एव व्यबाधत स्पृधः प्रापश्यद्वीरो अभि पौंस्यं रणम् । अवृश्चदद्रिमव सस्यदः सृजदस्तभ्नान्नाकं स्वपस्यया पृथुम् ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-११३-४)
> *jajñāna eva vyabādhata spṛdhaḥ prāpaśyad vīro abhi pauṃsyaṃ raṇam | avṛścad adrim ava sasyadaḥ sṛjad astabhnān nākaṃ svapasyayā pṛthum || (ṛ. saṃ. 10-113-4)*
>
> अत्र चतुर्वेदस्वामिकृतभाष्यम्— यः परमेश्वरो जज्ञानः प्रादुर्भूतमात्रो मायया बालदशां स्वीकुर्वाणोऽपि सन् स्पृधः स्पर्धां कृतवतः शत्रून् पूतनादीन् कंसान्तान् व्यबाधत बाधितवान् । न केवलं दैत्यान् अपि तु शक्रादीनां गर्वमपीत्याह । यो अद्रिं पर्वतं गोवर्धनं अवृश्चत् उद्दधार । किमुद्दिश्य ? सस्यदो धान्यदात्र्यान् मेघाननवरतं वर्षमाणान् अवसृजत विसर्जितवान् । तेन पृथुं सामर्थ्यवन्तं नाकं इन्द्रलोकं स्वपस्यया मायया अस्तभ्नात् स्तम्भितवान् स्तम्भितशक्तिमकरोत् । अथ यौवनदशायामपि अभिपौंस्यं सर्वपुरुषार्थसाधकं रणं कुरुपाण्डवसंग्रामं वीरोऽपि सन् अपश्यत् ताटस्थ्येन दृष्टवान् न तु स्वयं युयुधे ।
> *atra caturvedasvāmi-kṛta-bhāṣyam — yaḥ parameśvaro jajñānaḥ prādurbhūtamātro māyayā bāladaśāṃ svīkurvāṇo'pi san spṛdhaḥ spardhāṃ kṛtavataḥ śatrūn pūtanādīn kaṃsāntān vyabādhata bādhitavān | na kevalaṃ daityān api tu śakrādīnāṃ garvam apīty āha | yo adriṃ parvataṃ govardhanaṃ avṛścat uddadhāra | kim uddiśya ? sasyado dhānyadātryān meghān anavarataṃ varṣamāṇān avasṛjata visarjitavān | tena pṛthuṃ sāmarthyavantaṃ nākaṃ indralokaṃ svapasyayā māyayā astabhnāt stambhitavān stambhitaśaktim akarot | atha yauvanadaśāyām api abhipauṃsyaṃ sarvapuruṣārthasādhakaṃ raṇaṃ kurupāṇḍavasaṃgrāmaṃ vīro'pi san apaśyat tāṭasthyena dṛṣṭavān na tu svayaṃ yuyudhe |*

**Here, Caturvedasvāmin's commentary:** the Supreme Lord, as soon as he was born, though by his māyā he had taken on the state of a child, struck down the enemies who contended with him — Pūtanā and the rest, ending with Kaṃsa; and not only the demons — he humbled the pride of Śakra (Indra) and the others too. He lifted the mountain Govardhana. For what purpose? He released the grain-giving clouds that rained without ceasing; and by his māyā he stopped the mighty heaven, Indra's world, rendering its power powerless. And in his youth too, though a hero, he only watched the Kurukṣetra battle — the battle that achieves every human end — standing aside; he did not fight himself. **Many would not find it right to accept an explanation of this kind.**

#### 14. Devasvami {.lv2}

His commentary itself is not available, but its existence is well confirmed through citations. He composed commentaries on the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra and Śrautasūtra; it is not impossible that such a man also wrote a commentary on the Ṛgveda.

**In Vimalabodha's commentary on the Mahabharata:**

> मया भोजजन्मेजयाचार्यदेवस्वामिवेदनिघण्टुविभ्राडनुवाकार्थपर्यालोचनेनायमर्थः कृतः ।
> *mayā bhoja-janmejayācārya-devasvāmi-vedanighaṇṭu-vibhrāḍ-anuvākārtha-paryālocanenāyam arthaḥ kṛtaḥ |*
>
> "This meaning has been arrived at by me through consideration of [the works of] Bhoja, Janmejaya, Ācārya Devasvāmin, the Veda-nighaṇṭu and the meaning of the Vibhrāḍ anuvāka."

That Devasvāmin wrote a commentary on the Mahābhārata has not been heard of so far — so the text Vimalabodha references here must be his Rigveda commentary instead.

**His period** is not definitively known. The Prapancha-hridaya records that Acharya Devasvami composed a Mimamsa-commentary (as an abridgment of Upavarsha's commentary), apparently based on the Shabara-bhashya. If this is the same Devasvami as the Rigveda commentator, he would predate the Vikrama era.

##### 15. Bhattabhaskara {.lv3}

His commentary has not been located anywhere, though he is known to have composed a commentary on the Aitareya Brahmana; he is also said to have written a Rigveda commentary.

#### 16. Uvata {.lv2}

In the Nighantu commentary (3-4-11), where the meaning of the word "amātya" is explained, a line by Uvata is quoted — on this basis, it can be conjectured that Uvata too composed a Rigveda commentary. (Dr. Raj's article, read at the Fifth Oriental Conference, p. 261)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 260</div>

But since this same citation also occurs in a Yajurveda commentary, whether Uvata composed a genuine Rigveda commentary remains genuinely ambiguous.

There is a commentary by Uvata on Katyayana's *Sarvanukramani*; this Anukramani commentary is excellent. Uvata also wrote an exposition of the Rik-pratishakhya. Therefore he may also have composed a commentary on the Rigveda.

#### 17. Haradatta {.lv2}

Composed a commentary on the Ashvalayana-mantra-patha text (manuscripts survive at Mysore, Madras, and Trivandrum); Devarajayajva's own Nighantu-bhashya cites Haradatta's commentary at several points. He also composed:

1. Ekagni-kanda-vyakhya
2. Apastamba-Grihyasutra-vyakhya — titled *Anakula*
3. Apastamba-Dharmasutra-vyakhya — titled *Ujjvala*
4. Ashvalayana-Grihyasutra-vyakhya — titled *Anavila*
5. Gautama-Dharmasutra-vyakhya — titled *Mitakshara*

The commentators discussed above are the principal ones. It is understood that many further commentators existed beyond these, but since their commentaries and related works cannot be located, their details are not covered here. Modern vernacular-language attempts at Vedic interpretation — such as those written in Hindi and other regional languages by scholars like Dayananda Sarasvati — have not gained full recognition among Vedic scholars, and given their comparatively lesser standing, there is no felt need to detail them here.

**— Chapter Thirteen (Commentators on the Rigveda) concludes here. —**

## Chapter Fourteen — Commentators on the Yajurveda

<div class="pgmark">original p. 261</div>

The matter that the Yajurveda has two divisions, the Śukla Yajurveda and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, was explained earlier. Of the Śukla Yajurveda, the Mādhyandina and Kāṇva branches, and of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda the Taittirīya branch, are renowned and especially in currency. Therefore we shall briefly make known the commentators of these three branches.

#### Commentators of the Mādhyandina branch of the Śukla Yajurveda {.lv2}

#### 1. Śaunaka {.lv2}

(time not known)

There are two manuscripts of the commentary composed by Uvaṭa on the Mādhyandina branch of the Yajurveda; one is the Kāśī copy and the other the Pune copy. In the Pune copy there is no Uvaṭa commentary for the Puruṣa-sūkta; in its place there is the commentary of Śaunaka.

> अस्य भाष्यं शौनको नाम ऋषिरकरोत् ।
>
> *asya bhāṣyaṃ śaunako nāma ṛṣir akarot |*
>
> "The sage named Śaunaka made the commentary on this."

He himself writes that the commentary on this was made by a sage named Śaunaka. This Śaunaka has also described the order of writing his commentary:

> प्रथमं विच्छेदः क्रियाकारकसंबन्धः समासः प्रमेयार्थव्याख्येति ।
>
> *prathamaṃ vicchedaḥ kriyākārakasaṃbandhaḥ samāsaḥ prameyārthavyākhyeti |*
>
> "First the separation [of words]; the relation of verb and case-roles; the compound; then the explanation of the meaning to be established."

That is: in this commentary first the words are separated, the construction is written, the compound words are analysed, and afterwards the purport (*tātparya*) is written. This is the order he follows.

He declares that the mantras are useful for sacrifices and also give a spiritual (*ādhyātmika*) meaning. In places, using such words as "*kecit*" ("some") and "*apare*" ("others"), he gives examples of the opinions of others. He gives meanings of words following the Nirukta.

> एवं योगिनोऽपि दीपनाद्देवाः ।
>
> *evaṃ yogino 'pi dīpanād devāḥ |*
>
> "Thus even the yogins [are called] *devāḥ* because of shining."

The opinion of the etymologists (*nairuktas*) is that the word *deva* acquired that name because it makes light (*prakāśa*).

We do not know much about this man. Only this much can be said: whether, as Uvaṭa has said, Śaunaka was one sage, or an ordinary person, he belonged to a very early time.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 262</div>

##### 2. Hariswāmī {.lv3}

(time about 638 C.E.)

In determining the time of Skandasvāmin, the first of the Ṛgveda commentators, these verses were quoted from the commentary on the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa composed by Hariswāmī:

> नागस्वामी तत्र ....श्रीगुहस्वामिनन्दनः ।
> तत्र याजी प्रमाणज्ञ आढ्यो लक्ष्म्या समेधितः ॥ ५ ॥
> तन्नन्दनो हरिस्वामी प्रस्फुरद्वेदवेदिमान् ।
> त्रयीव्याख्यानधौरेयोऽधीततन्त्रो गुरोर्मुखात् ॥ ६ ॥
> यः सम्राट् कृतवान् सप्त सोमसंस्थास्तथर्क्श्रुतिम् ।
> व्याख्यां कृत्वाथापयन्मां श्रीस्कन्दस्वाम्यस्ति मे गुरुः ॥ ७ ॥
>
> *nāgasvāmī tatra ....śrīguhasvāminandanaḥ |*
> *tatra yājī pramāṇajña āḍhyo lakṣmyā samedhitaḥ || 5 ||*
> *tannandano harisvāmī prasphuradvedavedimān |*
> *trayīvyākhyānadhaureyo 'dhītatantro gurormukhāt || 6 ||*
> *yaḥ samrāṭ kṛtavān sapta somasaṃsthās tathark-śrutim |*
> *vyākhyāṃ kṛtvāthāpayan māṃ śrīskandasvāmy asti me guruḥ || 7 ||*

(No translation of these verses is given in the source other than the following gloss.)

From this it is learnt that Hariswāmī was the grandson of one Guhasvāmī, the son of Nāgasvāmī, and the pupil of Skandasvāmin, who composed the commentary on the Ṛgveda. It has already been written that Skandasvāmin composed his commentary about 630 C.E.; Hariswāmī, his pupil, may be guessed to be of about the same time. And Hariswāmī himself has written his own time in his commentary on the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa:

> यदाब्दानां कलेर्जग्मुः सप्तत्रिंशच्छतानि वै ।
> चत्वारिंशत्समाश्चान्यास्तदा भाष्यमिदं कृतम् ॥
>
> *yadābdānāṃ kaler jagmuḥ saptatriṃśacchatāni vai |*
> *catvāriṃśat samāś cānyās tadā bhāṣyam idaṃ kṛtam ||*
>
> "When thirty-seven hundred years of the Kali [age] had gone, and forty more years, then was this commentary made."

The commentary on the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa was composed in the year 3740 of the Kali. The Christian era begins from Kali 3102. That is: the composing of Hariswāmī's commentary may be said to be 638 C.E. (3740 − 3102 = 638, as the source states). Sufficient evidence is not obtained to determine his time more firmly than this.

Besides the commentary on the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa, he has composed a commentary on the Kātyāyana Śrauta-sūtra too. As for his having composed a Yajurveda commentary, further evidence has not been obtained. In the library of the Raghunātha temple there is a work numbered 4509; it is the *pada-pāṭha* of the Rudrādhyāya. It is written that this *pada-pāṭha* follows the opinion of Hariswāmī. From this there is room to believe that Hariswāmī may have composed a commentary on the Yajurveda also.

##### 3. Uvaṭa {.lv3}

(time about 1042 C.E.)

Uvaṭa is the renowned one among the commentators on the Śukla Yajurveda. At the end of his commentary he has written his family, time and the like.

> आनन्दपुरवास्तव्यवज्रटाख्यस्य सूनुना ।
> उवटेन कृतं भाष्यं पदवाक्यैः सुनिश्चितैः ॥
> ऋष्यादींश्च नमस्कृत्य अवन्त्यामुवटो वसन् ।
> मन्त्राणां कृतवान् भाष्यं महीं भोजे प्रशासति ॥
>
> *ānandapuravāstavyavajraṭākhyasya sūnunā |*
> *uvaṭena kṛtaṃ bhāṣyaṃ padavākyaiḥ suniścitaiḥ ||*
> *ṛṣyādīṃś ca namaskṛtya avantyām uvaṭo vasan |*
> *mantrāṇāṃ kṛtavān bhāṣyaṃ mahīṃ bhoje praśāsati ||*
>
> "By Uvaṭa, son of the one called Vajraṭa, resident of Ānandapura, was the commentary made with well-determined words and sentences. Having bowed to the seers and the rest, Uvaṭa, dwelling in Avantī, made the commentary on the mantras while Bhoja ruled the earth."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 263</div>

Vajraṭa was his father. He was of the time of King Bhoja. Uvaṭa's place of residence was Avantī. The same intention is found in the Baroda, Pune and Kāśī readings of this commentary. That the time of King Bhoja was 1017–1059 C.E. is a matter known from history. Therefore Uvaṭa's time may be said to be about 1042 C.E.

The names Uvaṭa, Vajraṭa and the like are from the Kashmir side; they must probably have been Kashmiri Brahmins.

> इति श्रीमद्वज्रटभट्टोपाध्यायात्मजसकलनिगमविज्ञूडामणि [sic]
> श्रीमदुवटभट्टाचार्यविरचिते........चत्वारिंशत्तमोऽध्यायः ।
>
> *iti śrīmadvajraṭabhaṭṭopādhyāyātmajasakalanigamavijñūḍāmaṇi [sic] śrīmaduvaṭabhaṭṭācāryaviracite........ catvāriṃśattamo 'dhyāyaḥ |*
>
> "Thus [ends] the fortieth chapter, in the work composed by the venerable Uvaṭa Bhaṭṭācārya, son of the venerable Vajraṭa Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, crest-jewel of all the Vedas…" (The words *vijñūḍāmaṇi* are as printed; read probably *-vic-cūḍāmaṇi*.)

Since the respectful words *upādhyāya* and *bhaṭṭācārya* are used here, it can be said that he was of good family and famous.

Some special features of his commentary:

1. In general he follows and explains in the *yājñika* (ritual) manner. But in places he also sets forth [matters] in the spiritual manner.
2. He has quoted sentences from Yāska's Nirukta, the Nighaṇṭu and the Bṛhaddevatā. But he rarely tells the names of the authors.
3. It does not appear that he has seen the Yājuṣa-sarvānukramaṇī. At the beginning of the commentary he has written thus —

> गुरुतस्तर्कतश्चैव तथा शातपथश्रुतेः ।
> ऋषीन्वक्ष्यामि मन्त्राणां देवताश्छन्दसं च यत् ॥
>
> *gurutas tarkataś caiva tathā śātapathaśruteḥ |*
> *ṛṣīn vakṣyāmi mantrāṇāṃ devatāś chandasaṃ ca yat ||*
>
> "From the teacher, from reasoning, and likewise from the Śatapatha Śruti, I shall tell the seers of the mantras, the deities, and the metre."

That is: on the strength of the guru, *tarka* (that is, Nyāya-śāstra) and the Śatapatha-śruti, I shall write the ṛṣi, devatā and chandas of the mantras.

From this it is determined to this extent: the Yājuṣa-sarvānukramaṇī was of little use to the Mādhyandina branch, or that sarvānukramaṇī is not ancient.

He has composed three other works: the Ṛk-prātiśākhya-bhāṣya, the Yajuḥ-prātiśākhya-bhāṣya, and the Ṛk-sarvānukramaṇa-bhāṣya.

#### 4. Gauradhara {.lv2}

(time about 1292 C.E.)

Among the commentators on works such as the Mālatīmādhava there was a famous Kashmiri author named Jagaddharabhaṭṭa. His paternal grandfather was Gauradhara. This Jagaddharabhaṭṭa composed a work full of the flavour of devotion called Stutikusumāñjali. In this work he describes his lineage.

> पुरा पुरारेः पदधूलिभूषरः सरस्वतीस्वैरविहारभूरभूत् ।
> विशालवन्तश्रुतवृत्तिविश्रुतो विपश्चितां गौरधरः किलाग्रणीः ॥ १ ॥
> अनन्तसिद्धान्तपथान्तगामिनः समस्तशास्त्रार्णवपारदृश्वनः ।
>
> *purā purāreḥ padadhūlibhūṣaraḥ sarasvatīsvairavihārabhūr abhūt |*
> *viśālavantaśrutavṛttiviśruto vipaścitāṃ gauradharaḥ kilāgraṇīḥ || 1 ||*
> *anantasiddhāntapathāntagāminaḥ samastaśāstrārṇavapāradṛśvanaḥ |*

(Transcribed as printed; the second line is doubtful; the verse continues on the next page; no translation is given in the source of the verses themselves. Gist, editorial and tentative: "Of old there was one adorned with the dust of the feet of Śiva (the foe of Pura), the playground of Sarasvatī: Gauradhara, indeed foremost of the learned … who had reached the end of the path of endless doctrines, who had seen to the far shore of the ocean of all the śāstras".)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 264</div>

> ऋजुर्यजुर्वेदपदार्थवर्णना व्यनक्ति यस्माद्भुतविश्रुतं श्रुतं ॥ २ ॥
>
> *ṛjur yajurvedapadārthavarṇanā vyanakti yasmādbhutaviśrutaṃ śrutam || 2 ||*
>
> "…whose straightforward description of the meanings of the words of the Yajurveda makes manifest the wonderful, renowned, heard [tradition]."

Earlier there was an excellent scholar named Gauradhara, born of a good lineage and master of all the śāstras. He composed a pure commentary on the Yajurveda. The commentator Ratnakaṇṭha, writing the explanation of these verses, says:

> ताद्दृशस्य गौरधरस्य ऋजुर्निर्मला निर्दोषा च यजुर्वेद-
> पदानामर्थवर्णना भाष्यपद्धतिर्वेदविलासनाम्नी य-
> स्माद्भुतं च विश्रुतं प्रसिद्धं च श्रुतं व्यनक्ति प्रकटयति ॥
>
> *tādṛśasya gauradharasya ṛjur nirmalā nirdoṣā ca yajurveda-padānām arthavarṇanā bhāṣyapaddhatir vedavilāsanāmnī yasmādbhutaṃ ca viśrutaṃ prasiddhaṃ ca śrutaṃ vyanakti prakaṭayati ||*
>
> "Of such a Gauradhara, the straightforward, pure and faultless description of the meanings of the words of the Yajurveda — the commentary-method called *Vedavilāsa* — makes manifest, makes clear, what is wonderful, renowned, famous and heard."

Gauradhara composed a commentary on the Yajurveda named *Vedavilāsa*. One copy of this commentary is at Baroda. In it there is a commentary only for adhyāyas 26 to 31 and 38 to 40. At the end:

> इति ऋजुव्याख्याने संहितायां चत्वारिंशत्तमोऽध्यायः ।
> संवत् १५६४ फाल्गुन शुद्ध १४ भौमे लिखितं ॥
>
> *iti ṛjuvyākhyāne saṃhitāyāṃ catvāriṃśattamo 'dhyāyaḥ |*
> *saṃvat 1564 phālguna śuddha 14 bhaume likhitaṃ ||*
>
> "Thus the fortieth chapter in the *Ṛju-vyākhyāna* of the Saṃhitā. Written on Tuesday [*bhauma*], the 14th of the bright half of Phālguna, Saṃvat 1564."

So it is said: it was written in the year Saṃvat 1564, Phālguna śukla caturdaśī, Wednesday [as the Kannada prose of the source says "*budhavāra*"; the Sanskrit colophon as printed has *bhaume*, Tuesday — an inconsistency in the source, noted and not corrected].

He was the grandfather of Jagaddharabhaṭṭa. The editor of the Stutikusumāñjali determines that Jagaddhara composed the Stutikusumāñjali about 1352 C.E. It can be guessed that Gauradhara-bhaṭṭa wrote his commentary about 50 years before him; that is, the commentary was composed about 1292 C.E.

##### 5. Rāvaṇa {.lv3}

(first half of the 16th century C.E.)

In describing the history of the commentators on the Ṛgveda, the time of Rāvaṇa and so on has already been discussed. He was a writer of the early part of the 16th century C.E. It is learnt that he composed a commentary on the Yajurveda also. A copy of the Yajurveda commentary has not come to hand till now. The evidence is found that a Yajurveda commentary existed: there is a work called *Rudra-prayoga-darpaṇa*, composed by one Padmanābha. A manuscript of it, written in the year 1659 C.E., was with one Aṇṇāśāstri at Nāsik. At the beginning of this work Padmanābha himself says that when writing the Rudra commentary he wrote it on the basis of Rāvaṇa's Yajurveda commentary. Besides this, no other evidence has been found.

##### 6. Mahīdhara {.lv3}

(time about 1587 C.E.)

He was a resident of Kāśī. He wrote a Tantra work called *Mantra-mahodadhi*, and a commentary on it too. But in these no capacity of his own is seen. His is like a shadow of Uvaṭa's commentary. There is only this much difference between the two. In Uvaṭa's commentary

<div class="pgmark">original p. 265</div>

there is no sign that he has quoted sentences of the Kātyāyana Śrauta-sūtra. But Mahīdhara has put everything into his commentary on the basis of Sāyaṇa's commentary on the Kāṇva-saṃhitā. Mahīdhara's commentary has no great excellence.

A little discussion has been made about the time of this man. According to the view of some he was of the 12th century C.E. On this basis they quote the auspicious verse of the commentary:

> प्रणम्य लक्ष्मीं नृहरिं गणेशं भाष्यं विलोक्योवटमाधवीयम् ।
> यजुर्मनूनां विलिखामि चार्थं परोपकाराय निजेक्षणाय ॥ १ ॥
>
> *praṇamya lakṣmīṃ nṛhariṃ gaṇeśaṃ bhāṣyaṃ vilokyovaṭamādhavīyam |*
> *yajurmanūnāṃ vilikhāmi cārthaṃ paropakārāya nijekṣaṇāya || 1 ||*
>
> "Having bowed to Lakṣmī, Nṛhari and Gaṇeśa, and having looked at the commentaries of Uvaṭa and of Mādhava, I write the meaning of the Yajus mantras, for the benefit of others and for my own seeing." (*manūnām* is read as in the print.)

Here it is said that, relying on the commentaries of Uvaṭa and of Mādhava, he has written the commentary. These people say that this Mādhava was Veṅkaṭamādhava, and that Mahīdhara was in the 12th century. The source quotes in English:

"This view is further confirmed as Mahidhara, the commentator of the Sukla Yajurveda, who belonged to 1100. A.D. mentions a predecessor Madhava by name. This predecessor is probably to be identified with Madhava, son of Venkata." [sic: "Mahidhara", "Sukla", "1100. A.D.", as printed.]

But that this Mādhava is Sāyaṇa-Mādhava is clear from sentences quoted in other places in the commentary.

In the *Mantra-mahodadhi* Mahīdhara has himself written his own time:

> अब्दे विक्रामतो [sic] जाते बाणवेदनृपैर्मिते ।
> ज्येष्ठाष्टम्यां शिवस्याग्रे पूर्णो मन्त्रमहोदधिः ॥
>
> *abde vikrāmato [sic] jāte bāṇavedanṛpair mite |*
> *jyeṣṭhāṣṭamyāṃ śivasyāgre pūrṇo mantramahodadhiḥ ||*
>
> "In the year born of Vikrama, measured by *bāṇa, veda, nṛpa* [5, 4, 16], on the eighth of Jyeṣṭha, before Śiva, the Mantra-mahodadhi was completed."

In the commentary on this verse he has made the meaning clear as "*pañcacatvāriṃśaduttaraṣoḍaśaśatatame vikramasyāpāgte sati*"; that is, he has written that the *Mantra-mahodadhi* was finished on the day of Jyeṣṭha aṣṭamī of the year 1645 of the Vikrama era. Therefore, if it is supposed that the commentary was finished some years before this or after it, it can be said that the commentary was composed about 1587 C.E.

##### Commentators on the Kāṇva Saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda {.lv3}

##### 1. Sāyaṇācārya {.lv3}

(about 1315–1387 C.E.)

Sāyaṇācārya composed a commentary on the Kāṇva branch. In this the commentary on 20 adhyāyas has been found. The commentary on the remaining 20 adhyāyas has not been found. The commentary on the twentieth adhyāya... [sic: the source reads "of the second twenty"] must have been lost, or else the first twenty adhyāyas are those which Sāyaṇācārya wrote.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 266</div>

According to the opinion of Ananta, a commentator of this same branch, Sāyaṇācārya did not write a commentary on the last twenty adhyāyas.

> व्याख्याता कण्वशाखीयसंहिता पूर्वविंशतिः ।
> माधवाचार्यवर्येण स्पष्टीकृत्य न चोत्तरा ॥
>
> *vyākhyātā kaṇvaśākhīyasaṃhitā pūrvaviṃśatiḥ |*
> *mādhavācāryavaryeṇa spaṣṭīkṛtya na cottarā ||*
>
> "Of the Saṃhitā of the Kaṇva branch the first twenty [adhyāyas] were explained by the excellent Mādhavācārya, made clear; not the later [ones]."
>
> (From the Kāṇva-śākhā Yajurveda commentary that follows.)

It is not so easy to believe this view. This portion may also have been lost, like the last portion of the first kāṇḍa of the commentary on the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa.

In this commentary Sāyaṇācārya has quoted from works such as Manu, Prakāśātmācārya and his work of exposition (*Vivaraṇa*), the Vedānta-darśana, Jaimini, Kumārilabhaṭṭa, Bhāskarācārya, the Kātyāyana Sarvānukramaṇī, the Kātyāyana Śrauta, the Kāṇva Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa, Āpastamba, the Taittirīya, the Vāsiṣṭha-rāmāyaṇa and others.

In the Yajurveda, the divisions such as *khaṇḍa* are for the convenience of those who study the Veda; as Veṅkaṭamādhava and Ānandatīrtha said of the *vargas* and the other divisions of the Ṛgveda, Sāyaṇācārya too has accepted [this]. In the first adhyāya of the commentary these sentences are:

> माणवकानामावर्तनसौकर्याय खण्डिकाविच्छेदस्य बुद्धिमद्भि-
> रध्यापकैः कल्पितत्वात् । यथा बह्वृचानां तत्र तत्र सूक्त-
> मध्येऽपि वर्गविच्छेदः कल्पितः । यथा वा तैत्तिरीयकाणां
> वाक्यमध्येऽपि पंचाशच्छब्दसंख्यया विच्छेदः आवृत्ति-
> सौकर्याय कल्प्यते । तद्वदत्राप्यनुगंतव्यम् ।
>
> *māṇavakānām āvartanasaukaryāya khaṇḍikāvicchedasya buddhimadbhir adhyāpakaiḥ kalpitatvāt | yathā bahvṛcānāṃ tatra tatra sūktamadhye 'pi vargavicchedaḥ kalpitaḥ | yathā vā taittirīyakāṇāṃ vākyamadhye 'pi paṃcāśacchabdasaṃkhyayā vicchedaḥ āvṛttisaukaryāya kalpyate | tadvad atrāpy anugantavyam |*
>
> "For the facility of repetition by students, the division into *khaṇḍikā* has been devised by the wise …; just as for the Bahvṛcas the division into *vargas* is devised here and there even in the middle of a hymn; or as for the Taittirīyakas a division by a count of fifty words is devised, even in the middle of a sentence, for ease of repetition; so should it be followed here too." (One word in the first line is doubtful.)

By this [account], the Brāhmaṇas are expositions of the mantras. In the *upodghāta* he has said:

> "शतपथब्राह्मणस्य मन्त्रव्याख्यानरूपत्वात्"
>
> *"śatapathabrāhmaṇasya mantravyākhyānarūpatvāt"*
>
> "Because the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa is in the form of an exposition of the mantras."

With this same intention, in the commentary he quotes sentences of the Brāhmaṇa here and there.

##### 2. Ānandabodha {.lv3}

(1442–1542 C.E.)

He composed a commentary for the entire Kāṇva branch. At Pune there is a commentary on the first 20 adhyāyas. In the library of the Panjab University at Lahore it is from the 19th to the 38th adhyāya. Bhagavaddatta, who wrote the "History of Vedic Literature", has in his own library two parts. In one is the commentary on the 20th to the 39th adhyāyas, and in the second part is the commentary on the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad, the 40th adhyāya. Taken all together this makes one complete commentary.

At the end of every adhyāya the name "*Kāṇva-veda-mantra-bhāṣya-saṃgraha*" has been used for the work. At the end of the commentary on the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad, published by Ānandāśrama,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 267</div>

> इति श्रीमत्परमहंसपरिव्राजकाचार्यवर्यश्रीवासुदेव-
> पुरीपूज्यपादपरमकारुण्यासादितश्रीकृष्णभक्तिसाम्राज्यस्य
> श्रीमज्ज्ञातवेदभट्टोपाध्यायस्य सूनुना श्रीमदानन्द-
> भट्टोपाध्यायेन विरचिते काण्ववेदमन्त्रभाष्यसंग्रहे
> चत्वारिंशोऽध्यायः ।
>
> *iti śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryavaryaśrīvāsudeva-purīpūjyapādaparamakāruṇyāsāditaśrīkṛṣṇabhaktisāmrājyasya śrīmajjñātavedabhaṭṭopādhyāyasya sūnunā śrīmadānanda-bhaṭṭopādhyāyena viracite kāṇvavedamantrabhāṣyasaṃgrahe catvāriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ |*
>
> "Thus, in the *Kāṇva-veda-mantra-bhāṣya-saṃgraha* composed by the venerable Ānanda Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, son of the venerable Jātaveda Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, who obtained the empire of devotion to Kṛṣṇa through the supreme compassion of the revered feet of the venerable Vāsudeva-purī, teacher-supreme, the *paramahaṃsa* wanderer — the fortieth chapter."

From this it is learnt that the name of this work is *Kāṇvaveda-mantra-bhāṣya-saṃgraha*, and that his father was Bhaṭṭopādhyāya.

There are not sufficient grounds to state his time with certainty. From the Pune manuscript it can only be guessed that he was earlier than 300 years ago.

One Devayājñika wrote, about 1506 C.E., a work called *Iṣṭakāpūrṇa-bhāṣya*. In his commentary on the Yājuṣa-sarvānukramaṇī he has quoted something from a commentary on the Kāṇva-saṃhitā.

> उर्वन्तरिक्षमित्यस्य रक्षोघ्नं ब्रह्मदेवतेति एवं कण्वसंहिता-
> भाष्ये व्याख्यातमस्ति ।
>
> *urv antarikṣam ity asya rakṣoghnaṃ brahmadevateti evaṃ kaṇvasaṃhitā-bhāṣye vyākhyātam asti |*
>
> "Of [the mantra] 'urv antarikṣam', the demon-slaying one, the deity is Brahman — thus it is explained in the commentary on the Kaṇva-saṃhitā."

And —

> अग्निर्देवतेति माधवाचार्याः ।
>
> *agnir devateti mādhavācāryāḥ |*
>
> "'The deity is Agni' — so say the Mādhavācāryas."

These sentences are not in Sāyaṇācārya's commentary. Moreover, he does not indicate the deities in this manner. Therefore, if these sentences happen to be found in Ānandabodha's commentary, then his time can be stated with certainty.

##### 3. Anantācārya {.lv3}

(time: the first half of the 17th century C.E.)

Parts of his commentary are here and there. In the library of the Alwar State it is from the 32nd to the 40th adhyāya; at Pune, from the 32nd to the 40th (a copy of C.E. 1665); and at Madras from the 21st to the 30th adhyāya. The commentary on the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad, the 40th adhyāya, was printed by the Ānandāśrama publishers.

A manuscript of his commentary on the Prātiśākhya, written at the end of the 17th century C.E., is at Calcutta. In his work called *Kaṇva-kaṇṭhābharaṇa* he has quoted a commentary on the Yājuṣa-sarvānukramaṇī. This too is a work written in the early part of the 17th century C.E. And he has taken sentences from Sāyaṇācārya's work also. For these reasons it can be said that he composed his commentary in the first half of the 17th century C.E.

At the beginning of the Madras copy he has bowed to his father and mother, telling their names.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 268</div>

> वन्दे श्रीपितृचरणान् भट्टनागेशसंज्ञकान् ।
> यत्प्रसादादहं प्राज्ञः संजातो जडधीरपि ॥
> वन्दे भागीरथीमम्बां ...........गुणशालिनीम् ॥
>
> *vande śrīpitṛcaraṇān bhaṭṭanāgeśasaṃjñakān |*
> *yatprasādād ahaṃ prājñaḥ saṃjāto jaḍadhīr api ||*
> *vande bhāgīrathīm ambāṃ ...........guṇaśālinīm ||*
>
> "I bow to the revered feet of my father, named Bhaṭṭa Nāgeśa, by whose grace I, though dull-witted, have become learned. I bow to my mother Bhāgīrathī, [full of ...], endowed with virtues."

His father was Nāgeśabhaṭṭa, his mother Bhāgīrathī, his place of residence Kāśī. At the end of the Pune copy too the same intention occurs.

> अम्बा भागीरथी यस्य नागदेवः पिता सुधीः ।
> काश्यां वासः सदा सस्य चित्तं यस्य रमाप्रिये ॥
>
> *ambā bhāgīrathī yasya nāgadevaḥ pitā sudhīḥ |*
> *kāśyāṃ vāsaḥ sadā sasya cittaṃ yasya ramāpriye ||*
>
> "Whose mother is Bhāgīrathī, whose father is the wise Nāgadeva; whose residence is always at Kāśī; whose mind [is] on the beloved of Ramā [Viṣṇu]."

That he composed a commentary on the entire Kāṇva Saṃhitā is clear from this verse of the Madras copy:

> व्याख्याता काण्वशाखीयसंहिता पूर्वविंशतिः ।
> माधवाचार्यवर्येण स्पष्टीकृत्यै न चोत्तरा ।
> अतस्तां व्याकरिष्येऽहमनन्ताचार्यनामकः ॥
>
> *vyākhyātā kāṇvaśākhīyasaṃhitā pūrvaviṃśatiḥ |*
> *mādhavācāryavaryeṇa spaṣṭīkṛtyai na cottarā |*
> *atas tāṃ vyākariṣye 'ham anantācāryanāmakaḥ ||*
>
> "Of the Saṃhitā of the Kāṇva branch the first twenty were explained by the excellent Mādhavācārya, made clear; not the later. Therefore I, named Anantācārya, shall explain it."

Mādhavācārya expounded the first twenty adhyāyas of the Saṃhitā and left the remaining twenty. Therefore, he says, I shall explain the remaining twenty adhyāyas. The name of this commentary is "*Bhāvārtha-dīpikā*". Sometimes it is also called "*Veda-dīpa*".

> अमुना वेददीपेन मया नीराजितो हरिः ।
>
> *amunā vedadīpena mayā nīrājito hariḥ |*
>
> "By this lamp of the Veda Hari has been waved before [in lamp-worship] by me."

He wrote the commentary after studying the Kātyāyana sūtras, the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa, many ancient commentaries, and the Vedāṅgas such as the Nirukta. He declares that he composed the commentary not for the sake of showing off his scholarship, nor from greed for wealth, but solely for the satisfaction of the Supreme Self.

> कात्यायनकृतं सूत्रं ब्राह्मणं शतपथाभिधम् ।
> पुरातनानि भाष्याणि निरुक्ताद्यंगमेव च ॥
> आलोक्य सम्यग्बहुधा कृतं भाष्यमनुत्तमम् ।
> सन्ति भाष्याण्यनेकानि प्रणीतानि हि सूरिभिः ॥
> (पूना प्रति)
>
> *kātyāyanakṛtaṃ sūtraṃ brāhmaṇaṃ śatapathābhidham |*
> *purātanāni bhāṣyāṇi niruktādyaṃgam eva ca ||*
> *ālokya samyag bahudhā kṛtaṃ bhāṣyam anuttamam |*
> *santi bhāṣyāṇy anekāni praṇītāni hi sūribhiḥ ||*
> (Pune copy)
>
> "Having looked at the sūtra made by Kātyāyana, the Brāhmaṇa called Śatapatha, the ancient commentaries, and the Vedāṅga beginning with the Nirukta, a most excellent commentary has been made [by me] in many ways. There are indeed many commentaries composed by the learned."

> अनेकग्रन्थमालोच्य दीपिका क्रियते मया ।
> बहूनि सन्ति भाष्याणि प्रणीतानि हि सूरिभिः ॥
> न पाण्डित्याभिमानेन न च वित्तस्य लिप्सया ।
> दीपिका रच्यते किन्तु लक्ष्मीकान्तस्य तुष्टये ॥
> (मद्रास् प्रति)
>
> *anekagranthamālocya dīpikā kriyate mayā |*
> *bahūni santi bhāṣyāṇi praṇītāni hi sūribhiḥ ||*
> *na pāṇḍityābhimānena na ca vittasya lipsayā |*
> *dīpikā racyate kintu lakṣmīkāntasya tuṣṭaye ||*
> (Madras copy)
>
> "Having reflected on many works, a lamp [*dīpikā*] is made by me. There are indeed many commentaries composed by the learned. Not from pride of scholarship, nor from desire for wealth, is the lamp composed, but for the satisfaction of the Lord of Lakṣmī."

Besides having written a commentary on the Yajurveda, he wrote:

1. A commentary on the Śatapatha-brāhmaṇa — a manuscript copy is at Madras.
2. *Kaṇva-kaṇṭhābharaṇa* — likewise, at Madras.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 269</div>

3. *Yājuṣa-prātiśākhya-bhāṣya* — "*Padārtha-prakāśa*" — four manuscript copies of this are at Calcutta.
4. *Bhāṣika-sūtra-bhāṣya* — at the Asiatic Society, Calcutta.

These other works he also composed.

##### 4. Kālanātha {.lv3}

(time about C.E. 1192)

The name of his work is *Yajur-mañjarī*. This is not a commentary on the whole Yajurveda. Following the order of the Yājuṣa [*prakramaṇa*], it is in the form of exposition only for 250 mantras. At the beginning of the commentary there is this verse —

> विविच्य भाष्यं विविधांश्च कल्पा-
> नेतस्य तोषाय मुदा व्यतानीत् ।
> भट्टः स्वयंभूतनयोऽत्र विद्वान्
> श्रीकालनाथः सहकारिभावम् ॥
>
> *vivicya bhāṣyaṃ vividhāṃś ca kalpā-n etasya toṣāya mudā vyatānīt |*
> *bhaṭṭaḥ svayaṃbhūtanayo 'tra vidvān śrīkālanāthaḥ sahakāribhāvam ||*
>
> (The second half-verse is not syntactically clear in the print.)

That is: having examined the commentary and many *kalpas*, for the pleasure of the Mahārāja Devarāja, Kālanātha, son of Svayambhūbhaṭṭa, composed this commentary.

There are not many grounds to determine his time. The following verses help to some extent in finding who the Mahārāja Deva, his patron, was.

> अस्ति प्रशस्तं दिशि पश्चिमायां
> उच्चाभिधानं नगरं गरीयः ॥ ३ ॥
> उच्चैस्तनारध्वरगावगाहं
> तीर्थं परं पञ्चनदं पवित्रम् ॥ ४ ॥
>
> *asti praśastaṃ diśi paścimāyāṃ uccābhidhānaṃ nagaraṃ garīyaḥ || 3 ||*
> *uccaistanāradhvaragāvagāhaṃ tīrthaṃ paraṃ paṃcanadaṃ pavitram || 4 ||*

> क्षितीश्वराः क्षत्रपदावतंसा-
> स्तत्राविरासंस्तरुणप्रतापाः ।
> येषामभूत् वाघरनामधेयः
> प्ररूढशक्तिः प्रथमो नरेन्द्रः ॥
>
> *kṣitīśvarāḥ kṣatrapadāvataṃsā-s tatrāvirāsaṃs taruṇapratāpāḥ |*
> *yeṣām abhūt vāgharanāmadheyaḥ prarūḍhaśaktiḥ prathamo narendraḥ ||*

(The second verse is clearly legible; in the first, the words of the second half are doubtful.)

That is: in the western direction there is a large city by the name Ucca. Near it there is a holy place (*tīrtha-kṣetra*) called Pañcanada. Here many excellent Kṣatriya kings ruled. Their root-ancestor was one named Vāghara. In this line, Vāghara, Toloka, Rāma, Hariścandra, Sahadeva, Haṃsapāla, Maṅgala, Vīrapāla, Jayapāla and Mahārājadeva ruled. In the time of the last of these, Mahārājadeva, Kālanātha's *Yajur-mañjarī* was written.

There are two holy places called Pañcanada. Of these, the Pañcanada near Bhāvalpur must be the region pointed to by Kālanātha. Near it there is also a village called Ucca. Kālanātha may have described the genealogy of the kings of this place.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 270</div>

The manuscript copy in the Asiatic Society of Bengal is of the year 1523 C.E. Therefore Kālanātha must have been earlier than this. In all Kālanātha's works the names are those of Hindu kings. No sign of Muslim rule is seen. The entry of Muslims into the region he describes was after 1174 C.E. Therefore it can be said that he lived at the end of the 12th century C.E.

Those who quote from his work are few. His sentences are seen only in the *Śāstradīpikā* of Pārthasārathi Miśra. But the time of the *Śāstradīpikā* is not yet settled. Therefore nothing more can now be said about Kālanātha.

##### 5. Murāri Miśra {.lv3}

(time about C.E. 1342)

He wrote a work called *Pāraskara-mantra-bhāṣya*. This is not an independent Veda commentary. As he himself writes at the beginning, taking some matters from the Gṛhya commentary written by his father, he wrote a commentary on the mantras that occur in the Pāraskara Gṛhya sūtras.

> प्रणम्य पूर्वं पुरुषं पुराणं
> तथैव कात्यायनपादपद्मम् ।
> तनोति पारस्करमन्त्रभाष्यं
> मुरारिमिश्रः पितृगृह्यभाष्यात् ॥
>
> *praṇamya pūrvaṃ puruṣaṃ purāṇaṃ tathaiva kātyāyanapādapadmam |*
> *tanoti pāraskaramantrabhāṣyaṃ murārimiśraḥ pitṛgṛhyabhāṣyāt ||*
>
> "Having first bowed to the ancient Puruṣa, and likewise to the lotus feet of Kātyāyana, Murāri Miśra composes the commentary on the Pāraskara mantras, from his father's Gṛhya commentary."

> गृह्यप्रकाशाभिधभाष्यगर्भ-
> ज्ञैर्वेदमिश्रैर्विधिवत्प्रणीतम् ।
> आकृष्य बन्धुं विदधाति मन्त्रे
> मुरारिमिश्रः श्रुतितो विविच्य ॥
>
> *gṛhyaprakāśābhidhabhāṣyagarbha-jñair vedamiśrair vidhivat praṇītam |*
> *ākṛṣya bandhuṃ vidadhāti mantre murārimiśraḥ śrutito vivicya ||*
>
> (The first line is transcribed as printed; the word *jñre…* is doubtful and may stand for "Vedamiśra". Gist, editorial and tentative: "Drawing on the commentary called *Gṛhya-prakāśa*, duly composed by Vedamiśra [his father], Murāri Miśra, distinguishing from the Śruti, makes [the commentary] on the mantras.")

His father was Vedamiśra. He composed a work called *Gṛhya-prakāśa*. With the help of this work and of the Veda, he collected the matter and composed his *Pāraskara-mantra-bhāṣya*.

In the Asiatic Society of Bengal there is a *Mantra-bhāṣya*. This copy was written in 1370 C.E. The copy in the library of the Raghunātha temple was written in 1362 C.E. Therefore it can be said that this work was composed before 1362 C.E.

##### 6. Halāyudha {.lv3}

(time C.E. 1174–1199)

He composed a commentary on the Kāṇva-saṃhitā called "*Brāhmaṇa-sarvasva*". This work was printed at Kāśī in 1877 C.E. Many manuscript copies of it also are found.

Concerning him, Rāy Bahādur Manomohana Cakravartī wrote an essay in the journal of the Asiatic Society in 1915 C.E. And Kāṇe, in his History of Dharmaśāstra too, has written concerning Halāyudha. These two writers, taking as their basis this verse of the *Brāhmaṇa-sarvasva*, are of opinion that Halāyudha composed his works between 1174–1199 C.E.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 271</div>

> बाल्ये ख्यापितराजपण्डितपदं श्वेतार्चिबिम्बोज्ज्वल-
> च्छत्रोत्सिक्तमहामहस्तनुपदं दत्त्वा नवे यौवने ।
> यस्मै यौवनशेषयोग्यमखिलक्ष्मापालनारायणः
> श्रीमान्लक्ष्मणसेनदेवनृपतिर्धर्माधिकारं ददौ ॥
>
> *bālye khyāpitarājapaṇḍitapadaṃ śvetārcibimbojjvala-cchatrotsiktamahāmahastanupadaṃ dattvā nave yauvane |*
> *yasmai yauvanaśeṣayogyam akhilakṣmāpālanārāyaṇaḥ śrīmān lakṣmaṇasenadevanṛpatir dharmādhikāraṃ dadau ||*
>
> "In his boyhood [Lakṣmaṇasena] had given him the title of Royal Scholar [*rāja-paṇḍita*], …; in the freshness of his youth the glorious King Lakṣmaṇasena Deva, a Nārāyaṇa among all the guardians of the earth, gave him the office of Dharmādhikāra [judge of religious law], fitted for the remainder of his youth." (The middle of the first line is doubtful in the print.)

King Lakṣmaṇasena Deva gave him the office of Dharmādhikāra. This Lakṣmaṇasena Deva carried on the rule from 1169 to 1199 C.E. Therefore Halāyudha must have composed his works between 1174 and 1199 C.E.

In his commentary Halāyudha has taken help not only from many ancient works but also from the works of such as the Karka-bhāṣya on the Pāraskara Gṛhya sūtras, Mugudācārya's Veda-bhāṣya, Uvaṭa, Yajñapārśva and others. Of these he has taken help chiefly from Uvaṭa's commentary.

He composed not only the *Brāhmaṇa-sarvasva* but other works too. At the beginning of the *Brāhmaṇa-sarvasva* there is this verse —

> मीमांसासर्वस्वं वैष्णवसर्वस्वं यत्कृतश्शैवसर्वस्वम् ।
> पण्डितसर्वस्वमसौ सर्वस्वं सर्वधराणाम् ॥
>
> *mīmāṃsāsarvasvaṃ vaiṣṇavasarvasvaṃ yatkṛtaś śaivasarvasvam |*
> *paṇḍitasarvasvam asau sarvasvaṃ sarvadharāṇām ||*
>
> (The verse is not securely intelligible, and the source gives only the following sentence of explanation.)

He composed also works called *Mīmāṃsā-sarvasva*, *Vaiṣṇava-sarvasva*, *Śaiva-sarvasva* and *Paṇḍita-sarvasva*. But none of these has been found up to now.

#### 3. Ādityadarśana {.lv2}

He wrote two works called '*Mantra-vivṛti*' and '*Kaṭha-gṛhya-sūtra-vivaraṇa*'. The *Mantra-vivṛti* follows the Kaṭha mantra-text or the Cārāyaṇīya mantra-text. In the *Vivṛti* itself he has written an explanation of the Kaṭha Gṛhya sūtras. But again he has written the *Vivaraṇa* in a simple language. He has said this intention at the beginning of his *Vivaraṇa*.

> प्रायेण मन्त्रविवृतौ विवृतं मयेदं
> गुह्यं तथापि बहुभिः शबलीकृतत्वात् ।
> स्पष्टं सुयुक्तिलघुवाक्यविदामभीप्सि-
> तमिष्टं चिकीर्षुरहमत्र पुनर्विचित्रम् ॥
>
> *prāyeṇa mantravivṛtau vivṛtaṃ mayedaṃ guhyaṃ tathāpi bahubhiḥ śabalīkṛtatvāt |*
> *spaṣṭaṃ suyuktilaghuvākyavidām abhīpsitam iṣṭaṃ cikīrṣur aham atra punar vicitram ||*
>
> (Transcribed as printed; a few words are doubtful and the source gives only the gist: "Though I have mostly explained this secret in the *Mantra-vivṛti*, because it was made variegated by many [others], here again I wish clearly to do the desired thing for those who know well-reasoned short sentences.")

His time is not determined. Two persons have quoted his commentary: Brāhmaṇabala, the author of the work *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-pañcikā*, and Devapāla, the commentator on the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya-sūtra. Though it is clearly said that Ādityadarśana was earlier than these two, since the time of these two is itself undetermined, it cannot be said with certainty that Ādityadarśana belonged to this very time.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 272</div>

> यो वेददर्शन इति द्विजवर्गमुख्यः
> सत्यार्जवाशयविशुद्धगुणैः प्रसिद्धः ।
> आस्तिक्यनिर्मलमतिर्विहितानि चक्रे
> चारायणीयचरणैकगुणः प्रदाता ॥
>
> तस्माज्जातो विगतमत्सरमानसानां
> मन्त्रार्थतत्त्वविदुषां जयनिन्द्रियाणि ।
> श्लाघ्यः श्रुताभिजनमाधवरातशिष्य
> आदित्यदर्शन इमां विवृतिं व्यधत्त ॥
>
> *yo vedadarśana iti dvijavargamukhyaḥ satyārjavāśayaviśuddhaguṇaiḥ prasiddhaḥ |*
> *āstikyanirmalamatir vihitāni cakre cārāyaṇīyacaraṇaikaguṇaḥ pradātā ||*
> *tasmāj jāto vigatamatsaramānasānāṃ mantrārthatattvaviduṣāṃ jayanindriyāṇi |*
> *ślāghyaḥ śrutābhijanamādhavarātaśiṣya ādityadarśana imāṃ vivṛtiṃ vyadhatta ||*
>
> "He who was the chief of the twice-born, renowned for pure virtues of truthfulness and uprightness of mind, of an unsullied intellect in faith, who performed the prescribed rites, whose one virtue was the Cārāyaṇīya school, a giver — from him was born [Ādityadarśana], praiseworthy, of Vedic lineage, a pupil of Mādhavarāta, who composed this *Vivṛti*." (The words "*jayanindriyāṇi*" in the second verse are doubtful and are left outside the rendering.)

His father was Vedadarśana, who studied only the Cārāyaṇīya branch. One named Mādhavarāta was his guru. His work is the foremost among the Vedic commentaries.

#### 8. Devapāla {.lv2}

He did not write a separate mantra-commentary. What he composed is the commentary on the Kāṭhaka Gṛhya-sūtra. As is included within it, he composed a mantra-commentary also.

> "इति चारायणीयमन्त्रभाष्यं भट्टहरिपालकृतं समाप्तम् ।" (Punjab copy)
> *"iti cārāyaṇīyamantrabhāṣyaṃ bhaṭṭaharipālakṛtaṃ samāptam |"*
> "Thus ends the Cārāyaṇīya mantra-commentary made by Bhaṭṭa Haripāla."

> "इति चारायणीयमन्त्रभाष्यं कृतिः श्रीमदाचार्यवर्य-
> स्वामिभट्टारकहरिपालपूज्यपादानाम्" (काश्मीर प्रति)
> *"iti cārāyaṇīyamantrabhāṣyaṃ kṛtiḥ śrīmadācāryavarya-svāmibhaṭṭārakaharipālapūjyapādānām"* (Kashmir copy)
