It is on this basis that Jacobi and the Indian scholar B. G. Tilak dated the Veda. Both of them made the attempt in the same year (C.E. 1893), and each arrived at a conclusion of his own.

In the time of the Brahmanas there is an indication that the Mesha-saṅkramaṇa (the vernal equinox) began in the Krittika nakshatra; but in the Samhita portions, older than these, it is said that this saṅkramaṇa began in the Mrigashiras nakshatra. Calculating by the order of the nakshatras, it is known that the Mesha-saṅkramaṇa fell in Krittika in about 2500 BC and in Mrigashiras in about 4500 BC. On this basis Jacobi conjectures that the civilization of the Vedas lay between about 4500 and 2500 BC, and concludes that the Samhita we now have was gathered and put into book form in the latter half of this period. But Tilak goes back as far as 6000 BC.

Jacobi's conclusion has one more basis. In the Grihya-sutras a practice current at that time is described. When a newly married couple come to their home, they must look at the nakshatras: when the nakshatras begin to be seen, that is, after dark, the bridegroom shows his wife the Dhruva-nakshatra (the pole star) and says, "Like that nakshatra, may you live firmly with me." She addresses the nakshatra and prays, "You are firm; be gracious, that I too may be firm in the same way." From this one point can be known: the Dhruva-nakshatra spoken of must then have been a bright nakshatra appearing fixed near the north pole of the earth. As the earth goes round the sun, its north pole too turns slowly; in this turning

<div class="pgmark">original p. 340</div>

each nakshatra in turn comes near the north pole and is called the Dhruva-nakshatra. For one such circle to be completed takes 26,000 years. Among the nakshatras that become the Dhruva-nakshatra in turn, large nakshatras come only rarely. The present Dhruva-nakshatra is a small nakshatra of the Laghu-saptarshi group (the Little Bear), and it cannot be said that this same nakshatra was the Dhruva-nakshatra then. It is known that in 2780 BC there was another Dhruva-nakshatra. Therefore the time when this practice was current may be said to be the first half of the third millennium BC. This practice is not found anywhere in the Ṛgveda; therefore the Ṛgveda's period can boldly be said to be earlier than 3000 BC.

There are some faults in this argument. First, the very name *saṅkramaṇa* does not occur in the Vedas. Against the view that the Krittika nakshatra mentioned in the Shatapatha Brahmana (2-1-2-3) stays fixed in the east, the right meaning is that the Krittika nakshatra was seen for a long time in the eastern quarter (in 3000 BC), since Krittika does not rise exactly in the east; and this was so in about 1100 BC. Further, taking the beginning of the year over thousands of years: in some places one season and in other places another is called the beginning of the year, and the number of seasons in a year is not fixed either — there are 3, 4, 5 seasons, and so on. As for the Dhruva-nakshatra, it is not right either that a small nakshatra could not be the Dhruva-nakshatra and that it must have been a large one: since the sky in our country is clear, even a small nakshatra is seen distinctly. And since this practice is not even named in the Ṛgveda, it is wrong to conclude that the Vedas are earlier than this. The Veda does not mention every practice; so it is not proper to argue on this one alone.

Though it is not possible to accept the views of Jacobi and Tilak, they became one reason for scholars to re-examine the date of the Veda. There was one more reason for the re-examination to be needed. As historical research advanced, it became clear that 700–800 years were not enough for the Aryans to spread over the whole of our country. It is known that in the first parts of the Ṛgveda the Aryans were in the Punjab, and it is known from inscriptions that by about 300 BC the Aryans had occupied South India. It is a known fact that the Bodhāyana and Āpastamba branches were current in South India; so the Aryans must have entered South India still earlier — perhaps about 700 BC, for to occupy a country, spread the Brahmanical dharma and establish new branches here would take a long time.

If it is accepted that in 700–600 BC Aryan culture was spreading in the south, it is not possible to believe that the Aryans were in the Punjab in 1200 BC. In 500–600 years for the Aryans to conquer

<div class="pgmark">original p. 341</div>

a country as large as this is impossible; and to conquer people who were uncivilized and quarrelling among themselves, to make them cultured and to spread their literature among them is very hard to achieve. Therefore at least twice that time is needed. This is the view of **G. Buhler**.

But **Oldenberg** argued thus: 700 years is not a short time, and many changes can happen within it. Considering how much change took place in America in four hundred years, one may guess what can happen in 700 years.

But the political situation of America differs greatly from that of India. In the Vedic and Puranic period the occupation of the plains of the Hindu country by the Aryans was a very difficult and slow task; they had to fight for and win every step. Besides, it is known from the Veda that the composition of the Ṛgveda took a long time; among the mantras there are new mantras and old mantras, new ṛṣis and old ṛṣis.

**Bloomfield** notes that many Rigveda mantras recur repeatedly across different contexts within the text itself — showing that much of the Rigveda's material already existed in fixed, traditional form before being incorporated, later generations adapting it to their own needs.

The mantras of the Ṛgveda differ in language from the other mantras; the Brāhmaṇas, Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads differ from the Saṃhitās in many ways — in language, style, modes of worship and the civilization described. And by the time these Brāhmaṇas and the rest were composed, the four Saṃhitās were in use; moreover, the Saṃhitā portions were not understood at all by many people of that time.

The Vedas have not come to us in book form. Had writing been in use, the growth of the Vedas would not have needed so much time; but since everything had to be kept in memory and learned by mouth from one person to another, many centuries were needed for the whole Saṃhitā portion to come together. The Brāhmaṇas too must have taken many centuries to take full shape. Considering the many śākhās and sub-śākhās and the countless priests, it is established that all this was not possible in less than several centuries. In the same way, in the Upaniṣads too, differences of time, many generations of teachers and a tradition of centuries are understood.

From all this it is known that, though the Veda developed so far, the Aryans had come only from the Punjab as far as the Gangetic plain. If so much time was needed to occupy so small a region, how many centuries must it have taken to occupy the rest of North India, go on to the south and spread Brahmanism there? Therefore, as Oldenberg said, 700 years is no long span; it may be said not to be enough at all.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 342</div>

Max Müller, taking the spread of Buddhism (502 BC) as an anchor point, held that Vedic religion was already fully developed by then; Oldenberg showed that there must have been a gap of many centuries between the Upanishads and the beginning of Buddhism. There were creeds current before Buddhism which, like Buddhism, did not accept the Vedas as authority; Jainism is one of them, and it is known from reliable evidence that the founder of the Jains lived in about 750 BC. Beginning in this way, **G. Buhler** set out to prove that the Vedas are much earlier than the time now known; unfortunately he died before he could establish his theory.

A genuinely remarkable piece of evidence comes from **Boghazkoi** in Asia Minor: ancient artifacts discovered there by **Hugo Winckler** in 1907 CE included treaty documents from the ancient **Hittite Kingdom**. Among them, a treaty between the Hittites and the **Mitanni** kingdom, made in the **14th century BC**, survives in its concluding portion — where the two parties invoke their own deities as witnesses to the treaty. Among the named deities are **Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and Nasatya** — all recognizably Hindu deity-names. Why these names occur in this inscription became a great problem for scholars; each argued in his own way.

The historian **Meyer** holds that these deities belong to a shared ancient Aryan-Iranian heritage, predating the Aryans' eventual arrival in India — by the time the Aryans were spreading in Mesopotamia and Syria they were also spreading in India; in his view the composition of the mantras began from about the 15th century BC onwards. **Oldenberg** expresses the same opinion and says that there is not enough basis for saying that the Vedas are earlier than this.

It is quite impossible to say that these deities are others than the deities of our Veda. People used to migrate from this country to foreign lands now and then; in the same way people living in India with a Vedic culture may have gone to Asia Minor and other regions. This establishes one point: about the 14th century BC the Aryans had settled in the north-western provinces and had long been engaged in the worship of deities. If it is established from the Asia Minor inscriptions that the numerals of the Hindu country were also in use in that country, our above opinion would be strengthened.

**J. Hertel** argues the Veda's birthplace was not India at all, but Persia, dating its composition to the era of Zoroaster (550 BC). **G. Husing**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 343</div>

 went a step further and argued that Kānīta Pṛthuśravas, who occurs in the Ṛgveda, and the Scythian king Kānīta are one and the same, and that the Vedas were not yet complete even in the 2nd century BC. There is no proper basis in support of his view.

The very strong basis for saying that the Vedas are not older than three thousand years is the likeness — in religion, language and the like — between the Veda and the Avesta. But this likeness is easily explained in another way. If one or two facts are kept in mind it becomes very simple. First, the Indians and the Iranians belonged to one tribe, and even after separating the two were neighbours. As for the likeness in language: languages do not change according to any fixed rule; some change very fast and some very slowly. Languages connected with religion naturally change more slowly than the spoken tongue.

But it is also false that languages stay alike for thousands of years. The conclusions, made on the basis of astronomy or geology, that the Vedas are older than 16,000 or 25,000 years are groundless. By such figures one would have to suppose that peoples as skilful as the Hindus stayed in one state for thousands of years without making any progress at all; that is quite impossible. Besides, it is impossible to accept a break between the culture of the Samhita portion and that of the Brahmana portion. Further, Panini's Sanskrit and the Sanskrit of Ashoka's inscriptions are closely related to the Vedic language. If the Veda is accepted as 16,000–20,000 years old, the clear views stated above would have to be wrong.

**In summary, only this much can be said of the discussion so far:**

**1.** The attempt to date the Veda on the basis of Vedic statements connected with astronomy certainly fails; Vedic statements can bear many meanings.

**2.** Historical points — the names of Vedic deities in the inscriptions of Syria and other countries, and the likeness of the Hindu Aryans, the civilization of the Indo-Europeans and the civilization of the Veda — are very uncertain. But points recently come to light can push the Veda back to the 20th century BC.

**3.** Figures and points connected with language — the likeness of the Veda and the Avesta, and of the Vedic language and modern languages — do not allow any proper conclusion.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 344</div>

### Chapter Conclusion

**4.** The one result of these linguistic likenesses and differences is that they warn that it is wrong to push the Veda's date back indefinitely.

**5.** Since a proper conclusion is not possible from external evidence, the attempt must be made to decide by examining the whole literature of our country. The one strong basis is that the Vedas and Vedangas were all complete before the time when Parshvanatha, Mahavira and the Buddha spread their creeds. But if 1200 or 1500 [BC] is taken as the beginning of the Veda, it is not possible to account for the growth of the Vedas and Vedangas. It is therefore best to take the beginning of the Veda as about **4500–3000 BC** and its completion as about **1500–1000 BC**. Without going into the matter of a fixed date, the best course of all is to take a period neither very ancient nor so late as to be laughable.

**— This concludes the chapter on the Age of the Vedas. —**

# PART II: Sāyaṇācārya's Introduction to the Ṛgveda Commentary (Ṛgveda-bhāṣya-bhūmikā)

## Chapter 1. Invocatory Verses

*Original title: "Maṅgalācaraṇa"*
**Printed pages 345–349 of the source.**

### Title Page

**श्रीगणाधिपतये नमः।**
*śrī gaṇādhipataye namaḥ*
"Salutations to Sri Ganapati (Lord of the Ganas)."

**सायणाचार्यकृता ऋग्वेदभाष्यभूमिका**
*(Composed by Sayanacharya: The Introduction (Bhumika) to the Rigveda-Bhashya)*

**Kannada Translation of Sayanacharya's Rigveda-Bhashya-Bhumika**

### Opening

Shri Sayanacharya was a great scholar of the Vijayanagara royal court — highly accomplished in the Vedas, Vedangas, statecraft (rajaniti), the doctrines of Purva-Mimamsa, logic (tarka-shastra), grammar, and other disciplines, who had an elder brother, Madhavacharya, also a court scholar of King Bukka, unrivalled in all the shastras and the author of many learned works.

Seeing his scholarship, King Bukka ordered Madhavacharya to write a commentary on the Rigveda for the benefit of the world. Madhavacharya then said to King Bukka: "O great king, I have a younger brother named Sayanacharya. He is expert in all the shastras and knows everything about Vedic matters. If he is ordered to compose the commentary, he will compose it." Accordingly King Bukka summoned Sayanacharya and ordered him to compose a commentary on the Vedas.

Since the Yajurveda held particular usefulness for yajna-related matters, Sayana composed its commentary first, turning to the Rigveda only afterward. Following the ancient tradition of disciples, he opened his very first verse with an auspicious invocation (mangalacharana) honoring **Ganapati**:

> "āśīr-namaskriyā vā vastu-nirdeśo vā" — auspicious invocations take one of three forms: a blessing (āśīrvāda), a salutation (namaskāra), or a statement of the subject-matter (vastu-nirdeśa). Since the deity who removes obstacles (Vighneshvara/Ganapati) is especially favored at the start of any undertaking, Sayana composed his opening verse as a hymn of praise to this very deity, so that his own great endeavor might proceed free of obstacles.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 346</div>

**Verse 1:**

> वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस्तं नमामि गजाननम् ॥ १ ॥
>
> *vāgīśādyāḥ sumanasaḥ sarvārthānām upakrame | yaṃ natvā kṛtakṛtyāḥ syus taṃ namāmi gajānanam || 1 ||*
>
> "I bow to that elephant-faced one, bowing to whom, at the start of all undertakings, even the wise ones beginning with Vagisha (the Lord of Speech) become accomplished in their purpose."

That is: Chaturmukha-Brahma and other deities, before beginning yajnas, going to war, or any other undertaking, first bow to elephant-faced Ganapati and thereby become successful in their tasks. Sayana bows to this same obstacle-removing Ganapati so that the Rigveda-commentary he is about to begin may reach completion without hindrance.

Ganapati is famously known in the Puranas as "Vighnaraja" (Lord of Obstacles) — granting his worshippers success without hindrance. The Shiva Purana recounts that at the burning of Tripura, when Shiva set out to destroy the three cities without first worshipping Ganapati, the cities could not even be seen; only after worshipping Ganapati did they become visible, and the destruction proceeded effortlessly. Vishnu, Brahma, Indra, and other deities likewise began their own undertakings only after worshipping Ganapati first — and if even the gods do so, mortals certainly must. It is customary to worship Ganapati first at the start of education, marriage and other auspicious rites, vows, and deity-worship generally. Sayanacharya follows this same learned tradition here.

**Verse 2:**

> यस्य निःश्वसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तमहं वन्दे विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरम् ॥ २ ॥
>
> *yasya niḥśvasitaṃ vedā yo vedebhyo'khilaṃ jagat | nirmame tam ahaṃ vande vidyātīrtha-maheśvaram || 2 ||*
>
> "I worship him — Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara — whose very breath the Vedas are, and who, from the Vedas, fashioned this entire universe."

Having bowed to Ganapati, Sayana next bows to the Blessed Lord Ishvara — identifying his own guru, Vidyatirtha, with Maheshvara himself.

### English Translation of Sayana's Preface to the Rigveda

**1.** I bow down to the elephant-faced Ganapati, to whom (even all other) deities with the Lord of speech (Brihaspati or Brahma) at their head, bow down at the beginning of all their undertakings, and (thereby) become successful in their attempts.

**2.** I worship Him—Vidyatirtha, (my Guru) Who is (identical with) Maheswara, Whose breath the Vedas are, (and) Who from the Vedas created the whole world.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 347</div>

The Supreme Lord whose breath itself takes the form of the Vedas, and who created the whole universe from the Vedas themselves — that Maheshvara, the master of all the vidyas, or our guru named Vidyatirtha, who is the very form of the Lord, I bow to.

Vidyatirtha was the guru of Bharatitirtha, and Bharatitirtha was the guru of Madhavacharya; so Vidyatirtha was Madhava's paramaguru. According to the shastra saying "*guru reva maheśvaraḥ*" ("the guru alone is Maheshvara"), the disciple should regard the guru as Parameshvara himself. For these reasons, when Madhavacharya bows to Vidyatirtha-Maheshvara, he bows to both his guru and Maheshvara.

The Vedas are said to be the breath of Parameshvara: an Upanishad passage says that this Rigveda, Yajurveda and Samaveda are the breath of that great Being. Hence the Vedas have come forth from the mouth of the Supreme Self in the form of breath. Moreover, Parameshvara created the world with the help of the Vedas, and this Lord is the cause of all vidyas; from him all vidyas and shastras have arisen. Therefore, at the time of composing the Veda-commentary, Madhavacharya bows to Maheshvara (the guru) renowned by the name Vidyatirtha, who is the very form of all the Vedas and the lord of all vidyas, and so begins the work after making the auspicious invocation of bowing to Ishvara and the guru.

**Verse 3:**

> तस्यैव कटाक्षेण तादृशं दध्रे बुक्कमहीपतिः । आदिशन्माधवाचार्यं वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशने ॥ ३ ॥
>
> *tasyaiva kaṭākṣeṇa tādṛśaṃ dadhre bukka-mahīpatiḥ | ādiśan mādhavācāryaṃ vedārthasya prakāśane || 3 ||*
>
> "By that very [Maheshvara's] sidelong glance, King Bukka assumed such a form [became king], and directed Acharya Madhava to illuminate the meaning of the Vedas."

In this verse, Sayana states what occasioned this very undertaking. Through the grace of the aforementioned Vidyatirtha, King Bukka — himself born as a portion of the divine — commanded Madhavacharya to compose a commentary that would clearly explain the Vedas' meaning for the people's easy understanding.

Scripture holds that protecting the citizenry according to dharma is a king's foremost duty — "protection" meaning not merely removing hardship and the fear of enemies, but ensuring citizens come to understand the essential truths of the Veda, Shastra, Purana, and Itihasa, so that, walking the path of truth, they become worthy recipients of divine grace. Such governance is impossible without divine grace itself. And "*nāviṣṇuḥ pṛthivīpatiḥ*" — regarding Vishnu...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 348</div>

The phrase "*nāviṣṇuḥ pṛthivīpatiḥ*" is a smṛti saying that one without a portion of Vishnu cannot become a king — since protecting the world is Vishnu's own foremost task, a king who protects his citizens must be Vishnu's own portion, and no king can prosper without Ishvara's protection. King Bukka, holding this same divine favor, considered illuminating the Veda's meaning a task worthy of his position, and equal to accomplishing it.

**Verse 4:**

> स स्प्राह नृपतिं राजन् सायणार्यो ममानुजः । सर्वं वेत्त्येष वेदानां व्याख्याकृत्ये नियुज्यताम् ॥ ४ ॥
>
> *sa sprāha nṛpatiṃ rājan sāyaṇāryo mamānujaḥ | sarvaṃ vetty eṣa vedānāṃ vyākhyā-kṛtye niyujyatām || 4 ||*
>
> "He said to the king: 'O king, Sayanacharya is my younger brother; he knows everything of the Vedas — let him be appointed to the task of composing the commentary.'"

Hearing King Bukka's request, Madhavacharya addressed him: "O king, I have a younger brother named Sayana, a scholar accomplished across all the shastras — he may be commanded to compose the Veda-commentary."

**Verse 5:**

> इत्युक्तो माधवार्येण वीरबुक्कमहीश्वरः । अन्वशात् सायणाचार्यं वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशने ॥ ५ ॥
>
> *ity ukto mādhavāryeṇa vīra-bukka-mahīśvaraḥ | anvaśāt sāyaṇācāryaṃ vedārthasya prakāśane || 5 ||*
>
> "Thus addressed by Madhavacharya, the valiant King Bukka commanded Sayanacharya to illuminate the meaning of the Vedas."

Accordingly, King Bukka summoned Sayanacharya and commanded him to compose a Veda-commentary and make it widely known, for the world's benefit. *(Note: verses 4 and 5 are absent from some copies.)*

**Verse 6:**

> ये पूर्वोक्ते मीमांसे ते व्याख्यायातिसंग्रहात् । कृपालुर्माधवाचार्यो वेदार्थं वक्तुमुद्यतः ॥ ६ ॥
>
> *ye pūrvokte mīmāṃse te vyākhyāyātisaṃgrahāt | kṛpālur mādhavācāryo vedārthaṃ vaktum udyataḥ || 6 ||*
>
> "Having already expounded, in extremely concise form, the two aforementioned Mimamsas, the compassionate Madhavacharya now sets himself to explain the meaning of the Vedas."

This Madhavacharya was a scholar of great accomplishment, having already written commentaries on the Purva-Mimamsa and Uttara-Mimamsa systems for the convenience of learned readers; he now turns to illuminating the Vedas' meaning.

The Purva-Mimamsa and Uttara-Mimamsa are the final two of the six orthodox philosophical systems (Shad-darshanas) — Purva-Mimamsa composed by the sage Jaimini, and Uttara-Mimamsa (or Sharirika-Mimamsa, the Brahma-sutra).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 349</div>

The Vedanta-sutra (Brahma-sutra), known by several names, forms the basis of the Uttara-Mimamsa system, its various topics grounded specifically in the Upanishads — and it is on this same foundation that the present Veda-commentary is built. This sutra-text draws together the views of various traditional teachers and interprets other Vedantic works accordingly, and has itself become authoritative among the philosophical schools. Since these Purva- and Uttara-Mimamsa, among the six darshanas, are helpful to the meaning of the Veda, Madhavacharya first wrote commentaries on them and then set about the Veda-commentary; that is, he helped his younger brother Sayanacharya in the great task of composing the Veda-commentary.

**Verse 7:**

> आध्वर्यवस्य यज्ञेषु प्राधान्याद्व्याख्यातः पुरा । यजुर्वेदोऽथ होत्रार्थं ऋग्वेदो व्याकरिष्यते ॥ ७ ॥
>
> *ādhvaryavasya yajñeṣu prādhānyād vyākhyātaḥ purā | yajurvedo'tha hotrārthaṃ ṛgvedo vyākariṣyate || 7 ||*
>
> "Because of the primary importance of the Adhvaryu priest's role in yajnas, the Yajurveda was explained first; now, for the sake of the Hotr priest's task, the Rigveda is going to be explained."

That he composed the Yajurveda commentary first, before undertaking the Rigveda's, has already been stated — but why explain the Yajurveda first, when the Rigveda is the first among the Vedas? This verse gives the answer.

In yajnas, the **Adhvaryu** priest's role is primary — "*adhvaryurvā ṛtvijāṃ prathamo yujyate*" ("the Adhvaryu is indeed yoked first among the priests"), as the Yajurveda itself states. An Adhvaryu cannot perform his duties without thorough knowledge of the Yajurveda. Correspondingly, the **Hotr** priest must be deeply versed in the Rigveda. Yajnas involve four principal priests — Hotr, Adhvaryu, Udgatr, and Brahma — and though many assistant priests may participate in various rites, these four remain the principal officiants. The Hotr must have mastered Rigveda study along with its Shrauta (ritual-application) portion. Yajna-mantras fall into two categories: puronuvākyā and yajya; inviting the deities and directing the fire-offering is the Hotr's chief duty. The Adhvaryu, correspondingly, must thoroughly study the Yajurveda and diligently practice its Shrauta portion.

## Chapter 2. Purva-pakṣa — Even Though the Rigveda Holds the Foremost Place Among the Vedas, Was It Proper That Sayanacharya's First Commentary Was on the Yajurveda Rather Than the Rigveda?

*Original title: "Ṛgvedavu vēdagaḷalli agrasthānavannu paḍediddarū Sāyaṇācāryaru Ṛgvedakke modala bhāṣyavannu bareyade Yajurvēdakke bhāṣyavannu barēdudu ucitavē emba vicāradalli pūrvapakṣavu"*
**Printed pages 350–354 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 350</div>

The Udgatr priest, similarly essential in yajnas, must be well-versed in the Samaveda, reciting its prescribed hymns correctly during the ceremony — "*ayajño vā eṣa yo 'sāmā*" (a yajna without Sāman-singing is no yajna), as the Yajurveda states. The **Brahma** priest must know all four Vedas and be broadly versed in every ritual matter — overseeing the correct, sequential offering of oblations throughout the yajna, a role that stands above all the other three priests.

Having established this reasoning, Sayana explains: because the Adhvaryu's role is prominent, the Yajurveda commentary was needed and written first; now, because the Hotr's role likewise requires the Rigveda to be made accessible, he sets out to compose the Rigveda commentary next.

**Verse 8:**

> एकस्मिन् प्रथमोऽध्यायः संप्रदायानुसारतः । वृत्तैस्सावधानः सर्वं बोद्धुं शक्नोति बुद्धिमान् ॥ ८ ॥
>
> *ekasmin prathamo'dhyāyaḥ saṃpradāyānusārataḥ | vṛttaiḥ sāvadhānaḥ sarvaṃ boddhuṃ śaknoti buddhimān || 8 ||*
>
> "In this [work], the first chapter should be studied following tradition; a discerning student, attentively grasping it through repeated practice, becomes capable of understanding the whole."

That is: if this Rigveda's first chapter is studied in the traditional way — serving one's guru, receiving his grace, hearing the Veda directly from the guru's own mouth, and thoroughly absorbing its meaning through reflection — an intelligent student, well-trained by this, becomes capable of grasping the meaning of every subsequent chapter as well.

### Objection: Should the Rigveda's Commentary Have Come First?

> अत्र केचिदाहुः—ऋग्वेदस्य प्राथम्येन सर्वत्रामातत्वाद्बहिर्भूतं पूर्वमिति न्यायेनाभ्यर्हितत्वात्तद्व्याख्यानमादौ युक्तम् । प्राथम्यं च...
>
> *atra kecid āhuḥ — ṛgvedasya prāthamyena sarvatrāmnātatvād bahirbhūtaṃ pūrvam iti nyāyenābhyarhitatvāt tad-vyākhyānam ādau yuktam | prāthamyaṃ ca...*
>
> "Here, some argue: since the Rigveda is universally cited first everywhere [in the sacred tradition], by the principle that 'what comes first is [thereby shown to be] preeminent,' its commentary rightly ought to have been undertaken first. And regarding this primacy..."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 351</div>

**In the Purusha-sukta, it is proclaimed:**

> तस्माद्यज्ञात्सर्वहुत ऋचः सामानि जज्ञिरे । छन्दांसि जज्ञिरे तस्माद्यजुस्तस्मादजायत ॥ (RV 10-90-9)
>
> *tasmād yajñāt sarva-huta ṛcaḥ sāmāni jajñire | chandāṃsi jajñire tasmād yajus tasmād ajāyata ||*
>
> "From that all-oblation yajna, the Riks and Samans were born; the meters were born from it, and the Yajus arose from it."

That is: from that being called "sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ" (the thousand-headed Purusha) — from that Parameshvara, from that yajna fit for worship, all-encompassing — the Riks and other Vedas were born; likewise, this expresses Parameshvara's own self-manifestation in this form.

**And also this mantra:**

> इन्द्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुरथो दिव्यः स सुपर्णो गरुत्मान् । एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्त्यग्निं यमं मातरिश्वानमाहुः ॥ (RV 1-164-86)
>
> *indraṃ mitraṃ varuṇam agnim āhur atho divyaḥ sa suparṇo garutmān | ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanty agniṃ yamaṃ mātariśvānam āhuḥ ||*
>
> "They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni; and also that divine, well-winged Garutman. That which is One, the wise call by many names — they call it Agni, Yama, Matarishvan."

**And the followers of the Vajasaneyi tradition state:**

> तस्यैदिमातुरमं यजामं यजेत्येकं देवमेतस्यै व सा विसृष्टिरेष उ स्येव सर्वे देवा इति ॥ (Shatapatha Brahmana 14-4-2-12)
>
> *(A Shatapatha Brahmana passage affirming that the many deity-names ultimately refer to a single divine being, whose own creative act these names collectively describe; precise phrase-level construction is difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

That is, all these [deity-names] are ultimately spoken of Parameshvara alone.

Some argue as follows: whenever the Vedas are named together, the Rigveda is invariably mentioned first — and by the accepted principle that, among several items named together, the most preeminent is named first, the Rigveda's consistent first-mention establishes its preeminence. Its foremost position among the Vedas is made explicit in the Purusha-sukta, where — as cited above — the Rigveda is indeed named before the others. Therefore, this objection concludes, the Rigveda's commentary ought to have been undertaken first of all.

Here, "*tasmād yajñāt*" ("from that yajna") means from the Yajna-Purusha, or Parameshvara himself; and "*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*" ("the thousand-headed Purusha") means one with countless heads — that is, all-encompassing.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 352</div>

He is pervasive and omnipotent — this same **यज्ञ-पुरुष** (*yajña-puruṣa*, "the Yajna as Person," i.e. the great **पुरुष** *puruṣa* with a thousand heads described at Rigveda 10-90-1), called **परमेश्वर** (*parameśvara*, "the Supreme Lord"), is worshipped throughout every yajna, by everyone. Here "यज्ञ" (*yajña*) carries the sense of "**यजनीय**" (*yajanīya*) — "that to which sacrifice is offered," i.e., an object of worship — and "**सर्वहुतः**" (*sarvahutaḥ*) means "invoked/offered to by all" — that is, worthy of worship, invoked universally. This describes Parameshvara alone.

Here, an objection may be raised: is it a fixed rule that in Vedic mantras, any reference must refer to Parameshvara alone? Why, then, do some mantras invoke Agni, Indra, or other deities specifically, if the same underlying being is meant? The answer: though these deities are invoked separately in different mantras, since Parameshvara alone is omniscient, omnipotent, and all-pervading, he alone underlies and takes on all these various divine forms — so when a devotee invokes Agni, it is Parameshvara who is truly being invoked. The word "sarvahutaḥ," applied to Parameshvara, is thus without contradiction.

Further mantras confirm this same point — when people invoke Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, or Garutman under these differing names, wise scholars recognize that one and the same deity is being addressed throughout, whatever name is used. Or, alternatively: whichever name a deity is invoked under, the worshipper simply regards that name as referring to that same deity.

The followers of the Vajasaneyi (Shukla Yajurveda) tradition state something similar: though various deities appear worshipped under different names here and there, no genuinely separate deity is being worshipped — it is that same great deity existing in the forms of Indra and the others. Whichever deity is invoked or worshipped, Parameshvara alone is ultimately being addressed.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 353</div>

> न केवलमृचां पाठप्राथम्येनाभ्यर्हितत्वं किंतु यज्ञाङ्गदार्ढ्यहेतुत्वादपि । तथा च तैत्तिरीया आमनन्ति । यद्वै यज्ञस्य साम्ना यजुषा क्रियते शिथिलं तद्यदृचा तद्दृढमिति । (तै. सं. ६-५-१०-३)
> *na kevalam ṛcāṃ pāṭha-prāthamyenābhyarhitatvaṃ kiṃtu yajñāṅga-dārḍhya-hetutvād api | tathā ca taittirīyā āmananti | yad vai yajñasya sāmnā yajuṣā kriyate śithilaṃ tad yad ṛcā tad dṛḍham iti | (Taittiriya Samhita 6-5-10-3)*
>
> "The Riks' preeminence rests not merely on their being recited first, but also on their being the cause of firmness in the limbs of the yajna. Thus the Taittiriyas recite: 'Whatever in the yajna is done by Saman or Yajus is loose; what is done by a Rik, that is firm.'"

> तथा च सर्ववेदगतानि ब्राह्मणानि स्वाभिहितेऽर्थे विश्वासदार्ढ्याय तदेतदृचाभ्युक्तमिति ऋचमेवोदाहरन्ति ।
> *tathā ca sarva-veda-gatāni brāhmaṇāni svābhihite'rthe viśvāsa-dārḍhyāya tad etad ṛcābhyuktam iti ṛcam evodāharanti |*
>
> "And so the Brahmanas of every Veda, to make firm the confidence in what they themselves state, cite a Rik alone, saying 'this is declared by a Rik.'"

> मन्त्रकाण्डेष्वपि यजुर्वेदगतेषु तत्र तत्राध्वर्युणा प्रयोज्या ऋचो बहव आम्नाताः । साम्नां तु सर्वेषां ऋगाश्रितत्वं प्रसिद्धम् । आथर्वणिकैरपि स्वकीयसंहितायां ऋच एव बाहुल्येनाधीयन्ते । अतोऽन्यैः सर्वैर्वेदैरादृतत्वादभ्यर्हितत्वं प्रसिद्धम् ॥
> *mantra-kāṇḍeṣv api yajurveda-gateṣu tatra tatrādhvaryuṇā prayojyā ṛco bahava āmnātāḥ | sāmnāṃ tu sarveṣāṃ ṛgāśritatvaṃ prasiddham | ātharvaṇikair api svakīya-saṃhitāyāṃ ṛca eva bāhulyenādhīyante | ato'nyaiḥ sarvair vedair ādṛtatvād abhyarhitatvaṃ prasiddham ||*
>
> "In the mantra-portions of the Yajurveda too, many Riks to be used by the Adhvaryu are given here and there. That all Samans rest on Riks is well known. The Atharvanikas too recite mostly Riks in their own Samhita. Hence, because the Rik is honoured by all the other Vedas, its preeminence is well established."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 354</div>

...are prescribed in the Rigveda, in the Yajurveda and in the Samaveda. But where the procedure given in the Rigveda and those given in the Yajurveda and Samaveda differ, the Rigveda procedure is the principal one and the authority; the procedures of the Yajurveda and Samaveda are not to be heeded, and the Rigveda procedure holds firm — so the Yajurveda says plainly. Each Veda has its own Brahmana portion explaining the manner of performing yajna-rites — and in supporting their own statements, these Brahmanas cite "thus it is said in the Rigveda," using the Rigveda itself as authority. This confirms that the other Vedas and their Brahmanas rely on the Rigveda. Even in the Yajurveda's own mantra-section, the mantras the Adhvaryu priest must actually recite are often not found in his own Veda at all — the Rigveda's own Riks must be recited instead. As for the Samaveda, it is known to all that all its mantras are found in the Rigveda itself, and a large portion of the Atharvaveda likewise consists of Rigveda verses. Since every Veda relies upon the Rigveda in this way, and all revere it accordingly, the Rigveda's foremost, most venerable position is confirmed.

**The followers of the Chandogya tradition** recite Narada's own words to this effect:

> ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदमाथर्वणं चतुर्थमिति । (Chandogya Upanishad 7-12)
>
> *ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo'dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam ātharvaṇaṃ caturtham iti |*
>
> "O revered one, I have studied the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the fourth — the Atharvana."

**The followers of the Mundaka Upanishad** likewise state:

> ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेद इति । (Mundaka Upanishad 1-1-5)
>
> *ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo'tharvaveda iti |*
>
> "Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda."

Other Upanishadic traditions similarly prescribe the order of study for the whole body of mantras:

> ऋग्यजुःसामाथर्वाणश्चत्वारो वेदाः साङ्गाः सशाखाश्चत्वारः पादा भवन्तीति । (नृ. ता. १-२)
> *ṛgyajuḥsāmātharvāṇaś catvāro vedāḥ sāṅgāḥ saśākhāś catvāraḥ pādā bhavantīti | (Nṛ. Tā. 1-2)*
>
> "The four Vedas — Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman and Atharvan — with their aṅgas and śākhās, are the four feet." (Nṛsiṃha-Tāpanīya Upaniṣad 1-2)

## Chapter 3. Uttara-pakṣa's Defense — It Was Proper, for the Convenience of Yajna-Performance, to Compose the Yajurveda Commentary First

*Original title: "Yajñānuṣṭhānasaukaryakkāgi Yajurvēdakke modalu bhāṣyavannu racisidudu yuktavendu uttarapakṣasamarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 355–361 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 355</div>

The Chandogas first cite Narada's own words to Sanatkumara: "O revered one, I have studied the Rigveda, and also the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the Atharvaveda" — even here, listing all four Vedas studied, the Rigveda is named first. The Mundaka Upanishad likewise states: "The Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda — these are the four Vedas." The Tapaniya Upanishad, describing the "feet" of the sovereign mantra and prescribing the order of study, states: "The Riks, the Yajus, the Sama, and the Atharvana — the Vedas are these four; together with their limbs (the Vedangas) and their branches (shakhas), they form the four feet." Many more such examples could be cited. Wherever one looks, the Rigveda holds primacy — so it would only have been proper for this preeminent text to be commented upon first.

> एवं सर्वत्रोदाहरणीयम् । तस्मादृग्वेदस्य भूरिष्ठत्वादादौ व्याख्यानमुचितमिति । तान् प्रत्येतदुच्यते—
>
> *evaṃ sarvatrodāharaṇīyam | tasmād ṛgvedasya bhūriṣṭhatvād ādau vyākhyānam ucitam iti | tān pratyetad ucyate—*
>
> "Such examples can be cited everywhere. Therefore, given the Rigveda's preeminence, its commentary ought to have been undertaken first. To this, the following reply is given—"

### The Resolution (Siddhanta) Begins

> अस्त्येवं सर्ववेदाध्ययनकत्वात् आचारण ब्रह्मयज्ञ जपसाधा-ऋग्वेदस्यैव प्राथम्यम् । अर्थज्ञानस्य तु यज्ञानुष्ठानार्थत्वात् तु यजुर्वेदस्यैव प्रधानत्वात् व्याख्यानप्रयोगेऽदौ युक्तम् । तस्मात्प्राधान्यं काचिद् गेवाच—
>
> *asty evaṃ sarva-vedādhyayanakatvāt ācāraṇa brahmayajña japasādhā-ṛgvedasyaiva prāthamyam | arthajñānasya tu yajñānuṣṭhānārthatvāt tu yajurvedasyaiva pradhānatvāt vyākhyāna-prayoge'dau yuktam | tasmāt prādhānyaṃ kācid gevāca—*
>
> "It is indeed true that, so far as the practice of studying all the Vedas, the daily Brahma-yajna, muttering of mantras, and similar customary observances are concerned, the Rigveda holds primacy. But since understanding meaning (artha-jñāna) exists specifically for the purpose of performing yajnas — and since, for that purpose, the Yajurveda holds the primary place — it was proper for its commentary to be undertaken first. Therefore, whatever primacy [the Rigveda holds elsewhere]..."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 356</div>

...regarding the Yajurveda's meaning being essential for yajna-performance, the Yajurveda's commentary needed to be composed first. This same point, Sayana notes, is suitably supported by a verse of the Rigveda itself:

> ऋचां त्वः पोषमास्ते पुपुष्वान् गायत्रं त्वो गायति शक्वरीषु । ब्रह्मा त्वो वदति जातविद्यां यज्ञस्य मात्रां विमिमीत उ त्वः ॥ (RV 10-71-11)
>
> *ṛcāṃ tvaḥ poṣam āste pupuṣvān gāyatraṃ tvo gāyati śakvarīṣu | brahmā tvo vadati jātavidyāṃ yajñasya mātrāṃ vimimīta u tvaḥ ||*
>
> "One, having nourished it, tends the growth of the Riks; another sings the Gayatra chant among the Shakvari meters; the Brahmin speaks forth innate knowledge; and another measures out the proper form of the yajna."

Yaska, author of the Nirukta, briefly explains this verse's purport (Nirukta 1-8): it "determines the sphere of application of priestly duties" — that is, it explains which specific tasks each of the priests must perform, distinguishing their respective roles.

**Nirukta** is one of the six Vedangas (alongside Shiksha, Vyakarana, Chandas, Nirukta, Jyotisha, and Kalpa), in which Yaska clarifies the meaning of certain difficult Riks — the very first text composed in the form of a Rigveda commentary. Though the Aitareya Brahmana and similar texts also explain portions of the Veda, since the Brahmanas are themselves considered part of the Veda, no one calls them commentaries or bhashyas upon it. Yaska therefore stands as the first to attempt explaining the Veda's meaning as such. But since the Nirukta explains only select Riks here and there, and even there conveys only the hidden sense rather than the full meaning, understanding the Veda's meaning through the Nirukta's help alone remains impossible.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 357</div>

Yaska continues, explaining the verse's first quarter in detail:

> पुनरपि स एव प्रथमं पादं विवृणोति—'ऋचामेकः पोषमास्ते पुपुष्वान् होतर्गर्चानि' (नि. १-८) इति । अस्यायमर्थः—त्वशब्द एकशब्दस्य पर्यायो होतृविशेषणम् । होत्रेनामक एकः ऋत्विग्यज्ञकाले स्वीयवेदगतानामृचां पुष्टिं कुर्वन्नास्ते । भिन्नप्रदेशेष्वाम्नातानामृचां संघमेकत्र संसाद्यैतावदिदं शस्त्रमित्यर्चनं करोति । सेयं पुष्टिः । अर्चनीत्यस्यार्थवाच्यमृचेत्यर्थः । अर्च्यते प्रशस्यत इति देवविशेषः क्रियाविशेषस्त्प्रधनविशेषो वा अर्च्यते इत्युपलक्ष्यते इति ॥
>
> *(Yaska's own gloss on "ṛcāṃ tvaḥ poṣam āste pupuṣvān," explaining that the priest called Hotr, at the time of sacrifice, "nourishes" the Riks of his own Veda by gathering scattered verses from various places into one collected body and determining "this much constitutes this Shastra" — this gathering itself being the meaning of "nourishment" (puṣṭi); and that the word "Rik" derives from "arcana," meaning that which praises a particular deity, rite, or ritual instrument.)*

**Yaska then explains the second quarter of the same verse:**

> अथ द्वितीयं पादं विवृणोति—"गायत्रमेको गायति शक्वरीषुद्द्वाता गायत्रं गायतेः स्तुतिकर्मणः शक्वर्यो ऋचः, शक्नोतेः शक्न्यैः वृत्रमपीर्वत्तमशक्नदेतं तच्छिक्वरीणां शक्वरीत्वमिति विज्ञायत इति । (कौ. २३-२) अस्यायमर्थः—उद्गातृनामक एकः ऋत्विग्गायत्रशब्दाभिधेयं स्तोत्रं शक्वरीक्ब्याभिधेयश्च ऋग्गायति । धातूनामनेकार्थत्वेन स्तुतिक्रियावाचिनो गायधातोः श्रौढ्यं स्तोत्रं गायत्र...
>

<div class="pgmark">original p. 358</div>

> शब्दः । शक्वरीशब्दस्य शक्नोतिधातोः...इति ॥ वृत्रं शत्रुं हन्तुं शक्नोत्याभिर्गीर्भिरेषा वृक्वृत्तिः कस्मिंश्चिद्ब्राह्मणे विज्ञायत इति ॥
>
> *(The word "Shakvari" derives from the root "śak" ("to be able"); the sense "by means of these hymns, one is able to slay the enemy Vritra" is confirmed in a certain Brahmana text — the Kaushitaki Brahmana, 23-2.)*

That is: the Udgatr priest sings the "gayatra" hymn (from the root "gai," meaning an act of praise) using verses in the "Shakvari" meter (from "śak," to be able) — so named because, through these very hymns, Indra was empowered to slay Vritra, a connection explicitly confirmed in the Brahmana literature.

**Yaska then explains the third quarter of the verse:**

> अथ तृतीयं पादं विवृणोति—'ब्रह्मा को जाके जाके विद्यां वदति, ब्रह्मा सर्वविद्यः सर्वं वेदितुमर्हति ।' अस्यायमर्थः—ब्रह्मानामक एक ऋत्विग् जाके जाके कर्मणि तदोचितज्ञानं, प्रस्तुते प्रायश्चित्तकर्मणि विद्यामनुज्ञां वदति । ब्रह्मणः पश्चेष्टः सामक्येण संबोधितः सन् ओं प्रणिय इत्यनुजानाति । स च ब्रह्मा वेदत्रयोक्तसर्वकर्माभिज्ञः । तस्माद्योग्यतां वैद्यात्तत्र दृष्टज्ञातुं सति प्रमादे समाधातुं च समर्थ इति । तच्च सामर्थ्यं छन्दोगा आमनन्ति—
>
> *(Yaska's gloss: the Brahma priest speaks the appropriate knowledge/sanction for each rite as it occurs, granting approval — "Om, proceed" — for any required expiatory action; being learned in all rites of the three Vedas, he alone is qualified both to notice errors during the yajna and to correct them.)*

That is: the priest called Brahma speaks the proper sanction relevant to each specific rite in turn — granting permission for any expiatory rite (prayashchitta) that becomes necessary. Addressed with the proper request, he grants approval with "Om, proceed." Since this Brahma priest is versed in every rite prescribed across all three Vedas, he alone is capable of both recognizing errors in the yajna's performance and correcting them when they occur. This same capability is described by the followers of the Samaveda (Chandogas)—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 359</div>

> एष एव यज्ञस्पृष्ट मनश्च वाक् च वर्तनी तयोरन्यतरां मनसा संस्करोति ब्रह्मा, वाचा होताध्वर्युरुद्गाता चान्यतराम् इति ॥ (Chandogya Upanishad 4-16-1)
>
> *eṣa eva yajñas pṛṣṭa manaś ca vāk ca vartanī tayor anyatarāṃ manasā saṃskaroti brahmā, vācā hotādhvaryur udgātā cānyatarām iti ||*
>
> "This indeed is the yajna, having mind and speech as its twofold path; the Brahma corrects one of these [the mind-path] with his mind, while the Hotr, Adhvaryu, and Udgatr correct the other [the speech-path] with speech."

Even if an error occurs during the yajna, the whole rite need not be considered incomplete — it can be properly rectified through the mind, while the mantras of the three Vedas are recited through speech. The Hotr and his two counterparts (Adhvaryu, Udgatr) together correct the yajna's speech-path; but the Brahma alone corrects its mind-path, in its entirety, by himself. This is his special capability.

**Continuing the explanation of the third quarter:** while the yajna proceeds, the priest called Brahma instructs the other priests on precisely how each rite should be performed, being himself the most knowledgeable of all. Many subsidiary rites occur as part of a yajna's proper conduct, and the important ones require the Brahma priest's explicit sanction. For example, at the water-fetching rite, the Adhvaryu requests permission: "O Brahman, shall I fetch the water into this vessel?" — to which the Brahma replies, "Om, fetch it" — granting permission. Even pouring water from one vessel into another requires the Brahma's approval, since "apaḥ praṇayana" (the water-fetching rite) is itself an important ritual act — filling the "praṇīta" or "pūrṇa" vessel with water as a purificatory step. In all such ritual components, work may proceed only with the Brahma's sanction, since he alone is thoroughly versed in the ritual procedures laid out across all the Vedas, knowing precisely what should be done, and when — and he accordingly watches for errors throughout the yajna. Should an error occur through inattention, he identifies the necessary remedy and sets it right. The followers of the Samaveda (Chandogas) describe the Brahma's capability in just this way — describing the yajna as having both a mind-form and a speech-form.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 360</div>

...The yajna's mind-form consists in determining in the mind that ritual acts must be performed exactly thus (as prescribed by the shastras) and then acting accordingly; the yajna's speech-form consists in reciting the mantras and performing the corresponding external acts. Of these, the mind-form is the more essential and superior. The Brahma priest determines and rectifies this mind-form himself; the other priests — Hotr, Adhvaryu, and Udgatr — carry out the yajna's speech-form through their mantras. Since the yajna's principal component (its mind-form) is settled and corrected by the Brahma alone, his capability in the yajna exceeds that of all the others.

**Yaska now explains the fourth and final quarter of the verse:**

> अथ चतुर्थं पादं विवृणोति—'यज्ञस्य मात्रां विमिमात एकोऽध्वर्युरध्वर्युरध्वरयुरध्वरं युनक्त्यध्वरस्य नेतेति' । अस्यायमर्थः—अध्वर्युनामक एक ऋत्विग् यज्ञस्य मात्रां स्वरूपं विशेषेण निष्पादयति । मात्र्यते इति मात्रा, स्वरूपम् । तस्य स्वरूप्यं चाध्वर्यो...
>
> *(Yaska's etymological gloss identifying the Adhvaryu priest as the one who specially "measures out" — constructs — the essential form of the yajna; "mātrā" meaning that which is measured/constructed, deriving from the root "mā.")*

That is: the priest named Adhvaryu specially brings into being the essential form ("mātrā") of the yajna. "Mātrā" — that which is measured out — means the yajna's own proper form. And this constructive function is understood from the word "Adhvaryu" itself.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 361</div>

> नामनिर्वचनादेव गम्यते । अध्वर्युरित्यत्र भाण्डोस्क्यप्रक्रियाया अलुप्तमुकारं पुनः प्रकृष्याध्वरयुरिति नाम संस्थापनीयम् । अध्वरं युनक्तीत्यवयवार्थः । अध्वरस्य नेतेति तात्पर्यार्थ इति ॥
>
> *(Yaska's etymological demonstration: reversing the phonetic elision in "adhvaryu" restores the form "adhvarayu" — "he yokes the sacrifice" being the literal, component sense, and "leader of the sacrifice" its intended overall meaning.)*

That is: this is understood directly from the word's own etymology. In "Adhvaryu," by reversing the vowel-elision process, the form "Adhvarayu" is recovered — "he yokes the sacrifice" being the meaning of its parts, and "leader of the sacrifice" its intended sense.

Yaska further demonstrates this same idea:

> मन्त्रा मननाच्छन्दांसि च्छादनाच्च स्तोमः स्तवनाच्च यजुर्यजनेरिति । (Nirukta 7-12)
>
> *mantrā mananāc chandāṃsi cchādanāc ca stomaḥ stavanāc ca yajur yajaner iti |*
>
> "'Mantra' [derives] from manana (thinking/reflection); 'Chandas' from chādana (covering); 'Stoma' from stavana (praising); and 'Yajus' from yajati (to sacrifice)."

### The Culminating Conclusion

> एवं सत्यध्वर्युसंबन्धि यजुर्वेदे निष्पन्नं यज्ञशरीरमुपजीव्य तदपेक्षितौ स्तोत्रशस्त्ररूपावयवावितरेण वेद...
>
> *evaṃ saty adhvaryu-saṃbandhi yajurvede niṣpannaṃ yajña-śarīram upajīvya śeṣa-bhūtā stotra-śastra-rūpā sānagāthā itareṇa veda...*
>
> "Thus it being established that the yajna's own body is formed specifically within the Yajurveda, connected to the Adhvaryu — the remaining elements, in the form of hymn (stotra) and recitation (shastra), are supplied by the other Vedas..."

This is the pivotal conclusion of the entire discussion: since the yajna's essential body/structure resides in the Yajurveda, and the Rigveda and Samaveda merely furnish its accompanying hymn and recitation elements, the Yajurveda holds the dominant, foundational role — justifying why it was explained first. And since the Samaveda's own verses are entirely drawn from the Rigveda, between these latter two, the Rigveda rightly comes next — which is precisely the task Sayana now undertakes.

## Chapter 4. Purva-pakṣa — Since the Veda Has No Defining Marks or Proofs, No Such Text as "the Veda" Exists

*Original title: "Vēdakke lakṣaṇapramāṇādigaḷu illaddarinda vēdavemba granthavē illavendu pūrvapakṣavu"*
**Printed pages 362–367 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 362</div>

> द्वैयेन पूर्ग्येके इत्येव जीव्यस्य यजुर्वेदस्य प्रभुगुण व्याख्यानं युक्तम् । तत ऊध्वं साम्नामृगात्मकत्वादुभयोर्मध्ये प्रभुमके ऋग्व्याख्यानं युक्तमिति सिद्धे इदानीं व्याख्यायते ॥
>
> *(Concluding: since the yajna's essential body resides in the Yajurveda, its commentary rightly came first; and since the Samaveda is itself constituted of Riks, between the Rigveda and Samaveda, the Rigveda rightly comes next — this now being settled, the Rigveda-commentary is undertaken.)*

Keeping this reasoning in mind, Yaska Maharshi clarifies the etymology showing that the Yajurveda — the Adhvaryu's own Veda — holds the power to establish the yajna's essential form: "manana" (reflection) yields "mantra"; "chādana" (covering/binding together) yields "chandas"; "praising" yields "stoma." The yajna's principal form must therefore arise from the Yajurveda, with the Rik and Sama Vedas serving a supporting, auxiliary role. This establishes that the Yajurveda holds primacy for yajna-performance — justifying its commentary being composed first. And since every Samaveda mantra is itself found within the Rigveda, between these remaining two, the Rigveda rightly comes next. **Accordingly, the Rigveda-commentary now begins.**

### The Rigveda-Bhashya Proper Begins: A Logical Challenge to the Veda's Very Existence

> लक्षणप्रमाणराहित्याद्वेदस्यासद्भाव इति पूर्वः पक्षः
>
> *lakṣaṇa-pramāṇa-rāhityād vedasyāsadbhāva iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*
>
> "The objection that the Veda does not exist, for it lacks definition and proof—"

> ननु वेद एव तावन्नास्ति । कुतस्तदवान्तरभेद ऋग्वेदः ? तथा हि । कोऽयं वेदो नाम ? न हि तत्र लक्षणं प्रमाणं नास्ति । न च तदुभयव्यतिरेकेण किंचिद्वस्तु प्रसिध्यति । लक्षणप्रमाणाभ्यां हि वस्तुसिद्धिरिति न्यायविदां मतम् ॥
>
> *nanu veda eva tāvan nāsti | kutas tad-avāntara-bheda ṛgvedaḥ | tathā hi | ko'yaṃ vedo nāma | na hi tatra lakṣaṇaṃ pramāṇaṃ nāsti | na ca tad-ubhaya-vyatirekeṇa kiṃcid vastu prasidhyati | lakṣaṇa-pramāṇābhyāṃ hi vastu-siddhir iti nyāya-vidāṃ matam ||*
>
> "Objection: The Veda itself does not exist at all — how then can there be a subdivision of it called the Rigveda? Consider: what is this thing called 'Veda'? Neither a definition (lakṣaṇa) nor a proof (pramāṇa) of it exists. And without both of these, nothing whatsoever can be established — for it is the settled view of logicians (Naiyayikas) that the establishment of any entity requires both definition and proof."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 363</div>

...a distinguishing mark by which something can be pointed out. "Pramana" (proof) means stating separately, "this object bears such-and-such a mark" — the means by which an object's true nature is determined through its own characteristic marks. Logicians hold that a thing's real nature becomes known only through such proofs. Since the Veda has neither a definition nor a proof, how can the entity called "Veda" be established to exist at all?

**First attempted definition, and its refutation:**

> प्रत्यक्षानुमानागमेषु प्रमाणाविशेषेण किमो वेद इति तल्लक्षणमिति चेन्न, मन्वादिस्मृतिष्वतिव्याप्तेः । समयबलेन सम्यक्परोक्षानुभवसाधनमित्येतस्यागमलक्षणस्य तास्वपि सद्भावात् ।
>
> *pratyakṣānumānāgameṣu pramāṇāviśeṣeṇa kim eṣa veda iti tal-lakṣaṇam iti cen na, manv-ādi-smṛtiṣv ativyāpteḥ | samaya-balena samyak-parokṣānubhava-sādhanam ity etasyāgama-lakṣaṇasya tāsv api sadbhāvāt |*
>
> "If you say that, among the three valid means of knowledge — perception, inference, and revealed word (āgama) — the Veda is defined as the last of these, we reply: no. This over-extends to the Smritis of Manu and others as well, since the accepted definition of 'āgama' — 'that which serves as the means for correctly apprehending what is unseen (adṛṣṭa)' — applies equally to those Smritis."

**Second attempted definition, and its refutation:**

> अपौरुषेयत्वे सतीति विशेषणाददोष इति चेन्न, वेदस्यापि परमेश्वरनिर्मितत्वेन पौरुषेयत्वात् ।
>
> *apauruṣeyatve satīti viśeṣaṇād adoṣa iti cen na, vedasyāpi parameśvara-nirmitatvena pauruṣeyatvāt |*
>
> "If you say that adding the qualifier 'provided it is non-human in origin (apauruṣeya)' removes this flaw, we reply: no. For the Veda too, having been made by Parameshvara (the Supreme Person), is thereby of personal/human origin (pauruṣeya)."

**Third attempted definition, and its refutation:**

> शरीरधारिजीवनिर्मितत्वाभावादपौरुषेयत्वमिति चेन्न । सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुष इत्यादिश्रुतिभिरीश्वरस्यापि शरीरित्वात् ॥ कर्मफलरूपशरीरधारिजीवनिर्मितत्वाभावमात्रेणापौरुषेयत्वं विवक्षितमिति चेन्न । जीवविशेषैरग्निवाय्वादित्यैर्वेदानामुत्पादितत्वात् । ऋग्वेद एवाग्नेरजायत यजुर्वेदो वायोः सामवेद आदित्यात् (ऐ. ब्रा. ५-३२) श्रुतेरीश्वरस्याग्न्यादिप्रेरकत्वेन निर्मातृत्वं द्रष्टव्यम् ।
> *śarīradhārijīvanirmitatvābhāvād apauruṣeyatvam iti cen na | sahasraśīrṣā puruṣa ityādiśrutibhir īśvarasyāpi śarīritvāt || karmaphalarūpaśarīradhārijīvanirmitatvābhāvamātreṇāpauruṣeyatvaṃ vivakṣitam iti cen na | jīvaviśeṣair agnivāyvādityair vedānām utpāditatvāt | ṛgveda evāgner ajāyata yajurvedo vāyoḥ sāmaveda ādityāt (Ai. Brā. 5-32) śruter īśvarasyāgnyādiprerakatvena nirmātṛtvaṃ draṣṭavyam |*
>
> "If you say that 'non-human origin' means 'not made by an embodied living being,' we reply: no; for from texts such as 'the thousand-headed Purusha' the Lord too has a body. If you say that what is meant is only 'not made by a living being whose body is the fruit of karma,' we reply: no; for the Vedas were brought forth by particular living beings — Agni, Vayu and Aditya. From the text 'The Ṛgveda was born from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya' (Ai. Brā. 5-32), the Lord is to be understood as the maker, in that he impels Agni and the others."
>

<div class="pgmark">original p. 364</div>

Regarding the three proofs of knowledge — perception (**प्रत्यक्ष** *pratyakṣa*), inference (**अनुमान** *anumāna*), and revealed word (**आगम** *āgama*) — even if the last of these, "āgama," is proposed as the Veda's defining mark, this fails: since Manu's and other Smritis also possess this same "āgama" quality, the flaw of over-extension (**अतिव्याप्ति** *ativyāpti*) results, since they too would have to count as "Veda." A sound definition (**लक्षण** *lakṣaṇa*) must avoid three classical flaws:

- **अतिव्याप्ति** (*ativyāpti*, over-extension): the stated mark applies to other things too (e.g., defining milk as "that which is white" also catches lime).
- **अव्याप्ति** (*avyāpti*, under-extension): the stated mark fails to cover part of the intended thing (e.g., defining horses by "white color" excludes horses of other colors).
- **असंभव** (*asambhava*, impossibility): stating a quality the thing doesn't actually possess at all.

Whatever definition of "Veda" one proposes free of these three flaws will, since Manu's and similar Smritis share the same "āgama" quality, still fall into ativyāpti. The characteristic of being "āgama" therefore cannot serve as the Veda's true defining mark.

**Fourth attempted definition, and its refutation** (regarding embodiment):

If you say the "body" in question is specifically one produced by the karmic results of a past life — and that the Veda's own author has no such body, which is what you really mean by "non-human origin" — this too fails. For the Vedas are described as produced through such beings as Agni, Vayu, and Aditya: "The Rigveda was born from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya" — confirming that Parameshvara composed the Vedas at the instigation of Agni and the others.

**Fifth attempted definition, and its refutation** (mantra + brahmana):

You might next suggest that "Veda" simply names the collected body of mantras and brahmanas. This too fails — since no one has yet clearly established what precisely constitutes a "mantra" or a "brahmana." It is therefore clear that no adequate definition of the term "Veda" exists.

If, finally, you propose that "apauruṣeyatva" (non-human origin) itself simply *is* the Veda's defining mark — since the Veda is not made by any finite person — this too fails, for the Veda is itself [made by] Parameshvara.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 365</div>

Since it is made by someone, the quality of "personal origin" (pauruṣeyatva) necessarily follows — and countless texts are made by persons, so why should the Veda deserve any special regard on that basis? If the Veda is instead called apauruṣeya because no embodied living being made it — that too fails, since the Veda itself states "sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ" (the thousand-headed Purusha), affirming Ishvara's own possession of a body. And if apauruṣeya means merely "not made by one embodied through karmic result," this too fails: the Veda states it was born from special beings — Agni, Vayu, Aditya — the Rigveda from Agni, the Yajurveda from Vayu, the Samaveda from Aditya — meaning Parameshvara, who impels Agni and the others, is himself the true author of the Shruti. And if "Veda" simply names the collected group of mantras and brahmanas, that too fails, since no one has ever clearly determined what precisely qualifies as a "mantra" or a "brahmana." **The Veda, in short, has no valid defining characteristic whatsoever.**

**Turning to proof (pramana):**

> नापि तस्यावे प्रमाणं पश्यामः । ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदमथर्वणं चतुर्थम् (छान्दोग्य उपनिषद् ७-१-२) इत्यादिवाक्यं प्रमाणमिति चेन्न, तस्यापि वाक्यस्य वेदान्तःपातित्वेनात्माश्रयत्वप्रसंगात् । न खलु निपुणोऽपि स्वस्कन्धमारोढुं प्रभवति ।
>
> *nāpi tasyāve pramāṇaṃ paśyāmaḥ | ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo'dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam atharvaṇaṃ caturtham ity ādi-vākyaṃ pramāṇam iti cen na, tasyāpi vākyasya vedāntaḥpātitvenātmāśrayatva-prasaṅgāt | na khalu nipuṇo'pi svaskandham āroḍhuṃ prabhavati |*
>
> "Nor do we see any proof of its existence either. If you say that a statement such as 'O Lord, I study the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the fourth, the Atharvana' (Chandogya Upanishad 7-1-2) serves as proof — we reply: no. Since that very statement, being itself contained within the Veda, falls into the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya). Indeed, no one, however skilled, can climb upon his own shoulder."

> वेद एव द्विजातीनां निःश्रेयसकरः पर इत्यादिस्मृतिवाक्यं प्रमाणमिति चेन्न, तस्याप्युक्तश्रुतिमूलत्वेन निराकृतत्वात् । प्रत्यक्षादिकं शंकितुमप्ययोग्यम् । वेदविषया तु लोकप्रसिद्धिः सार्वजनीनापि नीलं नभ इत्यादिवच्च । तस्माल्लक्षणप्रमाणरहितस्य वेदस्य सद्भावो नांगीकर्तुं शक्यत इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥
>
> *veda eva dvijātīnāṃ niḥśreyasakaraḥ para ity ādi-smṛti-vākyaṃ pramāṇam iti cen na, tasyāpy ukta-śruti-mūlatvena nirākṛtatvāt | pratyakṣādikaṃ śaṅkitum apy ayogyam | veda-viṣayā tu loka-prasiddhiḥ sārvajanīnāpi nīlaṃ nabha ity ādi-vac ca | tasmāl lakṣaṇa-pramāṇa-rahitasya vedasya sadbhāvo nāṅgīkartuṃ śakyata iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||*
>
> "If you say that a Smriti-statement such as 'the Veda alone is the supreme means of ultimate good for the twice-born' serves as proof — we reply: no. Since this too, being rooted in Shruti itself, is rejected for the same reason. Perception and similar means aren't even worth considering here. As for the Veda's popular renown among people — however universal, it is like the common expression 'the sky is blue' [a mistaken notion]. Therefore, the existence of a Veda lacking both definition and proof cannot be accepted. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

**This concludes the objection (purva-paksha).** Sayana's own resolution follows next.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 366</div>

Not only that. We see no proof at all that those Vedas exist. If it's argued that the statement—

> ऋग्वेदं भगवोऽध्येमि यजुर्वेदं सामवेदमाथर्वणं चतुर्थम् ।
> *ṛgvedaṃ bhagavo'dhyemi yajurvedaṃ sāmavedam ātharvaṇaṃ caturtham |* (Chandogya Upanishad 7-1-2)
>
> "O Lord, I now study the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the fourth, the Atharvaveda"

—clearly proves the Vedas exist — that's not possible, since this very statement is itself part of the Veda (occurring within the Chandogya Upanishad), producing the fallacy of self-dependence: if the Veda's own authority is in question, how can a statement that is itself part of the Veda serve as proof? No man, however skilled, can climb up and sit upon his own shoulder.

If we cite the Yajnavalkya-Smriti's statement, "the Veda alone is the highest means of ultimate good for the twice-born," as proof that the Vedas exist — that too fails. All Smritis are rooted in Shruti — that is, they follow Shruti itself — so the very same fallacy of self-dependence arises here too. The Vedas' existence cannot be established through Smriti statements either.

In everyday affairs, no one can deny things visible to the eye — so shouldn't everyone accept perceptual proof? Should we accept the Veda's existence simply because the subject is widely renowned, and everyone visibly engages with Vedic matters? No — because many things considered "perceptually evident" in ordinary life turn out to rest on mere illusion, just as it is commonly (but falsely) held that the sky is blue-colored. Is this anything but illusion? Therefore, there is no valid basis for accepting that an entity called "Veda," lacking both definition and proof, exists. **This concludes the objection (purva-paksha).**

### A Methodological Note: Purva-Paksha and Siddhanta

When examining any subject, pointing out its flaws and objections through careful, reasoned argument to show "this is not correct" is called the **purva-paksha** (prior view, or objection). Correspondingly, resolving those very flaws and objections one by one, with sound reasoning, and firmly establishing the subject's true nature, is called the **siddhanta** (established conclusion). To properly grasp the subjects expounded in the shastras, tradition holds that the purva-paksha should be presented first, with the siddhanta established afterward.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 367</div>

This purva-paksha, siddhanta, and related components together form what is called an "adhikarana." Its definition:

> विषयोऽविषयश्चेति पूर्वपक्षस्तथोत्तरं । निर्णयश्चेति पञ्चाङ्गं शास्त्रेऽधिकरणं मतम् ॥
>
> "Subject-matter and doubt, together with the objection and its answer, and the determination — this combination is considered an 'adhikarana' in the shastras."

That is: an adhikarana comprises five distinct parts — the subject-matter (vishaya), the doubt (samshaya), the objection (purva-paksha), its answer, and the final determination (siddhanta). Each is examined in turn before the siddhanta is finally established as correct.

### The Resolution (Uttara-Paksha) Begins: Determining the Veda's Definition and Proof

> अत्रोच्यते । मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मकत्वं तावददुष्टं लक्षणम् । अत एवापस्तम्बो यज्ञपरिभाषायामाह । मन्त्रब्राह्मणयोर्वेदनामधेयमिति (आ. प. ३१) । तयोस्तु स्वरूपमुपरिष्टान्निर्णेष्यते
>
> *atrocyate | mantra-brāhmaṇātmakatvaṃ tāvad aduṣṭaṃ lakṣaṇam | ata evāpastambo yajña-paribhāṣāyām āha | mantra-brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam iti (Āpastamba Yajña-paribhāṣā 31) | tayos tu svarūpam upariṣṭān nirṇeṣyate*
>
> "To this we reply: the definition of the Veda as consisting of mantras and brahmanas is, in fact, faultless. This is precisely why Apastamba, in his Yajña-paribhāṣā, states: 'The name Veda applies to the mantras and the brahmanas' (Apastamba Yajña-paribhasha 31). As for determining the precise nature of each of these..."

We now state the resolution (samādhāna) to the objection. Calling the body of words comprising mantras and brahmanas "the Veda" is, in fact, a faultless definition. As for the objection that "mantra" and "brahmana" themselves remain undefined — the answer is that whatever the shastra-tradition designates as "mantra" is indeed mantra, and the remainder is brahmana. This is exactly why the great sage **Apastamba**, in his *Yajna-paribhasha-sutra*, states: "mantra-brāhmaṇayor veda-nāmadheyam" — the name "Veda" applies to both mantras and brahmanas together.

## Chapter 5. Siddhanta — the Veda Does Have Defining Marks and Proofs; and Why a Commentary Is Needed at All

*Original title: "Vēdakke lakṣaṇapramāṇādigaḷu iveyendu siddhāntasamarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 368–373 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 368</div>

This is accepted. This point will be settled further ahead. Similarly, on the question of "apauruṣeyatva," we shall clarify our stated definition later. The three types of proof — shruti (revealed word), smriti (tradition), and loka-vyavahara (common human practice) — must all be accepted together as establishing the Veda's existence.

Consider: jars and similar objects have no self-illuminating power — they depend on other light sources and cannot shine on their own. But does this mean *everything* luminous must depend on another's help to shine? The sun, moon, and stars shine of their own accord, without needing any external light. A pot's lack of self-illumination doesn't contradict the sun's genuine self-luminosity. Likewise: just because an ordinary human, however skilled, cannot climb onto his own shoulder, does that mean the Veda — possessing unlimited power — cannot illuminate itself the same way? No. **The Veda's power is unobstructed**, and it can therefore reveal and prove itself, just as it reveals everything else. The fallacy of self-dependence, then, simply does not arise for a text of such undiminished power. As those versed in ancient tradition say of the Veda's own unblunted power:

> "The Veda can make clear what has been, what is, and what is to be — what is near, and what is far off."

This being so, proof drawn from Smriti (itself rooted in the Veda), as well as proof drawn from common notoriety (rooted in both Shruti and Smriti), must also be accepted. **It therefore stands firmly established that the Veda, duly proven by both definition and proof, cannot be overturned by any skeptic.**

### A New Objection: Even If the Veda Exists, Is It Authoritative?

> ननु अस्तु नाम वेदाख्यः कश्चित् पदार्थः । तथापि नासौ व्याख्यानम् अर्हति । अप्रमाणत्वेनानुपयुक्तत्वात् । न हि वेदः प्रमाणम् । तल्लक्षणस्य तत्र दुःसंपादत्वात् । तथा हि । सम्य-…
> *nanv astu nāma vedākhyaḥ kaścit padārthaḥ | tathāpi nāsau vyākhyānam arhati | apramāṇatvenānupayuktatvāt | na hi vedaḥ pramāṇam | tal-lakṣaṇasya tatra duḥsampādatvāt | tathā hi | samya-…* *(the last word is divided at the page end and continues on p. 369)*

"Very well — we grant that the thing called 'Veda' exists. Still, it isn't worth commenting on, since it carries no authority (pramāṇya), and being without authority, it is of no real use. The Veda is of no authority. Why? Because you cannot show that the defining mark of valid proof (pramāṇa) resides in it." Some define "pramāṇa" as the instrument of right knowledge; others say it is the means of acquiring [knowledge] of what was not previously known.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 369</div>

> अनुभवसाधनं प्रमाणमिति केचिल्लक्षणमाहुः । अपरे तृषष्ट्यधिगतार्थगन्तृ प्रमाणमित्याचक्षते । न चैतदुभयं वेदे संभवति । मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मको हि वेदः । तत्र मन्त्राः केचिदबोधकाः । अम्यक् स त इन्द्र ऋष्टिरेको मन्त्रः । (ऋ. सं. १-१६९-३) यद्रिस्मिन् धायि तमपश्यया विददृक्षः । (ऋ. सं. ५-४४-८) सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतु (ऋ. सं. १०-१०६-६) इत्येवंजातीयान्यन्यान्यपि अपान्तमन्युस्त्रिपलप्रभर्मिः इत्यादयः (ऋ. सं. १०-८९-५) उदाहार्याः । न ह्येतैर्मन्त्रैः किंचिज्ज्ञेयार्थोऽवगच्छते । विशेषतः संभव एव यदा नास्ति तदा तस्य ज्ञानकारणसाधनत्वं च दूरास्थितम् ॥
>
> अनुभव-साधनं प्रमाणम् इति केचिल् लक्षणम् आहुः । अपरे तृ-षष्ट्य्-अधिगतार्थ-गन्तृ प्रमाणम् इत्य् आचक्षते । न चैतद् उभयं वेदे संभवति । मन्त्र-ब्राह्मणात्मको हि वेदः । तत्र मन्त्राः केचिद् अबोधकाः । ... न ह्य् एतैर् मन्त्रैः किंचिज् ज्ञेयार्थोऽवगच्छते । विशेषतः संभव एव यदा नास्ति तदा तस्य ज्ञान-कारण-साधनत्वं च दूरास्थितम् ॥
> *anubhava-sādhanaṃ pramāṇam iti kecil lakṣaṇam āhuḥ | apare tṛ-ṣaṣṭy-adhigatārtha-gantṛ pramāṇam ity ācakṣate | na caitad ubhayaṃ vede saṃbhavati | mantra-brāhmaṇātmako hi vedaḥ | tatra mantrāḥ kecid abodhakāḥ | ... na hy etair mantraiḥ kiṃcij jñeyārtho'vagacchate | viśeṣataḥ saṃbhava eva yadā nāsti tadā tasya jñāna-kāraṇa-sādhanatvaṃ ca dūrāsthitam ||*
>
> "Some define 'pramana' (valid proof) as 'the means of [right] experience.' Others say it is 'that which leads to knowledge of an object not previously known.' Neither definition applies to the Veda. For the Veda consists of mantras and Brahmanas — and among the mantras, some convey no discernible meaning at all: 'amyak sa ta indra ṛṣṭir' is one such mantra; 'yad rismin dhāyi tam apaśyayā vidad ṛkṣaḥ' is another; 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītu' another; and 'apāntamanyus tripala-prabharmiḥ' and similar besides may be cited. These mantras yield no discernible meaning whatsoever. And when there is no possibility of meaning at all, being a means or cause of knowledge is all the more remote."

We grant, then, that an entity called "Veda" exists — but what need is there to compose commentary on it? Since the Veda carries no valid authority (pramana) and yields no genuine use, commenting on it serves no purpose. The Veda cannot count as "pramana," since it lacks the defining marks proposed for valid proof: some define pramana as "the means productive of correct experience"; others define it as "that which reveals an object not previously known." Neither definition applies to the Veda. As already stated, the Veda consists of two parts — mantra and Brahmana. Taking the mantra portion first: does either definition of pramana apply there? It does not — and several mantras are cited here as examples: "amyak sa ta indra ṛṣṭi," "yad rismin dhāyi tam apaśyayā vidat," "sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītu," and "apāntamanyus tripala-prabharmā." These mantras convey no meaning at all. And if they convey no meaning whatsoever, then their serving as a means to correct knowledge becomes, quite obviously, altogether impossible.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 370</div>

> अधः स्विदासीदुपरि स्विदासीदिति (ऋ. सं. १०-१२९-५) मन्त्रस्य बोधकत्वेऽपि स्थाणुर्वा पुरुषो वेत्यादिवाक्यवत्संदिग्धार्थबोधकत्वान्न प्रामाण्यम् ॥
>
> *adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīd iti (RV 10-129-5) mantrasya bodhakatve'pi sthāṇur vā puruṣo vety ādi-vākyavat saṃdigdhārtha-bodhakatvān na prāmāṇyam ||*
>
> "The mantra 'adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt' (was it below, or was it above?) (RV 10-129-5), though it conveys some meaning, conveys only a doubtful, ambiguous sense — like the statement 'is it a post, or is it a man?' — and therefore lacks authority."

Take the mantra "adhaḥ svid āsīd upari svid āsīt." Even though its words convey a meaning of sorts, it leaves genuine room for doubt — much like asking whether something is a stump or a man. Since it fails to convey a settled, coherent meaning, how could such a mantra carry any authority?

> ओषधे त्रायस्वैनमिति (Taittiriya Samhita 1-2-1-1) मन्त्रे दर्भविषयः । (Ashvalayana Grihyasutra 1-17-8) स्वधिते मैनं हिंसीरिति क्षुरविषयः । (Ashvalayana Grihyasutra 1-17-9) श्रुणोत ग्रावाण (Taittiriya Samhita 1-3-13-1) इति पाषाणविषयः । एतेष्वचेतनानां दर्भक्षुरपाषाणानां चेतनवत्संबोधनं श्रूयते । द्वौ चन्द्रौ चन्द्रमसाविति वाक्यवद्विसंवादिबोधकत्वात्प्रामाण्यम् ॥
>
> *oṣadhe trāyasvainam iti mantre darbha-viṣayaḥ | svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīr iti kṣura-viṣayaḥ | śṛṇota grāvāṇa iti pāṣāṇa-viṣayaḥ | eteṣv acetanānāṃ darbha-kṣura-pāṣāṇānāṃ cetanavat sambodhanaṃ śrūyate | dvau candrau candramasāv iti vākyavad visaṃvādi-bodhakatvāt prāmāṇyam ||*
>
> "In the mantra 'oṣadhe trāyasvainam' ('O herb, protect him'), the subject is sacred grass (darbha). 'Svadhite mainaṃ hiṃsīḥ' ('O razor, do not harm him') concerns a razor. 'Śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ' ('Hear, O stones') concerns stones. In these, inanimate things — grass, razor, and stones — are addressed as though sentient beings. Such statements, conveying something self-contradictory (like saying 'there are two moons'), cannot carry authority."

That is: the mantras "O herb, protect him" address grass (darbha), "O razor, do not harm him" address a razor, and "Hear, O stones" address stones — in each case treating lifeless objects as if they were conscious beings capable of understanding and acting on a command. This, the objection argues, is as absurd as claiming there are two moons — and such statements therefore cannot possibly be authoritative.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 371</div>

> एक एव रुद्रो न द्वितीयाय तस्थे (Taittiriya Samhita 1-8-6-1) सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्रा अधि भूम्याम् (Taittiriya Samhita 4-5-11-1) इत्येतयोस्तु मन्त्रयोर्यावच्छिवमहं मौनीति वाक्यवद्व्याघातबोधकत्वादप्रामाण्यम् ॥
>
> *eka eva rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1-8-6-1) sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrā adhi bhūmyām (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4-5-11-1) ity etayos tu mantrayor yāvac chivam ahaṃ maunīti vākyavad vyāghāta-bodhakatvād aprāmāṇyam ||*
>
> "'Rudra is one alone; he does not stand as a second' (Taittiriya Samhita 1-8-6-1); and 'thousands upon thousands are the Rudras upon the earth' (Taittiriya Samhita 4-5-11-1) — these two mantras convey a plain self-contradiction, like a man declaring aloud, 'I am silent' — and are therefore without authority."

One mantra states that Parameshvara, as Rudra, exists alone with no equal second; another states there are thousands upon thousands of Rudras in the world. These two statements plainly contradict each other — like a man declaring, "as long as I live, I remain silent" — the very act of speaking the claim contradicts it. How can the claim of silence hold, once spoken aloud? A mantra conveying mutually contradictory meanings in this way cannot carry authority.

> आप उन्दन्त्विति (Taittiriya Samhita 1-2-1-1) मन्त्रे यजमानस्य क्षौरकाले जलेन शिरसः सेचनं ब्रूते । शुभिके शिर आरोह शोभयन्ती मुखं ममेति मन्त्रे विवाहकाले मंगलाचरणार्थं पुष्पनिर्मितायाः शुभकायाः वरवध्वोः शिरस्यवस्थानं ब्रूते । तयोश्च मन्त्रयोर्लोकप्रसिद्धार्थानुवादित्वादनधिगतार्थगन्तृत्वं नास्ति । तस्मात्स्मृतिभागो न प्रमाणम् ॥
>
> *āpa undantv iti mantre yajamānasya kṣaura-kāle jalena śirasaḥ secanaṃ brūte | śubhike śira āroha śobhayantī mukhaṃ mameti mantre vivāha-kāle maṅgalācaraṇārthaṃ puṣpa-nirmitāyāḥ śubhakāyāḥ vara-vadhvoḥ śiraśy avasthānaṃ brūte | tayoś ca mantrayor loka-prasiddhārthānuvāditvād anadhigatārtha-gantṛtvaṃ nāsti | tasmāt smṛti-bhāgo na pramāṇam ||*
>
> "The mantra 'āpa undantu' ('may the waters moisten him') states that water should be poured over the sacrificer's head at the time of shaving. The mantra 'śubhike śira āroha śobhayantī mukhaṃ mama' ('O beautiful one, ascend the head, adorning my face') states that a flower-garland should be placed on the bride's and groom's heads at marriage for an auspicious purpose. Since both mantras merely restate what is already commonly known, they fail to reveal anything previously unknown — and so this ritual-instruction portion too is not valid proof."

That is: these mantras merely describe customs already familiar from ordinary life — pouring water while shaving, placing a garland at a wedding — conveying nothing genuinely new. Since valid proof must reveal something not already known, even this portion of the Veda fails to qualify as pramana.

## Chapter 6. The Defining Characteristics of Mantras — Examination of the Related Mimamsa Sutras — Purva-pakṣa and Siddhanta

*Original title: "Mantragaḷa lakṣaṇādivicāravu — tatsambandhavāda Mīmāṃsāsūtragaḷa vimarśeyu — pūrvapakṣa mattu siddhāntagaḷu"*
**Printed pages 374–388 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 374</div>

> जलादिदृश्येण शिरःक्षेदनादेर्लोकसिद्ध्यैकपि तदभिमानिदेवतानुग्रहस्यअप्रसिद्धत्वाद्विषयस्यानाज्ञातार्थज्ञापकत्वम् । ततो लक्षणसद्भावात्स्वैर्मन्त्रैर्भागस्य प्रामाण्यम् ॥
>
> *jalādi-dṛśyeṇa śiraḥ-kṣedanāder loka-siddhy-aikapi tad-abhimāni-devatānugrahasyāprasiddhatvād viṣayasyānājñātārtha-jñāpakatvam | tato lakṣaṇa-sadbhāvāt svair mantrair bhāgasya prāmāṇyam ||*
>
> "Though acts such as pouring water while shaving the head are, by themselves, well known in ordinary life, the favor of the deity presiding over that act is not commonly known — so this subject matter does indeed reveal something previously unknown. Therefore, since the defining mark of valid proof is genuinely present, this mantra-portion is authoritative."

**This is Sayana's own resolution** to the preceding objection: while the *outward act* described (pouring water, placing a garland) may be common knowledge, the specific *divine favor* connected to performing it in the prescribed ritual manner is not — and it is precisely this previously-unknown element that the mantra reveals, satisfying the very definition of valid proof.

### Turning to Jaimini's Own Mimamsa-Sutras

> एकदेवाभिप्रेत्य भगवान् जैमिनिर्मन्त्राधिकरणे मन्त्राणां विवक्षितार्थत्वमसूत्रयत् (Purva Mimamsa 1-2-31 to 53) । तानि च सूत्राणि क्रमशः प्रवर्तयिष्यामः । तत्र पूर्वपक्षं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *eka-devābhipretya bhagavān jaiminir mantrādhikaraṇe mantrāṇāṃ vivakṣitārthatvam asūtrayat (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā 1-2-31 to 53) | tāni ca sūtrāṇi kramaśaḥ pravartayiṣyāmaḥ | tatra pūrvapakṣaṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "With this very idea in mind, the venerable Jaimini, in his section on mantras, formulated in sutra-form the doctrine that mantras carry an intended meaning (Purva-Mimamsa 1-2-31 to 53). We shall now present these sutras in their proper order — beginning with his own formulation of the objection (purva-paksha)."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 375</div>

A "sutra" is a sentence composed with the fewest possible words to convey many subjects concisely, without any loss of meaning. In ancient times, many rishis composed their treatises in this style — the Yoga, Vyakarana, and other philosophical schools (darshanas) are similarly composed, and, being terse, require commentary to unpack. We now turn to explaining several sutras from Jaimini's own Purva-Mimamsa-sutras concerning the meaning of mantras, beginning with the objection (purva-paksha) as Jaimini himself states it.
