> चेदर्थशास्त्रत (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-31) स विनाभिधेयो यस्य शास्त्रे ब्राह्मणवाक्ये तदर्थशास्त्रम् । तस्माच्चाविशक्तार्थो मन्त्र इत्यर्थः । इत्येवं हि । उक्तं हि (Taittiriya Samhita 1-1-8; Vajasaneyi Samhita 1-22) मन्त्रेण प्रथमप्रभनमुभयीयते । पुरोडाशं प्रथयिष्येति (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-2-8-4; Shatapatha Brahmana 1-2-2-8) ब्राह्मणेऽपि तदेवाभिप्रेत्य प्रस्तुतचोदनाय प्रवृत्तं ब्राह्मणवाक्यम् प्रवृत्तम् । तथा सति मन्त्रेणाप्ययमेवार्थो बोधाय प्रवृत्तः ।
>
> चेद् अर्थ-शास्त्रत (जैमिनि सुत्र १-२-३१) स विनाभिधेयो यस्य शास्त्रे ब्राह्मण-वाक्ये तद्-अर्थ-शास्त्रम् । तस्माच् चाविशक्तार्थो मन्त्र इत्य् अर्थः । ...
> *ced artha-śāstrata (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-31) sa vinābhidheyo yasya śāstre brāhmaṇa-vākye tad-artha-śāstram | tasmāc cāviśaktārtho mantra ity arthaḥ | ...*
>
> "The mantras convey no [independent] meaning, since there exists an 'artha-shastra' — a separate text explaining their meaning — namely, the Brahmana [portion]. Thus a mantra's meaning is unfixed/dependent [on the Brahmana]. For instance: it is said that the first application is conveyed through the mantra, and the statement 'I shall set forth the puroḍāśa cake' occurring in a Brahmana passage was made with this same intent, using the Brahmana's own sentence to direct the ongoing rite — showing that the mantra was employed to convey this very same meaning [already given by the Brahmana]."

That is: from the sutra "ced artha-shastrata" through to the sutra on "vidhi-shabda" (injunction-words), a single adhikarana (topic-section) runs, with each sutra explained in turn. The opening sutra's meaning: mantras have no independent meaning, because a separate "artha-shastra" (meaning-explaining text) — namely, the Brahmana — already exists to explain them. If a mantra genuinely had its own meaning, people would grasp it directly, with no need for an accompanying Brahmana passage. Since a Brahmana explanation *is* needed, this shows the mantra itself conveys no independent meaning — illustrated by the Brahmana statement "I shall set forth the puroḍāśa cake," used precisely to supply the meaning the mantra alone fails to convey.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 376</div>

For instance, the mantra "uru prathasva" refers to spreading out the purodāśa cake — and this same act is described in the Brahmana passage "purodāśaṃ prathayati" ("the Adhvaryu spreads the purodāśa"). Since the Brahmana merely restates what the mantra already conveys, what genuine use does such a Brahmana serve? If the mantra's meaning is already clear on its own, the Brahmana statement becomes pointless. But if instead the mantra's own meaning is what remains unclear, and the Brahmana serves to clarify its **viniyoga** — the procedure and context in which the mantra should be applied — then the Brahmana genuinely earns its purpose. On this view, if mere recitation of the mantra during the yajna is held to be its primary function, we must then accept that recitation serves some **adṛṣṭa** (unseen, imperceptible) purpose.

On this, the upholder of the doctrine to be controverted states another argument:

> ननूच्चारणार्थत्वे सत्यदृष्टं प्रयोजनं परिकल्प्येत । अर्थाभिधायकत्वे तु दृष्टं लभ्यते । तस्माद्ब्राह्मणस्यानुवादकत्वमभ्युपेत्यापि मन्त्रस्याभिधानार्थत्वमेवेत्याशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *nanūccāraṇārthatve saty adṛṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ parikalpyeta | arthābhidhāyakatve tu dṛṣṭaṃ labhyate | tasmād brāhmaṇasyānuvādakatvam abhyupetyāpi mantrasyābhidhānārthatvam evety āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "But if [the mantras] serve only for recitation, an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose would have to be posited, whereas if they convey meaning, a visible purpose is obtained; therefore, even granting that the Brāhmaṇa merely repeats, the mantra must serve to convey meaning — raising this doubt, he states the answer in a sūtra."

But suppose instead we say the very purpose of reciting mantras at the yajna is to convey their meaning — this would establish a **dṛṣṭa** (directly perceivable) purpose for the mantras. Between the two kinds of purpose, perceived and unperceived, an unperceived purpose should only be invoked when no perceived purpose can be found. If the Brahmana merely repeats the mantra's own meaning, then the meaning of mantras recited during the yajna...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 377</div>

We would have to accept that mantras do convey meaning in this sense. But if we accept that a mantra has this meaning-conveying capacity, another objection immediately arises — explained in the next sutra.

### "Vakya-niyamat" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-32)

> अग्निर्मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (RV 8-44-16) इत्येवमेव वाक्यं पठितव्यमिति मन्त्रे नियम उपलभ्यते । अर्थप्रत्यायनं तु मूर्ध्वाग्निरित्येवं वृत्त्यपि स्वेष्टेव भवत्येव । तस्मान्नियतपाठक्रमफलायोच्चारणमेव मन्त्रप्रयोजनम् । ननु पाठक्रमनियममात्रात्स्याद्यष्ट्वार्थज्ञेऽपि मन्त्रपाठक्रमबोधार्थं चेवेत्याशंक्य तत्र दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> अग्निर् मूर्धा दिवः ककुत् (र्व् ८-४४-१६) इत्य् एवम् एव वाक्यं पठितव्यम् इति मन्त्रे नियम उपलभ्यते । अर्थप्रत्यायनं तु मूर्ध्वाग्निर् इत्य् एवं वृत्त्यपि स्वेष्टैव भवत्य् एव । तस्मान् नियत-पाठ-क्रम-फलायोच्चारणम् एव मन्त्र-प्रयोजनम् । ...
> *agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut (RV 8-44-16) ity evam eva vākyaṃ paṭhitavyam iti mantre niyama upalabhyate | arthapratyāyanaṃ tu mūrdhvāgnir ity evaṃ vṛttyapi sveṣṭaiva bhavaty eva | tasmān niyata-pāṭha-krama-phalāyoccāraṇam eva mantra-prayojanam | ...*
>
> "It is a settled rule that the mantra 'agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut' must be recited in exactly this word-order, and no other. Yet conveying its meaning would work equally well in a rearranged form such as 'mūrdhāgnir...' Therefore, the mantra's purpose lies solely in its recitation according to a fixed word-order — for the sake of that order's own fruit, not for conveying meaning. One might object that even granting this fixed order, its purpose could still be to teach the proper recitation-sequence to someone who already knows the mantra's meaning. Anticipating this, Jaimini now formulates a further objection identifying an additional flaw in that view."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 378</div>

### "Buddha-shastrat" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-33)

> अग्नीदग्नीन् विहर (Taittiriya Samhita 6-3-1-2) इति एष मन्त्रः प्रयोगकाले पठ्यते । तच्चाग्निविहरणादिकमाग्नीध्रेणाध्ययनकाल एव स्वकर्तव्यत्वेन बुद्धम् । तस्य च बुद्धार्थस्य पुनर्मन्त्रेण शासनमनर्थकम् । न हि सोपानत्कः पादे प्रतिमुंचति । तस्मात् बुद्धस्यापि अर्थस्य स्मारणाय मन्त्रेण स्मारणमस्तीत्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> अग्नीद् अग्नीन् विहर (तैत्तिरीय संहिता ६-३-१-२) इति एष मन्त्रः प्रयोग-काले पठ्यते । तच् चाग्नि-विहरणादिकम् आग्नीध्रेणाध्ययन-काल एव स्वकर्तव्यत्वेन बुद्धम् । तस्य च बुद्धार्थस्य पुनर् मन्त्रेण शासनम् अनर्थकम् । न हि सोपानत्कः पादे प्रतिमुञ्चति । ...
> *agnīd agnīn vihara (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6-3-1-2) iti eṣa mantraḥ prayoga-kāle paṭhyate | tac cāgni-viharaṇādikam āgnīdhreṇādhyayana-kāla eva svakartavyatvena buddham | tasya ca buddhārthasya punar mantreṇa śāsanam anarthakam | na hi sopānatkaḥ pāde pratimuñcati | ...*
>
> "'Agnīd, distribute the fires' (Taittiriya Samhita 6-3-1-2) — this mantra is recited during the ritual performance. But distributing the fire and similar duties have already been learned by the Agnidh priest, as his own responsibility, during his period of study. Instructing him again, through a mantra, about something he already knows serves no purpose. Indeed, no one puts a second shoe on a foot that already wears one."

That is: the objection here is that mantras convey no meaning, since their sole function is recitation — not instruction, because reciting an already-known meaning serves no purpose. It was already established that mantras must follow a fixed recitation-order (per the previous sutra); now a further flaw is illustrated. "Agnīd agnīn vihara" is an injunctive mantra (vidhi-mantra), also called a "prescriptive" (preṣaṇa) mantra, recited during the yajna to direct the priest performing a task while he performs it. In every yajna, fire is kept burning in the Agnidh's own fire-pit before the ritual begins, and before the rites commence, this fire is carried from the Agnidh's altar to the other altars — this mantra commands precisely that act. But this mantra's meaning is already generally known to every priest participating in the yajna. What purpose is served by restating something everyone already knows?

In this connection there is a story in the Aitareya Brahmana (Ai. Brā. 2-5-4). In the sacrificial hall the gods and the asuras fought for position. The asuras were strong and drove the gods from every place; but they could not drive Agni out of the Agnidhra's place. The gods, taking refuge there, increased their strength and drove out the asuras, and on the other altars, where the asuras had put out the fire, they rekindled it from the fire on the Agnidhra's altar. It is on this basis that the rite called *agni-viharaṇa* is performed in sacrifices. The ṛk "*agninā'gniḥ samidhyate*" (ṛ. saṃ. 1-12-6) supports this very point.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 379</div>

Generally, yajnas employ sixteen priests, organized into four groups (**गण** *gaṇa*):

- **होतृगण** (*hotṛgaṇa*, Hotr-group) — मैत्रावरुण/प्रशास्त्र (*maitrāvaruṇa*/*praśāstra*), अच्छावाक (*acchāvāka*), ग्रावस्तुत् (*grāvastut*) — priests connected to the Rigveda.
- **अध्वर्युगण** (*adhvaryugaṇa*, Adhvaryu-group) — प्रतिप्रस्थाता (*pratiprasthātā*), नेष्टा (*neṣṭā*), उन्नेता (*unnetā*) — priests connected to the Yajurveda.
- **उद्गातृगण** (*udgātṛgaṇa*, Udgatr-group) — प्रस्तोता (*prastotā*), प्रतिहर्ता (*pratihartā*), सुब्रह्मण्य (*subrahmaṇya*) — Samaveda priests.
- **ब्रह्मगण** (*brahmagaṇa*, Brahma-group) — ब्राह्मणाच्छंसी (*brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*), आग्नीध्र (*āgnīdhra*), पोता (*potā*) — priests who must be learned across all the Vedas.

Altogether there are sixteen priests; with the yajamana, seventeen persons. But the Shatapatha Brahmana (10-4-1-9) states that a yajna should not be performed with seventeen priests — followers of the Kaushitaki shakha therefore appoint an eighteenth priest, the **सदस्य** (*sadasya*), who oversees the entire proceeding to ensure everything runs correctly (this appointment is not customary among Ashvalayana-shakha followers).

The mantra "Agnīd agnīn vihara," discussed above, is used specifically when carrying fire from the Agnidh's altar to the other altars. But the Agnidh and other priests such as the Adhvaryu already know their duties, and the meaning and purpose of the mantras, from their period of Vedic study. Restating what is already known is therefore pointless — as pointless, the objection says, as putting a second shoe over a foot already shod.

This might be answered as follows: what the mantras state may indeed already be known — but it could be forgotten through carelessness, and the mantras then serve a genuinely useful reminding function. Very well — let us grant that mantras can serve to remind priests of forgotten matters. But some mantras assert things that are outright impossible. This is addressed in the next sutra.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 380</div>

### "Avidyamāna-vacanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-34)

> चत्वारि शृंगा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य (RV 4-58-3) इति मन्त्रे आम्नायते । न खलु चतुःशृंगत्वादियुक्तं किंचिद्यज्ञसाधनं विद्यते यन्मन्त्रशाखेनास्मर्येत । ...
>
> *catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya (RV 4-58-3) iti mantre āmnāyate | na khalu catuḥ-śṛṅgatvādi-yuktaṃ kiṃcid yajña-sādhanaṃ vidyate yan mantra-śākhenāsmaryeta |*
>
> "The mantra states: 'four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands has it' (RV 4-58-3). But no sacrificial implement possessing four horns and the like actually exists, which this mantra could be supposed to remind the priest of."

Even granting mantras a memory-jogging function, this fails for mantras describing things with no real-world referent at all — like this famously cryptic verse. Since no such four-horned, three-footed, two-headed, seven-handed object exists among yajna implements, this mantra cannot serve even as a reminder of anything real.

### "Acetane'rtha-bandhanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-35)

> ओषधे त्रायस्वैनम् । श्रुणोत ग्रावाणः । इत्याद्यचेतनवचनेषु मन्त्रेषु चेतनोचितं रक्षणश्रवणादिकमर्थं बध्नाति । स च चेतनस्वापादुचितः ।
>
> *oṣadhe trāyasvainam | śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ | ity ādy acetana-vacaneṣu mantreṣu cetanocitaṃ rakṣaṇa-śravaṇādikam arthaṃ badhnāti | sa ca cetana-svabhāvād ucitaḥ |*
>
> "In mantras such as 'O herb, protect him' and 'Hear, O stones,' meanings befitting sentient beings — protection, hearing, and the like — are attached to statements addressed to inanimate things. But such meanings are properly suited only to conscious beings."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 381</div>

> नन्वभिमानिव्यपदेश इति (वे. सू. २-१-५) वैयासिकशास्त्रे सूत्रितत्वादोषध्याद्यभिमानिचेतनदेवतात्र विवक्ष्यतामित्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *nanv abhimānivyapadeśa iti (Ve. Sū. 2-1-5) vaiyāsikaśāstre sūtritatvād oṣadhyādyabhimānicetanadevatātra vivakṣyatām ity āśaṅkya doṣāntaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "It may be said that, since in the Vaiyasika Shastra the sutra 'abhimānivyapadeśaḥ' (Ve. Sū. 2-1-5) has been laid down, the conscious presiding deity of the herbs and the like should be understood here; to guard against this he states a further fault in the next sutra."

*Sutrartha:* qualities such as protecting and hearing, which are possible only in living beings, are attributed to inanimate things too; therefore the mantras are useless.

*Akshepa:* the mantra "oṣadhe trāyasvainam" (Tai. Saṃ. 1-2-1-1) is one that prays to the darbha (darbha belongs to the class of plants) at the time of the yajamana's shaving during his consecration: its meaning is "O darbha, protect this yajamana." Another mantra is "śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ" (Tai. Saṃ. 1-3-13-1), meaning "O stones, kindly hear what we pray." This mantra prays to the stones when the soma juice is pressed out with stones. In such mantras inanimate things such as darbha and stones are addressed. How can mantras containing such incoherent talk be worthy of respect?

*Samadhana:* the sage Vyasa, in his Vedanta-sutra, has said "abhimānivyapadeśaḥ" (Ve. Sū. 2-1-3); that is, the herbs and the rest have presiding deities. In the Taittiriya Samhita it is said "somo oṣadhīnām adhipatiḥ"; so it should be understood that in addressing the herb, the prayer is made to the moon, the presiding deity of the herbs. Since it is the presiding deities of the things that are addressed, there is no harm to the dignity of the mantra.

### "Artha-vipratiṣedhāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-36)

> अर्थविप्रतिषेधात् ॥ (जै. सू. १-२-३६) अदितिर्द्यौरदितिरन्तरिक्षम् (ऋ. सं. १-८९-१०) इति मन्त्र आम्नायते । यदेव द्यौस्तदेवान्तरिक्षमित्ययमर्थो विप्रतिषिद्धः । एवमेक एव रुद्रः (तै. सं. १-८-६-१) सहस्राणि सहस्रशो ये रुद्राः (तै. सं. ४-५-११-५) इत्यादिकमप्युदाहर्तव्यम् ।
> *arthavipratiṣedhāt || (Jai. Sū. 1-2-36) aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-89-10) iti mantra āmnāyate | yad eva dyaus tad evāntarikṣam ity ayam artho vipratiṣiddhaḥ | evam eka eva rudraḥ (Tai. Saṃ. 1-8-6-1) sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrāḥ (Tai. Saṃ. 4-5-11-5) ityādikam apy udāhartavyam |*
>
>
> "The mantra states: 'Aditi is Dyaus (Heaven), Aditi is Antariksha (the mid-region).' But to say that what is Dyaus is the very same as Antariksha is a self-contradiction. Similarly, one might cite here 'Rudra is one only' alongside 'the Rudras in their thousands.'"

The objection: since a single mantra identifies Aditi simultaneously with two distinct cosmic regions (Heaven and the mid-air), and separate mantras contradictorily describe Rudra as both singular and countless-in-thousands, such mutually inconsistent statements cannot be meaningful or authoritative.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 382</div>

> नसु त्वैमेव माता च पिता त्वैमेवेत्यादवन्तरिक्षादिरूपश्चेनादितिः स्तूयते । एवमेकस्यापि रुद्रस्य योगसामर्थ्याद्बहुमूर्तिस्वीकारोऽस्तु । ततो नार्थविप्रतिषेध इत्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *nanu tvaim eva mātā ca pitā tvaim eva ity ādav antarikṣādi-rūpaś cenāditiḥ stūyate | evam ekasyāpi rudrasya yoga-sāmarthyād bahu-mūrti-svīkāro'stu | tato nārtha-vipratiṣedha ity āśaṅkya doṣāntaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "[One might say:] just as we say of someone, 'you alone are my mother, and you alone are my father,' Aditi is likewise praised metaphorically in the form of Antariksha and similar epithets. Similarly, let it be granted that the one Rudra, through his own yogic power, assumes many forms. Therefore, there is no genuine contradiction of meaning. Anticipating this possible defense, [Jaimini] now formulates yet a further objection, identifying a different flaw."

*Sutrartha:* since the meanings stated in the mantras contradict each other, the mantras are not worthy of respect.

*Akshepa:* in the mantra "aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam" (ṛ. saṃ. 1-89-10) the contradictory meanings heaven and mid-air are applied to one person. Can contradictory qualities exist in one thing? If one says milk is white, that is the quality found in milk; can the opposite, black, be in milk? A sentence or mantra saying "milk is both white and black" is incoherent. Take another example: "eka eva rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe" (Tai. Saṃ. 1-8-6-1) says that Rudra is one only and there is no second. But in another place, "sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrā adhi bhūmyām" (Tai. Saṃ. 4-5-11-5) says that the Rudras are on this earth in thousands upon thousands. The meanings of these two mantras contradict each other, and it is hard to say which is right and which wrong. Since many mantras contain such mutually contradictory meanings, the mantras are not worthy of consideration.
---

<div class="pgmark">original p. 383</div>

### "Svādhyāyavad-vacanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-37)

> पूर्णिका नाम काचिद्योषिदवघातं करोति । तत्समीपे माणवकः स्वाध्यायग्रहणकालं कदाचिदवघातमन्त्रमधीते। न च तस्यार्थप्रकाशनविवक्षाऽस्ति, प्रतिमुशलप्रहारं तस्य मन्त्रस्यापश्यमानत्वात्पदग्रहणमात्रं इच्छत इव मन्त्रानभ्यस्यति। तत्र स्वाध्यायकाले पठितोऽप्यश्वं मन्त्रो यथा पूर्णिकां प्रति स्वार्थं न ब्रूते तथा कर्मकालेऽपि स्वार्थं न वक्ष्यति।
>
> *pūrṇikā nāma kācid yoṣid avaghātaṃ karoti | tat-samīpe māṇavakaḥ svādhyāya-grahaṇa-kālaṃ kadācid avaghāta-mantram adhīte | na ca tasyārtha-prakāśana-vivakṣā'sti, prati-muśala-prahāraṃ tasya mantrasyāpaśyamānatvāt pada-grahaṇa-mātraṃ icchata iva mantrān abhyasyati | tatra svādhyāya-kāle paṭhito'py evaṃ mantro yathā pūrṇikāṃ prati svārthaṃ na brūte tathā karma-kāle'pi svārthaṃ na vakṣyati |*
>
> "A certain woman named Purnika is pounding grain with a pestle. Nearby, a young brahmin student, engaged in his daily lesson, happens to be reciting the pestle-mantra (avaghāta-mantra). He has no intention of conveying its meaning — evident from the fact that he does not synchronize the mantra with each fall of the pestle; he seems merely intent on memorizing the words, and practices this mantra among others [without regard to Purnika's work]. Just as this mantra, though recited during study, conveys no meaning relevant to Purnika, so too it will convey no meaning even when recited during the actual ritual."

That is: just as a mantra's meaning goes unattended during rote study, so too its ritual application conveys no genuine meaning — since the objection holds that mantra-recitation and the accompanying ritual action (here, pounding grain) proceed with no real connection between them, mantras recited without understood meaning yield no fruit for the rite performed alongside them.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 384</div>

**Resolution to the Purnika objection:** there is no intention of conveying meaning when the student recites the mantra during rote study, and Purnika herself has no capacity to grasp it. But in yajna-rites proper, the Adhvaryu priest reciting mantras does know their meaning, does intend to convey it, and those present are capable of understanding it. The claim that mantras are meaningless does not hold.

> केषांचिन्मन्त्राणामर्थो विज्ञातुं न शक्यते । तद्यथा । अम्यक्स त इन्द्र ऋष्टिरस्मे (RV 1-169-3) इत्येको मन्त्रः । सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतू (RV 10-106-6) इत्यपरो मन्त्रः । ननु एतस्मान्मन्त्रार्थबोधायैव निगमनिरुक्तव्याकरणानि सन्तीत्याशंक्य दोषान्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *keṣāñcin mantrāṇām artho vijñātuṃ na śakyate | tad yathā | amyaksa ta indra ṛṣṭir asme ity eko mantraḥ | sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū ity aparo mantraḥ | nanv etasmān mantrārtha-bodhāyaiva nigama-nirukta-vyākaraṇāni santīty āśaṅkya doṣāntaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "The meaning of some mantras cannot be ascertained at all. For example: 'amyaksa ta indra ṛṣṭir asme' is one such mantra; 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū' is another. One might object that Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana exist precisely to illuminate such mantras' meaning — anticipating this, a further objection is formulated."

That is: since the meaning of numerous mantras cannot be properly determined at all — these two being prime examples — it follows that mantras exist merely for recitation, not meaning.

**A resolution is then offered:** it is precisely to explain such difficult mantras' meaning that disciplines like Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana arose; with their help, understanding mantra-meaning is readily achievable — the claim of impossibility does not hold.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 385</div>

### "Anitye-saṃyogān mantrānarthakyaṃ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-39)

> किं ते कृण्वन्ति कीकटेषु (RV 3-53-14) इति मन्त्रे कीकटो नाम जनपद आम्नातः । तथा नैचाशाखं नाम नगरं प्रमगन्दो नाम राजेत्येतद्वा अनित्या आम्नाताः । तथा च सति स्यात्प्रमगन्दात्प्राय मन्त्रो भूतपूर्व इति गम्यते । तदेवं नित्यस्य शास्त्रादिभिर्हेतुभिर्मन्त्रार्थप्रत्यायनार्थत्वं नास्ति । किंतूच्चारणादृष्ट्यार्थ इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥
>
> *kiṃ te kṛṇvanti kīkaṭeṣu iti mantre kīkaṭo nāma janapada āmnātaḥ | tathā naicāśākhaṃ nāma nagaraṃ pramagando nāma rājety etad vā anityā āmnātāḥ | tathā ca sati syāt pramagandāt prāya mantro bhūtapūrva iti gamyate | tad evaṃ nityasya śāstrādibhir hetubhir mantrārtha-pratyāyanārthatvaṃ nāsti | kintūccāraṇād ṛṣṭy-artha iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||*
>
> "In the mantra 'kiṃ te kṛṇvanti kīkaṭeṣu' (RV 3-53-14), a country named Kikata is mentioned; likewise a city named Naichashakha and a king named Pramaganda — all non-eternal, transient things. This being so, it follows that the mantra must postdate King Pramaganda's era. Thus, for these reasons — along with the shastra-based arguments already given — mantras serve no purpose in conveying meaning; their purpose lies instead in the unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa) obtained through mere recitation. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

That is: since mantras mention transient, historically-bound proper names — a country, a city, a king — accepting that mantras convey meaning would force one to admit the Vedas are non-eternal, contradicting the doctrine that they are beginningless (anādi) and non-human (apauruṣeya). Therefore, only the unseen fruit of recitation itself can be the mantras' purpose — no other fruit exists.

**This concludes the full nine-part objection (purva-paksha)**, spanning from "Buddha-shastrat" through this final sutra — nine separate arguments marshaled to establish that mantras serve recitation alone. **Jaimini's own resolution follows in the next sutra.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 386</div>

### A Methodological Note, then Jaimini's Own Resolution Begins

In his Purva-Mimamsa sutras, before establishing that mantras do carry meaning, Jaimini himself first gathered every possible objection on the subject and presented them as the purva-paksha. Sayanacharya, rather than composing his own independent arguments, works directly through Jaimini's own sutras — though in places he interprets them along a path somewhat different from the classical commentators (Shabara, Kumarila, and others), who did not, sutra by sutra, anticipate the siddhantin's coming resolution before commenting on each subsequent sutra.

One notable divergence: Mimamsakas do not generally accept resolutions like "lifeless objects have presiding deities" or "yogis possess extraordinary powers" as doing genuine argumentative work — Shabara's own commentary instead holds that merely reciting the mantras, without making their meaning the primary aim, involves no fault at all. Sayanacharya, however, resolves this very objection using the sutra "abhimānivyapadeśaḥ" of Vyasa's Vedanta-sutras ("the deities are the presiding spirits [of these objects]"). By anticipating objections this way throughout, Sayana's argument reads as complete and self-contained. We follow Sayanacharya's own interpretation of Jaimini's sutras from here onward.

**There, Jaimini formulates the siddhanta (resolution):**

### "Aviśiṣṭastu vākyārthaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-40)

> तुशब्देन मन्त्राणामुद्दिष्टार्थमुच्चारणमात्रं वारयति । क्रियाकारकसंबन्धेन प्रतीयमानो वाक्यार्थो लोकवेदयोरविशिष्टः । तथा सति यथा लोकेऽर्थप्रत्यायनायैव वाक्यमुच्चार्यते तथा वैदिकयागप्रयोगेऽपि दृश्यम् । मन्त्रेण प्रकाशितस्यार्थोऽनुष्ठातुं शक्यते न...
>
> *tu-śabdena mantrāṇām uddiṣṭārtham uccāraṇa-mātraṃ vārayati | kriyā-kāraka-sambandhena pratīyamāno vākyārtho loka-vedayor aviśiṣṭaḥ | tathā sati yathā loke'rtha-pratyāyanāyaiva vākyam uccāryate tathā vaidika-yāga-prayoge'pi dṛśyam | mantreṇa prakāśitasyārtho'nuṣṭhātuṃ śakyate na...*
>
> "The particle 'tu' (but) rules out the view that mantras exist merely for recitation with no intended meaning. The meaning of a sentence, understood through the relation between action and its agents/instruments, is the same whether in ordinary speech or in the Veda. Just as, in ordinary life, a sentence is uttered precisely to convey meaning, the same must hold in Vedic ritual application as well. What a mantra reveals can indeed be acted upon, not..."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 387</div>

> …त्वप्रकाशितः । तस्मान्मन्त्रोच्चारणस्यार्थप्रकाशनरूपं दृष्टमेव प्रयोजनम् । नन्वभ्रिरसि नारिरसीत्यारभ्य त्रैष्टुभेन त्वा छन्दसा ददे (तै. सं. ४-१-१-३) इति मन्त्र आम्नातः । तेनैव मन्त्रेण प्रतीतेऽप्यभ्र्यादाने पुनर्ब्राह्मणे तां चतुर्भिरभ्रिमादत्ते (तै. सं. ५-१-१-४) इति विधीयते । तदेतद्विधानं त्वत्पक्षे व्यर्थं स्यादित्याशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *…tv aprakāśitaḥ | tasmān mantroccāraṇasyārthaprakāśanarūpaṃ dṛṣṭam eva prayojanam | nanv abhrir asi nārir asīty ārabhya traiṣṭubhena tvā chandasā dade (Taittiriya Samhita 4-1-1-3) iti mantra āmnātaḥ | tenaiva mantreṇa pratīte'py abhryādāne punar brāhmaṇe tāṃ caturbhir abhrim ādatte (Taittiriya Samhita 5-1-1-4) iti vidhīyate | tad etad vidhānaṃ tvatpakṣe vyarthaṃ syād ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>

That is: mantra-meaning is established through the relation of action and its instruments, exactly as in ordinary speech — this holds equally for sacred and secular language alike. The word "tu" ("but") in this sutra rejects the earlier objection's claim that mantras serve merely recitation and not meaning; a new meaning, once revealed by a mantra, is what makes ritual action possible, and this alone is the mantra's directly observable (dṛṣṭa) purpose — not some purely "spiritual"/unseen one. Just as an ordinary sentence is uttered specifically to convey its meaning, so too must a Vedic mantra be understood as functioning the same way.

A further objection is then raised: consider the sequence of mantras running from "abhrir asi nārir asi" through "traiṣṭubhena cchandasā dade" — on your view, this passage fully describes the taking-up of the "ābhri" (a ritual implement). If so, the Brahmana's separate injunction "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" ("one takes up the ābhri with four [mantras]") becomes entirely redundant. Jaimini anticipates and answers this objection in the next sutra.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 388</div>

The general point: acting according to a purpose already understood is the aim [of ritual action] — one must be able to say *why* a given act is performed, since even if the act itself succeeds mechanically, uttering words devoid of meaning cannot explain "why" it was done. The reason each individual mantra is recited must be known; without this, others simply perform the action mechanically. Since this defeats the purpose behind ritual acts, a mantra's meaning must be understood as serving a genuinely observable (dṛṣṭa) purpose — as the Shabara-bhashya says. Meaning is therefore not a matter of unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose alone — it is directly observable purpose. To claim otherwise contradicts how language works in ordinary human affairs, where sentences are understood specifically to convey meaning; the same applies to Vedic sentences. The unseen fruit that arises specifically from the *act of recitation itself* is a separate matter — but understanding the meaning is what makes the resulting Dharmic fruit (dharma) possible, and this is what both types of purpose ultimately serve together.

If a mantra's meaning is granted, but the Brahmana's own separate injunction (e.g., regarding the fourfold use of the "abhri") becomes redundant given this — that objection was raised on the previous page. It is resolved as follows: this mantra alone does not specify by itself *how many mantras* constitute proper use of the "abhri" — that detail must be learned from elsewhere. Even granting the mantra's own meaning, the Brahmana statement "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" still serves an independent, non-redundant purpose, specifying the count — resolving the apparent contradiction between the objection and the resolution.

### "Guṇārthena punaḥ-śrutiḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-41)

> मन्त्रेण प्रतीतस्यैवार्थस्य ब्राह्मणे यत्पुनःश्रवणं तदेतच्चतुःसंख्यालक्षणगुणविधानार्थत्वेनोपयुज्यते । एतस्य विधानस्याभावे चतुर्णां मन्त्राणां मध्ये येन केनाप्येकेनाभ्रिरादीयेत । नन्विमामगृभ्णन्रशनामृतस्य (तै. सं. ४-१-२-१) इत्यश्वाभिधानीमादत्ते (तै. सं. ५-१-२-१) इत्यत्र मन्त्रसामर्थ्यादेव प्राप्तस्य रशनादानस्य पुनर्ब्राह्मणवाक्यं विनियोजकमाम्नायते । तदेतत्त्वन्मते व्यर्थमित्याशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *mantreṇa pratītasyaivārthasya brāhmaṇe yat punaḥśravaṇaṃ tad etac catuḥsaṃkhyā-lakṣaṇa-guṇa-vidhānārthatvenopayujyate | etasya vidhānasyābhāve caturṇāṃ mantrāṇāṃ madhye yena kenāpy ekenābhrir ādīyeta | nanv imām agṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya (Taittiriya Samhita 4-1-2-1) ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte (Taittiriya Samhita 5-1-2-1) ity atra mantra-sāmarthyād eva prāptasya raśanādānasya punar brāhmaṇa-vākyaṃ viniyojakam āmnāyate | tad etat tvanmate vyartham ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> *(The repetition in the Brāhmaṇa of a meaning already known from the mantra serves to enjoin a subsidiary detail, the number four; without it the abhri might be taken with any one of the four mantras. But in "imām agṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya … he takes the halter", where the taking of the halter already follows from the mantra's own power, the Brāhmaṇa sentence is again given as directing its use — on your view that is pointless; raising this doubt, he states the answer.)*

That is: where a mantra's own already-understood meaning is repeated in a Brahmana passage, that repetition is not redundant — it serves to specify a quantifying detail (here, that exactly four mantras are required), a detail the mantra by itself leaves open, since without such specification, a priest might assume he had the option to use any single one of the four mantras referenced.

## Chapter 7. The Definition of Pariṣaṅkhyā

*Original title: "Pariṣaṅkhyālakṣaṇa"*
**Printed pages 389–393 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 389</div>

The sutra's meaning: restating what is already said serves to indicate a distinctive point contained within it. Why repeat, in the Brahmana, what the mantra already states? Because the mantra contains a directive about the "abhri" (spade), followed by three further similar mantras — but if one simply followed the mantra alone, the act of taking up the tool could be completed using just one of the four, leaving the remaining three mantras' purpose unclear. The Brahmana resolves this by stating "caturbhir ābhrim ādatte" — one must recite all four mantras before taking up the tool. Since "caturbhiḥ" ("with four") appears nowhere in the mantra itself, without the Brahmana's help, an Adhvaryu might recite only one mantra of his choosing and consider the act complete — improperly performed by shastric standards. The Brahmana's repetition thus serves specifically to supply this missing detail.

But consider the Taittiriya Samhita's mantra "imām agṛbhṇan" ("I have grasped this") (Tai. Saṃ. 4-1-2-1), which clearly instructs taking up a rope. The Taittiriya Brahmana (Tai. Brā. 5-1-2-1) restates the same matter: "aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" ("one takes up the rope called ashva"). Here too, one might object that the mantra's application becomes redundant. Anticipating this, the sutra "parisaṅkhyā" follows.

### "Pariṣaṅkhyā" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-42)

> गर्दभाभिधानीं नादत्त इति निषेधः परिसंख्या । तदर्थमिदं ब्राह्मणवाक्यम् ॥
>
> *gardabhābhidhānīṃ nādatta iti niṣedhaḥ pariṣaṅkhyā | tadartham idaṃ brāhmaṇa-vākyam ||*
>
> "'One does not take up the rope called gardabha [donkey-rope]' — this implied prohibition is called pariṣaṅkhyā (exclusive specification). The Brahmana statement exists precisely for this purpose."

That is: the Brahmana's repetition here isn't redundant either — it implicitly *excludes* an alternative (a "donkey-rope," as opposed to the "horse-rope" specified), a specification the mantra alone cannot convey.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 390</div>

> …न्येन च प्राप्तं गर्दभरशनाया आदानं बाध्येतेति त्रयो दोषाः । नैवम् । गर्दभरशनाया अप्राप्तत्वात् । तथा हि । त्वत्पक्षे प्रकरणपाठान्यथानुपपत्त्या मन्त्रेणानेनादानं कुर्यादिति वाक्यं परिकल्प्यते । तेन च वाक्येन मन्त्रादानयोः संबन्धे सति पश्चात्किंविषयकमादानमिति वीक्षायां लिङ्गाद्रशनामात्रस्यादानमुपेत्य गर्दभरशनायाः प्राप्तिर्वक्तव्या । सा च विलम्ब्यत इत्यश्वाभिधानीमिति प्रत्यक्षेण वाक्येन । मन्त्रादानयोः संबन्धे सति लिङ्गाद्रशनामात्रे प्राप्तमादानमश्वाभिधानीमिति श्रुत्या विशेषे व्यवस्थाप्यते । ततो मन्त्रस्य निराकाङ्क्षत्वाद्गर्दभरशनाया अप्राप्तत्वान्नास्ति प्राप्तबाधः । अत एव निषेधार्थो न कल्प्यते । विध्यर्थश्च न त्यज्यते । तत्र कुतो दोषत्रयम् । ईदृशमप्राप्तिरूपमेव गर्दभरशनाया निवारणमभिप्रेत्य परिसंख्येति सूत्रितम् । ननूरु प्रथस्वेति प्रथयतीति ब्राह्मणस्य वैयर्थ्यं तदवस्थमेवेत्याशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *…nyena ca prāptaṃ gardabharaśanāyā ādānaṃ bādhyeteti trayo doṣāḥ | naivam | gardabharaśanāyā aprāptatvāt | tathā hi | tvatpakṣe prakaraṇapāṭhānyathānupapattyā mantreṇānenādānaṃ kuryād iti vākyaṃ parikalpyate | tena ca vākyena mantrādānayoḥ saṃbandhe sati paścāt kiṃviṣayakam ādānam iti vīkṣāyāṃ liṅgād raśanāmātrasyādānam upetya gardabharaśanāyāḥ prāptir vaktavyā | sā ca vilambyata ity aśvābhidhānīm iti pratyakṣeṇa vākyena | mantrādānayoḥ saṃbandhe sati liṅgād raśanāmātre prāptam ādānam aśvābhidhānīm iti śrutyā viśeṣe vyavasthāpyate | tato mantrasya nirākāṅkṣatvād gardabharaśanāyā aprāptatvān nāsti prāptabādhaḥ | ata eva niṣedhārtho na kalpyate | vidhyarthaś ca na tyajyate | tatra kuto doṣatrayam | īdṛśam aprāptirūpam eva gardabharaśanāyā nivāraṇam abhipretya parisaṃkhyeti sūtritam | nanūru prathasveti prathayatīti brāhmaṇasya vaiyarthyaṃ tadavastham evety āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> *(The pariṣaṅkhyā argument: the taking of the ass's halter is never reached, because the explicit word "aśvābhidhānīm" restricts the taking to the horse's halter before the ass's halter could be reached; so nothing already reached is set aside, no prohibitive sense need be imagined and the injunctive sense is not abandoned — hence none of the three faults.)*

The sutra's meaning: "This Brahmana statement is a prohibitive injunction (niṣedha-vidhi)." Before following Sayanacharya's own argument, it helps to understand the classical Mimamsa taxonomy of injunctive statements (**vidhi**) — sentences prescribing that a given act be performed in a given way. Mimamsa authorities recognize three kinds:

**(1) Apūrva-vidhi** ("wholly new" injunction) — a sentence prescribing an act knowable by no other means. "One who desires heaven should perform yajna"; "one should sprinkle the grain [with mantra]" — these are apurva-vidhis, since no alternative path exists to fulfill the stated aim.

**(2) Niyama-vidhi** (restrictive injunction) — where two possible methods exist for performing some act, and a sentence specifies that only one of them should be adopted.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 391</div>

The other method isn't explicitly negated — it simply becomes moot. Take "vrīhīn avahanti" ("he husks the grain [by pounding]"): to prepare the puroḍāśa cake, grain must be cleaned, husked, and ground. Husking need not be done only by pounding — peeling is equally conceivable — and this niyama-vidhi specifically prescribes pounding. Once pounding is followed, the occasion for peeling never even arises; no explicit prohibition is needed. Niyama-vidhi sentences apply precisely in such contexts, where the alternative was never independently established.

**(3) Pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi** — its defining characteristic:

> विधिर्द्व्यन्तमप्राप्ते नियमः स्यादुके गतिः । तत्र चान्यत्र च प्राप्ते परिसंख्येति कीर्त्यते ॥
>
> *vidhir dvy-antam aprāpte niyamaḥ syād uke gatiḥ | tatra cānyatra ca prāpte pariṣaṅkhyeti kīrtyate ||*
>
> "Where nothing else is otherwise attained, that instruction is 'vidhi'; where one of two paths is already established and the instruction directs toward one, that is 'niyama'; where both this and another alternative are equally attained, and one is exclusively specified, that is called 'pariṣaṅkhyā.'"

That is: where no path besides the stated one can accomplish a given task, it is vidhi; where either of two paths would work and only one is prescribed, it is niyama; where more than one path is simultaneously viable and one is exclusively singled out, it is pariṣaṅkhyā. Such a statement — prescribing that only one of several available options be taken, the rest set aside — may seem unnecessary, since the situation alone would suggest which path to take anyway; but it earns its purpose precisely by *prohibiting* the other paths.

Example: "**pañca pañca-nakhā bhakṣyāḥ**" ("the five five-clawed [animals] are edible") — meaning only these five specified clawed animals may be eaten; other animals may not, though there's no requirement that all five must be eaten. This is precisely why pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi differs from apūrva- and niyama-vidhi: failing to perform what is stated in the latter two counts as a defect (karma-lopa) in the rite, but this defect does not apply to pariṣaṅkhyā.

Pariṣaṅkhyā itself comes in two kinds: **Shrauti** (explicit, marked by words like "eva," "only") and **Lakshaniki** (implied, established through the sentence's own structure without such marker-words). The sentence under discussion belongs to this second, implied category — which is precisely why further discussion is needed.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 392</div>

The mantra "imām agṛbhṇan" is used in the fire-altar construction rite (agnichayana): bricks are needed for the fire-pit, horses and donkeys carry the required earth, and ropes are needed to lead them — this mantra is recited while taking hold of such a rope. Without the Brahmana statement "ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" ("thus he takes the horse-named rope"), the mantra might be recited while taking up either the horse's or the donkey's rope; this Brahmana statement clarifies that it should specifically accompany taking up the horse's rope, not the donkey's — precisely the pariṣaṅkhyā function.

An objection arises: without this Brahmana statement, three flaws would follow if the mantra alone were held to demand taking up any rope indiscriminately — abandoning the natural meaning of "ādāna/grahaṇa" (taking/holding), assuming a foreign meaning ("not taking"), and barring the donkey's rope, which the general word "rope" would otherwise include. As stated:

> श्रुतार्थस्य परित्यागः अश्रुतार्थस्य कल्पनात् । प्राप्तस्य बाधो द्वेषं परिसंख्या त्रिदोषणा ॥
>
> *śrutārthasya parityāgaḥ aśrutārthasya kalpanāt | prāptasya bādho dveṣaṃ pariṣaṅkhyā tridoṣaṇā ||*
>
> "Abandoning the stated meaning, constructing an unstated one, and barring what is otherwise independently established — pariṣaṅkhyā suffers from these three flaws."

Once the mantra is established as relating to the act of taking hold, the question becomes: taking hold of *what*? Since the mantra itself uses the word "rashanā" (rope), it must refer to taking hold of a rope in general. Once this general sense is established, taking up the donkey's rope also becomes "attained".

<div class="pgmark">original p. 393</div>

Taking up the donkey's rope only becomes "attained" after several intervening steps — merely reciting the mantra doesn't make it directly applicable; only after grasping various intervening matters does the donkey-rope possibility even arise. But once the Brahmana statement "ity aśvābhidhānīm ādatte" is understood, none of this difficulty arises: it becomes clear that the mantra must accompany taking up specifically the horse's rope. Since the donkey's rope was never genuinely "attained" as a live option, there's no room for the "barring what is established" flaw — and without that flaw, "abandoning one's own meaning" doesn't arise either. With neither flaw applicable, the sutra calls this a pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi precisely in the sense that it excludes the (never truly viable) taking of the donkey's rope.

On further reflection, however, this statement arguably isn't pariṣaṅkhyā in the strict classical sense at all — pariṣaṅkhyā's defining mark is excluding *other genuinely available* means to accomplish a task, but here no other means was ever truly possible. Once the Brahmana statement clearly prescribes the intended means without ambiguity, the question of grasping the unwanted donkey-rope never arises. This same point appears in the Tantravartika:

> ननु एवमप्राप्तिविधिरेवायं संजात इति न वक्तव्यम् । परिसंख्येति फलेनैवं अभिधानाद्दोषः । (तन्त्रवार्तिक)
>
> *nanv evam aprāpti-vidhir evāyaṃ saṃjāta iti na vaktavyam | pariṣaṅkhyeti phalenaivam abhidhānād doṣaḥ | (Tantravārtika)*
>
> "One might object: this then simply becomes an ordinary injunction (for something not otherwise attained), and the term 'pariṣaṅkhyā' should not apply. But calling it pariṣaṅkhyā on the strength of its resulting function, rather than its strict formal structure, involves no real flaw."

In sum, whether or not this statement technically counts as pariṣaṅkhyā, one point stands firmly established: there is no room whatsoever for the flaw the objector (pūrvapakṣin) alleges. The Brahmana statement conveys a genuinely new point not otherwise present in the mantra.

## Chapter 8. The Definition of Arthavāda

*Original title: "Arthavādalakṣaṇa"*
**Printed pages 394–411 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 394</div>

> सर्वथा तदर्थशास्त्रता नास्ति । यदि हि यदेवं मन्त्रवचनाश्चाप्युयात्रदेव प्रत्यक्षवचनेनोच्यते । तको वनमुत्सालभ्येमुहि ।
>
> *(A further technical clarification concluding the previous argument, on why a mantra and its explanatory Brahmana statement do not genuinely compete for authority; precise phrase-level construction is difficult to render exactly at this resolution.)*

Grammarians and rhetoricians, like the logicians (Naiyayikas), do not accept a real distinction between niyama-vidhi and pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi:

> नियमोऽप्यैक्या दर्शने परिसंख्यैव साक्षिकप्राप्तियुगपत्प्रिदोष्सावंकेरपीक्ष्यस्यविज्ञानात् । अक एव वैयाकरणानां मते परिसंख्यापि नियमश्चेत्युच्यते । (रसगंगाधर परिसंख्याप्रकरण)
>
> *(Arguing that niyama and pariṣaṅkhyā ultimately reduce to the same underlying logical operation — excluding a simultaneously available alternative — so grammarians treat pariṣaṅkhyā itself as a species of niyama.)*

What was termed pariṣaṅkhyā-vidhi in the previous sutra applies only to that specific case. The Taittiriya Brahmana contains the statement "uru prathasveti prathayati" (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-2-8-4) — the mantra recited while spreading the puroḍāśa cake. One might object that such Brahmana statements remain useless if the mantra already conveys this meaning. Jaimini answers with the next sutra.

### "Arthavādo vā" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-43)

> वाशब्दो न्यायार्थं वारयति । अस्वप्रत्यार्थवादकः । यज्ञपतिमेव तत्प्रथयतीति तेनार्थवादेन संबन्धाय ब्राह्मणे विधिः पठ्यते । ननु प्रथयतीत्येव प्रथनविधिः सिद्ध प्रथनमनुष्ठेयं यज्ञपतिमेवेत्यादिनार्थवादेन स्तोतव्यम् । तदेव तु प्रथनं कुतः प्राप्तमित्यस्याशंक्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *vā-śabdo nyāyārthaṃ vārayati | asvapratyarthavādakaḥ | yajñapatim eva tat prathayatīti tenārthavādena sambandhāya brāhmaṇe vidhiḥ paṭhyate | nanu prathayatīty eva prathana-vidhiḥ siddha prathanam anuṣṭheyaṃ yajñapatim eva ity ādinārthavādena stotavyam | tad eva tu prathanaṃ kutaḥ prāptam ity asyāśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "The word 'vā' (or) rules out [the claim of] uselessness. [The relevant Brahmana passage is] an arthavāda (eulogistic explanatory statement). The injunction is recited in the Brahmana specifically to connect with the arthavāda 'yajñapatim eva tat prathayati' ('it spreads out the yajamana himself'). One might ask: since 'prathayati' alone already establishes the injunction to spread, and the act of spreading is already prescribed, then praised through the arthavāda beginning 'yajñapatim eva' — from where, then, is the very act of spreading itself originally attained? Anticipating this doubt, [Jaimini] formulates the answer."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 395</div>

### "Mantrābhidhānāt" (Shabara-bhashya sentence)

> अध्वर्युः पुरोडाशमुद्दिश्य मन्त्रे प्रथस्वेत्येवमभिधत्ते । तस्मादभिधानादध्वर्युकर्तृकं प्रथनं प्राप्तम् । यथा लोके यः कुर्विति ब्रूते स कारयत्येव तथात्रापि यः प्रथस्वेति ब्रूते स प्रथयत्येव ।
>
> *adhvaryuḥ puroḍāśam uddiśya mantre prathasvety evam abhidhatte | tasmād abhidhānād adhvaryu-kartṛkaṃ prathanaṃ prāptam | yathā loke yaḥ kurv iti brūte sa kārayaty eva tathātrāpi yaḥ prathasveti brūte sa prathayaty eva |*
>
> "Referring to the puroḍāśa, the Adhvaryu states in the mantra: 'spread [it] out.' From this very statement, the act of spreading is established as the Adhvaryu's own task. Just as, in ordinary life, one who says 'do this' thereby causes it to be done, so too here, one who says 'spread' thereby performs the spreading."

Sutra's meaning: since a mantra's own hidden/deeper meaning can be directly examined, mantras are not without purpose. The word "vā" (or) here signals this. Connected with "uru prathasveti prathayati" ("spread wide," he spreads) is an arthavāda: "yajñapatim eva tat prathayati" ("it spreads out the yajamāna himself"). The Adhvaryu recites this mantra while spreading the puroḍāśa cake — and just as the cake expands, so too the yajamāna gains growth in wealth and grain, per this arthavāda's own intended meaning. The Brahmana statement exists precisely to connect this arthavāda to the mantra.

### On Arthavāda

According to the Mimamsakas, the Veda's overriding purpose is performing yajnas to obtain unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit — the Brahmanas prescribe the ritual acts, while the Samhita supplies the mantras recited while performing them. But Brahmana texts don't consist solely of injunctions (vidhi-vākya) — some portions fit neither prescription nor prohibition. Rather than dismiss these as meaningless (which would compromise the Veda's own defining coherence), Mimamsakas hold that such passages support the Veda's central purpose indirectly — setting aside their surface/literal sense to grasp a different, connective meaning tied to the injunctions nearby. Such statements are called **arthavāda**, generally either praising an enjoined act or condemning a prohibited one. Arthavāda divides into four kinds:

**(1) Praśaṃsā** — praise (of what is enjoined).
**(2) Nindā** — censure (of what is prohibited).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 396</div>

**(3) Parakṛti** — relating that some great person in the past performed the enjoined act.
**(4) Purākalpa** — narrating an ancient historical account.

These statements convey that fruit accrues from performing an enjoined act, helping a person decide whether to undertake it, by clarifying its good or bad aspects — supporting the injunctions in this way.

Corresponding to the three pramanas (perception, inference, revealed word), arthavādas are likewise classified into three kinds:

**(1) गुणवाद (Guṇavāda)** — where the stated meaning contradicts direct perception, it is called guṇavāda (a metaphorical statement). Example:

> आदित्यो यूपः ।
> *āditya yūpaḥ |*
> "The sun is the sacrificial post"

— taken literally this is meaningless; the intended sense is that the post, like the sun, shines with brilliance — brilliance being their shared quality (guṇa).

**(2) अनुवाद (Anuvāda)** — restating an already-known fact. Example:

> अग्निर्हिमस्य भेषजम् ।
> *agnir himasya bheṣajam |*
> "Fire is the remedy for cold"

— common knowledge to everyone.

**(3) भूतार्थवाद (Bhūtārthavāda)** — matters impossible to establish through perception or inference. Example:

> इन्द्रो वृत्राय वज्रम् उदयच्छत् ।
> *indro vṛtrāya vajram udayacchat |*
> "Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vritra"

On this third category, a genuine disagreement exists between Agama-authority proponents (like Badarayana and Sayana) and the Mimamsakas. Sayanacharya holds that rejecting the literal truth of bhūtārthavāda statements would render *all* texts — Veda, Purana, Itihasa alike — unauthoritative. The Mimamsakas instead hold that bhūtārthavādas must be read purely as praise or censure, not literal fact. But the Mimamsaka position doesn't fully hold up: consider that the "Ratrisatra" yajna's own mantras nowhere state the rite's fruit — that fruit appears only in the associated arthavāda. Even the Mimamsakas must therefore accept that arthavāda genuinely conveys authoritative new information in such cases.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 397</div>

The Mimamsakas' "fruit-authority" doctrine (that every Vedic statement is authoritative only insofar as it supports yajna-performance) meets genuine resistance in the Upanishads and Gita.

**In the Chandogya Upanishad:**

> तद्यथेह कर्मचितो लोकः क्षीयते एवमेवामुत्र पुण्यचितो लोकः क्षीयते (Chandogya Upanishad 8-1-6)
>
> *tad yathā iha karma-cito lokaḥ kṣīyate evam evāmutra puṇya-cito lokaḥ kṣīyate*
>
> "Just as here, a world built through action decays, so too, in the next world, a world built through merit likewise decays."

**And in the Bhagavad Gita:**

> यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः । वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः ॥ (Bhagavad Gita 2-47)
>
> *yām imāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadanty avipaścitaḥ | veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha nānyad astīti vādinaḥ ||*
>
> "That flowery speech which the unwise proclaim, O Partha, devoted to the letter of the Veda, declaring 'there is nothing else [beyond ritual fruit]'..."

That is: just as worldly fruit is transient, so too are the heavenly pleasures gained through yajna — both texts hold that those who claim yajna-fruit as the only, ultimate reward are "avipaścitaḥ," the unwise (i.e., the Mimamsakas).

**Returning to resolve the earlier fixed-word-order objection:** in statements like "uru prathasva," the word "prathayati" was construed as connected to an arthavāda — but then where does the actual injunction to spread the puroḍāśa come from? The sutra "mantrābhidhānāt" answers this: the Adhvaryu addresses the puroḍāśa directly — "O puroḍāśa, spread yourself out" — and by this address alone, it becomes clear that the Adhvaryu himself must perform the spreading. This mirrors ordinary experience: if one person tells another to do something, carrying it out becomes that person's own responsibility — no separate injunction is needed.

*(Note: "mantrābhidhānāt" is not itself one of Jaimini's own sutras — it is a Shabara-bhashya sentence Sayana has interspersed while working through Jaimini's sutras, itself carrying sutra-like concision, a technique commentators occasionally employ.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 398</div>

Even so, since word-order must not be altered (altering it produces nonsense), this sutra answers the objection that mantras yield only unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit.

### "Aviruddhaṃ param" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-44)

> परं द्वितीयसूत्रोक्तं स्यात्प्रत्ययं पूपस्वाकशंसाकसं न हि अयं साकल्क्रमनियमादृष्ट्यं निवारयामः ॥ किं तर्हि ॥ मन्त्रेण जायमानमर्थप्रत्यायनं दृष्टप्रयोजनत्वान्नोपेक्षितव्यमिति ब्रूमः । ननु प्रोक्षणीरासादय (Vajasaneyi Samhita 1-28) इति मन्त्रो बुद्धमेवार्थं शास्ति । तदयुक्तम् ।
>
> *paraṃ dvitīya-sūtroktaṃ syāt ... na hi ayaṃ sākala-krama-niyamādṛṣṭyaṃ nivārayāmaḥ || kiṃ tarhi || mantreṇa jāyamānam artha-pratyāyanaṃ dṛṣṭa-prayojanatvān nopekṣitavyam iti brūmaḥ | nanu prokṣaṇīr āsādaya iti mantro buddham evārthaṃ śāsti | tad ayuktam |*
>
> "What was said in the second sutra is not contradicted by us — we do not deny the unseen benefit of the fixed recitation-order. What then is our point? We say that the meaning-conveying function arising through the mantra, being a directly observable benefit, must not be overlooked. But doesn't the mantra 'prokṣaṇīr āsādaya' merely prescribe an already-known matter? That objection does not hold."

Sutra's meaning: what the second sutra states is not opposed to our view. The intent of "vākya-niyamāt" (the second sutra) was that altering the mantra's word-order yields an improper result — this we don't deny; reciting mantras does yield a fruit. But our own position is: reciting a mantra also produces knowledge of its meaning, which helps carry out yajnas properly — and this directly observable benefit (dṛṣṭa-prayojana) must not be neglected or denied. Mantras, in other words, possess both the unseen fruit the objector claims *and* a directly observable one.

**This answers the third original objection ("buddha-shāstrāt")** — recall the "agnīd agnīn vihara" example, objected to as useless repetition of already-known matter. Here, the Vajasaneyi Samhita's "prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" is cited: reciting this mantra, one places the mantra-sanctified water:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 399</div>

One must know this mantra for sprinkling the yajna's implements with sanctified water (prokṣaṇa) — like the fire-distribution act, already-known matter, restated. One might object this resembles wearing a shoe over another shoe.

### "Sampreṣakarmaṇo garhānupalambhe saṃskāratvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-45)

> संप्रेषकर्मणो गर्हा त्वदुक्त दोषो नोपलभ्यते । बुद्धस्यापि अर्थस्य मन्त्रेणानुसंस्करणान्नियमाद्दृष्टलक्षणस्य संस्कारस्य सद्भावात् । यच्चोक्तं चत्वारि शृंगेति मन्त्रेऽसंभवमेवार्थमभिधत्त इति तस्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *saṃpreṣa-karmaṇo garhā tvad-ukta doṣo nopalabhyate | buddhasyāpy arthasya mantreṇānusaṃskaraṇān niyamād dṛṣṭa-lakṣaṇasya saṃskārasya sadbhāvāt | yac coktaṃ catvāri śṛṅgeti mantre'saṃbhavam evārtham abhidhatta iti tasyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "The fault you alleged for acts commanded by 'presha' (directive) mantras is not actually found. Even for already-known matter, reciting the mantra confers an unseen refinement (saṃskāra) upon the act, following the established rule. As for the earlier objection that the 'four-horned' mantra states something self-evidently impossible, an answer to that follows too."

Sutra's meaning: since an injunctive statement conveys ritual refinement (saṃskāra), it escapes the objection. Mantras like "prokṣaṇīr āsādaya" and "agnīd agnīn vihara" are **presha-mantras** — directive mantras commanding that certain acts be performed. Their stated meaning may already be known, but reciting the mantra to re-announce the act carries a special unseen fruit precisely through following this rule.

Though one learns during study what acts must be performed at their proper time, this knowledge doesn't remain constantly active in memory — it stays latent. Some means is needed to bring it to conscious attention; one could try to recall it through deliberate focus alone, but the rule requiring the act be performed specifically accompanied by this mantra rules out other means of recollection. The claim that presha-mantras are meaningless therefore does not hold.

> यदि हि बोध एवावतिष्ठेत ततोऽनवकाशत्वं भवेत् । इह तु तदीयसंस्कारमात्रावस्थानात्तदभिव्यक्तिद्वारेणास्ति ज्ञानोत्पत्त्यवसर इति न मन्त्रानर्थक्यम् । (तन्त्रवार्तिके १-२-१५)
> *yadi hi bodha evāvatiṣṭheta tato'navakāśatvaṃ bhavet | iha tu tadīyasaṃskāramātrāvasthānāt tadabhivyaktidvāreṇāsti jñānotpattyavasara iti na mantrānarthakyam | (Tantravārttike 1-2-15)*
>
> "If the knowledge itself remained [present], there would be no room [for the mantra]; but here, since only its latent impression remains, there is occasion for knowledge to arise through its manifestation — so the mantras are not meaningless." (Tantravarttika 1-2-15)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 400</div>

That is: "if it remained actively in memory, recalling it via the mantra would be unnecessary. But here, the knowledge of which mantras accompany which acts remains in a hidden (sub-conscious) state, and the mantra helps bring it into conscious expression — so calling mantras meaningless is incorrect."

Whether "saṃskāra" is understood as conferring a special unseen fruit (imparting a new quality) or as awakening a hidden mental impression, either way mantras are established as meaningful and beneficial.

**This resolves the fourth objection ("avidyamāna-vacanāt")** — that mantras like "catvāri śṛṅgā" ("four horns") describe things never experienced in ordinary life.

### "Abhidhāner-arthavādaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-46)

> असतोऽर्थस्याभिधाने वाक्ये गौणस्यार्थस्योक्तिर्दृष्ट्या । तद्यथा । चत्वारो होतृचोद्गातृ-अध्वर्यु-ब्राह्मणाः अस्य कर्णः शृंगाणि । प्रातःसवनादयस्त्रयः पादाः । गार्हपत्यादीनि सप्त छन्दांसि हस्ताः । ऋग्वेदादिभिस्त्रेधा बन्धनम् । कामान्सृजतीति वृषभः । रोरवीति स्तोत्रं चादिशब्दात् पुनःपुनः करोति । महादेवः सोऽयं प्राणो यज्ञरूपो देवो मर्त्यानाविवेशेति मनुष्या द्विनात्वाधिकांशि । लोकेष्विव गौणप्रयोगा दृश्यन्ते । चित्रांगस्त्री हंसदन्तावली काश्यैवलकेशिनीत्येवं सद्यः स्त्रीयमानत्वात् । एवमोषधे त्रायस्वैनं, शृणोत ग्रावाण इत्याद्यचेतनसंबोधनानि स्तुतिपरत्वेन योजनीयानि । यस्मिन् सजन ओषधिः त्रायते तत्र वसनकर्ता त्रायत इति किमु वक्तव्यम् । तथा ग्रावाणोऽपि...
>
> *asato'rthasyābhidhāne vākye gauṇasyārthasyoktir dṛṣṭyā | tad yathā | catvāro hotṛ-cod-gātṛ-adhvaryu-brāhmaṇāḥ asya karṇaḥ śṛṅgāṇi | prātaḥ-savanādayas trayaḥ pādāḥ | gārhapatyādīni sapta chandāṃsi hastāḥ | ṛgvedādibhis tredhā bandhanam | kāmān sṛjatīti vṛṣabhaḥ | roravīti stotraṃ cādi-śabdāt punaḥ punaḥ karoti | mahādevaḥ so'yaṃ prāṇo yajña-rūpo devo martyān āviveśeti manuṣyā dvinātv-adhikāṃśi | lokeṣv iva gauṇa-prayogā dṛśyante | citrāṃgastrī haṃsa-dantāvalī kāśyaiva-lakeśinīty evaṃ sadyaḥ strīyamānatvāt | evam oṣadhe trāyasvainaṃ, śṛṇota grāvāṇa ity ādy-acetana-sambodhanāni stuti-paratvena yojanīyāni | yasmin sajana oṣadhiḥ trāyate tatra vasana-kartā trāyata iti kim u vaktavyam | tathā grāvāṇo'pi...*
>
> "When a sentence states something non-existent, we recognize a secondary/metaphorical meaning, based on precedent. As follows: the four priests — Hotr, Udgatr, Adhvaryu, and Brahma — are this sacrifice's 'horns.' The morning pressing and the other two pressings are its three 'feet.' The Garhapatya and other sacred fires, together with the seven meters, are its 'hands.' It is bound threefold through the Rigveda and the other Vedas. 'It fulfills desires' — hence it is called a 'bull' (vṛṣabha); it 'roars' — that is, the hymn of praise — and, from the word 'etc.,' does so repeatedly. This same great deity (Mahādeva), this life-breath in the form of the sacrifice, has entered mortals — hence humans having two principal [organs/heads] need not be taken too literally. Metaphorical usage is seen in ordinary life too — as when we call a woman 'swan-toothed' or 'Kashi's own curly-locked one,' describing her as embodying these qualities directly. Likewise, addresses to inanimate things — 'O herb, protect him,' 'hear, O stones' — should be understood as oriented toward praise. Where the herb itself is said to protect [the wearer], need it even be said that the one who prepares and ties it also protects him? Similarly, the stones too..."

This is the celebrated allegorical reading of the "four-horned bull" mantra: rather than describing a literal impossible creature, it poetically describes the yajna itself — its four priests as horns, its three daily pressings as feet, its seven meters as hands, and its threefold Vedic foundation as its binding — resolving the fourth objection entirely.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 401</div>

Sutra's meaning: in a context stating a non-existent thing, that sentence carries a special, secondary meaning. Where any sentence describes non-existent things, a different, secondary meaning must be construed — setting aside the apparent literal meaning. Non-Vedic literature uses such devices too: describing a river as "**चक्रवाकस्तनी**" (*cakravāka-stanī*, having chakravaka birds as her breasts), "**हंसदन्तावली**" (*haṃsa-dantāvalī*, rows of swans as her teeth), **काश** (*kāśa*) grass as her garment, **शैवल** (*śaivala*) moss as her hair — one naturally understands a meaning beyond the literal claim. The same principle applies to the objector's cited mantra "**चत्वारि शृङ्गा**" (*catvāri śṛṅgā*) — it need not describe a literal four-horned, three-footed creature at all:

**चत्वारि शृङ्गाणि** (*catvāri śṛṅgāṇi*, Four Horns) — the four principal priests carrying out the yajna's work: **होतृ** (*hotṛ*), **अध्वर्यु** (*adhvaryu*), **उद्गातृ** (*udgātṛ*), and **ब्रह्मा** (*brahmā*).

**त्रयः पादाः** (*trayaḥ pādāḥ*, Three Feet) — the morning pressing (**प्रातःसवन** *prātaḥ-savana*), midday pressing (**माध्यंदिनसवन** *mādhyandina-savana*), and evening pressing (**सायंसवन** *sāyaṃ-savana*).

**द्वे शीर्षे** (*dve śīrṣe*, Two Heads) — the **यजमान** (*yajamāna*, patron of the sacrifice) and his wife.

**सप्त हस्ताः** (*sapta hastāḥ*, Seven Hands) — the **गायत्री** (*gāyatrī*) and the other Vedic meters (seven in number).

**त्रिधा बद्धः** (*tridhā baddhaḥ*, Threefold Bound) — bound together through the Rigveda and the other Vedas.

**वृषभः** (*vṛṣabhaḥ*, Bull) — one who "rains down" (**वर्षति** *varṣati*) desired boons, like rainfall.

**रोरवीति** (*roravīti*, "Roars") — he who repeatedly recites the mantras in the form of **स्तोत्र** (*stotra*) and **शस्त्र** (*śastra*) (hymn and recitation).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 402</div>

**Great God (Maho Deva)** — this deity in the form of the yajna itself.
**Entered Mortals** — has taken abode within humans, meaning: the authority to perform this yajna belongs to human beings alone.

That is: this mantra's real purport is that the above elements are the principal constituents of every yajna-rite — not a description of some strange creature. Recognizing the secondary meaning elsewhere too shows the claim that mantras are meaningless to be groundless.

Similarly, sentences addressing inanimate objects serve to praise the associated act. "Oṣadhe trāyasvainam" belongs to the yajamāna's shaving-ritual: addressing the darbha grass, "protect the yajamāna," the point is — if the grass itself protects the yajamāna seated for shaving, how much more should the one performing the shaving protect him. Likewise "śṛṇota grāvāṇaḥ" ("listen, O stones"), recited before the dawn hymns (prātar-anuvāka): if even inanimate stones listen to these hymns, how much more attentively should the assembled learned Brahmins listen — this is the intended point.

**This resolves the objection raised in "Artha-vipratiṣedhāt"** — the alleged contradictions in "Aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam" (Aditi is both heaven and atmosphere) and "eka eva rudraḥ... sahasrāṇi sahasraśo ye rudrāḥ" (Rudra is one alone... yet thousands of Rudras exist).

### "Guṇāvadhi-vipratiṣedhāt syāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-47)

> यथा त्वमेव सिता त्वमेव मातेत्यत्र गौणप्रयोगादविरोधस्तद्वत् । एवमेकरुद्रदेवत्ये कर्मण्येको रुद्रः शतरुद्रदेवत्ये शतं रुद्रा इत्यविरोधः । यदुक्तं स्वाध्या...
>
> *yathā tvam eva sitā tvam eva mātety atra gauṇa-prayogād avirodhas tadvat | evam eka-rudra-devatye karmaṇy eko rudraḥ śata-rudra-devatye śataṃ rudrā ity avirodhaḥ | yad uktaṃ svādhyā...*
>
> "Just as in 'you alone are my father, you alone are my mother,' the metaphorical usage removes any contradiction, so too here: in a rite dedicated to a single Rudra-deity, there is one Rudra; in a rite dedicated to a hundred Rudra-deities, there are a hundred Rudras — no contradiction. As for what was earlier said regarding svādhyāya..."

That is: just as calling someone "both father and mother" carries an evident metaphorical sense without contradiction, the "one Rudra"/"thousand Rudras" statements simply describe different ritual contexts invoking different numbers of Rudra-deities — no genuine inconsistency remains.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 403</div>

> यमधीयानो माणवकः पूर्णिकायाः अवघातं न प्रकाशयितुमिच्छतीति तत्रोत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> *(Regarding the earlier objection that a student engaged in rote study has no wish to convey meaning connected to Purnika's grain-pounding, a further answer follows.)*

Sutra's meaning: since the metaphorical meaning indicated in the mantra is accepted, no room for genuine contradiction remains. In ordinary speech, "you alone are father, you alone are mother, you alone are everything" is a common expression — just as we don't take this literally, "aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam" doesn't literally mean Aditi *is* heaven and *is* the atmosphere; a secondary meaning must be grasped. Likewise, a rite addressed to a single Rudra invokes one Rudra-deity; one addressed to a hundred Rudras invokes a hundred — no contradiction arises.

**Turning to resolve the Purnika/rote-recitation objection** (from "svādhyāyavad-vacanāt"): the objector had argued that a mantra recited during rote study (illustrated by the woman "Purnika" pounding grain nearby) bears no genuine connection between mantra and act. The next sutra answers this.

### "Vidyā-vacanam-asaṃyogāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-48)

> वेदविद्याग्रहणकालेऽर्थस्य यदवचनं तदयज्ञसंयोगादुपपद्यते । न हि पूर्णिकाया अवघातो यज्ञसंयुक्तः । नापि माणवको यज्ञमनुतिष्ठति । अतो यज्ञानुपकारान्न तत्रार्थविवक्षा । यदप्युक्तं अम्यक्सा त इन्द्र । सृण्येव जर्भरी तुर्फरीतू इत्यादावर्थस्य ज्ञातुमशक्यत्वादनवबोध इति तत्रोत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
>
> वेद-विद्या-ग्रहण-कालेऽर्थस्य यद् अवचनं तद् अयज्ञ-संयोगाद् उपपद्यते । न हि पूर्णिकाया अवघातो यज्ञ-संयुक्तः । नापि माणवको यज्ञम् अनुतिष्ठति । अतो यज्ञानुपकारान् न तत्रार्थ-विवक्षा । ...
> *veda-vidyā-grahaṇa-kāle'rthasya yad avacanaṃ tad ayajña-saṃyogād upapadyate | na hi pūrṇikāyā avaghāto yajña-saṃyuktaḥ | nāpi māṇavako yajñam anutiṣṭhati | ato yajñānupakārān na tatrārtha-vivakṣā | ...*
>
> "That meaning goes unconveyed during Vedic study is explained by the absence of any connection to an actual yajna. Purnika's pounding is not connected to a yajna, nor is the student performing one — hence, since neither assists the yajna, there is no intention to convey meaning in that context. As for the claim that meaning cannot be determined in texts like 'amyaksā ta indra' or 'sṛṇyeva jarbharī turpharītū,' an answer to that follows next."

That is: the student's silence on meaning during rote study isn't evidence mantras lack meaning generally — it simply reflects that neither Purnika's work nor the student's recitation is actually part of a yajna. Where no yajna is being performed, there's no occasion to intend conveying meaning at all — this doesn't undermine the mantra's meaning when genuinely used in ritual context.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 404</div>

Sutra's meaning: during rote practice/study, since the mantra bears no connection to any yajna-related ritual act, no meaning is conveyed. The objection holds that meaning-grasping fails to occur during Vedic study — but when mantras are genuinely applied in yajnas, real efforts at conveying and understanding meaning take place; during mere memorization, no such occasion arises. In the pestle-mantra case, since Purnika's husking isn't part of a yajna, no rule ties the mantra's recitation to the pounding — and the student's own recitation likewise isn't yajna-related. Where no yajna-connection exists, the absence of meaning-knowledge is simply not a flaw at all.

**Resolving the "unintelligible mantras" objection ("avijñeyāt," Jai. Sū. 1-2-38):**

### "Śataḥ parama-vijñānam" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-49)

> विद्यमान एवार्थः प्रमादालस्यादिभिर्न विज्ञायते । तेषां निगमनिरुक्तव्याकरणवशेन धातुतोऽर्थः परिकल्पयितव्यः । तद्यथा । जर्भरी तुर्फरीतू इत्येवमादीन्यश्विनोरभिधानानि । तेषु हि द्विवचनान्तत्वं लक्ष्यते । आश्विनं चेदं सूक्तम् । अश्विनोः काममप्राः (ऋ. सं. १०-१०६-११) इति दर्शनात् । एतदेवाभिप्रेत्य निरुक्तकारो व्याचष्टे । जर्भरी भर्तारावित्यर्थस्तुर्फरीतू हन्तारावित्यर्थः (नि. १३-५) इति । एवममम्यक्सा त इत्यादावप्यूहनीयम् । यदप्युक्तं (ऋ. सं. ३-५३-१४) प्रमगन्दाद्यनित्यार्थसंयोगान्मन्त्रस्यानादित्वं न स्यादिति तत्रोत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> *vidyamāna evārthaḥ pramādālasyādibhir na vijñāyate | teṣāṃ nigamaniruktavyākaraṇavaśena dhātuto'rthaḥ parikalpayitavyaḥ | tad yathā | jarbharī turpharītū ity evamādīny aśvinor abhidhānāni | teṣu hi dvivacanāntatvaṃ lakṣyate | āśvinaṃ cedaṃ sūktam | aśvinoḥ kāmam aprāḥ (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-106-11) iti darśanāt | etad evābhipretya niruktakāro vyācaṣṭe | jarbharī bhartārāv ity arthas turpharītū hantārāv ity arthaḥ (Ni. 13-5) iti | evam amyak sā ta ityādāv apy ūhanīyam | yad apy uktaṃ (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-53-14) pramagandādyanityārthasaṃyogān mantrasyānāditvaṃ na syād iti tatrottaraṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
>
> "The meaning does exist, but goes unknown due to carelessness, laziness, or similar causes. In such cases, meaning must be constructed from the word's own verbal root, with the help of Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyakarana. For example: in the mantra containing 'jarbharī turpharītu,' words like 'jarbhari' are forms referring to the Ashvins — their dual number is discernible, and this sukta is itself an Ashvin-hymn."

That is: the meaning is genuinely present in such mantras, but goes unnoticed through carelessness or inattention — not because it's inherently absent. Careful etymological analysis via Nirukta and grammar, cross-checked against parallel passages, reveals that even the famously obscure "jarbhari turpharitu" refers to the twin Ashvin deities, confirmed by the dual grammatical forms and the hymn's overall Ashvin-context.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 405</div>

One can indeed determine the meaning of such texts. For difficult words like these, gathering other Vedic passages using similar constructions, with Nirukta and grammar's help, one determines the underlying verbal root and infers meaning accordingly. Working through the cited example: "jarbharī" and "turpharītū" are clearly dual-number words, occurring in verse 6 of Rigveda Mandala 10, Sukta 106 — a sukta dedicated to the Ashvins, confirmed by that same sukta's 11th verse, "aśvinoḥ kāmam aprāḥ" ("you fulfilled the Ashvins' desire"). Therefore "jarbharī" and "turpharītū" refer to the Ashvin deities. The Nirukta itself, holding this same view, glosses "jarbharī" as "those who nourish/give shelter" and "turpharītū" as "those who destroy [obstacles]." The same method of inference applies to "amyak sā ta" and similar texts.

**The ninth and final objection-sutra: "Anitya-saṃyogān mantrānarthakyaṃ."** The Veda mentions non-eternal things — Pramaganda, Babara, Prāvāhaṇi, and similar proper names of persons who lived and then perished. Either the claim that the Veda is beginningless (anādi) is false, the objector argues, or the Vedas have no meaning at all — mere recitation must be their sole purpose.

### "Uktvā anitya-saṃyogaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-50)

> प्रथमपादान्तिमाधिकरणे सोऽयमनित्यसंयोगदोष...
>
> *(Jaimini refers back to his own earlier treatment: this same objection regarding connection with non-eternal things was already raised and resolved in the final adhikarana of the Mimamsa-sutra's first pada — the answer given there applies equally here.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 406</div>

> उक्त्वा परिष्कृतः । तथा हि । तत्र पूर्वपक्षे वेदानां पौरुषेयत्वं वक्तुं काठकं कालापकमित्यादिपुरुषसंबन्धाभिधानं हेतूक्त्वा नित्यदर्शनाच्च (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-28) इति हेत्वन्तरं सूत्रितम् । कस्यायमर्थः । बबरः प्रावाहणिः अकामयत (Taittiriya Samhita 7-1-10-2) इत्यादि अनित्यानां बबरादीनामर्थानां दर्शनात्क पूर्वमसत्त्वाच्चौरुषेयो वेद इति तत्रोत्तरं सूत्रितम् । परं तु श्रुतिसामान्यात् (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-31) इति तस्यायमर्थः । यत्तु परं काठकादिसाम्यानं तत्त्ववचननिमित्तं । यत्तु परं बबराख्यनिमित्त दर्शनं तच्चापि सामान्यमात्रम् ।
>
> *(Jaimini's own summary, referring back to his earlier first-pada discussion: the objection there cited the human-derived names "Kathaka," "Kalapaka" (schools named after their teachers) and the appearance of transient proper names like "Babara" as evidence the Veda was composed by humans; the resolution held that such school-names simply reflect which sages transmitted a given recension, not authorship of the Veda's content itself, and that the "Babara" reference is a case of similar-sounding words rather than a genuinely non-eternal element within the Veda's own composition.)*

Sutra's meaning: the matter of non-eternal things occurring in the Veda has already been addressed. In the closing portion of the first pada of Jaimini's sutras, while establishing the Veda's non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva), this same flaw regarding non-eternal things was resolved — Sayanacharya now summarizes that earlier resolution here, beginning with "tathā hi" ("that is").

The objection there held that the Vedas, like Kalidasa's own works, were composed by human authors — supported by two points: first, the connection to named persons via titles like "Kathaka," "Kalapaka," and similar Vedic school-names:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 407</div>

...and the sutra "anitya-darśanāc ca" ("because non-eternal things are seen") further supports the Veda's supposed human origin — citing the mantra "babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata" and similar texts containing apparently non-eternal names, arguing these mantras couldn't predate the persons they name.

> परं तु श्रुतिसामान्यमात्रम् ।
>
> *paraṃ tu śruti-sāmānya-mātram |*
>
> "But this rests merely on a similarity of sounds."

This is Jaimini's answer: such words resemble ordinary words only in sound and letter-sequence, not in meaning. The siddhanta holds: "Kathaka," "Kalapaka," and similar terms denote different Vedic branches/schools; "Babara" and similar words merely resemble ordinary proper names in their letter-sequence — there was no actual person named "Babara." Rather, "babara" is the very sound wind makes while blowing — so "babaraḥ" here means "the wind that makes that sound," and "prāvāhaṇīḥ" means "one whose nature is to blow swiftly/forcefully." The same reasoning applies to words like "Pramaganda."

In this way, no flaw whatsoever remains regarding mantra-meaning — mantras genuinely exist to convey meaning, and each mantra should be applied precisely where its stated meaning holds genuine use.

**A further doubt arises:** the siddhanta-sutras have logically established that mantras reveal meaning and possess directly observable purpose — but one might object that no actual scriptural (śruti) statement supports this conclusion. Jaimini anticipates this and answers next.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 408</div>

### "Liṅgo'padeśas tad-arthavat" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-51)

> आग्नेय्याग्निध्रमुपतिष्ठेति श्रूयते । तस्यायमर्थः । अग्निदेवता यस्या ऋचः सेयमाग्नेयी । तयाग्निध्रस्थानमुपतिष्ठेति । अत्र ह्युपस्थानमुपदिशद्ब्राह्मणमग्ने नय (RV 1-189-1) इत्येवंरूपोपस्थाने मन्त्रप्रतीकं पठित्वा नोपस्थितिं किं तु आग्नेयीत्याख्येनोपदिशति ।
>
> *āgneyy āgnidhram upatiṣṭheti śrūyate | tasyāyam arthaḥ | agni-devatā yasyā ṛcaḥ seyam āgneyī | tayāgnidhra-sthānam upatiṣṭheti | atra hy upasthānam upadiśad brāhmaṇam agne naya ity evaṃ-rūpopasthāne mantra-pratīkaṃ paṭhitvā nopasthitiṃ kiṃ tu āgneyīty ākhyenopadiśati |*
>
> "It is heard: 'one should approach the Agnidh's platform with an Āgneyī [verse].' Its meaning: that Rik whose deity is Agni is called 'Āgneyī' — one should approach the Agnidh's platform with such a verse. Here, the Brahmana, in prescribing this approach, does not simply cite the opening words of the actual verse ('agne naya...') — instead, it prescribes it using the descriptive term 'Āgneyī.'"

Sutra's meaning: ritual terms are used precisely to indicate meaning. "Āgneyyāgnidhram upatiṣṭheta" is a Brahmana statement indicating the mantra to recite while approaching the Agnidh's platform for worship. "Āgneyyā" means "by the mantra whose presiding deity is Agni" — referring to the mantra beginning "agne naya." Rather than naming that mantra directly, the Brahmana uses the grammatically-derived (taddhita) term "āgneyī" ("Agni-related [verse]") — itself proof that the mantra is understood to carry genuine meaning, since only a meaning-bearing verse could be classified by its subject-deity this way. Since mantras thus demonstrably convey meaning, they must be recited at their proper application. Further proofs follow.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 409</div>

### "Ūhaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-52)

> प्रकृतानाम्नातस्य मन्त्रस्य विकृतौ समन्वेतार्थत्वाय तदुचितसदान्तरस्य प्रक्षेपेण पाठ ऊहः । शब्द्यथा । अन्वेनं माता मन्यतामनु पितानु भ्रातेति प्राकृते पशुविषये मन्त्रपाठः (Maitrayani Samhita 4-13-4) । तस्य च मन्त्रस्य विकृतौ पशुद्वये सत्यन्वेना माता मन्यताम् इत्युक्त्ये कर्तव्ये इहैकस्मिन्त्रे व्याख्यारूपं ब्राह्मणमेवमाम्नायते । न माता वर्धते न पितेति ।
>
> *prakṛtānām nātasya mantrasya vikṛtau samanvetārthatvāya tad-ucita-padāntarasya prakṣepeṇa pāṭha ūhaḥ | śabdyathā | anvenaṃ mātā manyatām anu pitānu bhrāteti prākṛte paśu-viṣaye mantra-pāṭhaḥ | tasya ca mantrasya vikṛtau paśu-dvaye saty anvenā mātā manyatām ity uktye kartavye ihaikasminttre vyākhyā-rūpaṃ brāhmaṇam evam āmnāyate | na mātā vardhate na piteti |*
>
> "Ūha (adaptation) means reciting a mantra, originally composed for one context, with an appropriately modified word substituted, so that it retains a fitting meaning when applied in a related but altered context. For example: 'anvenaṃ mātā manyatām anu pitānu bhrātā' ('may its mother, father, and brother approve of it') is the mantra-text prescribed for a single sacrificial animal. In the modified case of two animals, one might expect the dual form 'anvenā mātā manyatām' — yet the Brahmana's own explanatory gloss on this states: 'the mother is not increased, nor the father' [i.e., these terms remain singular regardless]."

Sutra's meaning: constructing suitable adapted words to fit a given context, when needed, is itself a proof that mantras carry meaning. The original mantra must sometimes be recited with slight modification across different contexts — changing certain words, or substituting others in their place — this practice is called **ūha** (adaptation), found here and there in ritual application. Consider the mantra recited while leading the sacrificial animal to the offering-place: "anvenaṃ mātā manyatām anu pitānu bhrātā" (may its mother, father, and brother approve of it):

<div class="pgmark">original p. 410</div>

its mother, father, and brother — may all these approve of this animal's sacrifice — this mantra is used as-is with a single animal. With two animals, it's modified to "**अन्येनौ माता...**" (*anyenau mātā...*); with many animals, to "**अन्येनान् माता...**" (*anyenān mātā...*) That is: the singular word becomes dual ("**एनौ**" *enau*, these two) or plural ("**एनान्**" *enān*, these), according to the animal-count. A Brahmana statement confirms this required adaptation, stating simply:

> न माता वर्धते न पिता ।
> *na mātā vardhate na pitā |*
> "The mother is not increased, nor the father."

Here, "vṛddhi" (increase) could mean either of two things: age-related growth (childhood through youth to old age), or grammatical number-change (the singular "mātā"/"pitā" becoming dual "mātarau"/"pitarau" or plural "mātaraḥ"/"pitaraḥ"). Age-related growth obviously cannot be denied — it's plainly observable. So the Brahmana's real point must be grammatical: the words "mātṛ" and "pitṛ" specifically should NOT change in number. Since this restriction applies only to those two words, it follows that the remaining word "enam" *must* instead take the appropriate dual or plural form depending on context.
