If mantras carried no meaning at all, why would this kind of careful word-adaptation even be necessary? This confirms that mantras do indeed convey genuine meaning.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 411</div>

### "Vidhi-śabdāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-53)

> मन्त्रव्याख्यानरूपो ब्राह्मणिकः शब्दो विधिशब्द इत्युच्यते । स चैवमाम्नायते । शतं हिमाः शतं वर्षाणि जीव्यासमेत्येवैतदाह (Shatapatha Brahmana 2-3-4-21) इति । तत्र शतं हिमा इत्येतद्व्याख्येयमन्त्रस्य प्रतीकम् । अवशिष्टं तु तस्य तात्पर्यव्याख्यानम् । मन्त्रस्याविवक्षितार्थत्वे तु किं नाम तात्पर्यं मन्त्रे व्याख्यायेत । तस्माद्विवक्षितार्था मन्त्राः प्रयोगकाले स्वार्थप्रकाशनायैवोच्चार्यन्त इत्याह ॥
>
> *mantra-vyākhyāna-rūpo brāhmaṇagataḥ śabdo vidhiśabda ity ucyate | sa caivam āmnāyate | śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsmety evaitad āha (Śa. Brā. 2-3-4-21) iti | tatra śataṃ himā ity etad vyākhyeya-mantrasya pratīkam | avaśiṣṭaṃ tu tasya tātparya-vyākhyānam | mantrasyāvivakṣitārthatve tu kiṃ nāma tātparyaṃ mantre vyākhyāyeta | tasmād vivakṣitārthā mantrāḥ prayoga-kāle svārtha-prakāśanāyaivoccārayitavyāḥ ||*
>
> "A Brahmana statement that takes the form of explaining a mantra is called a 'vidhi-śabda.' One such is recorded: 'śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam' ('may I live a hundred winters, a hundred years') — this is what is meant. Here, 'śataṃ himāḥ' is the pratīka (opening phrase) of the mantra being explained; the rest explains its purport. If the mantra carried no intended meaning at all, what purport could possibly be explained? This shows that mantras, carrying real intended meaning, are recited at their application specifically to reveal that meaning."

Sutra's meaning: vidhi-śabda words embedded in Brahmanas likewise support that mantras carry meaning. Brahmanas contain many mantra-explanatory statements (the earliest form of Vedic commentary) — such statements are called vidhi-śabda. In "śataṃ himāḥ śataṃ varṣāṇi jīvyāsam ity evaitad āha" (Shatapatha Brahmana 2-3-4-21), "śataṃ himāḥ" is the mantra-portion, and the rest explains its purport — that it means "may we live a hundred years." Had mantras no meaning, there would be no need to explain their purport at all. This too proves mantras carry genuine meaning.

### Summary Verse

> तत्र सङ्ग्रहश्लोकौ— मन्त्रा उरु प्रथस्वेति किमदृष्टैकहेतवः । यागेषूत पुरोडाशप्रथनादेश्च भासकाः ॥ ब्राह्मणेनापि तद्ध्यानान्मन्त्राः पुण्यैकहेतवः । न तद्ध्यानस्य दृष्टत्वाद्दृष्टं वरमदृष्टतः ॥ इति ॥ (जै. न्या. मा. १-२-४)
> *tatra saṅgrahaślokau — mantrā uru prathasveti kim adṛṣṭaika-hetavaḥ | yāgeṣūta puroḍāśa-prathanādeś ca bhāsakāḥ || brāhmaṇenāpi tad-dhyānān [?] mantrāḥ puṇyaika-hetavaḥ | na tad-dhyānasya dṛṣṭatvād dṛṣṭaṃ varam adṛṣṭataḥ || iti || (Jaimini-nyaya-mala 1-2-4)*
>

## Chapter 9. Examination of the Authority of the Brahmana-Portion (the Vidhi/Injunctive Mantras)

*Original title: "Brāhmaṇātmaka-mantrabhāgada prāmāṇyavicāravimarśeyu — vidhivākyapramāṇa samarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 412–419 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 412</div>

Here, the objector's (pūrvapakṣa) view is presented as a question, and the siddhanta as its answer.

**Question:** Do mantras like "uru prathasva" yield only an unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit, or do they clarify actual ritual procedures — such as spreading the puroḍāśa — in the yajnas where they occur?

**The objector's prima facie answer:** since Brahmana statements already explain the acts to be performed in yajnas, mantras must be said to yield only unseen merit (puṇya).

**Siddhanta:** mantras do not yield merit alone as their fruit — the meanings they express are clearly useful for performing yajna-related acts. A directly observable (dṛṣṭa) fruit is always the superior explanation; mantras therefore do convey meaning, contrary to the claim that mere recitation is their only purpose.

**A new question opens:** granting the mantra-portion's authority, does the Brahmana-portion itself carry the same authority?

> नन्वस्तु मन्त्रभागस्य प्रामाण्यम् । ब्राह्मणभागस्य तु न तद्युज्यते । तथा हि । द्विविधं ब्राह्मणम् । विधिरर्थवादश्चेति । तथा चापस्तम्बः । कर्मचोदना ब्राह्मणानि ब्राह्मणशेषोऽर्थवादः (आ. प. ३२-३३) इति । विधिरपि द्विविधः । अप्रवृत्तप्रवर्तनमज्ञातज्ञापनं चेति । आग्नावैष्णवं पुरोडाशं निर्वपन्ति दीक्षणीयम् (ऐ. ब्रा. १-१) इत्याद्याः कर्मकाण्डगतविधयोऽप्रवृत्तप्रवर्तकाः । आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् (ऐ. आ. २-४-१) इत्यादयो ब्रह्मकाण्डगता अज्ञातज्ञापकाः । तत्र कर्मकाण्डगतानां जर्तिलयवाग्वा वा जुहुयाद्गवीधुकयवाग्वा वा (तै. सं. ५-४-३-२) इत्यादिविधीनां नास्ति प्रामाण्यम् । प्रवृत्त्ययोग्यद्रव्यविधानेन सम्यगनुभवसाधनत्वाभावात् । अयोग्यत्वं च वाक्यशेषे समाम्नातम् । अनाहुतिर्वै जर्तिलाश्च गवीधु-…
> *nanv astu mantrabhāgasya prāmāṇyam | brāhmaṇabhāgasya tu na tad yujyate | tathā hi | dvividhaṃ brāhmaṇam | vidhir arthavādaś ceti | tathā cāpastambaḥ | karmacodanā brāhmaṇāni brāhmaṇaśeṣo'rthavādaḥ (Ā. Pa. 32-33) iti | vidhir api dvividhaḥ | apravṛttapravartanam ajñātajñāpanaṃ ceti | āgnāvaiṣṇavaṃ puroḍāśaṃ nirvapanti dīkṣaṇīyam (Ai. Brā. 1-1) ity ādyāḥ karmakāṇḍagata-vidhayo'pravṛttapravartakāḥ | ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt (Ai. Ā. 2-4-1) ity ādayo brahmakāṇḍagatā ajñātajñāpakāḥ | tatra karmakāṇḍagatānāṃ jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyād gavīdhukayavāgvā vā (Taittiriya Samhita 5-4-3-2) ity ādi-vidhīnāṃ nāsti prāmāṇyam | pravṛtty-ayogya-dravya-vidhānena samyag-anubhava-sādhanatvābhāvāt | ayogyatvaṃ ca vākyaśeṣe samāmnātam | anāhutir vai jartilāś ca gavīdhu-…*
>
> *(Establishing that Brahmana passages fall into two categories — vidhi (injunction) and arthavāda (explanatory eulogy) — and that vidhi itself divides further into "initiating an unperformed act" and "revealing something unknown." Certain ritual-procedure injunctions are then questioned as to whether they meet the standard of genuinely valid proof, given a following passage that appears to declare a related substance ritually unsuitable; the bhāṣya above was re-read from the better scan in the [?] pass.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 413</div>

> …श्चेति । तत्र ह्यारण्यतिलानामारण्यगोधूमानां चाहुतिद्रव्यत्वं निषिद्धम् । तस्माद्बाधितो जर्तिलादिविधिरप्रमाणम् । एवमैतरेयतैत्तिरीयादिब्राह्मणेषु तत्तन्नादृत्यं तत्तथा न कार्यमिति वाक्याभ्यां बहवो विधयो निषिद्धाः । अपि चैतरेयब्राह्मणेऽनुदितहोमं बहुधा निन्दित्वा तस्मादुदिते होतव्यमित्यसकृन्निगमितम् । तैत्तिरीयाश्च तथैवामनन्ति “यदनुदिते सूर्ये प्रातर्जुहुयात् । उभयमेवाग्नेयꣳ स्यात् । उदिते सूर्ये प्रातर्जुहोति” (तै. ब्रा. २-१-२-७) इति । पुनरपि त एवोदितहोमे दोषमामनन्ति— “यदुदिते सूर्ये प्रातर्जुहुयात् । यथातिथये प्रद्रुताय शून्यायावसथायाहार्यꣳ हरन्ति । तादृगेव तत् ।” (तै. ब्रा. २-१-२-१२) इति । तथैवातिरात्रे षोडशिनं गृह्णातीति विधिर्नातिरात्रे षोडशिनं गृह्णातीति निषेधेन बाध्यते । ज्योतिष्टोमादिष्वप्यनुष्ठानानन्तरमेव स्वर्गादिफलं नोपलभ्यते । न हि भोजनानन्तरं तृप्तेरनुपलम्भोऽस्ति । तस्मात्कर्मविधिषु प्रामाण्यं दुःसंपादम् ।
> *…ś ceti | tatra hy āraṇya-tilānām āraṇya-godhūmānāṃ cāhuti-dravyatvaṃ niṣiddham | tasmād bādhito jartilādi-vidhir apramāṇam | evam aitareya-taittirīyādi-brāhmaṇeṣu tat tan nādṛtyaṃ tat tathā na kāryam iti vākyābhyāṃ bahavo vidhayo niṣiddhāḥ | api caitareya-brāhmaṇe'nudita-homaṃ bahudhā ninditvā tasmād udite hotavyam ity asakṛn nigamitam | taittirīyāś ca tathaivāmananti “yad anudite sūrye prātar juhuyāt | ubhayam evāgneyaṃ syāt | udite sūrye prātar juhoti” (Tai. Brā. 2-1-2-7) iti | punar api ta evodita-home doṣam āmananti — “yad udite sūrye prātar juhuyāt | yathātithaye pradrutāya śūnyāyāvasathāyāhāryaṃ haranti | tādṛg eva tat |” (Tai. Brā. 2-1-2-12) iti | tathaivātirātre ṣoḍaśinaṃ gṛhṇātīti vidhir nātirātre ṣoḍaśinaṃ gṛhṇātīti niṣedhena bādhyate | jyotiṣṭomādiṣv apy anuṣṭhānānantaram eva svargādi-phalaṃ nopalabhyate | na hi bhojanānantaraṃ tṛpter anupalambho'sti | tasmāt karmavidhiṣu prāmāṇyaṃ duḥsaṃpādam |*
>
> *(Bhāṣya re-read in full from the better scan in the [?] pass: injunctions such as the jartila one are set aside by the prohibition of wild sesame and wild wheat; many injunctions are negated by "it should not be done so"; the Aitareya condemns the pre-sunrise homa while the Taittirīyas condemn the post-sunrise homa; "he takes the ṣoḍaśin at the atirātra" is set aside by "he does not take the ṣoḍaśin at the atirātra"; and the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma is not seen right after it, as satisfaction is seen right after a meal — so the authority of the ritual injunctions is hard to establish.)*

Let us accept the Samhita (mantra) portion as authoritative, as already established. But applying that same status to the **Brahmana portion** is not straightforward. Brahmanas fall into two kinds — **vidhi** (injunction) and **arthavāda** (explanatory statement). Apastamba's sutra defines them: "karma-codanā brāhmaṇāni" — statements that impel ritual acts are Brahmanas (vidhis); the remainder is arthavāda. Vidhi itself divides further into two kinds: those that initiate a not-otherwise-performed act, and those that reveal a previously unknown matter. Karma-kanda statements like "āgnāvaiṣṇavam..." and similar:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 414</div>

...belong to the first category. This statement's meaning: before beginning a yajna, the yajamana must undergo initiation (dīkṣā), called "dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi."

> सोमयागे प्रवृत्तस्य यजमानस्य संस्कारो दीक्षणम् । तस्मै च संस्कारस्य हेतुः कर्मविशेषो दीक्षणीयाच्च्यवाच्यः ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Ai. Brā. 1-1-1)
>
> *somayāge pravṛttasya yajamānasya saṃskāro dīkṣaṇam | tasmai ca saṃskārasya hetuḥ karma-viśeṣo dīkṣaṇīyāc cyavācyaḥ ||*
>
> "For the yajamāna undertaking a Soma-yaga, initiation (dīkṣaṇa) is the necessary consecration; the specific ritual act causing that consecration is termed 'dīkṣaṇīyā.'"

The yajamāna undertaking a Soma-yaga must undergo certain consecrations, including bodily purification — this purifying rite is called "dīkṣaṇīyā(-iṣṭi)," described in the Taittiriya Samhita's sixth kanda, first chapter, first anuvaka. In this iṣṭi, a puroḍāśa cake is offered to Agni and Vishnu together ("āgnāvaiṣṇava"). Since no one would undertake such an act without being told to, this statement counts as **apravṛtta-pravartaka** vidhi (initiating what wouldn't otherwise occur).

The second category of vidhi reveals previously unknown matters. "Ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt" ("in the beginning, this was the Self alone") and similar statements on the relationship between the individual soul and Brahman belong to the **brahma-kāṇḍa** — the Aranyakas and Upanishads. Since such truths cannot otherwise be known, this category is called **ajñāta-jñāpaka** vidhi (revealing the unknown). Vidhi thus divides into these two kinds.

But within the karma-kāṇḍa, statements like "jartilayavāgvā..." (concerning forest-grown sesame and wheat as valid oblation materials) lack genuine authority — since the same scriptural tradition elsewhere states that forest-grown sesame and wheat are *not* suitable oblation materials. A statement permitting the use of unsuitable substances cannot itself be considered authoritative.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 415</div>

Similarly, in the Aitareya, Taittiriya, and other Brahmanas, many matters are prohibited using phrases like "this should not be regarded" or "this should not be done that way." Consider two examples: the Aitareya Brahmana repeatedly condemns performing homa before sunrise as useless:

> "tasmād udite hotavyam" — "therefore, homa should be performed only after sunrise" — stated again and again.

The Taittiriya Brahmana states similarly through "yad anudite... juhoti" and related passages — if homa is performed before sunrise, the offering goes entirely to Agni rather than reaching Surya; therefore the morning-homa (prātar-homa) must occur only after sunrise. Yet the same tradition also criticizes performing it *after* sunrise:

> यदुदिते सूर्ये प्रातर्जुहुयात् । यथातिथये प्रयुतायै शून्यायावसथायागच्छेत् । आद्यैव स्यात् । (Taittiriya Brahmana 2-1-27)
>
> *yad udite sūrye prātar juhuyāt | yathātithaye pradutāyai śūnyāyāvasathāyāgacchet | ādyaiva syāt |*
>
> "If one performs the morning homa after the sun has already risen — it is like a guest arriving at an empty house after the food meant for him has already been sent away; it would have been better offered promptly."

Thus, contradictory statements exist on this exact same point.

**The Taittiriya Brahmana offers a mythological account explaining this:** long ago, Prajapati (Brahma), preparing to offer havis to Agni, was approached by Surya, who insisted the offering be made to him instead. Agni and Surya then debated and reached an agreement: daytime homa belongs to Surya, nighttime homa belongs to Agni — a reasonable arrangement, since Surya's influence predominates by day and Agni's by night. Therefore, homa performed before sunrise (still counted as "night") belongs to Agni, while homa from sunrise to sunset belongs to Surya. Daytime homa thus belongs to Surya, nighttime homa to Agni.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 416</div>

A homa performed contrary to this arrangement, the argument holds, fails to reach its intended deity and becomes useless. Similarly, the Atiratra yajna's rule requiring the Shodashi-stotra and Shastra is directly contradicted by another passage prohibiting their use in that same rite. And while the Jyotishtoma yajna is said to secure heaven (with similar specific fruits attributed to other yajnas), none of these outcomes can be verified through direct experience — unlike "eating brings satisfaction," which is confirmed by observation. Since karma-kāṇḍa vidhi statements' promised fruits cannot be similarly verified, the objection concludes they carry no authority whatsoever.

**Before proceeding, a clear understanding of yajnas' actual structure is needed** — their main ritual components, subdivisions of injunction, method of performance, and technical vocabulary — to properly follow the Mimamsa-sutras' argument. We therefore briefly explain the classification of yajnas here.

**Yajnas are of two kinds: सोमयज्ञ (Soma-yajña) and हविर्यज्ञ (Havir-yajña)** — Soma-juice as the offering-substance defines the former; ordinary havis (oblation material) the latter. Soma-yagas divide into three kinds:

**एकाह (Ekāha)** — completed within a single day.
**अहीन (Ahīna)** — completed within two to twelve days.
**सत्र (Sattra)** — continuing beyond twelve days.

Among Ekāhas, the most important is the **ज्योतिष्टोम (Jyotiṣṭoma)**, itself of seven kinds (the "seven संस्था *saṃsthā*"):

1. अग्निष्टोम (Agniṣṭoma) 2. अत्यग्निष्टोम (Atyagniṣṭoma) 3. उक्थ्य (Ukthya) 4. षोडशी (Ṣoḍaśī) 5. वाजपेय (Vājapeya) 6. अतिरात्र (Atirātra) 7. आप्तोर्याम (Āptoryāma)

Of these, **Agnishtoma is the primary form**, the remaining six being its variants — hence Agnishtoma is called the "prakṛti" (base form) and the other six the "vikṛti" (modified forms). In the Agnishtoma, the udgatr and his assistants together sing 12 Stotras (Sama-chants), and after each Stotra-recitation, the accompanying priests — Maitravaruna, Brahmanacchamsi, Achchavaka, and others:

<div class="pgmark">original p. 417</div>

...recite the corresponding Shastra-mantras for each Shastra in turn. Below are the Stotras performed across the three pressing-sessions (savana) — morning, midday, and third/evening — along with their accompanying Shastra-mantras:

**Prātaḥ-savana (Morning Pressing)**

| # | Stotra-gāna (Chant) | # | Shastra-mantra |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra | 1 | Ājya-śastra |
| 2 | Ājya-stotras | 2 | Prayuga-śastra |
| 3 | " | 3 | Ājya-śastra |
| 4 | " | 4 | " |
| 5 | " | 5 | " |

**Mādhyandina-savana (Midday Pressing)**

| 6 | Mādhyandina-pavamāna-stotra | 6 | Marutvatīya-śastra |
| 7 | Pṛṣṭha-stotra | 7 | Niṣkevalya-śastra |
| 8 | " | 8 | " |
| 9 | " | 9 | " |
| 10 | " | 10 | " |

**Tṛtīya-savana (Third/Evening Pressing)**

| 11 | Ārbhava-pavamāna-stotra | 11 | Vaiśvadeva-śastra |
| 12 | Agniṣṭoma-sāman | 12 | Agni-māruta-śastra |

The yajna takes its name "**अग्निष्टोम**" (*Agniṣṭoma*) from the final (12th) Stotra listed here, the "Agnishtoma-sāman."

- In the **उक्थ्य** (*Ukthya*) samstha, beyond these 12, three additional Ukthya-stotras and three Ukthya-shastras are added.
- In the **षोडशी** (*Ṣoḍaśī*), one further Stotra-Shastra is added to the 15 above, making 16 total.
- In the **अतिरात्र** (*Atirātra*), twelve more Stotra-Shastras are added.

It is clear that each successive samstha builds upon the Stotra-Shastras of the one before it. But in the Atiratra, one Stotra from the preceding Shodashi samstha...

—is contradicted by the vidhi—

> नातिरात्रे षोडशिनं गृह्णाति ।
> *nātirātre ṣoḍaśinaṃ gṛhṇāti |*
> "In the Atiratra, one does not take up the Shodashin [cup]."
>
> Moreover, heaven and the like are said to be the reward of the jyotishtoma and other sacrifices. But nobody gets heaven immediately after performing a sacrifice, whereas the satisfaction after taking food is immediate.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 418</div>

Whether to include or omit a given Shastra remains disputed — the Sankhyayana-shrauta, Ashvalayana-shrauta, and Kaushitaki-brahmana all include the Shodashi, while the Aitareya Brahmana omits it entirely. In this yajna (Atiratra), 12 Stotra-Shastras are sung through the night, and at sunrise a Sandhi-stotra is recited; since the rites go on all night, the yajna is perhaps called "Atiratra." According to the other Brahmanas, in the Atiratra the 15+1 Stotra-Shastras of the Shodashi together with these 12 make 28 Stotra-Shastras in all; but according to the Aitareya, leaving out the Shodashi, the 15 Stotra-Shastras, the 12 Stotras of the Atiratra and the 3 Sandhi-stotras (the Sandhi-stotra being counted as three) make 30 Stotra-Shastras. Thus there are differences even about one and the same yajna. Atyagnishtoma, Vajapeya, and Aptoryama see comparatively less common use.

**A further, genuinely significant contradiction arises among the "revealing-the-unknown" (ajñāta-jñāpaka) vidhis of the brahma-kāṇḍa:**

> अज्ञातज्ञापकेषु ब्रह्मविधिष्ठ्वपि परस्परविरोधान्नास्ति प्रामाण्यम् । आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् (Aitareya Aranyaka 2-4-1) इत्यैतरेयेण आमनन्ति । असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत् (Taittiriya Aranyaka 8-7) इति तैत्तिरीयकाः । सोऽयं विरोधः । तस्माद्येव विधिभागः सर्वोऽप्यप्रमाणमिति प्राप्ते ब्रूमः ॥
>
> *ajñāta-jñāpakeṣu brahma-vidhiṣv api paraspara-virodhān nāsti prāmāṇyam | ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt ity aitareyeṇa āmnanti | asad vā idam agra āsīt iti taittirīyakāḥ | so'yaṃ virodhaḥ | tasmād eva vidhi-bhāgaḥ sarvo'py apramāṇam iti prāpte brūmaḥ ||*
>
> "Even among the brahma-kāṇḍa's 'revealing the unknown' vidhis, no authority exists, due to mutual contradiction. The Aitareyins state: 'ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt' (in the beginning, this was the Self alone). The Taittiriyas state: 'asad vā idam agra āsīt' (in the beginning, this was non-being alone). This is a direct contradiction. Given this, the entire vidhi-portion is claimed to be without authority — to which we now respond—"

Just as karma-kāṇḍa contains contradictions, the brahma-kāṇḍa does too — hence its statements are likewise claimed as unauthoritative. The Aitareya Aranyaka (Aitareya Upanishad 1-1) states that at the world's beginning, the Self (ātman) alone existed; the Taittiriya Aranyaka states instead that at the beginning, only "asat" (non-being/void) existed — a direct contradiction between these two Upanishadic statements.

**Given that the entire vidhi-portion — both karma-kāṇḍa and brahma-kāṇḍa — stands accused of lacking authority, a resolution now follows, establishing the vidhi-portion's genuine authority.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 419</div>

> अस्त्वेवं जर्तिलादिविधेरप्रामाण्यं तदर्थस्याननुष्ठेयत्वात् । अनुष्ठेयस्त्वर्थ उपरितने— “अजक्षीरेण जुहोति” इति (तै. सं. ५-४-३-२) वाक्ये विधीयते । तत्प्रशंसार्थमत्र जर्तिलादिकमनूद्य निन्द्यते । यथा गवामश्वानां च प्रशंसार्थम्— “अपशवो वा अन्ये गोअश्वेभ्यः” (तै. ब्रा. ३-९-१०-२) इति वाक्येनार्थवादरूपेणाजादीनां पशुत्वं निन्द्यते तद्वत् । एवं तर्ह्यजादेर्यथा वस्तुतः पशुत्वमस्ति तथा जर्तिलादिविधिरत्र निन्द्यमानोऽपि क्वचिच्छाखान्तरे भवेदिति चेत् भवतु नाम । प्रामाण्यमपि तच्छाखाध्यायिनं प्रति भविष्यति । यथा गृहस्थाश्रमे निषिद्धमपि परान्नभोजनमाश्रमान्तरेषु प्रामाणिकं तद्वत् । अनेन न्यायेन सर्वत्र परस्परविरुद्धौ विधिनिषेधौ पुरुषभेदेन व्यवस्थापनीयौ । यथा मन्त्रेषु पाठभेदः शाखाभेदेन व्यवस्थितस्तद्वत् । तैत्तिरीया वायव स्थोपायव स्थ (तै. सं. १-१-१) इति मन्त्रमामनन्ति । वाजसनेयिनस्तूपायव स्थेत्येतं भागं नामनन्ति (वा. सं. १-१) प्रत्युत शतपथब्राह्मणे (१-७-१-३) स भागोऽनूद्य निराकृतः । तथा सूक्तवाकमन्त्रे शाखान्तरपाठं निराकृत्य पाठान्तरं तैत्तिरीया आमनन्ति । यद्ब्रूयात्सूपावसाना च स्वध्यवसाना चेति प्रमायुको यजमानः स्यात् (तै. सं. २-६-९-६) इति निराकरणम् । सूपचरणा च स्वधिचरणा चेत्येव ब्रूयादिति (तै. सं. २-६-९-६) पाठान्तरोपदेशः । तत्रानुष्ठातृपुरुषभेदेन व्यवस्था । तद्वद्विधिषु द्रष्टव्यम् । षोडशिग्रहणादिदूषणं त्वश्रुतमीमांसावृत्तान्तस्य तवैव शोभते । पूर्वमीमांसायां दशमाध्यायस्याष्टमपादे षोडशिनो ग्रहणाग्रहणविकल्पो निर्णीतः । (जै. सू. १०-८-६) द्वितीयस्याध्यायस्य प्रथमपादे कालान्तरभावि-…
>
> *astv evaṃ jartilādi-vidher aprāmāṇyaṃ tad-arthasyānanuṣṭheyatvāt | anuṣṭheyas tv artha uparitane — “ajakṣīreṇa juhoti” iti (Tai. Saṃ. 5-4-3-2) vākye vidhīyate | tat-praśaṃsārtham atra jartilādikam anūdya nindyate | yathā gavām aśvānāṃ ca praśaṃsārtham — “apaśavo vā anye go-aśvebhyaḥ” (Tai. Brā. 3-9-10-2) iti vākyenārthavāda-rūpeṇājādīnāṃ paśutvaṃ nindyate tadvat | evaṃ tarhy ajāder yathā vastutaḥ paśutvam asti tathā jartilādi-vidhir atra nindyamāno'pi kvacic chākhāntare bhaved iti cet bhavatu nāma | prāmāṇyam api tac-chākhādhyāyinaṃ prati bhaviṣyati | yathā gṛhasthāśrame niṣiddham api parānna-bhojanam āśramāntareṣu prāmāṇikaṃ tadvat | anena nyāyena sarvatra paraspara-viruddhau vidhi-niṣedhau puruṣa-bhedena vyavasthāpanīyau | yathā mantreṣu pāṭha-bhedaḥ śākhā-bhedena vyavasthitas tadvat | taittirīyā vāyava sthopāyava stha (Tai. Saṃ. 1-1-1) iti mantram āmananti | vājasaneyinas tūpāyava sthety etaṃ bhāgaṃ nāmananti (Vā. Saṃ. 1-1) pratyuta śatapatha-brāhmaṇe (1-7-1-3) sa bhāgo'nūdya nirākṛtaḥ | tathā sūktavāka-mantre śākhāntara-pāṭhaṃ nirākṛtya pāṭhāntaraṃ taittirīyā āmananti | yad brūyāt sūpāvasānā ca svadhyavasānā ceti pramāyuko yajamānaḥ syāt (Tai. Saṃ. 2-6-9-6) iti nirākaraṇam | sūpacaraṇā ca svadhicaraṇā cety eva brūyād iti (Tai. Saṃ. 2-6-9-6) pāṭhāntaropadeśaḥ | tatrānuṣṭhātṛ-puruṣa-bhedena vyavasthā | tadvad vidhiṣu draṣṭavyam | ṣoḍaśi-grahaṇādi-dūṣaṇaṃ tv aśruta-mīmāṃsā-vṛttāntasya tavaiva śobhate | pūrvamīmāṃsāyāṃ daśamādhyāyasyāṣṭamapāde ṣoḍaśino grahaṇāgrahaṇa-vikalpo nirṇītaḥ | (Jai. Sū. 10-8-6) dvitīyasyādhyāyasya prathamapāde kālāntarabhāvi-…*
>
> "We grant that the vidhi regarding forest-grown sesame ('jartila') and similar substances lacks authority, since its stated content is not actually meant to be performed. The act that genuinely IS meant to be performed is prescribed in the following clause: 'ajakṣīreṇa juhoti' ('one offers with ajakṣīra'). The mention of jartila and similar substances there merely restates them in order to condemn them — just as, in praising cows and horses, the statement 'other animals besides cow and horse are non-animals [in ritual value]' (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-9-10-2) uses an arthavāda-style condemnation of goats and similar animals' status as sacrificial animals, without literally denying they are animals."

## Chapter 10. Examination of the Authority of the Arthavāda Portion

*Original title: "Arthavādabhāgada prāmāṇyavicāradalli Mīmāṃsāsūtragaḷa vimarśanapūrvaka pūrvapakṣasiddhāntagaḷa samarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 420–464 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 420</div>

> फलसिद्ध्यर्थमपूर्वं निर्णीतम् (Purva Mimamsa 2-1-5) इति पूर्वमीमांसायां प्रथमाध्यायस्य चतुर्थपादे कारणत्वेन चाकाशादिषु यथा व्यवदिष्टोक्तेः (Vedanta Sutra 1-4-14) इत्येष्टसूत्रे जगत्कारणे परमात्मनि श्रुतेर्विप्रतिपत्तिर्निराकृता । द्वितीयस्याध्यायस्य प्रथमपादारम्भाधिकरणे कैत्स्न्यपदेशान्नेति चेन्न धर्मान्तरेण वाक्यशेषात् (Vedanta Sutra 2-1-17) इति सूत्रे तैत्तिरीयवाक्यगतस्यासच्छब्दस्य न शून्यपरत्वं किंत्वव्याकृत-स्थावस्थेति निर्णीतम् । तथा जैमिनिस्तोऽभिनवसूत्रे विधिश्च वाक्यं धर्मे प्रमाणमिति प्रतिज्ञायोक्ष्टिकसूत्रे तत्प्रामाण्यं समर्थयामास (Purva Mimamsa 1-1-2-5) व्यासोऽपि शास्त्रयोनित्वसूत्रे (Vedanta Sutra 1-1-3) वेदान् शास्त्रस्य प्रामाण्यं प्रतिज्ञाय, तत्तु समन्वयात् (Vedanta Sutra 1-1-4) इत्यादिसूत्रैः समर्थयामास । तस्मादमीमांसकस्य कव पूर्वोक्तस्कान्यो दुष्परिहारः । अको विधिभागस्य प्रामाण्यं सुस्थितम् ॥
>
> अर्थवादभागस्य प्रामाण्यं महता प्रयत्नेन जैमिनिः समर्थयामास तत्सूत्राणि व्याख्यास्यन्ते । (जै. सू. १-२-१ — १८) तत्र पूर्वपक्षं सूत्रयति ॥
> *arthavādabhāgasya prāmāṇyaṃ mahatā prayatnena jaiminiḥ samarthayāmāsa tatsūtrāṇi vyākhyāsyante | (Jai. Sū. 1-2-1 — 18) tatra pūrvapakṣaṃ sūtrayati ||*
>
> "Jaimini established with great effort the authority of the arthavāda portion; his sutras (Jai. Sū. 1-2-1 to 18) will be explained. There he first states the objection."
>
> *(A capstone argument citing the Vedanta-sutra and Purva-Mimamsa-sutra by name: showing that the apparent contradiction over the world's cause is resolved because "asat" (non-being) in the Taittiriya passage doesn't mean literal nothingness but rather the unmanifest/undifferentiated state — consistent with the Self being the world's true cause; and that both Jaimini and Vyasa establish the Veda's authority through their respective sutra-systems. The overall conclusion: the entire vidhi-portion's authority stands firmly established.)*

Sūtra's argument now resolves the objection fully: the statements "jartilayavāgvā vā juhuyāt gavīdhukayavāgvā vā" and "anāhutir vai jartilāś ca gavīdhukāś ca" (cited as contradictory) genuinely do lack authority — but without any actual flaw, since these vidhi-statements were never meant to be followed in the first place. The truly prescribed oblation-substance — goat's milk — appears shortly after, in "ajakṣīreṇa juhoti." Goat's milk is the excellent oblation-substance; jartila and gavidhuka were mentioned first, and then declared unsuitable, precisely to praise goat's milk by contrast — that is, jartila and similar substances...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 421</div>

The vidhi-statements should be understood as arthavāda. Many such statements exist. The Taittiriya Brahmana states:

> अपशवो वा अन्ये गोऽश्वेभ्यः ।
> *apaśavo vā anye go'śvebhyaḥ |*
> "Apart from cows and horses, there are no [true] beasts."

This doesn't literally deny goats' status as animals — its real point is that cows and horses are superior in this context. There's a maxim:

> न हि निन्दा निन्द्यं निन्दितुं प्रवर्तते, अपि तु विधेयं स्तोतुम् ।
> *na hi nindā nindyaṃ ninditum pravartate, api tu vidheyaṃ stotum |*
> "Censure is not truly meant to condemn what's censured, but rather to praise what's prescribed."

Statements of censure aim to elevate what's prescribed, not genuinely denigrate what's censured. The same logic applies to jartila: its real point is praising goat's milk as the superior oblation-substance. If goats count as valid "beasts" in some other Vedic school, jartila might likewise be a valid oblation-substance there too — but this would apply only to followers of that particular school.

**A household-duty example illustrates this same principle:**

> परपाकरुचिर्न स्यात् ।
> *parapākarucirna syāt |* (Yajnavalkya Smriti 1-112)

— prohibits eating others' food for a householder;

> भिक्षार्थी ग्राममाश्रयेत् ।
> *bhikṣārthī grāmam āśrayet |*

— requires a sannyasi to beg for alms in the village (food from others being his only means);

> ब्रह्मचर्ये स्थितो नैकमन्नमद्यादनापदि ।
> *brahmacarye sthito naikam annam adyād anāpadi |*

— requires a Brahmachari student to eat from *many* households rather than just one, except in genuine hardship. What's prohibited in one life-stage (āśrama) is thus prescribed in another.

Following this same reasoning, mutually contradictory injunctions and prohibitions should be applied according to the specific person following them. Even mantras show this pattern across different schools (śākhā) — a rule stated in one context becomes prohibited in another. The Taittiriya Samhita contains the mantra:

> वायवस्थोपायवस्था देवो वः ।
> *nāyavastho-pāyavasthā devo vaḥ |*

The same mantra appears in the Vajasaneyi Samhita too — but there, only "**न आयवस्था देवो वः**" (*nāyavasthā devo vaḥ*) appears, omitting "upāyavasthā" entirely. The Vajasaneyi Samhita's own Brahmana...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 422</div>

The Shatapatha Brahmana debates the "nāyavastho-pāyavastha" reading and then rejects it. Likewise the Taittiriyas, in the sūktavāka mantra, reject one reading and teach instead the alternative: "sūpacaraṇā ca svadhicaraṇā cety eva brūyāt." Whichever reading is stated belongs to followers of that specific school (śākhā) — another school prescribes a different reading. In all such cases, the correct reading is determined by who recites or performs it. The same principle applies to vidhi-statements generally: whether a statement functions as injunction or prohibition must be judged relative to the specific person performing the act.

**Turning to resolve the Ātman/Asat contradiction:** "ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt" means the Self alone existed before creation; "asad vā idam agra āsīt" means only the unmanifest form called "asat" existed — these two Shruti statements appear directly contradictory. The answer is given in the Brahma-sutra, first adhyaya, fourth pada, fourteenth sutra:

> "कारणत्वेन चाकाशादिषु यथा व्यपदिष्टोक्तेः"
> "kāraṇatvena cākāśādiṣu yathā vyapadiṣṭokteḥ" (Vedanta Sutra 1-4-14)
>
> *(As with the sky and other elements, designated according to their causal role — the "asat" reference likewise describes Brahman's own unmanifest, pre-creative state as cause, not literal non-existence.)*

Badarayana, and Jaimini following him, hold that all the Upanishads together establish one and the same underlying doctrine: that Brahman alone is eternal — a conclusion drawn from the Upanishads as a whole.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 423</div>

...the subject already established; the apparent contradictions we find are only superficial, not genuinely opposed in real intent — on this foundation, Badarayana and Jaimini composed their respective works.

Regarding creation, contexts do differ over which entity was created first, and one place calls the cause of creation "sat" (being), another "asat" (non-being) — apparently opposed views. The Vedanta-sutra answers this:

Though schools differ over the *sequence* and specific entities of creation, no genuine difference exists regarding **Brahman itself** as the ultimate cause — the same Brahman is called the cause of the sky in one place and other elements elsewhere (Vedanta Sutra 1-4-14). Sequence-related statements are not decisive on their own; not every created thing is even named in them. The Taittiriya Upanishad explains this matter fully, establishing that the creator is one alone.

**On the specific meaning of "asat":** the Brahma-sutra's third adhyaya, first pada, addresses the Taittiriya Upanishad's own "asad vā idam agra āsīt":

> "असद्-व्यपदेशान् नेति चेन् न धर्मान्तरेण वाक्य-शेषात्"
> "asad-vyapadeśān neti cen na dharmāntareṇa vākya-śeṣāt" (Vedanta Sutra 2-1-17)
>
> "If it be objected that, because it is called 'non-existent' [Brahman cannot be its cause] — we say no, since the remainder of the passage indicates a different attribute [i.e., an unmanifest state, not literal non-existence]."

Using the word "asat" does not mean nothing at all existed at the beginning. Here, "asat" doesn't mean "void" — it means "not-sat," that is, not yet in a clearly manifest form, existing instead in an unmanifest state. This meaning is confirmed by the statements that follow in the same passage. Therefore, "sat" and "asat" carry no real, fundamental difference: one indicates the manifest state, the other the unmanifest state preceding manifestation — "asat" simply marks this distinct, pre-manifest condition, not literal nothingness.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 424</div>

That is: since the flaws alleged in the objection do not actually hold, vidhi-statements stand established as authoritative. Jaimini and Badarayana both affirm this in their own foundational sutras.

> "चोदना-लक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः"
> "codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-2)
>
> "Dharma is that which is characterized by [Vedic] injunction."

In this sutra, Jaimini establishes that dharma is whatever is conducive to a person's ultimate good — and since vidhi-statements themselves state which acts are conducive to that good, vidhi-statements are thereby authoritative. This authority is further affirmed by the sutra known as the "autpattika-sutra":

> "औत्पत्तिकस् तु शब्दस्यार्थेन सम्बन्धस् तस्य ज्ञानम् उपदेशोऽव्यतिरेकश् चार्थेऽनुपलब्धे तत् प्रमाणं बादरायणस्यानपेक्ष्यात्"
> "autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena sambandhas tasya jñānam upadeśo'vyatirekaś cārthe'nupalabdhe tat pramāṇaṃ bādarāyaṇasyānapekṣyāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-5)
>
> "The relationship between word and meaning is innate; knowledge of this relationship constitutes instruction; and where no perceivable contradiction exists [in the matter concerned], this instruction is itself valid proof — because, per Badarayana, it [dharma] depends on nothing else for its validity."

Word and word-meaning are both naturally arising and eternal — every phoneme is eternal, not created. The entire Veda is likewise "shruta" (heard/revealed) — eternal and faultless. For dharma and its karmic fruits, the Veda alone is authoritative, since these cannot be known through perception or inference. Jaimini himself anticipates every conceivable objection here and answers each in his own systematic way — only a full study of the Mimamsa-shastra can properly evaluate whether his conclusions hold.

**Vyasa parallels this in the Brahma-sutra:**

> "śāstra-yonitvāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1-1-3)

Sayanacharya glosses this sutra two ways: (1) "śāstrasya yoniḥ (brahma)" — the Supreme Self alone is the cause of all shastras, including the Vedas; or (2) "śāstre yoniḥ yasya" — he for whom the shastras alone serve as the basis of being known. This is affirmed further in "tat tu samanvayāt" ("and this, from harmonious coherence [across scripture]").

<div class="pgmark">original p. 425</div>

This second meaning is the better-known one; the first is merely the general sense — it isn't especially significant to say the creator of the whole universe also created the shastras. What matters is that shastra be the sole reliable means for knowing such a being — this is Badarayana's real point. But if it's objected that, since many differing statements exist within the Veda itself, treating all shastras as pointing to the Supreme Self risks the Veda's own authority — this is answered by:

> "तत् तु समन्वयात्"
> "tat tu samanvayāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1-1-4)
>
> "But that [Brahman as the unified meaning of all Vedantic texts] is established through their coherence/harmony."

The apparent mutual contradiction is not genuine — it only appears so on the surface; all seemingly conflicting statements must be harmonized as ultimately pointing to the Supreme Self. Indeed, most of the Brahma-sutras exist precisely to resolve such apparent contradictions. As the Nirukta states, for one unfamiliar with Mimamsa-shastra:

> "नैष स्थाणोर् अपराधो यद् एनम् अन्धो न शक्नोति"
> "naiṣa sthāṇor aparādho yad enam andho na śaknoti" (Nirukta, Naighantuka-kanda, Purvashatka 1-5-1)
>
> "It is not the post's fault that a blind man cannot see it."

That is: if a blind man fails to see the tree-stump before him, the fault isn't the stump's — and likewise, it's only reasonable that someone unfamiliar with Purva-Mimamsa cannot grasp the Vedas' true meaning.

**The vidhi-portion's authority is now fully established. Turning to the second kind of Brahmana content — arthavāda —** the sage Jaimini takes great pains to establish its authority as well. The objection's opening sutra:

> "आम्नायस्य क्रियार्थत्वाद् आनर्थक्यम् अतदर्थानां तस्माद् अनित्यम् उच्यते"
> "āmnāyasya kriyārthatvād ānarthakyam atadarthānāṃ tasmād anityam ucyate" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-1)
>
> "Since revelation exists for the sake of ritual action, whatever doesn't relate to that action is meaningless — and is therefore called 'anitya' (non-eternal/non-authoritative)."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 426</div>

> ...अर्थवादा इवम् आम्नायन्ते । सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित १-५-१-१) । स आत्मनो वपाम् उदखिदत् (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित २-१-१-४) । देवा वै देवयजनम् अध्यवसाय दिशो न प्राजानन् (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित ६-१-५-१) इति । यस्माद् ईदृशस्य वाक्यस्य विवक्षितार्थः कश्चिद् अपि नास्ति तस्माद् इदं वाक्यम् अनित्यम् उच्यते ।
> ...arthavādā ivam āmnāyante | so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam (Taittiriya Samhita 1-5-1-1) | sa ātmano vapām udakhidat (Taittiriya Samhita 2-1-1-4) | devā vai devayajanam adhyavasāya diśo na prājānan (Taittiriya Samhita 6-1-5-1) iti | yasmād īdṛśasya vākyasya vivakṣitārthaḥ kaścid api nāsti tasmād idaṃ vākyam anityam ucyate |
>
> *(Introducing three specific arthavada examples cited as apparently meaningless: "he wept — that is Rudra's Rudra-ness"; "he removed his own layer of fat"; "the gods, having settled on the sacrificial ground, did not yet know the directions." Since such passages seem to convey no genuine intended meaning, the objection concludes they are "anitya" — lacking the eternal authoritative status of the rest of the Veda, even if not literally separate from it.)*

Sutra's meaning: since all Vedic statements are established as pointing to ritual action, arthavāda statements — those unrelated to any ritual act — carry no genuine intended meaning at all, and are therefore called "anitya" (non-eternal/non-authoritative) — this is the objection. While all Vedic statements are meant to convey ritual action, the Veda also contains passages like these:

**(1)** "so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam" (Taittiriya Samhita 1-5-1) — "He wept; because he wept, that is Rudra's own Rudra-ness [i.e., the origin of his name]."

**(2)** "sa ātmano vapām udakhidat" (Taittiriya Samhita 2-1-1) — "He peeled off his own layer of fat and cast it into the fire."

**(3)** "devā vai devayajanam adhyavasāya diśo na prājānan" (Taittiriya Samhita 6-1-5) — "The gods, having fixed a place for the divine sacrifice, could not identify that place."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 427</div>

No genuine meaning could be intended for such statements — hence they're called "anitya." This doesn't mean they lack the Veda's general beginninglessness; even with an eternal word-sequence, from the standpoint of meaning, these statements lack the defining trait shared by the rest of the Veda — impelling ritual action. In this sense, they're "anitya" much like ordinary poetic statements.

### "Śāstra-dṛṣṭa-nirodhāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-2)

Sutra's meaning: since arthavādas contradict both shastra and direct experience, the arthavāda-portion is not authoritative.

> शास्त्र-विरोधो दृष्ट्य्-अविरोधः शास्त्र-दृष्ट्य्-अविरोध इति त्रिविधो विरोधोऽर्थवादेष्व् उपलभ्यते । तथा हि । स्तेनं मनोऽनृतवादिनी वाग् इत्य् अत्र क्रियमाणं मानसं चौर्यं वाचिकम् अनृत-वदनं च प्रतिषेध-शास्त्रेण विरुद्धम् ।
> śāstra-virodho dṛṣṭy-avirodhaḥ śāstra-dṛṣṭy-avirodha iti trividho virodho'rthavādeṣv upalabhyate | tathā hi | stenaṃ mano'nṛtavādinī vāg ity atra kriyamāṇaṃ mānasaṃ cauryaṃ vācikam anṛta-vadanaṃ ca pratiṣedha-śāstreṇa viruddham |
>
> *(Establishing three kinds of contradiction found in arthavādas: contradiction with shastra, contradiction with direct sensory observation, and contradiction between one shastra passage and another. The example given: "stenaṃ mano'nṛtavādinī vāk" ("the mind is a thief, speech a teller of lies") — contradicting the prohibitive shastra rules against theft and lying, since it seems to claim the mind and speech, not the person, commit these acts. The further passages cited in the Sanskrit are given as (Tai. Brā. 2-1-2), (Mai. Saṃ. 1-4-11) and (Tai. Saṃ. 6-1-1-1).)*

Sūtra's meaning: since arthavādas contradict both shastra and direct experience, the arthavāda-portion cannot be authoritative — this establishes a threefold taxonomy of contradiction found across various arthavāda passages, to be worked through with specific examples.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 428</div>

Statements like "so'rodīt" might lack authority regarding dharma-matters specifically, but their literal meaning must still be accepted as authoritative in itself — so one cannot claim they entirely lack authority. However, some arthavāda statements' meanings directly contradict perceptual and other proofs — such statements genuinely must be called unauthoritative, and on this basis, the next sutra argues for extending non-authority to all arthavādas.

**Three kinds of contradiction found in arthavādas, each illustrated:**

**Śāstra-virodha** (contradiction with shastra) — a view opposed to the Veda's own stated intent:

> स्तेनं मनः ।
> *stenaṃ manaḥ |*
> "The mind is a thief" — [continuing] "speech a teller of lies." One might wrongly conclude theft and lying are thereby permitted — directly contradicting the prohibitive shastra against theft and falsehood.

**Dṛṣṭa-virodha** (contradiction with direct experience):

> तस्माद्धूम एवाग्नेर्दिवा दृश्यते । नार्चिः । तस्मादर्चिरेवाग्नेर्नक्तं दृश्यते । न धूमः ॥
> *tasmād dhūma evāgner divā dṛśyate | nārciḥ | tasmād arcir evāgner naktaṃ dṛśyate | na dhūmaḥ ||* (Taittiriya Brahmana 2-1-12)
> "By day only smoke is seen, not flame; by night only flame is seen, not smoke" — contradicting our ordinary observation.

> न चैतद्विद्मो वयं ब्राह्मणा वा स्मोऽब्राह्मणा वा ॥
> *na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā ||* (Maitrayani Samhita 1-4-11)
> "We don't even know whether we are brahmins or not" — likewise contrary to experience.

**Śāstra-dṛṣṭa-virodha** (undermining the Veda's own authority) — where one Vedic statement damages another's credibility:

> स्वर्गकामो यजेत ।
> *svargakāmo yajeta |*
> "One desiring heaven should perform yajna" — clearly asserting heaven's existence. Yet:

> को हि तद्वेद यद्यमुष्मिन् लोकेऽस्ति वा न वा ॥
> *ko hi tad veda yad yamuṣmin loke'sti vā na vā ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 6-1-1-1)
> "Who indeed knows whether that [heavenly world] exists or not" — directly undermines the authority of the very statement promising heaven as yajna's reward.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 429</div>

In this way, since these passages contradict shastra and experience, the arthavāda-portion is not authoritative. "So'rodīt" and similar statements are inauthoritative for lacking purpose; "stenaṃ manaḥ" and similar are inauthoritative for contradicting other proofs. But one might still argue that fruit-declaring arthavāda statements should count as authoritative. Anticipating this, the objector offers a further reason.

### "Tathā phalābhāvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-3)

> यथा मानान्तर-विरुद्धम् अर्थवाद्य् उक्तं तथा फलम् अस्याप्य् अविद्यमानम् एव दृश्यते । तथा हि गर्गत्रिरात्रं प्रशत्यै क्रियते । क्षोभक्रेष्य मुखं य एवं वेदेति (तन्द्य महब्रह्मन २०-१६-६) दर्श-पूर्णमासयोर् वेदाभिमर्शनं प्रशत्यै क्रियते । अस्य प्रजायां वाजी जायते य एवं वेदेति । न च वयं वेदितॄणां तत्-फलम् उपलभामहे ।
> yathā mānāntara-viruddham arthavādy uktaṃ tathā phalam asyāpy avidyamānam eva dṛśyate | tathā hi gargatrirātraṃ praśatyai kriyate | kṣobhakreṣya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ vedeti (Tandya Mahabrahmana 20-16-6) darśa-pūrṇamāsayor vedābhimarśanaṃ praśatyai kriyate | asya prajāyāṃ vājī jāyate ya evaṃ vedeti | na ca vayaṃ veditṝṇāṃ tat-phalam upalabhāmahe |
>
> *(Establishing that just as some arthavādas contradict other proofs, others promise fruits that simply aren't observed in practice — the "Gargatriratra" ritual promising renown, and the darsha-purnamasa's mantra-repetition promising a swift, vigorous descendant, neither being confirmed by actual experience among those who know these rites.)*

Sutra's meaning: since the fruits arthavādas promise are never actually observed, they are inauthoritative. As with the previous sutra's contradiction-based argument, here the objection turns to unfulfilled promises. The "Gargatrirātra" is performed for renown; the arthavāda "kṣobhakreṣya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ veda" claims a certain effect for one who understands this correctly — yet this isn't borne out by experience. In the Darsha and Purnamasa yajnas, Vedic mantras are recited repeatedly with the aid of kusha-grass, and the promised fruit — stated in "asya prajāyāṃ..." — is that the performer's lineage will gain grain-abundance.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 430</div>

...this alone is the claimed fruit of this ritual-knowledge — but no one who knows this rite is ever seen to attain it. Since it declares an unattainable fruit, arthavādas are inauthoritative.

Statements like "śobhate'sya mukhaṃ" declare both worldly and perishable fruits. Whichever fruit is claimed, it might go unobserved even by those who perform the act — so such statements should be conceded as purposeless. But what of arthavādas promising specifically *other-worldly* (āmuṣmika) fruits, unfalsifiable by ordinary observation? Surely their authority must be granted? The next sutra argues even these fail.

### "Anyānarthakyāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-4)

> एवं हि श्रूयते । पूर्णाहुत्या सर्वान् कामान् अवाप्नोति । पशुबन्ध-याजी सर्वाल् लोकान् अभिजयति । तरति मृत्युं तरति पाप्मानं तरति ब्रह्म-हत्यां योऽग्निष्टोमेन यजते य उ चैनम् एवं वेदेति ।
> evaṃ hi śrūyate | pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān avāpnoti | paśubandha-yājī sarvāl lokān abhijayati | tarati mṛtyuṃ tarati pāpmānaṃ tarati brahma-hatyāṃ yo'gniṣṭomena yajate ya u cainam evaṃ vedeti |
>
> *(Citing three parallel arthavada promises: "one attains all desires through the Purnahuti offering"; "one who performs the pashubandha sacrifice conquers all worlds"; "one who performs the Ashvamedha, and understands it correctly, crosses beyond death, sin, and the crime of killing a brahmin." Since these three separate rites each claim to grant the very same all-encompassing rewards — attaining all desires, conquering all worlds, crossing all evils — at least two of the three promises must be redundant if the third alone already delivers everything; this excess undermines the reliability of such promised fruits generally, extending the charge of non-authority even to other-worldly-fruit arthavadas.)*

Sutra's meaning: all other arthavāda statements likewise serve no genuine purpose.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 431</div>

If authority is granted to even one other-worldly-fruit statement, then since it alone secures all kinds of fruit, the remaining fruit-statements become purposeless. Three examples (all from the Taittiriya Samhita/Brahmana):

**1.**

> पूर्णाहुत्या सर्वान् कामानवाप्नोति ।
> *pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān avāpnoti |*
> "By the Purnahuti (final oblation), one attains all desires." — "It suffices to perform the Purnahuti; all desired ends are fully accomplished." (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-8-10-5)

**2.**

> पशुबन्धयाजी सर्वाँल्लोकानभिजयति ।
> *paśubandha-yājī sarvāl lokān abhijayati |*
> "One who performs the pashubandha (animal sacrifice) conquers all worlds." — "For one who performs the pashubandha rite, all worlds become attained."

**3.**

> तरति मृत्युं तरति पाप्मानं तरति ब्रह्महत्यां योऽश्वमेधेन यजते य उ चैनमेवं वेदेति ।
> *tarati mṛtyuṃ tarati pāpmānaṃ tarati brahma-hatyāṃ yo'śvamedhena yajate ya u cainam evaṃ vedeti |*
> "He crosses beyond death, sin, and the killing of a brahmin, who performs the Ashvamedha and understands it correctly." — "One who performs the Ashvamedha yajna — even one who merely knows its proper procedure — is capable of conquering death and removing sins. More than that: even the grave fault of killing a brahmin is thereby removed." (Taittiriya Samhita 5-3-12-2)

Every householder must perform the rite called **Agnyadheya** before he becomes qualified to perform Agnihotra. If performing just one Purnahuti — itself only a component of the Agnyadheya rite — already fulfills every desired end, what purpose do the subsequent Agnihotra and related rites even serve?

**On the Purnahuti itself:** among the fire-offerings performed within Shrauta, Smarta, and Grihya rites, many "pradhana-homas" (principal offerings) are made to the yajna's chief deities. Afterward, "prayashchitta-homas" (expiatory offerings) remedy any lapses, followed by the "svishtakrit" offering, and finally the "Purnahuti" — the very last oblation of the sequence.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 432</div>

When all worlds are attained through the pashubandha yajna alone, what special benefit remains from performing the Jyotishtoma and similar yajnas? And since mere *study* of the Ashvamedha mantra removes even brahmin-slaying sin, undertaking the arduous actual Ashvamedha rite would become the work of a fool. Isn't it beyond doubt, then, that arthavāda-statements declaring such purposeless acts and fruits are inauthoritative? A response to this follows.

**A digression on yajna classification, for context:** Sayanacharya's introduction and commentary cites many portions from Mimamsa texts throughout — properly following these arguments requires familiarity with yajnas, so a brief technical outline follows here.

Vedic yajnas are of two kinds: **(1) Shrauta-yajna** and **(2) Grihya-yajna**. Taking Grihya-yajnas first — also called **Pakayajnas** — their procedures are described across various Grihya-sutras, using the fire called "Grihyagni." Pakayajnas exist in seven varieties (samsthas) across all traditions — no more, no less:

**Per the Gopatha Brahmana (1-5-23):**
1. सायंप्रातर्होम (*Sāyaṃprātar-homa*) 2. स्थालीपाक (*Sthālīpāka*) 3. नवयज्ञ (*Navayajña*) 4. बलि/वैश्वदेवबलि (*Bali*/*Vaiśvadeva-bali*) 5. पितृयज्ञ (*Pitṛyajña*) 6. अष्टक (*Aṣṭaka*) 7. पशु (*Paśu*)

**Per the Gautama Dharmasutra (1-8-10):**
1. अष्टक (*Aṣṭaka*) 2. पार्वण (*Pārvaṇa*) 3. श्राद्ध/मासिकश्राद्ध (*Śrāddha*/*Māsika-śrāddha*) 4. श्रावणी (*Śrāvaṇī*) 5. आग्रहायणी (*Āgrahāyaṇī*) 6. चैत्री (*Caitrī*) 7. आश्वयुजी (*Āśvayujī*)

**Per Dhurtasvami's commentary on the Apastamba Yajna-paribhasha-sutra:**
1. औपासनहोम (*Aupāsana-homa*) 2. वैश्वदेव (*Vaiśvadeva*) 3. पार्वण (*Pārvaṇa*) 4. अष्टक (*Aṣṭaka*) 5. मासिश्राद्ध (*Māsi-śrāddha*) 6. सर्पबलि (*Sarpa-bali*) 7. ईशानबलि/शूलगव (*Īśāna-bali*/*Śūlagava*)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 433</div>

Pakayajnas differ according to each branch's own tradition. Among Shrauta-yajnas too, there are two kinds: Soma-yajnas (using Soma-juice for homas) and Havir-yajnas (using ordinary havis). Soma-yajnas were briefly introduced earlier (page 416).

**हविर्यज्ञ (Havir-yajña)** number seven across all traditions — no disagreement on the count, though which specific rites are included varies by school:

**(1) Per Sayanacharya's own Aitareya-Brahmana-bhashya (Ai. Brā. Bhā. 5-7):**
अग्न्याधेय (*Agnyādheya*), अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), दर्शपूर्णमास (*Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*), आग्रयण (*Āgrayaṇa*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), दाक्षायणयज्ञ (*Dākṣāyaṇa-yajña*), कौण्डपायिनायन/सौत्रामणि (*Kauṇḍapāyina-māyana* or *Sautrāmaṇi*)

**(2) Per Dhurtasvami's Yajna-paribhasha-sutra commentary:**
अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), दर्शपूर्णमास (*Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*), आग्रयण (*Āgrayaṇa*), पिण्डपितृयज्ञ (*Piṇḍa-pitṛyajña*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), निरूढपशुबन्ध (*Nirūḍha-paśubandha*), सौत्रामणि (*Sautrāmaṇi*)

**(3) Per the Gautama Dharmasutra (1-8-20):**
अग्न्याधेय (*Agnyādheya*), अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), दर्शपूर्णमास (*Darśa-pūrṇamāsa*), आग्रयण (*Āgrayaṇa*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), निरूढपशुबन्ध (*Nirūḍha-paśubandha*), सौत्रामणि (*Sautrāmaṇi*)

**(4) Per the Gopatha Brahmana (1-5-23):**
अग्न्याधेय (*Agnyādheya*), अग्निहोत्र (*Agnihotra*), पौर्णमासी (*Pūrṇamāsī*), अमावास्या (*Amāvāsyā*), नवेष्टि (*Naveṣṭi*), चातुर्मास्य (*Cāturmāsya*), पशुबन्ध (*Paśubandha*)

**On the दर्शपूर्णमासेष्टि (Darsha-Purnamasa-iṣṭis)** — performed at new moon and full moon, called "**इष्टि**" (*iṣṭi*) — these form the structural foundation for all other iṣṭis, identical in both ritual technique (tantra) and essential form. The main offering-substance for the **पुरोडाश** (*puroḍāśa*) is rice flour or wheat flour, boiled in milk to become "puroḍāśa," prepared separately in earthen-dish fragments called "**कपाल**" (*kapāla*). The first homa addresses Agni: the puroḍāśa baked in eight kapalas ("**आग्नेयमष्टाकपालम्**" *āgneyam aṣṭākapālam*) is offered. The second homa addresses Agni and Soma jointly: the puroḍāśa in eleven kapalas ("**आग्नीषोमीयमेकादशकपालम्**" *āgnīṣomīyam ekādaśakapālam*) is offered. Different deities correspondingly require different numbers of kapalas.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 434</div>

These ishtis require four priests: **(1) अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu)** — performs all the technical/procedural work; **(2) होतृ (Hotṛ)** — recites mantras and invites the deities; **(3) ब्रह्मा (Brahmā)** — oversees the correct performance of the above two; **(4) आग्नीध्र (Āgnīdhra)** — Brahma's assistant.

The rites described so far occur on the new-moon or full-moon day itself, but preliminary rites are performed the day before: in the morning, the **अग्न्याधान (Agnyādhāna)** rite (placing kindling in the Garhapatya, Ahavaniya, and Dakshinagni fires with mantras); then the yajamana is ritually shaved, eats the midday meal, and, standing near the three fire-pits, takes certain vows (**व्रतग्रहण** *Vratagrahaṇa*) — after which he is considered "dīkṣā-bound." That night, both he and his wife (also diksha-bound) must remain within the sacrificial hall; the yaga proper begins the following morning.

After the Agnihotra: **(1)** priest-selection (**ऋत्विग्वरण** *Ṛtvigvaraṇa*); then, for minor deities' favor, the **प्रयाज (Prayāja)** rites (subsidiary to the main act); **(2)** one Ajya-homa (ghee-offering) each to Agni and Soma; **(3)** the puroḍāśa offered first to Agni (eight kapalas), then jointly to Agni-Soma (eleven kapalas) — the yajna's central act. Between these two, a softly-recited Ajya-homa to Agni-Soma jointly is called **उपांशुयाग (Upāṃśu-yāga)**; **(4)** the **सुहुतकृत्/शिष्टकृत् (Śiṣṭikṛt)** rite, offering the remainder of the puroḍāśa already used; **(5)** finally, the **अनुयाज (Anuyāja)s** — homas addressing three [further] deities.

### पूर्णाहुति (Pūrṇāhuti)

The final, principal offering made at the close of the Agnyadhana is called **Pūrṇāhuti**. Agnyadhana is also called **अग्न्याधेय (Agnyādheya)** — meaning the establishing or consecration of fire within the sacrificial hall. This Shrauta-fire consecration [is undertaken by] a householder [following his] marriage.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 435</div>

The main ritual act one gains the right to perform only after undertaking householder-life (**गार्हस्थ्य** *gārhasthya*) requires establishing three fires: **गार्हपत्य (Gārhapatya)**, **आहवनीय (Āhavanīya)**, and **दक्षिणाग्नि (Dakṣiṇāgni)**.

A square platform is built in the middle of the yajna-hall — to its west, a long rectangular pit for the Garhapatya-fire; to its east, a circular pit for the Ahavaniya-fire; to its south, a semicircular pit for the Dakshinagni-fire. The Garhapatya represents the yajamāna himself (as "**गृहपति**" *gṛhapati*, household-master); the Ahavaniya belongs to the deities, so all deity-offerings must be made there; other homas use the Dakshinagni.

**Preliminary rites the day before:** the Adhvaryu brings fire from a fixed source into the Garhapatya-pit. The yajamāna, with his wife, enters the yajna-hall that evening and keeps vigil through the night — solely to keep the Garhapatya-fire burning, continually feeding it kindling.

**The next morning**, fire is newly produced through "**अग्निमन्थन**" (*Agni-manthana*, fire-churning), with a horse readied for the occasion. The Adhvaryu ignites a stick from this new fire and places it in the Garhapatya-pit while the Brahma priest performs the Sama-chant. A procession then forms: the Adhvaryu carrying fire leads, the horse follows, then the yajamāna. The horse, facing west, places one leg into the Ahavaniya-pit; the Adhvaryu touches the fire to the horse's foot before placing it in the pit. He then carries fire once more from the Garhapatya into the Dakshinagni-pit. Everyone circumambulates the fires, and the horse is released.

**This is the moment of Pūrṇāhuti.** Ghee is melted over the Garhapatya-fire; the Adhvaryu, using a wooden ladle called "**जुहू**" (*juhū*), offers it into the Ahavaniya-fire while reciting Yajus mantras — further mantras follow with further offerings. Since the Adhvaryu performs this homa on the yajamāna's behalf, the yajamāna touches the Adhvaryu throughout. This final offering is what's called **Pūrṇāhuti** — the last act of the Agnyadhana rite. Even after this yajna concludes, the yajamāna must remain bound by certain observances for some further days. In this yajna...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 436</div>

The Garhapatya-fire must never go out, day or night — this rule doesn't apply to the other two fires. Every householder must perform this Agnyadhana; one who completes it properly is called **"Āhitāgni"** (one who has established the fire) — a status required before any other Shrauta yajna can be undertaken. Purnahuti is the final act of Agnyadhana as described, though two differing views exist on whether Agnyadhana properly concludes with a homa or with an ishti.

### Agnihotra

Every householder who is an Ahitagni must perform this rite daily. In the morning, addressing the Sun-deity, one recites—

> ॐ भूर्भुवस्स्वः । ॐ सूर्यो ज्योतिर्ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा ।
> *oṃ bhūr bhuvas svaḥ | oṃ sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā |*

—and offers a homa in the Ahavaniya-fire, using milk as the offering-substance — heated in an earthen vessel over the Garhapatya-fire, then offered using wooden spoons: a small "**स्रुव**" (*sruva*), and a larger "**अग्निहोत्रहवनी**" (*agnihotra-havanī*). Four or five sruva-dips of milk are transferred into the larger spoon for offering.

The Garhapatya-fire must always stay lit. The yajamāna, with his wife, enters the fire-hall and lights the Ahavaniya and Dakshinagni from it, offers a kindling-stick homa in the Ahavaniya, and then, once consumed, offers two milk-portions with the agnihotra-havani spoon — the first addressing the Sun (with mantra), the second addressing Prajapati (without mantra). He then similarly offers two milk-portions in the Garhapatya (for Agni-Grihapati, then Prajapati) and two more in the Dakshinagni (for Agni-Annapati, then Prajapati). The heated milk isn't offered undivided; the leftover portion is consumed by the yajamāna himself.

The evening rite follows the same structure, but addresses Agni instead of Surya, with the mantra—

> अग्निर्ज्योतिर्ज्योतिरग्निः स्वाहा ।
> *agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā |*

—the evening Agnihotra must be performed at sunset.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 437</div>

There is disagreement on the morning homa's exact timing — before or after sunrise (see the earlier account on page 415 of this work).

### पशुबन्ध (Paśubandha, or निरूढपशुबन्ध Nirūḍha-Paśubandha)

Among the many animal-sacrifice varieties, one is obligatory: the **निरूढपशुबन्ध (Nirūḍha-Paśubandha)**, performed on the rainy season's full-moon or new-moon day (some hold it should instead fall at the winter/summer Sankranti transitions). Six priests officiate: अध्वर्यु (Adhvaryu), होतृ (Hotṛ), ब्रह्मा (Brahmā), आग्नीध्र (Āgnīdhra, Brahma's assistant), प्रतिप्रस्थाता (Pratiprasthātā, Adhvaryu's assistant), and मैत्रावरुण (Maitrāvaruṇa, Hotr's assistant).

As in the ishtis, a platform is built; east of the Ahavaniya-pit, at a slight distance, a further platform called "**पशुक** (*Pāśuka*)" is constructed, atop which a smaller platform, "**उत्तरवेदि** (*Uttaravedi*)," is built. A pole (**यूप** *Yūpa*), five cubits long, is planted one cubit into the ground there, to which the sacrificial animal is tied. Numerous small mantric acts follow. Before the main homa, eleven "**प्रयाज** (*Prayāja*)" offerings are performed, each accompanied by its own "**आप्री** (*Āprī*)" hymn of praise.

The main homa follows immediately, dedicated to **इन्द्र (Indra)** and **अग्नि (Agni)**. The animal's fat and other portions are consecrated with mantras; the Adhvaryu offers the puroḍāśa and fat as homa, while the Maitravaruna and Hotr recite the appropriate Anuvaka-verses and "**याज्या** (*Yājyā*)" mantras respectively. An offering to please Agni ("**रुद्र** *Rudra*" in this ritual context) follows — the **शिष्टिकृत्-होम (Śiṣṭikṛt-homa)** — then "**इडाभक्षण** (*Iḍā-bhakṣaṇa*)," the partaking of the leftover offering ("iḍā") by the yajamāna, priests, and all present.

This completes the yajna's central portion, though further minor acts remain before the rite concludes properly: the "**अनुयाज** (*Anuyāja*)" offerings (using curd-mixed ghee as the substance, honoring eleven deities), followed by the "**उपयाज** (*Upayāja*)" — the Adhvaryu's assistant, the Pratiprasthata, offering the animal's meat without mantra-recitation — performed only in animal-sacrifice yajnas specifically.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 438</div>

This act doesn't occur in the ishtis. Finally, the yajamāna's wife performs "**Patnī-saṃyāja**" — offering the sacrificial animal's tail as homa in the Garhapatya-fire.

This yajna-matter has been explained only very briefly here; the full procedural detail, together with the relevant sutra-meanings, will be given more extensively elsewhere.

### "Abhāgi-pratiṣedhāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-5)

> न पृथिव्याम् अग्निश् चेतव्यो नान्तरिक्षे न दिवीत्य् एतस्य च दिवि प्रतिषेध-भागित्वं नास्ति । तत्र चयनस्य कृनगस्याभावात् । मा भूत्य् अर्षि निषेधानां प्रामाण्यं । बबरः प्रावाहणेर् अमयतेऽस्मायशऋचादीनां पूर्व-पुरुषन्यत्तन्ताभिधायिनाम् निरोधानुपलम्भाद् अस्तु प्रामाण्यम् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> na pṛthivyām agniś cetavyo nāntarikṣe na divīty etasya ca divi pratiṣedha-bhāgitvaṃ nāsti | tatra cayanasya kṛnagasyābhāvāt | mā bhūty arṣi niṣedhānāṃ prāmāṇyaṃ | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇer amayate'smāyaśaṛcādīnāṃ pūrva-puruṣanyattantābhidhāyinām nirodhānupalambhād astu prāmāṇyam ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> *(Introducing the objection that certain arthavada prohibitions apply to circumstances that could never actually occur — e.g., a rule against building a fire-altar "in the sky" makes no sense, since no one would ever attempt to build a sacrificial fire-altar in the sky in the first place. Such prohibitions, having nothing genuine to prohibit, are argued to be purposeless, extending the charge of non-authority even to the prohibitive class of arthavada statements.)*

Sutra's meaning: since the prohibitive statements found within arthavāda address situations that could never arise, arthavāda is not authoritative on these grounds either.

Granting, as the previous sutras argued, that fruit-promising statements lack authority — this same flaw shouldn't extend to prohibitive statements, since no view anywhere opposes them; one might therefore argue prohibitive arthavadas at least remain authoritative. Anticipating this, the objector raises a further point: since prohibitions address impossible situations, they too serve no purpose. The Taittiriya Samhita contains a statement regarding fire-altar construction (agni-chayana) — declaring that fire should not be established "on earth," "in the atmosphere," or "in the sky".

<div class="pgmark">original p. 439</div>

...a falcon-shaped altar is customarily constructed (in the Agni-chayana rite) — this Soma-related form being a portion of Prajapati, whom the rite addresses. The fire is established upon a golden plate (symbolizing the Sun), atop which a human-shaped golden image (representing Prajapati) is set, surrounded by layered bricks ("svayamātṛṇṇāḥ") thought to occupy the positions of earth, atmosphere, and sky — the whole rite depicting the creation of the universe, with the yajamāna coming to feel unity with Prajapati and the mantra-invoked deities.

**Returning to the objection:** this cited arthavada indicates fire should be established upon the golden plate — specifically excluding earth, atmosphere, and sky. Very well, let prohibitive statements lack authority — but surely narrative statements like "Pravāhaṇa's son Babara desired" carry no such doubt, containing only a sage's own historical account with no contradictory content at all? Anticipating this defense, the next sutra follows.

### "Anitya-saṃyogāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-6)

> बबरादि-रूपेणानित्येनार्थेन संयोगे सत्य् अस्य वाक्यस्य ततः पूर्वम् अभावात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवत् पौरुषेयत्वं प्रसज्येत । किं बहुना । सर्वथापि नास्त्य् अर्थवादानां प्रामाण्यम् इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥
> babarādi-rūpeṇānityenārthena saṃyoge saty asya vākyasya tataḥ pūrvam abhāvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavat pauruṣeyatvaṃ prasajyeta | kiṃ bahunā | sarvathāpi nāsty arthavādānāṃ prāmāṇyam iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||
>
> बेबरादि-रूपेणानित्येनार्थेन संयोगे सत्य् अस्य वाक्यस्य ततः पूर्वम् अभावात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवत् पौरुषेयत्वं प्रसज्येत । किं बहुना । सर्वथापि नास्त्य् अर्थवादानां प्रामाण्यम् इति पूर्वः पक्षः ॥
> *bebarādi-rūpeṇānityenārthena saṃyoge saty asya vākyasya tataḥ pūrvam abhāvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavat pauruṣeyatvaṃ prasajyeta | kiṃ bahunā | sarvathāpi nāsty arthavādānāṃ prāmāṇyam iti pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ ||*
>
> "Since this statement mentions a transient thing in the form of 'Babara' and similar, this statement could not have existed before that person — implying, like statements by Kalidasa and similar poets, a human origin. In short: arthavādas have no authority whatsoever. — Thus concludes the objection (pūrvapakṣa)."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 440</div>

This doubt should not be prolonged; however one looks at it, arthavādas plainly lack authority — this concludes the objection.

### The Siddhāntin's Resolution Begins

> "विधिना त्व् एक-वाक्यत्वात् स्तुत्यर्थेन विधीनां स्युः"
> "vidhinā tv eka-vākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-7)
>
> "But since arthavādas form a single syntactical unit together with their corresponding vidhi, they must be understood as existing to praise those very vidhis."

> तुशब्दोऽर्थवादानाम् अप्रामाण्यं वारयति । वायुर् वै क्षेपिष्ठा देवता वायव्यं श्वेतम् आलभेत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित २-१-१-१) इत्य् आदिना विधिना सैकवाक्यत्वाद् धर्मे प्रामाण्यम् । न च विधि-वाक्य-स्यार्थ-वादात् नैः सर्वे क्षेत्रण सदास्ति-यसंपूर्के स्तार्थ-वादानां नास्त्येक-योग इति शङ्कनीयम् । तेष्व् अर्थ-वादानां पुरुष-प्रवृत्ति-मात्र-कांक्षतां विधीनां स्तुत्यर्थ-स्येनोपयुक्ताः स्युः । स्तुत्या च पुरुष-प्रवृत्ति-श्रवण । तेनार्थ-वादानां प्रमाद-शमिते-क्षेपाणीय-क्त्वा तस्मिन् एवैकवाक्यता-प्रत्य् आसत्वाच्-छन्क्य्-अकः ॥
> tuśabdo'rthavādānām aprāmāṇyaṃ vārayati | vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta (Taittiriya Samhita 2-1-1-1) ity ādinā vidhinā saikavākyatvād dharme prāmāṇyam | na ca vidhi-vākya-syārtha-vādāt naiḥ sarve kṣetraṇa sadāsti-yasaṃpūrke stārtha-vādānāṃ nāstyeka-yoga iti śaṅkanīyam | teṣv artha-vādānāṃ puruṣa-pravṛtti-mātra-kāṃkṣatāṃ vidhīnāṃ stutyartha-syenopayuktāḥ syuḥ | stutyā ca puruṣa-pravṛtti-śravaṇa | tenārtha-vādānāṃ pramāda-śamite-kṣepāṇīya-ktvā tasmin evaikavākyatā-praty āsatvāc-chanky-akaḥ ||
>
> *(This dense commentary establishes: since arthavādas are grammatically and syntactically bound to the vidhi-statement they accompany — forming one continuous unit of meaning — the entire combined statement takes on the vidhi's own authority. The arthavāda's role is specifically to encourage a person's motivation to act on the injunction, through praise, and this "praise function" is what grants it derivative authority — not any standalone claim to convey new facts.)*

Sutta's meaning: arthavādas exist to praise the very meaning conveyed by vidhi-statements — this is the point of censuring them independently. Since one accepts the objector's own earlier concession that vidhi-statements are proven authoritative through the sutras, that same authority extends here: the very first sutra, "vidhinā tv eka-vākyatvāt stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syuḥ," establishes that both vidhi and arthavāda together form a single grammatical unit — and, being one unit, the arthavādas relevant portions in the current discussion are themselves praise-statements strengthening the vidhi's own force.

The word "**tu**" ("but") in this sutra rejects the objection's claim of arthavāda's non-authority. Since arthavādas like "vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā" form one syntactical unit with vidhis like "vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta," they too must be authoritative guides to religious duty. Nor need we doubt this on grounds that vidhis are verbally...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 441</div>

complete in themselves apart from arthavāda, such connection would be pointless. That's not so — vidhi-statements depend on human motivation to act, and arthavādas, by praising and emphasizing the vidhi, are precisely what generates that motivation. A person is moved to undertake a course of action specifically upon hearing it praised.

That is: the objection held that vayu is an especially swift deity, and offering the "vāyavya-śveta" (white goat) to him yields fruit quickly — while other deities' offerings yield fruit more slowly — and therefore, one should offer this goat to Vayu specifically. Following this reasoning, the arthavāda's own authority isn't independent; it exists purely to support this same vidhi's force, and neither is authoritative apart from the other. Where a vidhi's own arthavāda-portion doesn't literally align word-for-word with it, the vidhi and its associated arthavāda mustn't be assumed unrelated — arthavādas exist precisely to make a person eager to perform the enjoined act; this is the arthavāda's whole purpose. Recognizing this resolves the difficulty in every arthavāda passage.

**A further objection anticipated:** the sutra just given establishes authority through syntactical unity — but one could still argue that some arthavāda portions were mistakenly inserted through scribal error, and should therefore be disregarded despite appearing embedded within vidhi-passages. Jaimini answers this too.

### "Tulyaṃ ca sāṃpradāyikam" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-8)

> अनध्यायः वर्जनादि-नियम-पुरस्सरं गुरु-संप्रदायाद् अध्ययनं यत् तत् साम्प्रदायिकम् । तच् च विधि-समार्थवादानां समानम् । तस्मात् तद्-विधेव समानम् । न च शास्त्र-दृष्टि-विरोधाच् चैव समर्थ-वादे षु न भवति । न सं शास्त्र-दृष्टि-विरोधाच् चैव शेषम् अर्थ-वादे षु न पृच्छति ।
> anadhyāyaḥ varjanādi-niyama-purassaraṃ guru-saṃpradāyād adhyayanaṃ yat tat sāmpradāyikam | tac ca vidhi-samārthavādānāṃ samānam | tasmāt tad-vidheva samānam | na ca śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodhāc caiva samartha-vāde ṣu na bhavati | na saṃ śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodhāc caiva śeṣam artha-vāde ṣu na pṛcchati |
>
> *(Establishing that the tradition of study — passed down through the guru's own lineage, with the observance of restraints such as holy days — applies equally to vidhi and arthavāda portions alike, since both are transmitted through the very same unbroken chain. This equal transmission itself proves both classes of statement share the same authoritative status, ruling out the possibility that arthavāda was carelessly or erroneously introduced.)*

Sutra's meaning: since arthavāda-statements have been studied, generation after generation, following the same tradition as vidhi-statements, no error can have crept into them in transmission.

Just as there are vidhis such as not studying on "anadhyāya" (non-study) days — these too have come down through the same guru-lineage, passed on faithfully according to tradition. In this same transmission-line...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 442</div>

Everyone already accepts that transmission-errors cannot occur in vidhi-statements. Since vidhis and their arthavādas have both come down through the very same unbroken tradition, no cause exists for error to affect the arthavāda portion any differently.

But one might still object: given the apparent contradiction with shastra and direct perception, can we really accept that no error-flaws exist in these vidhi-arthavāda passages? The next sutra answers this.

### "Aprāptā cānupapattiḥ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-9)

> स्तेनं मन इत्यादौ शास्त्र-विरोधाद् अनुपपत्तिः प्राप्ता । प्रयोगे हि श्रेयादीनाम् उच्यमाने शास्त्र-विरोधः स्यात् । न चात्र श्रेयं कर्तव्यम् इति प्रयोग उच्यते । किन्तु श्रेय-शब्दार्थ एव प्रयोग-भाक् । तस्माच् छब्दार्थ-वचन-मात्रेण शास्त्र-विरोधाभावाद् अयम् अर्थवाद उपपन्न एव ।
> stenaṃ mana ityādau śāstra-virodhād anupapattiḥ prāptā | prayoge hi śreyādīnām ucyamāne śāstra-virodhaḥ syāt | na cātra śreyaṃ kartavyam iti prayoga ucyate | kintu śreya-śabdārtha eva prayoga-bhāk | tasmāc chabdārtha-vacana-mātreṇa śāstra-virodhābhāvād ayam arthavāda upapanna eva |
>
> स्तेनं मन इत्यादौ शास्त्र-विरोधाद् अनुपपत्तिः प्राप्ता । प्रयोगे हि स्तेनादीनाम् उच्यमाने शास्त्र-विरोधः स्यात् । न चात्र स्तेनं कर्तव्यम् इति प्रयोग उच्यते । किन्तु स्तेन-शब्दार्थ एव प्रयोग-भाक् । तस्माच् छब्दार्थ-वचन-मात्रेण शास्त्र-विरोधाभावाद् अयम् अर्थवाद उपपन्न एव ।
> *stenaṃ mana ityādau śāstra-virodhād anupapattiḥ prāptā | prayoge hi stenādīnām ucyamāne śāstra-virodhaḥ syāt | na cātra stenaṃ kartavyam iti prayoga ucyate | kintu stena-śabdārtha eva prayoga-bhāk | tasmāc chabdārtha-vacana-mātreṇa śāstra-virodhābhāvād ayam arthavāda upapanna eva |*
>
> ननु स्तुत्यर्थेन विधीनां स्युरिति यदुक्तं तदसद्व्यधिकरणत्वात् । वेतसशाखया चावकाभिश्चाग्निं विकर्षत्यापो वै शान्ताः (तै. सं. ५-४-४-३) इत्यत्र वेतसावके विधीयेते आपः स्तूयन्त इति वैयधिकरण्यमित्याशंक्याह ॥
> *nanu stutyarthena vidhīnāṃ syur iti yad uktaṃ tad asad vyadhikaraṇatvāt | vetasaśākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣaty āpo vai śāntāḥ (Tai. Saṃ. 5-4-4-3) ity atra vetasāvake vidhīyete āpaḥ stūyanta iti vaiyadhikaraṇyam ity āśaṅkyāha ||*
>
>
> "In statements like 'stenaṃ manaḥ' (the mind is a thief), the objection of contradiction with shastra was raised. If theft and similar acts were being literally enjoined, that would indeed contradict shastra. But no injunction to actually commit theft is being stated here — rather, only the *meaning of the word* 'thief' is being conveyed [metaphorically, describing the mind's tendency]. Since it merely states a word's sense without prescribing literal action, no contradiction with shastra arises, and this arthavāda stands perfectly coherent."

Sutra's meaning: it is not correct to say vidhi-arthavāda statements cannot be accepted as authoritative. Contradiction could only arise if these statements conveyed a literal, action-oriented command — but they convey only the meaning of the words themselves, not a prescription for actual performance. Therefore, they carry authority.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 443</div>

It is not correct that "stenaṃ manaḥ" and similar statements become inauthoritative through shastra-contradiction — since they say nothing about actual yajna performance at all. Shastra-contradiction would arise only if theft were being literally prescribed for performance; nowhere does this happen — only the literal word-meaning of "theft" occurs, without any action-oriented sense. Since the mere presence of this word produces no genuine shastra-contradiction, this arthavāda retains its authority.

**A further, genuinely subtle objection now arises:** granting that arthavādas exist to praise vidhis — forming, together, one complete sentence — surely the vidhi-portion alone should be accepted as authoritative, while the arthavāda-portion, addressing an entirely *different* subject, cannot be? Consider:

> "वेतस-शाखया चावकाभिश् चाग्निं विकर्ष्यापो वै शान्ताः" (तै. सं. ५-४-४)
> "vetasa-śākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣyāpo vai śāntāḥ" (Tai. Saṃ. 5-4-4)

Here, "vetasa-śākhayā cāvakābhiś cāgniṃ vikarṣati" ("one draws away the fire using branches of the vetasa and avaka plants") is the vidhi-portion. "Āpo vai śāntāḥ" ("waters indeed possess a calm nature") is a separate statement. What connection does water's calm nature have with extinguishing fire using plant-branches? Given such apparently unrelated subject-matter combined within a single vidhi-arthavāda passage, how can we accept its authority as a unified whole? — This is the objection. The resolution is given in the next sutra.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 444</div>

### "Guṇavādas tu" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-10)

> तुशब्दो वैयधिकरण्य-दोषं वारयति । गुणवादो ह्य् अत्र विवक्षितः । यथा लोके कश्मीराभिजनो देवदत्तः कश्मीरेषु स्तूयमानेषु स्तुतम् आत्मानं मन्यते एवम् अत्राप्य् अपो जाते वेतसावके अप्सु स्तुतासु स्तुते एव भवतः । शान्ताभ्योऽद्भ्यो जातत्वाद् वेतसावके स्वयम् अपि शान्ते सत्या यजमानिनम् आच्छमयत इष्टैतादृशस्य गुणस्य वाच्यत्वाभिप्रेत ।
> tuśabdo vaiyadhikaraṇya-doṣaṃ vārayati | guṇavādo hy atra vivakṣitaḥ | yathā loke kaśmīrābhijano devadattaḥ kaśmīreṣu stūyamāneṣu stutam ātmānaṃ manyate evam atrāpy apo jāte vetasāvake apsu stutāsu stute eva bhavataḥ | śāntābhyo'dbhyo jātatvād vetasāvake svayam api śānte satyā yajamāninam ācchamayata iṣṭaitādṛśasya guṇasya vācyatvābhipreta |
>
> तुशब्दो वैयधिकरण्य-दोषं वारयति । गुणवादो ह्य् अत्र विवक्षितः । यथा लोके कश्मीराभिजनो देवदत्तः कश्मीरेषु स्तूयमानेषु स्तुतम् आत्मानं मन्यते एवम् अत्राप्य् अपो जाते वेतसावके अप्सु स्तुतासु स्तुते एव भवतः । शान्ताभ्योऽद्भ्यो जातत्वाद् वेतसावके स्वयम् अपि शान्ते सत्या यजमानिनम् आच्छमयत इष्टैतादृशस्य गुणस्य वाच्यत्वाभिप्रेत ।
> *tuśabdo vaiyadhikaraṇya-doṣaṃ vārayati | guṇavādo hy atra vivakṣitaḥ | yathā loke kaśmīrābhijano devadattaḥ kaśmīreṣu stūyamāneṣu stutam ātmānaṃ manyate evam atrāpy apo jāte vetasāvake apsu stutāsu stute eva bhavataḥ | śāntābhyo'dbhyo jātatvād vetasāvake svayam api śānte satyā yajamāninam ācchamayata iṣṭaitādṛśasya guṇasya vācyatvābhipreta |*
>
> "The word 'tu' (but) rules out the flaw of mismatched subject-matter. A figurative statement (guṇavāda) is intended here. Just as, in ordinary life, a person native to Kashmir, upon hearing Kashmir praised, considers himself praised — likewise here, the vetasa and avaka plants, being born in water, are themselves praised whenever water is praised. Being born from calm-natured waters, the vetasa and avaka plants are themselves calm-natured, and thereby pacify [any harm affecting] the yajamāna — this very quality is what the statement intends to convey."

That is: this text figuratively means simply, "O vetasa and avaka plants, sprung from the holy waters and therefore yourselves holy — drive away all evil from this yajamāna."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 445</div>

Sutra's meaning: in such statements, one portion states a quality belonging to what the other portion describes — so the two portions of the statement do share a genuine mutual connection. The word "tu" (but) resolves the flaw of "vaiyadhikaraṇya" (mismatched subject-matter) — where a vidhi addresses one thing and its arthavāda seems to address another entirely. As in ordinary life: "when Kashmir is praised, Devadatta, native to Kashmir, considers himself praised too" — likewise, praising "waters are calm" implicitly praises the vetasa and avaka plants growing in that water, since they share water's calm nature and thereby pacify misfortune for the yajamāna. Stating this shared quality is the arthavāda's whole purpose.

**A second example of this same principle:**

> सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् । यद् अप्क्षीयत कद् रजतं हिरण्यम् अभवत् स्वाप्कर्जतं हिरण्यम् अदक्षिणम् उत्पृजद् घि यो बर्हिषि ददाति पुरस्तात् संवत्सराद् ध्य् ए रुदन्ति तस्माद् बर्हिषि न देयम् ॥
> so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam | yad apkṣīyata kad rajataṃ hiraṇyam abhavat svāpkarjataṃ hiraṇyam adakṣiṇam utpṛjad ghi yo barhiṣi dadāti purastāt saṃvatsarād dhy e rudanti tasmād barhiṣi na deyam || (Taittiriya Samhita 1-5-1)
>
> सोऽरोदीद् यद् अरोदीत् तद् रुद्रस्य रुद्रत्वम् । यद् अपक्षीयत तद् रजतं हिरण्यम् अभवत् स्वापकर्जतं हिरण्यम् अदक्षिणम् । उत्पृज्य हि यो बर्हिषि ददाति पुरस्तात् संवत्सराद् अस्य रुदन्ति तस्माद् बर्हिषि न देयम् ॥
> *so'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam | yad apakṣīyata tad rajataṃ hiraṇyam abhavat svāpakarjataṃ hiraṇyam adakṣiṇam | utpṛjya hi yo barhiṣi dadāti purastāt saṃvatsarād asya rudanti tasmād barhiṣi na deyam ||*
>
> "He wept; because he wept, that is Rudra's own 'Rudra-ness.' What flowed out [from his weeping] became silver-gold; silver-gold is therefore not fit as a sacrificial fee. For whoever, discarding [this warning], gives it upon the sacrificial grass — within that year, there is weeping in his household. Therefore it should not be given upon the sacrificial grass."
