**This is the resolution.** The corresponding **vidhi** (injunction) here simply states: silver should not be given as the priest's fee at a sacrifice. The "Rudra wept" narrative is an **arthavāda** built entirely to reinforce that one rule — deriving the god Rudra's name from the root for "weeping," and then figuratively tying that weeping to silver ("what flowed from his tears became silver"). The intended, purely figurative point is simple: if silver is given as payment, there will be "weeping" — misfortune — in that household within the year. Sayana states plainly that there is **no literal truth** in the story that Rudra's tears turned into silver; the narrative exists solely to emphasize and recommend the vidhi against paying priests in silver, through a vivid, memorable etymological pun.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 446</div>

That is: "He (Rudra) wept — that is, cried. Because he wept, he came to be named 'Rudra.' The tears that fell from him became silver. Therefore, silver — being the very form of Rudra's tears — should not be given as sacrificial fee. If silver were given, within one year, weeping would befall the yajamāna and his household — meaning, a death might occur among his relatives. Therefore, silver should not be given in yajna." Here, the prohibition against silver (the vidhi) and the arthavāda align perfectly — declaring that avoiding silver means avoiding grief is exactly this arthavāda's purpose.

**Another example:**

> प्रजापतिर् वा इदम् एक आसीत् स अकामयत प्रजाः सृजेयेति स आत्मनो वपाम् उदखिदत् ताम् अग्नौ प्रास्रष्ट्राग् स्रजनस्यापरस्याम् अभवत् प्राग् अप्य् असमभवत् तस्या एतद् देवतायै अलभत तथैव स प्रजाः पशून् असृजत यः प्रजा-कामः पशु-कामः स्यात् स एतं प्राजापत्यं पशुं प्रजापतिम् एव स्वेन भागधेयेनोपधावति प्रजया पशुना
> prajāpatir vā idam eka āsīt sa akāmayata prajāḥ sṛjeyeti sa ātmano vapām udakhidat tām agnau prāsraṣṭrāg srajanasyāparasyām abhavat prāg apy asamabhavat tasyā etad devatāyai alabhata tathaiva sa prajāḥ paśūn asṛjata yaḥ prajā-kāmaḥ paśu-kāmaḥ syāt sa etaṃ prājāpatyaṃ paśuṃ prajāpatim eva svena bhāgadheyenopadhāvati prajayā paśunā (Taittiriya Samhita 2-1-1-4)
>
> "Prajāpati alone existed in the beginning. He desired: 'let me create offspring.' He tore out his own [abdominal] entrails and offered them into the fire. From that, before an[other] came into being, [a hornless goat] was born. He offered it to that same deity. In that same way, he created offspring and cattle. Therefore, whoever desires offspring and cattle should approach this Prajapati-goat — Prajapati himself — through his own portion, with offspring and cattle [as the sought result]."

That is: Prajapati, desiring offspring and cattle, tore out his own entrails and offered them as homa; from this, a hornless goat was produced. One desiring children, grandchildren, and cattle can obtain this benefit through a hornless goat. Stating this quality of the hornless goat — and thereby praising the underlying vidhi — is this arthavāda's whole purpose.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 448</div>

...the divine [deities], despite their divinity, were once ignorant of this — recognizing this, we should not consider it false just because it seems strange. As in the example: "if you drink guḍūcī (an herb), the hair on your head will grow" — such statements, even when their literal claim seems dubious, are accepted as encouraging trust in the wider practice.

Having now shown resolutions to the shastra-contradiction cases, we turn to those raised as contradicting direct sense-perception: "stenaṃ manaḥ, anṛtavādinī vāk" — and a further doubt about how arthavāda statements' apparent absurdity should be resolved is addressed via the next sutra.

### "Rūpātprayāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-11)

> हिरण्यं हस्ते भवत्य् अथ गृह्णाति त्यकं विधिः स्तोकमयम् अर्थवाद उच्यते । यथा लोके किम् पुरुषा देवदत्त एव । पूज्यते इव? देव-दत्ते पूज्यमाने पूज्यं स्वयम् इत्य् उच्यते ।
> hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti tyakaṃ vidhiḥ stokamayam arthavāda ucyate | yathā loke kim puruṣā devadatta eva | pūjyate iva? deva-datte pūjyamāne pūjyaṃ svayam ity ucyate |
>
> *(Introducing a new sutra concerned with arthavāda passages whose surface form appears to contradict what we plainly observe — here, gold "being in the hand" before the priest actually grasps it — resolved by recognizing this as ordinary hyperbolic emphasis, the same way one might say "isn't Devadatta the only person who matters" without literally denying every other person exists.)*

Sutra's meaning: statements whose surface appearance seems inconsistent [with reality], being simply common usage, must be understood as intending an emphatic (exaggerated) sense — not as literal factual claims.

As with the earlier examples ("stenaṃ manaḥ, anṛtavādinī vāk"), this next arthavāda-statement is used only to encourage a person toward what's genuinely worth pursuing — not to convey a literal factual claim. Gold [in the phrase] "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavati"...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 449</div>

We now explain the arthavāda praising the vidhi "haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" (Maitrayani Samhita 4-8-2-3). "Kimṛṣiṇā devadatta eva pūjayitavyaḥ" ("What! Is Devadatta the only person worthy of honor?") — such an expression doesn't imply others aren't worthy; it exists solely to *emphasize* Devadatta's own worthiness. Likewise, "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" ("gold comes to be in the hand, then he grasps it") — this arthavāda praises the vidhi that gold should be taken as sacrificial fee, by declaring gold's own preciousness.

In the same way, "stenaṃ manaḥ" ("the mind is a thief") should be read figuratively: thieves remain hidden and unseen; the mind too stays hidden within the body, unseen. Since concealment is a shared quality between thieves and the mind, the mind is compared to a thief — stating this figurative sense is exactly this statement's purpose.

Likewise, "anṛtavādinī vāk" ("speech is a false-speaker"): since speech is commonly observed, in ordinary human life, to speak falsely, one must grasp the figurative sense here too, setting aside a literal reading. As for "hiraṇyaṃ haste bhavaty atha gṛhṇāti" — that gold visibly sits in the hand is plain to everyone, not hidden or false at all; this arthavāda's purpose is simply to praise the vidhi by declaring gold worth wearing on the hand.

**On these falsehood-statements, the Taittiriya Brahmana adds:**

> अनृतं वै वाचा वदति । अनृतं मनसा ध्यायति । चक्षुर् वै सत्यम् । अद्या हि घृताह अदर्शम् इति । सत्यैव ॥
> anṛtaṃ vai vācā vadati | anṛtaṃ manasā dhyāyati | cakṣur vai satyam | adyā hi ghṛtāha adarśam iti | satyaiva || (Taittiriya Brahmana 1-14)
>
> "Speech indeed speaks falsehood; the mind indeed dwells on falsehood — but the eye is indeed truthful, for when one says 'I saw [it] today,' that itself is truth."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 450</div>

A sentence carries two kinds of meaning: one, the direct meaning conveyed by the words themselves — "the fire burns"; another, a further meaning conveyed indirectly through that literal sense as a stepping-stone — the "secondary meaning" (gauṇārtha), as in "Devadatta burns like fire," where "burning" must be reinterpreted (through anger, desire, etc.) to fit Devadatta sensibly. The first is the primary meaning; the second, the secondary meaning — meaning derived by pointing at a shared quality.

Having thus resolved the shastra-contradiction objection, we turn to the dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction with direct perception) examples — statements like "dhūma evāgnir divā dadṛśe" (only smoke, not flame, is visible by day) — addressed in the next sutra.

### "Dūra-bhūyastvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-12)

> अग्निर् ज्योतिर् ज्योतिर् अग्निः स्वाहा सायं जुहोति । सूर्यो ज्योतिर् ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा प्रातर् इत्य् एतौ विधी स्तोतुं सोऽर्थवादः । यस्माद् अर्चिर् दिना न दृश्ये तस्मात् केषां प्रयोक्ष्ये यस्माद् रात्रौ प्रयोक्ष्ये इत्य् एतं तयोर् मन्त्रयोः स्मृतिः क तस्माद् अग्नि-मन्त्रेण रात्रौ प्रयोक्ष्य इति । भूमार्चिस् सोमदर्शनोऽस्य प्राप्तिः । भूम्या दूर-भूयस्य गुणस्य विशिष्टे । भूम्य् असि हि दूरे पर्येऽग्न्येर् वैश्वादयोऽपि न विशिष्ट्या दृश्यन्ते । किं तु कृष्णा-दृश्येन तेषां दर्शनाभाव एव ।
> agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā sāyaṃ juhoti | sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā prātar ity etau vidhī stotuṃ so'rthavādaḥ | yasmād arcir dinā na dṛśye tasmāt keṣāṃ prayokṣye yasmād rātrau prayokṣye ity etaṃ tayor mantrayoḥ smṛtiḥ ka tasmād agni-mantreṇa rātrau prayokṣya iti | bhūmārcis somadarśano'sya prāptiḥ | bhūmyā dūra-bhūyasya guṇasya viśiṣṭe | bhūmy asi hi dūre parye'gnyer vaiśvādayo'pi na viśiṣṭyā dṛśyante | kiṃ tu kṛṣṇā-dṛśyena teṣāṃ darśanābhāva eva |
>
> अग्निर् ज्योतिर् ज्योतिर् अग्निः स्वाहा सायं जुहोति । सूर्यो ज्योतिर् ज्योतिः सूर्यः स्वाहा प्रातर् इत्य् एतौ विधी स्तोतुं सोऽर्थवादः । यस्माद् अर्चिर् दिना न दृश्ये तस्मात् केषां प्रयोक्ष्ये । यस्माद् रात्रौ प्रयोक्ष्ये इत्य् एतम् उभयोः मन्त्रयोः स्मरणं । तस्माद् अग्नि-मन्त्रेण रात्रौ प्रयोक्तव्य इति । भूयांश् चर्चिषो दर्शनम् अस्य प्राप्तिः । भूम्या दूर-भूयस्त्व-गुणस्य विशेषः । भूम्यां हि दूरे पर्य् अग्नेर् वैश्वादयोऽपि न विशेषेण दृश्यन्ते । किं तु कृष्णा-दृश्यत्वेन तेषां दर्शनाभाव एव ।
> *agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā sāyaṃ juhoti | sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā prātar ity etau vidhī stotuṃ so'rthavādaḥ | yasmād arcir dinā na dṛśye tasmāt keṣāṃ prayokṣye | yasmād rātrau prayokṣye ity etam ubhayoḥ mantrayoḥ smaraṇaṃ | tasmād agni-mantreṇa rātrau prayoktavya iti | bhūyāṃś carciṣo darśanam asya prāptiḥ | bhūmyā dūra-bhūyastva-guṇasya viśeṣaḥ | bhūmyāṃ hi dūre pary agner vaiśvādayo'pi na viśeṣeṇa dṛśyante | kiṃ tu kṛṣṇā-dṛśyatvena teṣāṃ darśanābhāva eva |*
>
> "'Agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā' [is offered] in the evening; 'sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā' [is offered] in the morning — this arthavāda exists to praise these two vidhis. Since flame is not visible by day, [one might ask] for what purpose should I use [the fire-mantra then]? — and since [it should be] used at night, this itself is the recollection [rationale] behind the two mantras: therefore the Agni-mantra must be used at night. The greater visibility of the flame [at night] is what's actually being conveyed — a distinction owing to the sheer distance [between earth and the visible daytime sky-glow]. For at a distance, in daylight, even conspicuous things like [smoke and] fire's other features are not seen distinctly — not because they don't exist, but simply because their dark-visible quality goes unseen [against the bright sky]."

Sutra's meaning: the "smoke by day, flame by night" arthavāda isn't a false claim about physical reality — it explains, and thereby reinforces, exactly which mantra (Sun or Agni) belongs to which time of day, with the visibility difference serving as a memorable, praise-oriented justification rather than a literal scientific claim. The two vidhis are "agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāheti sāyaṃ juhoti" and "sūryo jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāheti prātaḥ" (Ai. Brā. 5-5-6).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 451</div>

These are the two vidhis this arthavāda exists to praise. Since flame isn't visible by day, the sun-mantra suits the morning; since flame alone is visible at night, the fire-mantra suits the night — "day, the sun-mantra" is the praise these vidhis (mantras) receive.

The objection held this contradicts direct perception — flame *is* visible before our eyes, so how can the text say otherwise? The resolution: if a fire burns at a distance during daylight, the sun's superior brightness prevents the flame from being visible — only the dark smoke registers. This is confirmed by ordinary experience: with sufficient distance, even trees atop a hill lose their distinct shape and look like mere blades of grass. The same principle applies here.

**Turning to the second dṛṣṭi-virodha example:** "na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā" — "we don't even know whether we are brahmins or not." The next sutra addresses this.

### "Straparādhātkartuśca putradarśanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-13)

> प्रवरे प्रव्रियमाणे ब्रूयाद् देवाः पितरः इत्य् अस्य विधीस् ताकोऽयम् अर्थवादः । यदि यजमानो देवाः पितर इत्य् आदि-मन्त्रेण प्रवरम् अनुमन्त्र्येत इदानीम् अब्राह्मणो ब्राह्मणो भवेद् इत्य् असु-मन्त्रिणस् स्तुतिः । न चैतद् इति एतद् अज्ञान-वचनं दुर्जनत्व-गुणेन तत्र प्रयुज्यते । यत्र...
> pravare pravriyamāṇe brūyād devāḥ pitaraḥ ity asya vidhīs tāko'yam arthavādaḥ | yadi yajamāno devāḥ pitara ity ādi-mantreṇa pravaram anumantryeta idānīm abrāhmaṇo brāhmaṇo bhaved ity asu-mantriṇas stutiḥ | na caitad iti etad ajñāna-vacanaṃ durjanatva-guṇena tatra prayujyate | yatra...
>
> प्रवरे प्रव्रियमाणे ब्रूयाद् देवाः पितरः इत्य् अस्य विधेर् उपस्तुताकोऽयम् अर्थवादः । यदि यजमानो "देवाः पितरः" इत्य् आदि-मन्त्रेण प्रवरम् अनुमन्त्र्येत, तदानीम् अब्राह्मणोऽपि ब्राह्मणो भवेद् इत्य् अस्य मन्त्रस्य स्तुतिः । "न चैतद् विद्मः" इत्य् एतद् अज्ञान-वचनं दुर्जनत्व-गुणेन तत्र प्रयुज्यते । यत्र...
> *pravare pravriyamāṇe brūyād devāḥ pitaraḥ ity asya vidher upastutāko'yam arthavādaḥ | yadi yajamāno "devāḥ pitaraḥ" ity ādi-mantreṇa pravaram anumantryeta, tadānīm abrāhmaṇo'pi brāhmaṇo bhaved ity asya mantrasya stutiḥ | "na caitad vidmaḥ" ity etad ajñāna-vacanaṃ durjanatva-guṇena tatra prayujyate | yatra...*
>
> "'When the ancestral lineage (pravara) is about to be recited, one should say 'devāḥ pitaraḥ' (the fathers are as gods)' — this arthavāda exists to praise this vidhi. If the yajamāna were to recite his lineage using the mantra beginning 'devāḥ pitaraḥ,' then even one not [genuinely] a brahmin by birth would become a brahmin [through this recitation] — this is the praise conveyed for this mantra. The statement 'we do not know this' [regarding our own paternity] is an admission of uncertainty applied here on account of the difficulty of [verifying] such matters with certainty. Where..."

*(This introduces a genuinely striking rationale: since a child's biological paternity can never be verified with absolute certainty by ordinary means, the arthavāda's admission of doubt over lineage serves — somewhat paradoxically — to elevate the ritual recitation of ancestry itself as the more reliable and praiseworthy means of establishing one's brahmin status, rather than undermining the practice.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 452</div>

> स्त्रिया अपराधो भवति तत्र कर्तुर् उत्पादयितुर् जारस्यापि पुत्रो दृश्यते । अतः पत्युपपत्योर् उभयोः पुत्र-दर्शनात् कैदृश्यं ज्येष्ठ इदृशम् इति दुर्ज्ञानम् । अनेनाभिप्रायेण प्रयुक्तान् नास्ति तत्र दृष्टि-विरोधः । न हि तत्र दृश्यमानं स्व-ब्राह्मण्यम् अपह्रियत इव "न चैतद् विद्म" इत्य् असत्यसत्वम् ।
> striyā aparādho bhavati tatra kartur utpādayitur jārasyāpi putro dṛśyate | ataḥ patyupapatyor ubhayoḥ putra-darśanāt kaidṛśyaṃ jyeṣṭha idṛśam iti durjñānam | anenābhiprāyeṇa prayuktān nāsti tatra dṛṣṭi-virodhaḥ | na hi tatra dṛśyamānaṃ sva-brāhmaṇyam apahriyata iva "na caitad vidma" ity asatyasatvam |
>
> स्त्रिया अपराधो भवति तत्र कर्तुर् उत्पादयितुर् जारस्यापि पुत्रो दृश्यते । अतः पत्युपपत्योर् उभयोः पुत्र-दर्शनात् कीदृश्यम् ज्यायस इदृशम् इति दुर्ज्ञानम् । अनेनाभिप्रायेण प्रयुक्ताव् न अस्ति तत्र दृष्टि-विरोधः । न हि तत्र दृश्यमानं स्व-ब्राह्मण्यम् अपह्रियत इव "न चैतद् विद्मः" इत्य् असत्य-सत्त्वम् ।
> *striyā aparādho bhavati tatra kartur utpādayitur jārasyāpi putro dṛśyate | ataḥ patyupapatyor ubhayoḥ putra-darśanāt kīdṛśyam jyāyasa idṛśam iti durjñānam | anenābhiprāyeṇa prayuktāv na asti tatra dṛṣṭi-virodhaḥ | na hi tatra dṛśyamānaṃ sva-brāhmaṇyam apahriyata iva "na caitad vidmaḥ" ity asatya-sattvam |*
>
> "Where a woman commits an offense [of infidelity], the son may be seen to belong to her actual paramour, the true begetter. Therefore, given the possibility of the son belonging to either the husband or the paramour, which of the two is genuinely the case remains difficult to know with certainty. Understood with this intent, no contradiction with direct perception arises here — for one's own visible brahmin-status isn't thereby actually denied; the statement 'we do not know this' does not assert something false."

Sutra's meaning: because of a woman's infidelity, a son born [to her] might in fact be her lover's son (rather than her husband's) — therefore that son's true lineage cannot be determined with full certainty.

The statement "na caitad vidmo vayaṃ brāhmaṇā vā smo'brāhmaṇā vā" (Mai. Saṃ. 1-4-11) ("we don't know whether we are brahmins or not") is spoken by the officiating priests — who are, by definition, always brahmins. So why would doubt about one's own brahmin-status even arise? Isn't everyone supposed to simply know their own caste? The resolution: in ordinary human affairs, when a son is born, whom does he properly belong to — mother or father? A son always belongs to the father (not the mother), and it is well-established, both by common recognition and by shastra, that a son belongs to whichever caste his father belongs to. But in some cases, through a mother's infidelity, the son born to her may in fact have been fathered by her lover — in which case, though publicly treated as his legal father's son, he is, in strict truth, the lover's son, and takes the lover's own caste. Such situations are not at all uncommon in ordinary life. Therefore, as stated above, genuine doubt can arise even regarding whether "we" (the officiants) are truly brahmins — and this example is accordingly classified as a case of dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction with direct perception).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 453</div>

"Pravare pravriyamāṇe brūyād devāḥ pitaraḥ" (Maitrayani Samhita 1-4-11) is the vidhi: when reciting one's pravara (ancestral lineage), one should recite the mantra "devāḥ pitaraḥ." If the yajamāna does so, then even a non-brahmin becomes a brahmin through that mantra's power — this is the praise conveyed. The admission "na caitad vidma" ("we do not know") isn't a firm claim of ignorance, but a statement that certainty is genuinely unattainable: where a woman has erred, her son may in fact be her lover's child; since he is then socially treated as son to both the husband and the lover, whose son he truly is remains genuinely unclear — hence no contradiction with direct perception. "Na caitad vidma" is not meant to deny one's own plainly-evident brahmin status.

**Having resolved dṛṣṭi-virodha, we turn to the shastra-contradiction example still outstanding:** "ko hi tad veda yad yamuṣmin loke'sti vā na vā" ("who indeed knows whether that heavenly world exists or not"). The next sutra resolves this doubt.

### "Ākālikeṣṭā" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-14)

> दिक्षाश् चीकास्थानश् चास्थंश द्वार-विधिः । तस्य शेषोऽयं को हि तद् वेदेति । धूमाद्य्-अप्रद्रवस-परिकरेण प्रत्यक्षेण फलेन द्वार-विधिः स्तूयते । स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिरूपं तु फलम् आकालिकम् । अकाले भवम् आकालिकम् । विप्रुष्टकालीनं न त्रिदानीम्-तनम् इत्य् अर्थः । तस्येष्टा प्राप्तिम् इच्छा । सा च को हि तद् वेदेत्य् अज्ञयोऽस्थानस्य कारणम् । यथा भाविकालिकः पौत्र प्रसौत्रादि त्वं को निश्चेतुं शक्नुते । तद्वत् स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिर् भाविकालीनेत्य् गुण-योगाद् इष्टयोपस्थिते इष्टाभिप्रायः ।
> dikṣāś cīkāsthānaś cāsthaṃśa dvāra-vidhiḥ | tasya śeṣo'yaṃ ko hi tad vedeti | dhūmādy-apradravasa-parikareṇa pratyakṣeṇa phalena dvāra-vidhiḥ stūyate | svarga-prāptirūpaṃ tu phalam ākālikam | akāle bhavam ākālikam | vipruṣṭakālīnaṃ na tridānīm-tanam ity arthaḥ | tasyeṣṭā prāptim icchā | sā ca ko hi tad vedety ajñayo'sthānasya kāraṇam | yathā bhāvikālikaḥ pautra prasautrādi tvaṃ ko niścetuṃ śaknute | tadvat svarga-prāptir bhāvikālīnety guṇa-yogād iṣṭayopasthite iṣṭābhiprāyaḥ |
>
> दिक्ष्वातिकासन-करोति द्वार-विधिः । तस्य शेषोऽयं "को हि तद् वेद" इति । धूमाद्य्-अप्रदृश्य-सापरिकरेण प्रत्यक्षेण फलेन द्वार-विधिः स्तूयते । स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिरूपं तु फलम् आकालिकम् । अकाले भवम् आकालिकम् । विप्ररुष्ट-कालीनं न तद्-इदानीम्-तनम् इत्य् अर्थः । तस्येष्टा प्राप्तिम् इच्छा । सा च "को हि तद् वेद" इत्य् अज्ञान-वचन-कारणम् । यथा भावि-कालिकः पौत्र-प्रपौत्रादि-भावः को निश्चेतुं शक्नोति । तद्वत् स्वर्ग-प्राप्तिर् भावि-कालीनेत्य् अत्र गुण-योगाद् इष्टवती उपस्थितेत्य् अभिप्रायः ।
> *dikṣvātikāsana-karoti dvāra-vidhiḥ | tasya śeṣo'yaṃ "ko hi tad veda" iti | dhūmādy-apradṛśya-sāparikareṇa pratyakṣeṇa phalena dvāra-vidhiḥ stūyate | svarga-prāptirūpaṃ tu phalam ākālikam | akāle bhavam ākālikam | vipraruṣṭa-kālīnaṃ na tad-idānīm-tanam ity arthaḥ | tasyeṣṭā prāptim icchā | sā ca "ko hi tad veda" ity ajñāna-vacana-kāraṇam | yathā bhāvi-kālikaḥ pautra-prapautrādi-bhāvaḥ ko niścetuṃ śaknoti | tadvat svarga-prāptir bhāvi-kālīnety atra guṇa-yogād iṣṭavatī upasthitety abhiprāyaḥ |*
>
> "'Dikṣvātikāsana-karoti' is the 'dvāra' (doorway) vidhi [performed] on the east side [of the altar]. 'Ko hi tad veda' ('who indeed knows this') is the arthavāda completing that vidhi. The dvāra-vidhi is praised through an immediately observable result, involving smoke and similar visible signs. But the fruit in the form of attaining heaven belongs to a *future* time. 'Ākālika' means 'occurring at [some] non-present time' — that is, it pertains to a time yet to come, not the present moment. 'Iṣṭā' means the desire for its attainment. And 'ko hi tad veda' is precisely the reason this admission of not-knowing is stated — just as no one can say with certainty whether a grandson or great-grandson will be born [to them] in the future, likewise, heaven's attainment, belonging to future time, is here connected with this same quality — this is the statement's intended meaning."

That is: no one doubts whether a *future* good — a grandchild not yet born — will actually occur; such uncertainty about future events is simply the nature of anything not-yet-present. In exactly the same way, "who indeed knows whether heaven exists" isn't a skeptical denial of heaven's reality — it merely acknowledges that heaven's attainment, being a *future* fruit, shares this same natural uncertainty that all future outcomes carry. The statement doesn't undermine the vidhi's authority at all; it simply reflects how one properly speaks about anything belonging to time yet to come.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 454</div>

When statements like "**स्वर्गकामो यजेत**" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) declare that heaven and similar worlds exist, statements like "**को हि तद्वेद**" (*ko hi tad veda*), which appear to cast doubt on this, are classified as śāstra-dṛṣṭi-virodha (contradiction damaging the shastra's own authority).

**The resolution:** "ko hi tad veda," cited by the objector, is actually the closing portion of a longer statement about ritual "openings" (atikāśa) —

> दिक्ष्वातिकाशान् करोति ।
> *dikṣv-ātikāśān karoti |* (Taittiriya Samhita 6-1-1)

— occurring in the ancient-lineage section of the Soma-yaga discussion. Without grasping the whole statement, its final fragment cannot be properly understood in isolation. "**अतिकाश**" (*atikāśa*) refers to doorway-openings made on the eastern and other sides of the yajna-platform, allowing smoke to escape freely — this is the passage's directly observable, immediate benefit (dṛṣṭa-phala).

Heaven's attainment, by contrast, is a *future* fruit — it doesn't materialize immediately. It's therefore entirely natural to express uncertainty about exactly *when* it will occur; "ko hi tad veda" exists precisely to convey this. The sutra's word "**आकालिक**" (*ākālika*, आकाले भवम् आकालिकम् *ākāle bhavam ākālikam*) means "occurring at another [future] time" — not the present, but the time to come. No one can say with certainty what will become of children not yet born; likewise, no one can specify with certainty exactly when a future fruit like heaven's attainment will occur. This uncertainty about *timing* is what "ko hi tad veda" conveys — not doubt about heaven's *existence*.

Notably, slightly earlier in this very same passage, it's stated plainly:

> अम्बर्हिः को हि देवलोके मनुष्यलोकात् ।
> *ambarhiḥ ko hi devaloke manuṣyalokāt |*

— that the divine world and the human world are interwoven with each other. This confirms unambiguously that no genuine doubt about the existence of heaven and similar worlds is intended anywhere here.

**Turning to the last remaining shastra-dṛṣṭi-virodha example** —

> शोभतेऽस्य मुखं य एवं वेद ।
> *śobhate'sya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ veda |* (Tandya Mahabrahmana 20-16-6)

— the next sutra explains this.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 455</div>

### "Vidyā-praśaṃsā" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-15)

> सोऽयं गर्गत्रिरात्र-विधेः शेषः । तद्-विषयं वेदनम् अस्ति मुख-शोभा-हेतुः किम् उतानुष्ठानम् इति स्तूयते । यथा कर्णाभरणादिना मुखं शोभितं भवत्य् एवं वेदितुस् त्व् एव विकसितं वदनं शोभितम् इव शिष्यैर् उदीक्ष्यते । अतः शोभा-सादृश्य-गुण-योगात् शोभत इत्य् उच्यते ।
> so'yaṃ gargatrirātra-vidheḥ śeṣaḥ | tad-viṣayaṃ vedanam asti mukha-śobhā-hetuḥ kim utānuṣṭhānam iti stūyate | yathā karṇābharaṇādinā mukhaṃ śobhitaṃ bhavaty evaṃ veditus tv eva vikasitaṃ vadanaṃ śobhitam iva śiṣyair udīkṣyate | ataḥ śobhā-sādṛśya-guṇa-yogāt śobhata ity ucyate |
>
> सोऽयं गर्गत्रिरात्र-विधेः शेषः । तद्-विषयं वेदनम् अस्य मुख-शोभा-हेतुः किम् उतानुष्ठानम् इति स्तूयते । यथा कर्णाभरणादिना मुखं शोभितं भवत्य् एवं वेदितुस् त्व् एव विकसितं वदनं शोभितम् इव शिष्यैर् उदीक्ष्यते । अतः शोभा-सादृश्य-गुण-योगात् शोभत इत्य् उच्यते ।
> *so'yaṃ gargatrirātra-vidheḥ śeṣaḥ | tad-viṣayaṃ vedanam asya mukha-śobhā-hetuḥ kim utānuṣṭhānam iti stūyate | yathā karṇābharaṇādinā mukhaṃ śobhitaṃ bhavaty evaṃ veditus tv eva vikasitaṃ vadanaṃ śobhitam iva śiṣyair udīkṣyate | ataḥ śobhā-sādṛśya-guṇa-yogāt śobhata ity ucyate |*
>
> "This [statement] is the complement of the Gargatriratra vidhi. Merely knowing about that rite is itself said to be a cause of facial radiance — how much more so its actual performance! Just as ear-ornaments and similar adornments make a face radiant, so too a knower's beaming face is regarded by his students as radiant. This is stated on the basis of a shared quality resembling literal radiance."

Sutra's meaning: this is a statement made in praise of knowledge itself. "Śobhate'sya mukhaṃ ya evaṃ veda" (Tā. Ma. Brā. 20-16-6) ("his face shines, whoever knows this") is the Gargatriratra vidhi's companion arthavāda. The point: mere knowledge of this rite brings radiance to the face — how much more so its actual performance? Just as ear-ornaments enhance a face's radiance, knowing the Gargaratri and similar Vedic portions produces a genuine effect on the mind, which then emanates outward and becomes visible on the face as an unprecedented glow. The difference between the countenance of one endowed with knowledge and humility, and that of an ignorant fool, is perceptible even to ordinary people — so a Veda-scholar's facial radiance becomes swiftly apparent to his students and others.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 456</div>

...one recognizes: since the words emanating from such a man's mouth are pleasant to hear, coherent, and enthusiastic, his face is compared to something radiant — this is the intended sense here. "Shobha" (radiance) thus applies equally to wearing ornaments and to acquiring learning.

**Resolving the "swift descendant" example** ("asya prajāyāṃ vājī jāyate ya evaṃ veda") — this arthavāda companions the vidhi about reciting the Veda to one's son. Following the same a-fortiori logic already established: the son of a Veda-learned father becomes learned himself through his father's instruction, then serves as officiating priest in yajnas, thereby earning substantial wealth — hence food and livelihood come to him. This is the meaning of "a swift one is born to his offspring." Stating this quality is what connects the arthavāda to its vidhi — the arthavāda praises the vidhi's own underlying value.

**A note on "kaimutika-nyāya"** (a fortiori reasoning), used throughout these resolutions: derived from "kim uta tasya bhāvaḥ," meaning "how much more, or how much less." An illustrative verse:

> यौवनं धन-सम्पत्तिः प्रभुत्वम् अविवेकिता । एकैकम् अप्य् अनर्थाय किम् उ यत्र चतुष्टयम् ॥ सर्वाविनयानाम् एकः स्थानम् आयतनं किम् उत समन्वकम् ॥
> yauvanaṃ dhana-sampattiḥ prabhutvam avivekitā | ekaikam apy anarthāya kim u yatra catuṣṭayam || sarvāvinayānām ekaḥ sthānam āyatanaṃ kim uta samanvakam ||
>
> "Youth, wealth, power, and lack of discernment — even a single one of these can lead to ruin; how much more so when all four occur together! [Any] one alone is a source and dwelling-place for every kind of impropriety — how much more so when they converge!"

That is: imagine a person possessing these four qualities — youth, wealth, authority, and lack of judgment. Youth alone risks entanglement with others' spouses and similar misdeeds; wealth alone breeds attachment to sense-pleasures, neglect of duty, and cruelty toward the poor; authority alone leads to harming others; lack of discernment alone leaves no wrongdoing unattempted. Each single vice is sufficient to ruin a person's worth on its own. Four...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 457</div>

When these four vices converge, what more need be said? There's no doubt whatsoever that his worthiness is entirely destroyed. This logical device — comparing two things and pressing home the conclusion that follows — is precisely its purpose.

**Returning to resolve the "redundant fruit" objection ("anyānarthakyāt"):** "pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān āpnoti" and similar statements are explained next.

### "Sarvatvamādhikārikaṃ" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-16)

> पूर्णाहुतिं जुहुयाद् इत्य् अस्य विधेः शेषोऽयं । सर्व-कामावाप्ति-हेतुत्वेन स्तूयमानं पूर्णाहुतिर् इति सूच्यते । यथा सर्वे ब्राह्मणा भोजयितव्या इत्य् अत्र सर्वत्वं स्व-गृह-गत-ब्राह्मण-विषयं । एवं पूर्णाहुत्याः कर्म-सङ्गत्ये यत् फलं तस्याधिकारे प्रस्तावे सम्भावितं तद्-विषयं सर्वत्वं द्रष्टव्यम् । पूर्णाहुतेर् अभावे कर्माङ्ग-विकलं भवति । तच् चेन् नैश्चल्यं पूर्णाहुत्या समाधीयत इत्य् एष कामः । तस्मिन् सम्ये सत्याहवनीयाद्य्-अग्नि-होत्रादि-कर्मसु योग्यो भवतीत्य् अयम् अप्य् एष कामः । कैश् च कर्मभिस् तैस् तैस् फलं प्राप्यत इति कामान्तरम् ।
> pūrṇāhutiṃ juhuyād ity asya vidheḥ śeṣo'yaṃ | sarva-kāmāvāpti-hetutvena stūyamānaṃ pūrṇāhutir iti sūcyate | yathā sarve brāhmaṇā bhojayitavyā ity atra sarvatvaṃ sva-gṛha-gata-brāhmaṇa-viṣayaṃ | evaṃ pūrṇāhutyāḥ karma-saṅgatye yat phalaṃ tasyādhikāre prastāve sambhāvitaṃ tad-viṣayaṃ sarvatvaṃ draṣṭavyam | pūrṇāhuter abhāve karmāṅga-vikalaṃ bhavati | tac cen naiścalyaṃ pūrṇāhutyā samādhīyata ity eṣa kāmaḥ | tasmin samye satyāhavanīyādy-agni-hotrādi-karmasu yogyo bhavatīty ayam apy eṣa kāmaḥ | kaiś ca karmabhis tais tais phalaṃ prāpyata iti kāmāntaram |
>
> पूर्णाहुतिं जुहुयाद् इत्य् अस्य विधेः शेषोऽयं । सर्व-कामावाप्ति-हेतुत्वेन स्तूयमानं पूर्णाहुतिर् इति सूच्यते । यथा सर्वे ब्राह्मणा भोजयितव्या इत्य् अत्र सर्वत्वं स्व-गृह-गत-ब्राह्मण-विषयं । एवं पूर्णाहुत्याः कर्म-सङ्गत्ये यत् फलं तस्याधिकारे प्रस्तावे सम्भावितं तद्-विषयं सर्वत्वं द्रष्टव्यम् ।
> *pūrṇāhutiṃ juhuyād ity asya vidheḥ śeṣo'yaṃ | sarva-kāmāvāpti-hetutvena stūyamānaṃ pūrṇāhutir iti sūcyate | yathā sarve brāhmaṇā bhojayitavyā ity atra sarvatvaṃ sva-gṛha-gata-brāhmaṇa-viṣayaṃ | evaṃ pūrṇāhutyāḥ karma-saṅgatye yat phalaṃ tasyādhikāre prastāve sambhāvitaṃ tad-viṣayaṃ sarvatvaṃ draṣṭavyam |*
>
> "This is the complement of the vidhi 'one should offer the Purnahuti.' The Purnahuti is praised as the cause of obtaining all desired ends. Just as, in 'all brahmins should be fed,' the word 'all' refers only to the brahmins present in one's own household [not literally every brahmin everywhere] — so too here, the 'all' [in the Purnahuti's praise] should be understood as restricted to the specific fruit relevant to the ritual context (adhikāra) in which the Purnahuti occurs, given its connection to that particular rite. Its absence would leave that particular ritual act incomplete; ensuring its stability/completeness is the specific 'desire' addressed here — and, at that proper ritual moment, becoming fit for the Ahavaniya-fire, Agnihotra, and similar acts is likewise this same 'desire.' Different rites yield their own respective fruits through their own respective means."

Sutra's meaning: the word "sarva" (all), occurring in such statements, must be understood as scoped specifically to the ritual context at hand — not as an unrestricted, universal claim covering literally every possible desire across all rites.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 458</div>

so the word 'all' here depends on the qualified performer entitled to it — or, alternatively, pertains only to the specific ritual act named there.

> पूर्णाहुत्या सर्वान् कामानवाप्नोति ।
> *pūrṇāhutyā sarvān kāmān avāpnoti |*

is the concluding portion of the vidhi—

> पूर्णाहुतिं जुहुयात् ।
> *pūrṇāhutiṃ juhuyāt |*

That is, this statement is the final component of just the Purnahuti-rite's own context — not a claim about literally every desire attainable through any offering whatsoever. One cannot, for instance, obtain sky-flight powers through the Purnahuti — nothing of that kind is claimed here. Just as saying "today, all the rice should be cooked" means only the rice in one's own house (not all the rice in the world), and "all brahmins should be fed" means the brahmin-guests present at one's own house — "sarva" (all) is used in this restricted sense throughout. Likewise here: "all fruits" means the desires specifically attainable through the ritual acts (like Adhana) relevant to this particular context — obtainable through the Purnahuti-homa alone.

The Adhana rite currently underway would otherwise remain deficient; the Purnahuti remedies this deficiency — **that** is one benefit. By completing the Adhana rite through the Purnahuti, one gains qualification to perform subsequent rites (Agnihotra, and homas in the Ahavaniya and other fires) — a **second** benefit. And the fruit promised by shastra for properly performing these subsequent rites is **yet another** benefit. If it's asked whether these same benefits might apply equally to other oblations besides the Purnahuti — very well, let it be so; what is lost to us by that? Praising the Purnahuti in this way loses nothing at all.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 459</div>

Very well — Purnahuti is merely a component of one ritual act, and its fruit-declaring Shruti-statement, being arthavāda, is oriented purely toward praise, since it concerns substance, consecration, and ritual acts performed for another's (i.e., a further) sake. But "paśubandha-yājī sarvāl lokān abhijayati" ("one who performs pashubandha conquers all worlds") both prescribes an act *and* declares its own principal fruit — if we accept the Purnahuti resolution as given, doesn't one of these two statements become purposeless? The next sutra resolves this.

### "Phalasya karmaniṣpattesteṣāṃ lokavatparimāṇataḥ sārato vā phalaviśeṣaḥ syāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-17)

> पृथिव्य्-अन्तरिक्ष-स्वर्-गेषु तमलोक-अभिजय-रूपं फलं पशुबन्ध-कर्मणा निष्पाद्यत इति शेषः । इतरेषां च प्रेणादीनां फलानां कर्मान्तरेण परिमाणाधिक्यं सारत्वं वा सम्पद्येत । ततः फल-विशेषः स्याद् इति नास्त्य् अनर्थक्यम् । लोक-वद् अपि प्रत्यक्ष-प्रमाणः दृष्टान्तः । यथा लोके निष्टिकिनः खारी-परिमितापि रीणे री श्रियं निष्पाद्य अन्तरेन पुनः क्रिये सति परिमाणाधिक्यं भवति । यथा वा निष्ठेन वस्त्र-मात्रं अल्पे निष्पद्यकेन तु सार-भूतं संकुलम् । तथा भोगाधिक्यं भोग-सारत्वं वा कर्मान्तरेण दृश्यम् । ब्रह्म-हत्याया अपि मानस्याः स्वल्पाया वेदन-मात्रेण तरणं कायिक्या महत्या अश्वमेधेन इति नास्त्य् अनर्थक्यम् ।
> pṛthivy-antarikṣa-svar-geṣu tamaloka-abhijaya-rūpaṃ phalaṃ paśubandha-karmaṇā niṣpādyata iti śeṣaḥ | itareṣāṃ ca preṇādīnāṃ phalānāṃ karmāntareṇa parimāṇādhikyaṃ sāratvaṃ vā sampadyeta | tataḥ phala-viśeṣaḥ syād iti nāsty anarthakyam | loka-vad api pratyakṣa-pramāṇaḥ dṛṣṭāntaḥ | yathā loke niṣṭikinaḥ khārī-parimitāpi rīṇe rī śriyaṃ niṣpādya antarena punaḥ kriye sati parimāṇādhikyaṃ bhavati | yathā vā niṣṭhena vastra-mātraṃ alpe niṣpadyakena tu sāra-bhūtaṃ saṃkulam | tathā bhogādhikyaṃ bhoga-sāratvaṃ vā karmāntareṇa dṛśyam | brahma-hatyāyā api mānasyāḥ svalpāyā vedana-mātreṇa taraṇaṃ kāyikyā mahatyā aśvamedhena iti nāsty anarthakyam |
>
> *(Establishing that the fruit of "conquering all worlds" — across the terrestrial, mid-heaven, and celestial realms — is obtained through the pashubandha rite specifically, while other rites performed further can yield an increase in the same fruit's degree or quality, not a wholly separate fruit. The parallel given: just as a fixed amount of raw grain, when processed, might yield the same quantity of a superior grade, or a greater quantity of an ordinary grade, depending on how it's worked — so too, rites performed in addition to the pashubandha can enhance the degree or quality of the "world-conquest" already secured, rather than rendering the pashubandha's own promised fruit redundant. Similarly, the "crossing beyond mental brahmin-slaying sin through mere knowledge" (a smaller sin) versus "crossing beyond even grave bodily brahmin-slaying sin through the Ashvamedha" reflects the same scaling principle — no genuine redundancy exists.)*

That is: no true redundancy exists between such fruit-statements. Just as in ordinary life, the same quantity of raw material, processed differently, might yield either a greater quantity of an ordinary product or the same quantity of a superior one — rewards across different rites can likewise differ in *degree* or *quality* rather than being entirely separate, competing claims. The Pashubandha secures "conquest of all worlds" as its base fruit; further rites performed afterward enhance that same fruit's magnitude or refinement, rather than duplicating or invalidating it.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 460</div>

Sutra's meaning: variations in how ritual acts are performed produce corresponding variations in their fruits — differing in either quantity or quality, just as in ordinary human affairs.

Since the Pashubandha secures the yajamāna all worlds — earth, atmosphere, heaven, and beyond — and other rites promise similar fruits, what special value does the Pashubandha specifically offer? Answer: other rites do secure heaven and similar worlds, and so does Pashubandha — but through Pashubandha, one obtains a *more excellent* fruit than what other rites yield. Consider an ordinary example: one nishka (gold coin) buys one khāri of rice; two nishkas buy two khāris — an increase in *quantity*. Or, one nishka buys ordinary cotton cloth; two nishkas buy silk — an increase in *quality*. The first shows quantitative increase; the second, qualitative increase (silk being superior to cotton).

A further illustration: imagine two farmers cultivating separate fields. One farms carelessly — minimal ploughing, no fertilizer, weeds left unpulled. The other farms attentively — proper ploughing, timely fertilizer, weeding, and protection from pests and birds. At harvest time, both obtain grain — but not equally. One gets little, the other gets his due measure.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 461</div>

Both obtain grain, but not equally — this depends on the effort each invested. The same holds for rites: one yajna's fruit might be doubled by another, or differ in quality/richness rather than quantity — such variation in enjoyment (degree or refinement) arising from different rites is entirely understandable. A mentally-committed, comparatively minor sin like brahmin-slaying can be removed merely through others declaring it (with repentance); a grave, physically-committed sin of the same kind requires the Ashvamedha to remove it. Therefore, no genuine flaw of purposelessness (ānarthakya) applies to any of these statements.

**Now, addressing the two final examples:** the "nāntarikṣe na divi" (misplaced-prohibition) case, and the "babaraḥ prāvāhaṇiḥ" (non-eternal-name) case — the next sutra resolves both.

### "Aṃśayor arthe śleṣṭham" (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-18)

> अंशयोर् उदाहरणयोर् उत्तरं पूर्वोक्तेनैव द्रष्टव्यम् । अन्तरिक्षादौ चयन-निन्दा-रूपोऽर्थवादो हिरण्यं निधाय चेतव्यम् इत्य् अस्य विधेः शेषः । अतोऽत्र स्तुत्यर्थेन संयोगः समाहित इति प्राग्-उक्त-प्रकारेणैव समाधानम् । अन्तरिक्षे चयनस्यासम्भावाद् एव निषेधानुपपत्तिर् इति चेत् । भण्यताम् । ईशं तु बबराख्येन पुरुषेण मनुष्येण न विवक्षितः । किं तु बबर-ध्वनि-युक्तः प्रकर्षेण वहन-शीलो वायुर् वनस्पत्य्-आदि-शाखां निष्के विनाशयेऽविवक्षिते इष्टेद् उकरं प्रशस्तेन वहन-शीलो वायुर् वनायुर् वनाशान्तिश् चेतोकरं प्रस्थानाधिकरणे प्रोक्तं भावित-दोषाणां परि-...
> aṃśayor udāharaṇayor uttaraṃ pūrvoktenaiva draṣṭavyam | antarikṣādau cayana-nindā-rūpo'rthavādo hiraṇyaṃ nidhāya cetavyam ity asya vidheḥ śeṣaḥ | ato'tra stutyarthena saṃyogaḥ samāhita iti prāg-ukta-prakāreṇaiva samādhānam | antarikṣe cayanasyāsambhāvād eva niṣedhānupapattir iti cet | bhaṇyatām | īśaṃ tu babarākhyena puruṣeṇa manuṣyeṇa na vivakṣitaḥ | kiṃ tu babara-dhvani-yuktaḥ prakarṣeṇa vahana-śīlo vāyur vanaspaty-ādi-śākhāṃ niṣke vināśaye'vivakṣite iṣṭed ukaraṃ praśastena vahana-śīlo vāyur vanāyur vanāśāntiś cetokaraṃ prasthānādhikaraṇe proktaṃ bhāvita-doṣāṇāṃ pari-...
>
> अंशयोर् उदाहरणयोर् उत्तरं पूर्वोक्तेनैव द्रष्टव्यम् । अन्तरिक्षादौ चयन-निन्दा-रूपोऽर्थवादो "हिरण्यं निधाय चेतव्यम्" इत्य् अस्य विधेः शेषः । अतोऽत्र स्तुत्यर्थेन संयोगः समाहित इति प्राग्-उक्त-प्रकारेणैव समाधानम् । अन्तरिक्षे चयनस्यासम्भावाद् एव निषेधानुपपत्तिर् इति चेत्, भण्यताम् । इह तु "बबर" आख्येन पुरुषेण मनुष्येण न विवक्षितः, किं तु बबर-ध्वनि-युक्तः प्रकर्षेण वहन-शीलो वायुः विवक्षितः । ...
> *aṃśayor udāharaṇayor uttaraṃ pūrvoktenaiva draṣṭavyam | antarikṣādau cayana-nindā-rūpo'rthavādo "hiraṇyaṃ nidhāya cetavyam" ity asya vidheḥ śeṣaḥ | ato'tra stutyarthena saṃyogaḥ samāhita iti prāg-ukta-prakāreṇaiva samādhānam | antarikṣe cayanasyāsambhāvād eva niṣedhānupapattir iti cet, bhaṇyatām | iha tu "babara" ākhyena puruṣeṇa manuṣyeṇa na vivakṣitaḥ, kiṃ tu babara-dhvani-yuktaḥ prakarṣeṇa vahana-śīlo vāyuḥ vivakṣitaḥ | ...*
>
> "The answer for both these two remaining examples is to be understood exactly as already given. The arthavāda describing the [impossible] altar-construction on earth, air, or sky, taking the form of a censure, is the complement of the vidhi 'one should establish [the fire] having placed gold [beneath it].' Therefore, as already explained, its connection here serves a praise-oriented purpose, resolved in precisely the same manner as before. If it be objected that since building an altar in the sky is impossible, the prohibition itself is out of place — we reply: as already stated, [remember our earlier resolution]: here, 'Babara' does not refer to an actual man named Babara, but rather to the wind, characterized by the 'babara' sound, whose nature is to blow with great force..."

**This closes the entire arthavāda objection cycle.** Both remaining examples are answered by simply invoking resolutions already established: the "impossible prohibition" is, once again, understood as praise-oriented arthavāda attached to a genuine vidhi, and "Babara" is, exactly as resolved in the last adhikarana of the first pada, understood as onomatopoeia for wind's sound — not a historical person's name at all, closing off any claim that the passage depends on a "non-eternal" human referent.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 462</div>

> कृतत्स्वाद् अर्थवादानाम् अस्ति प्रामाण्यम् ॥ तत्र संग्रह-श्लोकाः । वायुर् वा इत्य् एवम् आदेर् अर्थवादस्य मानता । न विधेयेऽस्ति धर्मे किं किं वासौ तत्र विद्यते ॥ विध्य्-अर्थवाद-शब्दानां मिथोऽपेक्षा-सापेक्षया । नास्त्य् एक-वाक्यता धर्मे प्रामाण्यं संभवेत् तथा ॥ विध्य्-अर्थवादौ साकाङ्क्षौ प्राशस्त्य्-पुरुषार्थयोः । तेनैकवाक्यता तस्माद् अनादानं धर्म-मानके ॥
> kṛtatsvād arthavādānām asti prāmāṇyam || tatra saṃgraha-ślokāḥ | vāyur vā ity evam āder arthavādasya mānatā | na vidheye'sti dharme kiṃ kiṃ vāsau tatra vidyate || vidhy-arthavāda-śabdānāṃ mitho'pekṣā-sāpekṣayā | nāsty eka-vākyatā dharme prāmāṇyaṃ saṃbhavet tathā || vidhy-arthavādau sākāṅkṣau prāśasty-puruṣārthayoḥ | tenaikavākyatā tasmād anādānaṃ dharma-mānake ||
>
> *(Concluding summary verses, restating in condensed form: statements like "vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā" possess genuine authority; vidhi and arthavāda words, being mutually interdependent, form a single unified sentence — and precisely because of this eka-vākyatā (sentence-unity), no separate authority-claim need be denied to either portion where dharma is concerned; both are, together, oriented toward praising and accomplishing the highest human end. The verses are cited as (Jai. Nyā. Mā. 1-2-1).)*

Thus, since no genuine cause for lack of authority exists among the three portions present in the Veda — mantra, vidhi, and arthavāda — and since authority has now been established for each of these contested categories, **the Veda's authority, in every respect, stands proven.**

Sutra's meaning: the matter of these final two statements ("abhāgi-pratiṣedhāt," Jaimini Sutra 1-2-5, and "anitya-saṃyogāt," Jaimini Sutra 1-2-6) was already explained earlier — see the discussion on pages 438–439 above. "Na pṛthivyām agniś cetavyo nāntarikṣe na divi" (Taittiriya Samhita 5-2-12-2) — the arthavāda declaring that fire-altar construction should not occur on earth, atmosphere, or sky — is the complement of the vidhi "hiraṇyaṃ nidhāya cetavyam" (Taittiriya Samhita 5-2-7-1): "having placed a golden plate, one should establish [the fire] upon it." As already explained under the "praise-oriented" principle, this same resolution applies: granting that fire-altar construction in the sky is indeed impossible...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 463</div>

To clarify the vidhi's own primacy — that fire-altar construction must occur only upon a golden plate — the statement

> न पृथिव्यां नान्तरिक्षे न दिवि ।
> *na pṛthivyāṃ nāntarikṣe na divi |*
> "Fire-altar construction should not occur on earth, atmosphere, or sky"

serves as arthavāda. Read together, vidhi and arthavāda produce one coherent, complete meaning, with no genuine contradiction: the vidhi requires its praise-oriented arthavāda, and the arthavāda requires its vidhi — neither stands without the other, and together they form a single unified sentence.

**Turning to the already-known-fact example:**

> वायुर्वै क्षेपिष्ठा ।
> *vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā |*
> "The wind indeed blows most swiftly"

— a well-known fact restated — is likewise the companion of a vidhi concerning the animal-offering (paśu-vidhi). Read together with that vidhi, the arthavāda's meaning fits appropriately. These two examples together resolve the objection raised in "abhāgi-pratiṣedhāc ca."

**And resolving "anitya-saṃyogāt":**

> बबरः प्रावाहणिरकामयत ।
> *babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata |*

— the surface reading suggests "a man named Babara, son of Pravahana, desired [this]" — but this is not correct. "**बबरः**" (*babaraḥ*) — connected to the sound "ba-ba-ra" — and "**प्रावाहणिः**" (*prāvāhaṇiḥ*) — "that which blows forth forcefully" — together mean: the wind, which blows forcefully while making the "ba-ba-ra" sound, something we ourselves observe at all times. This proper understanding was already established in the final adhikarana of the first pada of Jaimini's sutras.

**In this way, resolving each flaw raised in the objection one by one, and providing coherent explanations, the siddhānta stands established: arthavāda statements are not without authority — they carry genuine authority.** Some summary verses from the extensive Jaimini-nyaya-mala are now cited to illustrate this conclusion, explained as follows—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 464</div>

In the Kamya-pashu-kanda section, two connected statements occur: **(1)** "vāyavyaṃ śvetam ālabheta bhūtikāmaḥ" — "one desiring prosperity should offer a white [animal] to Vayu" — the vidhi; **(2)** "vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyum eva svena bhāgadheyenopadhāvati sa enaṃ bhūtiṃ gamayati" — "since Vayu is the swiftest-natured deity, the wind-god swiftly grants prosperity to his own worshipper" — the arthavāda.

If it's asked whether the arthavāda words here, being independently capable of conveying complete sense on their own, are truly authoritative in matters of dharma — some argue that vidhi and arthavāda, being separate, unconnected statements, means arthavāda carries no such authority. But the correct view: the arthavāda praises the vidhi. Without it, a person, told merely "offer a white animal to Vayu," might hesitate — why perform this act at all, what fruit results? The arthavāda resolves this doubt directly, stating that prosperity comes swiftly through this offering — thereby motivating action. Since vidhi and its praising arthavāda are thus mutually connected, arthavāda carries the same authority in matters of dharma that vidhi does.

**Closing summary verses:**

> वेदोक्ते हेत्व्-अपेक्षत्वा-स्यास्ति विधेर् मानता इति चेत् । सत्यस्यै स्तुति-द्वारा नास्त्य् एति गुरुर् जगौ ॥ युक्तो वायुः क्षिप्रम् एव फलप्रद इति आको वायव्यम् आलभेत...
> vedokte hetv-apekṣatvā-syāsti vidher mānatā iti cet | satyasyai stuti-dvārā nāsty eti gurur jagau || yukto vāyuḥ kṣipram eva phalaprada iti āko vāyavyam ālabheta...
>
> *(If it be asked whether the vidhi's authority depends on a reason stated in the Veda, the teacher [Jaimini] declares: through the medium of praise, [that reason] is not absent. "Vayu, being fittingly swift, grants fruit quickly" — this indicates why one should offer the white animal to Vayu specifically...)*

## Chapter 11. Refuting, with Proper Proofs, the Claim That the Veda Is of Human Origin — the Defense of Apauruṣeyatva

*Original title: "Vēdavu puruṣaracitavemba vādavannu pramāṇapurassaravāgi nirākarisi vēdāpauruṣeyatvasamarthaneyu"*
**Printed pages 465–475 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 465</div>

...quickly gives fruit — this arthavāda instills the confidence needed to motivate action, making the vidhi's dependence on arthavāda's help genuinely necessary; an incomplete vidhi lacking this support would not be authoritative — this concludes the objection.

**The siddhānta's resolution:** if acts are performed with a desire for fruit — just as serving and pleasing a king yields reward — then pleasing a deity likewise yields fruit, and the scripturally-authoritative vidhi needs no further external proof. Stating that a fruit-giving deity should be worshipped conveys the *praiseworthiness* of the act itself; since vidhi and arthavāda together convey "the praiseworthy act should be performed," their mutual connection is thereby established, and the siddhānta concludes: vidhi statements are indeed authoritative.

**A summary reflection:** the Veda's karma-kāṇḍa (ritual-action portion) discusses attainable actions; its jñāna-kāṇḍa (knowledge portion) discusses the established truth of the Self. Only the karma-kāṇḍa concerns the Mimamsakas, who divide it into mantra, vidhi, and arthavāda — this framework doesn't apply to jñāna-kāṇḍa. Since no genuine cause for doubt remains regarding these three portions, and each is accepted as inherently self-authoritative, the entire Veda stands established as authoritative.

### A New Major Topic: The Statement of the Veda's Human Origin, Followed by Establishment of Its Non-Human Origin

> नन्व् एवम् अपि वेदस्य पौरुषेयत्वेन विप्रलम्भक-वाक्यवद् अप्रामाण्यं स्यात् । पौरुषेयत्वं च प्रथम-साध्ये पूर्वपक्षे जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास (पुर्व मिमम्स १-१-२७–३२) । वेदांश्ये सन्निकर्षं पुरुषाख्या ॥
> nanv evam api vedasya pauruṣeyatvena vipralambhaka-vākyavad aprāmāṇyaṃ syāt | pauruṣeyatvaṃ ca prathama-sādhye pūrvapakṣe jaiminiḥ sūtrayāmāsa (Purva Mimamsa 1-1-27–32) | vedāṃśye sannikarṣaṃ puruṣākhyā || (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-27)
>
> नन्व् एवम् अपि वेदस्य पौरुषेयत्वेन विप्रलम्भक-वाक्यवद् अप्रामाण्यं स्यात् । पौरुषेयत्वं च प्रथम-साध्ये पूर्वपक्षे जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास । वेदेऽंश्ये सन्निकर्षं पुरुषाख्या ॥
> *nanv evam api vedasya pauruṣeyatvena vipralambhaka-vākyavad aprāmāṇyaṃ syāt | pauruṣeyatvaṃ ca prathama-sādhye pūrvapakṣe jaiminiḥ sūtrayāmāsa | vede'ṃśye sannikarṣaṃ puruṣākhyā ||*
>
> "But even granting all this, might the Veda still be unauthoritative on account of its human origin — like the speech of one who utters a deliberate falsehood? Jaimini formulates, as the very first matter to be established, the objection (pūrvapakṣa) asserting the Veda's human origin: 'Within Vedic portions, there occurs mention connecting to specific persons' (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-27)."

This opens a genuinely major new discussion — one of the most significant debates in all of Mimamsa philosophy: whether the Veda is of human authorship (pauruṣeya) or entirely without human origin (apauruṣeya). Jaimini himself first states the objection favoring human authorship, before Sayana works through its resolution.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 466</div>

> तेऽत्र दृष्टान्ततया समुच्चीयन्ते । यथा रघुवंशादय इदानीम्-तनास् तथा वेदा अपि । न तु वेदा अनादयः । अत एव वेद-कर्तृत्वेन पुरुषा आम्नायन्ते । व्यासासिकं भारतम्, वाल्मीकीयं रामायणम् इत्य् अत्र यथा भारतादि-कर्तृत्वेन व्यासादिं व्यपदिश्य आम्नायन्ते तथा काथकं कौथुमं तैत्तिरीयम् इत्य् एवं तथा वेद-शाखा-कर्तृत्वेन कथादीनाम् आख्यातत्वाद् वेदाः पौरुषेयाः । नन्व् इतीनाम् एव सतां वेदानाम् अध्याय-वंश-सम्प्रदाय-प्रवर्तकत्वेन काठकादि-समाख्या स्याद् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> te'tra dṛṣṭāntatayā samuccīyante | yathā raghuvaṃśādaya idānīm-tanās tathā vedā api | na tu vedā anādayaḥ | ata eva veda-kartṛtvena puruṣā āmnāyante | vyāsāsikaṃ bhāratam, vālmīkīyaṃ rāmāyaṇam ity atra yathā bhāratādi-kartṛtvena vyāsādiṃ vyapadiśya āmnāyante tathā kāthakaṃ kauthumaṃ taittirīyam ity evaṃ tathā veda-śākhā-kartṛtvena kathādīnām ākhyātatvād vedāḥ pauruṣeyāḥ | nanv itīnām eva satāṃ vedānām adhyāya-vaṃśa-sampradāya-pravartakatvena kāṭhakādi-samākhyā syād ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "These [book-examples] are cited here as parallel illustrations: just as the Raghuvamsha and similar works belong to recent times, the Vedas too [are argued to be recent] — the Vedas are not beginningless. This is precisely why persons are cited as the Veda's authors. Just as, in 'Vyāsāsikaṃ Bhāratam' (Vyasa's Bharata) and 'Vālmīkīyaṃ Rāmāyaṇam' (Valmiki's Ramayana), Vyasa and others are explicitly named as authors, so too, in 'Kāthakam,' 'Kauthumam,' 'Taittirīyam,' and similar [Vedic school-names], Katha and other [sages] are named as authors of their respective Vedic branches — the Vedas are therefore of human origin. [An objector might counter:] perhaps such names as 'Kathaka' arose simply because these individuals were the ones who established the tradition of study and transmission [of an already-existing text] — anticipating this, the answer follows in the next sutra."

Sutra's meaning: some hold that the Vedas were composed by human authors, because the Veda's various portions bear many names — and these names are the names of the persons who composed them. Jaimini himself first constructs this objection in his Purva-Mimamsa-sutra, before establishing the Veda's non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) in response.

Some argue that the Vedas, like recent literary works, were composed by specific persons not long ago. Their reasoning: everyone knows the Raghuvamsha and similar works, composed by poets like Kalidasa, are recent compositions. By the same logic, the Vedas too are recent works composed by certain persons. The word "ca" ("too") in the sutra signals this comparison — just as Raghuvamsha and similar works are human-composed, so too are the Vedas.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 467</div>

It cannot be said the Vedas are beginningless — it is customary to attach the names of composers alongside them, exactly as with "Vyāyasikaṃ bhāratam" (Vyasa's Bharata) and "Vālmīkīyaṃ rāmāyaṇam" (Valmiki's Ramayana), which clearly name their authors. Similarly, "Kāthaka," "Kauthuma," "Taittiri," and "Pippalāda" name the actual composers of their respective Vedic branches. Therefore, the Vedas are human-composed works. (This concludes the first argument of the objection.)

**A possible counter-response, and a further objection anticipating it:** some might reply that Katha and similar figures were merely teachers who established a tradition of study — their students' recitation-lineage simply came to bear the teacher's name, without implying literal authorship. Anticipating and questioning this defense, a further sutra advances another argument.

### "Anitya-darśanāc ca" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-28)

> अनित्या जनन-मरणवन्तो बबरादयो वेदे श्रूयन्ते । बबरः प्रावाहणिर् अकामयत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित ७-१-१०-२) कुसुरुबिन्द औद्दालकिर् अकामयत (तैत्तिरिय सम्हित ७-२-२-१) इति । तथा सति बबरादिभ्यः पूर्वम् अभावाद् अनित्या वेदाः । विमतं वेद-वाक्यं पौरुषेयं सांक्यत्वात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवद् इत्य् अनुमान-समुच्चयार्थश् च कारः ॥
> anityā janana-maraṇavanto babarādayo vede śrūyante | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata (Taittiriya Samhita 7-1-10-2) kusurubinda auddālakir akāmayata (Taittiriya Samhita 7-2-2-1) iti | tathā sati babarādibhyaḥ pūrvam abhāvād anityā vedāḥ | vimataṃ veda-vākyaṃ pauruṣeyaṃ sāṃkyatvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavad ity anumāna-samuccayārthaś ca kāraḥ ||
>
> अनित्या जनन-मरणवन्तो बबरादयो वेदे श्रूयन्ते । बबरः प्रावाहणिर् अकामयत । कुसुरुबिन्द औद्दालकिर् अकामयत इति । तथा सति बबरादिभ्यः पूर्वम् अभावाद् अनित्या वेदाः । विमतं वेद-वाक्यं पौरुषेयं वाक्यत्वात् कालिदासादि-वाक्यवद् इत्य् अनुमान-समुच्चयार्थश् च "च"-कारः ॥
> *anityā janana-maraṇavanto babarādayo vede śrūyante | babaraḥ prāvāhaṇir akāmayata | kusurubinda auddālakir akāmayata iti | tathā sati babarādibhyaḥ pūrvam abhāvād anityā vedāḥ | vimataṃ veda-vākyaṃ pauruṣeyaṃ vākyatvāt kālidāsādi-vākyavad ity anumāna-samuccayārthaś ca "ca"-kāraḥ ||*
>
> "Non-eternal beings, subject to birth and death — Babara and similar figures — are spoken of in the Veda: 'Babara, son of Pravahana, desired [this]' (Taittiriya Samhita 7-1-10-2); 'Kusurubinda, son of Uddalaka, desired [this]' (Taittiriya Samhita 7-2-2-1). This being so, the Vedas cannot have existed before Babara and these other figures — therefore the Vedas are not beginningless. The disputed Veda-statement is of human origin, since it is a statement [like any other] — just like statements by Kalidasa and similar poets. The word 'ca' (also) here links this inferential argument to what was said before."

Sutra's meaning: since the Vedas contain descriptions of non-eternal things — names of persons and similar — the Vedas, discussing such non-eternal matters, are themselves non-eternal, that is, composed by persons. (This is a further objection.)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 468</div>

In the Veda, statements occur: "babaraḥ prāvāhaṇeḥ kāmayata" ("Babara, son of Pravahana, desired") and "kusurubinda auddālakir akāmayata" ("Kusurubinda, son of Uddalaka, desired"). Since Babara and Kusurubinda are human, they're subject to birth, death, and similar changes — non-eternal beings. Statements discussing such figures necessarily postdate their birth; these Vedic passages cannot have existed before those persons lived. Therefore, the Vedas are non-eternal — and, like the works of poets such as Kalidasa, human-composed. The word "ca" ("also") in the sutra marks this as an additional argument, beyond the earlier human-authorship claim, specifically establishing the Veda's non-eternality.

**Having thus completed the objection — that the Veda is human-composed and, discussing non-eternal things, is itself non-eternal — the siddhānta (resolution), that the Veda is in fact apauruṣeya (non-human in origin) and eternal, is now established in the sutras that follow.**

### The Siddhāntin's Resolution Begins

### "Uktaṃ tu śabda-pūrvakam" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-29)

> तु-शब्दो वैमानाम् अनित्यत्वं वारयति । शब्दस्य वेद-रूपस्य कथादि-पुरुषेभ्यः पूर्वत्वम् अनादित्वं प्राचीनैर् एव सूत्रे उक्तम् । "औत्पत्तिकस् तु शब्दस्यार्थेन सम्बन्धः" (पुर्व मिमम्स १-१-५) इत्य् अस्मिन् सूत्रे औत्पत्तिक-शब्देन सर्वेषां शब्दानां वेदानां तद्-अर्थानां तद्-उभय-सम्बन्धानां च नित्यत्वं प्रतिज्ञायोक्तराभ्यां शब्दाधिकरण-वाक्याधिकरणाभ्याम् उपसादितत्वात् तर्हि कथाद्य्-आख्याया गतिः का शङ्क्य सम्प्रदाय-प्रवर्तनापेक्षयैव उपसद्यत इत्य् उत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> tu-śabdo vaimānām anityatvaṃ vārayati | śabdasya veda-rūpasya kathādi-puruṣebhyaḥ pūrvatvam anāditvaṃ prācīnair eva sūtre uktam | "autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena sambandhaḥ" (Purva Mimamsa 1-1-5) ity asmin sūtre autpattika-śabdena sarveṣāṃ śabdānāṃ vedānāṃ tad-arthānāṃ tad-ubhaya-sambandhānāṃ ca nityatvaṃ pratijñāyoktarābhyāṃ śabdādhikaraṇa-vākyādhikaraṇābhyām upasāditatvāt tarhi kathādy-ākhyāyā gatiḥ kā śaṅkya sampradāya-pravartanāpekṣayaiva upasadyata ity uttaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "The word 'tu' (but) rules out the [claim of] non-eternality [regarding sound]. That the sound constituting the Veda existed prior to — and independently of — Katha and similar persons was already stated by the ancient [sages] in the sutra: 'the connection between word and meaning is innate/original' (Purva Mimamsa 1-1-5). In this sutra, by the term 'autpattika' (innate), the eternality of all words, of the Vedas, of their meanings, and of the very relationship between the two, was already established through both the assertion and its subsequent proof, across the sections on word (śabdādhikaraṇa) and sentence (vākyādhikaraṇa). One might then ask: what, then, is the actual purpose of names like 'Kathaka'? Anticipating this doubt, the answer is that such names arise solely from the need to designate who established a given tradition [of transmission] — this is now formulated as the resolution."

**This is the pivot of the entire debate.** The Veda's own sound (śabda) is eternal and precedes even sages like Katha — already established earlier in the very foundational discussion of word-meaning relationships. The names "Kathaka" and similar do not indicate authorship at all — they simply mark which teacher established a particular tradition of transmission.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 469</div>

Sutra's meaning: it was already established that words — including those constituting the Vedas — are eternal. The word "tu" rules out the claim of non-eternality: the Veda's own sound-form existed even before figures like Katha, its beginninglessness having already been established through a sequence of prior sutras — from "karmaike tatra darśanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-6) through "liṅgadarśanāc ca" (1-1-23), in 18 sutras, the eternality of words was established; this is the sixth adhikarana of the first pada of the first adhyaya of Jaimini's own Purva-Mimamsa-sutra. (These 18 sutras are not explained in this Bhashya-Bhumika; interested readers may consult them there; they are not set out here for fear of the book growing too long.)

In the sutra "autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena sambandhaḥ" (Jai. Sū. 1-1,5), the word *autpattika* (natural, eternal) makes the pledge that the relation between all words and their meanings is eternal, and this is established in the adhikaranas that follow. (The 18 sutras mentioned above are the śabda-adhikaraṇa; the adhikarana made of the three sutras that follow is the vākya-adhikaraṇa. These sutras are not explained in this Bhumika.)

**One might then ask: why, then, do names like "Kathaka" appear at all?** The next sutra answers: these names arose because these persons propagated Vedic knowledge through teaching and recitation.

### "Abhyāsa-pravacanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-30)

> अस्त्य् एव आख्याया गतिः । तेषां परं बबराद्य्-अनित्य-दर्शनं । यद् उक्तं तस्य किम् उत्तरम् इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> asty eva ākhyāyā gatiḥ | teṣāṃ paraṃ babarādy-anitya-darśanaṃ | yad uktaṃ tasya kim uttaram ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "There does indeed exist [a valid] explanation for these names. As for the remaining objection — the appearance of non-eternal figures like Babara — what answer can be given to that? Anticipating this doubt, the resolution is formulated next."

Sutra's meaning: this is the correct interpretation of names like "Katha" and similar. This resolves the entire naming-based objection. But regarding mantras that discuss non-eternal beings like Babara — what should be said about this? The next sutra answers this remaining doubt.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 470</div>

Sutra's meaning: it is customary to name each Vedic branch (śākhā) after the celebrated rishi who traditionally taught it, according to a fixed method, to his students, after becoming proficient in that portion.

Take the Kāthaka-śākhā as an example: this doesn't mean the branch was *composed* by a man named Katha — rather, teachers who mastered that branch taught it to their students in a fixed, traditional sequence, and among them was one particularly gifted teacher named Katha, after whom the branch came to be named. The same holds for other branches.

**Very well — but what of "Babara" and similar words referring to non-eternal persons?**

### "Paraṃ tu śruti-sāmānya-mātram" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-31)

> यत् परं बबरादिकं तच् छब्द-सामान्यम् एव न तु मनुष्यो बबर-नामकोऽत्र प्रतिपाद्यते । बबर-ध्वनि-युक्त प्रवहन-स्वभावस्य वायोर् वचः शक्यत्वात् । ननु वेदे क्वचिद् एवं श्रूयते । वनस्पतिः सत्रम् आसत सर्पाः सत्रम् आसतेति । तत्र वनस्पतीनाम् अचेतनत्वात् सर्पाणां चेतनत्वेऽपि विद्या-रहितत्वात् तद्-अनुष्ठानं न सम्भवति । अत उन्मत्त-बाल-प्रलपित-मद्रकाणि इत्य् आदिर् वेदो मनुष्य-कृत इत्य् आशङ्क्योत्तरं सूत्रयति ॥
> yat paraṃ babarādikaṃ tac chabda-sāmānyam eva na tu manuṣyo babara-nāmako'tra pratipādyate | babara-dhvani-yukta pravahana-svabhāvasya vāyor vacaḥ śakyatvāt | nanu vede kvacid evaṃ śrūyate | vanaspatiḥ satram āsata sarpāḥ satram āsateti | tatra vanaspatīnām acetanatvāt sarpāṇāṃ cetanatve'pi vidyā-rahitatvāt tad-anuṣṭhānaṃ na sambhavati | ata unmatta-bāla-pralapita-madrakāṇi ity ādir vedo manuṣya-kṛta ity āśaṅkyottaraṃ sūtrayati ||
>
> "The remaining case — 'Babara' and similar — is simply a matter of shared sound; no man actually named Babara is being spoken of here. The wind, characterized by the sound 'babara' and whose very nature is to blow forth (pravahana), is capable of being described this way. But one might object: don't we find such statements as 'the trees performed a sattra [ritual session]; the serpents performed a sattra'? Trees are insentient; serpents, though sentient, lack knowledge — for either to actually perform such a rite is impossible. Given this, and given examples like the babble of a madman or child ('jaradgavo gāyati madrakāṇi'), it would seem the Veda must be human-composed after all. Anticipating this doubt, the resolution follows in the next sutra."

Sutra's meaning: among Vedic words, some words resembling persons' names are simply that — ordinary shared words. They do not actually indicate any specific human person.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 471</div>

In the case under examination, though the word "Babara" appears to name a man, it is not actually a proper name — merely an ordinary word. Combined with the sound "ba-ba-ra," it means "wind blowing forcefully." "Babara" is therefore not any man's name.

**Now, regarding statements like "vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata"** (the plants/trees performed the sacrifice) and "sarpāḥ satram āsata" (the serpents performed the sacrifice): since trees are insentient, and serpents, though sentient, lack the faculties of learning and understanding, neither could genuinely participate in a yajna. Given such statements resembling the meaningless babble of madmen or small children — like "jaradgavaḥ kambalapādukābhyāṃ dvāri sthito gāyati madrakāṇi..." — one might conclude the Veda cannot be non-human in origin, and must have been composed by some unwise person. The next sutra answers this.

### "Kṛte cāviniyoge syāt karmaṇaḥ samatvāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-32)

> यदि ज्योतिष्टोमादि-वाक्यं केनचित् पुरुषेण क्रियेत तदानीं कृते तस्मिन् ज्योतिष्टोमे स्वर्ग-साधनत्वे ज्योतिष्टोमस्य विनियोगो न स्यात् । साध्य-साधन-भावस्य पुरुषेण ज्ञातुम् अशक्यत्वात् । श्रुत्युक्तत्व तु विनियोगो । ज्योतिष्टोमेन स्वर्ग-कामो यजेतेति । न चैतद् उक्त्वा वाक्य-सादृश लौकिक-वाक्यवद् व्यवहरण इति कर्तव्यता-रूपाप्सि प्रभेर् अस्पीताया भावनाया अवगमात् । लोके हि ब्राह्मणासोज्जेदिकिपिधौ किं केन कथमित्य् आकाङ्क्षायां तृप्तिं दुग्ध-पशादि-संसादि-परिवेषण-प्रकारेणेति यद् वेच्यते तथा ज्योतिष्टोम-विधाव् अपि स्वर्गम् उद्दिश्य सोमेन द्रव्येण दीक्षणीयाद्य्-अङ्गोपकार-प्रकारेणेत्य् एत्येते कथमुक्त्वा वाक्य-सदृशं भवेत् ।
> yadi jyotiṣṭomādi-vākyaṃ kenacit puruṣeṇa kriyeta tadānīṃ kṛte tasmin jyotiṣṭome svarga-sādhanatve jyotiṣṭomasya viniyogo na syāt | sādhya-sādhana-bhāvasya puruṣeṇa jñātum aśakyatvāt | śrutyuktatva tu viniyogo | jyotiṣṭomena svarga-kāmo yajeteti | na caitad uktvā vākya-sādṛśa laukika-vākyavad vyavaharaṇa iti kartavyatā-rūpāpsi prabher aspītāyā bhāvanāyā avagamāt | loke hi brāhmaṇāsojjedikipidhau kiṃ kena kathamity ākāṅkṣāyāṃ tṛptiṃ dugdha-paśādi-saṃsādi-pariveṣaṇa-prakāreṇeti yad vecyate tathā jyotiṣṭoma-vidhāv api svargam uddiśya somena dravyeṇa dīkṣaṇīyādy-aṅgopakāra-prakāreṇety etyete kathamuktvā vākya-sadṛśaṃ bhavet |
>
> *(Establishing that no human could have devised the jyotiṣṭoma ritual specifically as a means to heaven, since the cause-effect relationship between this ritual and that reward is fundamentally beyond ordinary human observation — only revealed knowledge could establish such a connection. If the Veda's ritual-injunctions were merely human invention, they would resemble ordinary practical speech (like a cooking recipe explaining how to satisfy hunger through familiar, observable means), but they do not — the Veda instead prescribes specific ritual acts toward an entirely unverifiable, unobservable future goal, which no human composer could have devised on their own experience.)*

Sutra's meaning: had a human composed statements about the Jyotishtoma and similar rites, the assertion that this specific rite serves as the means to attain heaven simply could not have followed such composition — because no human being can perceive that a given ritual act and its future heavenly result stand in a genuine cause-and-effect relationship. Yet the Veda does contain exactly this kind of assertion, unverifiable by any human means.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 472</div>

> शब्दः स शब्दार्थ इति न्याय-विद आहुः । ज्योतिष्टोमादि-वाक्यस्य विधायकत्वाद् अनुष्ठाने तात्पर्यम् । वनस्पत्य्-आदि-सत्र-वाक्यस्यार्थवादत्वात् संशंसायां तात्पर्यम् । न चाविद्यमानेनापि कर्मणा शक्यते । अचेतना अविद्यांसोऽपि सत्रम् अनुष्ठितवन्तः । किं पुनस् तेऽनाविद्यांसो ब्राह्मणा इति सत्र-स्तुतिः । ...
> śabdaḥ sa śabdārtha iti nyāya-vida āhuḥ | jyotiṣṭomādi-vākyasya vidhāyakatvād anuṣṭhāne tātparyam | vanaspaty-ādi-satra-vākyasyārthavādatvāt saṃśaṃsāyāṃ tātparyam | na cāvidyamānenāpi karmaṇā śakyate | acetanā avidyāṃso'pi satram anuṣṭhitavantaḥ | kiṃ punas te'nāvidyāṃso brāhmaṇā iti satra-stutiḥ | ...
>
> *(A closing argument: the jyotiṣṭoma-type statements are genuine injunctions aimed at real ritual performance, while the trees/serpents statements are arthavāda — praise-oriented, not literal factual claims. Their real point: "even insentient trees and ignorant serpents managed to complete a sacrificial session — how much more so learned brahmins!" — the very same a-fortiori praise-logic seen throughout the earlier arthavāda discussion, not evidence of human authorship at all.)*

That is: nor can this be compared to a madman's babble — the jyotiṣṭoma injunction, like any everyday command, implicitly carries its goal, its means, and its method. Just as "feed the brahmins" naturally prompts the questions why, with what, and how — answered as "to satisfy them," "with rice," "accompanied by vegetables and broth" — so too the jyotiṣṭoma command carries heaven as its stated goal, soma as its instrument, and the prescribed subsidiary rites as its method. How could this resemble a madman's talk?

**Closing summary verse:**

> तस्मान् नास्ति वेदस्य पौरुषेयत्वम् । अत्र संग्रह-श्लोकः । पौरुषेयं न वा वेदनास्त्य् अपौरुषेयता । काथकादि-समाख्यानाद् वाच् छास्य वाक्यवत् । समाख्यानं प्रवचनाद् आचार्यत्वाच् च तत् पराहतम् । तत्-कर्तृ-स्मालम्भेन स्यात् कोऽपौरुषेयते ॥
> tasmān nāsti vedasya pauruṣeyatvam | atra saṃgraha-ślokaḥ | pauruṣeyaṃ na vā vedanāsty apauruṣeyatā | kāthakādi-samākhyānād vāc chāsya vākyavat | samākhyānaṃ pravacanād ācāryatvāc ca tat parāhatam | tat-kartṛ-smālambhena syāt ko'pauruṣeyate || (Jaimini-nyaya-mala 11-8)
>
> "Therefore, the Veda has no human origin. Summary verse: is the Veda human-composed, or not? [The objection holds it is,] on account of names like 'Kathaka' and its being a collection of statements — but this naming is refuted, [properly] explained instead by teaching-activity and preceptorship. And by touching upon [correctly identifying] its true, non-human 'author' [i.e., the eternal Word itself], how could its non-human-origin status be anything but established?"

**Badarayana's parallel argument, via the Vedanta-sutra:**

> ननु भगवता बादरायणेन वेदस्य ब्रह्म-कार्यत्वं सूत्रितम् । "शास्त्र-योनित्वात्" इति (वेदन्त सुत्र १-१-३) ऋग्वेदादि-शास्त्रत्वाद् वृद्ध-सर्वज्ञ इति सूत्रार्थः । बाधम् । नैतावता पौरुषेयत्वं भवति । मनुष्य-निर्मितत्वाभावात् ।
> nanu bhagavatā bādarāyaṇena vedasya brahma-kāryatvaṃ sūtritam | "śāstra-yonitvāt" iti (Vedanta Sutra 1-1-3) ṛgvedādi-śāstratvād vṛddha-sarvajña iti sūtrārthaḥ | bādham | naitāvatā pauruṣeyatvaṃ bhavati | manuṣya-nirmitatvābhāvāt |
>
> … अत एव च नित्यत्वम् । (वे. सू. १-३-२९) इति । श्रुतिस्मृती चात्र भवतः । वाचा विरूप नित्यया । (ऋ. सं. ८-७५-६) इति श्रुतिः । अनादिनिधना नित्या वागुत्सृष्टा स्वयंभुवेति स्मृतिः । तस्मात्पौरुषेयत्वदोषशंकयानुदयान्मन्त्रब्राह्मणात्मकस्य वेदस्य निर्विघ्नं प्रामाण्यं सिद्धम् ॥
> *… ata eva ca nityatvam | (Ve. Sū. 1-3-29) iti | śrutismṛtī cātra bhavataḥ | vācā virūpa nityayā | (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-75-6) iti śrutiḥ | anādinidhanā nityā vāg utsṛṣṭā svayaṃbhuveti smṛtiḥ | tasmāt pauruṣeyatvadoṣaśaṅkayānudayān mantrabrāhmaṇātmakasya vedasya nirvighnaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ siddham ||*
>
>
> *(Anticipating an objection: doesn't Badarayana's own Vedanta-sutra state that the Veda arises from Brahman? This might seem to concede a kind of "authorship" after all — but Sayana clarifies that Brahman's causing the Veda's existence doesn't make it "pauruṣeya" in the objectionable sense, since it was never fashioned by an embodied human being.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 473</div>

Sutra's meaning: though many seemingly incoherent statements ("**वनस्पतयः सत्रमासत**" *vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata* — "the trees performed the sacrifice," and similar) occur in the Vedas, they exist only to clarify certain ritual acts and their proper relationships.

**Working through the reasoning with a concrete example:** suppose someone claims a man composed

> ज्योतिष्टोमेन स्वर्गकामो यजेत ।
> *jyotiṣṭomena svargakāmo yajeta |*
> "One desiring heaven should perform the jyotiṣṭoma" Any man could say "perform the jyotiṣṭoma" — but no man can foresee that this specific act yields that specific future fruit. Humans have the capacity to perform acts, not to know which acts yield which unobservable future results. Such statements resemble a sovereign's authoritative command, requiring three essential components: **bhāvya** (the fruit sought), **karaṇa** (the means/instrument), and **itikartavyatā** (the proper method). Just as "feed the brahmins" implies satisfaction (goal), food (instrument), and accompaniments like vegetables and soup (method) — "perform the jyotiṣṭoma" implies heaven (goal), soma (instrument), and the full consecration-and-subsidiary-rite sequence (method). How could such a carefully structured statement resemble a madman's ravings?

**But this same explanation doesn't cleanly cover "**वनस्पतयः सत्रमासत**" (*vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata*)** — true, and a different kind of explanation is needed there. When interpreting a sentence, one must take the complete statement as a whole; taking only one fragment and declaring it senseless is not a fair reading.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 474</div>

How could it be otherwise? Examining a sentence's preceding and following context resolves what first seemed inconsistent. The "**वनस्पतयः सत्रमासत**" (*vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata*) statement, connected as it is with jyotiṣṭoma-type sattra statements, is not comparable to a madman's ravings. Logicians hold that a word's meaning shifts with context: statements like the jyotiṣṭoma exist to declare a duty — that is their function; statements like this are arthavāda, existing purely to convey praise, regardless of whether their literal content is possible or impossible. The point isn't literal plausibility — it's the praise itself: "if even insentient, unknowing creatures managed to perform such a rite, how much more should sentient, learned brahmins do so!" — this a-fortiori eulogy of the sattra-yajna is the statement's whole purpose.

**Siddhānta — the true conclusion:** names like "Kathaka" and "Kauthuma" do not indicate the persons who composed those Vedic branches — they were composed by no human being at all. Because these figures traditionally taught those branches to their students, the branches came to bear their names.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 475</div>

...became customary. Unlike the Raghuvamsha and similar works of Kalidasa and other poets — which always close each canto with an author's colophon, "iti kālidāsa-kṛtau" ("thus, in the work composed by Kalidasa") — no such author's name-marker appears anywhere in the Vedas. Therefore, the Vedas are not human-composed; they are apauruṣeya.

**A closing summary verse, in question-and-answer form:**

> "Is the Veda of human origin? Yes, since it is known by titles such as Kathaka, and since it is made up of sentences that have the same nature as other sentences." — "No: these titles refer to men who taught the Veda, not composed it. And that other argument has already been refuted by the fact that no author's name is mentioned."

**A doubt then arises:** hasn't the holy Badarayana himself stated that the Veda is the work of Brahman? — "śāstra-yonitvāt" (Vedanta Sutra 1-1-3), meaning Brahman is omniscient, having created the Rigveda and all other shastras. Granted — but this doesn't establish the Veda's *human* origin; it was not made by a [mere embodied] person. This same Badarayana, in the Devatā-adhikaraṇa section, establishes that for all beings who have not attained final liberation, the Veda is eternal, like the sky itself — "ata eva ca nityatvam" (Ve. Sū. 1-2-29) ("and for this very reason, its eternality follows").

**Both Shruti and Smriti confirm this:**

> श्रुति: "वाचा विरूप नित्यया" (ऋ. सं. ८-७५-६)
> *Śruti: "vācā virūpa nityayā" (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-75-6)* ("with eternal speech, O Virūpa")
> स्मृति: "अनादिनिधना नित्या वागुत्सृष्टा स्वयंभुवा । आदौ वेदमयी दिव्या यतः सर्वाः प्रवृत्तयः ॥" (ब्रह्मसूत्र शांकरभाष्य १-३-८२)
> *Smṛti: "anādinidhanā nityā vāg utsṛṣṭā svayaṃbhuvā | ādau vedamayī divyā yataḥ sarvāḥ pravṛttayaḥ ||" (Brahmasūtra Śāṅkarabhāṣya 1-3-82)* ("beginningless and endless, eternal is the speech emitted by the Self-existent One; divine, made of the Veda, from which all activities proceed")

**Therefore, no possibility of an authorial flaw arises for the Veda — it has no author at all. The authority of the Veda, comprising both mantra and Brahmana, thus stands firmly and unobstructedly established.**

## Chapter 12. Determining the True Nature of Mantra and Brahmana, Through Their Defining Marks

*Original title: "Mantra mattu Brāhmaṇagaḷige iruva lakṣaṇavē modalāda svarūpanirṇayavu"*
**Printed pages 476–486 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 476</div>

### Determination of the True Nature of Mantra and Brahmana

> nanu mantra-brāhmaṇātmakatvaṃ vedasya na yuktam | tayoḥ svarūpasya nirṇītum aśakyatvāt | naivam | dvitīyādhyāyasya prathamapāde saptamāṣṭamādhikaraṇayor nirṇītatvāt | saptamādhikaraṇam ācacaṣṭe—
>
> "But it may be objected: defining the Veda as 'consisting of mantra and Brahmana' is not sound, since it's impossible to determine the precise nature of these two categories. Not so — this has been clearly established in the seventh and eighth adhikaranas of the first pada of the second adhyaya [of Jaimini's Purva-Mimamsa-sutra]. The seventh adhikarana states—"

> अहे बुध्निय मन्त्रं म इति मन्त्रस्य लक्षणम् । नास्त्यस्ति नास्य नास्त्येतदव्याप्त्यादेरवारणात् ॥ याज्ञिकानां समाख्यानं लक्षणं दोषवर्जितम् । तेऽनुष्ठानस्मारकादौ मन्त्रशब्दं प्रयुंजते ॥ (जै. न्या. वि. २-१-७) ॥
> *ahe budhniya mantraṃ ma iti mantrasya lakṣaṇam | nāsty asti nāsya nāsty etad avyāptyāder avāraṇāt || yājñikānāṃ samākhyānaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ doṣavarjitam | te 'nuṣṭhānasmārakādau mantraśabdaṃ prayuṃjate || (Jai. Nyā. Vi. 2-1-7) ||*
>
