> "But it may be said, if the mastery of the text is in this way an object of human desire, only inasmuch as it subserves that knowledge of the meaning to which the real fruit is attached, then that knowledge is a chief object of desire, and the mastery of the text, as an object of desire, must be held to be subordinate to it. Why, then, should not the injunction be stretched so far? To this he says—
>
> **If the injunction is taken to extend to the fruit-bearing knowledge, the Veda would never be read as a whole.**
>
> For what is the fruit of the knowledge of the meaning? It is the performance of the sacrifice. That being so, the brahmin whose business it might be to perform the Brihaspatisava rite, let us say, would study the texts for that rite only. He would not study the text for, let us say, the Rajasuya sacrifice. For beginning, carrying on, and concluding that sacrifice would mean no reward to him. And so with others.
>
> He shows that his own view is not exposed to this objection."

**Sutra's meaning:** if study is held to extend all the way to complete understanding and successful ritual application, only those portions of the Veda directly useful to whichever specific rite one personally intends to perform could ever justify being studied — making comprehensive Vedic study impossible. (This concludes the objection.)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 513</div>

The purpose of understanding the Veda's meaning is to perform the rites it describes. Given this, shouldn't it suffice for someone intending the Brihaspatisava yajna to learn only that rite's own mantras — skipping, say, the Rajasuya's mantras entirely, especially since only kshatriyas (not brahmins) may perform Rajasuya at all? Whether this creates a genuine flaw in requiring *complete* Vedic study is addressed next.

### "कृत्स्नप्राप्तिर्जपार्थेति" (Sutra 7)

*"Kṛtsnaprāptir japārtheti"*

> न चाबोधकत्वेऽर्थावबोध एव न सिध्येदिति शङ्कनीयम् । प्रमाणस्य प्रमेयबोधकत्वस्वाभाव्यात् । लौकिकाप्तवाक्यानामन्तरेणैव विधिं बोधकत्वदर्शनादित्याह ॥
> *na cābodhakatve'rthāvabodha eva na sidhyed iti śaṅkanīyam | pramāṇasya prameya-bodhakatva-svābhāvyāt | laukikāpta-vākyānām antareṇaiva vidhiṃ bodhakatva-darśanād ity āha ||* (sūtra, printed ॥ ७ ॥, and bhāṣya re-read from the better scan in the [?] pass)
>
> "**The mastery of the whole text of the Veda is required for that recitation of the whole in which the spiritual sacrifice consists.**
>
> Nor need you doubt and say that if the injunction be not taken to extend to the knowledge of the meaning, such knowledge will not be obtained at all. It is the nature of words establishing a doctrine to inform us with regard to that which is to be established, and so we see in every-day life the words of weighty men instructing us without any injunction of Scripture to that effect. It is so here, he says.
>
> **The text instructs of its own accord, as in the case of every-day talk.**
>
> The next objection that occurs to him is this. If we take the reward contemplated by the injunction to lie in a knowledge of the meaning, then the injunction applies to every..."

**Sutra's meaning:** complete study serves the purpose of japa (recitation); through japa, an unseen fruit results. Nor need one worry that the meaning would not be obtained at all unless the injunction extends to knowledge of it's meaning — a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) naturally conveys what needs to be known by its own inherent nature, just as, in ordinary life, the words of respected persons instruct us without needing any separate scriptural command authorizing them to do so. The Vedic text, likewise, instructs of its own accord.

### "लोकवन्नैजो बोध इति" (Sutra 8)

*"Lokavan naijo bodha iti"*

> ननु बोधस्य विधिफलत्वे बोधकाममुद्दिश्य विधातुं शक्यत्वात्सुलभोऽधिकारी स्यादित्याशङ्क्य प्राप्तिपक्षेऽपि प्राप्तिकाम…
> *nanu bodhasya vidhiphalatve bodhakāmam uddiśya vidhātuṃ śakyatvāt sulabho'dhikārī syād ity āśaṅkya prāptipakṣe'pi prāptikāma…* (continues on p. 514; sūtra, printed ॥ ८ ॥, and bhāṣya added from the better scan in the [?] pass)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 514</div>

man who desires to know that meaning, and is not liable to non-fulfilment on account of the absence of any one qualified to fulfil it (for he who desires to know the meaning is ipso facto so qualified).

**Sutra's meaning:** just as in ordinary speech a specific meaning is naturally conveyed, so too the injunction fully conveys its own intended primary meaning.

**A doubt now arises:** if the injunction's purpose were merely to know the Veda's meaning, it would apply only to those already desiring to understand — but everyone naturally desires this anyway, making a separate injunction pointless. Alternatively, if the purpose were mere memorization, an eight-year-old upanayana-invested boy would already qualify — a trivially obvious point. Setting this aside, the objector raises a sharper criticism: that the very "desire to understand meaning" the opponent relies upon doesn't actually exist in any coherent sense.

### "सोऽकाम्यः प्राग्बोध्य भानाभानयोरिति" (Sutra 9)

*"So'kāmyaḥ prāg bodhya bhānābhānayor iti"*

> बोध्यस्याग्निहोत्रादिलक्षणवेदार्थस्याध्ययनात्प्राक् संध्योपासनादिवत्पित्राद्युपदेशत एव भाने सिद्धत्वादेव सोऽर्थबोधो न काम्यः । अभाने कामयितुमशक्यः । ज्ञात एव विषये कामनानियमात् । ननु सामान्यतो ज्ञाते…
> *bodhyasyāgnihotrādi-lakṣaṇa-vedārthasyādhyayanāt prāk saṃdhyopāsanādivat pitrādy-upadeśata eva bhāne siddhatvād eva so'rthabodho na kāmyaḥ | abhāne kāmayitum aśakyaḥ | jñāta eva viṣaye kāmanā-niyamāt | nanu sāmānyato jñāte…* *(Sūtra and bhāṣya re-read from the better scan in the [?] pass; the earlier heading had run the bhāṣya together as the sūtra. The sūtra number is printed ೯ = 9.)*

> "**The meaning to be learned was either already known or not before the study of the text which is enjoined. In either case it cannot be an object of desire.**
>
> If the meaning of Vedic passages about the agnihotra and other sacrifices be already known from parental instruction as is the case with the knowledge of the evening rite and the like, then, as the knowledge is there already, it cannot be an object of desire. If it be not known, it cannot be desired. Desire is limited to an object which is known."

This raises a genuinely elegant epistemological dilemma: desire, by its very nature, can only take a *known* object as its target — one cannot coherently desire something one has no conception of at all. So the meaning to be gained through study is either already known beforehand (in which case there's nothing left to desire), or genuinely unknown (in which case it cannot be desired at all, since one cannot desire the wholly unknown). Either way, "desire to understand the Veda's meaning" collapses as a coherent basis for the study-injunction's purpose.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 515</div>

You will perhaps say that a thing may be known in a general way, and yet there be desire to know it more particularly — or that even with regard to a matter known in all its particulars through parental instruction, there may still be desire to know it *authoritatively* (confirmed through scripture). Even granting this, Sayana holds that referring this injunction to knowledge-of-meaning remains impossible.

### "Uddeśāyogād iti" (Sutra 10)

> अग्निहोत्रादि-विशेष-ज्ञानानां न तावद् ईश उद्दिश्य विशेषाकारेणोद्देशः सम्भवति । अनन्तत्वात् सामान्याकारेणोद्देशे सामान्यम् एव विधि-फलं स्यान् न तु ज्ञान-विशेषः ।
> agnihotrādi-viśeṣa-jñānānāṃ na tāvad īśa uddiśya viśeṣākāreṇoddeśaḥ sambhavati | anantatvāt sāmānyākāreṇoddeśe sāmānyam eva vidhi-phalaṃ syān na tu jñāna-viśeṣaḥ |
>
> "**Because the reference is unsuitable.**
>
> The reference could not include the knowledge of each and every sacrifice such as the agnihotra. For they are endless, and if the reference were made general, the reward of the injunction would have to be made general also. It could not lie in a particular kind of knowledge. Therefore such a reference is unsuitable."

**Sutra's meaning:** the desire underlying the study-injunction cannot coherently refer to knowledge of every single specific rite (agnihotra and countless others), since these are effectively endless; and if the reference were made general instead, the injunction's reward would likewise become merely general, never landing on any specific piece of knowledge at all. Either way, positing "desire to understand meaning" as the injunction's basis fails to hold up.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 516</div>

**Sutra's meaning:** since the reference [to specific knowledge] cannot properly be established. Because knowledge related to Agnihotra and similar rites is effectively endless, no single piece of specific knowledge could ever be pinpointed as the injunction's real target — and if reference were made general instead, the injunction's own fruit would likewise become merely general, never landing on anything specific. Therefore, framing the injunction's purpose this way doesn't hold up.

**A fresh doubt now arises:** if Vedic recitation isn't done with reference to meaning at all, how would the Veda's own purport (tātparya) ever become known? Sayana answers that purport is established directly by the force of the words themselves.

### "तात्पर्यं शब्दादिति" (Sutra 11)

*"Tātparyaṃ śabdād iti"*

> "**The purport from the words. (Reading by conjecture.)**
>
> If you conjecture the meaning of the Veda without studying it, then to learn the text of the Veda with the intention of knowing its meaning would be useless in this world. But it is not so. Learning the text of the Veda is not enough, but to know its meaning is also necessary, because such doubts as the Vedas are composed by men and the like will vanish with the help of Mimamsa Sastra."

**Sutra's meaning:** the intended meaning can be surmised directly from the force of the words themselves. If the injunction's purpose were only to know the meaning, then reciting the words in studying the Veda would become pointless in the world. But this isn't so: merely learning the text isn't sufficient — understanding its meaning is genuinely necessary too, since doubts like "the Vedas were composed by human authors" are resolved only with the help of Mimamsa-shastra.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 517</div>

**But this cannot mean word-recitation without meaning is useless** — for grasping meaning without recitation is equally impossible. If mere recitation sufficed on its own, resolving doubts about the Veda itself (human authorship, non-eternality, and similar) would become impossible, and the entire Vichara-shastra (Purva-Mimamsa) would become pointless.

**Sutra's meaning:** reciting the Veda with a specific purpose — understanding its meaning, intending to perform yajnas — removes sin in this world. If the study-injunction excluded the aim of understanding meaning, then Mimamsa-shastra (which exists precisely to examine Vedic meaning) would become entirely purposeless. The resolution follows.

### "विचार उत्तरविधिप्रयोक्ते उपसद्यत इति" (Sutra 13)

*"Vicāra uttara-vidhi-prayokte upasadyata iti"*

> "**The Mimansa has the place because it rests on later injunctions.**
>
> The injunctions which teach the various sacrifices meet us as we study the Veda with its Angas. But without decisive knowledge founded on a removal of all the difficulties which present themselves, these injunctions cannot be carried out. They therefore imply a careful consideration of sacrifices (the Purva Mimansa) for the resolution of doubts with..."

**This is a genuinely elegant argument:** as one studies the Veda together with its Angas, one naturally encounters the various sacrificial injunctions — but these injunctions cannot actually be carried out without first resolving the genuine interpretive difficulties they raise. This practical necessity is precisely what draws the careful study of Mimamsa into the picture — not because the original study-injunction directly commands it, but because it is unavoidably implied by what full compliance with the *later* sacrificial injunctions actually requires.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 518</div>

**Sutra's meaning:** the injunction that follows makes the Vichara-shastra necessary. Injunctions concerning ritual-portions (kratu) appear scattered throughout Vedic study — but merely knowing the bare injunction, without grasping the Veda's meaning, cannot resolve their mutual contradictions or genuine doubts, nor yield the decisive knowledge needed for actual performance. Purva-Mimamsa-shastra therefore becomes necessary precisely for this purpose — resolving meaning-doubts and enabling correct ritual performance.

**A genuinely sharp counter-objection follows:** the "Uttara Mimamsa" (the investigation into Brahman) is reached simply through hearing its own relevant injunction ("one should inquire into Brahman") — no help from Purva-Mimamsa is needed there. So the injunction to *hear* naturally incites toward its own expressly enjoined object, and sacrifice-injunctions likewise incite toward what is subservient to them. But if the study-injunction is held to extend all the way to the *sense* of the words — reaching, through that sense, all the way to actual sacrifice-performance — then the specific injunctions commanding particular sacrifices become entirely superfluous, since sacrifice-performance would already follow automatically from the general study-injunction alone.

> "The injunction to hear expressly commands an investigation of Brahma (the Uttara Mimansa). Things being so, you must see that it is only right that the injunction to hear should incite a man to what is in it expressly enjoined, and the injunctions as to sacrifices incite him to what is subservient to that. But your view would make the injunction as to sacrifice of no effect. For if the injunction to study the Veda extends to the sense of the words, then through the sense the injunction will run up to the performance of the sacrifice, and the performance of the sacrifice being thus obtained from this injunction, the specific injunction to perform the sacrifice is superfluous and useless."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 519</div>

If Vichara-shastra study were obtained purely through the study-injunction, that injunction would have to cover every act all the way through attaining heaven itself — making the specific rite-injunctions redundant, since performance would follow automatically from study alone.

**A sharpened version of the objection:** the study-injunction binds only brahmins, kshatriyas, and vaishyas (the three higher classes) — so if Vichara-shastra follows from that same injunction, would this same class-restriction and compulsion apply equally to the investigation into *sacrifices* (kratu-vichara), or to the investigation into *Brahman* (Brahma-vichara) too? If the former, we agree entirely with you — that's established doctrine on both sides.

### "Ato nityaḥ kratu-vicāras traivarṇika-mātrasyaiva" (Sutra 14)

> युपकरणे प्रश्वायुपश्रवणापुक्तवत् त्रैवर्णकानां नित्य आगत इत्य् अर्थः । द्वितीयेऽङ्गीकराम इत्य् आह ॥
> yupakaraṇe praśvāyupaśravaṇāpuktavat traivarṇakānāṃ nitya āgata ity arthaḥ | dvitīye'ṅgīkarāma ity āha ||
>
> "You will perhaps say that the injunction to study the Veda is binding on the three higher classes and on them alone, and that it is only by basing the obligation to consider the meaning on that injunction that we can obtain for that duty an exactly similar compulsion and restriction. Do you want such for the investigation into sacrifices or for the investigation into Brahma? If the first, it is as much a matter of established doctrine with us as with you.
>
> **Therefore this investigation into sacrifices is compulsory, but only in the case of the three higher classes.**
>
> 'Therefore' because the evils attendant on a neglect to study the Veda have been set out.
>
> But if you mean the second, we reject that altogether."

**Sutra's meaning:** kratu-vichara (investigation into yajnas and similar ritual acts) is a duty binding only on the three [twice-born] classes — obligatory, not optional; failing to undertake it brings pratyavāya (transgression, sin). On this specific point — that rite-investigation belongs only to the three classes — both sides genuinely agree; there's no disagreement here. **But Brahma-vichara (inquiry into Brahman) is different**, as the next sutra explains.

## Chapter 15. Censure of One Who Studies Without Knowledge of the Veda's Meaning, and Praise of Such Knowledge

*Original title: "Vēdārthajñānavilladē adhyayanamāḍuva puruṣana ninde mattu vēdārthajñānada praśaṃseyu"*
**Printed pages 520–538 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 520</div>

### "Brahma-vicāraḥ punaḥ paramahaṃsasyaiveti" (Sutra 15) — "The Investigation into Brahma Is for the Sannyasi Alone"

> नित्य आगतसङ्ग इति ॥
> nitya āgatasaṅga iti ||

**Sutra's meaning:** Brahma-vichara belongs only to the paramahamsa (the renunciate sannyasi). For a sannyasi, Brahma-vichara is a nitya (obligatory) duty — Brahma-jijnasa (the desire to know Brahman) is the sannyasi's own duty; his mind must remain constantly attached to Brahman.

**A further important qualification now follows** — that knowledge of meaning, though not commanded by the study-injunction itself, IS enjoined elsewhere:

> ननु क्षा नित्य-अध्ययनस्याक्षर-ग्रहणान्त एवार्थ-ज्ञानम् अविहितं स्यात् । मैवम् । वाक्यान्तरेण तद्-विधानात् । ब्राह्मणेन निष्कारणो धर्मः षडङ्गो वेदोऽध्येयो ज्ञेयश् चेति तद्-विधिः । तत्र निष्कारण-शब्देनाध्ययन-ज्ञानयोः काम्यत्वं निवार्यते । अर्थज्ञाने पुरुष-प्रवृत्तिकरं वचनम् इदं शाखान्तरगतं निरुक्त-कारो यास्क एवम् उदाहार । अथापि ज्ञान-प्रशंसा भवत्य् अज्ञान-निन्दा च ॥
> nanu kṣā nitya-adhyayanasyākṣara-grahaṇānta evārtha-jñānam avihitaṃ syāt | maivam | vākyāntareṇa tad-vidhānāt | brāhmaṇena niṣkāraṇo dharmaḥ ṣaḍaṅgo vedo'dhyeyo jñeyaś ceti tad-vidhiḥ | tatra niṣkāraṇa-śabdenādhyayana-jñānayoḥ kāmyatvaṃ nivāryate | arthajñāne puruṣa-pravṛttikaraṃ vacanam idaṃ śākhāntaragataṃ nirukta-kāro yāska evam udāhāra | athāpi jñāna-praśaṃsā bhavaty ajñāna-nindā ca ||
>
> "The injunction to study the Veda, therefore, goes no further than the letter of Scripture. But you are not to suppose that a knowledge of the meaning is not also enjoined. It is, but in another text: '**A brahmin must be able to repeat and must understand the meaning of disinterested virtue in the shape of the Veda with its six Angas.**' By the word 'disinterested' the idea that the one or other duty is matter of desire (so that there might be brahmins who wish them, and are therefore qualified) is barred."

That is: without any hope of reward, a brahmin must study the Veda together with its six Angas — which convey dharma — and must also understand its meaning. This is itself a vidhi (injunction). The word "niṣkāraṇa" (disinterested/without ulterior motive) is used precisely to rule out treating either study or understanding as merely optional, desire-driven acts; both are obligatory regardless of any hoped-for reward. This makes clear that Vedic study accompanied by meaning-comprehension is indeed required.

**Two texts from another Shakha**, cited by Yaska the author of the Nirukta, incite people toward studying the Veda's meaning: "Here follows the praise of knowledge and the censure of ignorance:—"

<div class="pgmark">original p. 521</div>

A brahmin cannot study according to personal preference — it is simply his obligatory duty. Therefore, Vedic study and understanding its meaning are both nitya (obligatory), never kāmya (optional). Yaska, the Nirukta's author, cites two verses from another Shakha that motivate people toward understanding meaning — verses praising knowledge and censuring ignorance:

> sthāṇur ayaṃ bhāra-hāraḥ kilābhūd adhītya vedaṃ na vijānāti yo'rtham | yo'rthajña it sakalaṃ bhadram aśnute nākam eti jñāna-vidhūta-pāpmā ||
>
> यद् गृहीतम् अविज्ञातं निगदेनैव शब्द्यते ॥
> yad gṛhītam avijñātaṃ nigadenaiva śabdyate ||
>
> "He is a mere post holding up a weight who learns the Veda but does not understand the interpretation thereof: he who knows the meaning of the Veda wins every good thing; his sins are destroyed by that knowledge, and he goes to heaven.
>
> The Veda learnt and recited but not understood is dry fuel thrown upon ashes; it will never blaze up."

*(Nirukta 1-18; Taittiriya Aranyaka 2-15 cited within.)*

These two mantras comprise four half-mantras. Of these, the half-mantra "yo'rthajña..." eulogizes knowledge of the Veda's meaning; the other three half-mantras blame the want of that knowledge. One who knows the Veda's meaning obtains every good thing in this world; and when he dies, his sins having been destroyed by that knowledge, he attains heaven.

**The Taittiriyas quote a mantra and an interpretative brahmana** which clearly teach this doctrine of rewards in both worlds accruing to one who understands—

> yo'rthaṃ jānāti so'yam iha loke sakalaṃ śreyaḥ prāpnoti | tathā tena jñānena pāpakṣaye sati mṛtaḥ svargaṃ prāpnoti | tad etad aihikāmuṣmikaṃ ca jñāna-phalaṃ taittirīyā mantropodāharaṇena tad-īyatāt paryābhidhāyi-brāhmaṇena ca smṛti-lekhuḥ | tad eṣābhyukta | yo'rvāṅ uta vā purāṇo vedaṃ vidyāṃ samabhito vadaṃs tān āditya eva te pariṇadanti | sarve agniṃ dvitīyaṃ tṛtīyaṃ ca haṃsam iti | yāvatīr vai devatāḥ sarvā vedavidi brāhmaṇe vasanti | tasmād brāhmaṇebhyo vedavidbhyo dive dive namaskuryān nārhalīlaṃ kīrtayet — etā eva devatāḥ prīṇāti (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2-15)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 522</div>

**The mantra is as follows:**

> योऽर्वाङ् उत वा पुराणे वेदं विद्वांसम् अभितो वदन्त्य् आदित्यम् एव ते परिवदन्ति सर्वे । अग्निं द्वितीयं तृतीयं च हंसम् ॥
> yo'rvāṅ uta vā purāṇe vedaṃ vidvāṃsam abhito vadanty ādityam eva te parivadanti sarve | agniṃ dvitīyaṃ tṛtīyaṃ ca haṃsam ||
>
> "Those who, whether of recent or of ancient times, speak all around against a man learned in the Veda — they are in truth speaking against Aditya (the Sun) himself; and against Agni as the second, and the Hamsa (Vayu) as the third."

**This is explained as follows:** all the gods dwell in the brahmin who knows the Veda. Therefore a man should do daily honour to brahmins who know the Veda, and speak no harsh word to them. Thus shall he please all the gods.

> yāvatīr vai devatāḥ sarvā vedavidi brāhmaṇe vasanti | tasmād brāhmaṇebhyo vedavidbhyo dive dive namaskuryāt | nārtha-līlaṃ kīrtayet — etā eva devatāḥ prīṇāti ||

**By "knowing the Veda" here is meant being versed in the Veda's meaning.** Two classes of persons may be meant: the knower of the Veda may be a teacher of modern times well versed in all fourteen sciences; or he may be one of the men of old, such as, for example, [the ancient rishis]—

The passage further establishes that merely reciting without understanding does not confer these benefits: one who does not truly comprehend the Veda's meaning is like a mere pillar bearing a load. Nor does mere recitation alone attain heaven or accomplish worldly success — the honour, worship, and material support extended to such a mere reciter yield correspondingly little.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 523</div>

Vyasa. The men who, drunk with the pride of their learning, or their wealth, or their high birth, and believing themselves to be wise, revile a knower of the Veda of either kind, revile, firstly, Aditya, and after Aditya, Agni, and after Agni, Hansa. "Hansa" here is a name of Vayu, so called because he is always in motion ("hanti").

That he who knows the Veda bears the form of Agni, Vayu, and Aditya is revealed in a text of Scripture: "He has fellowship, it is said, with Agni, Vayu, and Aditya." But—

*(The Sanskrit passage at the head of the page, ending "… yāskena kācid ṛg udāhṛtā", closes with the reference (Nirukta 1-19).)*

One who studies the Veda without understanding its meaning is like a pillar bearing a load. One who genuinely understands the Veda's meaning gains all prosperity, and through the knowledge he has attained, destroys his sins and attains heaven. Reciting the Veda by heart without grasping its meaning is like a heap of cold ashes (the fire gone out) — however much dry fuel is thrown upon it, no flame will ever catch. In just this way, Veda-recitation without meaning-comprehension is fruitless.

Of the two mantras above, the portion beginning "yo'rthajña..." praises the investigation of the Veda's meaning; the remaining three half-verses (lines) censure the lack of it. One who understands the Veda's meaning attains all prosperity in this world, and after death attains heaven. Regarding this two-worldly fruit of Vedic knowledge, the Taittiriyas cite a mantra together with its explanatory Brahmana passage:

> योऽर्वाङ् उत वा पुराणो वेदं विद्वांसम् अभितो वदन्त्य् आदित्यम् एव ते परिवदन्ति सर्वे । अग्निं द्वितीयं तृतीयं च हंसम् इति ॥
> yo'rvāṅ uta vā purāṇo vedaṃ vidvāṃsam abhito vadanty ādityam eva te parivadanti sarve | agniṃ dvitīyaṃ tṛtīyaṃ ca haṃsam iti ||
>
> "Whoever — whether of recent or of ancient times — speaks all around against one learned in the Veda, truly all such men are reviling Aditya himself; and Agni as the second; and Hamsa as the third."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 524</div>

> यावतीर्वै देवताः सर्वा वेदविदि ब्राह्मणे वसन्ति । तस्माद्ब्राह्मणेभ्यो वेदविद्भ्यो दिवे दिवे नमस्कुर्यात् । नार्थलीलं कीर्तयेत् । एता एव देवताः प्रीणाति ॥
> *yāvatīr vai devatāḥ sarvā vedavidi brāhmaṇe vasanti | tasmād brāhmaṇebhyo vedavidbhyo dive dive namaskuryāt | nārtha-līlaṃ kīrtayet — etā eva devatāḥ prīṇāti ||* (Taittiriya Aranyaka 2-15)
>
> "As many deities as there are — all dwell within the Veda-knowing brahmin. Therefore one should offer daily reverence to Veda-knowing brahmins, and should never publicize their faults. By this alone are those very deities pleased."

**Meaning:** those who censure Veda-knowers, whether of recent or ancient times, are in truth censuring Aditya (the Sun) — and along with him, Agni and Vayu as well.

All deities reside within the brahmin who has studied the Veda and understood its meaning. One should therefore offer daily reverence to such Veda-meaning-knowing brahmins, and never speak ill of them; through this, the deities themselves become pleased and gracious.

**Note on terminology:** the word "vedavid" used in the original means specifically one who has studied the Veda *and understood its meaning* — that is, one who genuinely comprehends the Veda's sense. Such knowers are of two kinds: (1) contemporary ones — teachers skilled in all fourteen sciences (vidyā-sthānas) of the present age; and (2) ancient ones — Vyasa and similar rishis of former times. Both alike deserve honour.

**Who reviles them:** those who, with only a little learning of their own, become proud through mere book-learning (vidyā-mada), or through wealth (dhana-mada — pride that they have all the wealth they need), or through birth (kula-mada — believing themselves born in the highest lineage) — such arrogant persons, believing themselves great scholars who know all the shastras, revile these two classes of Veda-knowers (whether modern or ancient) in various ways —

<div class="pgmark">original p. 525</div>

They censure them. In this way, one who censures first incurs the sin of censuring Aditya; through that, he incurs the sin of censuring Agni; and beyond that, the sin of censuring Vayu ("Hamsa"), so called because he is always in motion.

**Why does censuring a Veda-knower amount to censuring Aditya, Agni, and Vayu?** Because scripture states that one who has understood the Veda's meaning becomes of the very nature of Aditya, Agni, and Vayu—

> अग्नेर्वायोरादित्यस्य सायुज्यं गच्छति ।
> *agner vāyor ādityasya sāyujyaṃ gacchati |*
> "He attains sāyujya (union/fellowship) with Agni, Vayu, and Aditya." And not these three deities alone: all deities dwell within one who has understood the Veda's meaning. **For this reason, one who knows the Veda's meaning is himself of the nature of all the gods.** Therefore, one should offer daily reverence to such brahmins accomplished in Vedic meaning, whether seen in person or recalled to mind. Should one even perceive a fault in them, it must not be broadcast. By doing so, that is, by remembering the knowers of the Veda's meaning, all the deities presiding over the Veda dwell in his heart; and one who remembers and reveres them thereby pleases those deities.

**A critical terminological point:** this refers specifically to one who *understands* the Veda's meaning — not to mere recitation-study alone. Note that the text uses "vedam adhīyānam" (studying the Veda) versus "vedavid" (knowing the Veda) as distinct terms — and it is precisely "vedavid" that scripture employs here. Thus, one who understands the Veda's meaning is to be honoured by all living beings as an embodiment of all the deities; such a knower of Vedic meaning is rightly blessed in both worlds.

**In contrast:** one who studies the Veda without understanding its meaning merely carries a load. "Like a post" (sthāṇu) in the text is a simile — "post" meaning the dry, branchless stump of a tree: just as it is fit only to be burned as fuel and will never again bear flower or fruit, so he who merely recites the Veda without comprehension will not, indeed, be outcasted — but that is all. The performance of the sacrifice, and heaven, are not his fruit.

The word "kila" in the text indicates that what is said is a matter of common knowledge. Even in ordinary experience, we see that the brahmin versed in the Veda's meaning receives greater honour — in the form of gifts and the like — than the mere reciter.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 526</div>

One who memorizes the Veda without understanding its meaning is not thereby outcasted — that is the only "fruit," and no more. He does not gain the ability to perform yajnas, nor obtain heavenly rewards or any further human aim.

The word "kila" in the original indicates a matter of common worldly knowledge: even in ordinary experience, a reciter who understands the Veda's meaning receives greater honour and greater gifts, while a mere reciter who has learned only from his guru without comprehension receives less honour than the one who knows the meaning. Reciting the Vedic text taught by the guru, without knowing its meaning, gives the reciter no knowledge of the Veda's meaning and inspires him in nothing. Does firewood thrown where there is no fire burn, however dry it is? Likewise the words a reciter utters, though they are Vedic words, carry little weight; only if he utters them knowing their meaning does great fruit arise.

**A genuinely important etymological argument now follows:** what, indeed, is the Veda? What is the meaning of the word "Veda"? Why is that name given? The word "veda" derives from the root meaning "to know" (√vid) — because it makes known the means of attaining human aims that cannot be known through ordinary worldly experience. On this basis, Sayana explains the very meaning of the term:

> प्रत्यक्षेणानुमित्या वा यस् तूपायो न बुध्यते । एतं विन्दन्ति वेदेन तस्माद् वेदस्य वेदता ॥
> pratyakṣeṇānumityā vā yas tūpāyo na budhyate | etaṃ vindanti vedena tasmād vedasya vedatā ||
>
> "**A means which is not learned by perception or inference is learned from the Veda: and that is why the Veda is so called.**"

That is: whatever means of attaining human ends cannot be grasped through direct perception or through inference — precisely because the Veda makes such means known, the Veda bears the name "Veda." **Therefore, if the Veda is to keep its character of being Veda in the true and proper sense of the word, its meaning must be apprehended** — merely learning the text as a book does not fulfill what the name itself signifies.

On this subject, Yaska cites a verse from the Rigveda (Nirukta 1-19)—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 527</div>

> उत त्वः पश्यन् न ददर्श वाचम् उत त्वः शृण्वन् न शृणोत्य् एनाम् । उतो त्वस्मै तन्वं वि सस्रे जायेव पत्य उशती सुवासाः ॥
> uta tvaḥ paśyan na dadarśa vācam uta tvaḥ śṛṇvan na śṛṇoty enām | uto tvasmai tanvaṃ vi sasre jāyeva patya uśatī suvāsāḥ || (Rigveda Samhita 10-71-4)
>
> "One, though seeing, has not seen Speech; another, though hearing, does not hear her. But to yet another she has revealed her own body — as a loving, well-clad wife reveals herself to her husband."

**Yaska gives the purport of the first two lines as follows:** "The first half of this verse speaks of the ignorant man as one who, seeing Speech, does not see her, and hearing her, does not hear her."

**The meaning is this:** the text, in its first half, speaks of the man who does not apprehend the Veda's meaning. One man, complete in his knowledge of the *words* only, sees Speech in the form of the Veda — but does not see her properly. For where no consideration has been given to grammatical questions, such as the [proper analysis of word-forms]...

That is: this man doesn't genuinely comprehend the Veda's meaning. Grammar and its auxiliary disciplines, Mimamsa and its allied inquiries — without study of these, one does not properly grasp the Vedic word. As the Taittiriya Samhita states, one who understands merely the word-forms without their meaning is like a man who takes only a share of what he might obtain.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 528</div>

He who has not learned to substitute "te" for "sa" and "gamayanti" for "gamayati," when the sentence "ādityān eva..." takes the place of the sentence "vāyum eva...," how can he give even a correct text?

**A second man**, with a view to apprehend the Veda's meaning, has heard, indeed, Grammar and the other Angas — but he too, not having studied the Mimamsa, does not properly hear Speech in her form as Veda. Take, for example, the text—

> यावतोऽश्वान् प्रतिगृह्णीयात्तावतो वरुणांश्चतुष्कपालान्निर्वपेत् ।
> *yāvato'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt tāvato varuṇāṃś caturkapālān nirvapet |*
> "As many horses as one should accept, that many four-kapala Varuna-offerings one should make"

Here Grammar by itself goes to show that it is the man who *accepts* a gift of horses who has to make atonement. But in the Mimamsa it is proved that it is the *giver* who must do so.

**Explanation of the verse's first half (pādas 1 and 2):** the first quarter-verse concerns the person regarding the Veda's meaning: one who studies the Veda merely as text (word-forms alone), without meaning, does not truly see the very form of Vedic speech.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 529</div>

Nor does he obtain genuine knowledge. He cannot properly grasp Vedic statements, and many doubts arise. Whether the Vedic sentence he recites is singular or plural remains unclear to him. Take these two statements as an example:

> वायुम् एव स्वेन भागधेयेनोपधावति स एनं भूतिं गमयति ॥
> vāyum eva svena bhāgadheyenopadhāvati sa enaṃ bhūtiṃ gamayati || (Taittiriya Samhita 2-1-1-1)
>
> आदित्यान् एव स्वेन भागधेयेनोपधावति ते एनं भूतिं गमयन्ति ॥
> ādityān eva svena bhāgadheyenopadhāvati te enaṃ bhūtiṃ gamayanti || (Taittiriya Samhita 2-3-1-1)

The first sentence ends with "gamayati" (singular); the second ends with "gamayanti" (plural). Which of these two words is correct in which case? Without grammatical training, doubt arises about the first sentence's "gamayati" and the second's "gamayanti," and one cannot resolve it. Since the first sentence has a singular agent (Vayu), it requires the singular verb "gamayati"; the second has a plural agent (the Adityas), requiring the plural "gamayanti." Without knowing grammar, such doubts remain unresolved. **But knowing grammar alone still isn't sufficient** — without Mimamsa-shastra, a person still cannot properly understand the Veda's meaning, and many doubts persist. For instance:

> यावतोऽश्वान् प्रतिगृह्णीयात् तावतो वरुणांश् चतुर्कपालान् निर्वपेत् ॥
> yāvato'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt tāvato varuṇāṃś caturkapālān nirvapet || (Taittiriya Samhita 2-3-12-1)

In this mantra the agent, verb and other words are all bound by the rules of grammar, so there is no ground for doubt; but if one sets out to explain the sentence on the basis of the grammatically correct words, this statement indicates that the person who *accepts* the horses must perform the required ishti (homa). However, examined through Mimamsa's own reasoning (Jaimini Sutra 3-4-30), it is definitively established that the person who *gives* the gift must perform this ishti.

**Therefore the first half of the verse speaks of these two classes of ignorant people** [one lacking grammar, one lacking Mimamsa].

**The purport of the third line is thus given by Yaska:** "But to another she unfolds her body, that is, reveals herself." In this clause the verse speaks of knowledge or the revelation of the meaning. The meaning of this is as follows: the "api" of Yaska is a synonym for the "uto" of the text. Particles have various meanings; "uto" here is used in the sense of "but," to distinguish the next case from that of the two ignorant men already referred to. The man who has gone about to correctly apprehend the meaning of its indi[vidual words] —

<div class="pgmark">original p. 530</div>

individual words by the help of Grammar and the other Angas, and their purport taken as a whole by the help of the Mimamsa — to him alone the Veda unfolds her form. The clause "svaṃ..." in Yaska explains the meaning of the individual words in the text. The clause "jñānam..." explains the purport. In this clause — that is, the third line here — the text speaks of that right knowledge which is able to throw light on the meaning of the Veda.

Without knowing Mimamsa-shastra, one cannot properly grasp the Veda's meaning — this is what—

> श‍ृण्वन्न शृणोति ।
> *śṛṇvan na śṛṇoti |*
> "Hearing, he does not hear"

—conveys. Both these lines—

> उत त्वः पश्यन्न ददर्श वाचम् । उत त्वः शृण्वन्न शृणोत्येनाम् ।
> *uta tvaḥ paśyan na dadarśa vācam | uta tvaḥ śṛṇvan na śṛṇoty enām |*

—refer to persons lacking knowledge of Grammar and Mimamsa-shastra respectively.

**The third line's meaning:**

> उतो त्वस्मै तन्वं वि सस्रे ।
> *uto tvasmai tanvaṃ vi sasre |*

— Speech reveals her own body [i.e., her true form and meaning] to such a person. Here "uto" functions as "api" (also/but). Thus, unlike the previously mentioned persons who lack grammatical and Mimamsa training, the one who does possess both attains genuine understanding: with Grammar's help he grasps word-meanings, and with Mimamsa's help he grasps overall purport — and to him alone the Veda's own form is revealed. The words "svaṃ" (own) and "jñānam" (knowledge) respectively indicate word-meaning and purport-meaning. Therefore, understanding the Veda's meaning properly requires both Grammar and Mimamsa-shastra as necessary aids — this is the third line's purport.

**The purport of the fourth line is thus given by Yaska:** "A simile is given in the last line. As a wife [reveals herself] to the husband of her desire, clothed in fair raiment after her flowers. By 'fair raiment' is meant auspicious raiment. He is the husband of her..."

That is—

> जायेव पत्य उशती सुवासाः ।
> *jāyeva patya uśatī suvāsāḥ |*

— just as a wife, at the auspicious time, adorns herself in fine garments and approaches her husband, so does Vedic Speech reveal herself to the knower of her meaning. Here, one who understands the Veda's meaning is called her "husband" (pati) — meaning the learned scholar who genuinely knows the Veda's sense.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 531</div>

desire on account of the season. As he looks at her and listens to her — this is the eulogy of the meaning.

**The meaning of this is as follows:** the last (fourth) line illustrates the third line's meaning by a simile. The word "kāmayamāna" explains the "uśatī" of the text. Through the day, busy with the work of the house, she may have been in a dirty dress, but when night comes she makes herself neat. Why? "Her desire is to him on account of the season." As the husband gazes eagerly on such a wife and listens kindly to the meaning of what she says, so this man, versed in all the fourteen sciences, has full vision of the secret of the Veda's meaning, and lovingly takes to himself the twofold meaning — dharma and brahma — which the Veda teaches. **This is the eulogy of him who knows the meaning of the Veda.**

**Yaska quotes another text saying, "The text that follows explains this further:"**

> उत त्वं सख्ये स्थिरपीतम् आहुर् नैनं हिन्वन्त्य् अपि वाजिनेषु । अधेन्वा चरति माययैष वाचं शुश्रुवाꣳ अफलाम् अपुष्पाम् ॥
> uta tvaṃ sakhye sthirapītam āhur nainaṃ hinvanty api vājineṣu | adhenvā carati māyayaiṣa vācaṃ śuśruvām̐ aphalām apuṣpām || (Rigveda Samhita 10-71-5)
>
> "Him they call firm-established in friendship, yet they do not urge him forward in the contests. He wanders on with an illusion that yields no milk — having heard Speech that bears neither fruit nor flower."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 532</div>

**The meaning is this:** the verse of Scripture immediately following "uta tvaḥ paśyan..." serves to explain that verse's meaning further — it is able to set out that meaning very clearly. How? We shall show. Of him — that is, of the man versed in the fourteen sciences — they say that, standing firmly in the friendship of the Word, he has drunk of the nectar of the Veda's meaning. Those who genuinely know are the ones who say so. And they refer to that friendship with the Veda spoken of in the text—

> सचिविदम् ।
> *sacividam |*

The one who understands the Veda's meaning gains the Veda's own friendship; those without such understanding do not obtain it. Regarding those lacking Vedic knowledge, they wander—

> अधेन्वा मायया ।
> *adhenvā māyayā |*
> "With an illusion that yields no milk"

—like a cow that gives no milk, their Veda-recitation yields no genuine fruit. Such a person, though he has heard Vedic speech, has heard speech—

> अफलामपुष्पाम् ।
> *aphalām apuṣpām |*
> "Bearing neither fruit nor flower"

This censures those who merely recite without comprehension: their recitation is barren, producing neither the "flower" (dharma-knowledge) nor the "fruit" (brahma-knowledge) that the Veda properly yields.

*(Reference cited within: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4-4-22.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 533</div>

**सखायम्** (*sakhāyam*)..." Or the meaning may be that such a one is here described as drinking abundance of nectar in heaven in the enjoyment of the Vedas' friendship.

**On "वाजिनेषु" (*vājineṣu*):** by the word "**वाजिनः**" (*vājinaḥ*) in the text is meant lords of words (vācāṃ inaḥ) — or those who are eloquent in the assemblies. The man versed in the Veda's meaning sits among them, but they cannot touch him, because they cannot contend with him in argument.

**But that other man**, engaged in the study of the recited text alone, is a hearer of the Word stripped of its flower and its fruit. **The flower of Scripture is the knowledge of religious duty (dharma)** which is expounded in the Veda's prior section; **its fruit is the knowledge of brahma**, which is taught in the latter section. As in nature we see that the flower produces the fruit, so the religious duties — such as that of learning the Veda — beget, through the instrumentality of the fulfilment of these duties, the desire for that knowledge of brahma, which is the fruit.

**Meaning of this verse, continued:** the mantra's words—

> सचिविदं सखायम् ।
> *sacividaṃ sakhāyam |*

—convey its explanation. One who understands the Veda's meaning becomes, as it were, the Veda's own friend; this arises from his engagement with Vedic meaning. Such a Veda-meaning-adept is genuinely established in the nectar of that meaning. Alternatively—

> सख्ये स्थिरपीतमाहुः ।
> *sakhye sthirapītam āhuḥ |*

—may mean: he becomes a friend even to the deities dwelling in heaven, and there drinks the nectar of immortality.

> yat pūrṇānandaikabodhas tad brahmāham asmīti kṛtakṛtyo bhavati ||
>
> "When there is that single realization of perfect bliss — 'I am that Brahman' — one becomes fulfilled, having accomplished all that is to be done."

**This very man**, reciter of a Veda stripped of such flower and fruit, walks with an illusion that seems a cow, but is no cow. A cow that has just given birth to a calf, and is therefore in milk, is called "dhenu" — because it is the cause of excitement on account of the pleasure it gives. That is the etymology of the word. Now the Word, in the shape of the Veda, to him who recites it merely, yields no such milk as the knowledge of religious duty and Brahma. It is no cow, but a deceptive illusion. It is like the image made by magicians that wears the shape of a cow, but is no cow. **Walking with this illusion, the man referred to does not obtain the chief end of man.**

*(Note on the Veda's twofold structure explained here: the karma-kanda's dharma-teaching is the "flower"; the jnana-kanda's brahma-knowledge is the "fruit" — just as in the ordinary world flowers precede and produce fruit, so ritual duty precedes and generates the desire for brahma-knowledge.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 535</div>

Because it is an illusion of deceptive form — a magical image conjured by Indrajala-magicians through the power of their own mantras, taking on the appearance of a cow. Just as no milk can be obtained from such an illusory cow, so no genuine human purpose is served by Vedic recitation devoid of meaning-comprehension. In this way, through examples, Yaska sets out clearly both the praise of knowledge and the censure of ignorance. **And since, in worldly usage, whatever is praised is precisely what people undertake, and the Veda's meaning is here praised, it must be concluded that understanding its meaning is itself enjoined** — merely memorizing the Veda by heart is not the injunction's full sense.

**Moreover, in the Nakshatreshti chapter**, each utterance regarding a sacrifice's fruit asserts, with Scripture's own authority, that the fruit of the sacrifice and of the *knowledge* of it are one and the same:

> यथा ह वा अग्निर् देवानाम् अन्नादः एवं ह वा एष मनुष्याणां भवति य एतेन हविषा यजते य उ चैनद् एवं वेद ॥
> yathā ha vā agnir devānām annādaḥ evaṃ ha vā eṣa manuṣyāṇāṃ bhavati ya etena haviṣā yajate ya u cainad evaṃ veda || (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-1-4-1)
>
> "Just as Agni is the eater of food among the gods, so indeed does he become among men — he who sacrifices with this oblation, and he who likewise knows this."

**For this reason too, it is clear that the knowledge of a sacrifice is as much matter of injunction as the sacrifice itself.**

*(Further citations woven in here: Jaimini Sutra 1-2-15 on fruit-praise; Taittiriya Samhita 2-2-5-4 on the "svargāya hi loko'yaṃ darśa-pūrṇamāsau" formulation — establishing that where scripture praises the fruit of both performance and knowledge equally, both alike carry injunctive force.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 536</div>

view to the fruit thereof as the sacrifice itself is. **A similar train of reasoning will show that all the Brahmanas contain precepts enjoining a knowledge of the sacrifice.**

**Here a doubt arises:** has not Jaimini, in the "**विद्याप्रशंसा**" (*Vidyāpraśaṃsā*) sutra, expressly ruled that the rewards assigned to the knowledge of the Veda are of the nature of eulogy? What of that? The language of eulogy may employ a reward which actually exists as well as one which does not. For example, in the precept with regard to the propitiatory sacrifice necessary when a mistake has been made in the course of the performance of the New and [Full Moon rites]—

In the Nakshatreshti section, each ishti's fruit-statement, ritual procedure, and purpose-explanation are given together. As stated:

> यथा ह वा अग्निर्देवानामन्नादः एवं ह वा एष मनुष्याणां भवति य एतेन हविषा यजते य उ चैनदेवं वेद ।
> *yathā ha vā agnir devānām annādaḥ evaṃ ha vā eṣa manuṣyāṇāṃ bhavati ya etena haviṣā yajate ya u cainad evaṃ veda |* (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-1-4-1)
>
> "Just as Agni consumes the offerings made to the deities, so does the person who performs this yajna, and likewise the one who *knows* it, become an eater of food among men." That is: whoever performs this rite, and whoever understands it correctly, alike obtain abundant food and similar goods, and become esteemed among people.

Here the mantra conveys both the ritual procedure and its fruit — so the mantra itself is authoritative regarding meaning, and the meaning must be understood, since without understanding, no fruit accrues. This same reasoning applies generally: throughout the Brahmana statements, Vedic injunctions clearly require that their meaning be understood.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 537</div>

**A doubt arises here:** Jaimini himself, in his "Vidyāpraśaṃsā" sutra (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-15), states that fruits obtained through Vedic-meaning-knowledge are of the nature of praise (arthavāda). What of that? The language of praise can employ both a fruit that genuinely exists and one that does not. **Example:** in the Darsha and Purnamasa yajnas, if some lapse occurs, an expiatory rite becomes necessary — and in the very injunction prescribing that expiation, heaven is stated as the fruit of those yajnas:

> "स्वर्गाय हि लोको दर्श-पूर्णमासाव् इज्येते"
> "svargāya hi loko darśa-pūrṇamāsāv ijyete" (Taittiriya Samhita 2-2-5-4)
>
> "For the sake of the heavenly world are the Darsha and Purnamasa sacrifices performed."

Here the Vedic statement declares that Darsha-Purnamasa yajnas are performed for attaining heaven — and this heaven-fruit is genuinely stated in the mantra itself. On this matter, in interpreting the meaning of statements conveying fruit, the Acharya (the shastra's propounder) cites two verses:

> इच्छाम्य् एवार्थवादत्वं वचसो ऽन्यपरत्वतः । यथावस्त्वभिधायित्वान् न त्व् अभूतार्थवादता ॥ इज्यते स्वर्गलोकाय दर्श-दर्शौ यथा तथा । न त्व् अभूतार्थवादत्वं पापलोक-श्रुतिर् यथा ॥
> icchāmy evārthavādatvaṃ vacaso 'nyaparatvataḥ | yathāvastvabhidhāyitvān na tv abhūtārthavādatā || ijyate svargalokāya darśa-darśau yathā tathā | na tv abhūtārthavādatvaṃ pāpaloka-śrutir yathā ||
>
> "**I accept the character of eulogy [in such statements], since the words point toward another purpose — yet not the character of stating what is factually non-existent**, since they do speak of things as they actually are. 'It is sacrificed for the heavenly world' — thus in the Darsha and similar rites; there is no assertion of non-existent fact here, unlike a scriptural mention of [some fictitious] world."

**A further doubt:** if a yajna's fruit accrues from mere knowledge of it, doesn't actual performance become a useless farce? **That difficulty is removed by the consideration that rewards may vary in quantity or quality.** They cite on this point a sutra of Jaimini's:

> फलस्य कर्म-निष्ठत्वात् तेषां लोकवत् परिमाणतः सारतो वा फल-विशेषः स्यात् ॥
> phalasya karma-niṣṭhatvāt teṣāṃ lokavat parimāṇataḥ sārato vā phala-viśeṣaḥ syāt || (Jaimini Sutra 1-2-17)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 538</div>

**"Each rite must needs have its reward. Distinctive rewards must therefore, as in daily life, refer to increase in quantity or in quality."**

We have already explained this sutra and illustrated it by the text "tarati brahma-hatyāṃ yo'śvamedhena yajate ya u cainam evaṃ veda" (see page 460 above) — one who performs the Ashvamedha, and likewise one who knows it, crosses beyond the sin of brahmin-slaying.

**The Chandogas have a text in which the performance of a sacrifice accompanied by knowledge is expressly preferred to a sacrifice performed without knowledge:**

> तेनो भौ कुरुतो यश् चैतद् एवं वेद यश् च न वेद । नाना तु विद्या चाविद्या च । यद् एव विद्यया करोति श्रद्धयोपनिषदा तद् एव वीर्यवत्तरं भवति ॥
> teno bhau kuruto yaś caitad evaṃ veda yaś ca na veda | nānā tu vidyā cāvidyā ca | yad eva vidyayā karoti śraddhayopaniṣadā tad eva vīryavattaraṃ bhavati || (Chandogya Upanishad 1-1-10)
>
> "Both perform [the rite] — he who knows it thus, and he who does not. But knowledge and ignorance are quite different things. Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upanishadic understanding — that alone becomes more powerful (vīryavattara)."

It is true that the injunction here has special reference to a knowledge of the Veda's Angas. **But the same thing holds good by analogy for all the other parts of a knowledge of the Veda.**

**Do you ask why I am so devoted to a knowledge of the Veda? Why do you hate that knowledge as you do?** I have shown you how often and greatly it is eulogised. And nowhere do we see it condemned. But just as the merit got by good works goes after death —

## Chapter 16. Exposition of the Anubandha-catuṣṭaya (Subject, Purpose, Relation, Qualified Person) Regarding the Veda

*Original title: "Vēdaviṣayadalli viṣaya, prayōjana, sambandha, adhikāri emba anubandhacatuṣṭayada nirūpaṇe"*
**Printed pages 539–545 of the source.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 539</div>

...with the soul, so, and in no other way, the merit got by knowledge accompanies the dead man. As it is said in the Scripture of the Vajasaneyins:

> तं विद्या-कर्मणी समन्वारभेते पूर्व-प्रज्ञा च ॥
> taṃ vidyā-karmaṇī samanvārabhete pūrva-prajñā ca || (Shatapatha Brahmana 14-7-2-3)
>
> "Knowledge, action, and prior wisdom follow him [after death]."

**Therefore, as it is clear that a knowledge of the Veda's meaning is as much matter of positive injunction as is the study of its text, we are now in that view about to expound the Veda.**

**Meaning:** enough — why this devotion to Vedic meaning-knowledge? Why do you expound its praise and its meaning with so much labour? Would it not be enough simply to say that the Veda's meaning should be known? To this we must reply: we have faith in meaning-knowledge, but why do you hate it so? The praises given for meaning-knowledge have been shown in particular detail above, and nowhere in this discussion is such knowledge condemned. Furthermore: just as the auspicious and inauspicious karmas a person performs follow him after death into his next life, so too does the unseen fruit acquired through Vedic-meaning-knowledge accompany him into that next life. Thus the Vajasaneyins (Shukla-Yajurveda followers) declare: "taṃ vidyā-karmaṇī samanvārabhete pūrva-prajñā ca" — knowledge, action, and prior wisdom follow the person and accompany him after death. **Therefore, since meaning-knowledge, just like study itself, is scripturally enjoined, expounding the Veda's meaning is genuinely necessary.**

### Determination of the Four Preliminaries: Subject-Matter, Purpose, Relation, and Qualified Persons

Before listeners can be expected to engage in the study of any work, they must be told what its subject-matter is, of what use it is, what are its relations, and whom it concerns. **These four heads are therefore next given.** The subject of this commentary is the—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 540</div>

**Veda, which is to be commented on. Its use is to make the meaning of that Veda plain. Its relation is that of a commentary to the work which is to be commented on. And they who desire such knowledge are they whom it concerns.**

This is all it is usual to give under this head. **But if the Veda, as distinguished from the commentary on the Veda which is our undertaking, were without subject, use, and so on, the commentary too would want these in the second and higher degree. Therefore I shall state the four with regard to the Veda also.**

**The Veda's own subject-matter is dharma.** As the Purusharthanushasana states: "dharma-brāhmaṇe vaidyaka-vedyo" — and again, in his second sutra: "codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ", "dharma is that whose defining mark is Vedic injunction." Since dharma is precisely what is knowable through Vedic injunction and not through perception, the Veda's subject-matter is dharma.

**Regarding whether dharma can be perceived directly:** dharma is not accessible to direct perception (pratyakṣa) — this is established by the sutra "pratyakṣam animittaṃ vidyamānopalambhanāt" (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-4). Nor can inference apprehend it, since it has no mark (liṅga) to infer from. Therefore, the Veda alone is the authority regarding dharma.

**Further supporting citation:**

> धर्मो विश्वस्य जगतः प्रतिष्ठा लोके धर्मिष्ठं प्रजा उपसर्पन्ति धर्मेण पापम् अपनुदति धर्मे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं तस्माद् धर्मं परमं वदन्ति ॥
> dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā loke dharmiṣṭhaṃ prajā upasarpanti dharmeṇa pāpam apanudati dharme sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ tasmād dharmaṃ paramaṃ vadanti || (Taittiriya Aranyaka 10-63-7)
>
> "Dharma is the foundation of the whole universe; in this world, people approach one most established in dharma; through dharma one drives away sin; in dharma all things are established — therefore they call dharma the highest."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 541</div>

**Dharma and brahma, in that order, are the subject-matter respectively of the two sections into which the whole Veda is divided.** Why? Because these two cannot be obtained from any other source. As it is laid down in the Purusharthanushasana—

> धर्मब्रह्मणी वेदैकवेद्ये ।
> *dharma-brahmaṇī vedaika-vedye |*
> "Dharma and brahma are to be learned from the Veda only."

Those who know tradition cite also here the second sutra of Jaimini with its twofold restriction—

> वेद एव धर्मस्य प्रमाणम् । वेद एव प्रमाणं न त्वन्यत् ।
> *veda eva dharmasya pramāṇam | veda eva pramāṇaṃ na tv anyat |*
> "The Veda is the only authority for dharma; the Veda is that authority and nothing else."

To establish the former of these propositions, Jaimini in his fourth sutra shows that dharma is not cognizable by our senses.

**The four preliminaries, applied:** dharma is the puruṣārtha (human aim); the Vedic statements themselves establish this. Regarding **relation (sambandha)**: the Veda stands as the expounder (pratipādaka) and dharma-brahma as what is expounded (pratipādya) — this is their mutual relation. Regarding **qualified persons (adhikārī)**: the three twice-born classes (traivarṇika) are those entitled to knowledge of the Veda's meaning. Regarding **purpose (prayojana)**: attaining dharma and brahma-knowledge respectively. Regarding **subject (viṣaya)**: dharma in the karma-kanda, brahma in the jnana-kanda.

**Note distinguishing Veda from Purana:** dharma and brahma-knowledge are obtainable *only* from the Veda; the Puranas and similar texts, though they discuss these matters, derive their authority from the Veda rather than standing as independent sources.

**Summary of the four preliminaries required before undertaking any text:** (1) the principal subject-matter treated in the work; (2) the purpose or benefit gained from studying it; (3) the relation between the text and its subject-matter; (4) who is qualified to undertake it — that is, which person should study it. These four qualities must be present.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 542</div>

Without these present in a work, listeners will not undertake to read it. Therefore these four qualities are now stated regarding the Veda itself. **The Veda is the subject (viṣaya); understanding its meaning is the purpose (prayojana); the Veda is primary and the commentary secondary — this is their relation (sambandha); and one who wishes to understand the Veda's meaning is the qualified person (adhikārī).** Since this subject is universally known and expounded within the Veda itself, one might doubt whether the commentary has any subject at all — and to resolve that doubt, these four qualities as stated above apply equally to the Veda itself.

**The Veda's two great divisions:** as stated earlier, karma-kanda and jnana-kanda are its two main portions. Karma-kanda expounds yajna-procedures and ritual methods; jnana-kanda expounds brahma-knowledge. Therefore, for these two portions, **dharma and brahma respectively are the subject-matter** — no other work whatsoever expounds dharma and brahma independently. On this the Purusharthanushasana states:

> धर्मब्रह्मणी वेदैकवेद्ये ।
> *dharma-brahmaṇī vedaika-vedye |*

— dharma and brahma are knowable through the Veda alone. Those learned in tradition cite here two of Jaimini's own sutras:

> चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ।
> *codanā-lakṣaṇo'rtho dharmaḥ |* (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-2)

—and—

> चोदनैव प्रमाणमेव ।
> *codanaiva pramāṇam eva |*

— the twofold restriction meaning that dharma is knowable through Vedic injunction alone, and cannot be grasped through direct perception. As Jaimini states in his fourth sutra:

> प्रत्यक्षमनिमित्तं विद्यमानोपलम्भनात् ।
> *pratyakṣam animittaṃ vidyamānopalambhanāt |* (Jaimini Sutra 1-1-4)

**Why dharma cannot be perceived:** dharma must be performed for one's own ultimate good, or must first be known before being performed — it is thus an object of knowledge, not of direct perception. It cannot be seen with the eyes; nor can it be known by inference, for a thing that the senses cannot reach cannot be inferred. Since the senses can grasp only what falls within their range, dharma cannot be apprehended by the senses at all. **Therefore dharma is knowable through the Veda alone.**

> "Perception is not a cause there, because perception deals with things that are, not with things that are to be." **Dharma will arise after the sacrifice producing it has been performed:** it does not exist before, and perception is therefore useless here. Nor even afterwards can dharma be apprehended by the senses, because it is destitute of form. That is the reason why it is commonly called "**adṛṣṭa**," that which is unseen. Nor is the second source of knowledge, inference, available here. Why? On account of the absence of characteristic marks. You will perhaps say that joy and sorrow are such characteristic marks for dharma and adharma. True. But they are given as such in the Veda itself. **Therefore the Veda is the only authority for religious duty.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 543</div>

There is no other way; since we have already established the Veda's authority, we must accept that dharma, as stated in the Veda, is authoritative.

**Dharma is not an object of perception.** The eyes reveal only what stands before them. Dharma arises only *after* the act producing it has been performed — it does not exist beforehand; and even afterward it remains beyond the senses, being destitute of form and similar sensible qualities. Therefore dharma is called "adṛṣṭa" (unseen). Nor can inference apprehend it, since no characteristic mark (liṅga) is available for it. One might object that pleasure and pain serve as such marks for dharma and adharma respectively — but the Veda itself is what tells us this. **Therefore the Veda alone is authoritative for dharma.**

One who performs dharma becomes happy; one who performs adharma becomes miserable. Seeing a happy person we conclude he has performed dharma; seeing a miserable one, that he has performed adharma. Pleasure and pain are indeed marks of dharma and adharma — this is precisely the point.

**On brahma:** although differing from dharma, inasmuch as it is something already in existence, **brahma can be known only from the shastra** — as is taught in the second section of the third sutra of the Uttara Mimamsa. As the commentator explains: "The meaning is that the shastra is the only authority for the truth that brahma is the cause of the birth, life, and death of the world." We can quote a text of Scripture too:

> "न वेदाविन् मनुते तं बृहन्तम्"
> "na vedāvin manute taṃ bṛhantam" (Taittiriya Brahmana 3-12-9-7)
>
> "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One."

Previous teachers have shown that this text has its application in the doctrine we are considering. **The other kinds of evidence — perception and inference — are of no use here, for brahma is without either form or characteristic marks.**

**Therefore, since they cannot be obtained from any other source, dharma and brahma are the subject-matter of the Veda.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 544</div>

Therefore dharma and brahma — the Veda's own subject-matter — are knowable through the Veda alone; there is no other means. **And knowledge of dharma and brahma is the immediate use (prayojana) of the Veda.**

Nor need we doubt lest such knowledge — like that, for example, that the earth has seven continents, or that a certain king is going somewhere — has no relation to any end of man. In ordinary usage, statements such as "the earth is bounded by seven islands" or "this king is going there" convey a genuine meaning, yet yield no human benefit to the hearer. Is the Veda's meaning to be understood in that same way? No, it is not — for from ordinary worldly statements a person gains little, whereas from knowledge of the Veda's meaning both dharma and brahma are attained, and thereby the human aims are accomplished.

**That dharma yields human benefit is praised in Scripture thus:**

> धर्मो विश्वस्य जगतः प्रतिष्ठा लोके धर्मिष्ठं प्रजा उपसर्पन्ति धर्मेण पापमपनुदति धर्मे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं तस्माद्धर्मं परमं वदन्ति ॥
> *dharmo viśvasya jagataḥ pratiṣṭhā loke dharmiṣṭhaṃ prajā upasarpanti dharmeṇa pāpam apanudati dharme sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ tasmād dharmaṃ paramaṃ vadanti ||* (Taittiriya Upanishad 63-7)
>
> "Dharma is the support of the whole world: throughout the world people flock to him who has most dharma. A man puts away his sin by means of his dharma; everything rests upon dharma. Therefore they call dharma man's highest good."

That is: dharma bears up this entire world; the people of the world approach the one established in dharma. By dharma sin is destroyed. Why? Because all things rest upon dharma alone. Therefore dharma is called the highest.

**Dharma restrains a king in act to strike, and to the weaker of two disputants brings victory as from a king's help:** truly it is an object of desire to men. As it is said in the Scripture of the Vajasaneyins, in the Srishti chapter:

> तच्छ्रेयोरूपमत्यसृजत धर्मं तदेतत्क्षत्रस्य क्षत्रं यद्धर्मस्तस्माद्धर्मात्परं नास्त्यथो अबलीयान्बलीयांसमाशंसते धर्मेण यथैव राज्ञैवम् ॥
> *tac chreyo-rūpam atyasṛjata dharmaṃ tad etat kṣatrasya kṣatraṃ yad dharmas tasmād dharmāt paraṃ nāsty atho abalīyān balīyāṃsam āśaṃsate dharmeṇa yathaiva rājñaivam ||* (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1-4-14)
>
> "He created dharma, that excellent form. This dharma is the kshatra (ruling power) of the kshatriya itself; therefore there is nothing higher than dharma. And so the weaker hopes to overcome the stronger by means of dharma, just as one does by the help of a king."

When two people quarrel, even a weak man in the right can, with the strength of justice, defeat a powerful wrongdoer — just as he might with a king's backing. **Therefore dharma accomplishes the human aims desired by all.**

**That knowledge of brahma conduces to man's desire is the theme of many texts of Scripture:**

> ब्रह्मविदाप्नोति परं ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवति तरति शोकमात्मवित् ।
> *brahmavid āpnoti paraṃ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati tarati śokam ātmavit |* (Taittiriya Upanishad 2-1-1; Mundaka Upanishad 3-2-9; Chandogya Upanishad 7-1-3)
>
> "The knower of brahma attains the Supreme. He who knows brahma becomes brahma itself. The knower of the Self crosses beyond sorrow."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 545</div>

The Vajasaneyins (followers of the Shukla-Yajurveda) state, in the Srishti (creation) chapter:

> तच्छ्रेयोरूपमत्यसृजत धर्मं तदेतत्क्षत्रस्य क्षत्रं यद्धर्मस्तस्माद्धर्मात्परं नास्त्यथो अबलीयान्बलीयांसमाशंसते धर्मेण यथा राज्ञैवम् ॥
> *tac chreyo-rūpam atyasṛjata dharmaṃ tad etat kṣatrasya kṣatraṃ yad dharmas tasmād dharmāt paraṃ nāsty atho abalīyān balīyāṃsam āśaṃsate dharmeṇa yathā rājñaivam ||* (Shatapatha Brahmana 14-4-2-26)

**Meaning:** thereafter He created dharma, that form of excellence. That itself is dharma. That very dharma is the kshatriya's own ruling power; nothing whatsoever is higher than it. Just as a person relies upon a king, one who relies upon dharma — even the weak — becomes strong.

**And the Taittiriya states** — "ब्रह्मविदाप्नोति परम्" *brahmavid āpnoti param* (Taittiriya Upanishad 2-1) — the knower of brahma attains the Supreme. **The Chandogya Upanishad states** — "ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवति" *brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati* — one who knows brahma becomes brahma itself (attaining oneness with brahma). **And "तरति शोकमात्मवित्" *tarati śokam ātmavit*** (Chandogya Upanishad 7-1-3) — one who knows the Self crosses beyond sorrow; for him there is no misery. In such statements throughout Scripture, the human benefit arising from brahma-knowledge is well established.

### The Qualified Person (Adhikārī)

**He who desires both kinds of knowledge is he who should study the Veda. He must be a man of one of the three higher castes.** The woman and the shudra, it is true, need that knowledge; but they have not been invested with the sacred thread — they have not gone over the Veda as a scholar with his guru does. **That they should meddle with the Veda is therefore expressly forbidden.** They must be taught dharma and brahma by means of the Puranas and the like.

**Therefore, the scope of the Veda lies in the knowledge of its meaning communicated to men of the three higher classes.**

### Relation (Sambandha)

**Lastly, of its relations.** To dharma and brahma it stands in the relation of that which teaches to the doctrine which is taught. To the knowledge of its own meaning it stands in the relation of that which produces to that which is produced. To men of the three higher castes it stands in the relation of that which benefits to that which is benefited. **Thus have I stated to those who are about to listen to me the four things commonly required**—

## Chapter 17. The Six Aṅgas of the Veda ("Lower Knowledge") — Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Chandas, Jyotiṣa: Their Purpose, and Why Each Must Be Studied

*Original title: "Aparavidyegaḷendu hēḷalpaḍuva vēdada ṣaḍaṅgagaḷa upayōgavēnu? Avannu ētakkāgi kaliyabēku?"*
**Printed pages 546–584 of the source.**

>
>

<div class="pgmark">original p. 546</div>

**Further on relation:** since the Veda expounds dharma and brahma, the Veda is the expounder (pratipādaka — the primary text) and dharma-brahma knowledge is what is expounded (pratipādya — its exposition). Therefore the Veda and dharma-brahma knowledge stand in the mutual relation of expounder and expounded. Likewise, dharma-knowledge arises *from* the Veda: the Veda is generative (janaka) and the knowledge generated (janya) — so they stand in the relation of producer and produced. And with respect to persons of the three twice-born classes, the relation is that of benefactor and beneficiary: those qualified receive the benefit, while dharma and brahma-knowledge confer it.

**Thus the four preliminaries — subject (viṣaya), purpose (prayojana), relation (sambandha), and qualified person (adhikārī) — have now been fully explained.** Knowing these, let the listeners now attend with composed minds to my exposition of the Veda's meaning.

### The Veda Together with Its Six Angas Constitutes the "Lower Knowledge" (Aparā Vidyā)

**The Veda is obscure, but it is the object of the Shiksha and the other Angas to expound its meaning.** That is why these Angas are included by the Atharvanikas in a sacred text to be found in their Mundaka Upanishad, under the term "lower knowledge" (aparā vidyā):

> द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्म यद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च । तत्रापरा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेदः शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति । अथ परा यया तदक्षरमधिगम्यते ॥
> *dve vidye veditavye iti ha sma yad brahmavido vadanti parā caivāparā ca | tatrāparā ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo'tharvavedaḥ śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam iti | atha parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate ||* (Mundaka Upanishad 1-1-4)
>
> "'Verily, there are two kinds of knowledge to be known' — so say those who know brahma — 'the higher and the lower.' Of these, the lower is: the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda, Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (ritual), Vyakarana (grammar), Nirukta (etymology), Chhandas (metre), and Jyotisha (astronomy). But the higher is that by which the Imperishable is attained."

**The reason for this classification:** the karma-kanda, being a means toward dharma-knowledge and requiring the six Angas as instruments, is called the "lower knowledge" (aparā vidyā); while the Upanishads, being the means to the supreme human aim of brahma-knowledge, are called the "higher knowledge" (parā vidyā).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 547</div>

Because the Veda is extremely profound — its words intricately joined and its meaning deep and hidden, hard to grasp — the six Angas beginning with Shiksha have arisen to make its meaning rightly known. For this very reason those who know the Atharvaveda, in the Mundaka Upanishad, call the Vedas with the six Angas the "lower knowledge" (aparā vidyā)—

> द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्म यद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च । तत्रापरा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेदः शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति । अथ परा यया तदक्षरमधिगम्यते ॥
> *dve vidye veditavye iti ha sma yad brahmavido vadanti parā caivāparā ca | tatrāparā ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo'tharvavedaḥ śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam iti | atha parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyate ||* (Mundaka Upanishad 1-1-4)

**Meaning:** knowledge is of two kinds — parā and aparā. Of these, aparā consists of: the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, Shiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana-shastra, Nirukta, Chhandah-shastra, and Jyotisha — these ten together are called aparā ("lower") knowledge. The knowledge that makes known the imperishable, beginningless Parabrahman is called parā. The Vedas with the six Angas teach the karma-kanda and are the cause of the means to dharma-knowledge; therefore the name aparā suits them. Therefore, this "lower" is no name of contempt; it merely means that dharma is a means, while attaining the highest human end — brahma-knowledge, of which the Upanishads are the source — is the "higher" (parā) knowledge.

### The Veda's Angas: The Definition of Śikṣā

> वर्णस्वराद्यच्चारणप्रकारो यत्प्रोक्तश्च ते सा शिक्षा । तथा च त्रैत्तिरीयाणामुपनिषदारम्भे समानुक्रियारूपणम् ।
> *varṇa-svarādy-uccāraṇa-prakāro yat proktaś ca te sā śikṣā | tathā ca traittirīyāṇām upaniṣad-ārambhe samānukriyā-rūpaṇam |* — वर्णः स्वरो मात्रा बलं साम सन्तान इत्युक्तः शिक्षाध्यायः । (Taittiriya Aranyaka 7-2)

That is: it is called Śikṣā because it teaches the method of pronouncing letters, accents, and similar matters. As it is said at the very beginning of the Taittiriyas' own Upanishad: "We shall now explain Śikṣā — varṇa (the letter), svara (the accent), mātrā (the quantity), bala (the force), sāma (uniform delivery), santāna (joining) — these are the six themes of the Śikṣā chapter."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 548</div>

**"Varṇa" (letter)** here means a and the other letters of the alphabet. The doctrine of the alphabet is clearly laid down in the work on Śikṣā, which is one of the Angas.

**By "svara" (accent)** is meant the udātta and other accents. The doctrine of the accents is given there too:

> उदात्तानुदात्तस्वरितः त्रयः स्वराः ।
> *udāttānudāttasvaritas trayaḥ svarāḥ |*
>
> "Udātta, anudātta, and svarita are the three accents."

**"Mātrā" (quantity)** refers to the distinction between short and long syllables, and the like. This, too, is defined in the same book.

**Under the term "bala" (force)** is included a reference both to the organ and the effort of pronunciation. The passage—

> अष्टौ स्थानानि वर्णानाम् ।
> *aṣṭau sthānāni varṇānām |*
> "Eight are the places [of articulation] of the letters"

— deals with the former subject (the organ); the passage—

> अचोऽस्पृष्टं यनस्त्विषत् ।
> *aco'spṛṣṭaṃ yanastviṣat |*
> "The vowels are unobstructed; the semivowels are [produced] with slight contact"

— with the latter (the effort).

**"Sāma" (uniform delivery)** means the even, level tone of the recitation, unmarked by any special rise or fall. This too is described in the same treatise.

**"Santāna" (joining)** means the un-interrupted linking together of accented and unaccented syllables into a single continuous flow, without pause — the euphonic combination (sandhi) that binds the Veda's own words together seamlessly.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 549</div>

As said before, knowledge of the six Angas beginning with Śikṣā is necessary for understanding the Veda's meaning. **We now examine closely the subjects treated in Śikṣā and the other Anga-works; whoever wishes to know more should consult the original works such as the Pāṇinīya-śikṣā.**

Regarding varṇa (letter), svara (accent), mātrā (quantity), bala (force), sāma (uniform delivery), and santāna (joining) — there is a separate Śikṣā work for each Veda, and many authors have written many kinds of Śikṣā-works for each Veda; they are known by the names of their authors: Pāṇinīya-śikṣā, Nāradīya-śikṣā, Bhāradvāja-śikṣā and so on. Followers of the Taittiriya Shakha specifically begin their own Upanishad with the following passage—

> शीक्षां व्याख्यास्यामः । वर्णः स्वरः । मात्रा बलम् । साम सन्तानः । इत्येषः शीक्षाध्यायः ॥
> *śīkṣāṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ | varṇaḥ svaraḥ | mātrā balam | sāma santānaḥ | ity eṣaḥ śīkṣādhyāyaḥ ||* (Taittiriya Upanishad 1-2)

That is: we shall now expound Śikṣā. Varṇa, svara, mātrā, bala, sāma, santāna — these constitute the six-part subject-matter treated in this Śikṣā-chapter. Varṇa refers to the letters of the alphabet and their explanation.

> त्रिषष्टिश्चतुःषष्टिर्वा वर्णाः संभवतो मताः । प्राकृते संस्कृते चापि स्वयं प्रोक्ताः स्वयम्भुवा ॥
> *triṣaṣṭiś catuḥṣaṣṭir vā varṇāḥ sambhavato matāḥ | prākṛte saṃskṛte cāpi svayaṃ proktāḥ svayambhuvā ||* (Śikṣā 3)

That is: in Sanskrit and in Prakrit — the languages in use other than Sanskrit — the letters number sixty-three or sixty-four, as Brahma himself has said. The details of the accents beginning with udātta are given there too—

> उदात्तश्चानुदात्तश्च स्वरितश्च स्वरास्त्रयः ।
> *udāttaś cānudāttaś ca svaritaś ca svarās trayaḥ |* (Śikṣā 11)

**"Svara" here means: udātta, anudātta, svarita — three types of accent.** Some works discuss a fourth kind too, called pracaya; but the wise say the primary threefold distinction stands—

### Definition of "Santāna" (Joining)

**"Sāma" (uniform delivery) is the same as samya**, by which term is meant here a mode of recitation which avoids such faults as being too quick, or too slow, or being singsong, and has the virtues of sweetness and the like. The faults are given in the passage beginning "giti sighri sirahkampi"; the virtues are given in the passage beginning "madhuryam aksharavyaktih."

**"Joining" (santāna)** refers to the rules for putting words together. When *vayu* stands before *yahi*, you must substitute *vayav*. When *indragni* stands before *agatam*, the final vowel...

**On accent:** by "svara" people commonly mean any of several kinds of accent found in different treatises — but the source treatises themselves generally speak of three svaras. The pronunciation of these svaras —

<div class="pgmark">original p. 550</div>

of the first word remains unchanged. This is a part of the subject which, as being discussed in Vyakarana, is omitted in the Śikṣā.

The udātta and prachaya accents are pronounced without any difference. When the anudātta is spoken, the syllable is pronounced lowered; when the svarita is pronounced, it is raised a little. In writing, the udātta and the prachaya accents carry no mark. But syllables that stand without a mark at the beginning of a mantra, and syllables that come without a mark after an anudātta, are to be understood as udātta syllables. The anudātta syllable is marked with a small horizontal stroke below the syllable; the svarita carries a small vertical stroke above the syllable. **As an example, one mantra is shown here with its accent-marks in place**—

> **अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं य॒ज्ञस्य॑ दे॒वमृ॑त्विज॑म् ।**
> **होता॑रं रत्न॒धात॑मम् ॥**
> *agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñasya devám ṛtvíjam | hótāraṃ ratnadhātamam ||* (Rigveda Samhita 1-1-1)
>
