> "I praise Agni, the household priest, the divine minister of the sacrifice, the invoker, the bestower of treasures most abundant."

**In this mantra, the udātta letters are:** gni, ro, jña, va, tvi, hoꞮ, dhā.
**The anudātta letters are:** a, pu, ya, de, ṛ, ta.
**The svarita letters are:** mī, ḷe, ta, jaꞮ, tā, ta.
**The prachaya (level/neutral) letters are:** le, taꞮ, raꞮ, ra, mam.
— And so on for the rest.

### On "Mātrā" (Quantity)

**"Mātrā"** means the specific duration required to pronounce a given letter — whether short or long — and how long that pronunciation should take. This is now discussed—

### "Prasave dīrghaḥ plutaśced iti kāla-niyamādi arthaḥ" (Sutra)

**Meaning:** the letter pronounced in the time taken to utter the vowel a is called hrasva (short); this is called one mātrā. Letters such as ā and ī, pronounced in the time of two mātrās, are called dīrgha (long). Letters pronounced in the time of three mātrās are called pluta (prolated). In the first example sentence the syllable is a pluta of three mātrās, and the numeral 3 is customarily written to show it; there is also a pluta of two mātrās, as in the second example sentence.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 551</div>

example, in the case of the word **indraśatru** pronounced with the wrong accent."

The reference is to the text of Scripture:

> इन्द्रशत्रुर्वर्धस्व ।
> *indraśatrur vardhasva |* (see Nirukta 2-16; Shatapatha Brahmana account of Tvashtri's error)
>
> "May you grow, O slayer of Indra."

If "indraśatru" in this text were intended to mean "enemy, destroyer of Indra," the word would be a tatpuruṣa compound, and in accordance with the rule "samāsasya" (the compound's accent-rule), it would have the acute accent on the...

**This is a well-known cautionary tale.** If "indraśatru" is to mean "he who slays Indra", the compound must be a tatpuruṣa ("Indra's slayer"), and then its last syllable must carry the udātta accent. But the word in the mantra has the udātta on its first syllable, and the last syllable (tru) is not udātta; so it is a bahuvrīhi, meaning "he whose slayer is Indra", that is, one to be slain by Indra. Because of this change of accent the sense reversed: Tvashtri, who sacrificed to obtain a son who would slay Indra, obtained one who was slain by Indra, and harm came to him instead of the fruit.

### On "Bala" (Force)

**"Bala"** means the place and the effort of articulation. "Place" (sthāna) is the part of the mouth to which the tongue is applied when a letter is pronounced; the Śikṣā says there are eight places, throat, palate, teeth, lips and the like. The vowels (a and the rest) are untouched: in pronouncing them the tongue touches no part of the mouth. The semivowels (ya, ra, la, va) are "īṣat" (slightly) touched. This manner of pronouncing a letter by touching the tongue to the palate and the other parts of the mouth is called "effort" (prayatna).

*(The Kannada text quotes here* तत्राष्टौ स्थानानि वर्णानाम् (शि. १३) — *tatrāṣṭau sthānāni varṇānām (Śikṣā 13).)*

### On "Sāma" (Uniform Delivery)

**"Sāma"** (sāmya, uniformity) means that, in pronouncing words, rules such as which letter is to be recited short and which long make the word uniform. One must not recite too hastily, nor drag out the letters too slowly. Without such faults, the words must be pronounced clearly and sweetly to the ear (audibly). This manner of pronunciation is called "sāmya".

The faults of recitation are given in the passages:

> गीती शीघ्री शिरःकम्पीत्यादिना (शि. ३२) । उपांशु दष्टं त्वरितमित्यादिना (शि. ३५)
> *gītī śīghrī śiraḥkampīty ādinā (Śikṣā 32) | upāṃśu daṣṭaṃ tvaritam ity ādinā (Śikṣā 35)*

### On "Madhurya" (Sweetness)

> माधुर्यमक्षरव्यक्तिरित्यादिना (शि. ३-३)
> *mādhuryam akṣara-vyaktir ity ādinā* (Śikṣā 3-3)

**When reciting the Veda's letters**, one must recite in such a way that letters like hrasva (short), dīrgha (long), saṃyukta-akṣara (conjunct letters), alpaprāṇa (unaspirated), and mahāprāṇa (aspirated) are pronounced clearly and distinctly, sweetly and without confusion, each properly articulated. **This is a virtue of correct recitation.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 552</div>

### "Santāna" (Joining) — continued

**Santāna** means the arrangement of joining according to the rules of saṃhitā or sandhi. In the sentence "vāyav ā yāhi", vāyo + ā becomes vāyav ā by the change of o to av, and sandhi results. In the sentence "indrāgnī ā gatam", indrāgnī + ā gatam undergoes no sandhi at all, and the original form remains as it was. Since many such rules of sandhi are explained at length in the science of grammar, the Śikṣā leaves them aside without explaining them.

Failing to properly know the rules laid down in the Śikṣā text — whether errors of accent or errors in letters — leads to serious fault when reciting a mantra. If a mantra is recited with either wrong accent or wrong letters, its very meaning becomes altered from its intended sense. Such a defective mantra becomes fruitless (aphala) — or worse, it directly harms the very person who recites it. There are traditional accounts of this. In particular, a well-known account, still preserved in the Taittiriya Shakha tradition, tells of such a case—

> मन्त्रो हीनः स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्या प्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह । स वाग्वज्रो यजमानं हिनस्ति यथेन्द्रशत्रुः स्वरतोऽपराधात् ॥ इति (शि. ५२)
> *mantro hīnaḥ svarato varṇato vā mithyā prayukto na tam artham āha | sa vāgvajro yajamānaṃ hinasti yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt || iti (Śikṣā 52)*
>
> "A mantra defective in accent or in letter, wrongly employed, does not convey that meaning; that word-thunderbolt injures the yajamāna, as 'indraśatru' did through the fault of accent."

Previously, when Tvashtri was performing Prajapati's yajna, desiring to have a son who would kill Indra, he made a homa-offering into Agni with the mantra—

> स्वाहेन्द्रशत्रुर्वर्धस्व ।
> *svāhendraśatrur vardhasva |*
> "Svāhā! May you grow, O slayer of Indra"

Because of an accent-error within it, instead of achieving the intended result, harm befell the very yajamāna who performed the yajna. **This same matter is explained by the mantra given in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda.**

> त्वष्टा हतपुत्रो वीन्द्रꣳ सोममाहरत्तस्मिन्निन्द्र उपहवमैच्छत तं नोपाह्वयत पुत्रं मेऽवधीरिति स यज्ञवेशसं कृत्वा प्रासहा सोममपिबत्तस्य यदत्यशिष्यत तत्त्वष्टाऽऽहवनीयमुपप्रावर्तयत्स्वाहेन्द्रशत्रुर्वर्धस्वेति स यावदूर्ध्वः पराविध्यति तावति स्वयमेव व्यरमत ॥ (तै. सं. २-४-१२-१)
> *tvaṣṭā hataputro vīndraṃ somam āharat tasminn indra upahavam aicchata taṃ nopāhvayata putraṃ me'vadhīr iti sa yajñaveśasaṃ kṛtvā prāsahā somam apibat tasya yad atyaśiṣyata tat tvaṣṭā''havanīyam upaprāvartayat svāhendraśatrur vardhasveti sa yāvad ūrdhvaḥ parāvidhyati tāvati svayam eva vyaramata || (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2-4-12-1)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 553</div>

What we need is the mantra "svāhendraśatrur vardhasva". When Tvashtri Prajapati performed the sacrifice, intending to obtain a son who would slay Indra, and made the offering in the fire, the accent of the word "indraśatru" was changed and the sense changed with it: instead of "the son who slays Indra" it became "the son who is slain by Indra", and harm came instead of the fruit. Let us consider how the change of accent came about. For "indraśatru" to mean the son who slays Indra, it would have to be a tatpuruṣa compound ("Indra's slayer"), and its last syllable would then have to be udātta. But the word used in the mantra has the udātta on its first syllable, and the last syllable (tru) is not udātta. So the word is a bahuvrīhi instead of a tatpuruṣa, and the meaning changes accordingly.

Because of this change of accent the sense of the mantra reversed: instead of producing a slayer of Indra, the sacrifice produced one to be slain by Indra, and the sacrificer received harm instead of the fruit. This shows how essential correct accent is:

> इन्द्रः शत्रुर्यस्य ।
> *indraḥ śatrur yasya |*

— this is the bahuvrīhi's genuine intended sense.

**Meaning:** if "indraśatru" is a tatpuruṣa, it means "slayer of Indra" and has the udātta on its last syllable; the word in the mantra has the udātta on its first syllable and is therefore a bahuvrīhi, "he whose slayer (śatru) is Indra", that is, one to be slain by Indra. By this change of accent the sense reversed and, instead of the fruit, harm came to the sacrificer. **From this it is clear how essential correct knowledge of the Śikṣā is for avoiding such faults of accent, letters and the like.**

### The Second Anga: Kalpa

**Kalpa, the second Anga, means the Sutras of Ashvalayana, Apastamba, Baudhayana and other authors.** For the science is so called because the sacrifice is confirmed (**kalpyate**) by it.

**Here you will perhaps start the following dilemma.** Does Ashvalayana in his book follow the order of the mantra portion of the Rigveda, or does he follow that of the brahmana portion? Not the former. Because his first words are, "We shall first expound the—"

<div class="pgmark">original p. 554</div>

**"New and Full Moon sacrifices" (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1-1-3).** Now the first hymns of Rig Veda are nowhere used throughout the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Nor the latter either. Because the Brahmana starts from the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, saying, "At the dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice they offer the puroḍāśa cake in eleven platters."

**To this we answer:** the mantra portion of Rig Veda follows the order in which the hymns must be recited — for example, in that recitation before the supreme Spirit, which we call the **brahma-yajña** [the "sacrifice of Brahman," i.e., Vedic recitation as a spiritual offering]. It does not follow the order in which the sacrificial rites are performed. This brahma-sacrifice is thus enjoined:

> यत्स्वाध्यायमधीयीतैकामप्यृचं यजुः साम वा तद्ब्रह्मयज्ञः ॥
> *yat svādhyāyam adhīyītaikām apy ṛcaṃ yajuḥ sāma vā tad brahma-yajñaḥ ||* (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2-10-6)
>
> "Let a man recite his own Veda, or one verse only of his own Veda, be it Rig, Yajur, or Sama; that is the spiritual sacrifice."

**Meaning:** in this brahma-yajña japa, the mantras beginning with the first Rik of the Saṃhitā are to be recited in the order in which they stand in the Saṃhitā. Likewise, at the vācaḥ-stoma sacrifice, in which all the Riks, all the Yajus mantras and all the Sāman mantras are to be recited, the order given by the traditional authorities is to be accepted.

The Mantra-kāṇḍa (the Saṃhitā) is thus arranged for japa in the brahma-yajña and the like, not for showing the order of performing sacrifices; therefore, although the order of the Mantra-kāṇḍa is not found in Āśvalāyana's Kalpa-sūtra, there is no contradiction in it.

The same traditional order is to be followed wherever the whole Mantra-kāṇḍa is employed, as in the recitation prescribed as an expiation.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 555</div>

**If it be asked** why uses are stated for mantras that are not in the Rigveda Saṃhitā, this is no fault. The use established in another Brāhmaṇa for mantras recited in another Śākhā has to be stated here by the principle of gathering together the qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya). The logicians say that one rite rests on all the Śākhās; therefore Kalpa, like Śikṣā, is needed.

**In all cases where a recitation of the whole mantra portion is commanded, the traditional order must be rigidly followed.**

So far the Vedānga Śikṣā has been dealt with; now the books of Kalpa, the sūtra-works, are examined. Kalpa means the works that set out the rules for performing sacrifices, the application (viniyoga) of mantras and the order of performing the sacrifice. They were composed in sūtra form by great sages such as Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba and Bodhāyana. For the Rigveda the Kalpa-sūtras composed by Āśvalāyana are the chief ones; for the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, Āpastamba, Bodhāyana and others composed Kalpa-sūtras; the other Vedas and other Śākhās also have Kalpa-sūtras composed by other sages. This has already been explained in detail (see page 32). According to the rites the sūtra-works are of many kinds: Śrauta-sūtra, Gṛhya-sūtra, Dharma-sūtra, Paribhāṣā-sūtra and so on. Of these the Śrauta-sūtra is the chief, so we shall examine it here. **In composing his Śrauta-sūtra, what order did Āśvalāyana follow?**

Did he follow the order of the Mantra-kāṇḍa (the mantras used in the sacrifice), or the order given in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa? He did not follow the first. At the beginning of his work he opens the section on the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice, saying—

> दर्शपूर्णमासौ तु पूर्वं व्याख्यास्यामः ।
> *darśa-pūrṇamāsau tu pūrvaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ |*
> "We shall first expound the Darsha and Purnamasa rites"

(Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1-1-3). The mantras at the beginning of the Rigveda Saṃhitā, such as the first Rik, are nowhere used in the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice; therefore the order of the Mantra-kāṇḍa was not followed. Did he follow the second, the order of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa? That too is not so. For at the beginning of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa come the mantras connected with the dīkṣaṇīyā rite, as in the passage—

> आत्मानं वेदपुरोडाशं निर्वपति दीक्षणीयेष्ट्यादौ कल्पम् ।
> *ātmānaṃ veda-puroḍāśaṃ nirvapati dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭy-adau kalpam |*
> "At the dikshaniya sacrifice they offer the purodasa cake in eleven platters"

(Aitareya Brahmana 1-1) — the mantras connected with the dīkṣaṇīyā rite come first there. So the order of the Brāhmaṇa too was not followed.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 556</div>

**Here one special point must be made.** The Mantra-kāṇḍa (the Saṃhitā, comprising the Riks) is an order fixed for recitation (japa) in the brahma-yajña and the like; it was not arranged for showing the order of performing sacrifices. **The brahma-yajña is enjoined thus:**

> यत्स्वाध्यायमधीयीतैकामप्यृचं यजुः साम वा तद्ब्रह्मयज्ञः ॥
> *yat svādhyāyam adhīyītaikām apy ṛcaṃ yajuḥ sāma vā tad brahma-yajñaḥ ||* (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2-10-6)

"Let a man recite his own Veda — even a single verse of his own Veda, whether Rig, Yajur, or Sama — that is the spiritual sacrifice." **This is what it means.** In this brahma-yajña the mantras beginning with the first Rik of the Saṃhitā are to be recited in the order in which they stand in the Saṃhitā. Likewise, at the vācaḥ-stoma sacrifice, in which all the Riks, Yajus and Sāman mantras are to be recited, the order given by the traditional authorities is to be accepted.

And at the Ashvina sacrifice, while the Ashvina-shastra is being recited, it is enjoined—

> सूर्यो नोदियादपि सर्वा दाशतयीरनुब्रूयात् ।
> *sūryo nodiyād api sarvā dāśatayīr anubrūyāt |*

— that is, before the sun rises one should finish reciting all the mantras called *dāśatayā*. And again—

> रिच्यत इव वा एष प्रेव रिच्यते यो याजयति प्रति वा गृह्णाति, याजयित्वा प्रतिगृह्य वानश्नन् त्रिः स्वाध्यायं वेदमधीयीत ॥
> *ricyata iva vā eṣa preva ricyate yo yājayati prati vā gṛhṇāti, yājayitvā pratigṛhya vānaśnan triḥ svādhyāyaṃ vedam adhīyīta ||* (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2-16)

— that is, one who, out of desire for wealth, officiates at sacrifices for the unqualified or accepts forbidden gifts is as it were emptied: he loses his good name in this world and has no good state hereafter, so he must perform penance, fasting and reciting his own Veda three times.

**It is true that the Brahmana of the Rig Veda begins with the dīkṣaṇīya rite.** But that rite is merely a modification of the New and Full Moon sacrifice to which it makes constant reference. So Ashvalayana did well to begin his exposition with his latter rite.

**It has thus been shown that the second Anga, the Kalpa Sutra, stating as it does the application of the various texts, is useful in teaching the performance of the sacrifice.**

**You will say**, let Ashvalayana, if he pleases, give the application of the Samidheni verses "pra vo vajah" and the like. But what does he mean by giving the application of such...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 557</div>

**verses as, for example,**

> नमः प्रवक्त्रे ।
> *namaḥ pravaktre |* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1-2)

**which are no part of the revealed text of the Rig Veda at all? He is not in fault. He does well, &c.**

Regarding this, **"इषे त्वा"** (*iṣe tvā*) and the other Yajurveda mantras: since these mantras are arranged in the order of performing the sacrifice, Apastamba and the other great sages composed their Kalpa-sutras following the order found there. Since that order is in the Veda itself, it is natural that the same order is followed in japa, recitation and the like.

**Ashvalayana** begins his Kalpa-sutra with the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice. In the Aitareya Brahmana the dīkṣaṇīyā rite is stated first. But since the dīkṣaṇīyā rite is a modification of the Darsha-Purnamasa, and it is proper to state the model rite first and the modification afterwards, Ashvalayana was right to state the Darsha-Purnamasa first. (The matter of model rites and modifications has been explained earlier.) **Therefore, since the Kalpa-sutras, by stating the application of mantras, teach the order of performing the sacrifice, they are of service.**

**Then let Ashvalayana state the application** of the Samidheni Riks (the mantras said when the fire is kindled and the fuel sticks are laid on), such as—

> प्र वो वाजाः ।
> *pra vo vājāḥ |*

**and similar verses** — granted. But why state the application of mantras that are not in the revealed Rig Veda text at all? — This is not a fault. All the texts that bear on a particular sacrifice should, **in accordance with the "गुणोपसंहारन्याय" (*guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya*)** (the principle of gathering together whatever qualities are relevant), be given, in whatever Shakha they are found. **Logicians say that each rite rests on all the Shakhas; therefore Kalpa, like Śikṣā, must be attended to.**

### The Third Anga: Vyākaraṇa (Grammar) — Its Purpose Set Out Through Its Defining Characteristics, in the Manner Shown by Vararuchi and Patañjali

<div class="pgmark">original p. 558</div>

**Vyākaraṇa** is useful in determining the precise form of a word and its meaning, through the instruction it gives regarding roots (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), and similar matters. Likewise, in the **Aindravāyavagraha-brāhmaṇa**, it is recounted—

> वाग्वै पराच्यव्याकृतावदत्तेते देवा इन्द्रमब्रुवन्निमां नो वाचं व्याकुर्विति। सोऽब्रवीद्वैषा मह्यं चैव वायवे च सह गृह्णाथा इति। तस्मादिन्द्रवायू सहैव गृह्णाति। तामिन्द्रो मध्यतोऽवक्रम्य व्याकरोत्। तस्मादियं व्याकृता वागुद्यते ॥
> *vāg vai parācy avyākṛtāvadat | te devā indram abruvan vi māṃ no vācaṃ vyākuruv iti | so'bravīd vaiṣā mahyaṃ caiva vāyave ca saha gṛhṇāthā iti | tasmād indra-vāyū sahaiva gṛhṇāti | tām indro madhyato'vakramya vyākarot | tasmād iyaṃ vyākṛtā vāg udyate ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 6-4-7-3)
>
> "**In old days Speech was indiscreet.** The gods came to Indra, and said, 'Separate Speech for us into its parts.' He said, 'Give me and Vayu a boon, let us take it together.' **Therefore, the Aindravayava [offering] is taken together.** Then Indra took Speech by the middle, and divided it into its parts. **And that is the origin of Speech divided into parts (vyākṛta).**"

**Meaning:** in ancient times, Speech (Vāk) existed only in an undivided, unanalyzed form — it had not yet been separated into its constituent parts, and was thus spoken in a scattered, indistinct manner. Perceiving this defect, the gods approached Indra and requested him to properly divide Speech into its parts. Indra agreed on the condition that this task be shared jointly with Vayu — hence the well-known "Aindravayava" oblation, offered to Indra and Vayu together, commemorates this shared undertaking. Indra then took hold of Speech at her very middle and divided her methodically into her constituent parts. From this act arose "vyākṛta vāk" — Speech properly analyzed and divided — which is precisely what the science of **Vyākaraṇa** ("grammar," literally "the analysis/division [of speech]") takes as its own subject-matter and derives its very name from.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 559</div>

**The meaning of this is as follows:** in old days a text like "agnim īḷe purohitam" was an indiscrete sound like the roar of the sea. And there was no book to help distinguish in it between roots, affixes, words, and sentences. Then Indra, at the request of the gods, being propitiated by a boon in the form of an offering of soma poured into one vessel for him and Vayu, divided Speech in the middle, and established the divisions between roots, affixes, and the like. **And that is why all can now recite Speech as it has been analysed by Pāṇini and other great sages.**

**The special use of this analysis of words, or Grammar, is shown by Vararuchi in the Vārtika**—

> रक्षोहागमलाघ्वसन्देहाः प्रयोजनम् ।
> *rakṣohāgama-lāghva-sandehāḥ prayojanam |* (Katyayana's Vartika on Paṇini's Ashtadhyayi)
>
> "Protection, comprehension of [the sense of] transmitted [Vedic texts], brevity, and removal of doubt — these are the purposes [of Grammar]."

**These and other uses are explained in the Mahābhāṣya by Patañjali as follows:**—

**"Rakṣā"** [protection] — the protection of the Veda [refers to preserving Vedic texts from corruption]. "**Pradhānaṃ ca ṣaḍbhis sneha-vyākaraṇam**" [Grammar is chief among these six, being the means of proper linkage]. "**Pradhāne ca kṛto yuktaḥ phalāt tṛptavati**" [Being primary, its fruit is complete]. "**Alpākṣaraṃ cābhyeyaṃ vyākaraṇam**" — Grammar is to be studied precisely because it is concise, [and thereby valuable]. "**Bṛhaspatiḥ riṃ nyāya vidyaṃ varṣa-sahasraṃ pratipada-doktvā śakalanāṃ śabdānām**" [Brihaspati taught the doctrine of words, syllable by syllable, for a thousand years]. "**Śabba-kṣatrāṃ**" [thus the science of words] "**Indrāya prāha**" — [and] taught it to Indra. "**Divyaṃ varṣa-sahasram adhyayana-kālaḥ**" — the period of study extended for a thousand celestial years. "**Aṃśaṃ ca na jagāma**" — and even then, he did not reach the end of it. "**Ādyas tu punar api paramāyāḥ bhagavatī sa kala-sad-āvaga-nu bhūta kuta sarva śabda-tāvagena sakala-sad-āva-vagenaḥ kuta sarva-pradeśāvena caitāyaṃ vyākaraṇam**" — [this concise treatise on] Grammar, [treating] all the requisite subjects, teaches "using appropriate speech" as its purpose.

**"Laghu-tvam"** [brevity] — a shortened word, used quickly (śīghra), is preferable. **"Sandehe"** — where doubt arises whether a particular is or is not a word: is it "sthūla" or "sthūlā," is it "śva" or "śvā" — [Grammar resolves this]. **"Kartā"** [the agent] — as with "dāśvaḥ" — [the one who has given]. **"Anavadyaṃ kṛta-śrī"** — [Grammar renders speech] faultless. **"Ubhaya-taḥ"** — on both sides. **"Duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato vā varṇato vā"** — **a word [used] incorrectly, whether in accent or in letter, [causes fault]. "Mithyā-prayukto na tam artham āha"** — [a] wrongly-used [word] does not convey that meaning [it is intended to]. **"Sa vāgvajro yajamānaṃ hinasti**" — **that word becomes a thunderbolt, and strikes the sacrificer**. **"Duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svaratovā"** — this is confirmed [by scripture] — **"yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt"** — as in the case of "indraśatru" mispronounced in accent. **"Tasmāt yajñeṣu prayoktavyaṃ śreyaḥ vyākaraṇam**" — **therefore, in sacrifices, Grammar should be properly employed.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 560</div>

**On "Rakṣā" (Protection):**

> रक्षार्थं वेदानामध्येयं व्याकरणम् ।
> *rakṣārthaṃ vedānām adhyeyaṃ vyākaraṇam |*
>
> "**Grammar should, in the first place, be studied for the protection of the Vedas.** Only he who knows the laws under which letters are dropped, or added, or modified, will be able adequately to guard the Vedas, and to understand their meaning."

**On "Ūha" (Adaptation):**

> ऊहः खल्वपि ।
> *ūhaḥ khalv api |*
>
> "**Uha [adaptation] comes next.** The texts are not given in the Veda in all the required genders and cases. They must needs be altered when used at the sacrifice, to suit the particular occasion. No one ignorant of Grammar can make the necessary alterations. **Grammar should therefore be studied for this reason also.**"

**On "Āgama" (Scriptural Authority/Tradition):**

> आगमः खल्वपि ।
> *āgamaḥ khalv api |*
>
> "**Scripture comes next.** There is the text, 'A brahmin should learn and understand disinterested virtue in the shape of the Veda with six Angas.' Among the six Angas, Grammar is important. **Effort spent on what comes first must be fruitful.**"

**Meaning:** among the six Angas, Grammar is spoken of as foremost. Since effort expended on the primary [Anga] is what truly bears fruit, one should first make the effort to study Grammar specifically. This is what "āgama" (scriptural authority) establishes as the reason for studying Grammar.

**On "Laghu" (Ease):** Grammar is to be studied so that the Veda may be understood easily; the account of Brihaspati and Indra on the next page shows why.

**On "Sandeha" (Doubt):** where genuine uncertainty arises regarding whether a word is being used correctly — for example, doubt about whether the intended sense is being properly conveyed by a given form — only knowledge of Grammar dispels such doubt and confirms the word's true, correct application.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 561</div>

**On "Lāghava" (Brevity/Conciseness) — continued:**

> लाघवार्थं व्याकरणमध्येयम् ।
> *lāghavārthaṃ vyākaraṇam adhyeyam |*
>
> "**Next, Grammar should be studied for conciseness' sake.** Brihaspati taught Indra the science of words for a thousand years of the gods, giving him one word after another. He never got to the end. Yet Brihaspati was the teacher, and Indra was the scholar, and the lesson lasted for a thousand years of the gods. And still he did not get to the end. Nowadays if a man is long-lived, he may reach a hundred years. How can he apprehend, much less learn to use rightly, all words if taught them word by word?"

**On "Sandeha" (Removal of Doubt):**

> संदेहार्थं च व्याकरणमध्येयम् ।
> *sandehārthaṃ ca vyākaraṇam adhyeyam |*
>
> "**Lastly, Grammar should be studied for the removal of doubts.** The priests recite the text**—**"

> स्थूलपृषतीमग्निवरुणमनड्वाहमालभेत ।
> *sthūlapṛṣatīm agnivaruṇam anaḍvāham ālabheta |*
>
> "**One should offer a great-spotted [cow] [belonging] to Agni-Varuna, and a bull.**"

"Here no one but a grammarian can say how the compound '**sthūlapṛṣatī**' is to be taken. He decides by the accent. If the acute accent were on the last syllable of the compound, the word would be a **karmadhāraya** (descriptive compound, meaning 'great and spotted'). As it is, the compound has the accent on its first member, and it is therefore a **bahuvrīhi** (possessive compound, meaning 'she who has great spots')."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 562</div>

**"Moreover, there are these further uses of Grammar":**

> तेऽसुरः दुष्टः शब्दः यदधीतम् यस्तु प्रयुङ्क्ते अविद्वान्सह विभक्तिं कुर्वन्ति यो वा इमं चत्वारि उतत्वः सक्तुमिव सरस्वतीं दसम्यं पुत्रस्य सुदेवोऽसि वरुणः ।
> *te'suraḥ duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ yad adhītam yas tu prayuṅkte avidvān saha vibhaktiṃ kurvanti yo vā imaṃ catvāri uta tvaḥ saktum iva sarasvatīṃ dasamyaṃ putrasya sudevo'si varuṇaḥ |* (Mahabhashya, Paspashahnika)
>
> "**'Te'suraḥ, duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ, yad adhītam, yas tu prayuṅkte, avidvān saha, vibhaktiṃ kurvanti, yo vā imaṃ, catvāri, uta tvaḥ, saktum iva, sarasvatīm, dasamyaṃ putrasya, sudevo'si varuṇaḥ.'**"

### "Te'suraḥ" (The Asuras)

> हेळयो हेळयः इत्यसुरा उच्चरन्तः पराजिता । तस्माद्ब्राह्मणेन म्लेच्छितवै नापभाषितवै मलेच्छो ह वा एष यदपशब्दः ॥
> *heḷayo heḷayaḥ ity asurā uccarantaḥ parājitāḥ | tasmād brāhmaṇena mlecchitavai nāpabhāṣitavai | mleccho ha vā eṣa yad apaśabdaḥ ||* (Mahabhashya, Paspashahnika)
>
> "**The Asuras shouted 'heḷayo heḷayaḥ' (he 'rayo he 'rayaḥ) and were defeated. Therefore a brahmin should not speak the language of the barbarian, should not use bad forms. The word 'mleccha' here is equivalent to 'apaśabda' [incorrect speech]. Let us study Grammar that we may not be Mlecchas.**"

### "Duṣṭaḥ Śabdaḥ" (The Corrupted Word)

> दुष्टः शब्दः स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्याप्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह । स वाग्वज्रो यजमानं हिनस्ति यथेन्द्रशत्रुः स्वरतोऽपराधात् ॥
> *duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato varṇato vā mithyā-prayukto na tam artham āha | sa vāg-vajro yajamānaṃ hinasti yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt ||* (Mahabhashya, Paspashahnika)
>
> "**A word with a wrong accent or a wrong letter is used in vain since it does not convey the same meaning: it is a spoken thunderbolt that will destroy the sacrificer, as, for example, the word 'indraśatru' with the accent misplaced.**"

<div class="pgmark">original p. 563</div>

Now the discussion of Grammar, the chief among the Vedāṅgas, is taken up. Grammar too is of use in determining the form of a word and its meaning, by showing the divisions such as root (prakṛti) and suffix (pratyaya). So it is said also in the **Aindravāyavagraha-brāhmaṇa**—

> वाग्वै पराच्यव्याकृतावदत् एते देवा इन्द्रमब्रुवन् इमां नो वाचं व्याकुर्विति सोऽब्रवीद्वैषा मह्यं चैव वायवे च सह गृह्णाथा इति तस्मादिन्द्रवायू सहैव गृह्णाति तामिन्द्रो मध्यतोऽवक्रम्य व्याकरोत् तस्मादियं व्याकृता वागुद्यते ॥
> *vāg vai parācy avyākṛtāvadat | ete devā indram abruvan imāṃ no vācaṃ vyākuruv iti | so'bravīd vaiṣā mahyaṃ caiva vāyave ca saha gṛhṇāthā iti | tasmād indra-vāyū sahaiva gṛhṇāti | tām indro madhyato'vakramya vyākarot | tasmād iyaṃ vyākṛtā vāg udyate ||* (Taittiriya Samhita 6-4-7-3; see page 558 above)

**Meaning:** in the beginning, Speech spoke unclearly (avyākṛta — undivided). Then the gods approached Indra, asking, "Divide this Speech of ours [into parts] for us." He agreed, saying, "Give this offering jointly to me and to Vayu." Because of this, [the offering] is given jointly to Indra and Vayu even now (the Aindravāyava). The gods agreed. Then Indra took hold of Speech at her very middle and divided her methodically. That is why what we now recite is "vyākṛta vāk" — Speech that has been analyzed and divided into her proper constituent parts.

**In ancient times a text like "agnim īḷe purohitam" was an undivided sound, like the roar of the sea, without the divisions of root, suffix, word and sentence.** Then Indra, requested by the gods and pleased with the boon that he and Vayu might take the soma juice in one vessel, separated that undivided Speech in the middle and established the divisions such as root and suffix throughout. **So this Speech, analysed (vyākṛta) by Pāṇini and other great sages by the rules of grammar, is recited by all — this is the sense.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 564</div>

What the use of this Grammar is, Vararuchi has shown in his Vārtika—

> **रक्षोहागमलाघवसंदेहाः प्रयोजनमिति ।**
> *rakṣohāgamalāghavasandehāḥ prayojanam iti |* (Katyayana's Vartika; see page 559 above)

"**Rakṣā** (protection), **ūha** (adaptation), **āgama** (scriptural priority), **lāghava** (brevity), and **sandeha**-removal — these are the purposes [of Grammar]." Patañjali has explained these purposes, and others, clearly in his Mahābhāṣya.

**Rakṣā (Protection):** Grammar is to be studied in order to protect the Vedas, that is, to preserve the Vedic texts as they are, so that they are not altered by pronunciation and the like and no variant readings or losses arise. One who knows the changes of letters caused by loss, addition and the like will keep the Vedas intact, and such a grammarian can understand the Veda well.

**Ūha (Adaptation):** In the Vedic mantras the genders, numbers, cases and the like are not used so strictly; and at the sacrifice the mantras have to be used with some change of number, case and the like to suit the occasion. One who does not know Grammar cannot make such changes. So that one may know which number and which case to supply on each occasion, Grammar must be studied.

**Āgama (Scripture):** The scriptures say that a brahmin, without desiring any reward, must study the Veda with its six Angas, which is of the nature of dharma, and must understand its meaning. Among the six Vedāngas Grammar is the chief. Effort spent on studying this chief Anga is fruitful. Therefore Grammar must be studied.

**Lāghava (Ease):** Grammar is to be studied so that the Veda may be understood easily. Once Brihaspati, the teacher of the gods, tried to teach Indra the science of words, and taught the peculiarities of the form and derivation of each word in the Veda for a thousand years by the divine reckoning; yet he did not reach the end. The teacher was Brihaspati, the learner Indra, and the time a thousand divine years; still it was not finished. Nowadays the longest life of a man is about a hundred years; how could he learn the science of words by taking each word in turn? Therefore Grammar must be studied so that the use of words may be learned easily and quickly.

**Sandeha (Removal of Doubt):** When the right meaning of words is to be fixed, many doubts arise. Grammar must be studied to remove them.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 565</div>

religious merit accrues to him from his knowledge of the right form, religious demerit must accrue to him from his knowledge of the wrong form. **In fact, more demerit than merit. For wrong forms are many, right are few. Every word has many corruptions. Take the word**

> गौः ।
> *gauḥ |*

**Corrupt forms of it are**

> गवी, गोणी, गोपोतलिका ।
> *gavī, goṇī, gopotalikā |*

**and the like. As for the man who does not know how to put words together, his ignorance is his safety."**

**Asaṃdeha (Freedom from Doubt):** knowing the meanings of words correctly is called freedom from doubt (asaṃdeha). This is a fundamental requirement for grammatical study. Understand it this way—

> स्थूलपृषती मासि आलभेत ।
> *sthūlapṛṣatī māsi ālabheta |*

— this sentence involves ambiguity: how should the compound "**sthūlapṛṣatī**" be understood? Or should one understand it as—

> स्थूलः पृषती ।
> *sthūlaḥ pṛṣatī |*

— (a karmadhāraya compound, "she who is both great and spotted")? Or as a bahuvrīhi compound, "she whose spots are great"? Without knowledge of Grammar, this cannot be resolved. Only a grammarian, on the basis of the accent, can determine whether this is a bahuvrīhi or a karmadhāraya compound, and thereby settle the meaning correctly. Here, in this sentence, the accent falls on the compound's *first* member — establishing it definitively as a bahuvrīhi, meaning "one who possesses great spots," rather than "great and spotted" as a mere descriptive pairing. In a karmadhāraya the two words are independent, with no relation of qualifier and qualified; in a bahuvrīhi the whole compound qualifies another, principal word ("she whose spots are great"); so the two analyses give different meanings. Therefore Grammar must be studied to remove such doubts.

Besides these, Grammar has many further uses; they are stated in sūtra form and each is explained at length. These sūtras are: **rakṣā, śabdaḥ, uditvaṃ, iyaśca, prayukte, avidvāṃsa, vibhaktiṃ kurvanti, yo vā imāṃ, catvāri, uta tvaḥ, saktum iva, sāraśvatīṃ, dasamyaṃ putrasya, sudevoṣi varuṇeti** ||

**Te'surāḥ (The Asuras):** those demons, at one time (in battle), pronounced a wrong word and were therefore defeated. Instead of shouting the cry "he 'rayo he 'rayah" (O enemies!),

<div class="pgmark">original p. 566</div>

they pronounced l in place of r and said "helayo helayah" (layah = destruction); so they met with laya, that is, destruction and defeat. Therefore a brahmin must not become a mleccha, that is, he must not speak a corrupt word as the mlecchas do; a corrupt word is itself mleccha. Grammar should be studied so as not to utter such corrupt words.

**"Duṣṭaḥ Śabdaḥ"** (The Corrupted Word) — this term has already been discussed above (see page 552 [the indraśatru account]). It occurs in the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā as follows:

> दुष्टः शब्दः स्वरतो वर्णतो वा मिथ्याप्रयुक्तो न तमर्थमाह । स वाग्वज्रो यजमानं हिनस्ति यथेन्द्रशत्रुः स्वरतोऽपराधात् ॥
> *duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato varṇato vā mithyā-prayukto na tam artham āha | sa vāg-vajro yajamānaṃ hinasti yathendraśatruḥ svarato'parādhāt ||* (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 52)

If in a word the accent or a letter is lost or changed, it is a corrupted word (duṣṭa śabda). Such a use of a word does not convey the intended meaning but speaks a wrong one. Therefore the use of a corrupted word brings harm to the sacrificer, as a thunderbolt strikes an enemy. The word "indraśatru" used with a changed accent is the example. Therefore, to avoid such faults, that is, to avoid using a corrupted word, Grammar should be studied.

**"Yad Adhītam"** (What Has Been Studied) — from the Nirukta (1-6-1), stated thus—

> यदधीतमविज्ञातं निगदेनैव शब्द्यते । अनग्नाविव शुष्कैधो न तज्ज्वलति कर्हिचित् ॥
> *yad adhītam avijñātaṃ nigadenaiva śabdyate | anagnāv iva śuṣkaidho na taj jvalati karhicit ||* (Nirukta 1-6-1)

**Meaning:** whatever is studied by rote alone, without understanding, and merely recited mechanically, without genuine comprehension of the Veda's meaning — it will never blaze up, like dry fuel thrown where there is no fire, never bursting into flame. Therefore, one should study Grammar specifically in order to understand the Veda's meaning correctly.

**"Yas tu Prayuṅkte"** (He Who Rightly Applies It) — Grammar is to be studied in order to know how words are to be used on each occasion. On this the sage Katyayana says—

> यस्तु प्रयुङ्क्ते कुशलो विशेषे शब्दान्यथावद्व्यवहारकाले ।
> *yas tu prayuṅkte kuśalo viśeṣe śabdān yathāvad vyavahāra-kāle |* (see page 564 above)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 567</div>

> सोऽकनन्तेमाप्रोत्येति जयं परत्रे वाग्योगविद्दुष्यति चापशब्दैः ॥
> *so'kanantemāprotyeti jayaṃ paratre vāg-yoga-vid duṣyati cāpaśabdaiḥ ||* (Kashika/grammatical tradition, on the value of correct usage)

**Meaning:** the wise man who, in the performance of rites as in worldly dealings, uses faultless good words as the occasion requires, gains fame in this world and endless victory (the best state) in the next world. But one who knows the right use of words, if he uses corrupt words, will not escape harm.

**Who is harmed here? The one who knows the right use of words.** Why is harm done to one who knows? Because such a man can tell a good word from a bad one; if, with that knowledge, he still uses a corrupt word, what is it but harm? From good use of words dharma arises; in the same way from the use of corrupt words adharma, that is, sin, arises. Or: if, though he knows, he uses a corrupt word, a greater sin comes to him. Ordinarily good words (correct words that are not corrupt) are very few; corrupt words are the more numerous. Every word has many corrupt forms. For example the word "gauḥ" (cow) has many corrupt forms in common use, such as "gāvī," "goṇī," "gopotalikā."

Someone may say that he used corrupt words from ignorance, that is, without knowing, because he had no knowledge of grammar. But to plead ignorance in this way is wrong, and it must not be done. If a man, without knowing it, kills a brahmin or drinks wine, does he not become an outcast even though he did it from ignorance? So, whether done knowingly or from ignorance, bad deeds do not escape punishment. In the same way, one who does not know the use of words and, in his ignorance, uses corrupt words does not escape adharma. And the one who knows the use of words and, by the strength of his knowledge, uses good words will surely gain dharma; since he has the knowledge, he should use good words only.

**Jaimini and other Mīmāṃsakas insist one must know what constitutes dharma, and equally know what constitutes adharma** — precisely for this purpose. Both must be known: to perform dharma, and to avoid adharma. Even here [in the Śikṣā's own account], "śabda" (correct word) and "aśabda" (incorrect word)...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 568</div>

One must know both. Knowing the correct word, and knowing how it should be applied; knowing the incorrect word, and knowing how it should be avoided in application — **for this very reason, Grammar should be studied.**

**"Avidvāṃsaha"** (The Ignorant) — regarding this term, since it discusses those who are ignorant of Grammar, it has been treated already in similar contexts. Since it discusses persons devoid of grammatical knowledge, it treats the fault of using improper forms — this is given here as an example—

> अविद्वांसः प्रत्यभिवादे नानोऽयं ये न पुंसि विदुः । कामं तेषु तु विप्रेष्यं स्त्रीष्विवानायं वदेदिति ॥
> *avidvāṃsaḥ pratyabhivāde nāno'yaṃ ye na puṃsi viduḥ | kāmaṃ teṣu tu vipreṣyaṃ strīṣv ivānāyaṃ vaded iti ||* (Nirukta 1-19)

"**But the unlearned, who do not know that, in responding to a salutation, they should protract the vowel — in approaching them, he should simply say, as he would to a woman, 'Here am I.'**"

**Meaning:** as said in this verse, when a young student (vaṭu) salutes, he states his pravara (the names of the chief sages of his gotra) and salutes with "I, sir, salute you". The one saluted blesses the student by saying "Long life to you, Devadatta, may you prosper", pronouncing the last syllable of the student's name with a pluta of three mātrās. When he salutes an unlearned man who does not know how to bless with the pluta, the one who has gone away and returned must salute without reciting the pravara and the rest, simply saying "I salute", as he would salute women. Since such is the rule, to receive salutations in a learned assembly and the like one must be learned through the study of Grammar and the other sciences; an unlearned man receives no such honour. Therefore, to win honour, Grammar should be studied.

**"Vibhaktiṃ Kurvanti"** (They Adapt the Case-endings) — those who know the order of performing the sacrifice say that the prayājas must be made "with case-endings", that is, in reciting the prayāja mantras (the prayājas are the principal offering-mantras of the sacrifice) the case-endings must be adapted to the occasion so that the meaning fits. Without a knowledge of Grammar one cannot recite the prayāja mantras with the right case-endings. Therefore Grammar should be studied.

> प्रयाजाः सविभक्तिकाः कार्त्स्न्या इति —
> *prayājāḥ savibhaktikāḥ kārtsnyā iti* — "The priests recite the text 'prayajah savibhaktikah karyah.' But without Grammar this precept cannot be complied with. Let us study Grammar then for this reason."

**"Yo Vā Imām"** (He Who [Analyses] This [Speech]) — the man who is able to divide the Vedic sentences word by word, and the accents and letters at the pauses according to the rules of svara-sandhi—

<div class="pgmark">original p. 569</div>

Whoever can resolve these according to the rules — only such a person is fit to be a priest. One who cannot properly divide sentences, syllables, or word-portions; who cannot distinguish accent-differences, letter-differences, or the boundaries within a compound; who cannot properly identify [ritually] related words — such a person is unfit to serve as priest in yajna and similar rites. **Therefore, only one who is thoroughly versed in Grammar is fit for priesthood.**

**Here, to illustrate the analysis of words and accented letters, we give the following example from the Rigveda**—

> वायवा याहि दर्शतेमे सोमा अरंकृताः । तेषां पाहि श्रुधी हवम् ॥
> *vāyav ā yāhi darśateme somā araṃkṛtāḥ | teṣāṃ pāhi śrudhī havam ||* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1-2-1)

**This ṛk is in the Gāyatrī metre.** Dividing its first half into its two pādas gives "vāyav ā yāhi darśata | ime somā araṃkṛtāḥ ||". In the pada-division "darśateme" becomes "darśata, ime": the syllable "te" is ta + i, two letters joined in sandhi, and the accent shifts slightly as well (the anudātta of "te" passes to "i"). So in pada-division one letter of the Saṃhitā may become two; a short letter may become long (indrāvaruṇa vām aham = indrāvaruṇā | vām | aham, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1-18-7); a long letter may become short (sa ghā naḥ sūnuḥ = saḥ | gha | naḥ | sūnuḥ, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1-27-2); and the accent may change. The ṛtvij must know all this well. **Therefore Grammar must be studied.**

### "Catvāri" (Four)

**This particular topic is important** — regarding it, the explanation of this ṛk has been given earlier (see page 40)—

> चत्वारि शृङ्गा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य । त्रिधा बद्धो वृषभो रोरवीति महो देवो मर्त्यां आ विवेश ॥
> *catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya | tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ ā viveśa ||* (Rigveda Samhita 4-58-3)
>
> "**With four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands in Bull, penned up in three places roars mightily; a great god has entered mortals.**"

Since this mantra holds a hidden meaning, many commentators have construed it in many ways. The poet Rājaśekhara, in the second chapter of his Kāvyamīmāṃsā, says that it describes the form of the Word (śabda) as the Great God; Yāska, the author of the Nirukta, says it sets forth the form of the Yajña-puruṣa (Nirukta 13-7). Sāyaṇācārya, commenting on the sūkta in which the mantra stands, explains it in five ways, because the sūkta's deities are Agni, Sūrya, Āpas (waters), cows and ghṛta (ghee) … *(It continues on the next page.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 570</div>

Following the view of the Nirukta-authors, Agni, in the form of the sacrifice, is the chief deity; and since the sun, like Agni, is luminous, this mantra is said to speak of both, and Sayana has explained the meaning in his commentary accordingly. Those who know Grammar say that this mantra refers to the Word-Brahman (shabda-brahman). In the same way many others explain it in many ways. **The following is the way the grammarians explain the meaning** —

> चत्वारि शृङ्गा त्रयो अस्य पादा द्वे शीर्षे सप्त हस्तासो अस्य । त्रिधा बद्धो वृषभो रोरवीति महो देवो मर्त्यां आ विवेश ॥
> *catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya | tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ ā viveśa ||* (Rigveda Samhita 4-58-3; see page 569 above)

**From this, the following meanings can be explained:**

**Catvāri Śṛṅgā** (Four Horns) — from the standpoint of Grammar: noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga), and particle (nipāta) — these are the four kinds of word-categories.

**Trayo Asya Pādāḥ** (Its Three Feet) — past (bhūta), future (bhaviṣyat), and present (vartamāna) — these are the three time-divisions.

**Dve Śīrṣe** (Two Heads) — nominal endings (subanta-padas) and verbal endings (tiṅanta-padas) — these two types of word-terminations.

**Sapta Hastāso Asya** (Its Seven Hands) — the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh cases (vibhakti) — these seven case-endings.

**Tridhā Baddhaḥ** (Bound in Three Places) — held fast by the three articulatory places: throat, chest, and head — these three points [of pronunciation].

**Vṛṣabhaḥ** (The Bull) — since it showers down (varṣaṇa) blessings upon what is desired, it is called Vṛṣabha (the Bull, "the shower-er").

**Roravīti** (It Roars Mightily) — from the root "ru," meaning to make a sound (śabda-karma) — hence its use here.

**Mahoo Devaḥ** (The Great God) — the great god, that is, the Word-Brahman (shabda-brahman).

**Martyān** (Into Mortals).

**Ā Viveśa** (Has Entered) — meaning: has entered into, taken possession of. That is, Grammar should be studied so that we may attain union (identity) with that great god.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 571</div>

**Or this verse may be quoted under the heading "Catvāri"** — since it belongs to the sutra as an illustrative example, we may cite here another well-known verse—

> चत्वारि वाक्परिमिता पदानि तानि विदुर्ब्राह्मणा ये मनीषिणः । गुहा त्रीणि निहिता नेंगयन्ति तुरीयं वाचो मनुष्या वदन्ति ॥
> *catvāri vāk parimitā padāni tāni vidur brāhmaṇā ye manīṣiṇaḥ | guhā trīṇi nihitā neṃgayanti turīyaṃ vāco manuṣyā vadanti ||* (Rigveda Samhita 1-164-45)
>
> "**There be four divisions of speech: brahmins who are wise know all four; but three lie hid in their secret place and do not move; the fourth part of speech men speak.**"

**"Manīṣiṇaḥ"** means "manasā īśinaḥ" (those who are masters through the mind). "**Guhā**" is a Vedic form for "guhāyam" (in the secret place), as is also "**nihitā**" for "nihitāni" (placed/deposited). "**Turīyaṃ vāco manuṣya vadanti**" — that is, it is the fourth part of speech only that is current among men.

**This verse too has been explained in many ways by many commentators. In the Nirukta-pariśiṣṭa, in expounding this mantra, it is said that many scholars have explained the four divisions of speech in various ways—**

**The four classes of speech are, according to the seers (ṛṣis), the syllable Om together with the three vyāhṛtis "bhūḥ," "bhuvaḥ," "svaḥ"; according to the grammarians, noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga) and particle (nipāta);**

**according to the performers of sacrifice (yājñikas), mantra, kalpa, grammar and the language people use in worldly dealings; according to the Nirukta-authors, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda and the language of worldly dealings; according to some (those who study the elements of nature), the speech of serpents, of birds and of small creeping creatures, together with the language of worldly dealings; and according to the upholders of the Self (ātma-pravādins), the speech found in cattle, in birds, in beasts and in man.**

**In this way many have explained it in many ways.**

**The main sense is this:** words are divided into four kinds, and all of them are known to intelligent brahmins. Of these four groups of words, three lie hidden in the cave and do not move, that is, being concealed they are not perceived by anyone; the fourth division, the web of words, is in use among men, and this men call speech. Here "manīṣiṇaḥ" means those who are able to understand by deliberating well in the mind, that is, the intelligent.

In the Veda, when speaking of a thing kept secret from everyone, it is usual to say that it lies hidden in a cave.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 572</div>

Here "**Guhā**" means "guhāyām" (in the cave). Things in a cave are not seen by ordinary people, so it has become usual to say, in speaking of what is secret, that it is in the cave. The fourth part of speech ("turīya") is the part that is current among men.

### "Uta Tvaḥ" (Moreover, One)

> उत त्वः पश्यन्न ददर्श वाचमुत त्वः शृण्वन्न शृणोत्येनाम् । उतो त्वस्मै तन्वं विससे जायेव पत्य उशती सुवासाः ॥
> *uta tvaḥ paśyan na dadarśa vācam uta tvaḥ śṛṇvan na śṛṇoty enām | uto tvasmai tanvaṃ visasre jāyeva patya uśatī suvāsāḥ ||* (Rigveda Samhita 10-71-4; see page 527 above)

"**One seeing does not see Speech: one hearing does not hear her; to one she unfolds her form as a loving wife shows herself to her husband in fair garments.**"

"**'Moreover, one seeing does not see, and hearing does not hear her.'** This half of the verse refers to the ignorant man. But to one she unfolds, that is, reveals her form..."

### "Sakhya" (Friendship)

> सख्यम् इव तमुलूना पुरुषेभ्यो रयस्ते धीरा मनसा नाचमक्रत । अत्रा सखायः सख्यानि जानते भद्रैषां लक्ष्मीर्निहिताधि वाचि ॥
> *sakhyam iva tam ulūnā puruṣebhyo rayas te dhīrā manasā nācam akrata | atrā sakhāyaḥ sakhyāni jānate bhadraiṣāṃ lakṣmīr nihitādhi vāci ||* (Rigveda Samhita 10-71-2)

**This mantra** has been explained by Yaska in the ninth section of the fourth chapter of his Nirukta. As grain (flour) is sifted by winnowing in a winnowing basket, the wise (those who know Grammar) sift speech with the mind (they consider well the nature of words and the like and then speak). By doing so they cultivate friendship with speech (they use good words and speak well). In the words they speak a blessing endowed with right marks resides (their words are well-formed and auspicious).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 573</div>

A man who sees yet does not see, and hears yet does not hear: though he sees with the eye and hears with the ear, he has no knowledge of the meaning of words, so nothing is understood by him; he only pronounces the words, without knowing their meaning. This is said of the man who is not learned. About the learned man the next part says: as a wife, wearing fair garments and adorned with every ornament, comes to her husband out of desire, and the husband looks at her with great regard and speaks to her lovingly, so the Vedas (or words) offer their body, that is, reveal their hidden meaning, to the man learned in the sciences; the learned man can well understand the nature of words and their special meaning. We have already explained the meaning of this Rik at length (see page 528). Therefore Grammar must be studied.

**"'As a loving wife shows herself in fair garments to her husband.' As a wife full of love for her husband puts on her fair attire and shows herself to him, so Speech reveals herself to the wise. Let us study Grammar that Speech may reveal herself to us."**

### "Saktum Iva" (Like Purified Grain)

> यत्रा सखायः सख्यानि जानते सक्तुमिव तितउना पुनन्ति । अत्रा धीरा धिय एनाभिरेकं गूहन्ति गुह्यमविशेषु शीकैः ॥
> *yatrā sakhāyaḥ sakhyāni jānate saktum iva titaunā punanti | atrā dhīrā dhiya enābhir ekaṃ gūhanti guhyam aviśeṣu śīkaiḥ ||* (Rigveda Samhita 10-71-2)

"**Where wise men draw speech hither and thither in their mind, purifying it as men purify grain with a winnowing basket — there friends learn what friendship is: a gracious fortune is upon their words.**"

**"The word 'saktu' here [is] derived from 'sacati': it means 'hard to purify.' Or we may take it from 'kasati,' become by transposition 'sakati.' In that case it would mean**..."

**Meaning:** the word "saktu" (ground grain/meal) here — its derivation according to Grammar can be traced through the verbal root "√sac" (to associate/adhere), yielding the sense of "that which is difficult to purify [thoroughly]." Alternatively, deriving it through transposition from the root "√kas", it may convey the sense "opened out, blossomed". This shows how the very meaning of a single word — its etymological source, and hence its true sense — depends entirely on grammatical analysis.

**This mantra** raises the question: what is that road, so hard to travel, to union with speech, that is, to the true nature of speech? It is the path that concerns speech, the science of words (shabda-shastra). **Who knows it? The authorities on Grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra).** Why? Because in the speech of the grammarians the words are well-marked.

> भद्रैषां लक्ष्मीर्निहिताधि वाचि — इषां वाचि भद्रा लक्ष्मीर्निहिता भवति ।
> *bhadraiṣāṃ lakṣmīr nihitādhi vāci* — *iṣāṃ vāci bhadrā lakṣmīr nihitā bhavati |*

"**A gracious fortune is upon their words.**" — that is, since the words in the speech of the grammarians are well-marked (endowed with the right marks), the auspicious Lakshmi dwells in their speech.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 574</div>

**Main import:** those who know Grammar analyze the defining characteristics of words, [correctly identifying] which forms carry genuine meaning and which are mere sound without proper sense. This is one path; another arises through genuine scholarly effort and depth of learning; this too grants a person the respect due to true knowledge. Therefore, one must study Grammar.

### "Sāraswatīm" (The Sarasvati Rite) — Explained Under the Heading "Ahitāgni Yajamāna's [Expiatory Rite for] Incorrect Usage"

> अहिताग्निर्यजामनश्चेत्प्रयुङ्क्ते सारस्वतीमिष्टिं निर्वपेदिति ॥
> *ahitāgnir yajamānaś cet prayuṅkte sārasvatīm iṣṭiṃ nirvaped iti ||*

**Meaning:** if the yajamāna, [whose Agnyadhana has already been performed] (an "āhitāgni" — see the earlier discussion), makes an error, he must perform this specific rite of atonement, which is well-established. If, having already performed the sacred fire-establishment rite, the āhitāgni proceeds and makes an error in the mantras during a subsequent yajna (specifically, in the course of performing the daily Agnihotra ritual), he must perform the "Sāraswatī iṣṭi" (an expiatory rite dedicated to Sarasvati) to atone for it — this is required. **Therefore, to avoid having to perform such expiatory rites, one should study Grammar.**

### "Daśamyāṃ Putrasya" (On the Tenth Day, for the Son)

**On the day fixed for the son's naming-ceremony**, following the birth, the traditional custom is to select a name. Regarding this:

> पुत्रस्य दशम्यां नाम कुर्यात्, द्व्यक्षरं चतुरक्षरं वा, अन्तस्थादिकं वा, आद्यन्तस्थं वा, कृद्रूपं वा, न तद्धितान्तम् ॥
> *putrasya daśamyāṃ nāma kuryāt, dvy-akṣaraṃ catur-akṣaraṃ vā, antasthādikaṃ vā, ādy-antasthaṃ vā, kṛd-rūpaṃ vā, na taddhitāntam ||*

**"'Let him name the boy on the tenth day after his birth. He must make the name of the sonants, with y, r, l or v in the beginning or middle, and the visarga at the end, of two syllables or four, a kṛt-formation, and not ending in a taddhita.' But without a knowledge of..."**

**Meaning:** the person's name should either begin with, or have in its middle, a semivowel (y, r, l, or v) [i.e., an "antasthā" consonant], and should end with the visarga. It should be two syllables in length, or four; it should be formed as a "kṛt"-derivative (from a verbal root, via primary suffixes), and must never be a "taddhita"-derivative (a secondary derivative formed from another noun). Whoever wishes to properly assign a name according to these precise grammatical rules must, without exception, possess knowledge of Grammar; without it, this precept cannot be properly carried out.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 575</div>

### "Sudevo Asi" (Thou Art a Glorious God) — Found in the Rigveda Samhita

> सुदेवो असि वरुण यस्य ते सप्त सिन्धवः । अनुक्षरन्ति काकुदं स्रुत्यं सुमिवा मव ॥
> *sudevo asi varuṇa yasya te sapta sindhavaḥ | anukṣaranti kākudaṃ srutyaṃ suṣirāmiva ||* (Rigveda Samhita 8-69-12)

"**Thou art a glorious god, Varuna, thou along whose throat the seven streams flow as through a hollow pillar.**"

**Meaning:** here, "the seven streams" refer to the seven grammatical cases (vibhakti). "**Kākut**" means the tongue. "**Kākuda**," the place where the tongue resides, therefore refers to the palate. "**Ūrmi**" or "**sūrmi**" is a stout, hollow pillar made of iron [used as a metaphor for the throat/vocal passage through which speech, in its sevenfold grammatical case-forms, flows].

**In this same way, the uses of Grammar given in the Vārtika are to be added here as well** — "**siddhe śabdārtha-sambandhe**..." [and so on, as previously discussed].

### Next, the Use of the Nirukta

**The name [Nirukta] implies a collection of words uttered (ukta), so, however, that they do not depend on each other for their meaning (nir).** Accordingly, the revealed enumeration of words — which begins "**gauḥ gma jma kṣa kṣama**" and ends "**vasavaḥ vajinaḥ devapatnayo devapatnayaḥ**" — forms a book throughout which there is no...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 576</div>

**"Ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ kāṇḍaṃ dvitīyaṃ naigamaṃ tathā | tṛtīyaṃ daivataṃ ceti samāmnāyas tridhā sthitaḥ ||**

**Gaurādyeṣāraḍ vyakta-mādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ mataṃ | jahādyaṃ vyavasānāntaṃ naigamaṃ saṃprakīrtitam ||**

**Agnyādi-devataśabdaṃ devatā-kāṇḍam ucyate | agnyādi devī-ūrjahatuḥ akhilaṃ kṣiti-devatāḥ ||**

**Nāyā-ādi-devaśabdaṃ tyā aṃkaraṃ tariṣadaṃ devatāḥ |**

**Ganādi-devaśabdaṃ samāmnāyam adhi tvate iti ||"**

*ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ kāṇḍaṃ dvitīyaṃ naigamaṃ tathā | tṛtīyaṃ daivataṃ ceti samāmnāyas tridhā sthitaḥ || gaurādyeṣāraḍ vyaktam ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ mataṃ | jahādyaṃ vyavasānāntaṃ naigamaṃ saṃprakīrtitam || agnyādi devatā-śabdaṃ devatā-kāṇḍam ucyate | agnyādi devi ūrjahatuḥ akhilaṃ kṣiti-devatāḥ ||*

**"Nighaṇṭu is a well-established name for a book in which groups of synonymous words are chiefly taught; such are the ten Nighaṇṭus (Amarasiṃha, Vaijayantī, Halāyudha and the rest) of common usage."**

**This Nirukta is divided into three chapters, as is shown in the commentary on the Anukramaṇikā.**

"**First the Naighaṇṭuka chapter, second the Naigama, third the Daivata, thus is the Samāmnāya divided into three parts.**

**"The Naighaṇṭuka is considered to be the part beginning with 'gauḥ' and ending 'apare': the part beginning with 'jahā' and ending with 'ulbaṃ ribīsam,' they declare to be the Naigama.**

**"The part beginning with 'Agni,' and ending with 'Devapatnyaḥ' is called the Devatā chapter. From Agni to Urjahati is the host of gods that are on the Earth.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 577</div>

> वायोर्भगान्तमन्तरिक्षदेवतानां सूर्यादि देवपत्न्यन्तं दिवि देवतानाम् ॥
> *vāyor bhagāntam antarikṣa-devatānāṃ sūryādi devapatny-antaṃ divi devatānām ||*

"**Let the section from Vayu to Bhaga be for the gods in mid-air; and that from Surya to Devapatnyah for the gods in heaven.**"

"**So the whole Samāmnāya from 'Gauḥ' to 'Devapatnyaḥ' is studied.**"

**Nighaṇṭu is a well-established name for a book which contains chiefly lists of synonyms.** As for example, such books as Amarasiṃha, Vaijayantī, Halāyudha, and others are spoken of as the "ten Nighaṇṭus." In the same way, the first chapter of our book, which gives a list of synonyms, is called a Nighaṇṭu. There are three adhyāyas in this chapter. In the first, we have names of things, such as the earth and the other worlds, and space and time; in the second, we have the names of things such as men and the limbs of men; in the third, we have qualities, such as multitude or shortness, belonging to both classes of things.

**This is what the following verse conveys**:

> प्रथमाध्याये भूम्यादि-लोकानाम् आकाश-कालयोश्च नामानि । द्वितीये पुरुषादीनां तदङ्गानां च संज्ञाः स्युः । तृतीये तूभयोरपि साधारणा बहुत्वाल्पत्वादि-गुणवाचकाः शब्दāḥ ||
> *prathamādhyāye bhūmyādi-lokānām ākāśa-kālayoś ca nāmāni | dvitīye puruṣādīnāṃ tad-aṅgānāṃ ca saṃjñāḥ syuḥ | tṛtīye tūbhayor api sādhāraṇā bahutvālpatvādi-guṇa-vācakāḥ śabdāḥ ||*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 578</div>

So far the necessity of Grammar for understanding the Veda has been explained at length; now the use that is gained from the Nirukta is explained. A work that explains the meaning of words so that the sense is had without the help of another is called Nirukta (nir + ukta): the meaning that arises from a word does not depend on another word. Thus this Nirukta begins with the words "Gauh, gma, jma, kshma, ksha, kshama" and ends with "vasavah, vajinah, devapatnyah, devapatnyah"; for understanding the meaning of words in it no other help (parāpekṣā) is needed, because it is stated clearly in each place that so many words are names of the earth and so many are names of gold. This Nirukta is divided into three kāṇḍas, as is shown in the Anukramaṇikā-bhāṣya—

**On this point the Anukramaṇikā-bhāṣya says**—

> आद्यं नैघण्टुकं काण्डं द्वितीयं नैगमं तथा । तृतीयं दैवतं चेति समाम्नायस्त्रिधा स्थितः ॥
> गौरादि पापूरणपर्यन्तमाद्यं नैघण्टुकं मतम् । जहादि व्यवसानान्तं नैगमं संप्रचक्षते ॥
> अग्न्यादिदेवपत्न्यन्तं देवताकाण्डमुच्यते । अग्न्यादिदेवी ऊर्जाहुत्यन्तक क्षितिगतो गणः ॥
> वाय्वादिदेवो भगान्ताः स्वन्तरिक्षस्थ देवताः । सूर्यादिदेवपत्न्यन्ता द्युस्था देवता इति ॥
> गणादिदेवपत्न्यन्तं समाम्नायमधीयत इति ॥
>
> *ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ kāṇḍaṃ dvitīyaṃ naigamaṃ tathā | tṛtīyaṃ daivataṃ ceti samāmnāyas tridhā sthitaḥ ||*
> *gaurādi pāpūraṇa-paryantam ādyaṃ naighaṇṭukaṃ mataṃ | jahādi vyavasānāntaṃ naigamaṃ saṃpracakṣate ||*
> *agnyādi-devapatny-antaṃ devatā-kāṇḍam ucyate | agnyādi devī ūrjāhutyantaka kṣiti-gato gaṇaḥ ||*
> *vāyv-ādi-devo bhagāntāḥ svāntarikṣa-stha devatāḥ | sūryādi-deva-patyantā dyu-sthā devatā iti ||*
> *gaṇādi-deva-patny-antaṃ samāmnāyam adhīyata iti ||*
>
> "The first section (kāṇḍa) is Naighaṇṭuka, the second is likewise Naigama, and the third Daivata — thus the Samāmnāya stands in three parts. From 'gauḥ' up to 'pāpūraṇa' is held to be the first, Naighaṇṭuka; from 'jahā' to 'vyavasāna' is proclaimed as Naigama. From 'agni' up to 'devapatnī' is called the Devatā-kāṇḍa; from Agni's own [group] up to Ūrjāhuti is the host of deities dwelling on Earth. From Vāyu onward, ending with Bhaga, are the deities dwelling in the mid-region (antarikṣa); from Sūrya onward, ending with the Devapatnīs, are the deities dwelling in heaven (dyuloka). Thus, from 'gaṇa' onward, ending with 'devapatnī,' the Samāmnāya is studied."

**Meaning:** this Nirukta has three kāṇḍas: the first, Naighaṇṭuka, the second, Naigama, the third, Daivata. In the Daivata kāṇḍa the words from "Agni" to "Ūrjāhuti" denote the host of deities on earth, from Vāyu to Bhaga the deities of the mid-region, and from Sūrya to the Devapatnīs the deities of heaven. The word "**nigama**" means Veda. **For Yaska, when citing a Vedic text, constantly uses the formula, "And there is a nigama with regard to this."** Because the second chapter, which is the fourth adhyāya, deals with words that, for the most part, occur in the Veda, it is therefore called Nigama.

**The reason why the third chapter, which is the fifth adhyāya, is called Daivata is plain.**

**The whole book, consisting of five adhyāyas or three chapters, is thus called Nirukta, because it teaches the meanings of words that stand in the lists perfectly independent of each other**.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 579</div>

**other. Yaska composed the commentary on it in twelve adhyāyas, beginning**

> समाम्नायः समाम्नातः ।
> *samāmnāyaḥ samāmnātaḥ |*

**and ending**

> तस्यास्तस्यास्तद्भाव्यमनुभवत्यनुभवति ।
> *tasyas tasyas tad-bhāvyam anubhavaty anubhavati |*

**This commentary also is called Nirukta. Because the supposed elements of each word are here fully (nir) set out (ukta). For in his book, after having declared the fourfold division of words into nouns, verbs, prepositions, and particles, Yaska declares that particles fall into (nipatanti) various meanings. Having thus analysed the term "nipāta," he gives an example. "Na" means only prohibition in common talk: in the Veda it means both (prohibition and comparison). In the text**

> नेन्द्रं देवममंसत ।
> *nendraṃ devam amaṃsata |*

**it means prohibition. In the text**

> दुर्मदासो न सुरायाम् ।
> *durmadāso na surāyāṃ |*

**Meaning:** the particles are used in various, even mutually opposed, meanings, and so this group of words has come to be called "nipāta". For example, the word "na"...

**"Nigama" means the Veda, because Yaska calls the sentences he cites here and there from the Vedas "nigama" sentences.** In the second kāṇḍa, the fourth chapter, words that are for the most part found in the Veda are explained; so this kāṇḍa has come to be called Naigama.

**In the third kāṇḍa, the fifth chapter, mostly the names of the deities are given; so this kāṇḍa is called the Daivata kāṇḍa.**

**The book of three kāṇḍas in five chapters is called Nirukta because in it the meanings of words are given without dependence on any other (parāpekṣā).** Yaska composed a commentary on this work in twelve chapters in all. This commentary too is called Nirukta; because in it the meanings of the parts of each word are stated without remainder, the name suits it by derivation. In that work, after stating that there are four kinds of words, noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga) and particle (nipāta), he says that the particles are used in various meanings, and so the group is called nipāta. For example, **"na" ordinarily means only prohibition in common speech; but in the Veda it carries both senses — prohibition and comparison.** In the text—

> नेन्द्रं देवममंसत ।
> *nendraṃ devam amaṃsata |*

—it means prohibition. In the text—

> दुर्मदासो न सुरायाम् ।
> *durmadāso na surāyāṃ |*

—...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 580</div>

**it means comparison. This is the example given in the Nirukta for the double use of the particle 'na,' as meaning both 'no' and 'if' in the Veda, whereas in common talk it means 'no' only. We shall have frequent occasion in the course of our commentary to cite similar etymologies given by this author.**

**Nor need it be feared that these etymologies have no foundation in fact. For some of them are given in the brahmanas.**

> तदाहुतीनामाहुतित्वम् (ऐ. ब्रा. १-१-२) । तमिदन्द्रं सन्तमिन्द्र इत्याचक्षते (ऐ. आ. २-४-३) । यदप्रथयत् तत्पृथिव्यै पृथिवित्वम् (तै. ब्रा. १-१-३-७) ।
> *tadāhutīnāmāhutitvam (ai. brā. 1-1-2) | tamidandraṃ santamindra ityācakṣate (ai. ā. 2-4-3) | yadaprathayat tatpṛthivyai pṛthivitvam (tai. brā. 1-1-3-7) |*
>
> **"This is that in virtue of which the āhutis are so called." Therefore they call him "Indra." "Because he stretched it out (aprathayat)," that is why the earth (pṛthivī) is so called.**

**The author himself will also be found citing brahmanas in proof of the etymologies he gives.**

**It is true that the etymology of some words can be learned from Grammar. But not all.** Wherefore the author says—

> तदिदं विद्यास्थानं व्याकरणस्य केवलं शब्दलक्षणे न सर्वेषां पदानां निर्वचनं सिद्ध्येत् ।
> *tad idaṃ vidyā-sthānaṃ vyākaraṇasya kevalaṃ śabda-lakṣaṇe na sarveṣāṃ padānāṃ nirvacanaṃ siddhyet |*
>
> "**Therefore this science is the essence of Grammar and establishes the proper sense of the words. Therefore the Nirukta is useful towards the understanding of the Veda.**"

**Meaning:** it means comparison as well, not merely prohibition. This is precisely the illustration the Nirukta itself gives — how the particle "na" carries a double sense within the Veda, though in ordinary conversational usage it means only "no." Throughout our own commentary, we shall have frequent occasion to cite similar etymological derivations given by this author (Yaska), and there is no need to fear that such derivations have no factual grounding — many of them are directly supported by statements found in the Brahmana portions themselves.

**For example:** "This is the reason why the offerings (āhutis) are called āhutis." "Therefore they call him Indra." "He stretched out (aprathayat) [the earth] — therefore the earth is called Pṛthivī." Such etymological explanations, based on scriptural authority, are found scattered throughout many places, and our author (the composer of the Nirukta) himself cites such Brahmana-passages in support of the etymologies he offers.

**It is true that some words' etymologies can indeed be derived through Grammar alone.** But this doesn't hold for *all* words — Grammar's own rules cannot, by themselves, fully derive the meanings of every single word. Therefore, the author of this treatise states:

**"Therefore this science (the Nirukta) is the essence of Grammar and helps to determine the proper sense of words."**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 581</div>

**"Kārtsnyaṃ svārthasādhakaṃ ca"** (Nirukta 1-15) — for this reason, this shastra (Nirukta) properly determines the meanings of words that are not otherwise settled by any means. **Therefore, Nirukta must be studied specifically for the sake of the Veda's meaning.**

### The Fifth Anga: Chandas (Metrics)

**Just as, in the sacrificial rites, various matters are described as ritually obligatory in certain cases**—

> गायत्र्युष्णिगनुष्टुब्बृहती पङ्क्तिस्त्रिष्टुब्जगत्यौ छन्दांसि सप्त ।
> *gāyatry-uṣṇig-anuṣṭub-bṛhatī-paṅktis-triṣṭub-jagatyau chandāṃsi sapta |*
>
> "**As, for example, in the text, 'Therefore seven plus four metres are recited in the prataranuvakya.' Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, are the seven metres. The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables. The Uṣṇik has four more, and thus consists of twenty-eight syllables. So the others may be worked out, as the Anuṣṭubh for example, each containing a greater number of syllables than the one before.**"

**Let me give another text**:

> ब्राह्मणं गायत्र्या यजेत् क्षत्रियं त्रिष्टुभा ।
> *brāhmaṇaṃ gāyatryā yajet kṣatriyaṃ triṣṭubhā |*
>
> "**He should say the fire for a Brahmin with Gāyatrī verses, for a Kshattriya with Triṣṭubh verses, and**"...

**Meaning:** because in ritual matters, certain specific meters are prescribed as obligatory to use in various contexts, one must study the science of metrics (Chandas-shastra) in order to properly know these meters, distinguish them correctly, and apply the right meter in the right context. This is precisely why the fifth Anga — Chandas — exists and must be studied.

**On this point, our own tradition gives the following explanation.** The seven principal meters are: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī. Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables; Uṣṇik has four syllables more, thus consisting of twenty-eight; and in the same way each of the following meters, Anuṣṭubh and the rest, contains more syllables than the one before it.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 582</div>

**for a Vaishya with Jagatī verses." Now in a matter of this kind, it is not easy without the Chhandas book to apprehend the distinction between the different metres, as that is laid down in the technical rules given there. I can quote a third text**—

> गायत्रीभिर्ब्राह्मणस्याग्निं यजेत् त्रिष्टुभा राजन्यस्य त्रिष्टुभा वैश्यस्य जगत्या । ओतत्तत्त्वं यजेत् ॥
> *gāyatrībhir brāhmaṇasyāgniṃ yajet triṣṭubhā rājanyasya triṣṭubhā vaiśyasya jagatyā | otat tattvaṃ yajet ||* (Taittiriya Brahmana 1-1-9-6)
>
> "**With Gāyatrī verses one should sacrifice the fire for a Brahmin, with Triṣṭubh verses for a Rajanya (Kshatriya), with Jagatī verses for a Vaishya.**"

**Meaning:** the proper procedure for the fire-establishment rite (Agnyādhāna) for a Brahmin is to use Gāyatrī-metered mantras; for a Kshatriya, it must be done with Triṣṭubh-metered mantras; for a Vaishya, one must use Jagatī-metered mantras. In this way, this treatise establishes precisely which meters apply to which specific rites for each of the three classes.

**The Kannada adds that the same Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (1-2-1) lays down, for the Ādhāna, three Gāyatrī-metre mantras for the Brahmin, three Triṣṭubh-metre mantras for the Kshatriya and three Jagatī-metre mantras for the Vaishya; only the first pāda of each Ṛk is given there, and the whole mantra can be learnt from the Veda. The characteristics of metres such as the Gāyatrī, which can be learnt from the metrical feet (magaṇa, yagaṇa and so on), cannot be learnt without a book on metres.**

**I can also cite another text**:

> यो ह वा अविदितार्ष-च्छन्दो-दैवतेन मन्त्रेण योजयति स्खलितं गच्छति कूपे वा पतति भूयश्च तस्मादृचā yajño'vidvāṃsam eva śāsti prakāśyate iti ॥
> *yo ha vā avidita-arṣa-chando-daivatena mantreṇa yojayati skhalitaṃ gacchati kūpe vā patati bhūyaś ca tasmād ṛcā yajño'vidvāṃsam eva śāsti prakāśyate iti ||*
>
> "**The man who sacrifices or teaches by means of a mantra whose rishi, metre, and devatā he does not know, runs up against a post, or falls into a well, or perishes utterly: his guilt is increased. Therefore for every mantra he must know all these.**"

**Meaning:** whoever performs a yajna or teaches a mantra without knowing the rishi (its seer), chandas (its metre), or devatā (its deity), stumbles as he goes, or falls into a well; his fault becomes even greater than before. Therefore, one must know the rishi, meter, and deity of every mantra one recites.

**Therefore, the Chhandas book on metres is useful for this knowledge.**

### The Sixth Anga: Jyotiṣa (Astronomy) — Its Purpose and Significance Determined

<div class="pgmark">original p. 583</div>

**The use of the Jyotiṣa is thus given in that book itself: "To establish the times and reasons for sacrifices."** There are texts prescribing all manner of times. The text "**saṃvatsaraṃ**" and similar refers to periods of years. The text "**vasante**" and similar refers to months. The text "**māsi māsi**" and similar refers to months. The text "**yaṃ kāmayeta**" refers to half-months. The text "**ekāṣṭakāyāṃ**" and similar refers to days. The text "**kṛttikāsu**" and similar refers to the nakṣatras (lunar mansions).

> ज्योतिषस्य प्रयोजनं तस्मिन्नेव ग्रन्थेऽभिहितम् । यज्ञकालार्थसिद्धय इति । कालविशेषविधयश्च श्रूयन्ते । संवत्सरमेतद्व्रतं चरेत्संवत्सरमुख्यं भृत्वेत्येवमादयः संवत्सरविधयः । वसन्ते ब्राह्मणोऽग्निमादधीत । ग्रीष्मे राजन्य आदधीत । शरदि वैश्य आदधीतेत्याद्या ऋतुविधयः । मासि मासि पृष्ठान्युपयन्ति । मासि मास्यतिग्राह्या गृह्यन्त इत्याद्या मासविधयः । यं कामयेत वसीयान्स्यादिति तं पूर्वपक्षे याजयेदित्याद्याः पक्षविधयः । एकाष्टकायां दीक्षेरन् फल्गुनीपूर्णमासे दीक्षेरन् (तै. सं. ७-४-८-१) इत्याद्यास्तिथिविधयः । प्रातर्जुहोति सायं जुहोतीत्याद्याः प्रातःकालादिविधयः । कृत्तिकास्वग्निमादधीत । (तै. ब्रा. १-१-२-१) इत्याद्या नक्षत्रविधयः । अतः कालविशेषानवगमयितुं ज्योतिषमुपयुज्यते ॥
> *jyotiṣasya prayojanaṃ tasminneva granthe 'bhihitam | yajñakālārthasiddhaya iti | kālaviśeṣavidhayaśca śrūyante | saṃvatsarametadvrataṃ caretsaṃvatsaramukhyaṃ bhṛtvetyevamādayaḥ saṃvatsaravidhayaḥ | vasante brāhmaṇo 'gnimādadhīta | grīṣme rājanya ādadhīta | śaradi vaiśya ādadhītetyādyā ṛtuvidhayaḥ | māsi māsi pṛṣṭhānyupayanti | māsi māsyatigrāhyā gṛhyanta ityādyā māsavidhayaḥ | yaṃ kāmayeta vasīyānsyāditi taṃ pūrvapakṣe yājayedityādyāḥ pakṣavidhayaḥ | ekāṣṭakāyāṃ dīkṣeran phalgunīpūrṇamāse dīkṣeran (tai. saṃ. 7-4-8-1) ityādyāstithividhayaḥ | prātarjuhoti sāyaṃ juhotītyādyāḥ prātaḥkālādividhayaḥ | kṛttikāsvagnimādadhīta | (tai. brā. 1-1-2-1) ityādyā nakṣatravidhayaḥ | ataḥ kālaviśeṣānavagamayituṃ jyotiṣamupayujyate ‖* (the Kannada below also cites Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1-32-1 for "saṃvatsaram etad vrataṃ caret")

**"Month by month" and similar** [texts refer to] monthly regulations for the sake of prosperity. **"Yaṃ kāmayeta**" [expressing whatever a person] desires — this is the fortnight-regulation. "**Ekāṣṭakāyāṃ**" is the day-regulation. "**Kṛttikāsu**" is the nakṣatra-regulation.

**This is the meaning: the Jyotiṣa serves the purpose belonging to yajnas and similar rites specifically because the treatise itself declares this.** Since all yajnas and similar acts must be performed at their properly appointed times, determining that time correctly is the primary purpose which the science of Jyotiṣa serves. There are many mantras in the Veda that indicate particular times; some of them are given below—

**The text on keeping this vow for a year (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1-321)** is a rule that states the length of a year: the vow is to be observed for one whole year.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 584</div>

**"Saṃvatsaram ukhyaṃ bhṛtvā"** (Taittiriya Brahmana 1-5-3-4) — this too establishes the correct measure of the year's timing.

> वसन्ता ब्राह्मणस्याग्निमाधीयेत । ग्रीष्मे राजन्यस्य भवति । मुखं वा एतद्संवत्सरस्य यद्वसन्तः । यो वसन्ते ब्राह्मणमाधत्ते मुखत एव भवति । अथो योऽभिजितं वसन्तमेव प्रजापतिमाधत्ते । ग्रीष्मे राजन्यस्यादधीत ग्रीष्मो वै राजन्यस्य ऋतुः । शरदि वैश्यस्यादधीत शरत् वै वैश्यस्य ऋतुः ॥
> *vasantā brāhmaṇasyāgnim ādhīyeta | grīṣme rājanyasya bhavati | mukhaṃ vā etad-saṃvatsarasya yad vasantaḥ | yo vasante brāhmaṇam ādhatte mukhata eva bhavati | atho yo'bhijitaṃ vasantam eva prajāpatim ādhatte | grīṣme rājanyasyādadhīta grīṣmo vai rājanyasya ṛtuḥ | śaradi vaiśyasyādadhīta śarad vai vaiśyasya ṛtuḥ ||* (Taittiriya Brahmana 1-1-2)

**Meaning:** in spring (vasanta) a Brahmin should perform the Ādhāna; by performing the fire-establishment in spring, the Brahmin's own season, he becomes endowed with brahmanic radiance (brahmavarcas). In the same way a Kshatriya is to perform the Ādhāna in summer (grīṣma), whereby he becomes full of valour; and a Vaishya in autumn (śarad), whereby he becomes possessed of cattle and other wealth.

**This mantra speaks of the seasons (ṛtu).**

**"Māsi māsi pṛṣṭhāny upayanti māsi māsy atigrāhyā gṛhyante**" (Taittiriya Samhita 7-5-1) — these and similar mantras indicate a period measured by a month.

**"Yaṃ kāmayeta vasīyān syād iti taṃ pūrvapakṣe yājayet**" (Taittiriya Samhita 2-23-1) — this and similar [texts] refer to the fortnight-measure regulations.

**"Ekāṣṭakāyāṃ dīkṣeran …… phalgunīpūrṇamāse dīkṣeran**" (Taittiriya Samhita 7-4-8-1) — this and similar [texts] refer to the day-timing regulations.

**"Prātar juhoti, sāyaṃ juhoti**" (Taittiriya Brahmana 2-1-2-7) and similar [texts] give the daily timing regulations.

**"Kṛttikāsv agnim ādadhīta**" (Taittiriya Brahmana 1-1-2-1) and similar [texts] give the nakṣatra-timing regulations.

**Therefore the Jyotiṣa is useful for knowing the particular times and for performing sacrifices accordingly.**

**That these six books, which we have shown to be helps to the understanding of the Veda, are 'Angas' or limbs of the Veda, is declared in the Śikṣā itself:**
