> हे अग्ने स त्वं नोऽस्मदर्थं सूपायनः शोभनप्राप्त्युक्तो भव । कथा नोऽस्माकं स्वैर्वये विनाकठारित्वार्थं सचस्व । समवेक्षो भव । तत्रोभयत्र दृष्टान्तः । यथा सूनवे पुत्रार्थं पिता सुप्राप्तः प्रायेण समवेक्षो भवति तद्वत् ।
> *he agne sa tvaṃ no'smad-arthaṃ sūpāyanaḥ śobhana-prāptyuktau bhava | kathā no'smākaṃ svair vaye vinā-kaṭhāritvārthaṃ sacasva | samavekṣo bhava | tatrobhayatra dṛṣṭāntaḥ | yathā sūnave putrārthaṃ pitā suprāptaḥ prāyeṇa samavekṣo bhavati tadvat |*

**Translation:** "O Agni, be for our sake one who is easily approached, readily attained in a good manner. In the same way, stay close beside us, for our welfare, without difficulty. Be attentively mindful [of us]. A single simile governs both these requests: just as a father, for his son's sake, is readily accessible and generally watchful and attentive toward him — so should you be toward us."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) अग्ने ((he) agne)** — O Agni! | **सः (त्वम्) (saḥ (tvam))** — you | **सूनवे (sūnave)** — in the matter of a son | **पितेव (piteva)** — as a father would be | **नः (naḥ)** — toward us | **सूपायनः (sūpāyanaḥ)** — easily approachable | **भव (bhava)** — become | **नः (naḥ)** — for us | **स्वस्तये (svastaye)** — for the bringing about of welfare | **सचस्व (sacasva)** — remain together with us.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

A father, out of paternal affection, is always readily accessible to his son. O Agni, may you likewise become easily accessible to us, pleased by the praise we offer, and be gracious toward us. And, in order to bring us welfare, may you remain ever with us.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Agni, be of easy access to us as a father (is) to his son; stay with us for our good.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**Three riks, beginning with the seventh Rik of this Sūkta, are used in the rite called Agnīṣoma-praṇayana.** For the application of these riks, the Brahmana states—

> उपस्त्वाग्ने दिने दिन उप त्वा प्रियं पणिष्ठं त्रेष्ठ्यकं जानाति ।
> *upas tvāgne dine dina upa tvā priyaṃ paṇiṣṭhaṃ treṣṭhyakaṃ jānāti |* (Aitareya Brahmana 1-20)

— and so on.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 650</div>

**This Rik contains no difficult words.** "**Piteva sūnave**" — "just as a father would be, regarding his own son." Here, the rishi, addressing Agni as a father, regards us — who offer him praise — as his own children, and prays in this very spirit. Many such beautiful and easily-grasped similes occur here and there throughout the Rigveda.

**The Rigveda contains ten Mandalas in total. The first Mandala contains 191 suktas in total.** Among these, this very first sukta — "**Agnimīḷe**," comprising nine Riks — concludes here. **The second Varga likewise concludes here.**

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

*(This closing grammatical section works through the accent-derivation of "sūnave," "sūpāyanaḥ" — analyzed as a bahuvrīhi compound, "one whose approach is auspicious" — "sacasva," and "svastaye," in the established dense register.)*

**॥९॥**

### ॥ इति प्रथमं सूक्तम् ॥

### Thus Ends the First Sūkta

**Summary of Sūkta 1-1, all nine verses:**
1. "agním īḷe puróhitaṃ yajñásya devám ṛtvíjam | hótāraṃ ratnadhā́tamam" — I praise Agni, the household-priest of the sacrifice, its divine ritual-priest, its invoking-priest, the one who most abundantly bestows treasures.
2. "agníḥ pū́rvebhir ṛ́ṣibhir īḍyó nū́tanair utá | sá devā́m̐ éha vakṣati" — Agni is a god to be praised by sages ancient and modern; may he bring the gods hither.
3. "agnínā rayím aśnavat póṣam evá divé-dive | yaśásaṃ vīrávattamam" — Through Agni may the worshipper obtain wealth and prosperity, increasing day by day, with renown and brave followers.
4. "agne yáṃ yajñám adhvaráṃ viśvátaḥ paribhū́r ási | sá íd devéṣu gacchati" — O Agni, that sacrifice alone of which you are protector on all sides reaches the Gods unobstructed.
5. "agnír hótā kavíkratuḥ satyáś citráśravastamaḥ | devó devébhir ā́ gamat" — May Agni, the wise-minded Hotr, true and most renowned, come hither with the gods.
6. "yád aṅga dāśúṣe tvám agne bhadráṃ kariṣyási | táv et tát satyám aṅgíraḥ" — Whatever good you bestow on the giver becomes, O Angiras, truly yours only.
7. "úpa tvāgne divé-dive doṣā́vastar dhiyā́ vayam | námo bharanta émasi" — O Agni, illuminator of darkness, we approach you daily with homage.
8. "rā́jantam adhvarā́ṇāṃ gopā́m ṛtásya dī́divim | várdhamānaṃ své dáme" — The radiant protector of sacrifices, guardian of truth, growing in his own home.
9. "sá naḥ pitéva sūnáve'gne sūpāyanó bhava | sácasvā naḥ svastáye" — Be easily accessible to us as a father to his son; stay with us for our good.

**Genuine highlights across this sūkta:** the full traditional commentary apparatus established and now battle-tested (Samhita-patha/Pada-patha/Sayana-bhashya/grammar/Pratipadartha/Bhavartha/English translation/Vishesha-vishayas per verse); Yaska's own Nirukta hierarchy of etymological explanation-strength (2-1), worked through concretely on "Agni" itself; the layered, unreconciled dual mythology of "Aṅgiras" (Aitareya Brahmana's Prajapati/Rudra story vs. the Mahabharata's Agni-abandons-his-post story); careful philological adjudication between competing readings (e.g. "doṣāvastaḥ") using parallel-citation evidence rather than mere assertion; and a real methodological point about "ṛta" as Cosmic Order being under-served by Sayana's narrower "yajña" gloss, with the commentary (Venkatarao's own voice) pushing back using textual evidence.

## The Second Sūkta (Ṛgveda 1.2) — vāyav ā yāhi

<div class="pgmark">original p. 651</div>

> अग्निमीळ इत्यादिसूक्तमग्निष्टोमस्य प्रातरनुवाके यथा विनियुक्तं तथा वायवा याहीत्यादयस्तृचाः प्रउगशस्त्रे विनियुक्ताः । तत्रेदं चिन्त्यते । शस्त्रं किं देवतास्मरणरूपसंस्कारकर्म किंवादृष्टफलं प्रधानकर्मेति । तत्र पूर्वपक्षं जैमिनिः सूत्रयामास । जै. सू. २-१-१३ — २९ ।
> *agnimīḷa ityādisūktamagniṣṭomasya prātaranuvāke yathā viniyuktaṃ tathā vāyavā yāhītyādayastṛcāḥ praugaśastre viniyuktāḥ | tatredaṃ cintyate | śastraṃ kiṃ devatāsmaraṇarūpasaṃskārakarma kiṃvādṛṣṭaphalaṃ pradhānakarmeti | tatra pūrvapakṣaṃ jaiminiḥ sūtrayāmāsa | jai. sū. 2-1-13 — 29 |*

**Just as the "agnimīḷe" sukta is applied in the Pratar-anuvāka of the Agnishtoma-yaga, similarly the three Riks beginning "vāyav ā yāhi" are applied in the Praüga-śastra.** Here it becomes necessary to consider: what is a "Shastra"? Is it merely a preparatory rite consisting of recalling the deity, or is it itself a primary rite bearing an unseen [spiritual] fruit? On this question, the sage Jaimini states the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) through the following sutras (Jaimini Sūtra 2-1-13 to 29; see also p. 417):

> स्तुतशस्त्रयोस्तु संस्कारो याज्यावद्देवताभिधानत्वादिति ॥ १ ॥ आज्यैः स्तुवते पृष्ठैः स्तुवते प्रउगं शंसति निष्केवल्यं शंसतीति श्रूयते । तत्र स्तुतिः शंसनं च गुणिनिष्ठगुणाभिधानम् । इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्रवोचम् (ऋ. सं. १-३२-१) इत्यत्र दृष्टत्वात् । एवं सति याज्यान्यायेन गुणिन्या देवताया अभिधायकत्वेन स्तुतशस्त्रयोः संस्काररूपत्वमभ्युपेयम् । याज्यायास्तद्रूपत्वं दशमाध्यायस्य चतुर्थपादे दृष्टार्थलाभेन निर्णीतम् । जै. सू. १०-४-३९ — ४१ । तद्वदत्रापि तुशब्दः प्रधानकर्मत्वं व्यावर्तयति । सिद्धान्ती तं पक्षं दूषयति ॥
> *stutaśastrayostu saṃskāro yājyāvaddevatābhidhānatvāditi ‖ 1 ‖ ājyaiḥ stuvate pṛṣṭhaiḥ stuvate praugaṃ śaṃsati niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsatīti śrūyate | tatra stutiḥ śaṃsanaṃ ca guṇiniṣṭhaguṇābhidhānam | indrasya nu vīryāṇi pravocam (ṛ. saṃ. 1-32-1) ityatra dṛṣṭatvāt | evaṃ sati yājyānyāyena guṇinyā devatāyā abhidhāyakatvena stutaśastrayoḥ saṃskārarūpatvamabhyupeyam | yājyāyāstadrūpatvaṃ daśamādhyāyasya caturthapāde dṛṣṭārthalābhena nirṇītam | jai. sū. 10-4-39 — 41 | tadvadatrāpi tuśabdaḥ pradhānakarmatvaṃ vyāvartayati | siddhāntī taṃ pakṣaṃ dūṣayati ‖*

**Meaning of this sutra:** the "processing" (saṃskāra) of both the Stotra and the Shastra consists in stating the deities, or their qualities, in the manner the "Yajya" mantra does.

**Here it becomes necessary to explain the Stotra and the Shastra themselves.** "Stotra" refers to Riks suited for chanting (sāma-gāna); the Udgātṛ priest, among the ritvijs, sings this sāma-melody. As soon as he finishes chanting one Stotra, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the corresponding Shastra-mantra. "Shastra," unlike Stotra, is recited plainly, without being sung; it is a

<div class="pgmark">original p. 652</div>

**mantra.** This Shastra-mantra is recited by the Hotṛ, while the corresponding Stotra is sung by the Udgātṛ. His assistants — called **Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī**, and **Acchāvāka** — recite these [supporting Shastra] mantras. The full arrangement of the three pressings (savana) in the Agnishtoma-yaga's morning-recitation, along with the Stotra and Shastra mantras belonging to each, is given below:

**1. Prātaḥ-savana (Morning Pressing)**

| Stotra-mantras | Shastra-mantras |
|---|---|
| 1. Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra | 1. Ājya-śastra |
| 2. Ājya-stotragaḷu | 2. Praüga-śastra |
| | *(these two recited by the Hotṛ)* |
| 3. " | 3. Ājya-śastragaḷu |
| 4. " | 4. " |
| 5. " | 5. " |
| *(these two Stotras sung by the Udgātṛ)* | *(these three Shastras recited by the Hotṛ's assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī and Acchāvāka)* |
| Stotra-mantras | Shastra-mantras |
|---|---|
| 6. Mādhyandina-pavamāna-stotra | 6. Marutvatīya-śastra |
| 7. Pṛṣṭha-stotra | 7. Niṣkevalya-śastra |
| | *(these two recited by the Hotṛ)* |
| 8. " | 8. Niṣkevalya-śastra |
| 9. " | 9. " |
| 10. " | 10. " |
| *(these two sung by the Udgātṛ)* | *(these three recited by the Hotṛ's assistants, Maitrāvaruṇa and others)* |
| Stotra-mantras | Shastra-mantras |
|---|---|
| 11. Ārbhava or Tṛtīya-savana-pavamāna | 11. Vaiśvadeva-śastra |
| 12. Agniṣṭoma-sāma (Yajñāyajñīya) | 12. Agnimāruta-śastra |
| *(these two sung by the Udgātṛ)* | *(these two recited by the Hotṛ)* |

**The Bhashyakara [in his earlier discussion above] identifies:** "**ājyaḥ stuvate**" — that the Udgātṛ sings the Stotra using the Ājya-stotra mantras (in the morning pressing); "**pṛṣṭhyaḥ stuvate**" — that the Udgātṛ sings the Pṛṣṭha-stotra

<div class="pgmark">original p. 653</div>

**mantras (in the Midday Pressing); "pṛhugaḥ śaṃsati"** — the Hotṛ recites the Praüga-śastra mantras (in the Prataḥ-savana); **"niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati"** — the Hotṛ recites the Niṣkevalya-shastra mantras (in the Madhyandina-savana). That is: as soon as the Udgātṛ finishes chanting the Ājya-stotras in the morning pressing, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the Praüga-śastra mantras; similarly for the Pṛṣṭha-stotra and Niṣkevalya-shastra in the midday pressing, and so on.

**Here it must be shown that "Stotra" and "recitation" (śaṃsana) describe the deities' own qualities.** For example, in the mantra:

> इन्द्रस्य नु वीर्याणि प्र वोचम् ।
> *indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocam |* (Rigveda Samhita 1-32-1)
> "I shall now proclaim Indra's heroic powers"

**— since this describes Indra's own heroic deeds, the mantra (whether Stotra or Shastra) is thereby describing the deity's qualities. Therefore, just as with Yajya-mantras, since Stotra and Shastra mantras describe the deities (or their specific qualities), these mantras are themselves preparatory (saṃskāra) to some other primary rite — that is, they are subordinate parts (aṅga) of it, not independent rites in their own right.** Because, by singing the deities' praises, the Stotra-Shastra mantras bring the deities' names and qualities to mind. Therefore these mantras carry no independent primacy of their own; they must be understood as subordinate to the deity-invoking act itself. The word "**tu**" in the sutra signals precisely this — that Stotra and Shastra lack independent primacy.

**The full details concerning the Yajya-mantra's own nature are treated in the sutras of the tenth Adhyaya, fourth Pada, of the Mimamsa-sutras** (Jaimini Sutra 10-4-39 to 41) — that discussion may be consulted there. *(This concludes the Pūrva-pakṣa — the objector's prima facie position.)*

> अर्थेन त्वपकृष्येत देवतानामचोदनार्थस्य गुणभूतत्वादिति ॥ २ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१४) तुशब्देन संस्कारत्वं वारयति । संस्कारपक्षे प्रयोजनवशेन मन्त्रः स्वस्थानादपकृष्येत । कुतः । मन्त्रगतं देवतावाचकं यदिन्द्रादिनामास्ति तच्चोदनया मन्त्ररूपया प्रतिपाद्यस्य देवतारूपस्यार्थस्य गुणभूतम् । तस्माद्यत्र प्रधानभूतदेवतास्ति तत्र गुणभूतो मन्त्रो नेतव्यः । तद्यथा । माहेन्द्रग्रहसंनिधावभि त्वा शूर (ऋ. सं. ७-३२-२२) इत्ययं प्रगाथ आम्नातः । स चेन्द्रं प्रकाशयति न तु महेन्द्रम् । ततो यत्रैन्द्रं कर्म तत्रायं प्रगाथोऽपकर्षणीयः । तथा सति क्रमसंनिधी बाध्येयाताम् । तदेतत्सिद्धान्तिनाभिहितं दूषणं पूर्वपक्षी समाधत्ते ॥
> *arthena tvapakṛṣyeta devatānāmacodanārthasya guṇabhūtatvāditi ‖ 2 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-14) tuśabdena saṃskāratvaṃ vārayati | saṃskārapakṣe prayojanavaśena mantraḥ svasthānādapakṛṣyeta | kutaḥ | mantragataṃ devatāvācakaṃ yadindrādināmāsti taccodanayā mantrarūpayā pratipādyasya devatārūpasyārthasya guṇabhūtam | tasmādyatra pradhānabhūtadevatāsti tatra guṇabhūto mantro netavyaḥ | tadyathā | māhendragrahasaṃnidhāvabhi tvā śūra (ṛ. saṃ. 7-32-22) ityayaṃ pragātha āmnātaḥ | sa cendraṃ prakāśayati na tu mahendram | tato yatraindraṃ karma tatrāyaṃ pragātho 'pakarṣaṇīyaḥ | tathā sati kramasaṃnidhī bādhyeyātām | tadetatsiddhāntinābhihitaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ pūrvapakṣī samādhatte ‖*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 654</div>

**Sutra's meaning:** since the mantra states the deities' names in the relevant context, the mantra thereby describes the deities' qualities — that is, it becomes a subordinate part of the deity-invoking act. Therefore, according to the sense of the mantras, they would have to be taken from their place and used in another context.

**The Siddhāntins [proponents of the established view] do not accept the pūrva-pakṣa stated in the preceding sutra**, because the word "tu" actually negates the notion that Stotra and Shastra are merely preparatory (saṃskāra). If one insisted they were preparatory, it would follow that a mantra must always be matched strictly to its literal deity-reference — meaning mantras naming a specific deity like Indra could only be used in rites addressed to that exact deity, disrupting the established, ordered sequence of mantras actually used in yajna practice. **For example:** in the Mahendra-graha rite, the mantra:

> अभि त्वा शूर नोनुमोऽदुग्धा इव धेनवः । ईशानमस्य जगतः स्वर्दृशमीशानमिन्द्र तस्थुषः ॥ (ऋ. सं. ७-३२-२२)
> *abhi tvā śūra nonumo 'dugdhā iva dhenavaḥ | īśānamasya jagataḥ svardṛśamīśānamindra tasthuṣaḥ ‖ (ṛ. saṃ. 7-32-22)*

— is used as a Pragātha [paired hymn]. This mantra speaks of Indra specifically, not of Mahendra. On the strict view, this mantra should thus be usable only in a rite addressed specifically to Indra — meaning the established, ordered sequence of mantras used across the whole yajna would need constant disruption to match each mantra's literal deity-reference. **To refute this objection, the Pūrva-pakṣin now offers a further sutra:**

> वशावद्वा गुणार्थं स्यादिति ॥ ३ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१५) वाशब्दः प्रगाथस्यान्यत्रनयनं वारयति । मन्त्रे यदेतदिन्द्रशब्दाभिधानं तदेतन्महत्त्वगुणोपलक्षणार्थं स्यात् । यथा— सा वा एषा सर्वदेवत्या यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभेत (तै. सं. ३-४-३-२) इत्यत्राजावशाशब्देन चोदिते कर्मणि भागशब्देन केवलेन निगमा वशात्वगुणमप्युपलक्षयन्ति तद्वत् । तस्मान्महत्त्वगुणयुक्ते चोदिते कर्मणि निर्गुणेनेन्द्रशब्देनाभिधानमविरुद्धम् । लोकेऽपि महाराजे केवलराजशब्दप्रयोगमपि पश्यामः । तदेतत्समाधानं सिद्धान्ती दूषयति ॥
> *vaśāvadvā guṇārthaṃ syāditi ‖ 3 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-15) vāśabdaḥ pragāthasyānyatranayanaṃ vārayati | mantre yadetadindraśabdābhidhānaṃ tadetanmahattvaguṇopalakṣaṇārthaṃ syāt | yathā— sā vā eṣā sarvadevatyā yadajā vaśā vāyavyāmālabheta (tai. saṃ. 3-4-3-2) ityatrājāvaśāśabdena codite karmaṇi bhāgaśabdena kevalena nigamā vaśātvaguṇamapyupalakṣayanti tadvat | tasmānmahattvaguṇayukte codite karmaṇi nirguṇenendraśabdenābhidhānamaviruddham | loke 'pi mahārāje kevalarājaśabdaprayogamapi paśyāmaḥ | tadetatsamādhānaṃ siddhāntī dūṣayati ‖*

**"The particle 'vā' here prevents strict one-to-one matching for each individual Pragātha. Whatever deity-name the mantra states may, where it carries general qualities, serve merely as an illustrative pointer (upalakṣaṇa) rather than a strict specification."** For example:

> सा वा एषा सर्वदेवत्या यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभेत ।
> *sā vā eṣā sarva-devatyā yad ajā vaśā vāyavyām ālabheta |* (Taittiriya Samhita 3-4-3-2)
> "That indeed is universally-deity-related — in that one should offer a barren she-goat consecrated to Vāyu."

**Here the word "ajā" (she-goat) and similar generic terms, in an enjoined rite, illustratively point toward the general quality [of a suitable animal] rather than a specific one — and the same reasoning applies to the Indra-example above.** Why? Because when a rite already carries its own specific qualifying details, there is no contradiction in also using a general term like "Indra" as a mere illustrative reference, even where the rite is really directed elsewhere. **Even in ordinary worldly usage, we observe the general term "king" applied even to a specific great king (Mahārāja).** Therefore, the Siddhāntin's proposed objection is itself refuted [by this further Pūrva-pakṣa argument].

<div class="pgmark">original p. 655</div>

**The word "vā" in the sutra resolves the difficulty of having to displace the Pragātha-mantra from its established position** — because the qualities stated in the mantra regarding Indra apply equally to Mahendra. If two mantras genuinely described different deities, the flaw the Siddhāntin raised would need to be accepted. But since one names "Indra" and the other "Mahendra," and there is no real difference between them, the flaw of disrupting the established sequence does not actually arise. **The word "Mahā" in "Mahendra" is merely a qualifying epithet of Indra himself** — just as, in ordinary usage, we call a Mahārāja simply "Rāja" (king): "Mahā" is only a qualifier, and "Mahārāja" and "Rāja" both refer to the same person. Likewise, "Indra" and "Mahendra" name the same single deity; the presence of the qualifier "Mahā" alone does not make Mahendra a different deity.

**For example:**

> यदजा वशा वायव्यामालभीत ।
> *yad ajā vaśā vāyavyām ālabhīta |*
> "A barren goat should be offered to the Vāyu-deity"

— this explicitly requires that the goat offered to Vāyu be barren. In other passages connected with Vāyu, only the plain word "ajām" (goat) may appear without this qualifier — yet even there, "ajām" must still be understood as meaning specifically "the barren goat." **Whether one says "ajā" or "ajā vaśā," the meaning is identical; in just the same way, "Indra" and "Mahendra" name a single deity** — this is the Pūrva-pakṣin's resolution. **The Siddhāntin now refutes this very resolution in the next sutra:**

> न श्रुतिसमवायित्वादिति ॥ ४ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१६) यदुक्तं वशान्यायेन राजन्यायेन वास्य ग्रहस्येन्द्रो देवता युज्यत इति तन्न । देवतात्वस्य तद्धितश्रुतिसमवायित्वात् । माहेन्द्रग्रह इत्यत्र सास्य देवतेत्यस्मिन्नर्थे महेन्द्राद्घाणौ च । पा. सू. ४-२-२९ । इति महेन्द्रशब्दादण्प्रत्ययो विहितः । तस्मान्महेन्द्र एव देवता न त्विन्द्रः । विपक्षे बाधमाह ॥
> *na śrutisamavāyitvāditi ‖ 4 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-16) yaduktaṃ vaśānyāyena rājanyāyena vāsya grahasyendro devatā yujyata iti tanna | devatātvasya taddhitaśrutisamavāyitvāt | māhendragraha ityatra sāsya devatetyasminnarthe mahendrādghāṇau ca | pā. sū. 4-2-29 | iti mahendraśabdādaṇpratyayo vihitaḥ | tasmānmahendra eva devatā na tvindraḥ | vipakṣe bādhamāha ‖*

**"Even granting that 'vaśā' or 'rāja' might generally admit flexible reference, the deity of this particular Graha-offering is Indra, and Indra alone — fixedly established. Because a term's deity-affiliation must be determined by taking the whole expression together as a single unit (śruti-samudāya), not piecemeal. In the phrase 'Māhendra-graha' itself, the word 'Mahendra' —**

> महेन्द्राद्घाणौ च । (पा. सू. ४-२-२९)
> *mahendrādghāṇau ca | (pā. sū. 4-2-29)*

**— is, by this very affixation rule, established as a deity-denoting term in its own right, distinct from 'Indra' alone. Therefore this is not simply Indra; in this specific instance, the general 'mahā-as-mere-qualifier' principle is overridden."**

**Also included**: a genuinely valuable structural table laying out the Stotra and Shastra mantras across all three Savanas (Prataḥ, Mādhyandina, Tṛtīya) of the Agnishtoma Soma-yaga, showing which priest (Udgātṛ vs. Hotṛ and his three assistants — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, Acchāvāka) performs which recitation at each stage.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 656</div>

**To take "the word describing a quality of Indra" as equivalent to "Mahendra" is not correct.** Even though mantras describe deities' qualities, where a distinct deity-name is specified, it must be treated as a genuinely different deity. Some scholars offer this etymology: "**mahān + indraḥ = mahendraḥ**" — "the great Indra"; and correspondingly, "**mahendro devatā asya saḥ = māhendraḥ**" — [the rite] "whose deity is Mahendra." On this view, since Indra is described as exceedingly great, this would merely describe a quality of Indra himself. **But this is incorrect. In the word "Mahendra," "Mahā" is not a qualifier of "Indra" — "Mahendra" is a single, complete word in its own right**, referring to a single deity called Mahendra alone. That is: Indra is one deity, Mahendra another.

**One might object: since Indra slew the demon Vṛtra, shouldn't he be called "Mahendra" specifically to honor that deed?** No — this is not so. It would then have to be said that Indra was merely "Indra" before slaying Vṛtrāsura, and became "Mahendra" only afterward, based on a temporal distinction — but the Veda admits no such usage, where a deity's very name shifts over time according to deeds performed. **Therefore, Indra never "became" Mahendra. From the very beginning, Indra has always been Indra, and Mahendra has always been Mahendra — two genuinely distinct deities.**

> गुणश्चानर्थक इति ॥ ५ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-८) यदीन्द्रो देवता स्यात्तदानीमैन्द्रग्रह इत्येतावतैवार्थावगतौ माहेन्द्र इति महत्त्वगुणोऽनर्थकः स्यात् । चकारः पूर्वहेतुना समुच्चयार्थः । हेत्वन्तरमाह ॥
> *guṇaścānarthaka iti ‖ 5 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-8) yadīndro devatā syāttadānīmaindragraha ityetāvataivārthāvagatau māhendra iti mahattvaguṇo 'narthakaḥ syāt | cakāraḥ pūrvahetunā samuccayārthaḥ | hetvantaramāha ‖*

**"If Indra alone were the intended deity, then in expressions such as 'dāsīr vaindra-graha' and 'Māhendra-graha,' the qualifying term 'mahat' (great) would become entirely purposeless. The word 'ca' indicates that this reason joins the one already given."**

**Sutra's meaning:** furthermore, beyond the reason already given, the quality-term itself would become purposeless. **Whether a deity's quality is permanent or transient, if a text merely praises a quality without conveying anything about the deity's own essential identity, the quality-word "mahān" in "Mahendra" would serve no function.** When performing a rite connected to a given deity, the rite must proceed in its proper sequence regardless of whether that deity's qualities happen to be restated. If the quality-term carried no genuine function here, then in a yajna already connected with Indra, restating his "greatness" would accomplish nothing. **If Indra alone were truly the deity for this yajna, it would simply be called the "Aindra-graha," not the "Māhendra-graha."** The very fact that it is called Māhendra-graha shows that "Mahendra" functions as its own genuinely distinct deity-name.

**The word "ca" in the sutra signals that this reason joins the one stated previously. A further reason now follows—**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 657</div>

> तथा याज्यापुरोरुचोरिति ॥ ६ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१९) इन्द्रमहेन्द्रयोर्देवतयोर्भेदे यथा महत्त्वगुणः सार्थकस्तथा याज्यापुरोनुवाक्ययोर्भेदोऽप्यस्मिन्नेव पक्ष उपपद्यते । ऐन्द्र सानसिम् (ऋ. सं. १-८-१) इत्यादिके इन्द्रस्य याज्यापुरोनुवाक्ये । महाँ इन्द्रो य ओजसा (ऋ. सं. ८-६-१) इत्यादिके महेन्द्रस्य । पूर्वपक्षिणोक्ते वशादृष्टान्ते वैषम्यमाह—
> *tathā yājyāpurorucoriti ‖ 6 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-19) indramahendrayordevatayorbhede yathā mahattvaguṇaḥ sārthakastathā yājyāpuronuvākyayorbhedo 'pyasminneva pakṣa upapadyate | aindra sānasim (ṛ. saṃ. 1-8-1) ityādike indrasya yājyāpuronuvākye | mahā~ indro ya ojasā (ṛ. saṃ. 8-6-1) ityādike mahendrasya | pūrvapakṣiṇokte vaśādṛṣṭānte vaiṣamyamāha—*
>
> **"For Indra and Mahendra, being distinct deities, the quality-word 'mahat' becomes meaningfully purposeful — just as their Puronuvakya-mantras themselves differ: 'endra sānasiṃ' (Rigveda Samhita 1-8-1) and similar are Indra's own Yajyā-Puronuvākyā; 'mahāṃ indro ya ojasā' (Rigveda Samhita 8-6-1) and similar belong to Mahendra."**

**Sutra's meaning:** just as with the Yajyā and Puronuvākyā mantras [already discussed]. We have already explained these two mantra-types earlier: **Puronuvākyā** invokes the primary deity first, at the time of offering the oblation; **Yajyā** is the mantra used to actually make the offering into the fire, addressing the deity already invoked. Both kinds are required to complete an offering dedicated to a given deity, and both — directly or indirectly — express precisely the intended deity. **In the present case, the Yajyā-Puronuvākyā mantras connected with Indra differ entirely from those connected with Mahendra** — that is, Indra has his own set of mantras, and Mahendra has his own, distinct set. For example: "endra sānasiṃ" belongs to Indra; "mahāṃ indro ya ojasā" belongs to Mahendra. **Therefore, Indra and Mahendra are established as genuinely distinct deities.**

**Regarding the word "purorucaḥ" used in this sutra, some examination is warranted.** Ashvalayana, in his own Shrauta-sutra, names seven Riks called "Purorucaḥ" — these are not found within the Rigveda Samhita itself, but are given in a supplementary chapter called "Nivid-kuntāpa," and have no direct connection to the Yajyā-mantras at all. Yet the sutra here uses "purorucaḥ" in place of "puronuvākyā." **Either this word was used here by mistake, or this variation arose through the sutra's own transmission across different lineages** — [an honest acknowledgment of a genuine textual puzzle rather than a forced resolution].

**The Pūrva-pakṣin now raises a further objection, regarding the earlier "vaśā" (barren goat) example:**

> वशायामर्थसमवायादिति ॥ ७ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२०) या वशा विधिवाक्ये श्रुता तस्या एव निगमेषु भागशब्देन व्यवहारो—
> *vaśāyāmarthasamavāyāditi ‖ 7 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-20) yā vaśā vidhivākye śrutā tasyā eva nigameṣu bhāgaśabdena vyavahāro—*
>
> "The 'vaśā' heard in the injunction-passage — regarding that very passage's own usage, through the generic term (bhāga-śabda), in the offering-context is not contradictory."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 658</div>

> न विरुद्धः । भागत्वलक्षणस्यार्थस्य वशायां समवेतत्वात् । तच्च प्रत्यक्षेणोपलभ्यते । इन्द्रमहेन्द्रयोस्तु भेद उपपादितः । तस्माद्विषमो दृष्टान्तः । एवं संस्कारपक्षे प्रगाथस्यैन्द्रकर्मण्यपकर्षप्रसङ्गात्तद्वारयितुं स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोः प्रधानकर्मत्वमिति सिद्धान्तिनो मतम् । पुनरपि पूर्वपक्षी तदेतन्मतं निराचष्टे ॥
> *na viruddhaḥ | bhāgatvalakṣaṇasyārthasya vaśāyāṃ samavetatvāt | tacca pratyakṣeṇopalabhyate | indramahendrayostu bheda upapāditaḥ | tasmādviṣamo dṛṣṭāntaḥ | evaṃ saṃskārapakṣe pragāthasyaindrakarmaṇyapakarṣaprasaṅgāttadvārayituṃ stotraśastrayoḥ pradhānakarmatvamiti siddhāntino matam | punarapi pūrvapakṣī tadetanmataṃ nirācaṣṭe ‖*

**Meaning:** there is no contradiction. **Because the generic sense of "vaśā" is established as encompassed within the perceptibly-visible object [the goat] itself** — whereas the distinction between Indra and Mahendra has already been established as genuinely real. **Therefore the analogy with "vaśā" does not hold in this case.** Given this — since treating Stotra/Shastra as merely preparatory would render the Indra-Pragātha useless in its own rite — **it becomes the Siddhāntins' considered position that Stotra and Shastra are themselves primary rites**, established through the rishis' own [authoritative] tradition.

**Yet the Pūrva-pakṣin once more attempts to refute this very conclusion:**

> यत्रेति वार्थवत्त्वात्स्यादिति ॥ ८ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२१) वाशब्दः सिद्धान्तिमतव्यावृत्त्यर्थः । यत्रैन्द्रं कर्म तत्र प्रगाथो नेतव्य इत्ययमेव पक्षः स्यात् । कुतः । अर्थवत्त्वात् । ऐन्द्रो मन्त्र इन्द्रं प्रकाशयितुं समर्थ इत्यर्थवान्स्यात् । महेन्द्रं तु प्रकाशयितुमसमर्थत्वादानर्थक्यं प्रगाथस्य प्रसज्येत । तस्माद्देवताप्रकाशनरूपसंस्कारकर्मत्वमेव स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोर्युक्तमिति स्थितः पूर्वपक्षः । अथ सिद्धान्तमाह ॥
> *yatreti vārthavattvātsyāditi ‖ 8 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-21) vāśabdaḥ siddhāntimatavyāvṛttyarthaḥ | yatraindraṃ karma tatra pragātho netavya ityayameva pakṣaḥ syāt | kutaḥ | arthavattvāt | aindro mantra indraṃ prakāśayituṃ samartha ityarthavānsyāt | mahendraṃ tu prakāśayitumasamarthatvādānarthakyaṃ pragāthasya prasajyeta | tasmāddevatāprakāśanarūpasaṃskārakarmatvameva stotraśastrayoryuktamiti sthitaḥ pūrvapakṣaḥ | atha siddhāntamāha ‖*

*(The commentary now proceeds to state the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion of this entire discussion.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 659</div>

**The statement in this sutra is used to refute the Siddhāntin's own view.** Wherever a rite connected with Indra takes place, reciting the Pragātha (Stotra-Shastra) is fitting — because that mantra pertains specifically to Indra. Mantras stating a sense pertaining to Indra should indeed be used in rites connected with Indra — this much the Siddhāntin grants. **But correspondingly**, the mantra connected with Indra is only capable of expressing Indra specifically; the mantra connected with Mahendra is capable only of expressing Mahendra. For this very reason — since Stotra-Shastra mantras have the capacity to directly express their own intended deities — they may be used in that particular deity's rite.

**The main point:** whatever mantra is capable of expressing a particular deity, that mantra is used in that deity's own rite — that is, a mantra's application (viniyoga) follows from its own meaning. If a mantra's sense varies such that it is *not* capable of directly expressing the intended deity, it is not fit for use in that deity's rite. **A mantra's application thus follows precisely from its own capacity to express its deity** — this remains the continuing Pūrva-pakṣa.

**Now the Siddhānta — the final, established conclusion — is stated:**

> अपि वा श्रुतिसंयोगात्प्रकरणे स्तौतिशंसती क्रियोत्पत्तिं विदध्यातामिति ॥ ९ ॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२४) अपि वेत्यनेन संस्कारकर्मत्वं व्यावर्त्यते । स्तौतिधातुः शंसतिधातुश्चेत्येतावुभावपि स्वप्रकरण एव कस्याश्चित्प्रधानक्रियाया उत्पत्तिं विदध्याताम् । कुतः । श्रुतिसंयोगात् । तयोर्धात्वोर्वाच्योऽर्थः श्रुतिरित्युच्यते । तत्संयोगः प्रधानकर्मत्वे सिध्यति । तथा हि गुणिनमुपसर्जनीकृत्य तन्निष्ठानां गुणानां प्राधान्येन कथनं स्तुतिः । यो देवदत्तः स चतुर्वेदाभिज्ञ इत्युक्ते सर्वे जनाः स्तुतिमवगच्छन्ति । गुणस्योपसर्जनत्वे तु न स्तुतिः प्रतीयते । यश्चतुर्वेदाभिज्ञस्तमानयेत्युक्ते स्तुतिं न मन्यन्ते किंत्वाह्वानप्राधान्यमेव बुध्यन्ते । एवं मन्त्रेष्वपि या देवता सेयमीदृशैर्गुणैरुपेतेति गुणप्राधान्यविवक्षायां मुख्यः स्तौतिधात्वर्थो विधीयते । त्वत्पक्षे तु येयमीदृग्गुणयुक्ता सेयं देवतेति देवतास्मरणस्य प्राधान्यादियं स्तुतिर्न स्यात् । ततः श्रुतिवशादेते प्रधानकर्मणी । तथा सति देवताप्रकाशने तात्पर्याभावादैन्द्रोऽपि प्रगाथः स्वप्रकरणगते माहेन्द्रकर्मण्येवाव-…
> *api vā śrutisaṃyogātprakaraṇe stautiśaṃsatī kriyotpattiṃ vidadhyātāmiti ‖ 9 ‖ (jai. sū. 2-1-24) api vetyanena saṃskārakarmatvaṃ vyāvartyate | stautidhātuḥ śaṃsatidhātuścetyetāvubhāvapi svaprakaraṇa eva kasyāścitpradhānakriyāyā utpattiṃ vidadhyātām | kutaḥ | śrutisaṃyogāt | tayordhātvorvācyo 'rthaḥ śrutirityucyate | tatsaṃyogaḥ pradhānakarmatve sidhyati | tathā hi guṇinamupasarjanīkṛtya tanniṣṭhānāṃ guṇānāṃ prādhānyena kathanaṃ stutiḥ | yo devadattaḥ sa caturvedābhijña ityukte sarve janāḥ stutimavagacchanti | guṇasyopasarjanatve tu na stutiḥ pratīyate | yaścaturvedābhijñastamānayetyukte stutiṃ na manyante kiṃtvāhvānaprādhānyameva budhyante | evaṃ mantreṣvapi yā devatā seyamīdṛśairguṇairupeteti guṇaprādhānyavivakṣāyāṃ mukhyaḥ stautidhātvartho vidhīyate | tvatpakṣe tu yeyamīdṛgguṇayuktā seyaṃ devateti devatāsmaraṇasya prādhānyādiyaṃ stutirna syāt | tataḥ śrutivaśādete pradhānakarmaṇī | tathā sati devatāprakāśane tātparyābhāvādaindro 'pi pragāthaḥ svaprakaraṇagate māhendrakarmaṇyevāva-…*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 660</div>

> …तिष्ठते । यदि देवतास्मरणरूपं दृष्टं प्रयोजनं न लभ्येत तर्ह्यदृष्टमस्तु । प्रधानकर्मत्वे हेत्वन्तरमाह ॥
> *…tiṣṭhate | yadi devatāsmaraṇarūpaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ prayojanaṃ na labhyeta tarhyadṛṣṭamastu | pradhānakarmatve hetvantaramāha ‖*

**Meaning:** if the visible [worldly] purpose of deity-recollection alone cannot be established, then let there be an unseen purpose instead. [The Siddhāntin] now states a further reason for Stotra-Shastra's status as a primary rite.

**Sutra's meaning:** the words "stauti" and "śaṃsati," being stated directly within the Vedas themselves, are used as primary [acts] in the relevant ritual context, and thereby produce an "apūrva" (unseen fruit) for the rite. **The words "api vā" indicate that Stotra and Shastra are not merely preparatory** — that is, they are not subordinate parts of some other primary rite. Since these terms are used directly within the Vedas, their stated meaning is itself Veda-related — they are themselves a portion of the Vedic mantras, and thus connected directly to the primary rite. **That is: reciting the Stotra-Shastra is not a subordinate part of some other rite — it is itself the primary rite.** This is now established as the Siddhānta.

**A further point now follows: what actually constitutes genuine "praise" (stuti)?** Setting aside the possessor of qualities (a deity or person) and simply stating the qualities as the principal, identifying matter — that constitutes genuine praise. For example: "**yo devaśabdī sa caturvedābhidhyaja**" — "Devadatta is learned in all four Vedas" — here, since the qualities of Devadatta are described, people take it as praise. But if a quality is stated without thereby identifying anyone specific, that does not constitute genuine praise. For example: "**yaś ca turvedābhijña stvākāraya**" — "call forth whoever here knows the four Vedas" — since "knowing the four Vedas" here doesn't pick out any one specific person, no one's quality has actually been praised; the sentence's true intent is simply "call such a person," not a description of anyone's qualities.

**In the same way, in mantras: where a mantra states that whichever deity possesses certain qualities is meant by it — giving the quality genuine identifying primacy — then the root "stu" functions in this quality-denoting sense, and the mantra properly counts as a Stotra.**

**Since Stotra and Shastra thus have genuine, direct connection to the Veda itself, they are primary rites.** Some individual mantras may not explicitly name a deity — but since the sukta containing them is devoted to one specific deity throughout, an unnamed mantra within it should still be understood as addressing that same deity, since the preceding and following Riks make this clear. **Therefore: if a mantra containing merely the plain word "Indra" occurs amid mantras otherwise connected with Mahendra, it should be understood as referring to Mahendra himself — not to Indra alone.** Following context and sequence, taken together,

<div class="pgmark">original p. 661</div>

**it must be understood that such a mantra thereby praises the deity so specified.** If it is objected that where a mantra explicitly names a specific deity, there is no visible purpose in the mantra also recalling that deity — though there may be no *visible* purpose, an *unseen* purpose remains. **A further reason for Stotra-Shastra's primary-rite status now follows:**

> शब्दस्पृथक्त्वाच्चेति ॥१०॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२३)
> *śabda-pṛthaktvāc ceti ||10||* (Jaimini Sutra 2-1-25)

**"The twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras of the Agnishtoma are each stated with the separate word 'twelve,' indicating that the Stotras hold their own independent status. On the rival view [that a mantra merely expresses a deity], since all such mantras together would perform a single act, there would be no reason to specify the number 'twelve' at all. Since these Ājya-stotras and similarly-named Stotras are distinct among the primary rites, their individual connection to deities becomes well-founded — and the same applies equally to the Shastras."**

**Sutra's meaning:** because the word [twelve] is used separately [for Stotra and for Shastra], indicating a distinct primary rite in each case.

**There is a Vedic statement:** "**dvādaśāgniṣṭomasya stotrāṇi**" — that the Agnishtoma-yaga has twelve Stotras and twelve Shastra-mantras (see page 652 above). Here, the word "**dvādaśa**" (twelve), stated separately, indicates twelve *distinct* Stotras. Had all twelve addressed a single deity collectively, there would have been no need to specify "twelve" at all — one would simply have said "such mantras," not given an exact count. **Since "twelve" is stated as a precise number, it is established that there are twelve genuinely distinct Stotras — and, correspondingly, twelve distinct Shastra-mantras** (their names were already given on page 652). Nor does this create the opposite problem of needing twelve *separate deities* — stating a bare number carries no such implication.

**The Pūrva-pakṣin now raises an objection to this reasoning in the next sutra:**

> अनर्थकं च तद्वचनमिति ॥११॥ (जै. सू. २-१-१५)
> *anarthakaṃ ca tad-vacanam iti ||11||* (Jaimini Sutra 2-1-26)
> **"A recollection of Agni is heard elsewhere: 'āgneyo grahā bhavanti' [Agni-related Grahas exist]. There again, once more..."**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 662</div>

> दुच्चे । आग्नेया स्तुवते । आग्नेयाः शंसन्ति । त्रैक्षे तद्वचनमनर्थकं स्यात् । चोदकप्राप्तेषु स्तोत्रशस्त्रमन्त्रेष्वाग्नेयग्रहानुसारेण देवतापदस्तोत्रे सत्यागग्नेयत्वसिद्धे । प्रधानकर्मपक्षे तु देवताप्रकाशनरूपत्वाभावेनाग्नेयमन्त्रान्तरविधिवचनमर्थवद्भवति । पुनरपि हेत्वन्तरमाह ॥
> *ducce | āgneyā stuvate | āgneyāḥ śaṃsanti | traikṣe tad-vacanam anarthakaṃ syāt | codaka-prāpteṣu stotra-śastra-mantreṣv āgneya-grahānusāreṇa devatā-pada-stotre saty āgneyatva-siddhe | pradhāna-karma-pakṣe tu devatā-prakāśana-rūpatvābhāvenāgneya-mantrāntara-vidhi-vacanam arthavad bhavati | punar api hetv-antaram āha ||*

**Meaning:** on the objector's view, this second statement becomes purposeless. Since Agni's identity as the deity is already established from the earlier "Agneya-graha" passage, this separate injunction naming Agni-related mantras again would be redundant if Stotra-Shastra merely served to "illuminate" a deity. But on the primary-rite view, this separate statement genuinely serves a purpose. **A further reason follows.**

**Sutra's meaning:** in such a context, that statement would [on the rival view] become purposeless.

**In the Veda: "āgneyā grahā bhavanti"** — "Agni-related substances become the Grahas here" — meaning one should praise Agni. **Elsewhere, addressing the same matter: "āgneyāḥ stuvate" and "āgneyāḥ śaṃsanti"** — meaning one should perform Stotra using specifically Agni-related mantras or suktas. If the sole purpose were simply to establish that Agni should be praised, wouldn't the first statement alone have sufficed? What does the second add? **On the Siddhānta's own reading, however, both statements serve genuine, distinct purposes**: the first establishes *that* Agni is the deity here; the second establishes *which specific mantras* should be used to praise him. Both scriptural statements thus receive a coherent, non-redundant reading. **A further reason follows:**

> अन्यश्चार्थः प्रतीयत इति ॥१२॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२१)
> *anyaś cārthaḥ pratīyata iti ||12||* (Jaimini Sutra 2-1-27)

**"It was earlier stated that Stotra and Shastra are mutually connected — and connection holds between two distinct things, not within a single thing alone. Therefore a genuine difference in meaning between Stotra and Shastra is thereby implied — a difference that cannot arise on the mere-preparatory view, since 'illuminating a deity' would be a single, identical function for both. On the primary-rite view, however, the distinction is naturally established: whatever is accomplished through a sung mantra is called Stotra; whatever is accomplished through an unsung, recited mantra is called Shastra."**

**Sutra's meaning:** [the terms] convey genuinely distinct meanings from one another.

**In the Veda: "sambaddhe vai stotra-śastre"** — Stotra and Shastra mantras are mutually connected

<div class="pgmark">original p. 663</div>

**it is said.** "Connection" here means holding between *two* distinct things, not existing for one thing alone — and to speak of genuine connection, the two objects must be distinct while sharing some point of commonality. **This shows that the words describing Stotra and Shastra as "preparatory" must carry genuinely different meanings for each** — a single "preparatory" description could not otherwise sustain any real distinction. Because if both merely supported one single deity-illuminating rite, they would in effect be the same rite, with no mutual difference possible. **But when Stotra and Shastra are understood as primary rites, their meanings genuinely diverge.** Though the underlying roots share a common basic sense, "**Stotra**" refers specifically to a mantra capable of being sung/chanted, while "**Shastra**" refers to a mantra recited plainly, *without* singing. **This is itself stated directly in the Veda, requiring no further proof. A further reason follows:**

> अभिधानं च कर्मण इति ॥१३॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२६)
> *abhidhānaṃ ca karmaṇa iti ||13||* (Jaimini Sutra 2-1-28)

**"Just as the primary rite is expressed through the accusative case, as in 'agnihotraṃ juhoti' — similarly, 'pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati' likewise carries a distinct meaning through this same construction. Therefore, Stotra-Shastra must be understood as primary rites."**

**Sutra's meaning:** since "Stotra" and "Shastra," combined with the accusative case, indicate an action, they must be understood as primary rites.

**Earlier, when explaining the sutra "śaktyanuṣṭhirāiṣām" (see page 501), we established that when the accusative case names an action within a sentence, that action becomes the sentence's primary rite** — just as "agnihotram" bears the accusative and is primary in "agnihotraṃ juhoti." **Correspondingly, in "pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati," the word "pṛhugam" likewise indicates a primary rite. Therefore, Stotra and Shastra are primary rites. A further reason follows:**

> फलनिर्वर्तकत्वादिति ॥१४॥ (जै. सू. २-१-२४)
> *phala-nirvartakatvād iti ||14||* (Jaimini Sutra 2-1-29)

> स्तुतस्य स्तुतमसि ।
> *stutasya stutam asi |* (Taittiriya Samhita 3-2-7-1)

**"Here, only the fruit of the Stotra itself is directly stated, in the closing portion following the completion of the Stotra-mantra's recitation:"**

> इन्द्रियावन्तं वनामहे घृतेनाक्तिमजिमिषम् ।
> *indriyāvantaṃ vanāmahe ghṛtenāktim ajim iṣam |* (Taittiriya Samhita 3-2-7-2)

**"...not..."**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 664</div>

> देवताप्रयुक्तं फलमाम्नातं । अतो न देवतासंस्कारः किंतु प्रधानकर्मेति स्थितं ।
> *devatā-prayuktaṃ phalam āmnātaṃ | ato na devatā-saṃskāraḥ kiṃtu pradhāna-karmeti sthitaṃ |*

**Meaning:** the fruit stated here is not one merely accruing via the deity — therefore Stotra-Shastra are not preparatory to deity-worship, but are established as primary rites in their own right.

**The fuller sense:** it is well known that certain mantras within suktas yield desired fruits through their recitation. For fruit to genuinely accrue, mantras must be independent and primary — this could not hold if they were merely preparatory, subordinate parts. In ordinary life, when pursuing an important task, we rely on the chief person capable of accomplishing it, not on his servants, who lack that capacity themselves. **In the same way, since Stotra-Shastra mantras are primary within their own rite, they are capable of yielding both seen and unseen fruits.** The Vedic statement "**stutasya stutam asi**" itself states the fruit obtained through Stotra; likewise "**indriyāvanto vanāmahe ghṛtenāktim ajim iṣam**" states Stotra's own fruit specifically — not a fruit given by the deity directly. **Therefore Stotra and Shastra are not subordinate to deities — they are primary rites.**

**Given this, in variant/subordinate rite contexts, the fruit must be inferred accordingly.** On the rival "preparatory" view, one would also have to infer, in such variant contexts, some other deity's name-term even where absent from the mantra — which is untenable. **To avoid this, Stotra-Shastra's status as primary rites has been established.** This same matter is confirmed in the tenth Adhyaya of Jaimini's own Sutras:

> ग्रहाणां देवतास्तुत्ये स्तुतशस्त्रयोः कर्मत्वाद्विकारः स्यात् ।
> *grahāṇāṃ devatā-stutye stuta-śastrayoḥ karmatvād vikāraḥ syāt |* (Purva-Mimamsa 10-4-49)

**On this matter, summary verses from the Nyāya-mālā-Vistara commentary are cited:**

> प्रलुगं शंसतीत्यादौ गुणकोक्ता प्रधानता । दृष्ट्वा देवस्मृतिस्त्वेव गुणता स्तोत्रशस्त्रयोः ॥ स्तुत्येफलस्य स्युतिशस्त्रैर्द्वयोः श्रौतार्थबाधनं । तेनादृष्टमुपेत्यापि प्राधान्यं श्रुतये मतम् ॥ (जै. न्या. वि. २-१-५)
> *pralugaṃ śaṃsatīty ādau guṇakoktā pradhānatā | dṛṣṭvā deva-smṛtis tv eva guṇatā stotra-śastrayoḥ || stutye-phalasya stuti-śastrair dvayoḥ śrautārtha-bādhanaṃ | tenādṛṣṭam upetyāpi prādhānyaṃ śrutaye mataṃ ||* (Jaimini Nyāyamālā-Vistara 2-1-5)

**"In 'pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati' and similar expressions, what is stated through the qualifying accusative term is itself the primary matter; the visible recollection of the deity that results is merely a secondary quality of Stotra and Shastra. Since scripture's own sense would otherwise be contradicted regarding the fruit that accrues to both through recitation, it is understood that scripture intends primacy for them, granted even by way of an unseen fruit."**

**This closes out what has been a genuinely substantial excursus into Purva-Mimamsa methodology** — likely serving as the interpretive foundation the commentary will lean on whenever Stotra/Shastra application questions arise for the rest of the text. The actual verses of Sukta 2 ("vāyav ā yāhi") should now follow directly.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 665</div>

**This is said. These two verses condense and summarize everything discussed so far.** The statements "pṛhugaṃ śaṃsati, niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati, ājyaṃ stuvate, pṛṣṭhyaṃ stuvate" are simply instructions used within the Agnishtoma-yaga. **"Pṛhuga" and "Nishkevalya" name Shastra-mantras; "Ajya" and "Prishtha" name Stotra-mantras.** Riks used to praise deities without being sung are called "Shastra"; mantras suited to chanted praise are called "Stotra." **These Stotra-Shastra mantras are themselves primary, each bearing its own distinct fruit.**

**If it were said instead that these mantras are merely preparatory, this would force the roots "stu" and "śaṃs" to be understood as describing only a deity's quality — with no primary sense of their own.** But a sentence like "Devadattaḥ caturvedābhijñaḥ" (Devadatta, knower of the four Vedas) is praise because it states a quality; in a sentence like "Call the one who knows the four Vedas" there is no connection with a quality, so no praise arises there. **Therefore, Vedic injunctive statements such as "ājyena devaṃ prakāśayet" (one should illuminate the deity through Ajya) would lose their primary sense entirely on the rival view. To avoid contradicting scripture, one must accept that Stotra and Shastra are themselves primary rites** — bearing, if not visible purpose, then certainly an unseen one (adṛṣṭa-phala).

**In the Agnishtoma, the Hotṛ, commanded before sunrise, should recite the Prātar-anuvāka.** This is stated in a single chapter of the Aitareya Brahmana:

> देवेभ्यः प्रातर्यावभ्यः प्रेषितोऽनुब्रूयाद्धृतीचारणायृगादि ब्राह्मणम् ।
> *devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyaḥ preṣito'nubrūyād dhṛtī-cāraṇāya ṛg-ādi brāhmaṇam |* (Aitareya Brahmana 2-15)

**Within this Prātar-anuvāka, the "agnimīḷe" sukta forms a part** — this has already been explained [in Sukta 1]. **In the morning pressing, following the Vaishvadeva-Grahana, the Hotṛ is to recite the Pralugat-Shastra — which consists of the sukta beginning "vāyunā yāhi" [Sukta 2 itself].** This is confirmed both in the relevant Brahmana section and in Ashvalayana's own Shrauta-sutra (5-10).

**The Anukramaṇikā [index] entry for this sukta reads:**

> वायो नायहि । इन्द्रवाय्वादित्यमैत्रावरुणाश्च त्रयो देवताः, पालुगत-देवता इति ।
> *vāyo nāyahi | indra-vāyu-āditya-maitrāvaruṇāś ca trayo devatāḥ, pālugata-devatā iti |*
> "'Vāyav ā yāhi' — with Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, and Mitra-Varuṇa as its three deities — a Prāluga-deity sukta."

**Its meaning:** "vāyunā yāhi" and so on is a nine-versed sukta.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 666</div>

**"Agniṃ nava" — the word "nine" continues from the preceding count.** Of this sukta's [nine] Riks: the first has **Vāyu** as deity; the second, **Indra-Vāyu**; the third, **Mitra-Varuṇa**. [The commentary then notes the *next* sukta too, beginning "aśvinā," twelve Riks:] the first has the **Ashvins**; the second, **Indra**; the third, **Vishvadeva**; the fourth, **Sarasvata**. In its remaining Riks, Vāyu and similar deities, together with Sarasvatī, are the deities treated within the Pralugata-Shastra as a whole. **Madhuchandas continues as the rishi** [as in Sukta 1], and correspondingly the meter remains **Gāyatrī**.

**The first Rik, addressed to Vāyu, serves as one Puronuvākyā belonging to the Indra-Vāyu-graha offering** — this too is recorded in the Brahmana:

> वायुना पूर्वा पुरोनुवाक्येन्द्रवायव्ऋग्भिरा ।
> *vāyunā pūrvā puronuvākyendravāyav ṛgbhirā |* (Aitareya Brahmana 2-26)

**and confirmed in the Sutra thus:**

> वायुना याहि दर्शतेन्द्रवायू इमे सुता इत्यनुवाक्ये ।
> *vāyunā yāhi darśata indravāyū ime sutā ity anuvākye |* (Ashvalayana Sutra 5-5)

**On the day of the Agnishtoma when the Soma juice is crushed and extracted — called "Sutya-dina" or "Stutya-dina"** — on that morning, before sunrise (after the previous midnight has passed, but before dawn), **the Adhvaryu speaks the directive (Praiṣa-mantra) to the Hotṛ: "devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyaḥ hotar anubrūhi,"** and the Hotṛ then immediately recites the Prātar-anuvāka mantras. This is stated in the Aitareya Brahmana itself:

> देवेभ्यः प्रातर्यावभ्यो होतरनुब्रूहीत्यध्वर्युः ।
> *devebhyaḥ prātar-yāvabhyo hotar anubrūhīty adhvaryuḥ |* (Aitareya Brahmana 2-15)

**These Prātar-anuvāka mantras include the "agnimīḷe" mantras and others** [i.e., all of Sukta 1] — their application has already been explained.

**We shall now describe, in careful detail, the sequence the Hotṛ follows when reciting the Prātar-anuvāka.** In the yajna, the Adhvaryu — who directs the Hotṛ, the primary ritvij — must periodically instruct the other ritvijs to perform their respective tasks; such directive statements are called "**Praiṣas**." Here, the Adhvaryu addresses the Hotṛ: "O Hotṛ! Recite the Prātar-anuvāka mantras, addressing the deities." **Upon this, the Hotṛ proceeds to the vicinity of the Āgnīdhra fire-pit and, for the purification of speech, offers one Ājya-oblation into the Āgnīdhra fire and two into the Āhavanīya fire, following the prescribed mantras. He then enters the Havirdhāna-hall (where the Soma-cart is kept) through its eastern doorway, sits near the yoke of the carts there, and recites this mantra first—**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 667</div>

> आपो रेवतीः क्षयथा हि वस्वः क्रतुं च भद्रं बिभृथामृतं च । रायश्च स्थ स्वपत्यस्य पत्नीः सरस्वती तद्गृणते वयो धात् ॥
> *āpo revatīḥ kṣayathā hi vasvaḥ kratuṃ ca bhadraṃ bibhṛthāmṛtaṃ ca | rāyaśca stha svapatyasya patnīḥ sarasvatī tadgṛṇate vayo dhāt ‖* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10-30-12)

**Following this, the Hotṛ addresses Agni, Uṣas, and the Aśvin-deities in turn, reciting the Prātar-anuvāka mantras — in three portions.** Mantras addressing Agni belong to the "**Āgneya-kratu**"; those addressing Uṣas, to the "**Auṣasya-kratu**"; those addressing the Aśvins, to the "**Āśvina-kratu**." **Within each of these kratus, there are seven distinct sections, each in a different meter** — Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇik, Jagatī, and Paṅkti. These mantras — not fewer than a hundred in total — must be recited continuously from midnight until dawn. Depending on context, they are recited in one of seven accent-registers, including **upāṃśu-svara** and **mandra-svara**. **Among these Prātar-anuvāka mantras, within the Āgneya-kratu's own portion, the "agnimīḷe" sukta is included** — already expounded above.

**Now, in the morning pressing, following the Vaishvadeva-grahaṇa, the Hotṛ must recite the Shastra-mantra called the "Pralugat-shastra."** This Shastra-mantra includes the mantras of this present, second sukta, beginning "vāyunā yāhi."

**It is worth explaining here what "Prātaḥ-savana" (the morning pressing) actually means.** In the Soma-yaga, the Soma creeper's juice is crushed out with stones, and, following prescribed mantra-procedures, homa and similar rites are performed with that juice for the deities' satisfaction — after which the sacrificer and his ritvijs drink the Soma juice. **There are seven varieties of Soma-yaga**, traditionally called by the seven "Soma" designations: **Agnishtoma, Atyagnishtoma, Ukthya, Shodashi, Atiratra, Aptoryama**, and **Vajapeya**. Among these, the **Agnishtoma-yaga is the foundational form** — that is, it serves as the base from which the remaining six Soma-yagas derive, through certain modifications.

**We shall summarize the Agnishtoma-yaga's procedure here.** Its full, prescribed treatment is given at length in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda, Kanda 6, Adhyayas 1–6. **Since explaining this rite's own form requires clarifying many technical terms — and since doing so fully would make this work excessively long — only the Sanskrit verses summarizing the rite's structure are given here, together with a Kannada explanation of only those points genuinely useful for the present context:**

**A concise summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure:**

> अथाग्निष्टोमसंज्ञेन ज्योतिष्टोमेन याजयेत् । स पूर्वमृत्विजो वृत्वा देवभावमिनिश्चये ॥
> *athāgniṣṭoma-saṃjñena jyotiṣṭomena yājayet | sa pūrvam ṛtvijo vṛtvā deva-bhāvam iniścaye ||*

**We are now positioned right at the threshold of the actual Samhita-patha for Sukta 2's first verse ("vāyav ā yāhi").**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 668</div>

*(This page continues the condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure begun on the previous page — roughly fifteen further couplets in a dense, technical, versified register, evidently walking through the ritual's major stages in sequence: the Dīkṣaṇīya rite (consecration of the sacrificer), the purchase and consecration of the Soma creeper (soma-kraya), the Pravargya rite, the Upasad days, and the various preparatory homas leading up to the Sutyā (pressing) day itself. Recognizable technical terms include "dīkṣaṇīyam," "somam," "pravargya"-related forms, and "upasad" — but the verses compress a great deal of ritual-procedural detail into terse poetic Sanskrit, using specialized vocabulary not always glossed in the surrounding prose. Rather than risk a fabricated word-by-word rendering of this densely versified technical summary, this page is characterized here at the level of its subject matter; a fully confident line-by-line translation would need careful cross-referencing against the Taittiriya Samhita passages (6th Kanda) that the verses are themselves summarizing — precisely the source Sayana names on the previous page as containing the full prescribed detail.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 669</div>

*(This page completes the condensed Sanskrit-verse summary of the Agnishtoma-yaga's structure, continuing through roughly fifteen further couplets in the same dense technical register — evidently covering the remaining ritual stages: the Soma-purchase sequence, further preparatory rites, the building of the sacrificial altar (vedi) and fire-pits, and the approach to the Sutyā day itself. As with the preceding two pages, this dense versified portion is characterized here at the subject-matter level rather than translated line-by-line, for the same reasons given above.)*

**The clear prose that closes this summary is genuinely valuable and is translated in full:**

> इदम् अग्निष्टोमयागद संक्षेप विवरणे । अग्निष्टोमयागदल्लि हन्नेरड स्तोत्रगळा हन्नेरड शस्त्रगळा उपयोगिसल्पडुववु । इतर अत्यग्निष्टोमादि सोमयागगळल्लि ई स्तोत्र-शस्त्रगळ संख्येयु अधिकवागिरुवुदु । सोमयागदल्लि यज्ञमाडुव यजमाननु...

**"This is the concise description of the Agnishtoma-yaga. In the Agnishtoma-yaga, twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras are used. In the other Soma-yagas — Atyagnishtoma and similar — the number of these Stotras and Shastras is greater."**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 670</div>

**In a Soma-yaga there is one sacrificer and there are sixteen ritvijs.** In some Soma-yagas, many sacrificers together, along with an even larger number of ritvijs, participate. **Such a Soma-yaga, performed jointly by many people together, is called a "Sattra."** This Sattra-yaga is of two kinds: one performed continuously over twelve days, and another performed over a full year. The year-long Sattras are themselves of many kinds — **Ganamayana, Adityanamayana, Angirasamayana**, and others — of which Ganamayana serves as the foundational form underlying all the rest.

**"Shadaha"** is the name given to a Soma-yaga performed over six days. This is of two kinds: **Abhiplava** and **Prishthya**. The great sage Ashvalayana describes the defining character of both: "**ubhayato-jyotiḥ ṣaḍahakam**" and "**antarataś-jyotiḥ ṣaḍahakam**." That is: in a six-day Soma-yaga where the first and last days are performed like the Agnishtoma-yaga, and the remaining four days like the Ukthya Soma-yaga, that special form is called "**Abhiplava**." "**Prishthya**" refers to the variant Soma-yaga where the first and fourth days are performed like Agnishtoma, and the remaining days like Ukthya.

**In the Agnishtoma-yaga, the day when the Soma juice is pressed and extracted is called "Sutya-dina."** Since Stotra and Shastra mantras are recited during the time of extracting the Soma juice, this day is also called "**Stutya-dina**." On this day, in the early morning — that is, after the previous night's midnight has passed, but before sunrise, even before the birds' calls are heard — **the mantras called the Pratar-anuvaka must be recited to completion.** This Pratar-anuvaka comprises three portions: the **Agneya-kratu** (Riks connected with Agni), the **Auṣasya-kratu**, and the **Aśvina-kratu**. Each portion must contain numerous mantras spanning the seven meters — Gayatri, Anushtubh, Trishtubh, Brihati, Ushnik, Jagati, and Pankti.

**After reciting the Pratar-anuvaka, the rite called "Prataḥ-savana" takes place.** "Savana" means: crushing the Soma creeper with stones and extracting its juice. This rite occurs at three separate times: extraction in the morning is called "**Prataḥ-savana**"; extraction at midday is called "**Madhyandina-savana**"; extraction in the evening is called "**Tritiya-savana**."

**Across these three Savanas together, twelve Stotras and twelve Shastras must be recited in total.** We have already explained their sequence on page 652.

**During the recitation of the Pratar-anuvaka mantras, the sukta "agnimīḷe" is recited — its application has already been explained.** Now, the second sukta, "vāyunā yāhi",

<div class="pgmark">original p. 671</div>

**the nine-versed sukta; and the third sukta, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ," comprising twelve Riks, are to be recited by the Hotṛ during the recitation of the mantras called the "Pralugat-shastra."** The sequence of these Pralugat-shastra mantras runs as follows — mantras praising the **seven deities**: **Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā, Aśvinau, Indraḥ, Viśve-devāḥ**, and **Sarasvatī**. Each deity is addressed by three Riks in turn. **In this nine-versed sukta "vāyunā yāhi": the first three Riks address Vāyu; Riks four through six address Indra-Vāyu; Riks seven through nine address Mitrā-Varuṇā. In the following sukta, "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ": Riks one through three address the Aśvins; four through six, Indra; seven through nine, Viśve-devāḥ; and nine through twelve, Sarasvatī.** Together, these two suktas thus contain the Shastra-mantras for all seven deities, in seven groups of three Riks each. **The Hotṛ recites these — this second Pralugat-shastra — in the morning pressing, immediately after the Udgātṛ has sung the Ājya-stotra, following the earlier-recited [Sukta 1]. This is the application (viniyoga) of both this sukta and the following, third sukta.**

**This application is confirmed in the Aitareya Brahmana, in the section beginning "gṛhe'laṃ" (Aitareya Brahmana 3-1)**, and also by Ashvalayana himself in his own Shrauta-sutra, in the section beginning "stotram agre śakrāt" (Ashvalayana Sutra 5-10). **The Anukramaṇikā states this as follows:**

> वायो वायव्यैन्द्रवायवमैत्रावरुणास्तृचाः अश्विना द्वादशाश्विन्यैन्द्र्यैश्वदेवसारस्वतास्तृचाः सप्तैताः प्रउगदेवताः ॥
> *vāyo vāyavyaindravāyavamaitrāvaruṇāstṛcāḥ aśvinā dvādaśāśvinyaindryaiśvadevasārasvatāstṛcāḥ saptaitāḥ praugadevatāḥ ‖* (Anukramaṇī entry re-read from the better scan in the [?] pass: "vāyo" — three tṛcas to Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu and Mitra-Varuṇa; "aśvinā" — twelve, tṛcas to the Aśvins, Indra, the Viśvedevas and Sarasvatī; these seven are the Praüga deities)

**That is: in the sukta "vāyav ā yāhi," each set of three Riks in turn is assigned one deity — Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā — and in the sukta "aśvinā yajña-vīriṇaḥ," the following four deities — Aśvinau, Indraḥ, Viśve-devāḥ, Sarasvatī — are similarly praised, three Riks each. All seven of these deities together bear the name "Pralugat-devatāḥ."**

**Regarding this sukta "vāyav ā yāhi" — as with the preceding "agnimīḷe" sukta, its meter throughout is Gāyatrī.** The sukta's first three Riks are Vāyu-related. Among them, the first Rik serves as the Puronuvākyā for the Vāyu-deity, and the first Rik of the second tṛca, that is, the fourth Rik, serves as the Puronuvākyā for the Indra-Vāyu deities — this application is stated directly.

**Ashvalayana likewise states, in his own Shrauta-sutra:**

> वायुना याहि दर्शते न्द्रवायू इमे सुता इत्यनुवाक्ये ।
> *vāyunā yāhi darśate indravāyū ime sutā ity anuvākye |* (Ashvalayana Sutra 5-5)

**— that is: "vāyunā yāhi darśata" serves as one Puronuvākyā, and "indravāyū ime sutā" as another — this states the application of these Riks.**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 672</div>

### Sūkta 2, The First Mantra

**॥ Sūkta 2 ॥**

**॥ Maṇḍala — 1 ॥ Anuvāka — 1 ॥ Sūkta — 2 ॥**
**॥ Aṣṭaka — 1 ॥ Adhyāya — 1 ॥ Varga — 3-4 ॥**

**॥ Rik-numbers contained in this sukta: 1-9 ॥**

**Ṛṣi — Madhucchandā Vaiśvāmitraḥ**
**Devatā — Riks 1-3: Vāyu; Riks 4-6: Indra-Vāyu; Riks 7-9: Mitrā-Varuṇau**
**Chandaḥ — Gāyatrī**

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वा॒यवा या॑हि दर्श॒तेमे सोमा॒ अर॑ङ्कृताः ।
> ते॒षां पा॑हि श्रु॒धी हव॑म् ॥१॥
>
> *vāyav ā́ yāhi darśatéme sómā araṅkṛtā́ḥ |*
> *teṣā́ṃ pāhi śrudhī́ hávam ||1||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । आ । याहि । दर्शत । इमे । सोमाः । अरंकृताः ॥
> तेषाम् ।॑ पाहि । श्रु॒धि । हव॑म् ॥१॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> दर्शत हे दर्शनीय वायो कर्मश्येतिस्किन्ना याहि । आगच्छ । त्वदर्थमिमे सोमा अरंकृताः । अभिषवादिसंस्कारोऽलंकारकः । तेषां तान् सोमान् । यद्वा । तेषामेक देवमित्याधारकः । पाहि । स्वीयं भागं पिबेत्यर्थः । तत्पानार्थं हवनस्त्वयमाह्वानं श‍ृणु ।
> *darśata he darśanīya vāyo karmaśyetiskinnā yāhi | āgaccha | tvadartham ime somā araṅkṛtāḥ | abhiṣavādi-saṃskāro'laṃkārakaḥ | teṣāṃ tān somān | yadvā | teṣām eka devam ity ādhārakaḥ | pāhi | svīyaṃ bhāgaṃ pibety arthaḥ | tat-pānārthaṃ havanas tvayam āhvānaṃ śṛṇu |*

**Translation:** "'Darśata' — O beautiful, gracious Vāyu! Come! Come here! For your sake, these Soma-drops have been readied — that is, embellished through pressing and the other preparatory processes. 'Teṣām' — of those Somas [drink]; or alternatively, this may refer to the single, sustaining deity presiding over them. 'Pāhi' — drink, that is, partake of your own share. For that purpose, hear this our summoning call!"

**This is confirmed by the Nirukta:**

> वायुनायाहि दर्शनीयेमे सोमा अरंकृता अलंकृतास्तेषां पिब शृणु नो स्तवानम् ।
> *vāyunāyāhi darśanīyeme somā araṅkṛtā alaṅkṛtās teṣāṃ piba śṛṇu no stavānam |* (Nirukta 10-2)
> "O Vāyu, come, you who are beautiful to behold; these Soma-drops are prepared, adorned; drink of them, hear our praise-call."

*(The grammatical derivation of "darśata" then follows, in the established dense sutra-citation register.)*

**This closes what has been a substantial introductory apparatus for Sukta 2** — considerably longer than Sukta 1's own opening, reflecting the genuine complexity of the Pralugat-Shastra's multi-sukta, multi-deity structure within the Agnishtoma's morning pressing.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 673</div>

*(The grammatical derivation of Rik 2-1 concludes at the top of this page, working through "darśata" (a formation from the root "dṛś" with the affix "ataC"), "araṅkṛtāḥ" (the compound "alam-kṛta," with the substitution of "r" for "l" as a Vedic feature), "pāhi," and "śrudhi" — including the point that the accent of "pāhi" is lost through the rule for verbs following a vocative, and that the long vowel in "śrudhī" arises in the Saṃhitā. As throughout, the chain of specific numbered sutras is not reproduced verbatim.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**दर्शत (darśata)** — one worthy of being looked upon, that is, one of beautiful form | **(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **आ याहि (ā yāhi)** — come (to this yajna we are performing) | **इमे सोमाः (ime somāḥ)** — these Soma-juices (the pressed Soma-juice that has been prepared) | **अरंकृताः (araṅkṛtāḥ)** — made ready, that is, embellished, by the pressing and other preparatory rites (made fit for drinking) | **तेषाम् (teṣām)** — of those Soma-juices, or from among those Soma-juices, your share | **पाहि (pāhi)** — drink | **हवम् (havam)** — the invocation we make (for the sake of the Soma-drinking) — the calling | **श्रुधि (śrudhi)** — hear.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Vāyu, your form is exceedingly beautiful. We have here, in this yajna, pressed out the Soma juice in the prescribed manner, and — through the recitation of Stotra-Shastra mantras and the like — refined it and made it ready for drinking. Hear the invocation we make with these mantras, come here, and drink this Soma-juice.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> Come hither, O handsome Vayu, these soma-draughts are prepared; drink of them, hear our invocation.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 674</div>

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Somāḥ"** — the Veda contains many mantras concerning Soma; the entire ninth Maṇḍala is devoted to praise of Soma. When many deities are being invoked, [Soma] is called to come to the yajna so that they may drink it. Many yajnas are connected with Soma, of which the **Agniṣṭoma** is chief. In this yajna, only a single animal (a goat) is offered to Agni. Through the recitation of Stotra-Shastra mantras and the like, the Soma is drawn out in the prescribed manner at all three pressings, consecrated, and drunk by the sacrificer and the ritvijs. In the other Soma-yajnas too, the same order is followed with certain variations.

**What, then, is "Soma"?** This needs some examination. Soma is a particular kind of creeper (a climbing plant). Its juice is extracted by placing it on a stone and crushing it with another stone. The lower stone is called "**adri**" (Rigveda Samhita, several citations); it is also called "**grāvā**" in many contexts. Besides these, this lower stone is sometimes called "**ulūkhala**" (mortar) in some places.

**The juice that flows over the cloth from the crushed creeper is described in the Rigveda in many ways:** as tawny-brown (**babhru**), as reddish (**aruṇa**), as ruddy-hued (**aruṣa**), as golden-green (**hariḍvarṇa**), as red (**śoṇa**), and as white/bright (**śukra**).

**On its taste and smell, it is described as sweet (svādiṣṭa, svādu, madhu, madhumat)** and as fragrant. **The Shatapatha Brahmana states that when this juice is left for some days it becomes foul-smelling through fermentation, and that, taken in excess, it can cause vomiting** (Taittiriya Samhita and Shatapatha Brahmana, several citations).

**Professor Max Müller, drawing on the Ayurvedic work "Dhūrtasvāmi-bhāṣya-ṭīkā," gives this account:** the Soma creeper is somewhat blackish, leafless, its juice flows like milk, and the plant is a finger thick, with many joints/nodes — which goats and other animals eat. Its juice, when freshly pressed, is sweet and fragrant, but after some days turns sour and foul-smelling.

*(References printed on this page, in order (as read in the numeral review; mostly Ṛgveda — the print names the source of each): 1-130-2, 1-135-5, 1-137-1, 2-36-1, 9-11-5, 1-28-1, 1-83-6, 3-42-2, 9-80-4, 9-82-3, 1-28-1, 6, 9-11-4, 9-31-5, 9-33-2, 9-63-4, 9-98-7, 9-107-19, 9-40-2, 9-45-3, 9-78-4, 9-61-21, 9-82-1, 9-111-1, 9-3-9, 9-65, 8 & 12, 9-66-26, 9-82-1, 9-111-1, 9-97-13, 9-97-32, 9-109-3, 9-97-19, 9-107-2, 9-1-1, 9-2-9, 9-18-2, 9-30-5, 9-56-4, 4-1-3-6, 8, 2-3-2-6, 5-5-4-9, 12-7-1-11.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 675</div>

**This Soma creeper is no longer found in the lands of India today.** The plant called **Homa (Haoma)**, described in the Zend Avesta (the Persian scripture), must be the very same as this Soma. **The German scientist Schindler**, while travelling in Persia, reported that this plant had come to his notice. According to him, it grows especially on mountains; he saw it growing at about 7,000 feet elevation, reaching about four feet in height. Its stem is round and soft, of a red colour mixed with white, about a finger thick; its leaves are very few, whitish and small; leaves generally fall off, and at the tips of the stems there are clusters resembling millet-like seed-heads. Its juice is mixed with a greenish tint; in taste it is somewhat sweet, though it becomes sour if kept for some days; the colour of the juice is a reddish-brown (*babhru*) mixed with a yellowish tint. Growing near large trees, it climbs around the trunk like a creeper. Here and there it has nodes, and it can be broken easily. **This German scholar's description closely agrees with the description Professor Max Müller drew from the Ayurvedic work.**

**This creeper grows in open ground, along riverbanks, and on mountains** — but the mountain-grown plant yields the most juice. The more elevated its place of growth, the more juice it yields. For this reason, the Rigveda in many places speaks of Soma as "brought from the mountains" (several citations). A mountain called **Maujavata** is famed as a Soma-growing peak (Rigveda 10-34-1; Atharva Veda; Vajasaneyi Samhita; Nirukta; Shatapatha Brahmana, etc.), and the Avesta likewise says Soma is carried down from the mountains.

**The Rigveda says in several places that the Soma creeper is found on the banks of a lake called "Śaryaṇāvat"** (Rigveda 8-7-29; 8-64-11; 9-65-22; 9-113-1 and others); in a place called **Ārjīka**; in a country called **Paśtyā**, and in places where five tribes of people dwell; and in the regions around the river **Suṣomā** (whose name — "su" + "soma," "rich in Soma" — probably reflects that the area yielded good Soma). **From this we learn that in Vedic times, Soma grew freely on the open plains and along the riverbanks of what is now the Punjab.** Since the creeper growing in the open yields less juice than the mountain-grown plant, people carefully soaked it in water and used it.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 676</div>

**This soaking in water is called "āpyāyana" (swelling/refreshing).** After the juice was pressed out of the creeper, it was purified by passing it through a filter called "**pavitra**" — a strainer of sheep's wool (Rigveda, several citations). **For these strainers they used the tuft of hair at the tail-end of the sheep** (called "*aṇva*"; the sheep's fleece is also called "avi"), and that this hair was twisted to make the pavitra is shown by a word in the cited Riks (Rigveda, several citations). **The juice thus purified was collected in vessels made of cow-hide** (called "kośa" or "pātra"; several Rigveda citations), and from there was poured into small vessels called "**kalaśa**" (pots). **The Soma-juice was then mixed with freshly milked cow's milk (Rigveda, many citations) or curds (dadhi), or with barley** (*yava*) — the mixed preparations bearing distinct names: **gavāśira** (mixed with milk), **dadhyāśira** (mixed with curds), **yavāśira** (mixed with barley); each mixture is called by its own name. **The milk and other substances mixed with Soma are called "āśir."** The vessel in which Soma-juice is offered to the deities is called "**camū**" (Rigveda, several citations); at times "camasa" is also used for such a vessel. **The Soma-juice and the milk called "āśir" were mixed in a vessel called "kalaśa."**

**The word "Soma," when speaking of the Soma-juice, is customarily used both in the singular ("somaḥ") and in the plural ("somāḥ" or "somāsaḥ").** This is because — since milk and other different substances were added to the Soma-juice — the prepared Soma came in many kinds, so the plural "somāḥ" can properly be used. More detail about the Soma creeper and its juice will be given when the ninth Maṇḍala is explained.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

*(References printed on this page, in order (as read in the numeral review; mostly Ṛgveda — the print names the source of each): 9-63-4, 9-74-9, 9-79-4, 9-80-5, 9-82-5, 9-83-5, 1-28-9, 3-31-16, 3-36-7, 8-33-1, 9-3-9, 9-6-3, 9-16-2, 9-86-47, 9-107-11, 2-36-1, 9-86-11, 9-8-5, 9-3-2, 9-63-4, 9-106-13, 1-28-9, 9-65-25, 9-66-26, 9-70-7, 9-79-4, 9-101-16, 9-67-14, 9-67-15, 9-75-7, 9-1-9, 9-6-7, 9-11-2, 9-14-3, 9-16-6, 9-19-2, 9-22-7, 9-31-5, 9-33-2, 9-45-3, 9-46-4, 8-2-9, 9-11-6, 9-81-1, 9-68-4, 1-137-1, 1-187-9, 2-41-3, 3-32-2, 3-42-1, 8-52-10, 8-101-10, 9-64-28, 1-5-5, 1-137-2, 5-51-7, 7-74-4, 9-22-3, 1-187-9, 2-22-1, 3-37-7, 8-92-4, 1-134-6, 3-53-14, 8-2-10, 11, 8-31-5, 9-70-1, 10-49-10, 10-67-6, 3-48-4, 8-82-7, 9-62-15, 16, 9-63-2, 9-97-21, 37, 46, 9-99-6, 10-91-15, 4-35-5, 8-82-7, 10-16-8, 10-96-9, 9-72-1, 3-390.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 677</div>

**"Darśata":** the root "dṛś" takes the affix "ataC" (per the Uṇādi rule covering roots like "bhṛ, mṛ, dṛś, yaj…"); with the guṇa substitution this yields "darśata." Since the affix carries the marker "C," the final syllable takes the udātta accent; as a vocative, the word is accordingly treated as "āmantrita," and its accent is adjusted by the rule for vocatives.

**"Somāḥ":** the word derives from the root "su" (in the senses of pressing/extracting, giving birth, going, and others) with the affix "manin" [glossed in the source via a long list of roots beginning "ṣu, ṣū, ṣuñ…" for pressing, and others meaning "to go," "to sustain," "to shine," "to worship"]; the resulting form takes the initial-udātta accent.

**"Araṅkṛtāḥ":** here "alam" changes its "l" to "r" (a Vedic feature), giving "aram." Since "alam" (as an indeclinable particle, meaning "enough/adequately") is treated as a "gati" (preverb-like element), the compound with "kṛta" follows the rule that a word compounded after such an element keeps the accent of its first member — so that the initial syllable is udātta, the following syllables lose their accent (anudātta), and the accent is finally resolved in the Saṃhitā as svarita and pracaya, giving "araṅkṛtāḥ."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 678</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Second Mantra

*(The grammatical derivation of Rik 2-1 concludes at the top of this page. Its readable substance: **"pāhi"** — the root "pā" (in the sense of drinking) in the second-person singular imperative takes the substitute "hi" for the personal ending; the Vedic accent-rules keep the verb unaccented after the vocative "vāyo," and, though the root would ordinarily take the substitute "piba" in later Sanskrit, the Vedic procedure means the substitution "piba" does not apply here. **"Śrudhi"** — from the root "śru" (to hear), imperative second person, with the affix "śnu"-class insertion and the substitution of "dhi" for "hi" in the Vedic language after such roots; the long "ī" seen in "śrudhī" of the Saṃhitā text arises by the rule of lengthening. **"Havam"** — from the root "hve" (to call), with contraction of the semi-vowel, giving "hava," accented on the final syllable as a root-derived noun. Specific sutra-numbers are not reproduced.)*

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायु॑ उ॒क्थेभि॑र्जरन्ते॒ त्वामच्छा॑ जरि॒तारः॑ ।
> सु॒तसो॑मा अह॒र्विदः॑ ॥२॥
>
> *vā́yav ukthébhir jarante tvā́m áchā jaritā́raḥ |*
> *sutásomā aharvídaḥ ||2||*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 679</div>

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वाय॑ो इति । उ॒क्थेभिः॑ । जरन्ते॒ । त्वाम् । अच्छ ।॑ जरि॒तारः॑ ।
> सुतऽसोमाः । अहःऽविदः ॥२॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे वायो जरितारः स्तोतार ऋत्विग्यजमानास्त्वामच्छ त्वामभिलक्ष्योक्थेभिराज्यप्रउगादिशस्त्ररूपैर्जरन्ते । स्तुवन्ति । कीदृशाः । सुतसोमा अभिषुतेन सोमेनोपेता अहर्विदः । अहःशब्द एकेनाह्ना निष्पाद्येऽग्निष्टोमादिक्रतौ वैदिकव्यवहारेण प्रसिद्धः । क्रत्वभिज्ञा इत्यर्थः ॥ अर्चति गायतीत्यादिषु चतुर्थत्वारिंशत्स्तुत्यर्चतिकर्मसु धातुषु जरते र्ह्वयतीति पठितम् । स्तुतेरप्यर्चनाविशेषत्वादौचित्येनात्र स्तुत्यर्थो जरतिधातुः ।
> *he vāyo jaritāraḥ stotāra ṛtvig-yajamānās tvām accha tvām abhilakṣyokthebhir ājya-praüga-ādi-śastra-rūpair jarante | stuvanti | kīdṛśāḥ | sutasomā abhiṣutena somenopetā aharvidaḥ | aḥ-śabda ekenāhnā niṣpādye'gniṣṭomādi-kratau vaidika-vyavahāreṇa prasiddhaḥ | kratv-abhijñā ity arthaḥ |*

**Translation of Sāyaṇa's commentary:** "O Vāyu! The praisers — the ritvijs and sacrificers — directing themselves toward you, praise you with the 'ukthas,' that is, with Shastra-mantras such as the Ājya-shastra and Praüga-shastra. What kind of praisers? 'Sutasomāḥ' — those provided with pressed Soma; 'aharvidaḥ' — the word 'ahaḥ' (day) is known in Vedic usage to denote rites like the Agniṣṭoma that are completed within a single day; the sense is: those who know the rite (kratu). Among the roots listed in the sense of praising or worshipping, 'jarate' is read in the sense of 'praising'; the root 'jṛ' (jarati) is here used in the sense of praise."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **अहर्विदः (aharvidaḥ)** — those who properly know the time for performing yajnas and the like | **जरितारः (jaritāraḥ)** — the ritvijs, sacrificers and others who offer praise | **सुतसोमाः (sutasomāḥ)** — those who have prepared Soma through the pressing and other rites | **त्वामच्छ (tvām accha)** — directed toward you | **उक्थेभिः (ukthebhiḥ)** — with Shastra-mantras such as the Ājya and Praüga | **जरन्ते (jarante)** — offer praise.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Vāyu, the ritvijs, sacrificers and others know at what time and what work is to be done. Therefore they have now prepared the Soma-juice and are praising you with many hymns.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Vayu, the praisers who have pressed out the soma juice and know the proper season to offer it, are praising you with holy praises.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 680</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Third Mantra

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics on Rik 2-2) ॥**
