**"Ukthebhiḥ"** does not mean sung Stotras; it means the Shastra-mantras such as the Pṛhuga and others, which are recited rather than chanted. **"Jarate"** — of the forty-four roots beginning "arcati" and "gāyati" [in the traditional list of praising-roots], the root "jṛ" is used in the sense of worshipping and singing, so "jarate" carries the sense of offering praise; likewise **"jaritāraḥ"** means "those who offer praise." **"Aharvidaḥ"** — in this word, "ahaḥ" means "day," referring to the Sutyā-day on which Soma-juice is pressed at the morning pressing and the others; this is a single day within the Agniṣṭoma. **"Sutasomāḥ"** — "those who have prepared the Soma-juice" — likewise makes clear that "ahaḥ" means the Sutyā-day specifically. Even so, one cannot say with certainty that the poet had precisely this sense in mind in using the word "aharvidaḥ."

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* The particle "accha" takes a lengthened vowel in the Saṃhitā by the rule that particles in mantras take lengthening. "**Sutasomāḥ**" is a bahuvrīhi compound ("those by whom Soma is pressed"), with the accent of the first member retained by the rule for bahuvrīhi. "**Aharvidaḥ**" is a compound whose final member, being a verbal derivative, keeps the stem accent.

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो॒ तव॑ प्रपृ॒ञ्चती॑ धे॒ना जि॑गाति दा॒शुषे॑ ।
> उ॒रू॒ची सोम॑पीतये ॥३॥
>
> *vā́yo táva prapṛñcatī́ dhenā́ jigāti dāśúṣe |*
> *urūcī́ sómapītaye ||3||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो॒ इति । तव॑ । प्रऽपृञ्च॒ती । धेना॑ । जिगाति । दा॒शुषे॑ ।
> उ॒रू॒ची । सोम॑ऽपीतये ॥३॥

<div class="pgmark">original p. 681</div>

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे वायो तव धेना वाक् सोमपीतये सोमपानार्थं दाशुषे दाश्वांसं दत्तवन्तं यजमानं जिगाति गच्छति । हे यजमान त्वयो दत्तं सोमं पास्यामीत्येवं वायुर्ब्रूते इत्यर्थः । कीदृशी धेना । प्रपृञ्चती प्रकर्षेण सोमसंपर्कं कुर्वती । सोमगुणं वर्णयन्तीत्यर्थः । उरूची उरूनस्वभूजमानान् गच्छन्ती । ये ये सोमयोजिनस्तान् सर्वान् स्वर्णयन्तीत्यर्थः ।
> *he vāyo tava dhenā vāk somapītaye soma-pānārthaṃ dāśuṣe dāśvāṃsaṃ dattavantaṃ yajamānaṃ jigāti gacchati | he yajamāna tvayā dattaṃ somaṃ pāsyāmīty evaṃ vāyur brūte ity arthaḥ | kīdṛśī dhenā | prapṛñcatī prakarṣeṇa soma-saṃparkaṃ kurvatī | soma-guṇaṃ varṇayantīty arthaḥ | urūcī urūn [bahūn] yajamānān gacchantī |*

**Translation:** "O Vāyu! Your 'dhenā' — your speech — goes, for the drinking of Soma, to the sacrificer who has given the oblation (dāśuṣe). The sense is: 'O sacrificer, I shall drink the Soma you have offered' — thus says Vāyu. What kind of speech? 'Prapṛñcatī' — bringing about, in an excellent manner, association with the Soma, that is, describing the Soma's excellence. 'Urūcī' — going to the many sacrificers; that is, it reaches every one of those who have prepared Soma."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **प्रपृञ्चती (prapṛñcatī)** — describing the qualities of the Soma | **तव (tava)** — your | **धेना (dhenā)** — speech | **सोमपीतये (somapītaye)** — for the drinking of Soma | **दाशुषे (dāśuṣe)** — to the sacrificer who offers [Soma], and | **उरूची (urūcī)** — to the many other sacrificers who offer you Soma | **जिगाति (jigāti)** — goes.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Vāyu, the sacrificer who performs the yajna, and many others besides, call you for the drinking of Soma. Your speech, pleased by the hymns they offer and by their Soma-drinking, will gladden the sacrificer who calls you to drink the Soma, and many others as well.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Vayu, your approving speech goes to the giver (of the oblation) and to many (others) who invite you for drinking Soma.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥**

**"Dhenā"** — many scholars have held many opinions about this word's meaning. Yāska, in his Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta), placed this word "dhenā" among the fifty-seven words meaning "vāk" (speech). Some take "dhenā" to mean "tongue" (jihvā).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 682</div>

On their view this Rik's sense would run: "O Vāyu, your long (that is, extended) tongue reaches the sacrificer who calls you for the drinking of Soma." **The German scholar Geldner**, after many investigations into the word "dhenā," concluded that it means "tongue" (in the sense of "speech," vāk); the sacrificer's Stotra (vāk), he says, generates in the deity a desire for the Soma-drinking. A Rik of the Rigveda supports this view: "**yaṃ te svadhāvan…**" (Rigveda 8-49-5). **But in a later study, this same scholar concluded that "dhenā" means "the milk-yielding cow's teat/milk-flow." According to Professor Max Müller, "dhenā" means "a stream of milk."** Both scholars hold that "dhenā" means "a cow that yields milk" and that the plural of the word denotes "the drinking of milk." **In the Veda, the word "dhenā" is used in a variety of senses in different contexts:**

(1) A Rik in which "dhenā" refers to a beloved woman: "*striyo hi dāsa āyudhāni cakre kiṃ mā karann abalā asya senāḥ…*" (Rigveda 5-30-9) — where "dhenā" is used for women who are objects of affection.

(2) "*ahan vyaṃsam uśadhag vaneṣv…*" and "*tvāvakro rathyo na dhenā rejante viśvā kṛtrimāṇi bhīṣā*" — in these Riks "dhenā" is used in the sense of "sister".

(3) "*viśvāḥ pinvathaḥ svasarasya dhenā anu vāmekaḥ pavir āvavarta*" (Rigveda 5-62-2) — here "dhenā" is used for a female animal, a cow.

(4) "*visṛṣṭadhenā bharate suvṛktir…*" and "*mādayasva haribhir ye ta indra viṣyasva śipre vi sṛjasva dhene*" (Rigveda 1-101-10) — here, from the root "dhe" (to drink), the word "dhenā" arises with the meaning "tongue," and this sense is still found in the later-literature word "**stanandhaya**" (a suckling child — "one who drinks milk").

<div class="pgmark">original p. 683</div>

**More Rigvedic uses of "dhenā"** (continuing the numbered list from the previous page):

(5) In several Riks — among them "*pitur…*" (Rigveda 3-1-9), "*samyak sravanti saritro na dhenā…*" (Rigveda 4-58-6), "*yad īm upa hvarate sādhate matir ṛtasya dhenā anayanta sasrutaḥ*" (Rigveda 1-141-1), "*dhiyo dhenā avasyavaḥ*", "*dhenā indrāvacākaśat*", "*viśaṃ-viśaṃ maghavā paryaśāyata janānāṃ dhenā avacākaśad vṛṣā*", "*indre dhenābhir iha mādayasva dhībhir viśvābhiḥ śacyā gṛṇānaḥ*", and "*vīreṇyaḥ kratur indraḥ suśastir utāpi dhenā puruhūtam ūtaye*" — the word is used in the senses of **speech, utterance, hymn of praise, and the act of praising.**

**M. Bloomfield**, in translating the Rik (10-104-10) cited above, remarks that the Vedic word "dhenā" is related to the Lithuanian word "*daina*" and the Avestan "*daena*." These words generally carry the senses of speech, song, hymn and lay. **Many scholars hold that in the Veda, "dhenā" chiefly and more often carries the sense of "speech, word."**

**"Prapṛñcatī"** — means "touching, making contact." **"Urūcī"** — "broad, extended, plentiful." The Bhashyakara has glossed this as "many sacrificers, performers of Soma-yajnas"; but "urūcī" may instead be taken simply as a qualifier of the word "dhenā." **"Somapītaye"** — the meaning of this word is clear; its use is especially frequent across many Riks.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* **"Prapṛñcatī"** — here, by the rule concerning words ending in the "śatṛ" affix and lacking the augment "num," the feminine-forming "ṅīp" affix (a "nadī"-class affix) is added, and the accent is treated accordingly: the word is accented on its final syllable, and the case-endings following it (such as "śas") likewise take the udātta accent.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 684</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Fourth Mantra

*(The grammar of "prapṛñcatī" concludes: the "ṅīp"-type affix's long "ī" takes udātta even though its marker would otherwise leave it unaccented.)*

**"Dhenā"** — listed in the Nirukta (Nighaṇṭu 1-11-39) among the fifty-seven words for "vāk" ("speech": *ślokaḥ, dhārā, dhenā, gnāḥ*, …); this is why "dhenā" is glossed as "speech." **"Jigāti"** — listed among the words expressing movement (Nighaṇṭu 2-14-113), where "jigāti" is glossed "gacchati" (goes).

**Grammar (summarized):** since "jigāti" is a verb of motion, the recipient noun takes the accusative/dative ("dāśvān" → "dāśuṣe") by the rule that verbs of going govern a fourth-case (dative) object of destination — hence the dative "dāśuṣe." **"Urūcī"** — the "ṣit"-marked class of words (with "gaurādi" nouns) takes the feminine affix "ṅīṣ," which brings its own accent. **"Somapītaye"** — though not a bahuvrīhi, the initial member's accent is retained by a special rule.

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> इ॒न्द्र॒वा॒यू इ॒मे सु॒ता उप॒ प्रयो॑भि॒रा ग॑तम् ।
> इन्द॑वो वामु॒शन्ति॒ हि ॥४॥
>
> *indravāyū imé sutā́ úpa práyobhir ā́ gatam |*
> *índavo vām uśánti hí ||4||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> इन्द्रवायू इति । इमे । सुताः । उप । प्रयःऽभिः । आ । गतम् ॥
> इन्दवः । वाम् । उशन्ति । हि ॥४॥

<div class="pgmark">original p. 685</div>

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> एतस्या ऋचा ऐन्द्रवायवग्रहे द्वितीयपुरोनुवाक्यारूपेण विशेषविनियोगः पूर्वमेवोक्तः । हे इन्द्रवायू भवदर्थमिमे सोमाः सुताः अभिषुताः । तस्माद्युवां प्रयोभिरन्नैरस्मभ्यं दात्व्यैः सहोपसा गतं । अस्मत्समीपं प्रत्यागच्छतम् । हि यस्मादिन्दवः सोमा वां युवामुशन्ति कामयन्ते तस्मादागमनमुचितम् । इन्द्रवायूशब्दस्यामन्त्रितस्याद्युदात्तत्वम् । प्रीणयन्ति भोक्तॄनिति प्रयांस्यन्नानि ।
> *etasyā ṛcā aindravāyava-grahe dvitīya-puronuvākyā-rūpeṇa viśeṣa-viniyogaḥ pūrvam evoktaḥ | he indravāyū bhavad-artham ime somāḥ sutāḥ abhiṣutāḥ | tasmād yuvāṃ prayobhir annair asmabhyaṃ dātavyaiḥ sahopasā gataṃ | asmat-samīpaṃ pratyāgacchatam | hi yasmād indavaḥ somā vāṃ yuvām uśanti kāmayante tasmād āgamanam ucitam | indravāyū-śabdasyāmantritasyādyudāttatvam | prīṇayanti bhoktṝn iti prayāṃsy annāni |*

**Translation:** "The specific application of this Rik — as the second Puronuvākyā in the Indra-Vāyu-graha offering — was stated earlier. O Indra and Vāyu! For your sake these Soma-juices have been pressed. Therefore, come to our side together with the foods (*prayas*) that are to be given to us, coming close to us. For, since the Soma-drops desire you two, your coming is fitting. [Grammar:] the vocative 'indravāyū' takes initial-syllable udātta. 'Prayas' means foods, 'those which please the eaters.'"

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) इन्द्रवायू ((he) indravāyū)** — O Indra and Vāyu! (for your sake) | **इमे (ime)** — these Soma-juices | **सुताः (sutāḥ)** — pressed (prepared so as to be fit for drinking) | **प्रयोभिः (prayobhiḥ)** — together with foods and other things that please us | **उपागतम् (upāgatam)** — come to our side | **हि (hi)** — because | **इन्दवः (indavaḥ)** — these Soma-juices prepared for you | **वाम् (vām)** — you two | **उशन्ति (uśanti)** — desire.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! These Soma-juices have been thoroughly pressed and made ready to be drunk. Come to our side to accept them, bringing food and other things that will please us. For these Soma-juices that we have prepared are awaiting you — that is, we watch for your arrival so that you may drink.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and Vayu, here are Soma-libations (poured out for you). Come with food for us. For, the soma-drops are desiring You.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 686</div>

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**This Rik, as already stated, is applied as the second Puronuvākyā in the rite called the Aindravāyava-graha.** In this Rik, and in the two Riks that follow, Indra and Vāyu are invoked together. **The joint invocation or joint praise of two deities is often found in the Rigveda** — for example: *Indra-Vāyū, Indrāgnī, Agnīṣomau, Indrāsomau, Somārudrā, Indrāviṣṇū, Dyāvāpṛthivī, Uṣāsānaktā* (or *naktoṣāsā*), and so on.

**"Ime"** — these (Soma-juices): that is, freshly pressed, made fit for drinking through the preparatory rites. **"Sutāḥ"** — this word, formed from the root "su" (to press), shows that Soma-creeper, crushed between stones and pressed out in the filter, has become fit for drinking. **"Prayobhiḥ"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "with foods" or "with meals." Since the word derives from the root "prī" (to please, to gladden), the sense "things that please, that bring joy to the mind" is entirely fitting. Moreover the Bhashyakara himself, in the Rik "*pra yad vo yajñe…*" — where "prayāṃsi" occurs (Rigveda 2-19-2) — glosses it as "dear things." **In the Rigveda this word is used in many places in the sense of "food fit for sacrifice."** **"Indavaḥ"** — Soma-juices mixed with various admixtures; the word derives from the root "und" (to wet/moisten): since Soma-juice is a liquid, "kledana" (moistening) is the sense; and "indu" is accordingly used in place of "soma" in many passages.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* **"Indravāyū"** — the vocative takes initial-udātta accent. **"Prayāṃsi"** — "those which please the eaters" — by analysis, "prayas" derives from the root "prī" (to please) with the affix "asun" (added after all roots, per the Uṇādi rule), giving "prī + as," with guṇa and substitution "prayas"; being formed with an accent-bearing affix, it is accented on the first syllable.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 687</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Fifth Mantra

*(The grammar of "prayobhiḥ" concludes: the affix-final "s" becomes "ru" and then visarga, giving "prayobhiḥ.")* **"Gatam"** — the root "gam," in the second-person dual imperative, has its personal ending elided by the Vedic rule ("bahulaṃ chandasi"), and the nasal of the root is dropped when the following affix is marked as "kit" or "ṅit"; hence "gatam," not to be mistaken for a form ending in the "kta" affix. **"Indavaḥ"** — from the root "und" (to moisten), the affix "un" is added and the initial "u" becomes "i," giving "indu"; the affix marker makes the word accented on its first syllable. **"Vām"** — the dual pronoun "yuvām" is replaced by the enclitic "vām," which is therefore unaccented. **"Uśanti"** — a verb, hence normally unaccented; but here it is joined with "hi," which blocks the loss of accent, so the verb retains its own accent; "hi" itself, being a particle, takes initial accent.

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायविन्द्र॑श्च चेतथः सु॒तानां॑ वाजिनीवसू ।
> तावा या॑त॒मुप॑ द्र॒वत् ॥५॥
>
> *vāyav índraś ca cetathaḥ sutā́nāṃ vājinīvasū |*
> *tā́v ā́ yātam úpa dravát ||5||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । इन्द्रः । च । चेतथः । सुतानाम् । वाजिनीवसू इति वाजिनीऽवसू ।
> तौ । आ । यातम् । उप । द्रवत् ॥५॥

<div class="pgmark">original p. 688</div>

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> अत्र चकारेणास्यः समुच्चीयते । संनिहितत्वाद्वायुरेव । हे वायो त्वमिन्द्रश्च युवामुभौ सुतानामभिषुतान्सोमान् चेतथः । जानीथः । यद्वा अभिषुतानां सोमानां विशेषणमित्यध्याहारः । कीदृशौ युवां । वाजिनीवसू । वाजिनीशब्दो यज्ञपुष्टोनामसु पठितस्तथास्य त्यासंभवात्रं गृह्यते । वाजोऽन्नं । तद्वत्यां हविःसंतत्तावस्ति सा वाजिनी । तस्यां वसतः इति तौ वाजिनीवसू । आमन्त्रितत्वादनुदात्तः । तौ तथाविधौ युवां द्रवत्क्षिप्रमुपसमीपे आ यातम् । आगच्छतम् ।
> *atra cakāreṇāsyaḥ samuccīyate | saṃnihitatvād vāyur eva | he vāyo tvam indraś ca yuvām ubhau sutānām abhiṣutān somān cetathaḥ | jānīthaḥ | … kīdṛśau yuvāṃ | vājinīvasū | vājinī-śabdo yajñapuṣṭo-nāmasu paṭhitaḥ … vājo'nnam | tadvatyāṃ haviḥ-saṃtatāv asti sā vājinī | tasyāṃ vasataḥ iti tau vājinīvasū | āmantritatvād anudāttaḥ | tau tathāvidhau yuvāṃ dravat kṣipram upa samīpe ā yātam | āgacchatam |*

**Translation:** "Here the word 'ca' combines [Indra] with the other deity — by proximity, Vāyu. O Vāyu, and Indra — you two — know the pressed Soma-juices. Or, as a qualifier of the pressed Somas, [it may be supplied]. What kind of pair are you? 'Vājinīvasū' — the word 'vājinī' is read among the words for 'sacrifice-nourishing'; 'vāja' means food. That in which there is a continuous stream of oblation-food is 'vājinī'; 'those two who dwell in it' are 'vājinīvasū' — unaccented as a vocative. You two, being such, come here quickly (*dravat*), near us."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **(त्वम्) इन्द्रश्च ((tvam) indraś ca)** — you, and Indra with you, both | **वाजिनीवसू (vājinīvasū)** — those who are chief in yajnas and the like furnished with oblation-portions | **(अतः तौ यूयम्)** — (you two, such as you) | **सुतानाम् (sutānām)** — of the pressed Soma-juices (that the Soma-juices are ready for drinking) | **चेतथः (cetathaḥ)** — know | **तौ (tau)** — you two, such | **द्रवत् (dravat)** — with alertness | **उप (upa)** — to our side | **आ यातम् (ā yātam)** — come.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! In yajnas equipped with oblation-shares and the like, you are honoured as chief. You know full well that the Soma-juice has been made ready for your drinking. Therefore, for the sake of drinking the Soma, come quickly to our side.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Vayu and Indra dwellers in the sacrifices, You are aware of these Soma-libations. You both come hither quickly.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 689</div>

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Vājinīvasū"** — many people have interpreted this word in many different ways. **The Bhashyakara** says that although "vājinī" is among the words that name Uṣas (the Dawn), that sense is impossible here and must be set aside; then "vāja" means food (the Vedic text says "*annaṃ vai vājaḥ*"), and "that in which there is oblation-food is 'vājinī'" — the sacrificial rite is thus called "vājinī" ("the yajna"). "*Tasyāṃ vasataḥ*" — "the two who dwell in it" are "vājinīvasū": the two who dwell in the yajna, hence so named.

**Authors of the Vedārtha-yatna [a modern commentary]** interpret the word thus: "vāji" means a horse, or a swift horse; "vasū" means those who possess them — that is, the two who possess swift horses. Or "vājinī" means "provided with horses" — a chariot; "vasū" means those who dwell or sit in it — those who sit in the chariot. Or "vājinī" may mean a mare, and "vasū" wealth — those who possess these. Or it may mean "givers." **The German scholar Grassmann** interprets "vājinīvasū" as "those who give abundant rewards."

**The Bhashyakara glosses the word "vājinī" in some places as "food"** (Rigveda 2-37-5; 3-42-5; 5-74-6, 7; 8-5-20; 8-9-4; 8-10-5; 8-22-7, 14, 18 and others); in some places as "sacrificial rite" (Rigveda 1-122-8; 3-42-5; 8-5-3, 12; 8-8-10; 10-96-8 and others); in some as "possessing food" (*annavatī*) (Rigveda 3-6-1; 6-61-6 and others); in some as "strong" (*balavatī*) (Rigveda 6-61-6 and others); and **"vasu" as "one who dwells"** (Rigveda 1-2-5) and as "wealth, riches" (Rigveda 3-42-5; 5-75-3; 8-5-3, 12, 20; 8-8-10; 8-9-4; 8-10-5; 8-22-7, 14, 18; 10-40-12; 10-96-8 and others).

**"Vasu"** is among the twenty-eight words for "wealth" in the Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2-10). Moreover, compounds ending in "vasu" are needed and found throughout the Rigveda, in which "vasu" generally means "wealth." A few examples follow:

**Śacīvasū** (Rigveda 1-139-5; 7-24-1; 8-60-12); **Sūryavasū** (Rigveda 7-68-3); **Vibhāvasuḥ** (Rigveda 1-44-10; 3-2-2; 5-25-2, 7; 8-43-32; 8-44-6, 10, 24; 8-93-25; 10-92-1; 10-118-4; 10-140-1 and others), and so on.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 690</div>

**Further compounds ending in "vasu" in the Rigveda:** **Viśvāvasuḥ** (10-85-21, 22; 10-139-4, 5); **Manāvasū** (5-74-1); **Viśvalāvasū** (1-182-1); **Svāvasuḥ** (5-44-7); **Tvāvasuḥ** (7-32-14); **Ṛtāvasū** (8-101-5); **Jenyāvasū** (7-74-3; 8-38-7); **Divāvasū** (8-34-1); **Dhiyāvasuḥ** (1-3-10; 1-58-9; 1-60-5; 1-63-9; 1-64-15; 3-3-2; 3-28-1 etc.); **Vṛṣaṇvasū** (1-111-1; 2-41-8; 4-50-10; 5-74-1; 8-5-24; 8-26-1, 2, 5 etc.); **Puruvasū** (1-47-10; 1-81-8; 2-1-5; 5-36-3; 6-22-4 etc.); **Prabhūvasuḥ** (1-57-4; 7-22-2; 8-45-36; 9-29-3; 9-35-6); **Vibhūvasuḥ** (9-72-7; 9-86-10); **Mahāvasū** (7-82-2); **Punarvasū** (10-19-1); **Aghṛṇīvasū** (8-60-20); **Ābharadvasuḥ** (5-79-3); **Akṣitāvasuḥ** (8-49-6); **Kṛtadvasū** (8-31-9); **Gūrtāvasuḥ** (10-132-1); **Pratadvasū** (8-13-27); **Radāvasū** (7-32-18); **Vidadvasuḥ** (1-6-6; 3-34-1; 5-39-1; 8-66-1); **Śatadvasuḥ** (1-119-1 etc.), and so on.

**In these words, "vasu" generally means "wealth."** In the Shatapatha Brahmana as well, the word occurs in "Amāvasu" (Śa. Brā. 1-6-4-2, 3) and in "Citrāvasu" (Śa. Brā. 2-3-4-22).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 691</div>

**"Vasu"** — in these two words it derives from the root "vas" (to dwell), and signifies "one who dwells." The Bhashyakara has followed this sense and explained accordingly here.

**The word "vājinīvatī"** — which is a derivative of "vājinī" — is used in the Rigveda as a qualifier of Uṣas (the Dawn) in several Riks (several citations). **Yāska, in his Nirukta, when explaining one of these Riks, glosses "vājinīvatī" as "annavatī" (possessing food).** There "vājinī" means "food"; and when explaining another Rik, he gives the same sense again.

**Sāyaṇācārya has explained "vājinī" as "a continuity of oblations"; likewise Skandasvāmin, in his own Vedabhāṣya, glosses "vājinī" as "a continuity of sacrifices."** Veṅkaṭamādhava, in explaining this word, interprets "*asmai vāsayitārau — vājinīvasū*" — hence for "vājinī," the principal senses that may be entertained are: (1) food or nourishment, (2) strength, and (3) speed. **"Vāji" is taken by some to mean "horse."** **Roth**, the scholar, translates "vājinīvasū" as "possessing quick horses." Since this word "vājinīvasū" is used by many rishis when praising deities such as Indra and the Aśvins, no single fixed sense has been established for it; it was evidently in common use, and especially frequent in yajnas involving Soma-drinking, so it is reasonable to suppose that Soma-juice and foods of every sort were freely offered in such rites.

**"Cetathaḥ"** — "you both know." **"Dravat"** — in the Nirukta (2-15-3), this word is listed among the twenty-six words expressing "quickly, swiftly."

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)* **"Vājinīvasū"** — although Yāska lists "vājinī" among the names of Uṣas, that sense does not fit here and is not adopted. "**Vājaḥ asyām asti**" — food is present in this: the affix "ini" is added after "vāja," and the "a" is dropped, then the feminine affix "ṅīp" is added, giving "vājinī." Then "vājinyāṃ vasataḥ" gives the compound "vājinīvasū," a vocative dual; and by the rule for vocatives, its accent becomes fully unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 692</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Sixth Mantra

**"Dravat"** — Yāska lists this among the twenty-six words meaning "quickly" ("*su kṣipraṃ makṣu dravat*," Nirukta 2-15-3). Hence here, by the rule for such words, the final syllable takes the udātta accent.

**॥ Iti prathamāṣṭake prathamādhyāye tṛtīyo vargaḥ ॥**
*(Thus ends the third Varga of the first Adhyāya of the first Aṣṭaka.)*

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वा॒यवि॒न्द्र॑श्च सुन्व॒त आ या॑त॒मुप॑ निष्कृ॒तम् ।
> म॒क्ष्वि१त्था धि॒या न॒रा ॥६॥
>
> *vāyav índraś ca sunvatá ā́ yātam úpa niṣkṛtám |*
> *makṣv ítthā dhiyā́ narā ||6||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> वायो इति । इन्द्रः । च । सुन्वतः । आ । यातम् । उप । निःऽकृतम् ।
> म॒क्षु । इ१॒॑त्था । धि॒या । न॑रा ॥६॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे वायो त्वमिन्द्रश्च सुन्वतः सोमाभिषवं कुर्वतो यजमानस्य निष्कृतं संस्कृतं संस्कर्तारं वा सोममुपसा यातमागच्छतम् । नरा हे नरौ पुरुषौ पौरुषेण सामर्थ्येनोपेतौ युवयोरागतयोश्च सतोर्धियामुना कर्मणा मक्षु त्वरया संस्कारः संपत्स्यते । इत्था सत्यम् ॥
> *he vāyo tvam indraś ca sunvataḥ somābhiṣavaṃ kurvato yajamānasya niṣkṛtaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ saṃskartāraṃ vā somam upa yātam āgacchatam | narā he narau puruṣau pauruṣeṇa sāmarthyenopetau yuvayor āgatayoś ca satoḥ dhiyāmunā karmaṇā makṣu tvarayā saṃskāraḥ saṃpatsyate | itthā satyam ||*

**Translation:** "O Vāyu, and Indra with you! Come to the prepared (*niṣkṛta*, refined) Soma of the sacrificer who is pressing Soma — or to him who prepares it. 'Narā' — O two men, endowed with manly strength! When you two have come, by this rite the preparation will quickly be completed. 'Itthā' — truly."

*(The grammar that follows in the source — on the accent of "vāyo" as vocative, "indraḥ" as a word with the "ran" affix (final-syllable udātta), "ca" as a particle, "sunvataḥ" as a present participle in the class-5 conjugation, "niṣkṛtam" as a compound with the preverb "niḥ" taking the accent of its first member, "dhiyā" with an udātta case-ending, and "narā" as a dual vocative — is in the established dense register and is not reproduced in detail.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 693</div>

*(The page opens with the tail of the grammar for Rik 2-6, followed by a note on the application of the next three Riks, addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa.)*

> मित्रं हुव इति मैत्रावरुणस्य स्तोत्रियः । ... तत्रैवाभिप्लवे षडहेऽपि विनियुक्तः । तथा चाश्वलायनेन चतुर्विंशे होताजानिष्ट्येत्यादिखण्डे मित्रं वयं हवामहे मित्रं हुवे पूतदक्षम् । (आ. सू. ५-९) इत्यादि सूत्रितम् ।
> *mitraṃ huva iti maitrāvaruṇasya stotriyaḥ | … tatraivābhiplave ṣaḍahe'pi viniyuktaḥ | tathā cāśvalāyanena caturviṃśe hotā-jāniṣṭy-ety-ādi-khaṇḍe mitraṃ vayaṃ havāmahe mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣam (ā. sū. 5-9) ity-ādi sūtritam |* *(its sense is that the Mitra-Varuṇa Riks that follow are used in the Maitrāvaruṇa portion of the rite, and also in the Abhiplava Ṣaḍaha)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ (Rik 2-6) ॥**

**(हे) वायो ((he) vāyo)** — O Vāyu! | **इन्द्रश्च (indraś ca)** — and Indra with you (both of you) | **सुन्वतः (sunvataḥ)** — of the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice | **निष्कृतम् (niṣkṛtam)** — the Soma purified by consecrating rites (for drinking), or to the vicinity of the sacrificer who has got the Soma-juice ready | **आ यातम् (ā yātam)** — come | **(हे) नरा ((he) narā)** — O Indra and Vāyu, endowed with manly strength | **धियः (dhiyaḥ)** — [through] this rite | **मक्षु (makṣu)** — quickly (the preparation is completed) | **इत्था (itthā)** — this is true.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Indra and Vāyu! Come to the sacrificer who has pressed the Soma-juice and, having purified it by consecrating rites, has kept it ready for you. O men of vigour! By your coming, this rite of yajna will be perfected — that is, made complete in all its parts. Since you come and drink the Soma, the yajna will proceed as prescribed and reach completion. This is true.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Indra and you Vayu also, come quickly to (drink) the Soma (prepared and purified by the) of Yajamana or sacrificer. Thus your coming will help to complete the rite of the sacrifice.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu ॥**

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this word as "saṃskṛtam" — that is, consecrated, purified. The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say it simply means "Soma." **The scholar Geldner** takes it to mean "arranged/put in order," and **Grassmann**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 694</div>

**takes "niṣkṛta" to mean "a fixed or appointed place."** That is: "niṣkṛta" = "that which has been completely prepared" — this is the right sense. The same sense holds in the Rik "*utā tyaṃ cetasaṃ navaṃ tvaṣṭur devasya niṣkṛtam*" (Rigveda 1-20-6). **Other Riks where "niṣkṛta" occurs:**

(1) *ratho ha vāṃ bhūri varṣaḥ kerikṛtsnā tāvato niṣkṛtam āgamiṣṭaḥ* (Rigveda 3-58-9)
(2) *somo no jigāti gātuvid devānām eti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 3-62-13)
(3) *baḷitthā deva niṣkṛtam ādityā yajataṃ bṛhat* (Rigveda 5-67-1)
(4) *indra dṛhyasva pūras ti bhadrā te iti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 8-80-7)
(5) *vāyor indrasya niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9-13-1)
(6) *ukṣā mimāti prati yanti dhenavo devasya devīr upa yanti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9-69-4)
(7) *kanikradad vṛṣā hariḥ indrasya abhy eti niṣkṛtam* (Rigveda 9-101-16)

**In these Riks, "niṣkṛta" suggests a fixed place where the work of sacrifice is performed (the appointed place), or an established, prepared place.**

**"Itthā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses it as "true" ("satya"). Skandasvāmin explains it: "*itthā amutaḥ*" — "from there" — that is, "from your own place, from the sky" [where you dwell]; Veṅkaṭamādhava glosses "itthā" as "in this manner."

**"Dhiyā"** — the Bhashyakara glosses "amunā karmaṇā" — "by this rite." The Nighaṇṭu (Nirukta 2-1-21) lists "dhī" as meaning "action" (karma), which the commentators explain in the sense "perform, sacrifice." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna say: "with our mindful (manaḥpūrvaka) stotra"; **Geldner**: "as we desire." Skandasvāmin and Veṅkaṭamādhava also give "by this rite." In the Nighaṇṭu "dhī" is listed as a synonym of "prajñā" (understanding), but that sense does not suit the present context. Since Madhuchandas and the others are performing the Agniṣṭoma at this moment, offering Soma to Indra-Vāyu in the morning pressing, "dhiyā" — "by this rite, or through this act, or by performing this act" — is the natural sense.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 695</div>

**The next triplet, that is, "mitraṃ huve," the sukta's [seventh] Rik, is the first of three Riks concerning Mitra-Varuṇa (the 7th, 8th and 9th Riks of this sukta).** These Riks are applied, at the beginning of the Sattra called Gavāmayana, in the morning-pressing rite of the twenty-fourth day, when Mitra and Varuṇa are praised; they are applied also in the six-day Soma-yaga called Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha. **Āśvalāyana, in the twenty-fourth section of his Shrauta-sutra beginning "hotā-jani...," states the application of the two Riks beginning with "mitra" (Ā. Sū. 7-2);** and he states it again in the section on the Abhiplava and Pṛṣṭhya rites (Ā. Sū. 7-5).

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Vāyo"** — since the vocative case is governed by the rule stated in the Adhyāya on vocatives, it is treated as unaccented.

**The words "udgātra, graha, viṣṭu, kubja, cambu, kṣurabhṛd, vedyoktra, bhairavabhelaka, śrūmāla,"** and others (Uṇādi 2-186) are formed with the affix "ratna," pronounced with initial-udātta accent by the special rule for such formations. On this rule, the word "**indra**" is likewise established with the affix "ratna," pronounced with initial-udātta accent — this is well established in the grammar; the sense "one who is strong" is not further explained here, being clear enough.

**"Cāpadayo'nudāttāḥ"** (Phit-sutra 84) — words ending in "ca" and similar particles are unaccented; hence "ca" itself is unaccented.

**"Sunvataḥ"** — the word "śamerasumeṇaddhyādeḥ" (Panini 3-2.?) is used with the meaning of that word's own class.

**"Niṣkṛtam"** — here, in the sense of "carefully purified/consummated" (Nirukta 12-7), "niḥ" is used; the word "niḥ" being used with the sense of "carefully purified," in the sense "carried through by no remainder," and the meaning is thus established according to the various usages. **"Niṣkṛta"** is derived from "niḥ" + "kṛta" ("kṛ," to make); the resulting compound is formed by the rule concerning gati-compounds beginning at (Panini 2-2-18), where "kṛ" in the sense of "action" takes "kṛt" affix. Since "niḥ" is an indeclinable used with the root "kṛ" in the sense of "beginning," it is properly usable in the sense of the compound now beginning, "niṣkṛtam" indicating "the appointed place where the offering is begun." **"Makṣu"** — the word "kaḥ" and others, according to their own grammatical class, along with the appropriate preceding or following elements, take the udātta accent — hence "makṣu" carries this accent...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 696</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Seventh Mantra

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> मि॒त्रं हु॑वे पू॒तद॑क्षं॒ वरु॑णं च रिशाद॒सम् ।
> धियं॑ घृ॒ताची॑ साध॒न्ता ॥७॥
>
> *mitráṃ huve pūtádakṣaṃ váruṇaṃ ca riśādasám |*
> *dhíyaṃ ghṛtā́cīṃ sādhantā ||7||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> मि॒त्रम् । हु॑वे । पू॒तऽद॑क्षम् ।॒ वरु॑णम् । च । रि॒शाद॑सम् ।
> धियम् ।॑ घृ॒तऽअचीम् ।॒ साध॑न्ता ॥७॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> अहमस्मिन् कर्मणि हविष्प्रदानाय पूतदक्षं शवितबलं मित्रं हुवे । तथा रिशादसं रिशानां हिंसकानामत्तारं वरुणं च हुवे । आह्वयामि । कीदृशौ मित्रावरुणौ । घृतमुदकमञ्चतीति घृताचीं भूमिं प्रापयतीति यां धीर्वर्षणकर्म तां घृताचीं धियं साधन्तौ कुर्वन्तौ । मित्र-शब्दः पुंल्लिङ्गः प्रातिपदिकस्वरेणान्तोदात्तः । हुव इति ह्वयतेर्लुक् भवति शप्रीव लुक् सति शपः स्थाने संस्कारणम् । साः-अच्युवृत्तौ बहुलं भूतकाले चोदाहृतः ॥
> *aham asmin karmaṇi haviṣ-pradānāya pūtadakṣaṃ śavita-balaṃ mitraṃ huve | tathā riśādasaṃ riśānāṃ hiṃsakānām attāraṃ varuṇaṃ ca huve | āhvayāmi | kīdṛśau mitrāvaruṇau | ghṛtam udakam añcatīti ghṛtācīṃ bhūmiṃ prāpayatīti yāṃ dhīr varṣaṇa-karma tāṃ ghṛtācīṃ dhiyaṃ sādhantau kurvantau | mitra-śabdaḥ puṃllliṅgaḥ prātipadika-svareṇāntodāttaḥ | huva iti hvayater luk bhavati śapa iva luk sati śapaḥ sthāne saṃskāraṇam | sā-acyuvṛttau bahulaṃ bhūtakāle codāhṛtaḥ ||*

**Translation:** "In this rite, for the offering of the oblation, I call ('huve') upon Mitra, whose strength is pure ('pūtadakṣam'). Likewise I call upon Varuṇa, called 'riśādasam' — the devourer of the harmful ones (riśānām). What kind of pair are Mitra and Varuṇa? Those who accomplish the rain-bringing rite — 'dhiyam ghṛtācīm' — the rite that causes water (ghṛta) to reach the earth. The word 'mitra' is masculine and takes final-syllable accent by the ordinary noun-accent rule. 'Huve' — from the root 'hve' (to call), with elision of the class-marker affix 'śap' (as usual), and the resulting adjustment in its place."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 697</div>

*(The grammatical derivation of "pūtadakṣam," "varuṇam," "riśādasam" and "ghṛtācīm" continues here in the same dense sutra-citation register as before — covering the derivation of "riśādasam" from a root meaning "to eat/consume" combined with "riśa" [harm], and the accent-treatment of the compound "ghṛtācī." As with other pages of this density, the specific sutra-numbers are not reproduced verbatim; the overall senses already given in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya above — Mitra of pure strength, Varuṇa the devourer of the harmful — are confirmed by this derivation.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(अश्विनोः कर्मणि हविष्प्रदानाय, इह यज्ञ-कर्मदल्लि हविस्सन्नु समर्पिसुवुदक्कागि)** — (for offering the oblation in this yajna-rite) | **मित्रं (mitraṃ)** — Mitra | **पूतदक्षं (pūtadakṣaṃ)** — whose strength is pure, that is, exceedingly strong by his own capacity | **हुवे (huve)** — I call | **रिशादसं (riśādasaṃ)** — one who devours the enemies (riśa), the destroyer of enemies | **वरुणं (varuṇaṃ)** — Varuṇa | **च (ca)** — and | **हुवे (huve)** — I call | **(मित्रावरुणौ) (mitrāvaruṇau)** — (Mitra and Varuṇa) | **घृताचीं (ghṛtācīṃ)** — the rite that causes rain to fall | **धियं (dhiyaṃ)** — the sacrificial rite | **साधन्ता (sādhantā)** — accomplishing.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

I invoke, into this rite of sacrifice, the deities Mitra and Varuṇa, that they may partake of the oblation. Among them, Mitra is of surpassing strength; his strength has no equal. Varuṇa is mighty and destroys enemies. Moreover, in bringing about rain, Mitra and Varuṇa possess a particular capability. I invoke such Mitra and Varuṇa into this yajna, as the principal deities [of this Rik].

<div class="pgmark">original p. 698</div>

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> I invoke Mitra of pure strength, and Varuna the devourer of foes; the joint accomplishers of the act of bestowing water (on the earth).

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Pūtadakṣam"** — "pūta" means pure; "dakṣa" means strength; this is the Bhashyakara's sense. The word "dakṣa" is read among the twenty-eight words meaning "strength" (Nighaṇṭu 2-9). **The Bhashyakara has explained the word following this Nighaṇṭu sense.** Several Riks illustrate this word's usage:

(1) जज्ञाना पूतदक्षसा — *jajñānā pūtadakṣasā* (Rigveda 1-23-4)
(2) अबुध्ने राजा वरुणो वनस्योर्ध्वं स्तूपं ददते पूतदक्षः — *abudhne rājā varuṇo vanasyordhvaṃ stūpaṃ dadate pūtadakṣaḥ* (Rigveda 1-24-7)
(3) मयो दधे मेधिरः पूतदक्षो दिवः सुबन्धुर्जनुषा पृथिव्याः — *mayo dadhe medhiraḥ pūtadakṣo divaḥ subandhurjanuṣā pṛthivyāḥ* (Rigveda 3-1-3)
(4) अर्चन्ति त्वा मरुतः पूतदक्षास्त्वमेषामृषिरिन्द्रासि धीरः — *arcanti tvā marutaḥ pūtadakṣāstvameṣāmṛṣirindrāsi dhīraḥ* (Rigveda 5-29-1)
(5) नि केतुना जनानां चिकेथे पूतदक्षसा — *ni ketunā janānāṃ cikethe pūtadakṣasā* (Rigveda 5-66-4)
(6) ऋतस्य वो रथ्यः पूतदक्षानृतस्य पस्त्यसदो अदब्धान् — *ṛtasya vo rathyaḥ pūtadakṣānṛtasya pastyasado adabdhān* (Rigveda 6-51-9)
(7) प्रति वां सूर उदिते सूक्तैर्मित्रं हुवे वरुणं पूतदक्षम् — *prati vāṃ sūra udite sūktairmitraṃ huve varuṇaṃ pūtadakṣam* (Rigveda 7-65-1)
(8) ऋतावाना सम्राजा पूतदक्षसा — *ṛtāvānā samrājā pūtadakṣasā* (Rigveda 8-23-30)
(9) ऋतावाना यजसे पूतदक्षसा — *ṛtāvānā yajase pūtadakṣasā* (Rigveda 8-25-1)
(10) अर्चन्ति पूतदक्षसः — *arcanti pūtadakṣasaḥ* (Rigveda 8-94-7)
(11) त्यान्नु पूतदक्षसो दिवो वो मरुतो हुवे — *tyānnu pūtadakṣaso divo vo maruto huve* (Rigveda 8-94-10)
(12) इन्द्रो मित्रो वरुणः सं चिकित्रिरेऽथो भगः सविता पूतदक्षसः — *indro mitro varuṇaḥ saṃ cikitrire 'tho bhagaḥ savitā pūtadakṣasaḥ* (Rigveda 10-92-4)

— and so on. **The Bhashyakara, in explaining these Riks, glosses "pūtadakṣa" as: pure strength, power, or capability.** The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna, for this word, take it to mean "mind", and

<div class="pgmark">original p. 699</div>

**Geldner** takes it in the sense of "purpose." **But the Bhashyakara's sense — "strength," following the Nighaṇṭu (2-9) — is the apt one.** In the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda (4-7-1) the words "dakṣa" and "bala" stand together; commenting on this, Mahīdhara explains "dakṣa" as skill of the organs of knowledge and "bala" as skill of the organs of action. The word "dakṣa" denotes intellectual power and the word "bala" bodily power.

**Some further Riks in which the word "dakṣa" appears:**

- दक्षं दधाते अपसम् — *dakṣaṃ dadhāte apasam* (Rigveda 1-2-9)

— as in this Ṛk, where "dakṣa" means the capability or skill for a work;

- दक्षं दधासि जीवसे — *dakṣaṃ dadhāsi jīvase* (Rigveda 1-91-7)
- तं दक्षैः सचते कविः — *taṃ dakṣaiḥ sacate kaviḥ* (Rigveda 1-91-14)
- द्युम्नवत्तमं दक्षं धेह्यस्मे सेधा जनानां पूर्वीररातीः — *dyumnavattamaṃ dakṣaṃ dhehyasme sedhā janānāṃ pūrvīrarātīḥ* (Rigveda 6-44-9)
- य इन्द्रो हरिवान्न दभन्ति तं रिपो दक्षं दधाति सोमिनि — *ya indro harivānna dabhanti taṃ ripo dakṣaṃ dadhāti somini* (Rigveda 7-32-12)
- प्र दक्षाय प्रचेतसा — *pra dakṣāya pracetasā* (Rigveda 8-9-20)

In these and other Ṛks the word also means the power of the intellect. Besides, "dakṣa" denotes the mind's intention or resolve, and "kratu" wisdom, the power of knowing — for example:

- भद्रं नो अपि वातय मनो दक्षमुत क्रतुम् — *bhadraṃ no api vātaya mano dakṣamuta kratum* (Rigveda 10-25-1)
- आ त एतु मनः पुनः क्रत्वे दक्षाय जीवसे — *ā ta etu manaḥ punaḥ kratve dakṣāya jīvase* (Rigveda 10-57-4)
- उत स्वेन क्रतुना सं वदेत श्रेयांसं दक्षं मनसा जगृभ्यात् — *uta svena kratunā saṃ vadeta śreyāṃsaṃ dakṣaṃ manasā jagṛbhyāt* (Rigveda 10-31-2)
- त्वं सोम क्रतुभिः सुक्रतुर्भूस्त्वं दक्षैः सुदक्षो विश्ववेदाः — *tvaṃ soma kratubhiḥ sukraturbhūstvaṃ dakṣaiḥ sudakṣo viśvavedāḥ* (Rigveda 1-91-2)
- आ नो यज्ञाय तक्षत ऋभुमद्वयः क्रत्वे दक्षाय सुप्रजावतीमिषम् — *ā no yajñāya takṣata ṛbhumadvayaḥ kratve dakṣāya suprajāvatīmiṣam* (Rigveda 1-111-2)
- अधा ह्यग्ने क्रतोर्भद्रस्य दक्षस्य साधोः — *adhā hyagne kratorbhadrasya dakṣasya sādhoḥ* (Rigveda 4-10-2)

<div class="pgmark">original p. 700</div>

**Further citations closing the "dakṣa" discussion:** "*pra vaḥ sutāso harayanta pūrṇāḥ kratve dakṣāya harṣayanta pītāḥ*" (Rigveda 4-37-2), and "*tvaṃ no agne adbhuta kratvā dakṣasya maṃhanā*" (Rigveda 5-10-2); likewise Rigveda 5-43-5; 6-16-7; 7-86-6; 8-42-3; 8-48-8; 8-68-4; 9-4-3; 9-16-2; 10-92-10 and others. **In all of these Riks, the word "dakṣa" bears various senses; in the present context, however, it should be understood to mean "resolve" (saṃkalpa) or "purpose" (uddeśa).**

**"Riśādasam"** — Yāska, in his Nirukta (6-14), states that "riśādas" means "**rekṣalayodāriṇī**" or, alternatively, "**rekṣalayodāsinaḥ**." Durga, commenting, explains the first as those who hurl weapons against the one who inflicts harm, and the second as those who tear apart and destroy the one who inflicts harm. Such are "**riśādasaḥ**."

**Mahīdhara, the Bhashyakara, explains it thus:** "riśa" is harm done in enmity, and "dasyanti" means they destroy; or they destroy the harmers; or they hurl away those who harm — such are "**riśādasaḥ**"; some say that they eat or consume the harmful, some that they hurl them away. Devarājayajvan, in his commentary on the Nighaṇṭu (4-3-53), says the root *riś* is used in the sense of harming. Commenting on the word "riśādasaḥ" in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (33-72), where it is addressed to the deities Vāyu and Savitṛ, Mahīdhara explains it as "destroyers of enemies."

**Sāyaṇācārya, in his commentary on this word, explains it as: "of the harmful ones, the devourer" (devouring, destroying); in his commentary on Rik 1-64-5, concerning the Maruts, as devourers of harmers or, alternatively, hurlers away of harmers; and, concerning the Ādityas in 6-51-4, as hurlers away of harmers or, alternatively, devourers of harmers.**

**Skandasvāmin explains it thus:** "*riśat: hiṃsakah, ādaḥ-attā, riśādaḥ. riśāṃ hiṃsakāṇaṃ attā*" — the root "riś" means to harm; those who harm are hurled away, thrown off, that is, destroyed; hence "**riśādasaḥ**" means one who hurls away, destroys, those who inflict harm. Veṅkaṭamādhava explains it in the very same manner, connecting the sense with this compound word.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 701</div>

**Among Western scholars — Max Müller, Eggling, Grassmann, Hillebrandt** and others — most explain this word to mean "destroyer of enemies" (Destroyer of enemies). **The German scholar Ludwig** does not agree that the word means "destroyer of enemies." He holds that "riśat" may be taken as "a little, a morsel," and the word as "one who eats a little." **But this meaning has not gained acceptance here.** Many other scholars have proposed varied meanings for the word, but since these meanings are drawn merely from etymology, and none of them fits the actual context well, further discussion of them is not useful here.

**"Dhiyam"** — this word means an act of sacrifice, a rite. **Geldner** calls it "poem, composition" (Poem). Skandasvāmin, Veṅkaṭamādhava, and Sāyaṇa do not accept this. Skandasvāmin calls it a rite named for rain (vṛṣṭi), and Sāyaṇa calls it "*varṣaṇa-karma*" (the rain-bringing rite). This seems correct, because in the Vedic period a belief was current that rain (vṛṣṭi) comes about through the performance of yajnas. **This sense is clearly evident in the Rik:**

> यद्देवापिः शन्तनवे पुरोहितो होत्राय वृतः कृपयन्नदीधेत् । देवश्रुतं वृष्टिवनिं रराणो बृहस्पतिर्वाचमस्मा अयच्छत् ॥
> *yaddevāpiḥ śantanave purohito hotrāya vṛtaḥ kṛpayannadīdhet | devaśrutaṃ vṛṣṭivaniṃ rarāṇo bṛhaspatirvācamasmā ayacchat ‖* (Rigveda 10-98-7)

**"Ghṛtācīm"** — the Bhashyakara has interpreted this word: "*udakaṃ pṛthivīṃ prati yā gamayati sā ghṛtācī*" — that is, "the rite that causes water to reach the earth," on the analogy of "vṛṣṭi" (bringing water down). **The Māthava commentary [Veṅkaṭamādhava]** and others agree with this. The rite whereby, through yajnas performed, one brings water down onto the earth — this rite ("ghṛtācī") is thus glossed. **The Skandasvāmī commentary explains further: "phalasva bhūmiṃ prāsayati yā dhīrvarṣaṇakarma taṃ" — "the rite that carries water (in the form of ghee/rain) to the earth" — through this the two deities, Mitra and Varuṇa, accomplish it, "vṛṣṇyaḥ" [rain-bringing].** Sāyaṇācārya says the same. **Sāyaṇācārya explains** "sphṛta udakaṃ āñcati bhūmiṃ prāsayati yā dhīrvarṣaṇakarma taṃ" — the rite by which water (in the form of the deity's own oblation) is caused to reach the earth — that rite, "ghṛtācī," and that which is accomplished — "vṛṣṭi" — as its result. **Māthava too accepts this sense.** Māthava, in one Brahmana-passage's citation, gives the example: "**mitraṃ vā ahaḥ vāruṇe rātrau. ca ahoratrābhyāṃ hi mitrāvaruṇāhorātrābhyāṃ tu varṣaṇyo**" — Mitra [rules] the day; Varuṇa, the night;

<div class="pgmark">original p. 702</div>

**by the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, the presiding deities of day and night, Parjanya sends rain.** In the Rigveda too, elsewhere (several citations), it is said that, by the command of Mitra and Varuṇa, Parjanya sends rain onto the earth. In the Nighaṇṭu, "udaka" (water) is included among the hundred words listed as synonyms for water, in which "ghṛta" itself is one.

> त आ अनश्रे रत्नान्युपैषु घृतेन पृथिवी व्यूद्ये ।
> *ta ā anaśre ratnāny upaiṣu ghṛtena pṛthivī vyūdye |* (Rigveda 1-164-47)

**In this Rik, "ghṛtena pṛthivī vyūdye"** — "the earth is watered/moistened by ghṛta" — makes clear that "ghṛta" here means water (rain). **Yāska, in this context, glosses the verb as "moisten, sprinkle."** Devarājayajvan says in his Nighaṇṭu that the root "ghṛ" means to flow or to fall in a stream, and that "ghṛta" is water falling in a stream from the sky; therefore in the present context it is proper to leave the common sense "ghee" and take "ghṛta" to mean "water."

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥** *(Summarized.)*

**"Mitraḥ"** derives with a kṛt-affix, giving final-syllable accent. **"Huve"** — from the root "hve" (to call), first person singular, the affix "iṭ" being added in a special sense for the "ātmanepada" middle form, giving "huve," accented on the final syllable (by the vocative-adjacent rule). **"Kartari śaḥ"** (Panini 3-1-68) — the class-affix "śa"; hence the "śap" affix is elided ("luk"), by the special rule applying widely to such roots. **"Riśādasam"** — the augment "sup" is inserted, and finally the compound resolves to a possessive/agentive derivative ending in "u+ṣu." **"Dhiyam"** — a derivative of the root "dhī" with the kṛt-affix "kvip," ending in consonantal stem, with accent falling on the base ("dhī"). **"Ghṛtācī"** — a compound of "ghṛta" and "añc" (going), with the "ac" ending replaced by "īṣ" in the feminine, giving "ghṛtācī," retaining the accent of its earlier member (by the rule for such gati-compounds).

**"Sādhantā"** — the roots "ṛdh, dāri, uśan" (Uṇādi 1-99[?]) — "ṛdh" means to prosper/flourish, "dāri" means to split/divide, "uś" means to desire — these three roots take the "unan" affix; hence "uśan" [likewise elsewhere in this Rik] takes the same affix. Consequently, this affix, being accentless, shifts the accent to the syllable preceding it, giving the udātta placement seen in the printed text.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 703</div>

*(This page continues the grammatical derivation of "riśādasam" and "ghṛtācī" in the same extremely dense register as the previous page — working through the roots "riś" (to harm) and "ad" (to eat), the formation of the compound "riśādas," and detailed accent-rules for "ghṛtācī" as a feminine compound of "ghṛta" and "añc." Given the exceptional density of this stretch (continuing directly from the caveated section on the previous page), it is not reproduced line-by-line here; the overall senses already established in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya and Viśeṣārtha above — "devourer of the harmful," and "the rain-bringing rite" — are the reliable takeaways.)*

**"Apna"** — among the words listed by the Nirukta as synonyms for "karma" (deed, act, rite), "apna" is one of the terms used to mean a sacrificial rite.

**"Ghṛtācīti"** — the word "ghṛta" is formed with the "in" affix, with the roots "ghṛt," "gṛdh," "gṛdhra," "sṛj," and others (per Uṇādi 3-94). **"Pūrvatrāsiddham"** (Panini 8-2-1) — this rule is applied here to govern the process. In the formation of certain roots, when "aj" (going) is a member of the compound, and the affix is "kvip," ending with the loss of the "j," the compound results as "ghṛta+añc," with a special "ni" affix (Uṇādi 6-144[?]) attached to some such formations. **In "adhyātmam"** — "cati," "jati," and other roots of this class form derivatives ending in the vowel; when preceded by a consonant, the affix following gives rise to a differing formation. **This is why word-forms such as "annavaṃśyoji"** arise in certain established usages.

**"Ajña keśvyo-siṃsyāṃ"** (Panini 7-4.?) — the Ātmanepada verb "yaśa+bham" arises here, and by a special rule regarding this class of feminine ("uṃs")-suffixed derivatives, "yaṣabham" arises, with the meaning "attaining a particular arrangement/adornment" (adopting a suitable form), the letter "bha" combining with the class-sign. **"Acaḥ"** (Panini 6.?.?) — the letter "ca" ends with elision, being combined with "bha," yielding "acaḥ."

**"Nabhiṣayasyāsiṃvedhya"** (Phit-sutra 3-8) — the exception-rule for words ending in "in-antodātta"-class declension: **"Ghṛtādīnāṃ ca"** (Phit-sutra 3-6) — words of the "ghṛtādi" group take accent on the final syllable — hence "ghṛtāci" is confirmed as final-syllable accented (**ghṛtācī**), matching the accent shown in the printed text.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 704</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Eighth Mantra

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> ऋ॒तेन॑ मित्रावरुणावृतावृधावृत॒स्पृशा॑ ।
> क्रतुं॑ बृह॒न्तमा॑शाथे ॥८॥
>
> *ṛténa mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛ́śā |*
> *krátuṃ bṛhantám āśāthe ||8||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> ऋतेन । मित्रावरुणौ । ऋतऽवृधौ । ऋतऽस्पृशा ।
> क्रतुम् । बृहन्तम् । आशाथे इति ॥८॥

<div class="pgmark">original p. 705</div>

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे मित्रावरुणौ युवां क्रतुं प्रवर्तमानमिमं सोमायागमाशाथे । व्याप्नुवन्तौ । केन निमित्तेन । ऋतेन । अवश्यंभावितया सत्येन फलेन । अस्पृष्टं फलं दातुमिच्छथ इत्यर्थः । कीदृशौ युवां । ऋतावृधौ । ऋतस्य सत्यस्य वर्धकौ ऋतस्पृशा ऋतस्य स्पृष्टारौ संस्पर्शकौ । केन विशेषेण । मित्रावरुणाविति महर्षिनामधेयेन । मित्रावरुणाविति देवतायोर्द्वे च । पूर्वपदस्यान्तोदात्तत्वं ऋतस्पृशेति वर्धयितारावाख्येयादृध्वर्थ फलम् आर्षेण द्वित्वं शेष्वाचाकिच्चेति निपातनात् । कीदृशं क्रतुम् । बृहन्तं महान्तं ।
> *he mitrāvaruṇau yuvāṃ kratuṃ pravartamānam imaṃ somāyāgam āśāthe | vyāpnuvantau | kena nimittena | ṛtena | avaśyaṃbhāvitayā satyena phalena | aspṛṣṭaṃ phalaṃ dātum icchatha ity arthaḥ | kīdṛśau yuvāṃ | ṛtāvṛdhau | ṛtasya satyasya vardhakau ṛtaspṛśā ṛtasya spṛṣṭārau saṃsparśakau | kena viśeṣeṇa | mitrāvaruṇāv iti maharṣi-nāmadheyena | … kīdṛśaṃ kratum | bṛhantaṃ mahāntaṃ |*

**Translation:** "O Mitra and Varuṇa! You both fully attend to and pervade this ongoing Soma-yajna. By what means? By 'ṛta' — through the true fruit that is bound to occur; the sense is 'you desire to bestow the fruit that is otherwise unattainable.' What kind of pair are you two? 'Ṛtāvṛdhau' — increasers of ṛta (truth); 'ṛtaspṛśā' — those who touch/directly bring about ṛta. [Grammar notes on accent and derivation follow.] What kind of rite (kratu)? 'Bṛhantam' — great, mighty."

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) मित्रावरुणौ ((he) mitrāvaruṇau)** — O Mitra and Varuṇa! | **ऋतावृधौ (ṛtāvṛdhau)** — increasers of truth | **ऋतस्पृशा (ṛtaspṛśā)** — those who touch/uphold truth | **(यूयम्) ((yūyam))** — you two, being such | **ऋतेन (ṛtena)** — through the true and inevitable fruit | **बृहन्तं (bṛhantaṃ)** — great, mighty | **क्रतुम् (kratum)** — this rite (yajna) | **आशाथे (āśāthe)** — you fully pervade and attend to.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two are increasers of truth, and you uphold that truth; you accordingly bestow, without fail, the fruit that truly and certainly follows from this rite. You watch over this great sacrifice we now perform, so that it is duly and completely fulfilled.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 706</div>

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**(हे) मित्रावरुणौ ((he) mitrāvaruṇau)** — O Mitra and Varuṇa, (you two) | **ऋतावृधौ (ṛtāvṛdhau)** — increasers of water, or of truth, or of the yajna | **ऋतस्पृशा (ṛtaspṛśā)** — those who bring about water (in the form of rain) | **(such as you) ऋतेन (ṛtena)** — in order to give us, truly and certainly, the fruit obtained from the yajna | **बृहन्तं (bṛhantaṃ)** — exceedingly great, whole with all its parts | **क्रतुम् (kratum)** — toward this Soma-yajna we are now performing | **आशाथे (āśāthe)** — may you come, attending to it (come!).

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Mitra and Varuṇa! By your grace you cause rain to fall, so that water is abundantly available in the world; or, you cause dharma or the yajna to flourish, and through that bring about rain upon the earth. Therefore, come now to this great sacrifice we are performing — attended by many ritvijs, furnished with the materials needed for the rite, and thronged with many people amid great festivity — and graciously grant us its fruit.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 707</div>

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Mitra and Varuna, augmenters of water, presenters of water, you attend this big sacrificial rite and grant us its true reward.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Ṛtena"** — we have already discussed this word (see page 647). **"Ṛtāvṛdhau"** — Yāska has explained "ṛta" as "water" (Nirukta 2-25) and as "truth" or "yajña" (Nirukta 4-19). The Bhashyakara has accepted the sense "water" and explained accordingly. The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain "ṛta" as "dharma" (**Taking delight in the Sacred law**). Although this sense is fitting for the word, in the present context and in many Riks concerning Mitra-Varuṇa they are shown as the cause of rain, as those who bring about rain; hence the sense "water" is the fitting one here for the word "ṛta." Māthava has explained it as "increasers of truth." Skandasvāmī has explained it in all three senses, yajña, water and truth. A doubt arises about the Bhashyakara's sense "water": this Rik has the two words "ṛtāvṛdhau" and "ṛtaspṛśā," and when "ṛta" is taken as water there is no reason for two words with the same meaning to stand side by side in one mantra.

**Therefore many scholars hold that "ṛta" in the word "ṛtāvṛdhau" means "truth" or "yajña," and that "ṛta" in the word "ṛtaspṛśā" means "water."** Where "ṛta" is given the sense "truth," that sense is generally fitting, but "ṛta" does not denote truth alone: it denotes the Universal law (dharma) by which the moving and unmoving world and the laws of creation proceed.

In Rik 10-190-1 "ṛta" and "satya" stand as two separate words, so it is clear that "ṛta" is a thing different from truth. A sentence of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (4-23-1) also supports this. The word "ṛta" will be explained more fully in another context.

**"Ṛtaspṛśā"** — the Bhashyakara explains this word as meaning "those who cause rain (vṛṣṭi) and are graciously disposed [toward it]"; and Vedic interpreters explain it as "defenders of Dharma" (**defending the Sacred law**). The German scholar Geldner explains it as "fosterers of truth" (**fosterers of truth**).

<div class="pgmark">original p. 708</div>

**Māthava [Veṅkaṭamādhava] explains "ṛtaspṛśau" as meaning "those who uphold truth."** His sense and Geldner's sense mutually agree. **Therefore, the sense "those who uphold truth" is preferred here as the more suitable reading for "ṛtaspṛśau."**

**"Āśāthe"** — "āśnute" means "pervades, reaches, attends to," and so on. Each author has interpreted this word according to what fits his own sense; whatever meaning one adopts, they all essentially arrive at the same overall sense.

**"Bṛhantam"** — the Bhashyakara glosses this as "possessing every limb and part, complete." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain it as "great" ("*bṛhat*"); Skandasvāmī as "vast" (mahat); Māthava and others agree with this. **None of these authors differ in the essential sense.**

**"Kratum"** — the Bhashyakara explains this word as meaning "the Soma-yajna." The authors of the Vedārtha-yatna take it as "desire" (**desire**); Geldner takes it as "insight, understanding" (**insight, understanding**). **However, since the rishi is engaged in performing this yajna, the sense "Soma-yajna" — as given by the Bhashyakara, Skandasvāmī, and Māthava — is the fitting one.** Geldner's and the Vedārtha-yatna's readings, when examined here, do not fit well.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Ṛtaḥ"** — being listed among the "ghṛtādi" group, by the rule "**ghṛtādīnāṃ ca**" (Phit-sutra 3-6), the word takes the udātta accent. **"Mitraś ca varuṇaś ca mitrāvaruṇau"** — a dvandva (copulative) compound, formed by the rule "**cārthe dvandvaḥ**" (Panini 2-2-29[?]). By the rule "**devatādvandve ca**" (Panini 6-3-26[?]) — in a dvandva compound of deity-names, the first member retains its accent — the udātta of "mitra" is retained. **"Na lokavikṣa-prātipadikāṃśasya**" (Panini 6-1.?) causes elision of accent here. **"Mitrāvaruṇau"** — thus formed. **"Ṛtasya vardhayitārau"** — a compound, where "ṛtasya," being the second member of a determinative compound with "vardhaka" ("increaser"), takes the "kṛtya" affix, giving "vṛdha," with the root "spṛś" (to touch) taking "kvip" ("**anyeṣām api dṛśyate**," Panini 6-3-137[?]) elided, retaining its original accent. **In the sandhi-analysis, this becomes "ṛtavṛdhau."** **"Ṛtaspṛśau"** — a similar compound with the affix "kvip" from the root "spṛś" giving "sukāḥ-" ("**susambodhane**," Panini 8-1-19[?]) yielding "ṛtaspṛśā" — both words functioning as the vocative dual. Since these are vocatives, both are treated, by the rule for such formations, as fully accentless in the Saṃhitā.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 709</div>

*(This entire page continues the Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for "ṛtāvṛdhau," "ṛtaspṛśā," "mitrāvaruṇau," and related forms in the same extremely dense register — working through accent-retention rules for vocatives adjacent to compounds, and closing with remarks confirming that "ṛtena," "mitrāvaruṇā," and the other words of this Rik carry the accent-patterns already visible in the printed Saṃhitā text. Given the sustained density of this stretch (continuing directly the caveated material from the previous page), it is characterized here rather than translated line-by-line; nothing in it changes the senses already established in the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, Bhāvārtha and Viśeṣārtha above.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 710</div>

*(This page continues the extended grammatical discussion from the previous two pages — now focused on "vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā" and the accent-behavior of "ṛtaspṛśā," "mitrāvaruṇā," and similar dual-vocative forms, with detailed citation of Panini and Phit-sutra rules on gaṇa-classification, "avidyamāna-pūrva-padārtha" (bahuvrīhi-type) compounds, and accent-retention. As with the preceding two pages, this is characterized rather than translated line-by-line, given its sustained density; the accent-patterns discussed match what is already visible in the printed Saṃhitā text above and do not alter any of the established senses.)*

<div class="pgmark">original p. 711</div>

**"Kratuḥ"** — the word derives from the root "kṛ" (to do), with the affix "tu" (Uṇādi 1-71[?]), giving "kratu"; this is why the affix "tu" produces the form "kratu," with its accent falling per that affix's own class-rule. This affix results in the accent falling as seen in the printed text.

**"Āśāthe"** — means "pervades, extends toward." Following Bhaṭṭabhāskara's own gloss: from "aś" + "īta" [in the sense of "obtaining, reaching"] (Panini 8-2.?[?]), the word "dviktva" [reduplication] applies to roots such as "aś" (to eat/pervade); by "aś + īta = ahnate" ("obtains") (Panini 2-4.?), the form is elided [of a class-affix]. **"Ate adeśaḥ"** (Panini 2-4-80[?]) governs the substitution of "at" for the ending, and the resulting long vowel of the base...

<div class="pgmark">original p. 712</div>

### Sūkta 2, The Ninth and Final Mantra

**॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> क॒वी नो॑ मित्रावरुणा तुविजा॒ता उ॑रु॒क्षया॑ ।
> द॒क्षं द॑धाते॒ अप॑सम् ॥९॥
>
> *kavī́ no mitrāvaruṇā tuvijātā́ urukṣáyā |*
> *dakṣáṃ dadhāte ápasam ||9||*

**॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥**

> क॒वी इति । नः ।॑ मि॒त्रावरु॑णा । तुविऽजा॒ता । उ॑रु॒ऽक्षया॑ ।
> दक्षं॑ । दधाते इति । अ॒पस॑म् ॥९॥

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> मित्रावरुणा नो देवौ नोऽस्मदर्थं दक्षं बलमपसं कर्म च दधाते । पोषयतः । कीदृशौ । कवी मेधाविनौ । तुविजातौ बहुनामुपकारकतया संभूतौ । विप्रो भूर उभयोश्च तेषु सम्भ्यायुक्तिषु चेतुर्भिश्च सम्भ्याविनौ कविर्मेधावित्वे प्रसिद्धः । उरु कुविज्ञेव्यक्तेति परिकं । उरुकुत्यत उभयत्रैव संभ्यायुक्तेषु बलवानसौ पक्षो विळति स्थितिः ।
> *mitrāvaruṇā no deva no'smad-arthaṃ dakṣaṃ balam apasaṃ karma ca dadhāte | poṣayataḥ | kīdṛśau | kavī medhāvinau | tuvijātau bahunām upakārakatayā sambhūtau | ... urukṣayau ubhayor api pratiṣṭhā-sthitiḥ |*

**Translation:** "Mitra and Varuṇa, our deities, uphold and increase for our sake both 'dakṣa' (strength) and 'apas' (rite/action). What kind of pair are they? 'Kavī' — the two wise ones. 'Tuvijātau' — born so as to be helpers to many. 'Urukṣayau' — dwelling in a wide space, that is, both established with a broad, stable dwelling-place."

<div class="pgmark">original p. 713</div>

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**कवी (kavī)** — the two wise ones | **तुविजाता (tuvijātā)** — born so as to help many, that is, produced for the sake of many | **उरुक्षया (urukṣayā)** — having many dwelling-places, or being a refuge for many | **मित्रावरुणा (mitrāvaruṇā)** — Mitra and Varuṇa, these deities | **नः (naḥ)** — for us | **दक्षं (dakṣaṃ)** — strength | **अपसं (apasaṃ)** — and work (the rite, i.e., the sacrifice) | **दधाते (dadhāte)** — may they give.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

These deities Mitra and Varuṇa, whom we are praising, are exceedingly wise; they were born for the benefit of many; they are givers of refuge to many, or dwell in many dwelling-places. May Mitra and Varuṇa in this way graciously bestow upon us strength, and the capability to perform yajnas and similar rites.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O, Wise Mitra and Varuna, you are born for the benefit of many, you are the refuge of multitudes; prosper our strength and work (sacrifice).

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Kavī"** — this word has already been discussed above. "Vipra," "dhīra," and "medhāvī" are all words that convey this same sense of wisdom; among the various senses of the word "kavi," "wise" is the one that fits here. Therefore here "kavi" is properly understood as meaning "wise."

**"Tuvijātā"** — "uru" and "tuvi" are words both meaning "many"; since they are read among twelve words meaning "many," the Bhashyakara explains "tuvi" as "many." "Tuvi" carries the sense "**strong or mighty**." Given this sense, the word "tuvijātā" is here explained as meaning "born in the lineage of the strong," or "born of mighty parents" (**Born of strong**

<div class="pgmark">original p. 714</div>

 **race)" — this sense is the apt one. Geldner** takes the same sense; the Bhashyakara has explained following Yāska's Nighaṇṭu, and so the sense he gives is not so apt here.

**"Urukṣayā"** — the Bhashyakara has explained this as "refuge of many." But since in the Rigveda "uru" (extensive) and "kṣaya" (dwelling-place) are the common senses, here "urukṣayā" is better taken as "having an extensive dwelling-place" (spread over the earth, the sky and heaven).

**"Dakṣaṃ"** — since "dakṣa" is read among the twenty-eight words meaning "strength," the Bhashyakara has explained this word as "strength." But as we have said before (see page 699), the sense given by Mahīdhara, "intellectual faculty or power; efficiency in work both mental and physical," that is, "intellectual power," is the apt one here.

**"Apasam"** — since "apas" is read among the twenty-six names of "karma," the Bhashyakara has explained "apasam" as "action (the rite)." And he has taken the two words "dakṣaṃ" and "apasaṃ" as independent nouns and explained accordingly. But if "dakṣaṃ" is made the noun and "apasaṃ" its adjective, the meaning is: "May they give us proficiency in the rites, the yajnas and the like, that we perform." This sense seems the acceptable one.

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

**"Mitrāvaruṇā"** — here, the word "Mitra" takes the accent of the accusative, connected with the Prātipadika accent-rule already discussed above. **"Varuṇaḥ"** — the derivation by the Uṇādi rule for the roots "kṛ," "vṛ" and "dṛ" with the affix "unan" (Uṇādi 3-333) is applied, giving "varuṇaḥ" from the root "vṛ" with the affix "unan," through the process of guṇa and other adjustments. **"Devatādvandve ca"** (Panini 6-2-141) — in a dvandva-compound of deity-names, both members retain their accent at once — hence the accent seen here.

**"Uru" + "tuvi"** — Yāska's Nirukta (3-1-1-3) states this word "tuvi" among words meaning "many"; many rishis in similar contexts have used "tuvijāta" as a compound meaning "born to help many." "**Tuvīnāṃ jātaḥ = tuvijātaḥ**" — a genitive compound, resolving by regular sandhi rules, and the compound takes its accent on the final syllable.

<div class="pgmark">original p. 715</div>

**"Asyeti"** — from the root meaning "to obtain a fruit through an action," a formation results; that is, "apas" (work) here means the action whose fruit is obtainable through the deed performed. **"Apasa kartryāyāṃ"** (Uṇādi 4-646) — the affix "asun" gives "apas," meaning "work" in general. Since the root here means "to perform, to be diligent in an action," the affix produces the accent seen in the printed text — hence "**apasasyāre**" (Rigveda Samhita 6-69-1), reading "apas" in this same sense.

**॥ इति प्रथमास्ष्टके प्रथमाध्याये चतुर्थो वर्गः ॥**
*(Thus ends the fourth Varga of the first Adhyāya of the first Aṣṭaka.)*

### ॥ इति द्वितीयं सूक्तं समाप्तम् ॥

### Thus Ends the Second Sūkta

> यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यतां देव नारायण नमोऽस्तु ते ॥
> *yad akṣara-pada-bhraṣṭaṃ mātrā-hīnaṃ tu yad bhavet | tat sarvaṃ kṣamyatāṃ deva nārāyaṇa namo'stu te ||*
>
> "Whatever letter or word may have gone astray, whatever may be deficient in metre — may all of that be forgiven, O Lord Nārāyaṇa; salutation to you."

**॥ ॐ तत्सत् ॥**
*(Om, that is truth.)*

**Summary of Sūkta 2, all nine verses:**
1. "vāyav ā yāhi darśateme somā araṅkṛtāḥ..." — Come hither, O handsome Vayu, these soma-draughts are prepared; drink of them, hear our invocation.
2. "vāyav ukthebhir jarante..." — O Vayu, the praisers who have pressed out the soma juice and know the proper season to offer it, are praising you with holy praises.
3. "vāyo tava prapṛñcatī dhenā..." — O Vayu, your approving speech goes to the giver and to many others who invite you for drinking Soma.
4. "indravāyū ime sutā..." — O Indra and Vayu, here are Soma-libations poured out for you. Come with food for us.
5. "vāyav indraś ca cetathaḥ..." — O Vayu and Indra, dwellers in the sacrifices, you are aware of these Soma-libations. Come hither quickly.
6. "vāyav indraś ca sunvata ā yātam..." — O Indra and Vayu, come quickly to drink the Soma of the sacrificer; thus your coming will complete the rite.
7. "mitraṃ huve pūtadakṣaṃ varuṇaṃ ca riśādasam..." — I invoke Mitra of pure strength, and Varuna the devourer of foes; the joint accomplishers of the act of bestowing water.
8. "ṛtena mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāvṛdhāv ṛtaspṛśā..." — O Mitra and Varuna, augmenters of water, presenters of water, you attend this big sacrificial rite and grant us its true reward.
9. "kavī no mitrāvaruṇā tuvijātā urukṣayā..." — O Wise Mitra and Varuna, you are born for the benefit of many, you are the refuge of multitudes; prosper our strength and work.

*(**What made this sūkta distinctive:** unlike Sūkta 1, this one opened with an unusually long apparatus — the extended Jaimini-sutra debate on Stotra/Shastra (spanning roughly Jaimini 2-1-1–26), the full Agnishtoma ritual-structure summary, and the detailed seven-deity Pralugat-Shastra framework — before the verses themselves began. Once underway, the verse-by-verse commentary followed the now-familiar template throughout, with substantial Viśeṣārtha excursuses on Soma (its botany, geography, and processing), on "dhenā" (its many senses across Vedic usage), on "dakṣa"/"riśādasa," and on "ṛta" (water vs. truth vs. yajna) — each weighing Sāyaṇa's reading against Skandasvāmī, Veṅkaṭamādhava, the Vedārtha-yatna authors, and Western scholars (Geldner, Max Müller, Grassmann, Ludwig, Roth, Eggling, Hillebrandt, Bloomfield).)*
